text:
The agency said it will solicit proposals from one or more of the companies to build a specific project at a site with an identified reactor technology, but it did not offer a target date, only stating it would happen in “the coming months,” according a Nov. 12 announcement.

The agency is set to decide on location and technology within the first six months of 2027 for the first 1 GW of capacity, but dates and scopes of the new solicitations would be confidential and covered by non-disclosure agreements, officials noted. “No public announcement will be issued unless or until a proposed project has been selected by NYPA,” the agency said.

The developer shortlist comes as New York Gov. Kathy Hochul unveiled on Nov. 18 the state's advanced nuclear energy "masterplan," a 30-point roadmap outlining how the 5 GW of capacity will be developed—which is set to be the largest such U.S. energy expansion in more than three decades. Also released was the state's policy white paper that proposes cost controls, revenue support mechanisms, site/developer prequalification, and open-book negotiations to prevent cost overruns, she said.

"Nuclear, I believe, is the most sustainable, the most reliable and ultimately, when it's all done, the most affordable way we can power our state,” Hochul said.

Firms on the Shortlist

Six of the selected companies could build either a large reactor, typically able to generate about 1 GW, or a small modular reactor (SMR) that could produce about 300 MW.

The firms, in alphabetical order, are: Avangrid, the parent company of utility companies New York State Electric & Gas and Rochester Gas & Electric; Elementl Power, which is currently proposing to build a 1.5-GW nuclear plant in Ohio by linking five 300-MW reactors; NextEra Energy, the parent company of Florida Power & Light, which operates nuclear plants; Oppenheimer Energy, a nuclear power developer founded by Charles Oppenheimer, grandson of nuclear pioneer J. Robert Oppenheimer; the Nuclear Co., a startup founded in 2024 that aims to build a 6-GW fleet of reactors using existing technology; and Turquoise Power, a technology-agnostic company that specializes in siting, financing, building, and operating small modular reactors.

The authority also selected four companies that would develop just the small nuclear reactors: Blue Energy, set to build a 2.5-GW hybrid power plant in Texas using both natural gas and nuclear power; Holtec International, which is developing 300-MW SMR technology and is also involved in decommissioning retired nuclear plants, including Indian Point north of New York City. Also shortlisted for this work is TerraPower, which is developing an innovative 345-MW reactor in Wyoming; and X-energy, a company that builds 80-MW nuclear reactors that can be linked, often in groups of four.

Earlier this year, the authority announced eight communities that are seeking to host a new nuclear plant, including Oswego County, which is already home to three nuclear reactors owned and operated by Constellation Energy. The developer and the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority have filed a grant proposal to the U.S. Energy Dept. for an early site permit to advance nuclear at the Nine Mile Point nuclear plant, which currently houses two of Constellation's reactors in the county.

Other upstate regions or locations that have agreed to host are Broome County; Jefferson County; Schuyler County; St. Lawrence County; Wayne County; the City of Dunkirk, located 40 miles southwest of Buffalo; and Eastman Business Park in Rochester, near the Robert Emmet Ginna nuclear plant.

In October, the U.S. Army also said that Fort Drum near Watertown was one of several U,S, bases chosen to work with private developers to host a new nuclear microreactor under the service's Janus program. The base will work with Westinghouse Electric Co. to deploy its 5-MW eVinci microreactor.

There are no sites being considered closer to New York City, despite efforts earlier this year by Energy Secretary Chris Wright and some lawmakers to propose restarting the Indian Point plant or reusing its reactors for a new facility. The proposal has faced strong community opposition.

Opponents in other areas also voiced concern. Graham Hughes, an environmental advocate in the Genesee-Finger Lakes region, argued that spending tens of billions of dollars on nuclear power would not lower costs or quickly decarbonize the grid. "We need the state to prioritize true renewables, not nuclear energy." he said.

Meeting Projected Energy Gaps

Driven by new large-load demand, New York will face its first statewide resource deficiency, about 225 MW, beginning in 2033, growing to more than 1.85 GW by 2036, the state’s grid operator said on Nov. 18.

“New generation and transmission resources take years to plan, permit, and build, so the reliability needs identified in this report must be addressed today,” Zach Smith, Independent System Operator senior vice president of system and resource planning, said in a statement

“Nuclear isn't just a response to near-term reliability concerns. It's really a long-term commitment around infrastructure investment," Todd Josefovski, NYPA senior vice president of nuclear energy development, told attendees of ENR’s NY-NJ Infrastructure Forum in September. “It's designed to last 60, 80, or even 100 years.”

Meanwhile, to prepare the next-generation advanced nuclear workforce, the authority also allocated the first $10 million of a pledged $40-million training fund to several state groups and schools—including $3.65 million to the Workforce Development Institute and New York State Building & Construction Trades Council and $1.06 million to the Manufacturers Talent Institute for construction craft training, and remaining funds to Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and several State University of NY campuses for training to include certifications and internships.

text:
Landmark Bipartisan Permitting Reform Bill Will Make It Easier To Build More Solar, Wind, Geothermal Projects In Nevada, Lowering Energy Costs & Creating Good-Paying Jobs

WASHINGTON, DC – Today, U.S. Senator Jacky Rosen (D-NV) released the following statement after voting in the Senate to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), landmark legislation that will make it easier to build more clean energy projects while keeping strong environmental regulations in place. This will help create more good-paying jobs, lower energy costs, and strengthen American energy independence, all while lowering net carbon emissions. Senator Rosen joined Democratic efforts to amend this legislation and remove sections reforming the National Historic Preservation Act, but they were blocked.

“As the state with the most solar jobs per capita and tremendous geothermal potential, Nevada stands to greatly benefit from historic federal investments in renewable energy projects that create good-paying jobs and lower energy costs, all while reducing carbon emissions. Unfortunately, current government red tape has made it nearly impossible to bring these clean energy projects online, which is why sensible reform like this bipartisan bill is needed,” said Senator Rosen. “While we fought to strengthen this bill, Senate Republicans refused to accept any changes and I believed we couldn’t squander this opportunity to lower energy costs for hardworking Nevada families. I’ve always been clear that making things more affordable for Nevada families and creating good-paying jobs are priorities for me, and this historic bipartisan bill will allow us to achieve both.”

Senator Rosen has been a strong supporter of Nevada’s clean energy economy. She has also been a strong supporter of Nevada’s solar industry, successfully leading the charge against solar tariffs that would have decimated the industry. Senator Rosen helped pass the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and Inflation Reduction Act, which have been making significant investments in Nevada’s clean energy economy and the jobs it supports.

description:
Washington — The Senate approved a long-sought bipartisan permitting reform bill on Thursday, following a major breakthrough on legislation that aims to cut costs by ramping up the speed of infrastructure and energy projects.
Thirty-one Democrats voted no, largely raising concerns that the bill would weaken environmental protections and lead to more fossil fuel projects.
While the bill does have the backing of some renewable energy leaders and developers, it also faced opposition from environmental groups.
Merkley acknowledged the bill could "turn the faucet potentially on" for renewable energy, but he said he's concerned Mr. Trump will continue to block wind energy projects.
In one all-caps X post, he argued the Trump administration could use the bill to approve fossil fuel projects while continuing to slow-walk renewable energy projects.
text:
Washington — The Senate approved a long-sought bipartisan permitting reform bill on Thursday, following a major breakthrough on legislation that aims to cut costs by ramping up the speed of infrastructure and energy projects.

In a 62 to 33 vote, the upper chamber passed the measure on a bipartisan basis. The bill now heads to the House. President Trump has expressed support for the deal.

Fifteen members of the Democratic caucus voted yes, along with virtually all Republicans. Thirty-one Democrats voted no, largely raising concerns that the bill would weaken environmental protections and lead to more fossil fuel projects. Republican Sens. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Josh Hawley of Missouri also voted no.

The vote follows years of on-and-off negotiations over how to speed up major infrastructure projects by streamlining the complicated permitting processes that can snag projects for years — an issue that has drawn more attention amid rising energy prices.

"This bill is years in the making," Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Thursday.

Supporters say the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, will make it easier to build both renewable energy and fossil fuel projects, along with the high-tension power lines that support them. Negotiators announced a breakthrough on the legislation in September, touting a "historic, bipartisan agreement to reform America's federal environmental review and permitting processes."

"This is a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects, certainly without giving up any of the strong protections for our environment," Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia said at the time.

Capito said the agreement represented "something that's become increasingly rare in Washington — Republicans and Democrats, sitting down, identifying a problem, and in this case a problem that has festered for at least a decade and more that impacts all Americans, and for us to sit down and work together to solve it." She said the American people "sent us here to do big things."

"This is a big thing," Capito said. "It's monumental, and it's legacy-setting."

GOP Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming, who worked alongside Capito on permitting reform efforts for years, stressed the need for the legislation in a floor speech this week, saying, "If we want life to be more affordable in America, we need to make it more affordable to build in America, but also more convenient — more efficient."

The Wyoming Republican said, "In America today, it takes too long, and it costs too much to build," putting the blame on Washington for slowing things down, as projects are put in the "regulatory penalty box — waiting to act, waiting to build, workers sitting on the sidelines."

Barrasso lauded the bill for streamlining environmental and judicial reviews and limiting lawsuits, calling them common-sense reforms. He argued that the legislation represented a "responsible path" for producing more energy and protecting the environment, saying, "We can do both."

But some progressives have balked at the legislation, arguing it could erode environmental protections and doubting Mr. Trump will allow renewable projects to be built. While the bill does have the backing of some renewable energy leaders and developers, it also faced opposition from environmental groups.

Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley of Oregon cited concerns about how it will affect states' rights to protect clean water and air, its implications for fossil fuel over renewable energy sources and how it could make it easier to build and power new data centers, along with its impact on the deficit. Sen. Ron Wyden, also of Oregon, opposed the bill as well, and sought a vote on an amendment to ban data centers on public lands.

The two senators have also expressed concern about how the bill could impact tribal rights.

"Embedded in this bill is a fundamental question about the direction we go regarding our responsibilities to this planet," Merkley said ahead of the vote Thursday.

Merkley acknowledged the bill could "turn the faucet potentially on" for renewable energy, but he said he's concerned Mr. Trump will continue to block wind energy projects. He argued that by allowing more natural gas and other fossil fuel projects, it will "open another floodgate for carbon that we won't ever be able to reverse."

After its passage in the Senate, the bill faces an uncertain future in the House, where opposition on multiple fronts has thrown into question whether the bill can make it through the lower chamber before year's end.

While some House Republicans have cited changes to the bill's provisions on transmission related to grid reliability, some House Democrats have also stressed that they would like to see the legislation altered. Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the ranking member on the House Natural Resources Committee, has raised doubts about the bill. In one all-caps X post, he argued the Trump administration could use the bill to approve fossil fuel projects while continuing to slow-walk renewable energy projects.

A spokesperson for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said earlier this month that he "supports the need for permitting reform," but argued the Senate's legislation "falls short in several areas."

"Leader Jeffries will not rubber-stamp legislation that emerges from the Senate without more constructive involvement with our caucus as we fight to make life more affordable for the American people," the spokesperson said.

Some opponents have also suggested that Democrats could have more leverage to negotiate next year, when the party takes control of the House and Senate. Mr. Trump will ultimately need to sign any bill. But others believe the push is only possible with a GOP governing trifecta at the helm.

Thune told reporters on Thursday that he didn't know whether the House would be able to pass the bill as is, or need to make changes, noting that it's "been litigated now for months."

"The best way to get anything done around here is for them to pick up the bill and pass it," Thune said. "If it were to go over there and then come back over here, I mean, I don't know what I can't predict what happens. So hopefully there'll be the critical mass there to move it. I don't know what else you can add to it or detract from it. I think it's been through the full monty when it comes to the legislating process."

text:
The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.

The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.

Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.

“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.

Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.

Datacentre developers have emerged as the world’s biggest corporate buyers of renewable energy to help fuel their servers which have a connection to local power grids. Despite this, the report showed that the appetite for fossil fuels is expected to grow even faster, particularly in the US and China.

By the end of the decade, around half of the electricity needed to power China’s AI datacentres will come from coal power plants, according to the IEA. The rest will come from renewable energy, with smaller amounts from nuclear reactors and very little from gas plants.

In contrast, the US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. There were plans for about 180GW of new gas-fired power plants linked to US datacentres in August this year, the agency said. That is almost as much new gas capacity as the total now installed across the European Union.

As a result of the growth in fossil fuel generation for datacentres, emissions associated with this sector were on track to rise by 70% by 2030, the IEA said.

The appetite for gas power among US datacentre developers is more than 16 times higher than in Canada, where the IEA identified plans for 11GW of gas generation to power their servers. In the rest of the world, AI developers have put forward plans for new gas plants with a combined capacity of just 4GW, the agency said.

This is because renewable energy is expected to play a greater role in supplying datacentres outside the US and China. In the EU, the IEA expects datacentres to rely on renewables for about 70% of their electricity by 2030 – followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and a very small amount of coal power.

The agency based its forecasts for the notoriously opaque industry on data showing the annual global shipment of AI servers, which have climbed eighteen-fold since 2020. It also used space-based imagery to track the buildout of 93 large “AI factories” around the world.

Its analysis suggests that the world’s datacentre capacity has climbed tenfold in the last 24 months to 17GW. By the time the AI factories were completed, their combined capacity was likely to be about 50GW, the IEA said.

The world’s existing stock of datacentres, including those with AI-optimised servers, now stands at 120GW, with 80% of this capacity in China, the US and the EU. A further 120GW will be built by the end of the decade under the IEA scenario often considered its central base case, of which three-quarters will be AI datacentres.

title: Ford F-150 Lightning Owner Saves Nearly $5,000 After 58,000 Miles, Showing Why the ...
description:

Another interesting perspective came from Scott Hildula, who is approaching 50,000 miles in his 2023 F-150 Lightning Lariat.
Why the Right Electric Truck Isn't Necessarily the Best Electric Truck for Everyone The F-150 Lightning's appeal extends beyond its operating costs.
After three and a half years and 58,000 miles, this owner has documented a meaningful financial advantage from driving an electric pickup.
text:
Electric pickup trucks have always presented an interesting dilemma for buyers. They promise lower operating costs, fewer maintenance requirements, and the convenience of charging at home, but those advantages don't necessarily make them the right choice for everyone. For drivers who regularly tow long distances or spend their days traveling between job sites, a gas-powered truck can still be the more practical option.

However, Guy Garnett recently shared a breakdown of his ownership expenses after three and a half years and 58,000 miles, and his calculations offer a compelling look at what happens when an electric pickup fits someone's driving habits.

"I had reason to do the math this morning, and in three and a half years and 58,000 miles, my F-150 Lightning has not used 2,600 gallons of gas and 9 gallons of motor oil compared to an equivalent of a gas F-150.

It has saved me a net $4,750 — Electricity cost me $4,400 less than gas, plus $250 in motor oil and $90 in oil filters that I didn’t have to buy.

It avoided a net 4 tons of CO2 emissions to date (savings to date of 16.5 tons, less 12.5 tons from manufacturing the batteries), and can be expected to save a total of 30 to 45 tons of CO2 over its useful life."

While the savings are impressive, understanding how the owner achieved them is more valuable than the dollar amount itself.

What The Savings Actually Tell Us

Over 58,000 miles, the owner's estimated savings work out to approximately 8.2 cents per mile. Of that amount, $4,400 came from the difference between gasoline and electricity expenses, while another $340 came from avoiding conventional engine oil and filter replacements.

His estimate of 2,600 gallons of gasoline also suggests that the comparable gasoline-powered F-150 would have averaged approximately 22.3 mpg.

That's a reasonable comparison for certain F-150 configurations, although actual fuel economy varies depending on the engine, drivetrain, driving conditions, and whether the truck is regularly towing or hauling.

What's particularly interesting is that most of the owner's savings came from energy costs rather than maintenance. Electricity accounted for more than 90% of the $4,750 difference.

However, electricity isn't universally inexpensive. Drivers paying higher residential electricity rates or relying heavily on public DC fast charging may see considerably smaller savings.

The same applies to gasoline prices, which vary significantly by location.

It's why the owner's experience shouldn't necessarily be interpreted as proof that every Lightning will save its driver nearly $5,000 over 58,000 miles. Instead, it demonstrates what becomes possible when an electric truck operates under favorable conditions.

I've previously explored a similar situation involving a business owner who replaced an entire gasoline-powered vehicle fleet with Ford F-150 Lightnings and reported reductions in operating expenses.

That experience reinforces an important distinction: For businesses and individuals who drive predictable routes and have reliable charging access, the Lightning's operating-cost advantages can become particularly meaningful.

Another Lightning Owner Approaching 100,000 Miles Highlights Additional Maintenance Savings

Fuel expenses are only part of the equation.

Unlike gasoline-powered pickups, the F-150 Lightning doesn't require conventional engine oil changes, spark plug replacements, or maintenance associated with an internal combustion engine's exhaust system.

However, another Lightning owner responding to the discussion pointed out an additional potential advantage that wasn't included in the original calculation.

Leo Foo, who says his truck is approaching 100,000 miles, shared:

"Also you don’t need to get brakes done if you use one pedal all the time. Almost 100k miles on my truck with occasional towing. Brakes are still great because I rarely use them."

Leo's experience highlights one of the less-discussed advantages of electric vehicles.

Rather than relying entirely on conventional friction brakes to slow the vehicle, the Lightning can use its electric motors to recover energy during deceleration. This reduces wear on brake pads and rotors, potentially extending their service life.

One-pedal driving makes this process particularly noticeable because lifting off the accelerator can slow the truck substantially without requiring the driver to press the brake pedal in many everyday situations.

Of course, conventional brakes remain essential, and owners still need to inspect and maintain them. Regenerative braking doesn't eliminate brake wear or prevent corrosion.

Nevertheless, Leo's experience suggests that some Lightning owners may realize maintenance savings beyond those included in the original $4,750 calculation.

For someone planning to keep a truck well beyond 100,000 miles, those differences could become increasingly relevant.

Does the F-150 Lightning Actually Save Owners Time?

Another interesting perspective came from Scott Hildula, who is approaching 50,000 miles in his 2023 F-150 Lightning Lariat.

While the original discussion focused on money, Scott argued that another benefit deserves attention.

"You are forgetting the most valuable commodity you saved with this truck: TIME! I’m just about to hit 50k miles on my 2023 Lariat and I plug it in when I get home and unplug it before leaving in the morning. No lines at the pump, no looking for better prices, just a momentary pause to connect when I’m already hearing the dogs bark at the window and picturing my wife making dinner. I really love the electric life!"

Scott makes a compelling point about the convenience of home charging.

For drivers who have access to a dedicated charging setup and travel relatively predictable distances, charging an electric vehicle can become something they barely think about.

Instead of stopping at gas stations, they simply plug in when they arrive home and begin the following day with a replenished battery.

But this convenience advantage can disappear when driving circumstances change.

Someone who regularly travels hundreds of miles for work, operates on tight schedules, or frequently tows heavy trailers may find that charging introduces additional complications.

In fact, previous Torque News reporting documented an F-150 Lightning owner whose 850-mile journey reportedly took approximately 16 hours compared with around 12 hours in his F-150 PowerBoost hybrid.

That four-hour difference illustrates why electric truck convenience cannot be evaluated solely through the experience of someone charging overnight at home.

Both owners can be correct about their experiences.

For Scott, plugging in at home eliminates an inconvenience. For someone regularly traveling long distances, the time spent charging could outweigh whatever time they save by avoiding gas stations during the week.

Why the Right Electric Truck Isn't Necessarily the Best Electric Truck for Everyone

The F-150 Lightning's appeal extends beyond its operating costs.

Its familiar pickup design, substantial onboard storage, available Pro Power Onboard functionality, and relatively conventional driving experience make it an interesting alternative to other electric trucks.

I've previously covered an owner who experienced several electric pickups, including models from Rivian and GMC, before ultimately favoring the Ford F-150 Lightning.

Experiences like these demonstrate why evaluating electric trucks requires more than comparing range estimates and purchase prices.

A truck that works exceptionally well for one owner may be frustrating for another.

For example, a Lightning owner who drives 40 miles daily, charges at home, and occasionally uses the truck for hauling could enjoy years of relatively inexpensive operation.

Meanwhile, a contractor who frequently travels between distant job sites while towing equipment may find that a gasoline-powered F-150 better accommodates their schedule.

The Bigger Picture Behind 58,000 Miles of Lightning Ownership

One important limitation of the original owner's calculations is that they focus on energy and selected maintenance expenses rather than total ownership costs.

Purchase price, depreciation, insurance, tires, financing, and potential repairs can all influence whether an electric truck ultimately costs less to own than its gasoline counterpart.

After three and a half years and 58,000 miles, this owner has documented a meaningful financial advantage from driving an electric pickup.

And when combined with other owners' experiences involving reduced brake wear and convenient home charging, his story illustrates why the Lightning can be an excellent fit for certain drivers.

Perhaps the most important takeaway is that electric trucks don't need to outperform gasoline pickups in every situation to justify their existence.

They simply need to perform exceptionally well in the situations that matter most to their owners.

Join the Conversation

Would nearly $5,000 in operating-cost savings over 58,000 miles make you consider an F-150 Lightning, or would factors such as charging time, towing range, and purchase price still push you toward a gasoline-powered truck?

And if you already own an electric pickup, have your real-world savings matched your expectations

I'd love to hear about your experiences in the comments below.

About The Author

Aram Krajekian is a young automotive journalist bringing a fresh and analytical perspective to the evolving automotive landscape by reporting on real-world ownership experiences and providing industry analysis. Based in North Carolina, he covers electric vehicles, trucks, and broader automotive trends with a focus on contributing a balanced evaluation. His reporting cuts through brand bias to provide readers with grounded insight into how vehicles perform for everyday drivers beyond marketing narratives.

Aram can be reached on X and LinkedIn for ongoing automotive coverage.

title: Senate passes permitting reform bill reining in data centers - USA Today
description:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Senate on Nov. 19 passed a massive bill to speed up energy project development, weakening environmental rules, while ensuring data centers pay their own way for the electricity they require.
The bill, which also bolsters clean energy sources like wind and solar, marked the most significant piece of permitting reform legislation that Congress has passed in years.
If not adopted by both chambers, the legislation would have to be reintroduced when the 120th Congress takes over in January.
The bipartisan bill, first introduced in September, would speed up federal environmental reviews of energy projects and make it easier for developers to get the power they need to run data centers.
The bill also aims to improve energy affordability, reduce emissions and strengthen the electric grid.
text:
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Senate on Nov. 19 passed a massive bill to speed up energy project development, weakening environmental rules, while ensuring data centers pay their own way for the electricity they require.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which locked senators on both sides of the aisle in painstaking negotiations over the past few months, passed on a 62-33 vote. The bill, which also bolsters clean energy sources like wind and solar, marked the most significant piece of permitting reform legislation that Congress has passed in years.

Still, it faces an uncertain future in the House of Representatives and a shrinking legislative window to fully pass on Capitol Hill. If not adopted by both chambers, the legislation would have to be reintroduced when the 120th Congress takes over in January.

While supporters of the bill hailed it as a victory for American manufacturing and infrastructure, critics such as Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Oregon, said it would "put the pedal to the floor" on data center development while running roughshod over the sovereignty of Native American tribes.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune said the legislation "cuts through decades of red tape that has made it unnecessarily difficult and costly to build things in America." He promised the bipartisan measure would create better roads and more jobs.

"The slow pace of our current permitting process has had an impact on everything from drinking water to bridge and road repairs. And those delays have consequences for the American people," he said on the Senate floor. "It’s estimated that this bill will save the average household hundreds of dollars each year."

The bill, however, has garnered scrutiny from tribal groups, who said it could infringe upon their treaty rights and endanger sacred sites. Despite last-minute efforts to address those concerns, many opponents in Indigenous communities ultimately weren't assuaged.

"This bill ran right over the top of them," Merkley said. "They are profoundly insulted."

What does the bill do?

The bipartisan bill, first introduced in September, would speed up federal environmental reviews of energy projects and make it easier for developers to get the power they need to run data centers. However, a provision outlined in the text would also charge extra for access to the electric grid, meaning the developer would have to pay more for power.

Proponents of the bill make up an unlikely coalition, including the oil and gas industry and the White House, as well as clean energy developers and global warming activists.

Backers assert the bill is tough but fair on developers, forcing them to pay the full cost of any upgrades while smoothing permits required for projects to move forward. The bill also aims to improve energy affordability, reduce emissions and strengthen the electric grid.

"BAAJA is a big step forward in our fight against climate change," Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-Rhode Island, wrote in a post on X, citing the 1.5 gigatons of emissions it would lower through 2040. "That's the same as taking nearly 35 million gas-powered cars off the road."

The bill has seen opposition from anti-data center groups, environmentalists and Indigenous groups, who argue that it would strip away environmental laws to accelerate the development of data centers powered by natural gas, accelerating the buildout of the artificial intelligence industry.

Environmental advocacy nonprofit Oil Change International called the legislation a "fossil fuel giveaway" and 17 Democratic state attorneys general wrote a letter seeking revisions to protect laws they say the bill could weaken, like the National Environment Policy Act and Clean Water Act.

text:
Just over two weeks after millions voted to oust the Republicans from control of Congress, leading Senate Democrats have joined the Trump administration in pressing the outgoing Republican majority to weaken some of the country’s most important environmental laws. The measure, which Senate Majority Leader John Thune promoted on the floor Thursday, bears the title “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act” (BAAJA).

The bill’s promise of cheaper energy and more jobs rests on the familiar argument of capitalist trickle-down economics. Its sponsors claim that if Congress makes it cheaper for corporations to build pipelines, refineries, power plants, data centers and transmission lines, workers will benefit through lower utility bills and new jobs. The bill requires no utility to cut residential rates and sets no minimum number of workers a developer must hire. Companies can distribute the savings to shareholders and reduce labor costs by doing the work with fewer workers.

On Thursday, November 19, the Senate passed BAAJA by a vote of 62–33, sending it back to the House. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York was one of 14 Democrats who voted for passage. Maine independent Angus King, who caucuses with the Democrats, also voted in favor. Republican senators Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah drafted the legislation with Democrats Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico. On Wednesday, the Senate voted 69–27 to adopt their package as a substitute amendment to H.R. 2347 and 65–31 to limit further debate.

The fossil fuel industry campaigned openly for passage. On November 6, the American Petroleum Institute, the Independent Petroleum Association of America, the Interstate Natural Gas Association of America, the gas export lobby LNG Allies and the National Mining Association signed a US Chamber of Commerce letter urging Congress to send the bill to Trump’s desk. Three days later, American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers issued its own appeal, arguing that the bill would “drive more investment in American energy and manufacturing.”

Under the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA), federal agencies must prepare a detailed environmental impact statement for major federal actions expected to significantly affect the environment. That obligation can apply to a federal agency’s own construction project or to its decision to grant a private developer a permit. BAAJA would exempt more decisions from review. Where review is still required, residents could prove in court that an agency failed to examine a project’s environmental consequences and still see construction proceed while the agency corrects its work.

The bill would allow states to issue permits to discharge pollutants into waterways for up to 10 years, double the current five-year limit under the Clean Water Act. The Interior Department could turn over to state agencies its responsibility under the Endangered Species Act for assessing how projects within their borders would affect threatened or endangered species. If a federal agency approved a project in violation of the National Historic Preservation Act, a court could order the agency to correct its errors, but the violation alone would give the court no authority to halt construction while the agency did so.

For developers, the bill spells out in dollars what a court victory could mean. Under Section 1402, a company that proves its permit was denied in bad faith or unreasonably delayed could recover economic damages and legal fees. If it meets the bill’s other conditions, it would also be entitled to an award equal to 50 to 100 percent of the project’s expected construction cost, payable from the US Treasury. On a $1 billion project, that provision alone could yield between $500 million and $1 billion. The Natural Resources Defense Council warned passage of the bill would result in “large taxpayer-funded corporate handouts.”

The restrictions on environmental lawsuits would reach well beyond the energy industry. In April, Maryland obtained a preliminary injunction halting the conversion of a warehouse into an immigration detention center after Immigration and Customs Enforcement failed to comply with NEPA. Under BAAJA, a judge could order the government to correct the same defect while contractors continued converting the warehouse. The American Civil Liberties Union warned that the bill would give ICE “a faster, cheaper path to building out a detention system.”

In a Senate speech on November 17, Thune blamed permitting delays on “cascading litigation from environmental groups and by agencies determined to study a project to death.” The agencies he accused of delay have lost many of the workers who carry out those studies. From January 2025 to March 2026, staffing in permitting-related occupations at six federal agencies fell by 20 to 30 percent, depending on the agency and occupation, according to an analysis published by the Federation of American Scientists. These workers include hydrologists who assess risks to drinking water, biologists who study threats to wildlife and engineers who evaluate proposed projects.

By exempting more projects from review and introducing automated tools to process public comments, the bill would give the Trump administration grounds to pursue further staffing cuts. On November 16, American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) Local 704, which represents about 1,000 Environmental Protection Agency workers in Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Ohio and Wisconsin, urged representatives from all six states to reject the legislation. “Every day, we use the legal tools provided by law to protect impacted communities and hold industry accountable,” the local wrote.

Four days earlier, the national AFL-CIO leadership had urged senators to vote for the same bill. “Passing BAAJA will show that our government is listening,” wrote Jody Calemine, the federation’s director of government affairs. Among those Congress has heard from are the oil refiners, pipeline operators and mining companies whose appeal for passage preceded the AFL-CIO’s by six days.

What would a family struggling to keep the heat on this winter receive under the bill? Heinrich has cited a Rhodium Group study projecting average household electricity savings of $50 to $78 a year in 2040. That comes to roughly $4 to $6.50 a month, 14 years from now.

The criminal US-Israeli war against Iran has already demonstrated how little protection the abundant domestic oil production affords American workers against a price shock, since it is the world market, not the US market alone, which determines prices. Most of the oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz before the war was bound for Asia. Yet when the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28 and tanker traffic through the strait collapsed, gasoline prices rose sharply in the United States. Brent crude entered April above $100 a barrel. By May 6, a gallon of regular gasoline in the US averaged $4.54, up 52 percent from before the war.

On November 17, US fighter aircraft again struck Iran, targeting what a US military official described as a missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Two days later, the Senate rejected a war powers resolution against the war on Iran, with 51 senators voting against and 48 in favor. The US-NATO proxy war against Russia in Ukraine is now in its fifth year. While senators of both parties promote the prospect of a few dollars a month in household savings by 2040, the Trump administration has requested $1.5 trillion for military spending in fiscal 2027. Federal debt reached $40.2 trillion at the end of September.

The premise of BAAJA—and of every “energy affordability” bill before it—is that energy is a commodity to be produced and sold for profit by private corporations, with the state’s role limited to subsidizing them and clearing away obstacles. Energy is not merely a commodity. It is the foundation of modern life—heat, light, transportation, industry, medicine.

The demand must be for the nationalization of the energy monopolies under the control of the working class, through which production and distribution are planned to meet human need rather than to maximize shareholder value. This nationalization will include no compensation to the wealthy shareholders who have profited from decades of price-gouging.

A family must be able to heat, cool and light its home regardless of its ability to pay. Meeting that need requires taking the energy monopolies into social ownership and placing decisions about generation, transmission, prices and environmental protection in the hands of workers and the communities they serve. That struggle requires a party of the working class, independent of the Democrats and Republicans, fighting for a socialist program.

text:
The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation's energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.

The legislation's sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

The vote sends the bill to the House and is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

The bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act.

Trump urged approval of the Senate bill, calling it a "BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE" in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, "lowering Energy Costs for American Families," Trump wrote.

Industry groups back bill, but environmentalists fear it would weaken safeguards

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more.

However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

"Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.," said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.

Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill "a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America" and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.

Democrats push for amendments

A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon's two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands.

Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels.

"Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn't tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that," Merkley said.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project's possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill.

"In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build," said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. "Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years" as they await approval by the federal government.

text:
The Senate on Thursday, in a 62-33 vote, passed a bipartisan permitting reform bill that aims to speed up the construction of major energy infrastructure like clean energy, transmission lines, and gas pipelines.

Passage of the Bipartisan Affordability and American Jobs Act was far from guaranteed. It took years of negotiations and caused a split within the climate movement, exposing fractures among green groups. Both clean and fossil fuel energy developers, among other business groups, were immediately on board. But four key senators also had to make changes in recent weeks to address concerns from Tribes, investor-owned utilities, and environmentalists in order to win more votes.

Those changes were enough to sway the utility industry’s lobbying group, The Edison Electric Institute, and the climate advocacy group Evergreen Action. But nearly every Democratic member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee ultimately voted against it on Thursday, excluding Rhode Island Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a lead negotiator of the deal. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) also voted no, in part over provisions narrowing Tribes’ consultation rights with the federal government over cultural and sacred sites.

The bill now heads the House, where a coalition of more than 100 moderate Democrats are warming to it. Some other members, including Reps. Jared Huffman (Calif.) and Rashida Tlaib (Mich.), are opposed and argue the party should hold out until next year when it controls Congress.

Supporters of BAAJA said this is their best shot at passing permitting reform, given President Donald Trump still has two years left in office and would likely veto a version pushed by Democrats. They also argue that enacting permitting reform is a way to deliver results as soon as possible for U.S. voters demanding that politicians make their lives more affordable and make data centers pay for their energy costs.

“We cannot keep holding out on permitting reform year after year, in the hopes that maybe, just maybe, we’re going to do it a little bit better next time,” Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said during floor debate. “This is our best option, not only for now, but likely for years to come.”

Building faster

There’s widespread agreement that it takes far too long to build energy projects in the U.S. The skyrocketing power demands of data centers, reshored manufacturing, and greater electrification of transportation and other industries has added new urgency to permitting reform. Utilities also need to continue upgrading the existing grid so it’s more resilient to extreme weather as global temperatures rise, primarily from burning fossil fuels.

BAAJA would set faster timelines for federal agencies to review and approve environmental permits for a long list of energy projects, as well as shorten the window parties have to sue from years to 150 days. The bill would also make it harder for courts to block projects under the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act, and Endangered Species Act. For example, construction could continue even if a court rules that a federal environmental review was deficient. Another section narrows the authority that states and Tribes have to deny projects over water pollution.

Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), another lead negotiator, said that advocacy groups have historically relied on litigation to stop “bad” projects, but that the existing permitting system slows down “good” projects too. That needs to change, especially given how much clean energy is stuck in congested grid queues.

Heinrich and Whitehouse, both longtime climate hawks, are betting that clean energy will win out over polluting fossil fuels because solar, wind, and storage are quicker to build and cheaper to operate — limiting the rise of greenhouse gas emissions and energy prices.

A forecast by the Rhodium Group supports their position, showing that BAAJA will accelerate long-haul transmission lines and therefore unlock a lot more clean energy. This could reduce the power sector’s emissions by between 1% and 18% by 2040 — mainly depending on clean energy’s price competitiveness with gas — even as LNG exports rise. Average annual household electricity bills would be $50 to $78 lower by the same year, the study found, compared to business as usual.

The emissions impact of behind-the-meter gas plants at data centers isn’t included in the forecast. But Rhodium Group said those plants are generally fueled by lateral gas pipelines that typically don’t cross state boundaries or need federal permits, meaning they wouldn’t be impacted much by provisions in BAAJA.

To help expedite transmission lines, the bill would give the federal government greater authority to approve projects when states block or delay them, as well as conduct oversight of utilities’ plans. State regulators could also refer a utility to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission for an investigation if they suspect local transmission planning is inefficient and overly costly to ratepayers.

An initial version of BAAJA would have eliminated utilities’ federal right of first refusal to upgrade existing lines and build new regional ones in their service territories, likely opening them up to greater competition from independent developers. However, those provisions were softened in the final bill, effectively retaining utilities’ right to replace aging corridors.

The Trump wild card

As part of the BAAJA compromise, senators also aim to lift Trump’s blockade of federal on solar and wind projects on federal lands and waters. So-called “permit certainty” provisions would ban any administration from vacating already issued permits, except under emergency scenarios — such as new information showing that a project harms national security, the environment, or human health — or in accordance with new laws or regulations.

The bill would allow any energy developer to sue federal agencies for “disparate treatment,” and outline criteria for proving it. The approach uses a 10-year lookback period to compare whether there’s a new pattern of delays or denials by an administration. Plaintiffs who win their case could collect between 50% and 100% of expected construction costs, “reasonable” litigation costs, and economic damages. Taxpayers would cover them under the federal government’s Judgement Fund.

The provisions are designed to deter future presidents from targeting specific energy technologies, as Trump is doing to renewables and former President Joe Biden did to oil and gas infrastructure.

Whitehouse has said he has assurances from administration officials that BAAJA’s “permit certainty” provisions would apply to a backlog of hundreds of clean energy projects across the Department of Interior and Pentagon, even as Trump has told reporters that he still won’t approve wind turbines.

Trump last week did endorse the bill on Truth Social, stating that it would ensure the U.S. can quickly build pipelines, mines, and power plants and lower energy costs for Americans.

BMW Group and E.ON have announced that drivers of the latest BMW cars can use the EV's vehicle-to-grid (V2G) capability can be paid to feed power back into the mains electricity grid.

The scheme requires one of the automaker's Neue Klasse sixth-generation eDrive vehicles, a bi-directional BMW Wallbox Professional and E.ON's V2G electricity tariff. Vehicles that ship with the V2G capability are the BMW i3, iX4 and iX5, plus the latest, sixth-generation iX3.

The joint collaboration began in February this year in Germany, but the range of vehicles shipping with V2G is now larger.

Under the scheme, a kilowatt-hour of power fed back into the grid via the onboard V2G technology is compensated at €0.42 (US$0.46) credit on their energy bill, up to maximum of €60 per month. Additionally, for every hour the vehicle is connected to the wallbox and the V2G facility is active, the customer receives a. The status of the vehicle's charge and the amount of money refunded are viewable in the driver's My BMW app.

Software developed by BMW and E.ON controls the ratio of EV charging and the energy from the EV's battery sent to the grid. The control system respects the desired minimum state of charge the driver has set to be reached by a specified departure time, and the process has no deleterious impact on battery life, the companies say.

E.ON and the BMW Group announced Germany's first commercial V2G service in September 2025, with the first model capable of V2G, the sixth-generation eDrive BMW iX3, shipping in February of this year.

All drivers of any hybrid or all-electric Mini or BMW can use the BMW app to ensure a vehicle is charged using lowest possible electricity tariff by stating their desired charge level and departure time. This capability is possible from any electricity supplier offering variable-rate tariffs, BMW says.

The BMW Group will produce high-voltage batteries for the US market at its Plant Woodruff facility in South Carolina, US, for the sixth-generation eDrive range. The first vehicle to benefit from the V2G-capable drive will be the iX5, which is due to be released in the first quarter of next year.

The iX5 will be the automaker's first all-electric vehicle assembled in the US, although the company aims to have six EV models produced domestically by 2030.

New solar designs are unlocking clean energy potential at extreme elevations in Austria.

The nation is heavily reliant on hydropower, yet during freezing winter months, electricity production drops sharply.

Reliable winter power generation is needed, but due to strict climate goals, imported fossil fuels can no longer provide it.

Widespread electric heat pump and electric vehicle adoption, along with expanding data centers and industrial electrification, is straining the grid.

Developers turned to high-altitude alpine regions that offer intense sunlight but first had to overcome harsh conditions.

How do cross-shaped solar trees solve this problem?

How Austria is experiencing increased grid strain and winter power deficits

Austria operates a fleet of 135 major hydroelectric plants and alpine reservoirs.

As the backbone of the nation’s electricity grid, hydropower provides approximately 54% to 67% of the total generation mix.

Seasonal rainfall and snowmelt deliver reliable, clean baseload energy.

Yet during the freezing winter months, hydroelectricity production drops sharply.

Sub-zero conditions lock precipitation into mountain ice and snow.

Run-of-river inflows then decline by more than 50% during peak cold snaps.

Meanwhile, Austria is experiencing major surges in national electricity consumption.

Widespread electric heat pump and electric vehicle adoption, along with expanding data centers and industrial electrification, is straining the grid.

The seasonal gap, combined with rising energy demand, is creating a significant power supply deficit.

To prevent blackouts, Austria usually relies on natural gas and imported electricity during winter.

A continued reliance on fossil fuels directly conflicts with national climate mandates to achieve 100% renewable electricity by 2030.

This makes accelerated green energy deployment urgent.

When standard solar generation fails during winter

Rapid solar power expansion is vital for balancing Austria’s electricity grid.

Photovoltaic arrays complement hydropower by generating clean electricity during the day.

This reduces pressure on mountain reservoirs.

Under Austria’s Renewable Expansion Act, the nation aims to add 11 GW of new solar capacity by 2030.

However, standard solar installations struggle during Austrian winters.

From November through February, low-lying valleys face heavy cloud cover, thick fog, and short daylight hours.

As heavy snowfall increases during the winter months, it buries flat, ground-mounted panels.

This blocks sunlight and stops clean power generation for weeks at a time.

To overcome the challenges of standard installations, developers turned to high-altitude alpine regions.

Above 6,500 feet, mountain peaks sit well above valley fog.

However, the mountain terrain presents extreme conditions that conventional solar racks cannot survive.

That is why Austrian clean-tech company HELIOPLANT created cross-shaped solar trees specifically designed for these harsh landscapes.

Unlock clean energy potential at high elevations

The Austrian Climate and Energy Fund supported this technology due to the distinct benefits offered by high-altitude alpine regions.

These high elevations are well above valley fog and experience intense, uninterrupted winter sunlight.

The cold ambient temperatures also increase photovoltaic efficiency.

Additionally, the surrounding snow reflects extra light onto the panels.

Now, HELIOPLANT’s innovative photovoltaic technology also addresses strong alpine winds, shifting glacier ice, and heavy snow loads.

The pilot system was installed on the Tiefenbach Glacier in Sölden, Austria, at roughly 9,800 feet.

The operational specifications of the cross-shaped solar trees

The elevated installations are anchored directly into the alpine terrain to resist shifting ice and extreme winds.

Aerodynamics help the tree-like structures to stay clear of snow accumulation.

The cross-shaped arms channel winds across the panel surfaces.

This automatically sweeps snow away, eliminating manual clearing.

Double-sided bifacial modules are mounted vertically and at steep angles.

Direct sunlight is captured by the front, while the back absorbs sunlight reflected from the white glacier snow.

These operational advantages have helped the Tiefenbach Glacier installation to deliver peak power output during winter.

From May to October 2026, assembly of the full expansion took place, scaling toward the planned total of 800 units.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation's energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices.

The legislation's sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths.

The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year.

The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act.

Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a "BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE" in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, "lowering Energy Costs for American Families," Trump wrote.

Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no.

Industry groups back bill, but environmentalists fear it would weaken safeguards

Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more.

However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure, saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.

"Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.," said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.

Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill "a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America" and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate.

Democrats push for amendments

A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon's two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands.

Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels.

"Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn't tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that," Merkley said.

Majority Republicans stymied Merkley's effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for "purely political purposes."

The bill's sponsors reneged on promises of "a robust amendment process," he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators.

"I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet," Merkley said.

Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project's possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill.

"In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build," said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. "Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years" as they await approval by the federal government.

"Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box," driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said.

The bill's four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation.

The four senators, who lead the chamber's energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.

"We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families," Lee said.

Co-sponsor calls bill 'the floor, not the ceiling' for legislative action on climate

Whitehouse, a longtime climate hawk who has been criticized by some allies for supporting the permitting bill, said the measure is "the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations," adding that he hopes "to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities" over the next two years.

But Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state said the bill has been rushed and its impacts are not fully considered.

Cantwell, who met Tuesday with tribal, outdoor recreation and conservation leaders, said the bill would undermine tribal nations and weaken protections for the nation's bodies of water, land and wildlife.

"Now is the time to slow this process down, to actually have a formal process" to debate and amend the bill, she said. "Don't sacrifice the Clean Water Act or hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty. We all need new sources of energy and power. But this bill, as it's currently drafted, is not the answer."

Oneida Nation Vice Chairman Jameson Wilson said the bill threatens the tribe's ability to protect its sacred spaces, ancestors, traditional ceremonies and culture. "Any effort to accelerate development must strengthen, not diminish and erode tribal sovereignty and meaningful consultation," he said.

Former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm, who led the agency in the Biden administration, said she understands those concerns, but believes recent changes by bill sponsors strengthen protections for tribal consultation and restore important state authority over water quality.

"A bigger Democratic majority can write a stronger bill," Granholm wrote in a social media post. "But it would still need this president's signature."

Sen. Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said he supports and even authored many provisions in the bill, such as streamlining transmission infrastructure.

But he voted no because the bill contains provisions he said would "irreparably harm California and the 109 federally recognized tribes who call California home." He said he cannot sacrifice the rights of tribal governments or California's environment.

Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, Rhode Island.

text:
A bipartisan bill moving through the Senate could reshape how the U.S. builds nuclear power plants.

The legislation, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), is a bill aimed at accelerating the approval processes for energy, infrastructure and manufacturing projects.

Introduced by Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island), the permitting bill remains on the Congress floor as lawmakers debate amendments and final passage.

Read More on News

Supporters argue BAAJA could help the U.S. meet rising electricity demand—including from data centers and artificial intelligence—while critics warn it could weaken environmental checks and public accountability.

What Is the BAAJA Bill? Summary Explained

BAAJA is a nearly 500-page proposal that would overhaul federal permitting and environmental review rules.

Negotiated by leaders of the Senate's Environment and Public Works Committee and Energy and Natural Resources Committee, it affects a broad range of projects, including power plants, transmission lines, pipelines, transportation infrastructure and industrial facilities.

Supporters say the current federal permitting system can take years or even decades to navigate, meaning projects are often delayed. The bill seeks to establish more predictable timelines and reduce bottlenecks.

Purpose of the Bill

The permitting bill is designed to speed construction of energy and infrastructure projects across the country.

"For far too long, our broken and outdated federal environmental review and permitting processes have stood in the way of energy reliability, secure jobs, modern infrastructure, and economic growth," Moore Capito said of the bill.

"The bipartisan reforms we secured in this deal will transform our nation's ability to power our economy and fuel future growth, while continuing to protect the land, water, and wildlife we all cherish."

And according to Lee, passing the bill would mean projects like the Hoover Dam, the Golden Gate Bridge, and the Empire State Building could be completed "in years, not decades."

"America still has the resources and the talent, but what too often stands in the way is a permitting system that takes too long and costs too much," he said.

"Our permitting system takes too long, costs too much, and leaves too much uncertainty for the people trying to build what our country needs."

Permitting delays have become an obstacle for large projects and have put a damper on domestic energy production and ways to strengthen the power grid.

Backers of the legislation say faster permitting could help lower costs and accelerate building the infrastructure needed to connect new power sources to the grid.

However, environmental and tribal groups have expressed concern that the measure would limit opportunities to challenge projects or seek additional review under existing laws.

How the Bill Could Change Nuclear Power

While BAAJA affects numerous industries, nuclear power has emerged as one of the sectors with the most to gain.

According to Scientific American, four amendments added to the bill focus specifically on nuclear regulation.

These amendments could streamline elements of the licensing and permitting process overseen by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC).

Permitting currently accounts for approximately 40 percent of the decade-long process of planning and constructing a new nuclear facility.

Industry supporters say those changes could be especially important for building small modular reactors and microreactors which could help supplement local energy needs.

For nuclear developers, the immediate impact of passing BAAJA could be shorter approval timelines and greater certainty over project schedules. This in turn makes it easier for companies to attract investment and bring new reactors online.

How the Bill Could Change Other Energy Infrastructure

The bill's impact would extend well beyond nuclear energy.

BAAJA backers say it could accelerate construction of interstate transmission lines needed to carry electricity from renewable energy projects to consumers.

Solar and energy-storage developers have argued that lengthy permitting processes can delay projects and increase costs.

The legislation could also benefit wind, geothermal and other renewable energy sources, while easing approval pathways for some oil and natural gas infrastructure, including pipelines.

When Could the Senate Vote on the Bill?

The Senate has already taken multiple procedural votes advancing BAAJA.

On November 18, senators voted 65-31 to invoke cloture on the legislation—moving it closer to a final vote. Earlier votes also advanced the bill with bipartisan support.
