title: Tesla's Cybercab raises concerns among automakers and battery suppliers - CHOSUNBIZ
description: Tesla’s Cybercab push threatens carmakers and battery demand Tesla's two-seat Cybercab robotaxi, which entered mass production this year, is raising…
text:
Tesla's two-seat Cybercab robotaxi, which entered mass production this year, is raising concerns among rival automakers and battery makers alike. Once the Cybercab goes on sale for personal use, it is expected to take a substantial share of demand for other vehicles. Tesla plans to produce the battery cells for the vehicle itself, meaning battery makers will also be affected.
Tesla's "Cybercab" is on display at Starfield Anseong in Anseong, Gyeonggi Province, on the 12th. The Cybercab is a two-seat Autonomous Driving taxi (robotaxi) with no steering wheel or pedals. /Courtesy of Yonhap News Agency
◇ Cybercab sales begin, threatening to upend auto industry
Tesla began taking preorders for personal-use Cybercabs from select U.S. consumers on the 13th, local time, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) and other outlets reported on the 20th. The price is $29,990 (about 40 million won). Buyers can pay a monthly subscription fee of $299 (about 400,000 won) for the full Autonomous Driving service. Vehicle deliveries are scheduled to begin next month.
The Cybercab is a two-seat electric vehicle designed exclusively for Autonomous Driving that Tesla unveiled in 2024. Because it operates with full Autonomous Driving without driver intervention, it has no steering wheel, accelerator or brake pedals, side mirrors or rear window. Unlike conventional electric vehicles that charge through a cable, it charges wirelessly by parking over a floor pad.
Tesla first unveiled the Cybercab in October 2024 and began mass production in February this year at Gigafactory Texas in the U.S. state of Texas. In September, it also began commercial robotaxi operations in parts of Austin, Texas.
Even when purchased by individuals, Cybercabs can be used only within existing robotaxi service areas. Tesla's robotaxis currently operate in only 8 U.S. cities: Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Houston and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando and Tampa in Florida.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk wrote on his X account that the company would sell the Cybercab throughout the United States once it receives regulatory approval. "I think the $299 monthly subscription fee is too expensive," Musk added. "$115 a month would be reasonable, the same as the FSD subscription fee." Full Self-Driving (FSD) is the full Autonomous Driving technology used in vehicles Tesla currently sells.
Visitors look at Tesla's "Cybercab," unveiled in Korea for the first time, at Starfield Anseong in Anseong, Gyeonggi Province, on the 12th. /Courtesy of Yonhap News Agency
The start of Cybercab sales has heightened tensions in the global auto market. An official at a Korean automaker said it would likely take more time before Cybercabs are fully permitted to operate because of regulatory and safety verification issues. But the official added, "Once they are fully commercialized, the very structure of the auto industry, which has existed for more than 100 years, will change, and many automakers will face a crisis."
Tesla is concentrating its resources on the Cybercab as it reorganizes its existing production facilities and redirects new investment. It plans to end Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas next year and use the newly available equipment and production lines to make Cybercabs. Ahead of European Union (EU) approval for operations, Tesla has also outlined plans to invest 3 billion euros (about 4.4 trillion won) in its Grünheide factory in Germany and produce Cybercabs there starting in 2029.
Tesla has discontinued the Model S large sedan and the Model X large sport utility vehicle (SUV) in succession since last year. With the Cybertruck also slated for discontinuation, the only models still on sale next year, apart from the Cybercab, will be the Model 3 midsize sedan and the Model Y midsize SUV. Tesla also plans to launch the Roadster electric sports car in 2028.
Musk is seen in the auto market as restructuring the business with a focus on mass-producing the Cybercab while adding a few driver-operated models, including the Roadster, for consumers who enjoy driving.
◇ Tesla moves to develop and produce its own battery cells
Automakers are not alone in feeling anxious about the Cybercab's arrival. Battery cell makers are closely watching the situation because demand could change if competition shifts in the auto market, which buys their products.
Tesla is building its capacity to develop and produce battery cells in-house. It currently receives battery cells from LG Energy Solution, Japan's Panasonic and China's Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. (CATL), among others. Panasonic mainly makes battery cells for Tesla vehicles produced in the United States, while CATL produces lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells for lower-priced trims of the Model 3 and Model Y. LG Energy Solution supplies nickel cobalt manganese (NCM) battery cells for higher-end trims of the Model 3 and Model Y.
The Cybercab is expected to take share from other vehicles and reduce demand for purchased battery cells. If Tesla equips it with cells produced in-house, outside battery makers will inevitably take a major hit.
Tesla has battery cell development and production facilities at 3 locations in the United States. Its Fremont, California, plant handles research and development (R&D) and pilot production of 4680 cylindrical battery cells. Designed to be 46 mm in diameter and 80 mm tall, the high-energy-density nickel cobalt manganese (NCM) battery is produced at the Gigafactory in Texas. The Nevada Gigafactory mass-produces lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells.
Tesla mass-produces 4680 cylindrical batteries at its Gigafactory in Texas, U.S. The photo shows workers on the job at the Texas Gigafactory. /Courtesy of Tesla website
Tesla's in-house-developed 4680 cylindrical battery cells are currently used in the Cybertruck and some trims of the Model Y produced in the United States. The Cybercab also uses these cells. The Roadster, scheduled to launch in 2 years, will also use 4680 cylindrical battery cells.
Tesla has recently been preparing to produce battery cells outside the United States as well. According to industry sources, Tesla said at an auto industry conference in Berlin on the 11th, "We plan to begin producing our own battery cells at the Grünheide factory in the middle of next year." Tesla has reportedly completed construction of a battery cell production facility inside the factory and is now installing equipment and making other preparations.
An official in the battery industry said, "Even the Model Y, which is currently very popular in Korea, uses CATL battery cells in its lower-priced trims, leaving Korean battery cell makers on the sidelines." The official added, "If the Cybercab's arrival reduces the market share of Hyundai Motor or German luxury car brands, which use a high proportion of NCM battery cells, Korean companies are also likely to suffer a knock-on effect."

Together, we aim to help the country attract private investment, create jobs and drive sustainable, inclusive growth," said Thomas Jacobs, IFC Division Director for the Levant, Yemen and Iraq.
Proceeds will finance projects to improve water efficiency, reduce non-revenue water, expand wastewater treatment and agricultural reuse, and strengthen water systems in water-stressed areas.
The projects reinforce IFC’s long-term commitment to private investment, sustainable growth, jobs, and financial inclusion in Jordan.
text:
Amman, Jordan, 19 November 2026—The International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, announced five investment and advisory agreements at the EU-Jordan Investment Conference to expand access to finance, mobilize private capital, strengthen energy infrastructure across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA), boost manufacturing and create jobs.

The agreements advance the World Bank Group's Country Partnership Framework for Jordan and align with the country's Economic Modernization Vision, targeting sectors where private investment can drive growth and jobs.

"Jordan has the talent, a strong investment climate, and the opportunities to attract private investment at scale. These agreements bring those strengths together with IFC’s support for small business finance, climate and water solutions, and high-tech sectors. Together, we aim to help the country attract private investment, create jobs and drive sustainable, inclusive growth," said Thomas Jacobs, IFC Division Director for the Levant, Yemen and Iraq.

The investments and agreements focus on five priorities:

Build water resilience: IFC is investing $100 million in Arab Bank’s adaptation and resilience blue bond, the first issued by a commercial bank in Jordan. Proceeds will finance projects to improve water efficiency, reduce non-revenue water, expand wastewater treatment and agricultural reuse, and strengthen water systems in water-stressed areas. The bond supports Arab Bank’s strategy to embed environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations in its business and operations to create long term value for its stakeholders and the communities in which it operates.

Unlock new capital for SMEs and trade: IFC is providing a $50 million financing package to Safwa Islamic Bank, in addition to $30 million from the OPEC Fund, to finance small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and sustainable projects. This marks Jordan's first Sharia-compliant financing dedicated to sustainability, including those led by SMEs. Safwa Islamic Bank is also a member of IFC's Global Trade Finance Program with a $50 million trade line to facilitate trade flows. The partnership aims to narrow the SMEs financing gap, strengthen competition, and enable trade, building on the World Bank’s green finance work with the Central Bank of Jordan. The project is supported by the Global SME Finance Facility (GSMEF), a blended-finance partnership funded by the UK's Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office and the Netherlands' Ministry of Foreign Affairs. GSMEF is a program that promotes financial inclusion and reduces the financing gap faced by underserved SMEs in emerging markets.

Scale up clean energy: IFC is investing $25 million in Catalyst MENA Climate Fund 2, including $10 million in blended finance equity from its Frontier Opportunities Fund. IFC has helped mobilize $127 million, mostly from Australian, European, and Gulf Cooperation Council-based companies and entities, and will support further mobilization through 2027. The fund intends to provide equity for solar, wind, energy efficiency, energy storage, and water treatment projects across MENA, focusing on Jordan, Egypt, Tunisia, and Morocco to improve energy access, resilience, and diversification. IFC advised the Fund on integrating a gender and a forced displacement lens into its operations and investments.

Position Jordan as a high-tech investment destination: In line with the strategic directions of the National Council for Future Technology, IFC is advising the Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship to assess Jordan’s semiconductor investment environment, with a focus on chip design and assembly, testing and packaging (ATP). The partnership, which also aims to strengthen conditions for high-tech investment, includes training to build the Ministry’s capacity, in collaboration with its investment promotion arm, Jordan Source, to attract and support investors. This advisory engagement is delivered in partnership with the Government of the Netherlands through the MENA PSD program.

Support textile manufacturing and women employment: IFC is partnering with Jerash Holdings to support the company’s expansion program. The project is expected to support the creation of more than 10,000 direct and indirect jobs including for women, who already make up about 74% of the workforce, and help enhance the company’s production capacity. In addition, IFC will support the company through an EDGE Gender Certification to improve working conditions, employability, and career progression opportunities for women.

The projects reinforce IFC’s long-term commitment to private investment, sustainable growth, jobs, and financial inclusion in Jordan. Jordan is one of IFC’s largest portfolios in the Middle East, with $919.7 million committed across 31 projects.

description:

text:
Continuing its commitment to sustainability — a core Denison value — the university powered up its largest solar array in June 2026.

The 10,800-panel unit, built on land north of campus, became the university’s 11th solar installation. Nearly 40% of Denison’s annual electricity now comes from renewable sources, at a time when demands on the electrical grid are escalating and energy costs are rising.

The new array will offset about 5.5 million pounds of carbon dioxide annually.

“This project marks a historic moment for the college,” said Jeremy King ’97, Denison’s director of sustainability. “This represents our largest single investment in sustainability to date and a significant milestone toward our goal of becoming carbon net zero by 2045.”

Denison has reduced its carbon footprint 50% since 2010, and King said the addition of the newest array — the largest solar installation at any Ohio university — could drive that total to 65%.

The solar arrays are just one way the university has lowered its greenhouse gas emissions. Other Denison initiatives to increase energy efficiency include:

Committing to a “green revolving loan fund” that has invested in more than 150 energy efficiency and water conservation projects across campus. One example is Denison’s transition to more compact fluorescent and LED lighting.

Hiring an energy consulting firm to create a master plan to reach its 2045 carbon net-zero goal. Denison has taken the firm’s report and turned it into an “energy road map.”

Moving away from steam heating in new and renovated buildings. Hot-water heating is more efficient, King said.

Electrifying more of the university’s heating systems, a process that allows Denison to use renewable energy as the source rather than fossil fuels.

Installing EV chargers and transitioning to electric vehicles when it comes time to replace vehicles in Denison’s fleet.

The university is even employing sheep to graze beneath the solar panels rather than rely on diesel-powered mowers and chemical management to keep the vegetation down. The practice illustrates Denison’s determination to take no shortcuts toward sustainability.

King said the university doesn’t purchase carbon credits — tradeable certificates allowing buyers to achieve sustainability goals by having third parties reduce carbon emissions elsewhere. Each credit equals one metric ton of carbon dioxide or other greenhouse gases.

“Our approach at Denison has been, ‘We’re not going to lean into buying our way out of our emissions,’” King said. “We’re actually going to reduce our emissions on campus. That’s more meaningful.”

The solar arrays have been a focal point in two Denison sustainability pledges. In 2010, Denison joined the American College and University Presidents’ Climate Commitment, pledging to become carbon neutral by 2030. Coming out of the pandemic, President Adam Weinberg and the campus sustainability committee decided carbon neutrality was not going to “move the needle,” King said, and “upped the ante” with its net carbon-zero goal for 2045.

Plans for the university’s latest and most ambitious solar array began in 2023, when campus partner Kokosing Solar authored a study illustrating the economic benefits.

Jake Preston, director of physical plant and capital projects, credits much of the project’s early development to James Gallick, Denison’s senior automation engineer. What started with Gallick sketching ideas “on a napkin” evolved through his technical analysis and collaboration with the project team into a 5.4-megawatt solar array.

Preston said it’s a worthy investment on multiple levels.

“There’s much more to the story than just producing solar volume,” he said. “This project helps us manage how much impact we have on the grid throughout the summer months. That’s not just a benefit to Denison, it’s a benefit to the whole grid. The fact that it is reducing our impact during the times when people need power the most pays dividends to everybody in the surrounding community.”

Preston said the demand for electricity in Licking County in the past three years has reached unprecedented levels. With soaring costs, Denison is reaping the benefits of a campus that runs on 40% renewable energy.

“There’s a real business case to be made for these projects,” he said.

text:
Los Angeles County Supervisor Kathryn Barger, U.S. Representative George Whitesides, and Assemblymember Pilar Schiavo are jointly seeking the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) continued partnership in securing stronger protections for residents impacted by the ongoing Chiquita Canyon Landfill crisis, including permanent relocation for affected families.

In a letter sent Wednesday, November 18, to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, the three elected officials requested that the federal agency expand its existing enforcement order governing the landfill to include more extensive temporary housing, improved air filtration, and permanent relocation options for residents who have endured years of noxious odors and disruptions to their daily lives.

“Families in Val Verde and Castaic have been living with this nightmare for more than four years, and they deserve lasting relief,” said Supervisor Kathryn Barger. “The EPA has been an important partner, and I appreciate their continued involvement. We’re asking for its continued help in building on the protections already in place and ensuring Chiquita Canyon Landfill provides meaningful solutions, including permanent relocation for families who have been deeply impacted.”

The request follows another incident at Chiquita Canyon Landfill on November 16 that prompted an emergency response from the Los Angeles County Fire Department and multiple regulatory agencies. In response, the County’s Department of Public Health issued a directive requiring the landfill to provide immediate relief to nearby communities.

The landfill subsequently announced temporary hotel accommodations and a relief center at Embassy Suites Valencia, with services scheduled to end November 20. However, the elected officials raised concerns about the limited assistance available to affected households.

According to their letter, the landfill had secured just 80 hotel rooms for an area encompassing approximately 1,200 households, highlighting the gap between available accommodations and the potential need for relief.

The lawmakers are asking the EPA to expand its existing Unilateral Administrative Order to require the landfill to provide expanded temporary housing by providing more hotel rooms and longer stays for impacted residents, higher-quality air purifiers certified by the California Air Resources Board, and resources to support permanent relocation for affected families.

The letter also acknowledges the EPA’s ongoing regulatory involvement and expresses appreciation for its collaboration with local and state agencies.

text:
“In both markets, the systems will shift midday solar output into the evening peak—addressing Texas’s tightest supply hours after sunset and supporting coal retirement goals in New South Wales,” said the company in a press release.

The fifth installation will be constructed in New South Wales, Australia, where stored renewable energy is needed to support regional coal retirement goals.

Balancing grid supply and demand

By capturing excess midday solar output and releasing it during peak demand, the systems will provide dispatchable electricity. This capability helps grid operators balance supply and demand in real time. As a result, the batteries will strengthen overall network reliability and reduce the need for fossil-fuel peaking power plants.

To build the five sites, X-ELIO has signed supply agreements with e-STORAGE, the energy storage solutions division of Canadian Solar. The combined capacity of the projects totals 590 MW / 1.43 GWh DC. Canadian Solar announced the multi-region deals at one of North America’s largest clean energy industry events.

All five installations will utilize e-STORAGE’s SolBank 3.0 technology. The units do not rely solely on external suppliers for core components. Instead, they are constructed using battery cells manufactured directly at Canadian Solar’s own facilities.

Alongside the battery enclosures, e-STORAGE is supplying the power conversion systems and plant controls needed to connect the units to local transmission networks. These components are designed in a smart way. They can work together to regulate power output and maintain grid stability during rapid shifts in demand.

Equipment shipments currently underway

Deployment is already in its early logistical stages, with equipment shipments currently underway. The five projects are scheduled to enter commercial operation across a two-year window in 2027 and 2028.

Beyond delivering the physical hardware, e-STORAGE will remain involved in the day-to-day performance of the assets. Each contract includes a 22-year long-term service agreement (LTSA). These agreements lock in ongoing maintenance and operational support across the full lifespan of the batteries.

Jeff Roy, President of e-STORAGE, noted that the deal marks the beginning of a global partnership with X-ELIO. He described the developer as a sector leader with a strong twenty-year track record in renewable energy.

“Having them place their trust in e-STORAGE’s products and team for the next 22 years is a positive reflection of our ability to successfully deliver projects across multiple regions with varying complexities,” concluded Roy.

text:
General Motors is seemingly on the hunt for a new chief executive to succeed current boss, Mary Barra, who has been in the top spot for over a decade.

According to a report published by The Wall Street Journal, GM has engaged an executive search firm to find potential candidates for the high-profile role. The outlet adds that Ms Barra’s replacement could come from within GM.

GM has thus far not issued a comment on the matter, and hasn't named a successor.

Reuters reported that following the release of the WSJ’s report on Ms Barra, shares in GM were up 1.5 per cent in afternoon trading.

Ms Barra started at GM in 1980 at 18 years old as a quality control checker. She climbed the company’s internal structure, eventually becoming the manager of the automaker's Detroit/Hamtramck factory.

She became the vice president of global manufacturing engineering in 2008, rapidly cycling through a series of high-ranking positions over the following six years before being named as chief executive in early 2014.

Ms Barra was the first woman to be named as the CEO of a major automaker. Female automotive CEOs have been few and far between, and have included former Citroen and Peugeot CEO Linda Jackson and Chrysler and Ram CEO Christine Feuell.

She has become GM's second-longest-serving CEO, after Alfred P. Sloan who helmed the automaker for 23 years from 1923 to 1946.

The 64-year-old’s time at the helm of GM has included many twists and turns.

Ms Barra oversaw the navigation of GM’s notorious faulty ignition switch scandal, which included the recall of millions of vehicles worldwide and compensation payouts to the families of 124 people that died as a result of the fault.

The CEO also presided over the sale of Opel and Vauxhall to Groupe PSA in 2017, and the shuttering of Holden in 2020 as GM shrank its global presence to focus on more profitable markets and vehicles.

She helped steer the direction of the mid-engined Chevrolet Corvette C8, as well as GM’s at times rocky shift into electric and autonomous vehicle development.

Under Ms Barra, GM invested heavily in its Cruise autonomous taxi division, only to shutter it late in 2024 after collisions and billions of dollars in losses.

The American automaker also invested heavily in electric vehicles (EVs), axing various combustion-powered vehicles and focusing on profitable combustion-powered full-size SUVs and pickup trucks to help fund EV development.

This included the rollout of so-called 'Ultium' EVs, including the range of Cadillac models now available in Australia.

Like many other automakers, GM subsequently reduced EV investment and walked back some of its goals – for example, between 2021 and 2022 it had confirmed Buick and Cadillac would become EV-only brands by 2030, but these plans were subsequently scrapped.

Again like other automakers, GM is in the midst of a battle with the Chinese car industry. The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, of which GM is a member, has repeatedly called for a ban on the sale, import or manufacturing of Chinese connected vehicles in the United States.

GM is also battling with declining demand in the crucial Chinese market, which is shifting away from non-Chinese brands at a rapid pace.

Earlier this year, GM renewed its 30-year-old 50-50 joint venture with Chinese giant SAIC Motor, extending it to 2047. GM plans to export more vehicles produced by its Chinese operations.

title: DOE Offers $2.8B Conditional Loan for 1.8-GW Wyoming Link Between Eastern and Western Grids
description:
Grid United’s Interregional Transmission Portfolio Grid United is developing a portfolio of five major transmission projects across the central and western U.S.
Along with Wyoming Intertie, the portfolio includes North Plains Connector, Three Corners Connector, Pecos West, and Southline Transmission Project.
Under the program, the DOE can contract for transmission capacity to help developers establish the commercial commitments necessary to advance construction.
In October 2026, the office closed a $5.1 billion financing package for Alliant Energy’s utilities in Iowa and Wisconsin.
The potential assignment of the federal loan to utilities that acquire transmission capacity could improve the economics of those agreements before construction begins.
text:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has offered up to $2.8 billion in conditional financing for Wyoming Intertie, a proposed 106-mile transmission project in southeastern Wyoming that could more than double existing power transfer capacity between the Eastern and Western Interconnections, the nation’s two largest synchronous grids. The federal loan, which could be assigned to utilities that acquire capacity on the line, would finance the majority of the independently developed project’s construction costs.

The DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) announced the conditional commitment on Nov. 17 for the up-to-1,800-MW project, under development by Houston-based independent transmission company Grid United. The project would expand transfer capability between the Southwest Power Pool (SPP) and Western Electricity Coordinating Council (WECC) regions.

Existing transfer capacity between the Eastern and Western Interconnections totals just 1,320 MW, according to Grid United’s October 2026 open house materials. The DOE estimates Wyoming Intertie could yield up to $39 billion in electricity cost savings across 17 states in the WECC and SPP regions, though the department did not detail the methodology underlying that projection in its announcement.

According to Grid United’s October financing fact sheet, the proposed loan would cover 80% of construction costs over a 30-year term that includes the construction period. The $2.8 billion excludes interest during construction. Loan disbursements would begin only after the project receives notice to proceed and enters construction.

Grid United separately estimates that the lower federal borrowing rate would yield more than $500 million in ratepayer savings compared with private market project financing. The company notes that the federal loan could be assigned to utilities that acquire capacity on the transmission line.

The DOE said the commitment advances President Donald Trump’s executive order “Strengthening the Reliability and Security of the U.S. Electric Grid” and builds on the department’s September project selections under the Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Advanced Transmission Technology Upgrades (SPARK) program.

Expanding Transfer Capacity Between Asynchronous Grids

The Eastern and Western Interconnections operate as separate, asynchronous alternating current (AC) systems that cannot exchange power directly over conventional AC transmission ties. Seven existing back-to-back high-voltage direct current (HVDC) converter facilities enable power transfers between the two interconnections, Grid United noted in Feb. 25, 2025, comments to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) on the North American Electric Reliability Corp.’s (NERC’s) Interregional Transfer Capability Study. The existing facilities are distributed across Montana, South Dakota, Nebraska, Colorado, and New Mexico, with individual ratings of 130 MW to 210 MW. Five date to between 1977 and 1988 and employ older line-commutated converter (LCC) technology.

Wyoming Intertie would connect the existing Aeolus substation near Medicine Bow in the Western Interconnection to a proposed HVDC back-to-back converter station near the Laramie River Station outside Wheatland. The transmission route extends through Wyoming’s Carbon, Albany, and Platte counties.

Documents suggest the converter station would employ voltage source converter (VSC) technology. In a back-to-back configuration, incoming AC power is converted to direct current (DC) and then back to AC at a single site, which allows power exchanges between grids without synchronization. According to Grid United’s financing fact sheet, the VSC equipment would provide rapid control of bidirectional power flows, voltage regulation, and support for black-start restoration. The latter capability could allow an energized grid to assist in the restoration of portions of the neighboring system after a major outage.

“As a networked grid infrastructure asset, Wyoming Intertie will not directly connect to any specific generation or demand source,” Grid United notes in its project materials. The line would accommodate power from all generation technologies and allow transfers in either direction according to real-time demand.

The additional capacity could allow grid operators to access surplus generation in one interconnection during supply shortages in the other, particularly during extreme weather events. Grid United also anticipates that geographic and meteorological diversity across the two systems, along with differences in their generation profiles, would allow utilities to import electricity during periods of lower production costs and provide Wyoming generators access to additional markets.

Commercial Development and Regulatory Approvals

Still, the federal financing commitment arrives relatively early in Wyoming Intertie’s development. Grid United has not publicly identified capacity customers in its announcement materials, though its financing fact sheet identifies commercial capacity contracts, acquisition of the full project right-of-way, receipt of federal, state, and local permits, and compliance with federal program requirements as key conditions of financial close.

The DOE’s conditional commitment also requires the project to satisfy technical, legal, environmental, and financial conditions before the department executes definitive financing agreements.

Grid United began field surveys in 2023, initiated acquisition of right-of-way options in 2024, and entered the federal Coordinated Interagency Transmission Authorizations and Permits (CITAP) process in 2025, according to its October 2026 development schedule.

Portions of the proposed route cross federally owned land and require environmental reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). At the state level, the project requires an Industrial Siting Certificate through the Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality. Carbon and Platte counties also require conditional use permits, though Albany County currently does not, according to Grid United’s October open house materials.

The developer anticipates concurrent state and county permitting processes in 2027 and 2028, followed by issuance of a federal environmental record of decision and a permitting notice to proceed in 2029. Construction of the transmission line and converter station could begin as early as 2030. Grid United projects commercial operation in 2032 or 2033, subject to HVDC equipment procurement.

Grid United’s October project overview notes that route development incorporates input from landowners, Tribal Nations, and local communities, and the alignment remains subject to regulatory approval. The project has also established a community investment program in partnership with the Wyoming Community Foundation. As of October 2026, the program had awarded $1.2 million to 73 organizations across the three host counties, with local community committees responsible for grant recipient selection.

Grid United’s Interregional Transmission Portfolio

Grid United is developing a portfolio of five major transmission projects across the central and western U.S. Along with Wyoming Intertie, the portfolio includes North Plains Connector, Three Corners Connector, Pecos West, and Southline Transmission Project. Several of the projects have secured federal support through programs established under the previous administration or advanced under the DOE’s more recent transmission initiatives.

The 3,000-MW North Plains Connector is an approximately 420-mile HVDC transmission line rated at up to 525 kV between Montana and North Dakota that would connect the Western Interconnection to the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) and SPP regions. In August 2024, the DOE selected the Montana Department of Commerce for up to $700 million in funding under the Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships (GRIP) program, established by the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. The award supports North Plains Connector and upgrades to the existing Colstrip transmission system. On Oct. 22, 2026, the North Plains Connector Utility Consortium confirmed finalization of the GRIP award at approximately $695 million. Of that amount, the transmission project will receive approximately $620 million as a subrecipient to the Montana Department of Commerce, primarily for transmission tower engineering and construction. The DOE and the Montana Department of Environmental Quality issued the project’s final environmental impact statement on Aug. 28, 2026.

Grid United’s 1,800-MW Three Corners Connector, a proposed 300-mile HVDC line rated at up to 525 kV, would connect the existing transmission systems near Pueblo, Colorado, and Guymon, Oklahoma. In September 2026, the DOE selected an application from Oklahoma’s Office of Management and Enterprise Services for negotiations under the SPARK program. The application seeks up to $250 million in federal funding, primarily for transmission tower engineering and materials. According to an Oct. 7 project announcement, the funding remains contingent on execution of a formal financial assistance agreement. Three Corners Connector could enter commercial operation as early as 2031.

North Plains Connector, Three Corners Connector, and Wyoming Intertie would all incorporate VSC technology, according to Grid United’s February 2025 FERC filing. Their combined proposed project ratings total 6,600 MW—five times the existing East-West transfer capability.

Grid United’s southwestern development portfolio includes Pecos West, a proposed HVDC project that would link El Paso, Texas, and southeastern New Mexico, and Southline, an approximately 280-mile, double-circuit, high-voltage transmission project that Grid United is co-developing with Black Forest Partners between New Mexico and Arizona.

Southline has secured federal support through a separate mechanism. The DOE selected the project’s first phase in 2023 and its second phase in 2024 for capacity contracts under the $2.5 billion Transmission Facilitation Program. Under the program, the DOE can contract for transmission capacity to help developers establish the commercial commitments necessary to advance construction. Payment for transmission service under such contracts does not begin until the infrastructure is operational and available to provide service.

Financing Independent Transmission Development

Grid United has previously identified limitations in existing transmission planning procedures that could complicate commercial development of interregional projects. In its February 2025 FERC comments, the company urged the commission to establish a framework under Order 1920, its long-term regional transmission planning and cost allocation rule, to explicitly evaluate the reliability benefits of interregional transmission investments.

“Additionally, many regions count this value operationally, but none that Grid United can find puts value on it proactively or for new lines,” the company wrote. Grid United argued that the omission reduces the assessed value of prospective interregional transmission investments and makes participant-funded projects more difficult to develop.

EDF’s Wyoming Intertie commitment represents a different application of federal financing from either infrastructure grants or capacity contracts. The office, formerly the DOE’s Loan Programs Office, has more than $289 billion in available loan authority and has concentrated its recent financing activity on baseload generation, transmission, and nuclear power projects, as POWER has reported.

In July 2026, EDF closed a $3.26 billion loan to AEP Texas for approximately 100 transmission projects that encompass roughly 2,800 miles of lines. In October 2026, the office closed a $5.1 billion financing package for Alliant Energy’s utilities in Iowa and Wisconsin.

While those transactions involved regulated utilities with established mechanisms for infrastructure cost recovery, EDF’s Wyoming Intertie commitment precedes fulfillment of the independent project’s commercial contracting requirements. The potential assignment of the federal loan to utilities that acquire transmission capacity could improve the economics of those agreements before construction begins.

The announcement follows EDF’s $4.2 billion conditional commitment to Vistra for nuclear power uprates in Ohio and Pennsylvania and its conditional commitment of up to $5 billion to Constellation for uprates at eight nuclear plants.

text:
NORTH CAROLINA (WTVD) -- Duke Energy customers in North Carolina will see higher electric bills beginning in January after the North Carolina Utilities Commission approved rate increases for Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress.

For residential customers using 1,000 kilowatt-hours per month, Duke Energy Carolinas customers can expect bills to increase by $6.53 per month beginning in January, followed by an additional $4.66 per month in 2028.

Duke Energy Progress customers using the same amount can expect an increase of $9.62 per month in 2027 and another $5.89 per month the following year.

The increases are raising concerns among some customers.

"People need to pay for food and shelter. Housing is going up, everything is going up. And it's very hard for people, working people, to make ends meet," said Donna Ford, a Henderson resident and member of Kerr Regional Citizen Voices.

"People's bills are going up. They're paying a greater percentage of their income for their electricity bills. The raise is going in effect in the middle of winter, when folks are going to need to turn the power on, turn the thermostat to keep it warm in the house," added Dan Crawford, Senior Director of Public Affairs with North Carolina League of Conservation Voters.

The Commission's order also establishes a new rate schedule for data center customers with loads above 50 megawatts and sets a 9.8% cap on Duke Energy's return on shareholder equity.

"We listened to our customers and worked closely with stakeholders to find a more cost-effective way forward. This outcome keeps affordability at the forefront while allowing us to make the investments needed to strengthen reliability and support North Carolina's continued growth. That balance is what we were working to achieve," Duke Energy North Carolina President Kendal Bowman said in a statement.

"Duke Energy made a record $5 billion profit last year. A billion with a 'b', and so allowing them to still get 9.5% (increase over two years is) still quite a bit, especially when consumers are already paying so much more for groceries, for gas," Crawford said.

Both Ford and Crawford want the General Assembly to take action to lower energy costs.

"We'd like to see protections from the General Assembly, not only with the rates, but for environmental protections and also to make these data centers pay their fair cost," Ford said.

"Some states have a cap on what some lower-income families pay as a percentage of their income. I would love to see the General Assembly explore that, see what that looks like. And then moving forward, we need to make data centers pay their fair share. They need to be bringing their own clean energy to the table and that's not been discussed yet in a real way," Crawford explained.

Days after the commission's vote, Treasurer Brad Briner announced Commissioner Donald van der Vaart would resign effective Jan. 1. No reason was publicly provided for his resignation. He concurred with portions of the commission's ruling but dissented on others, including how costs would be handled if customers driving new energy development leave and the approved return on equity.

"I appreciate Don's willingness to serve on the Utilities Commission and wish him the best," said Treasurer Brad Briner.

The order also includes $20 million in new funding from Duke Energy shareholders to help customers in need.

Sites repurposed: The completion of Isotope Row’s demolition within two months marks steady progress in the process of remediating and redeveloping land at Oak Ridge.

text:
The history of Oak Ridge cleanup: Built between the 1940s and the 1960s, the structures of Isotope Row housed the research and production of isotopes used for medical, industrial, and national defense purposes. Work at Isotope Row ceased in the 1990s, but not before the Oak Ridge Reservation—the larger site of which ORNL is a part—landed on the National Priorities List for cleanup of hazardous materials under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act in 1987.

Cleanup of Oak Ridge has progressed in phases since then, though some areas such as Isotope Row have required particularly specialized planning and processes because of the level of contamination of the remaining equipment and structures. While the demolition of Isotope Row’s physical structures began in September of this year, the milestone represents the culmination of efforts that began in earnest in 2020.

That year, contracted cleanup firm United Cleanup Oak Ridge (UCOR) started preparing the buildings for teardown. Working with the DOE’s Office of Science, the Oak Ridge Office of Environmental Management (OREM), and contractor UT-Battelle, they addressed utility infrastructure, combustible materials, contaminated structures such as gloveboxes and hot cells, and various forms of hazardous waste, including asbestos-containing materials. According to DOE-EM, crews encountered a notable challenge in removing the facilities’ overhead ventilation system, parts of which had been constructed using asbestos-blended concrete.

With the preparatory work completed this past June, crews were able to undertake demolition of Isotope Row’s buildings. The process began with the teardown of Building 3036, formally known as the Isotope Area Storage and Service Building. According to UCOR, the final building demolished was Building 3033, which had been used to process gaseous radioisotopes. The building’s materials contained elevated levels of tritium, which risked contaminating other structures if those structures were not demolished and the debris not removed beforehand.

DOE-EM estimates that about 12,000 square feet of buildings were torn down with the demolition of Isotope Row. Most of the demolition debris has been disposed of on-site.

Sites repurposed: The completion of Isotope Row’s demolition within two months marks steady progress in the process of remediating and redeveloping land at Oak Ridge. Even as recently as May 14, DOE-EM estimated that Isotope Row would be demolished by 2027. The DOE plans to use the space for future research missions.

text:
WASHINGTON — The bill would appear to many as a no-brainer for climate-conscious Democrats, allowing for the transmission of clean energy from wind farms in the Plains to the heavily populated pockets of the country like the Northeast.

But in a political twist, many of those same Democrats have proven to be some of the bill’s biggest critics, raising questions about exemptions for data centers, tribal opposition and threats to foundational federal environmental statutes like the Clean Water Act.

After a series of procedural votes, the Senate on Wednesday voted 65-31 to end debate on the legislation, with New Jersey’s Sens. Cory Booker and Andy Kim, both Democrats, each voting no.

“I wanted us to have a real debate about this, but I definitely don’t see everything that I wanted to see right now,” Kim told reporters at the Capitol on Tuesday before voting against the measure.

Kim said he was concerned about environmental protections, tribal input and had “questions about ICE detention facilities” in connection with the bill. Booker himself raised concerns that the bill has too many loopholes.

“I respect the work done on this bill with the goal of accelerating clean energy and building out our grid, but I do not believe it meets the mandate voters have charged us with to put a check on the corruption, chaos and cruelty of Trump’s administration,” Booker said in a statement, noting elements of the bill to eliminate environmental safeguards.

Easing transmission

At its core, the legislation — dubbed by sponsors as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (S.5653) — would accelerate the federal permitting process for energy projects, including electric transmission lines that are the vital sinew of power grids that bring electrons from where they are made to where they are consumed.

“It’s really awesome for transmission,” Nadine Sapirman, a volunteer with the Citizens’ Climate Lobby, a climate advocacy group, said in an interview with NJ Spotlight News.

In their advocacy, Sapirman and fellow supporters of the bill cite a growing backlog of renewable energy projects to receive approval and start operations.

“This bill would cut down on the time it takes to build a wind farm, to build a transmission line” by years, said Sapirman.

She traveled to Capitol Hill from New Jersey to lobby Congress in favor of the bill, arguing regions like the Great Plains, where wind power is strong, present a great opportunity for the country. “Hopefully we can get the electrons from where they’re generated to where they’re needed,” she said.

Electricity demand is only growing, and Sapirman said renewables, not fossil energy, can meet that demand. “We are as a country electrifying more,” she said. “This would be a really, really big climate win.”

Yet the hitch with some Democrats is that the legislation would also allow for the faster construction of oil and gas projects, a non-starter for many in the party, and it would weaken legal protections for tribes, states and local communities by revising bedrock federal laws.

“It turns the faucet wide open on more fossil electrons,” said Sen. Jeff Merkley of Oregon in a floor speech Tuesday.

In particular, the permitting bill would alter the text of the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act and the National Environmental Policy Act, the federal statute that regulates permits.

Environmental groups’ misgivings

Jim Walsh, policy director at Food & Water Watch, a national environmental group, said the bill could increase renewable electricity production in the country.

But it could also boost production of fossil energy projects, oil, gas and coal, further exacerbating human-made climate change. Instead of trying to ramp up renewable energy, he said the focus should be squarely placed upon zeroing out fossil sources.

Earth’s climate is sensitive to added greenhouse gas emissions. “It cares about whether we are trying to phase out or expand fossil fuels,” Walsh said in an interview.

A last-minute amendment adopted on Wednesday would provide exemptions to data centers, allowing them to install gas-powered turbines on their sites without notice, according to Merkley.

Still, an unusual collection of allies — from Senate Republicans and the White House on the political right to clean-energy firms and some climate hawks on the left — has amassed sufficient support to get the bill over its first significant hurdle: achieving 60 votes in the Senate.

That threshold is required to overcome the Senate’s filibuster, the procedural rule that requires a supermajority of senators to proceed on most legislation.

Final passage in the Senate is expected in the coming days, and the House has three legislative weeks scheduled before this Congress ends. If approved, the legislation would also need President Donald Trump’s signature.

Trump has said he supports the bill, as does the American Petroleum Institute, a federal trade group for oil and gas firms.

National organizations including the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council and the NAACP oppose the bill, as does the National Congress of American Indians, the largest and oldest Native advocacy group in the U.S.

Booker is one of several potential 2028 presidential candidates to vote against the measure, including Democrats Mark Kelly and Jon Ossoff of Arizona and Georgia, respectively, and Missouri Republican Josh Hawley.

“I am particularly concerned that the legislation would eliminate the courts’ authority to block the administration’s illegal projects, including ICE detention centers,” Booker said in a statement. “As written, the bill would weaken bedrock environmental laws and strip away important tribal sovereignty protections. For all of these reasons, I cannot support the bill in its current form.”

While final passage in the Senate is likely, passage in the House is uncertain.

Rep. Frank Pallone (D-6th), an influential voice on environmental policy, told reporters last week he had problems with portions of the text. “I have continued to try to do more for the protection of the environment and also address the tribal concerns,” Pallone said.

title: Midterm Elections Reset the Policy Landscape: Takeaways for Businesses Operating and ...
description:
Congressional oversight will become a more significant consideration for businesses across sectors.
Businesses should distinguish among existing statutory obligations, final regulations currently in effect, pending rules and policy initiatives whose durability remains uncertain.
The midterm results do not diminish—and may indeed increase in certain areas- the role of state and local governments in shaping major investments.
Companies evaluating U.S. projects should therefore assess federal developments alongside state and local requirements, community impacts and incentive conditions.
Consistent, constructive engagement with relevant federal, state and local stakeholders will also remain important.
text:
The midterm elections will change the balance of power in Washington without changing control of the executive branch, creating a divided policy environment for businesses for at least the next two years. Congress is poised to take a more active role in oversight, funding and scrutiny of federal programs, while the Trump Administration will retain authority to pursue the administration’s existing regulatory and enforcement agenda.

For companies operating or investing in the United States, the practical consequence of this shift will likely not be a wholesale change in law, but a more complex environment in which infrastructure development, government incentives, and corporate decision-making may receive closer attention from Congress, and state regulators may play a greater role.

1. Congressional oversight will become a more significant consideration for businesses across sectors.

Changes in congressional leadership are expected to bring new oversight priorities, with energy, artificial intelligence and technology, financial services, digital assets, health care, telecommunications and government contracting among the likely areas of focus. While Congress does not have the power to prosecute, it does have broad power to investigate, particularly where potential legislation or federal funds are involved. Companies should assess now—before the new Congress takes office—whether they are likely targets of Congressional inquiry and consider developing proactive response plans.

2. Federal incentives remain available, but government-supported projects will likely face additional scrutiny.

We expect significant federal financing to remain available for energy projects, but those financing decisions will likely be of keen interest to the new Congress. Current Department of Energy priorities include nuclear energy, fossil fuels and geothermal development, some of which may continue to attract bipartisan support. The election nevertheless increases the prospect of congressional scrutiny of major funding decisions and award processes. Companies receiving or seeking federal support should maintain clear documentation demonstrating compliance with program requirements, technical milestones and funding conditions.

3. Environmental policy may face greater congressional scrutiny without an immediate change in existing law.

Federal environmental agencies remain under executive control and will likely continue pursuing the administration’s regulatory agenda. The new Congress, however, can influence implementation of that agenda through oversight and appropriations. Timing also matters: major federal rules finalized late in an administration may, depending on statutory requirements, become eligible for disapproval by the next Congress under the Congressional Review Act. Businesses should distinguish among existing statutory obligations, final regulations currently in effect, pending rules and policy initiatives whose durability remains uncertain.

4. State and local governments will remain consequential to development and investment decisions.

The midterm results do not diminish—and may indeed increase in certain areas- the role of state and local governments in shaping major investments. Data centers, manufacturing facilities, energy projects and other developments may depend on state regulation, local approvals, infrastructure commitments and economic development incentives. Companies evaluating U.S. projects should therefore assess federal developments alongside state and local requirements, community impacts and incentive conditions. Changes in Washington may garner the most headlines, but many decisions affecting project viability will continue to be made at the state and local level.

5. Corporate governance and compliance provide continuity amid policy uncertainty.

The election changes the political environment, not the underlying legal obligations businesses already face. Existing statutes remain in force, executive agencies retain their responsibilities, and many regulatory requirements will continue regardless of congressional priorities. However, given potential increased Congressional oversight and shifting political winds, companies working on projects involving government funding, major infrastructure or other public commitments should ensure accurate documentation of key decisions and that they are following their established processes for procurement and bidding, given the possibility that these decisions may later be scrutinized in hindsight by politically-motivated actors. Consistent, constructive engagement with relevant federal, state and local stakeholders will also remain important.

The HYC400 packs up to 400 kW into a single unit. If you’ve stopped at an IONNA Rechargery, you may have already plugged into one.

The HYC1000 works differently. A separate power cabinet can send up to 1 MW across as many as eight vehicles at once, shifting power between them as their charging needs change. Operators can configure it with CCS or NACS plugs for passenger EVs or a Megawatt Charging System (MCS) plug for compatible heavy-duty trucks.

Three deadlines fall between Monday, Nov. 2, and Monday, Nov. 16, and each one is a grant or award round open to Pasadena small businesses. The first is the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) annual research solicitation for small businesses, which pays up to $100,000 per Phase I contract and closes at 8:59 p.m. Pacific time Sunday, Nov. 8. EPA small-business research contracts (Sunday, Nov. 8, 8:59 p.m. Pacific)

EPA’s Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) program funds proof-of-concept work on environmental technologies. Phase I awards run up to $100,000 for six months, and EPA offers up to an additional $6,500 for outside technical and business help such as market analysis or patent strategy, though that money is not guaranteed. Proposals must answer one of the solicitation’s topics, which fall in four areas: clean and safe water, air quality, sustainable materials, and safer chemicals. Examples include treating or detecting per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), preventing and recycling food waste, recovering critical minerals from lithium batteries, and improving lead test kits. Awards are contracts, and work is expected to begin in February 2027, when EPA anticipates making the awards.

Issued by: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, solicitation 68HERW26R0102; deadline 11:59 p.m. Eastern time. Requires an active System for Award Management (SAM) registration set to accept contracts or all awards, a Unique Entity Identifier, a U.S. Small Business Administration company registry ID, and a FedConnect account. Proposals are capped at 36 pages. Read EPA’s solicitation page and apply at https://www.epa.gov/sbir/how-apply-sbir-contract.

Route 66 legacy business grants (Thursday, Nov. 12, 11:59 p.m. local time)

The National Trust for Historic Preservation’s Preserve Route 66 Legacy Business Grant Fund pays for capital improvements, planning, and marketing at small, independently owned legacy businesses or businesses housed in historic or older buildings along the Route 66 corridor, which in Pasadena includes East and West Colorado Boulevard. Eligible capital work includes facade cleaning, sign and window restoration, awnings, outdoor seating, accessibility upgrades, and electrical and heating and cooling systems; planning money can cover business plans, energy audits, and preservation consultants. Grants generally range from $5,000 to $10,000, and no match is required.

Issued by: National Trust for Historic Preservation. The applicant must own the business, which must have a brick-and-mortar location, be a registered business in good standing in the state where it was formed and where it operates, and not be part of a national franchise; digital-only businesses are ineligible. Applications need three high-resolution photos, a project budget, a certificate of good standing, and the property owner’s consent if the applicant does not own the building. Preference goes to businesses tied to historically underrepresented communities and to those in economically distressed areas or affected by natural disasters. Read the grant guidelines at https://savingplaces.org/preserve-route-66-legacy-business-grant-fund.

$5,000 disaster-mitigation grants (Sunday, Nov. 15)

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation’s Readiness for Resiliency (R4R) Mitigation Grant program, supported by Verizon, awards $5,000 grants for projects that cut a small business’s disaster risk before an emergency: backup power, redundant communications, protection from flooding and water intrusion, structural fixes, or safeguards for critical equipment. Applicants propose their project in the application. To qualify, an owner completes the foundation’s disaster-preparedness checklist and a free Disaster Resilience course on Verizon’s Small Business Digital Ready platform. Recipients will be notified by Jan. 15, 2027, and must complete their projects by April 30, 2027.

Issued by: U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation. The course must be completed by Nov. 15. Applying also enrolls a business in the foundation’s separate R4R recovery program, which is open to businesses with 500 or fewer employees and an Employer Identification Number and offers another $5,000 if a qualifying disaster strikes their region. Read the foundation’s announcement and apply at https://www.uschamberfoundation.org/disasters/new-grant-program-helps-small-businesses-prepare-for-natural-disasters.

text:
November 19, 2026 – Ottawa, Ontario – Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat

The Government of Canada is committed to achieving net-zero emissions in its operations by 2050 as we build a cleaner, more competitive economy.

Today, the Honourable Shafqat Ali, President of the Treasury Board, announced the Government of Canada has established a national master standing offer for carbon dioxide removal (CDR) credits that will provide federal departments with access to credits from 19 projects across Canada.

Canada is the first national government in the world to establish competitive standing offers for permanent CDR credits, demonstrating how public procurement can advance innovative climate action and support emerging clean technology sectors.

Canada is building its way to a cleaner economy with four building blocks:

Build: by expanding our supply of non-emitting electricity

Switch: by powering our homes, businesses, and vehicles with non-emitting electricity

Transform: by improving energy efficiency

Innovate: by developing and scaling clean fuels and technologies

These standing offers support the “Innovate” pillar of Canada’s new approach to climate action by strengthening domestic expertise and generating economic and environmental benefits.

The selected projects use advanced technologies and processes to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and store it in natural reservoirs and products in Canada. To ensure quality, they must follow rigorous scientific protocols and undergo independent verification and certification aligned with international best practices.

The CDR credits will help address emissions from federal operations that are hard to decarbonize, such as the operation of National Defence’s air and marine fleets.

Carbon removal technologies are rapidly advancing, and Canada is well positioned to grow its carbon management sector through its expertise, favourable geology, and innovative companies. This initial procurement will help scale the sector while informing the Government of Canada’s long-term CDR strategy for greening operations.

text:
Free Enterprise Project Demands Answers as Congress Considers BAAJA and Trump Visits China

Washington, D.C. — As President Donald Trump confronts China’s economic and national security threats during his trip to Asia, the Free Enterprise Project (FEP) of the National Center for Public Policy Research is demanding that Wells Fargo disclose how much of its massive $500 billion sustainable-financing commitment supports projects dependent on Chinese-made equipment and materials.

In a shareholder proposal submitted yesterday, FEP calls on Wells Fargo to examine the extent to which its green financing supports Chinese supply chains instead of American manufacturing. The proposal comes as Congress considers the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), legislation intended to accelerate permitting for energy and infrastructure projects, including renewable-energy development.

“Washington is talking about strengthening American energy security while Wall Street may be financing the very Chinese industries that undermine it,” said FEP Executive Director Steve Milloy. “Wells Fargo has promised half a trillion dollars in sustainable financing. Shareholders deserve to know how much of that money ultimately supports Chinese solar panels, batteries, wind turbines and other so-called green technologies.”

Wells Fargo has committed to financing or facilitating $500 billion in sustainable finance by 2030, including investments in renewable energy, clean transportation and other environmental projects. The bank reports that it has already facilitated approximately $321 billion toward that goal.

But China dominates the manufacturing and processing of many technologies essential to the global green-energy industry.

According to the International Energy Agency, China accounts for approximately 85% of global solar supply-chain production capacity and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply-chain production capacity. That concentration raises serious questions about whether American financial institutions are increasing dependence on a geopolitical adversary in the name of environmental sustainability.

“Congress is preparing to make it easier to build energy projects under BAAJA, but who will actually benefit?” Milloy asked. “If those projects depend on Chinese equipment and materials, American banks could be helping strengthen China’s industrial dominance while calling it sustainable finance. That’s a question shareholders should not have to guess about.”

FEP’s proposal requests that Wells Fargo’s board prepare a report disclosing:

The estimated share of its sustainable-finance portfolio associated with projects relying on Chinese-origin solar panels, wind components, batteries, critical minerals and related equipment.

The share supporting projects that use American-made or other non-Chinese equipment and materials.

How Wells Fargo identifies the origins of equipment and materials used in financed projects.

The geopolitical, regulatory, reputational and forced-labor risks associated with dependence on Chinese supply chains.

The proposal does not seek to prohibit lending or dictate which projects Wells Fargo can finance. Instead, it seeks transparency about financial exposure, supply-chain vulnerabilities and the consequences for American industry.

The timing also coincides with President Trump’s visit to China, where economic competition, technology and trade tensions remain central concerns in the relationship between Washington and Beijing.

“President Trump is in Asia confronting the reality of America’s economic competition with China,” Milloy said. “Meanwhile, American shareholders have no clear picture of whether a major U.S. bank’s green-financing commitments are helping perpetuate our dependence on Chinese manufacturing.”

“Calling something ‘green’ doesn’t make it good for America,” Milloy added. “Wells Fargo owes its shareholders answers about where this money is going, whose industries are benefiting and what risks the bank is taking.”

The proposal has been submitted for inclusion in Wells Fargo’s 2027 proxy materials.

About

The Free Enterprise Project, an initiative of the National Center for Public Policy Research, is a leading shareholder activism and education program that works to hold corporate America accountable and defend free enterprise.

The National Center for Public Policy Research, founded in 1982, is a nonpartisan, free-market, independent conservative think tank. Contributions are tax-deductible and may be earmarked for the Free Enterprise Project. Sign up for email updates here.

title: Even the 'good guys' of AI are locking in fossil fuels - Grist.org
description:

A recent report found that the biggest data centers in the United States emit about as much carbon dioxide as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark.
Assuming humans avert an AI apocalypse, we’ll have to contend with the reality of living on a rapidly warming planet.

text:
Anthropic became one of the most valuable companies on the planet on Wednesday, valued at $1.5 trillion after its IPO. Known as one of the “good guys” of AI, Anthropic was founded by employees who left OpenAI over disagreements about ethics and safety. But despite the company’s emphasis on responsibility and preventing AI from killing everybody, one thing you don’t hear Anthropic talking about much is its contribution to climate change.

Ahead of the initial public offering this week, Greenpeace accused the company of “asking average investors to join them in throwing the planet into the climate furnace.” AI data centers are causing electricity demand to soar and fueling a surge in natural gas plants. A recent report found that the biggest data centers in the United States emit about as much carbon dioxide as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark. Anthropic is contributing to that: It reportedly signed a $3.4 billion deal with the Texas-based company OnePWR Solutions in September to power data centers with gas-fired engines — the largest known single purchase of its kind by an AI lab.

“It signals what direction they’re taking very clearly,” said Charlie Cray, a senior strategist at Greenpeace USA. The company is locking in fossil fuels at a time when scientists say the world is certain to overshoot the goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees C. Anthropic’s reputation for being the most responsible of the AI giants means it should be minimizing its climate impact, Cray argued: “Show the world that you can do it better.”

The company has been lauded for focusing on safety and “alignment,” trying to ensure that AI acts in accordance with human values — or as its website puts it, “training Claude to be helpful, harmless, and honest.” Earlier this year, Anthropic got into a dispute with the Pentagon when it refused to give the Department of War unrestricted use of AI for autonomous weapons and mass domestic surveillance. This summer, Dario Amodei, its CEO, called for the government to regulate the industry and for AI development to slow down. But Anthropic’s actions are decidedly less “aligned” with efforts to preserve the stable climate that allowed complex human civilizations to grow and flourish.

In the hundreds of pages of its IPO filings, the maker of Claude mentioned climate change sparingly, laying out a number of ways that the warming planet could threaten its business. One risk is higher operating costs: Anthropic said that higher temperatures “can increase the power consumption and water usage required to cool equipment at the facilities on which we depend.” In addition, fires, hurricanes, and floods amped up by climate change could disrupt its operations, it noted.

Environmental policies pose another set of risks to the company’s resource-intensive business. Anthropic acknowledged that some investors may choose not to invest in the company if its sustainability measures are seen as inadequate. On the other hand, implementing such goals “could be difficult to achieve or costly to implement,” it wrote in the filings, adding that navigating various climate and sustainability disclosure laws in California, the European Union, and the United Kingdom could require “significant time and resources.”

That good-guy reputation might also take a hit. The filings suggest that AI’s environmental harms could hurt Anthropic’s image, as its brand is “subject to heightened scrutiny with respect to perceived societal, environmental, labor, health, and safety-related impacts.”

“At least they admit that climate change is a threat when they say it’s a risk to their own operations,” Cray said, “but they’re not taking responsibility for their own contribution.”

In the broader public discussion about AI, concerns about global warming have been drowned out by a more immediate existential threat. One of Anthropic’s researchers, Jacob Coxon, accused the company of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives” when he resigned in September; then the lead of its alignment division, Evan Hubinger, said he thought there was a greater than 10 percent chance that “AI could kill all humans” within the next decade.

Assuming humans avert an AI apocalypse, we’ll have to contend with the reality of living on a rapidly warming planet. Some experts are trying to bring sustainability into the conversation about how to use AI responsibly. “The entire sector needs to be scrutinized closely as to what choices they make and how much transparency is in their reporting — which in this case, is not a lot,” Cray said. A recent analysis from the firm Integrum ESG compared Anthropic to 14 peer companies across the AI supply chain and found that all of them except Anthropic and SpaceX reported their direct greenhouse gas emissions and the indirect emissions from the energy they purchase (called Scope 1 and 2 emissions in energy wonk-speak).

Anthropic has pledged to cover the electricity price increases from its data centers so the public wouldn’t have to pay those costs and committed to “being a responsible neighbor” and addressing its environmental impacts, such as by deploying “water-efficient cooling technologies.” In June, it joined other major corporations in backing the carbon removal industry. (Anthropic did not respond to a request to comment.)

Cray has ideas for how Anthropic could apply its ethical standards to the problem of climate change. In addition to greater transparency, the company could commit to a timeline for powering its data centers with only renewable power and set firm climate targets. “They shouldn’t be building data centers that are powered by natural gas without a timeline for phasing that out and replacing it,” he said.
