title: The U.S. Government Once Tried To Get The Big Three To Sell 80 MPG Diesel-Electric ...
description:
The goal was a high-tech sedan that achieved at least 80 mpg.
Amazingly, the automakers succeeded in building family sedans that got 80 mpg or very close to it.
Run the numbers, and America’s quest to make 80 mpg sedans came at a cost of $1.05 billion per year, and that’s in 1990s money.
However, the gasoline-electric Prius fell short of the 80 mpg goal.
GM said that the Precept could run on diesel power, electric power, or both, and that in testing, it scored 80 mpg.
text:
Sometimes innovation doesn’t come by way of market forces, but necessity. The technologies of World War II and the space race are great examples, but even the auto industry has sometimes been pushed in a direction by forces beyond the whims of car buyers. One of those times was in the 1990s and the 2000s, when America tried to force a green revolution by having Detroit automakers build wild 80 mpg diesel-electric hybrid cars. The cars worked, but the program didn’t. Here is their story.

Back in the early 1990s, the federal government saw a disconnect between its research on environmental pollution and the technologies of the cars of the era. According to the United States Environmental Protection Agency, transportation was responsible for 32 percent of U.S. carbon dioxide emissions and was the fastest-growing polluter. America, like much of the world, was interested in a future where people could enjoy high-tech cars without them filling the air with harmful pollution. To achieve this, the federal government believed that cars needed a leap forward in technology, not just a gradual advancement.

It wasn’t just Washington and its agencies that saw a future in greener cars. Notably, in 1989, the California Air Resources Board kicked off its Zero-Emission Vehicle Program, which required that two percent of a large auto manufacturer’s total sales in California be zero-emission vehicles by 1998. California then planned for a future where, by 2003, ten percent of all cars sold in the state would be zero-emission.

On September 29, 1993, President Bill Clinton gathered the CEOs of Chrysler, Ford, and General Motors to announce the Partnership for a New Generation of Vehicles (PNGV). This initiative was a public-private partnership between the Big Three and the government, and promised to produce a mid-sized family car with three times the fuel efficiency of the average 1994 model-year sedan. The goal was a high-tech sedan that achieved at least 80 mpg. Part of the marketing of PNGV was that the program would also help secure the long-term competitiveness of domestic automakers against foreign competition.

Amazingly, the automakers succeeded in building family sedans that got 80 mpg or very close to it. They did so by pairing compact diesel engines with hybrid systems. One of them is the diesel-electric Ford Prodigy sedan shown below. But while the cars were real and promising, the program had problems that would ultimately lead to its demise.

The Partnership For A New Generation Of Vehicles

According to the Congressional Research Service (CRS) for the Library of Congress, the U.S. Department of Commerce led the program and coordinated related research between federal agencies. Participating agencies included the Department of Energy, the Environmental Protection Agency, the Department of Transportation, and the National Science Foundation. Representing the automakers was the United States Council on Automotive Research. Smaller players involved entities like individual investors and automotive suppliers.

The CRS notes that there was no direct federal funding for PNGV. Instead, federal funding – about $250 million per year – came from the research budgets of the affiliated government agencies. These agencies used that money to research engine technology, lightweight materials, hybrid systems, fuel cells, and emissions controls. More than half of the $250 million per year price tag came from the DOE’s energy conservation budget.

The majority of the funding for PNGV came from the automakers themselves. Collectively, Chrysler, Ford, and General Motors spent $800 million per year on the program. Run the numbers, and America’s quest to make 80 mpg sedans came at a cost of $1.05 billion per year, and that’s in 1990s money. In 2003, when the CRS report was published, that would have been the equivalent of $1.92 billion spent every year.

CRS says that PNGV had three main goals. The 80 mpg “supercar,” as the program called it, was only one. PNGV also sought to improve the quality of American manufacturing while also implementing new technologies. Those were ambitious enough, but PNGV also set baseline parameters for the cars beyond just fuel economy.

Each car had to seat up to six occupants, had to survive a minimum of 100,000 miles, had to meet or exceed EPA Tier 2 standards, be at least 80 percent recyclable, and cost about the same as existing mid-size sedans. To say that these were lofty goals would be an understatement. Remember, the automakers involved were working with 1990s technology, too.

At the time, there were competing ideas in the automotive industry. Automakers were already hard at work cooking up EVs for California’s zero-emission mandate. At the same time, these same automakers, as well as universities, were researching hybridization as a way to leapfrog the efficiency of internal combustion engines.

Pioneering EV engineer Alan Cocconi, who would become known for his work on the GM EV1 and for being a co-founder of AC Propulsion, also got involved. He converted a Honda Civic to electric drive and managed a real-world range of 118 miles. Cocconi drove the car from California to Washington, D.C. in an attempt to convince the federal government to push the PNGV into an all-electric path. Washington ignored Cocconi’s proposal, but that didn’t deter him. He would later become one of the architects behind Tesla’s eventual success.

According to the book, Car Wars: The Rise, The Fall, And The Resurgence Of The Electric Car, a pivotal moment in the PNGV program came on October 27, 1995, when Toyota unveiled the concept for the first Prius. PNGV researchers were blown away. They had been studying hybrid systems, and here Toyota was with a hybrid car that was entering production soon. Then, in January 1996, GM showed the world the EV1.

The Prius was apparently a catalyst of sorts. It proved that hybrid technology was a working way to dramatically improve fuel efficiency. However, the gasoline-electric Prius fell short of the 80 mpg goal. But the PNGV researchers had a cure. They would take hybrid power and pair it with an efficient diesel engine. This determination came in 1997, or four years after the launch of PNGV.

The ‘Supercars’

All of the Big Three settled on diesel-electric hybrid designs, and by December 1999, PNGV finally had something grand to show the world. Ford pulled the wraps off a sedan called the Prodigy, while Chrysler had the Dodge Intrepid ESX and General Motors had the Precept. All three cars were different flavors of the same idea.

I got to see the Prodigy in person when I went to the Ford Vault in Romulus, Michigan, and the car surprised me.

Here’s what Ford said about the Prodigy during the car’s debut at the 2000 Detroit Auto Show:

The new Ford Prodigy is a hybrid electric family car prototype able to achieve more than 70 miles per gallon fuel economy. The lightweight, aerodynamic and fuel-efficient Prodigy – which will be unveiled at the North American International Auto Show – demonstrates Ford’s progress in developing a hybrid electric family vehicle with mass appeal. “The vehicle represents an interim stage between our P2000 research programs and our plans for an affordable, production hybrid.” says Neil Ressler, vice-president – Research and Vehicle Technology.

The stylish, roomy Prodigy is designed to be stingy on fuel without sacrificing customer appeal in areas such as performance, affordability and roominess. The sedan is built on a lightweight platform, features a modern, aerodynamic design and is powered by a low storage requirement (LSR) hybrid electric powertrain. The Ford Prodigy features an aerodynamic design that enhances vehicle aesthetics while reducing air resistance. Prodigy’s 0.199 coefficient of drag – a measure of air resistance – is a 33-percent improvement compared with prior versions of the vehicle. Such a major improvement helps improve the vehicle’s fuel economy by 4 miles per gallon.

To enhance the vehicle’s aerodynamics, side-mounted cameras and onboard monitors are used in place of conventional side-view mirrors. The cameras provide a needed side view for the driver while not hindering air-flow around the vehicle. Variable ride height, grille shutters and shields under the car also add to the vehicle’s aerodynamic improvement. Prodigy’s platform is based on Ford’s extensive lightweight materials research. Prodigy’s total weight is 2,387 pounds, which is about 1,000 pounds lighter today’s family sedan. The significant weight reduction was achieved without sacrificing package efficiency. Prodigy is 30-percent lighter than today’s Taurus sedan, but – thanks to creative packaging and lightweight materials – passenger space and luggage capacity are the same. Prodigy’s low storage requirement hybrid electric propulsion system uses an aluminum DIATA (Direct Injection, Aluminum Through Bolt Assembly) engine, starter/alternator, automatically shifted manual transmission and high-power battery.

The Prodigy is a work of engineering art. The body is made from a mix of aluminum and composites to keep weight down, and helping the car slice through the air is a total absence of mirrors. Instead, where each mirror would be, there’s a little bullet-style camera that feeds video to dashboard screens inside.

The 1.2-liter DIATA common rail turbodiesel four made 74 HP and, according to the Department of Energy, had a thermal efficiency of “greater than 40 percent.” The DOE also stated that the DIATA diesel was remarkably quiet compared to other diesels, thanks in part to computer design tools and Ford’s fast-track development program with partner FEV Engine Technology. Ford also utilized an exhaust gas recirculation system to reduce NOx emissions.

The starter/alternator here was actually a 47 HP electric motor placed between the engine and the transmission. Combined with the gasoline engine, Ford quoted a total system output of 121 horsepower.

When the vehicle was on the move, the diesel engine did most of the work, but the electric motor was able to kick in to give an assist. Since the motor was also a starter/alternator, the system also allowed the engine to shut down when stopped. Then, when the engine needed to be called into action again, the motor was able to spin the engine back up in just 0.2 seconds, or as Ford said: “in the blink of an eye.”

All of this was good for 72 mpg, at first. But later, it was reported that Ford did meet the 80 mpg goal. Ford quoted a range of 660 miles, and like any true nerdy hybrid car, you got to see the status of the vehicle’s hybrid system through the vehicle’s internal screens. The car also had active aero in the form of a grille that opened to the air only when needed.

GM Made A Rear-Engine Diesel Hybrid

The GM Precept was equally as innovative. That car sported an air suspension, a heat pump climate control system, all-wheel-drive, electric doors, and an aluminum body. Like the Ford entry, it traded mirrors for cameras and screens.

A tiny 35-kW battery lived under the front seats, providing energy storage. The Precept was extra weird with a rear-mounted 1.3-liter three-cylinder turbodiesel engine, which was good for 54 HP. The engine drove the rear wheels through an automated-manual transmission, and there were also two electric motors. One motor lived in the rear with the engine, and a second was up front, which provided the AWD.

GM said that the Precept could run on diesel power, electric power, or both, and that in testing, it scored 80 mpg. The Precept featured a drag coefficient of 0.163, which was said to be GM’s slickest car ever at that time. Despite all the tech, GM also succeeded in shedding weight. The Precept weighed about 460 pounds lighter than a typical mid-size GM sedan.

Chrysler Went Plastic

Finally, there was the Dodge Intrepid ESX III, and what made this one special was its realism. DaimlerChrysler went through three iterations of this concept, beginning in 1996, and it seemed like Chrysler did honestly try to make this seem more like a normal car. Designers knew that a fully aluminum body was going to be far too expensive for production, so it draped the ESX in plastic body panels like a Saturn.

Power came from a 1.5-liter three-cylinder diesel built by Detroit Diesel. This engine made 74 HP and, when combined with an electric motor, was good for a total system power of 94 HP. Like the other cars, Chrysler went with an automated-manual transmission to combine manual fuel economy with the ease of use of an automatic. Chrysler called its box the “Electro Mechanical Automatic Transmission.” Meanwhile, a small lithium battery provided energy storage, and the car used regenerative braking to slow down and recharge that battery.

The Dodge was actually the least efficient of the trio, as Chrysler never advertised a rating higher than 72 mpg. However, in going through three iterations, Chrysler made great progress towards making a car that might have been able to be sold in a showroom. Reportedly, the first ESX concept was $60,000 more expensive to build than an equivalent Dodge Intrepid. By the ESX III, the gulf had narrowed to only $7,500. Chrysler was confident that, with more development, it could maybe get the ESX to a place where it could be produced. It even quoted a 60 mph acceleration time of 11 seconds and a weight of 2,250 pounds.

Yet, none of these cars reached production, and the reasons were numerous.

Why PNGV Failed

As the CRS notes, the choice of diesel power poisoned the program before the show cars even saw the light of day. Environmentalists said that the diesel engines were far too dirty and betrayed the purpose of the PNGV program. Some critics went as far as to argue that the diesels actually wouldn’t comply with the EPA’s Tier 2 emissions standards, which were a requirement of the program. According to CRS, environmental groups also questioned the honesty of the program. Some argued that PNGV was actually just a way for the government to delay increasing Corporate Average Fuel Economy standards.

That put the program on a bit of shaky ground, but it got even worse from there.

As I sort of hinted above, these cars were expensive bits of kit. Yes, Ford and GM both hit 80 mpg and Chrysler came close, but by Chrysler’s own admission, had it put the ESX III into production, it would have been much more expensive than an existing car. The Ford and GM entries used even more expensive materials. This meant that the program would, in theory, fail in two of its main objectives.

Then, there was a question about whether the automakers could even mass-produce these cars. Building one-off prototypes is one thing; actually tooling up a factory to crank them out in the tens of thousands is another.

Perhaps the biggest question of all was the government’s exact role in all of this. From CRS:

Another issue that was raised was whether the federal government should support this research at all, and that the program amounted to “corporate welfare.” According to the Cato Institute, “taxpayers should not be forced to help private companies develop profitable new products in the first place.” This concern contributed to a June 14, 2000 House of Representatives vote to eliminate funding for PNGV in the FY 2001 appropriations bill (P.L. 106-291), and to use the funds for debt reduction.

In the final conference, PNGV funding was reinstated. Because consumers generally do not make fuel economy a high priority, supporters of PNGV argued that it may be necessary for the federal government to intervene to limit petroleum dependence. Further, according to industry estimates, auto manufacturers spent three times as much as the government per year on PNGV research. A related issue is the question of whether the program “picked winners” through its selective technology focus.

Critics argued that too much funding was being directed at the technologies chosen for implementation in goal 3 of the partnership. PNGV supporters countered that research was continuing on topics unrelated to goal 3 (the supercar), but which may have helped the partnership meet goals 1 and 2 (improved domestic competitiveness, and implementation of new technologies in conventional vehicles, respectively). These technologies included research on fuel cells and other advanced technologies. Other concerns that were raised at the beginning of the partnership centered on questions of antitrust and intellectual property rights.

Ralph Nader called the program, “an effort to coordinate the transfer of property rights for federally funded research and development to the automotive industry.”

On January 8, 2002, with the support of the Big Three, President George W. Bush canceled the PNGV program, replacing it with the less ambitious Freedom Car program. For the most part, the project was forgotten. A couple of examples of the Ford Prodigy concept have been sold at auction, and one currently lives in the Ford Vault.

PNGV Did Move The Needle A Little

The PNGV program wasn’t a total waste. In developing 80 mpg sedans, engineers figured out new ways to reduce vehicle weight, new ways to clean up diesel exhaust emissions, and even reduced the cost of materials like aluminum, magnesium, and composites for automotive use. Ford used some of the styling cues from the Prodigy in the Fusion and the Five Hundred.

PNGV, like California’s old zero-emission program, seemed to have good intentions, but it might have been a bit too far ahead of its time. Today, hybrid cars are commonplace. Sure, they don’t use diesel engines and generally don’t use exotic materials, but they are affordable, and it’s entirely possible to hit or exceed 50 mpg with one.

But back in the 1990s, hybrids were a lot more novel, and for a while, Detroit and the U.S. government spent over a billion dollars a year to give America 80 mpg diesel-electric sedans. I wonder what would have happened had the project succeeded. Would diesel-electrics be commonplace today?

text:
WASHINGTON — The Department of the Interior today announced that the Marine Minerals Administration’s Outer Continental Shelf minerals lease sale offshore American Samoa, or Lease Sale PACM-1, generated $6 million in high bids during a live oral auction for two lease areas covering approximately 31,503,235 acres in federal waters offshore American Samoa.

Lease Sale PACM-1 marks the first-ever offshore critical minerals lease sale. Under Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum’s leadership, the Department is delivering on President Donald J. Trump’s Executive Order 14285, “Unleashing America’s Offshore Critical Minerals and Resources” to advance responsible development of America’s offshore critical mineral resources. The order established a national policy to responsibly develop offshore critical mineral resources, secure reliable domestic supplies and reduce U.S. dependence on supply chains controlled by foreign adversaries.

“This is the first time the United States has held an offshore critical minerals lease sale in the Pacific and a historic step for America’s energy and mineral security,” said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum. “Critical minerals are used in everything from electronics to defense systems. A dependable critical minerals supply chain is essential to American manufacturing and the technologies that power our economy and national defense. Today’s sale opens a path to learn more about the resources off the coast of American Samoa and assess whether they could contribute to a more reliable domestic supply."

“Critical minerals are essential to modern electronics, clean energy technologies and national defense,” said Acting MMA Director Mike Olsen. “A dependable supply chain helps American manufacturers withstand disruptions, and any future development would be subject to rigorous U.S. safety and environmental standards.”

The Final Leasing Notice was published in the Federal Register on October 20, 2026, outlining lease areas, fiscal terms and sale procedures. The two lease areas are located from 150 to 240 miles east of Pago Pago in water depths ranging from 4,630 to 20,100 feet (1,412 to 6,127 meters). The lease terms include a 20-year primary term and a structured royalty schedule starting at 2% for the first five years of production, transitioning to 5% for subsequent production years.

Results of the oral bid auction, which was livestreamed, will be posted at https://www.boem.gov/marine-minerals/potential-american-samoa-offshore-minerals-lease-sale with a final statistical summary to be released within 90 days.

Lease issuance does not authorize delineation, testing or mining activities. Once a lease is issued, the lessee has the right to conduct limited preliminary activities to better understand the lease area and an exclusive right to submit plans for testing, delineation and mining activities. Proposed delineation, testing or commercial mining would be subject to applicable environmental reviews and technical approvals administered by MMA and other partner agencies.

For more information about Lease Sale PACM-1, including lease terms, maps and bid results, visit https://www.boem.gov/marine-minerals/potential-american-samoa-offshore-minerals-lease-sale.

title: The Outlook for Data Center Tax Policy in the 120th Congress | Insights | Mayer Brown
description:
Summary of Data Center Tax Proposals Proposals that Impose New Excise Taxes on Data Centers Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR), who will become the Chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, the Committee with jurisdiction over tax policy, has introduced draft legislation that would impose an excise tax on data center gross revenue.
Senator Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) has published a policy white paper that proposes a 10% excise tax on data center gross revenue.
Senator Warner’s proposal would allow data centers to continue to utilize bonus depreciation if the data center met a sufficiently robust LEED certification.
Outlook for Data Center Tax Policies The new Democrat majorities in Congress believe that they have a mandate to target data centers including by making significant, negative changes in tax policy for data centers.
The President’s desire to ensure the extension of these policies could spur a broad tax policy negotiation that could become a vehicle for some of these data center tax proposals.
text:
Data centers are one of the most consequential political topics in the United States. Concerns over data center development and energy usage were major factors in the mid-term elections. There were at least 50 local ballot measures related to data centers in 13 states: Arkansas, California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio, and Wisconsin. In nearly every initiative, a majority of voters favored greater limits on data center development. In a CBS exit poll, 76 percent of voters said they would oppose the construction of a new data center in their community.

The 120th Congress will open with new and large Democratic majorities in both the House and Senate. Many of these newly elected Members campaigned against the expansion of data centers. However, the newly elected Democrat Members of Congress are not fully aligned on how to approach data center-related policies and stakeholders should be prepared to advocate on these tax policy proposals with these differences of opinion among Members in mind.

One of the campaign themes that emerged late in the election timeline were several proposals that would implement significant, negative changes to the tax environment for data centers. This Legal Update summarizes several key proposals, several of which have bipartisan support.

Summary of Data Center Tax Proposals

Proposals that Impose New Excise Taxes on Data Centers

Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR), who will become the Chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, the Committee with jurisdiction over tax policy, has introduced draft legislation that would impose an excise tax on data center gross revenue. The rate of the excise tax is “to be determined” and the legislation proposes a higher rate for data centers utilized by hyperscalers. Senator Bernie Moreno (R-OH) has introduced legislation that would impose an excise tax equal to the value of any tax or other financial incentive provided to a data center by a state or local government. Senator Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) has published a policy white paper that proposes a 10% excise tax on data center gross revenue.

Proposals that Prohibit Data Centers from Claiming Bonus Depreciation

The proposals noted above by Senators Wyden, Moreno, and Gallego would prohibit data centers from using bonus (100%) depreciation. In addition, legislation introduced by 30 House Democrats and legislation introduced by Senator Mark Warner (D-VA) would also prohibit data centers from using bonus depreciation. Generally, these proposals would classify property used in data centers as property that does not qualify for bonus depreciation. Senator Warner’s proposal would allow data centers to continue to utilize bonus depreciation if the data center met a sufficiently robust LEED certification.

Proposals that Prohibit Data Centers from Utilizing Opportunity Zones

The proposals noted above by Senators Wyden, Moreno, Gallego and the House Democrats would prohibit data centers from qualifying for Opportunity Zone benefits. Senator Josh Hawley (R-MO) has proposed a similar prohibition on data center use of Opportunity Zone benefits. These proposals would accomplish this prohibition in different ways but all have the same functional outcome.

Other Proposals

Senator Wyden’s draft legislation would also limit data center access to REITs and the R&D tax credit.

Outlook for Data Center Tax Policies

The new Democrat majorities in Congress believe that they have a mandate to target data centers including by making significant, negative changes in tax policy for data centers. At the same time it will take time for the new Congress to get organized. The first action item Members will take is to reintroduce the legislation described above in the new Congress. The number of proposals and Members supporting them is likely to increase. Congress will almost certainly hold hearings on data centers and tax policy. The proposals described above should be considered a starting point for legislation targeting the tax treatment of data centers, and other proposals and policies will certainly be proposed as well. For example, proposals to limit interest deductibility or other tax benefits could be proposed as well.

Because some of these proposals have bipartisan support, it is very possible that these proposals could gain momentum. While enactment as standalone legislation is unlikely, Congress could fold such legislation into other major must-pass legislative vehicles. For example, Congress needs to reauthorize the bipartisan infrastructure and highway spending program. To do so, Congress needs to find over $100 billion in additional revenue to pay for the infrastructure spending. Also, sometime in the second half of 2027, Congress will need to raise the statutory debt limit, and Congress may try to leverage that vote to include other policies, particularly those that raise new revenue and could be dedicated to the reduction in the national debt. Additionally, a number of important tax policies originally enacted in the One Big Beautiful Bill, such as “no tax on tips” and “no tax on overtime,” expire at the end of 2028. The President’s desire to ensure the extension of these policies could spur a broad tax policy negotiation that could become a vehicle for some of these data center tax proposals.

Further, House Democrats are considering establishing a select committee on artificial intelligence which could be modeled on the House Select Committee on China with subpoena power, its own staff, its own budget, and created by a full House vote. If a select committee on AI and data centers is modeled after the China Select Committee, it could become a launching pad for tax proposals. Many of the anti-China tax credit eligibility criteria that were included in the One Big Beautiful Bill traced their origins to the work of the China Select Committee. Representative Ted Lieu (D-CA) appears to be the frontrunner to chair this new select committee. Representative Lieu holds a degree in computer science and has said that the United States must continue building AI data centers to stay globally competitive with countries like China, warning that blocking construction locally would simply push the infrastructure abroad. However, he noted that development must be done thoughtfully with an emphasis on expanding renewable energy to handle rising power and water demands.

The Congressional calendar gives stakeholders some time to get organized and engaged on influencing the design and consideration of these proposals. However, that time is not infinite, and stakeholders should be engaging now to maximize their odds of success.

DETROIT, MI, UNITED STATES, November 19, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — Joyride Group—an integrated communications agency specializing in automotive, transportation, mobility technology and infrastructure—is celebrating two major honors recognizing the agency’s impact and leadership within the communications industry.

Joyride Group received Founded by Women’s Marketing & Communications Impact Award, while the agency’s Founder and CEO, Katelyn Davis, was named one of Crain’s Detroit Business’ 2026 Notable Leaders in Communications. Together, the accolades recognize the Detroit-based agency’s rapid growth, specialized industry expertise, and ability to deliver high-impact communications strategies for companies transforming mobility.

Founded in 2023, Joyride has quickly established itself as a strategic communications partner for startups, technology innovators, and industry leaders across the United States, Europe, and the Middle East. The agency was built on the belief that companies advancing the future of transportation need communications partners who understand the complexities of mobility innovation as deeply as they understand the power of storytelling.

“Building Joyride has always been about creating something different—an agency that combines deep industry expertise with creativity, strategy and meaningful impact,” said Davis. “To have both our team’s work and my leadership recognized in such a short period of time is incredibly rewarding. These honors reflect the talented people, innovative clients and incredible Detroit community that have helped make Joyride what it is today.”

Recognizing Impact in Mobility Communications

Joyride’s Marketing & Communications Impact Award from Founded by Women recognizes the agency’s ability to deliver measurable brand transformation through strategic communications. The award highlighted Joyride’s work supporting Electreon’s debut of the nation’s first public wireless electric vehicle charging roadway in Detroit, where a fully earned communications campaign generated 734 media placements, including coverage from NBC News, The Washington Post, the Associated Press, and TIME. The campaign exemplifies Joyride’s ability to translate complex mobility innovations into compelling stories that resonate with mainstream audiences and industry stakeholders, an approach the agency applies across electrification, autonomous mobility, public transit, and emerging transportation technologies.

Recognizing Leadership in Communications

Crain’s Detroit Business named Davis a 2026 Notable Leader in Communications, recognizing her leadership in building Joyride into a growing global mobility communications agency. With more than a decade of experience in automotive, transportation, and emerging technologies, Davis has helped innovative companies build influential brands while championing Detroit’s mobility ecosystem. Beyond her work at Joyride, she co-founded Detroit Moves, a community festival and forum focused on transportation innovation, and co-authored Women Driven Mobility: Rethinking the Way the World Moves, highlighting the role of women in shaping the future of transportation.

Together, the dual honors mark a significant milestone for Joyride as it continues to expand its reach and influence within the global transportation and mobility industry.

Through integrated capabilities spanning strategy and positioning, brand identity and creative, public relations and influence, content and marketing, and community and stakeholder engagement, Joyride helps companies build visibility, credibility, trust and momentum.

“Mobility is one of the most exciting and consequential industries in the world, but innovation alone doesn’t guarantee understanding, adoption or impact,” added Davis. “Strong communications play a critical role in connecting new ideas with the people and communities they are designed to serve. We’re proud to be building an agency that helps move not just businesses forward, but the entire mobility industry.”

As Joyride looks ahead, the agency remains focused on advancing the stories, technologies, and organizations driving the next era of transportation, while continuing to champion Detroit’s entrepreneurial and mobility communities.

Yet, the Trump administration has been particularly hostile to existing regulations on the environmental front, and has made significant policy reversals that are major setbacks to seriously addressing climate change.

text:
Climate change and the environment are not particularly “hot” issues with the electorate these days. It is way down the list of top concerns. Yet, the Trump administration has been particularly hostile to existing regulations on the environmental front, and has made significant policy reversals that are major setbacks to seriously addressing climate change.

That puts a big spotlight on a case in front of the Supreme Court right now—one where the county of Boulder, Colorado, is suing oil companies Suncor and ExxonMobil. The Supreme Court heard oral arguments in the case last month. Dozens of municipalities around the country are attempting to pursue similar actions.

As we have seen in other areas where government regulation has been viewed as too weak—such as social media and tobacco products—the courts have been used as an alternative way to create more socially responsive behavior on the part of industries. Judicially imposed major damage awards have a way of focusing industry attention and causing industries to tame practices where societal harms have clearly been demonstrated. In this case, Boulder is seeking financial compensation for everything from wildfires to reduced farm output.

The issue in the case before the Supreme Court is whether a local government can sue energy companies under state law and recover monetary damages for harms that have been inflicted in their local area that are clearly attributable to climate change. This has turned into a major political question, with members of Congress and a coalition of states along with the Trump Justice Department weighing in to support the oil companies, and a number of other members of Congress and other states submitting briefs in favor of Boulder's position.

title: Building the right way: Lessons from 20 years in The Dalles
description:
Growing alongside Wasco County Over these past two decades, Google has invested more than $7 billion in Oregon.
As Wasco County's largest taxpayer in recent years, we help fund services like North Wasco County School District and Mid-Columbia Fire and Rescue.
Building the right way Since we started building in The Dalles, we’ve worked to set the industry standard in developing data centers the right way.
Looking ahead To commemorate the anniversary, we're announcing two new programs in support of The Dalles: 20 for 20: Throughout 2027, we'll award $20,000 grants to 20 different organizations across Wasco County — one for each year we've called The Dalles home.
To the people of The Dalles and Wasco County: a sincere thank you for having us as neighbors for the past 20 years.
text:
In 2006, Google opened its first owned and operated data center in The Dalles, Ore. At the time, we didn't know whether it would grow beyond two small buildings with a few servers, let alone become the digital foundation for hospitals, banks, retailers, and other businesses in the region (and across the country).

Today, many of the innovations that shape how we approach data centers began there. As we mark this twenty-year milestone, we're reflecting on what we've built together with the local community, as well as what comes next.

Growing alongside Wasco County

Over these past two decades, Google has invested more than $7 billion in Oregon. As Wasco County's largest taxpayer in recent years, we help fund services like North Wasco County School District and Mid-Columbia Fire and Rescue. Throughout our time in Oregon, we’ve remained active members of the community: Googlers have volunteered more than 28,000 hours with nonprofits and schools around Oregon, while Google and its employees have given more than $35 million to organizations and nonprofits across the state.

In addition, for many families, our presence has meant building a career without leaving home. Over the last three years, our operations have supported an average of $862 million in state GDP each year. Our workforce in The Dalles spans a variety of backgrounds and includes a father-son duo, a pair of sisters, and many employees who have been with us for more than 15 years.

Building the right way

Since we started building in The Dalles, we’ve worked to set the industry standard in developing data centers the right way. This means paying our own way, working to keep energy affordable, creating local jobs, showing up as active participants in our communities, and protecting shared resources like power and water.

Since 2022, our data centers in The Dalles have achieved more than 80% carbon-free energy — which we’re continuing to support through our 100 MW wind agreement with Avangrid and our 50 MW “superhot” geothermal deal with Quaise. We’ve also partnered with the Oregon Hazards Lab on wildfire prevention and Columbia Gorge Food Bank (CGFB) on hunger relief programs.

We recirculate cooling water at least 10 times before it leaves our facilities, so every gallon goes further — leaving more for farms, families, and businesses that share the watershed. In the last three years, we’ve spent more than $38 million on local water infrastructure and replenishment projects. This includes $28 million in funding for water and sewer infrastructure and an aquifer storage and recovery (ASR) system — a project that functions like an underground water savings account for the city. Upon completion, we transferred the ASR system and associated groundwater rights to the City of The Dalles. And we developed our third campus at a former Superfund site, previously home to an old aluminum smelter, which now provides a source of jobs and tax revenue for the county.

Looking ahead

To commemorate the anniversary, we're announcing two new programs in support of The Dalles:

20 for 20: Throughout 2027, we'll award $20,000 grants to 20 different organizations across Wasco County — one for each year we've called The Dalles home. These grants are not only our “thank you” to the local community, but also our commitment to continue supporting local organizations that help the region thrive.

Energy Impact Fund: We're also launching a $10 million Energy Impact Fund to support energy affordability and efficiency for residents of the Columbia Gorge, with the first grant going to Energy Trust of Oregon.

Communities across the country are asking what it means to have a data center as a decades-long neighbor. The Dalles offers some insight: two small buildings became thousands of supported jobs, a lasting source of public revenue, and a local neighbor that is part of a thriving business community. To the people of The Dalles and Wasco County: a sincere thank you for having us as neighbors for the past 20 years. We're grateful for what we've built here, and we're committed to building responsibly together in the years ahead.

title: The Grid is a Decision: How Countries Can Connect More Renewable Energy
description:
To meet rising electricity demand and connect more renewable power, annual grid investment needs to reach around $600 billion by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
Connecting renewable power to agro-processing facilities, industrial zones and local businesses can create jobs and strengthen the financial viability of electricity networks.
In Viet Nam, a World Bank-supported project strengthened 500-kilovolt transmission infrastructure serving Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, improving reliability and renewable energy integration.
A renewable energy target without a grid plan is an ambition, not an implementation plan.
The decisions made now will determine not only how much renewable electricity countries can connect, but also where new industries can grow and essential services can improve.
text:
As countries meet for the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), Riad Meddeb, Head of Decarbonization and Sustainable Energy at the UN Development Programme (UNDP), and Denis Subbotnitskiy, Sustainable Development Officer at the UN Development Coordination Office, discuss why electricity grids are struggling to keep pace with renewable power. Delivering usable electricity depends on decisions made years before the need becomes urgent.

A solar or wind power project can be developed in one to five years. The new grid infrastructure needed to connect it to the electricity network, such as high-voltage power lines, can take five to fifteen years to plan, approve and build. Worldwide, more than 2,500 gigawatts of renewable power, storage and large electricity users, such as data centres, are queuing for a grid connection.

Long-term contracts to sell electricity from solar and wind farms help private investors secure a predictable income. Grids are different. They are often run by state-owned utilities and paid for through regulated electricity bills, so governments and regulators must first decide where new networks are needed, who will pay and how they will be managed.

To meet rising electricity demand and connect more renewable power, annual grid investment needs to reach around $600 billion by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).

The Global Grids Accelerator, launched by the UN Secretary-General in September, aims to help countries in Africa and South-East Asia turn grid priorities into projects ready for investment. These regions show what is at stake: Africa is home to most of the world’s people without electricity, while in South-East Asia, electricity demand has grown by around 6 per cent a year since 2015.

A reliable grid can help a factory run on more renewable power, a farmer refrigerate produce before it spoils, or a clinic keep essential equipment working. How countries build and manage their networks will shape future progress.

Using Existing Networks Better

How much power the grid can carry depends partly on operating rules. Electricity networks are planned to remain reliable at peak demand. The spare capacity available on existing lines for new projects therefore varies by location. Publishing this information, for example as online maps, helps developers find promising sites.

In South Africa’s 2022 competitive bidding round for renewable power, wind projects were passed over because grid capacity in the windy Cape provinces had already been allocated. In 2025, the regulator allowed more projects to connect on condition that they accept temporary limits on their output, with compensation — a change the grid operator estimates could make room for another 1,580 megawatts of wind power by 2028, where local lines can support it.

Technology can help too. The IEA estimates that technologies that let lines carry more power and route it along less busy paths could connect up to 330 gigawatts of new power generation, batteries and large users to existing networks without building new lines. Artificial intelligence (AI) can also improve forecasts of solar and wind output and help locate network breakdowns faster. This can shorten power cuts by 30 to 50 per cent. But utility rules often reward building new lines over making better use of existing ones.

Preparing Grids Before Demand Arrives

Kenya’s Lake Turkana wind farm shows what happens when power plants and power lines arrive out of sequence. The 310-megawatt farm was completed in January 2017, but its power line was only finished in September 2018. The wind farm’s contract guaranteed payment for electricity it could have supplied had the power line been ready. Consumers and public finances bore the cost of the mismatch.

Planning ahead is possible. India’s Central Electricity Authority prepared a transmission plan for 500 gigawatts of clean power capacity before most of that generation existed. Such planning must assess whether expected demand is realistic and allow for construction in stages, because lines built for users who never arrive still have to be paid for by utilities and consumers.

This means looking not only at where electricity will be generated, but also at where it can support economic activity. Connecting renewable power to agro-processing facilities, industrial zones and local businesses can create jobs and strengthen the financial viability of electricity networks. In Viet Nam, a World Bank-supported project strengthened 500-kilovolt transmission infrastructure serving Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, improving reliability and renewable energy integration. By the end of 2024, the country had established 447 industrial zones for factories, 143 still under construction, an indication of the industrial demand that grids will need to serve.

Turning these plans into infrastructure, however, depends on utilities’ financial health. A World Bank review found that only around 40 per cent of more than 180 utilities could cover operating costs and debt payments. Barriers included high costs, prices set below cost, power lost on the network, unpaid bills and poor planning.

Competitive bidding processes for power lines in Brazil and India show that grids can attract private capital. But even a priority power line requires feasibility studies, environmental and social assessments, a credible way to recover its costs and agreement on who bears which risks.

The COP31 Presidency has proposed raising electricity’s share of the energy that consumers use to 35 per cent by 2035. Countries need to plan for the grid as they turn national climate commitments into investment plans. Climate Promise: Forward, the UN system’s common framework for supporting implementation of those commitments, can help countries make that link.

Plans need to show where new power will be produced and used, identify what existing networks can accommodate and establish which investments need preparation now. A renewable energy target without a grid plan is an ambition, not an implementation plan.

Coordinating Delivery Through the UN System

Energy, industry, finance and planning ministries need to coordinate with regulators, land authorities, the private sector and local communities.

The Global Grids Accelerator, convened by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), the UN Office for Project Services (UNOPS) and Sustainable Energy for All, will bring together governments, development partners and investors to help countries strengthen grid planning and regional interconnections, modernise networks and mobilise finance for implementation. It builds on initiatives such as Mission 300 and the Programme for Infrastructure Development in Africa (PIDA), and the ASEAN Power Grid and the UN’s regional road map for Asia and the Pacific. Its co-conveners are already supporting countries on the ground.

In Mauritius, a Green Climate Fund project, supported by UNDP, worked with the national utility to install 18 megawatts of battery storage and new grid controls, allowing the grid to safely accommodate more than 200 megawatts of solar and wind power.

In Indonesia, the Southeast Asia Energy Transition Partnership, managed by UNOPS, helped prepare a modernised control centre for the Java–Bali grid system, which serves some 160 million people.

A power line can be a ten-year answer to a question a country has to ask today. The decisions made now will determine not only how much renewable electricity countries can connect, but also where new industries can grow and essential services can improve. The grid is a decision about where and how development will happen.

title: Newcleo's planned Savannah River MOX fuel fabrication plant gets Curio support
description:
The agreement, announced on November 16, would see Curio use its NuCycle nuclear fuel recycling technology to recover plutonium, uranium, and other materials from used fuel.
The Nuclear REFUEL Act passed in the House of Representatives on November 9 and, as of this writing, has been read twice in the Senate.
The MFFF: While several nations, including France, Belgium, and Switzerland, have used MOX fuel in their reactors for decades, the United States has not been producing MOX fuel during this time.
In 2005, the NRC approved a construction license for the Mixed Oxide Fuel Fabrication Facility (MFFF) at SRS.
In 2022, the DOE contracted Aecon-Wachs to assist in converting the MFFF facility into a plutonium processing plant.
text:
The agreement, announced on November 16, would see Curio use its NuCycle nuclear fuel recycling technology to recover plutonium, uranium, and other materials from used fuel. Newcleo would then use the materials to fabricate MOX fuel at its proposed facility. The two companies intend to collaborate on additional R&D activities to develop nuclear recycling technology.

Although Newcleo has not yet submitted a licensing application for the facility to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, it submitted a preapplication regulatory engagement plan on August 3, noting that it plans to apply for a license under 10 CFR Part 70. The move came approximately five weeks after the company submitted a regulatory engagement plan to the NRC for another project: its LFR-AS-200 lead-cooled fast reactor.

According to Newcleo, the MOX fuel it fabricates at its Savannah River facility would be compatible with its LFR-AS-200 reactors as well as other advanced reactors and certain existing light water reactor designs. Newcleo also aims to construct a reactor at SRS.

Additionally, Curio states that its NuCycle technology, which would produce the feedstock for the facility, aligns with the requirements of the Nuclear REFUEL (Recycling Efficient Fuels Utilizing Expedited Licensing) Act, which is currently under deliberation in Congress.

The Nuclear REFUEL Act: Originally introduced in the House of Representatives in December 2024 and reintroduced as part of the 119th Congress in June 2025, the Nuclear REFUEL Act proposes a redefinition of nuclear fuel “production facilities” under 1954’s Atomic Energy Act.

Under the new legislation, instead of being licensed as production facilities, reprocessing facilities producing uranium-transuranic mixed fuel would qualify for licensing under 10 CFR Part 70, the same regulatory framework that applies to other fuel facilities. Proponents of the Nuclear REFUEL Act say that this would streamline requirements for reprocessing and recycling facilities, including, presumably, a facility that uses Curio’s NuCycle technology.

The Nuclear REFUEL Act passed in the House of Representatives on November 9 and, as of this writing, has been read twice in the Senate. Should it become law, it would facilitate production of a type of nuclear fuel that the United States has explored but not yet produced commercially.

The MFFF: While several nations, including France, Belgium, and Switzerland, have used MOX fuel in their reactors for decades, the United States has not been producing MOX fuel during this time.

However, Newcleo’s proposed South Carolina facility is not the first MOX fabrication facility that has been attempted in the United States—or at Savannah River—in the 21st century. In 2005, the NRC approved a construction license for the Mixed Oxide Fuel Fabrication Facility (MFFF) at SRS.

The MFFF, which was to have been administered by the DOE’s National Nuclear Security Administration, was designed as a result of a bilateral agreement between the United States and Russia—the Plutonium Management and Disposition Agreement, enacted in 2000—to reduce both countries’ stocks of weapons-grade plutonium. The MFFF was to do so by processing plutonium into MOX fuel, which would render it less susceptible to proliferation efforts. The agreement between the two nations was bolstered at the April 2010 Nuclear Security Summit, at which the United States and Russia committed to disposing of 34 metric tons each of surplus weapons-grade plutonium.

However, construction delays and increasing costs led the Obama administration to issue a request to terminate work on the project for fiscal year 2017; the first Trump administration followed in fiscal year 2018 with a directive to pursue an option known as “dilute and dispose” for disposing of the surplus plutonium. On October 12, 2018, the DOE and NNSA sent the facility contractor a Notice of Termination to cease construction work on the MFFF, and on February 8, 2019, the NRC terminated the facility’s construction authorization.

Yet even that was not the end of the story for the MFFF. In 2022, the DOE contracted Aecon-Wachs to assist in converting the MFFF facility into a plutonium processing plant. The Savannah River Plutonium Processing Facility will produce plutonium pits to support the NNSA’s mission of nuclear deterrence; full authorization for construction of the facility was issued on October 15 of this year.

title: Rep. Roy Introduces Bill to Defeat Costly E15 Mandate Expansion
description:
Washington, D.C. — Today, Congressman Chip Roy (R-TX) introduced legislation to wind down the costly Renewable Fuels Standard (RFS), bolster domestic refining, give consumers more choice, and help Americans save more at the pump.

By eliminating costly government mandates and removing barriers to E15 and higher ethanol blends, we’re empowering the free market, expanding consumer choice, and strengthening America’s domestic energy sector,” said Rep. Roy.

title: Vision 2030: Decarbonizing and modernizing industry - Fresh Energy
description:
For decades, Fresh Energy has helped shape Minnesota’s clean energy landscape, driving progress across multiple critical sectors, including securing Minnesota’s landmark 100% clean electricity law.
The good news is that Minnesota’s industrial sector is adept at facing and adapting to transformational industrial challenges.
When it comes to decarbonizing industry, Minnesota has a huge advantage Minnesota enters this global industrial transition with significant strengths that put us steps beyond the competition.
Rather than viewing decarbonization as a threat to industry, Fresh Energy sees it as an opportunity to build the next generation of industrial competitiveness.
Fresh Energy’s approach to decarbonizing industry in Minnesota Industrial transformation requires more than technological innovation alone.
text:
For decades, Fresh Energy has helped shape Minnesota’s clean energy landscape, driving progress across multiple critical sectors, including securing Minnesota’s landmark 100% clean electricity law. Generating steady wins throughout the Electricity, Buildings, and Transportation sectors has built necessary momentum for and dedication to transforming the systems that power our economy. Today, as Minnesota continues its transition toward a carbon-neutral future, another sector that stands out as both a challenge and opportunity is Industry.

For more than a century, Minnesota’s economy has been driven by industrial activities. From mining and manufacturing to food processing, forest products, medical technology, and advanced materials, industrial facilities provide family-supporting jobs, anchor regional economies, and produce the goods that communities rely on every day. They are also among the most energy-intensive sectors in the state and a significant source of greenhouse gas emissions.

That’s why Vision 2030: Fresh Energy’s Strategic Framework elevated industrial decarbonization as a core area of focus. Achieving Minnesota’s climate goals while strengthening economic competitiveness requires reducing emissions from the industrial processes that form the foundation of our economy.

The Challenge: Decarbonizing industrial processes and driving long-term industrial resilience

In Minnesota, the industrial sector is the fourth-largest (and growing) source of greenhouse gas emissions in the state, and it accounts for about 18% of the state’s net emissions. Unfortunately, Industrial emissions are among the most difficult to reduce because industrial facilities rely on highly specialized processes that often require significant amounts of heat, continuous operations, and custom equipment. Solutions that work for one facility may not work for another, making industrial decarbonization more complex than other sectors.

In many cases, emissions from the industrial sector are tied to heat used in the manufacturing process (known as process heating) that has historically relied on fossil fuel combustion. Boilers, furnaces, kilns, dryers, steam systems, and similar process heating equipment are frequently central to industrial operations and are often inefficient, emissions-heavy systems compared to modern energy-efficient options like industrial heat pumps. However, adopting new, cleaner technology solutions can come with a list of challenges for an operator, so that change is often slow to come.

Transitioning industrial systems can be challenging for practical reasons. Companies have invested heavily in facilities and processes that are already optimized for production. Changes can require retraining workers, modifying operations, and accepting risks to productivity. New technologies can also require significant upfront investment and, in some cases, higher operating costs. As a result, industrial change often happens gradually.

While transitioning industrial systems involves cost and operational challenges, inaction carries risks of its own. Volatile energy prices, changing customer expectations, evolving supply chains, and increasing demand for lower-carbon products are reshaping global markets. Companies that adapt will be better positioned to compete in the decades ahead.

Industrial resilience and decarbonization are critical for Minnesota’s future

Minnesota’s industrial sector contributes billions of dollars annually to the state’s economy and supports hundreds of thousands of jobs across the state, with manufacturing serving as one of the state’s largest sources of high-wage employment. The resilience and future competitiveness of these industries will increasingly depend on their ability to access clean energy, improve efficiency, reduce emissions, and meet growing market demand for lower-carbon products.

Climate change and global supply chain constraints are creating new risks for businesses, infrastructure, and communities. Extreme weather, trade volatility, rising operating costs, and changing customer expectations are reshaping markets across the globe and in Minnesota — but what states and countries do now, at this time of change, will shape the future.

The good news is that Minnesota’s industrial sector is adept at facing and adapting to transformational industrial challenges. For example, in the mid-20th century when high grade iron ore reserves began to decline, industry leaders, researchers, and policymakers worked together to pioneer the completely new taconite “pelletization” process. That innovation transformed the global iron ore industry, preserved jobs on the Iron Range, and secured Minnesota’s place as a critical supplier of iron ore for generations and into the present.

Today, Minnesota faces another defining industrial opportunity. The question is not whether industry will evolve. The question is whether Minnesota will help lead that transformation.

When it comes to decarbonizing industry, Minnesota has a huge advantage

Minnesota enters this global industrial transition with significant strengths that put us steps beyond the competition. We have:

A highly skilled industrial, engineering, and manufacturing workforce

World-class research institutions advancing next-generation technologies

Globally significant natural resources and robust transportation infrastructure

Growing access to clean, reliable electricity

Established industrial supply chains and business networks

A strong foundation of supportive policies and programs

These key strengths position Minnesota to become a national leader in clean industrial development. Rather than viewing decarbonization as a threat to industry, Fresh Energy sees it as an opportunity to build the next generation of industrial competitiveness. The communities that successfully attract emerging industrial investment will capture jobs, supply chains, innovation, and long-term economic growth.

Fresh Energy’s approach to decarbonizing industry in Minnesota

Industrial transformation requires more than technological innovation alone. Success depends on aligning policy, infrastructure, markets, research, utility engagement, and investment strategies to support emerging technologies and help industrial facilities manage risk. Through supporting and advancing innovative policies and programs, Fresh Energy is working to create the conditions that enable cleaner industrial technologies and business models to succeed in Minnesota:

Supporting early movers

Fresh Energy works to identify emerging opportunities, connect stakeholders, and support projects that demonstrate new technologies in real-world settings. Early adopters may be large corporations pursuing sustainability goals or smaller businesses willing to test innovative approaches. Successful projects help reduce uncertainty, build confidence, and accelerate broader market adoption.

Building public-private partnerships

Industrial decarbonization requires collaboration. Utilities, manufacturers, policymakers, researchers, labor organizations, economic development leaders, and communities all play important roles in shaping the future industrial economy. Strong public-private partnerships can help de-risk investments, accelerate deployment, and position Minnesota to compete for major industrial projects.

Advancing market transformation

Technology alone does not transform markets. Policy, infrastructure planning, financing tools, and regulatory frameworks all influence whether innovative technologies can scale successfully. Fresh Energy works to advance policies that support investment, reward innovation, reduce barriers to deployment, and strengthen Minnesota’s competitive position in emerging industrial sectors.

Policy solutions that can move the needle

Fresh Energy believes policy is the most effective way to drive lasting climate and clean energy progress because it transforms entire systems. Policies create the rules, incentives, and market conditions that accelerate clean energy adoption across entire sectors. These are a few of the policy solutions the Industry team is focusing on:

Industrial electrification

Many industrial processes can be powered by electricity rather than fossil fuels. As Minnesota’s electric grid continues to become cleaner, industrial electrification represents one of the most important pathways for long-term emissions reductions.

Supporting electrification requires thoughtful planning, economic and tax incentives, and policies that encourage investment while maintaining reliability and affordability. As industrial electrification grows, Minnesota will also need continued investment in generation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure to ensure reliable and affordable power for future industrial growth.

Utility rate design

Electricity costs play a significant role in industrial investment decisions. Well-designed rate structures can help industrial facilities deploy cleaner technologies, lower operating costs, and take advantage of Minnesota’s growing clean energy resources.

Demonstration projects

Many promising industrial technologies remain in the early stages of commercialization. Targeted grants, financing tools, and demonstration programs can help validate performance, reduce uncertainty, and accelerate market adoption.

Strategic industrial development

Minnesota has an opportunity to compete for major industrial investments that align economic development and climate goals. Targeted incentives and coordinated planning can help attract projects that create jobs, strengthen supply chains, and support long-term industrial growth. In some cases, strategic industrial growth and electrification can improve utilization of the electric grid, helping spread infrastructure costs across more customers and supporting long-term affordability.

Looking ahead

Industrial decarbonization is a long-term transition driven by practical investments, evolving technologies, and strategic decisions about how Minnesota’s industries will compete in a changing economy.

In many cases, the most cost-effective emissions reductions begin with industrial efficiency. Improving controls, recovering waste heat, optimizing processes, upgrading equipment, and reducing energy consumption can lower costs while reducing emissions. As the old saying goes, the cheapest energy is the energy you never have to use.

For facilities that rely on industrial heat, electrification presents another significant opportunity. Technologies such as industrial heat pumps can provide low- and medium-temperature heat far more efficiently than conventional fossil fuel systems, often delivering multiple units of useful heat for every unit of electricity consumed. Equally important is ensuring that when aging equipment reaches the end of its useful life, companies evaluate modern alternatives rather than replacing old gas-fired systems with new ones that could lock facilities into decades of continued fossil fuel dependence.

At the same time, Minnesota is uniquely positioned to capitalize on emerging opportunities in cleaner manufacturing. Perhaps no sector better illustrates this potential than iron and steel production. Minnesota’s iron resources, mining expertise, manufacturing heritage, and growing clean energy economy create opportunities to attract new investment and support the next generation of lower-carbon manufacturing. Communities that successfully attract these investments will secure jobs, infrastructure, and long-term economic growth.

Beyond steel, innovation is accelerating across the industrial sector. Advanced electrification, thermal energy storage, hydrogen production, next-generation metallurgical processes, and other technologies are creating new opportunities to rethink how materials are produced and manufactured. Fresh Energy is working to help Minnesota prepare for and capitalize on these opportunities as they emerge.

Fresh Energy’s policy work on the industrial sector happens in the spaces where long-term energy and industrial decisions are made, including at the Minnesota Legislature, the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission, and state agencies. The work comes to life through utility planning proceedings, Integrated Resource Plans, utility rate cases, Future of Gas proceedings, and through regional partnerships and industry collaborations. Decisions made in these venues increasingly shape the affordability, availability, and reliability of the energy resources industrial facilities will need in the decades ahead.

Industrial decarbonization is about more than reducing emissions. Done well, it can strengthen Minnesota’s manufacturing base, attract investment, create high-quality jobs, improve energy productivity, and position the state as a leader in the next generation of industrial innovation.

Minnesota has a long history of adapting to economic and technological change. With the right policies, investments, and partnerships, it can continue that tradition while building a cleaner, more competitive industrial economy.

text:
Your browser doesn't support audio playback.

West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey filed lawsuits Wednesday against solar energy credit restrictions in New Jersey and Washington, D.C.

Currently, West Virginia’s solar energy producers are barred from selling solar energy credits in those markets and others. The filings follow a lawsuit filed by McCuskey in Pennsylvania in September, challenging similar restrictions.

All three states and D.C. are part of PJM Interconnection, which operates the grid across 13 states in total. Electricity generated in any of these states can serve customers in another.

Renewable energy laws in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and D.C. mandate electric suppliers obtain a certain percentage of their energy each year from renewable energy sources or buy renewable credits. But New Jersey and D.C., along with Pennsylvania, treat solar energy credits differently, requiring them to be purchased from producers located within their respective borders.

“The geographic restrictions serve no legitimate environmental or governmental purpose and as a result, the compliance costs in those states have skyrocketed while West Virginia solar energy producers are left facing unconstitutional trade barriers,” he said. “We should all be working toward a more efficient and reliable system, but rules like these stand in the way of progress, and ultimately all households and businesses pay the price.”

McCuskey argues the explicit geographic restrictions are violations of the Commerce Clause of the U.S. Constitution, discriminating against out-of-state industry.

The Commerce Clause is just one line of the U.S. Constitution, which gives Congress the power “to regulate commerce with foreign nations, among states, and with the Indian tribes.” According to Cornell Law School, Congress has often used the Commerce Clause to justify exercising legislative power over the activities of states and their citizens, leading to significant and ongoing controversy regarding the balance of power between the federal government and the states.

The lawsuits are asking the courts to strike down the geographic restrictions and open the markets to bring down costs for consumers on all sides.

title: Altilium: Building Britain's Sovereign Critical Minerals Supply Chain - UK Investor Magazine

text:
Backed by over £27 million in government funding and strategic investment from global industry leaders SQM and Marubeni, UK clean technology company Altilium is scaling its patented battery recycling technology to establish a sovereign supply chain for critical minerals essential to the UK’s national and economic security.

From EVs and renewable energy to advanced manufacturing and defence, the UK’s industrial future depends on securing reliable supplies of critical minerals, such as lithium, nickel and cobalt. The Government’s Critical Minerals Strategy sets ambitious targets to meet at least 10% of annul UK demand for critical minerals through domestic production and a further 20% through recycling by 2035.

Currently Britain remains reliant on overseas suppliers for these strategically important resources, with China dominating supply. As a recent report from the UK Parliament’s Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee warns, this dependence leaves key industries vulnerable to geopolitical tensions and supply chain disruption, prompting calls for greater investment in domestic processing and recycling capacity.

Transforming battery waste into a strategic resource

As the Critical Minerals report also notes, the UK possess significant quantities of minerals already in circulation. Every EV on Britain’s roads contains valuable materials, including lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite, which can be recovered and reused once they reach the end of their useful lives. With more than two million EVs now on UK roads, that represents a growing strategic resource.

Meanwhile, major gigafactory developments, including Agratas in Somerset and AESC in Sunderland, are creating new demand for battery materials and generating manufacturing scrap that will also need recycling.

By 2030, the Advanced Propulsion Centre estimates that 28,000 tonnes of battery waste could be recycled from manufacturing scrap and end-of-life batteries in the UK.

Plymouth-based Altilium is at the forefront of efforts to unlock the value of this growing domestic resource, developing the technology and industrial infrastructure needed to recover and refine critical minerals from battery waste here in the UK, transforming materials that might otherwise be exported for processing overseas into valuable resources for British industry.

The company, which was recently nominated for the prestigious Earthshot Prize, has made significant progress towards commercialisation during 2026, securing £18.5 million through the UK Government’s DRIVE35 programme to support construction of its ACT3 facility in Plymouth, the UK’s first commercial-scale recycling and refining facility.

The investment represents a significant step towards establishing a sovereign UK supply chain for critical battery materials. Building on the success of Altilium’s existing pilot operations, ACT3 will have the capacity to process material equivalent to approximately 24,000 electric vehicle batteries annually, recovering lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite for reuse in new batteries.

By developing domestic refining capacity alongside Britain’s emerging battery manufacturing industry, Altilium aims to retain more of the economic value of these materials in the UK, reduce reliance on imported supplies and create a more resilient, circular supply chain for British industry.

First-move advantage in a strategic growth market

Unlike companies focused primarily on dismantling and shredding batteries, Altilium is developing an integrated platform capable of recovering critical minerals and converting them into high-value materials for new battery production.

The company’s patented EcoCathode™ technology can recover over 95% of the cathode metals, including lithium, from end-of-life batteries, enabling the production of cathode active materials (CAM) that can be reused to manufacture new lithium-ion batteries, with up to 74% lower carbon emissions than mined materials.

This capability offers a potentially significant competitive advantage as cell manufacturers and OEMs seek secure, low-carbon sources of materials that meet increasingly demanding sustainability and recycled-content requirements.

Altilium has already demonstrated its technology through collaborative R&D projects with OEMs, including Nissan and JLR. These trials have shown that Altilium’s materials can deliver performance comparable to commercially available virgin materials, demonstrating that recycled battery materials can meet the demanding technical requirements of automotive manufacturers.

Scaling from innovation to industrial production

Beyond ACT3, Altilium continues to develop plans for its ACT4 industrial-scale facility, designed to be one of Europe’s largest battery materials recycling and refining operations, with capacity to recycle 150,000 batteries a year.

At full scale, ACT4 will have capacity to produce approximately 30,000 tonnes of CAM annually, establishing a significant domestic source of materials for Britain’s emerging battery manufacturing industry.

This phased approach, progressing from pilot validation to commercial demonstration and ultimately industrial-scale production, is designed to reduce technology risk while establishing the infrastructure and customer relationships needed for long-term growth.

Strategic investment supports the next phase

Alongside government support, Altilium has attracted backing from major international industry players, including SQM, one of the world’s leading lithium producers, and Japanese trading group Marubeni Corporation.

Both investors reaffirmed their commitment through follow-on investment in October 2026, providing further support for the company’s scale-up strategy.

In November, Altilium also launched a secondary share sale through Crowdcube, Europe’s leading private market investment platform, providing an opportunity for investors to acquire existing shares as the company enters its next stage of development.

The offering will enable eligible employees to realise some of the value they have helped create, while providing investors with an opportunity to acquire existing shares in a UK clean technology company at the forefront of securing critical materials essential for the UK’s national and economic security.

Christian Marston, Altilium COO, commented: “Our people have been instrumental in taking Altilium from an ambitious technology start-up to a business developing the infrastructure needed to build a new strategic industry for the UK. As we move towards commercial-scale operations, we want our employees to share in the success of the business and demonstrate that building innovative clean technology companies in the UK can create real financial value for the people behind them.”
