name: Indiana American Energy
title: Oak Ridge's AI Factory Moment: Lux, Nuclear Power, and the Next Data Center Frontier
description:
Rebuilding the Nuclear Fuel Supply Chain The expansion of advanced nuclear generation depends on another capability now receiving substantial investment around Oak Ridge: the domestic production of nuclear fuel.
DOE Opens the Door to Commercial AI Data Centers at Oak Ridge Alongside the nuclear investment, DOE is pursuing a separate initiative that could bring privately operated AI data centers directly onto federal property at Oak Ridge.
Electricians, mechanical contractors, controls specialists, commissioning professionals, and experienced project managers are already important constraints on large data center construction schedules.
Even the DOE initiative to make federal property available for private AI data center development must contend with those requirements.
For the data center industry, that convergence may prove to be Oak Ridge's most important contribution to the next frontier of digital infrastructure.
text:
For much of its history, Oak Ridge has been associated with the Manhattan Project and the subsequent development of America's nuclear research and production capabilities. Established during World War II, the community became home to major facilities for uranium enrichment, nuclear materials processing, scientific research, and ultimately high-performance computing.

Today, that legacy is being repurposed for a new generation of industrial development. The former K-25 uranium enrichment complex, once a critical part of the nation's atomic weapons program, has been transformed into the East Tennessee Technology Park (ETTP), where extensive environmental cleanup and redevelopment have made former federal property available for commercial use.

At an October 27 gathering in Oak Ridge, federal officials and nuclear industry representatives highlighted more than $15 billion in announced nuclear-related projects across the region, an investment wave subsequently documented in a November 17 DOE report on Oak Ridge's emerging energy hub. The investment figure largely represents planned private-sector development rather than completed capital spending. Regional officials also anticipate demand for thousands of construction workers over the next five years, with additional permanent manufacturing and operating positions potentially following as projects advance.

In March, DOE completed its largest Oak Ridge land transfer to date, conveying more than 700 acres for economic reuse. The transfer included a 624-acre parcel designated for Orano USA's planned uranium enrichment complex and a 77-acre parcel associated with Oklo's proposed nuclear fuel recycling development. Overall, more than 2,500 acres have been transferred from federal ownership for redevelopment, following decades of cleanup and the demolition of hundreds of former industrial structures.

For nuclear developers, the appeal is straightforward: large industrial sites, existing utility and transportation infrastructure, proximity to federal laboratories, and an established community of nuclear engineers, technicians, researchers, and specialized manufacturers.

For data center developers, the implications are somewhat different but no less relevant. Large AI campuses increasingly require industrial-scale sites with access to electrical infrastructure, water and cooling resources, and a workforce capable of constructing and maintaining highly specialized facilities. Brownfield redevelopment offers one potential alternative to entirely new industrial development, although it does not eliminate interconnection, environmental, or permitting requirements.

Oak Ridge's advantage is not simply available land. It is the concentration of technical capabilities and energy-related industries taking shape around that land.

TVA's Clinch River Project Marks a New Nuclear Milestone

One of the most consequential developments is occurring at TVA's Clinch River Nuclear Site near Oak Ridge.

On September 29, 2026, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) announced that it had approved a construction permit for Clinch River Unit 1, a planned 300-megawatt GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 small modular reactor (SMR). As Reuters reported at the time, the decision represented a major regulatory milestone for the commercialization of smaller nuclear generating units. The permit was formally issued on September 28.

The NRC completed its review in approximately 14 months, ahead of its original schedule. The approval is especially important because it establishes a licensing precedent for a reactor design that utilities and developers hope can eventually be deployed in multiple locations using standardized engineering and modular construction techniques.

The BWRX-300 is based on established boiling-water reactor technology but incorporates a smaller generating unit and greater reliance on modular construction than conventional large nuclear plants. Its nominal 300-MW output could offer utilities a means of adding substantial firm generation capacity without undertaking the construction of a traditional gigawatt-scale reactor.

That prospect has obvious significance for utilities serving fast-growing data center markets. AI infrastructure projects are creating demand for continuous, reliable power at scales that can exceed the capacity available from existing local electrical systems.

However, a construction permit is not equivalent to an operating reactor. TVA must still make a final investment decision, complete construction, and secure a separate operating license before Clinch River can generate commercial electricity. In its November 2026 financial filing, TVA confirmed that it had not yet decided whether to proceed with construction.

The project has also become part of a much larger international nuclear investment discussion. In March, the United States and Japan announced a proposed strategic investment initiative involving up to $40 billion in GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 projects in Tennessee and Alabama. The prospective development would encompass approximately 3 GW of generation, equivalent to ten 300-MW reactor units.

Federal officials have discussed the potential for additional reactor development in Tennessee and at TVA's Bellefonte site in Alabama. Those plans remain prospective and should not be confused with fully financed or approved construction projects. The $40 billion initiative also falls outside the approximately $15 billion in regional nuclear projects highlighted at the October Oak Ridge event.

Nevertheless, the proposal illustrates the scale of interest in creating a repeatable SMR deployment model that could eventually support expanding industrial and computing loads across the TVA service territory.

Kairos Power Connects Advanced Nuclear Development to Google's AI Infrastructure

While Clinch River represents an evolutionary approach to commercial nuclear generation, another Oak Ridge development is pursuing a more unconventional reactor technology with a direct connection to hyperscale data center energy procurement.

In April 2026, Kairos Power broke ground on its Hermes 2 Demonstration Plant at the former K-33 uranium enrichment site. The project is the company's first power-producing reactor deployment and a central component of its agreement with Google to develop advanced nuclear generating capacity.

Hermes 2 is designed to provide up to 50 MW of electricity to the TVA grid, helping support Google's data center operations in Tennessee and Alabama. Under the arrangement, TVA will purchase the electricity generated by the plant, with Google supporting the commercial development of the advanced nuclear technology.

The project is scheduled to begin operations in 2030, although that timeline remains subject to successful construction, licensing, testing, and commissioning.

As Data Center Frontier previously examined in David Chernicoff and Matt Vincent's Google Backs Advanced Nuclear at TVA's Clinch River as ORNL Pushes Quantum Frontiers, the arrangement reflects a growing convergence between hyperscale computing requirements and the development of advanced nuclear technologies.

Kairos is developing a fluoride salt-cooled, high-temperature reactor that uses TRISO fuel particles embedded in fuel pebbles. Rather than employing the pressurized water systems common to most existing commercial nuclear plants, the technology uses molten fluoride salt as a coolant.

Hermes 2 follows Hermes 1, a low-power demonstration reactor also under construction at Oak Ridge. Together, the projects are intended to establish the technical and operating foundation for larger commercial deployments.

Kairos is also investigating construction approaches that could influence the economics of future nuclear development, including factory-built components, modular assembly, precast concrete structures, and seismic isolation systems. Components are being manufactured at the company's Albuquerque, New Mexico, campus before shipment to Tennessee.

The significance for Google and the broader data center industry lies in the commercial structure as much as the reactor technology. Hyperscalers are increasingly becoming participants in the development of new generating resources, helping support projects whose capital costs and development risks historically would have been carried primarily by utilities and energy companies.

At the same time, the distinction between contracted nuclear energy and physically dedicated generation remains important. Hermes 2 is not a standalone plant supplying a single isolated Google data center. Its electricity will enter the TVA system, supporting a broader regional grid that serves Google's facilities alongside other customers.

Rebuilding the Nuclear Fuel Supply Chain

The expansion of advanced nuclear generation depends on another capability now receiving substantial investment around Oak Ridge: the domestic production of nuclear fuel.

Many proposed small modular reactors and microreactors require high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU), enriched to higher concentrations than the fuel typically used in conventional U.S. commercial nuclear reactors. Domestic production capacity remains limited, creating potential bottlenecks for reactor developers seeking to move from demonstration projects into commercial deployment.

The challenge extends beyond HALEU. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration's 2025 Uranium Marketing Annual Report, U.S.-origin enrichment services accounted for only 23% of separative work units purchased by operators of American civilian nuclear reactors in 2025. Foreign enrichment facilities provided the remaining 77%, underscoring the country's continued reliance on overseas capabilities.

Much of Oak Ridge's latest industrial development is directed toward addressing that imbalance.

Orano, LIS Technologies, Centrus, and BWXT

Orano USA is developing Project IKE, a planned $5 billion uranium enrichment complex on the 624-acre parcel transferred by DOE. The proposed 750,000-square-foot development is intended to become one of North America's largest enrichment operations.

DOE announced a $900 million award to Orano Federal Services earlier in 2026 to expand domestic low-enriched uranium production capacity. The NRC accepted the Project IKE license application for detailed technical review in May.

A more recent development illustrates the complexities of translating these investments into operating infrastructure. In November, the NRC's projected completion of the technical review shifted from April to June 2027 after the regulator granted additional time for Orano to respond to requests for information. As Nuclear Newswire reported November 13, the adjustment represents approximately two months of additional licensing review. Orano has indicated that the revised review schedule is not expected to delay its target for initial enrichment operations in 2031, although that remains dependent on licensing and execution.

Other manufacturers are advancing projects of their own.

In January, LIS Technologies announced approximately $1.38 billion in planned investment for a laser uranium enrichment facility at the former K-25 site, a project expected to create about 203 jobs. The company is pursuing a commercial application of laser isotope separation technology.

Centrus Energy announced plans to invest more than $560 million in an expansion of its Oak Ridge centrifuge manufacturing operations, with nearly 430 additional jobs anticipated. On October 29, Centrus reached a tangible manufacturing milestone when it began shipping newly manufactured centrifuges from Oak Ridge to Ohio for its uranium enrichment expansion.

BWX Technologies (BWXT) added another element in January with the opening of its Centrifuge Manufacturing Development Facility, supporting a National Nuclear Security Administration program to rebuild domestic enrichment capabilities for national security purposes. The company is participating in a federal program valued at approximately $1.5 billion.

These projects illustrate how Oak Ridge is becoming a manufacturing center for technologies essential to the long-term expansion of nuclear generation, even when the eventual power plants will be located elsewhere.

TRISO-X, Standard Nuclear, and the Advanced Fuel Market

Advanced reactor development also depends on the ability to manufacture specialized fuels at commercial scale.

TRISO-X, an X-energy subsidiary, completed vertical construction of its 214,000-square-foot TX-1 fuel fabrication plant in September and moved into interior construction and equipment installation. Once operational, the facility is expected to manufacture approximately 700,000 TRISO fuel pebbles annually, equivalent to five metric tons of uranium and enough fuel to support as many as eleven Xe-100 reactors.

In February, the NRC granted TRISO-X a 40-year special nuclear material license covering its TX-1 and planned TX-2 facilities. The company has also expanded its Oak Ridge property holdings and announced further fuel manufacturing and research development, with Tennessee officials associating the broader expansion with more than 1,100 prospective jobs.

As Chernicoff has examined in DCF's earlier feature, Nuclear's Next AI Test: Building at Scale, reactor technology is only one component of the emerging nuclear infrastructure equation. Commercializing advanced nuclear generation will also require fuel supply, manufacturing capacity, licensing, financing, and repeatable construction processes to develop in parallel.

Standard Nuclear is developing additional advanced fuel capacity in the same region. Construction is substantially complete at its new Oak Ridge production facility, with commissioning and authorization activities continuing. In its November 12 third-quarter update, the company reported progress toward a February 2027 target for DOE authorization to operate its new Tennessee and Idaho plants. Its existing Oak Ridge operation already manufactures TRISO fuel, and the company has established relationships with reactor developers including Radiant and Antares.

The downstream connections to data center power are beginning to emerge. Equinix has signed a preorder agreement for 20 of Radiant's planned Kaleidos microreactors, each designed to provide approximately 1 MW of electricity. Radiant announced a $280 million investment in 2025 to establish microreactor manufacturing and research operations in Oak Ridge, and is targeting expanded local assembly operations by late 2028.

Radiant is also participating in a significant federal microreactor initiative. In August, the company announced a U.S. Army agreement valued at up to $750 million under the Janus program, tied to development and deployment milestones for its Kaleidos units.

Although these compact reactors are not intended to replace the large power systems serving hyperscale campuses, they could eventually provide options for remote facilities, military installations, specialized industrial loads, and applications requiring resilient localized generation.

Oklo's Nuclear Fuel Recycling Ambitions

Oklo is pursuing a different part of the nuclear fuel cycle, with plans for an advanced fuel center involving investment of up to $1.68 billion at Oak Ridge.

The company has identified approximately 250 acres at the East Tennessee Technology Park for the proposed development, including property transferred from DOE to the community. The facility is intended to recover usable nuclear materials and support fuel production for Oklo's Aurora reactor technology and potentially other advanced nuclear systems.

Oklo has also been pursuing power arrangements with data center operators and other large electricity customers. Its recycling initiative adds another dimension to Oak Ridge's industrial development, connecting proposed reactor deployments with the longer-term challenge of fuel availability and management.

The broader significance is that Oak Ridge is assembling several components of an advanced nuclear supply chain within one region: enrichment technology, centrifuge manufacturing, specialized fuel fabrication, microreactor manufacturing, and potential fuel recycling.

Whether this industrial concentration can substantially accelerate commercial reactor deployment remains an open question. But the underlying capabilities address constraints that will matter increasingly as utilities and data center developers look toward nuclear energy for future capacity.

DOE Opens the Door to Commercial AI Data Centers at Oak Ridge

Alongside the nuclear investment, DOE is pursuing a separate initiative that could bring privately operated AI data centers directly onto federal property at Oak Ridge.

In September 2025, the department issued a request for proposals seeking private-sector partners interested in developing AI data centers and associated energy infrastructure on portions of the Oak Ridge Reservation. Two locations were identified: one at the East Tennessee Technology Park and another adjacent to Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

Oak Ridge was one of four DOE locations selected nationally for potential AI data center development, alongside Idaho National Laboratory, the Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant, and the Savannah River Site.

The prospective arrangements would place responsibility for financing, permitting, construction, operations, and eventual decommissioning on commercial developers. Those companies would also need to establish the necessary utility interconnection and power supply arrangements.

DOE has not publicly identified a developer selected for either Oak Ridge location.

That qualification matters. The designation of federal land for potential AI infrastructure development is not equivalent to a committed data center construction project, nor does it establish the availability of sufficient electrical capacity.

Still, the initiative represents a potentially important expansion of Oak Ridge's role. The region could become not only a research and manufacturing center for energy technologies used by data centers, but also a location for large-scale commercial computing facilities themselves.

ORNL Builds a Research Center for the Next Generation of Data Centers

The regional transformation is also taking place inside Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

In February 2026, ORNL launched its Next-Generation Data Centers Institute, an initiative specifically intended to address the technical challenges arising from the rapid growth of AI computing infrastructure.

The institute brings together researchers working in electrical engineering, thermal management, grid science, cybersecurity, materials, and high-performance computing. Tom King, a longtime leader in electric grid research, was appointed its director in July.

Unlike research programs focused principally on semiconductor or processor performance, the institute is examining the computing facility as an integrated energy system.

That distinction is increasingly important for AI data centers. Modern rack-scale computing systems are pushing cooling, power distribution, and facility design requirements well beyond those of traditional enterprise computing environments. Direct-to-chip liquid cooling, high-capacity coolant distribution networks, higher-voltage electrical architectures, and more sophisticated control systems are moving toward the center of facility engineering.

ORNL's existing supercomputing infrastructure offers a valuable environment for studying those challenges.

Frontier, the laboratory's exascale supercomputer, already provides extensive experience with large-scale high-performance computing operations and liquid cooling. Lux adds another AI-oriented platform with substantial GPU capacity, direct-liquid-cooled server infrastructure, and advanced Ethernet networking.

The Next-Generation Data Centers Institute is investigating cooling techniques that include direct-to-chip and two-phase liquid systems, improved thermal recovery, and methods of coordinating facility cooling operations with computing workloads. It is also examining how increasingly large computing loads can interact more flexibly with electrical networks.

For commercial data center operators, these are practical research questions. Higher rack densities have made cooling and power distribution fundamental determinants of achievable computing capacity. At the same time, utilities are looking for ways to accommodate large, concentrated electrical loads without undermining grid reliability or imposing excessive infrastructure costs.

The institute's work could help establish approaches for connecting workload scheduling, thermal management, and electricity consumption more directly to grid conditions.

Lux and the institute are distinct initiatives, but together they illustrate an important shift: AI infrastructure is becoming both the object of scientific research and a tool for conducting that research.

Fusion Adds Another Long-Term Energy Dimension

Oak Ridge's energy research ambitions also extend into fusion technology, although commercial deployment remains considerably further away than the nuclear fission projects currently under development.

In August, ORNL and Kyoto Fusioneering announced plans to establish UNITY-3, an advanced fusion breeding blanket test facility in East Tennessee. Kyoto Fusioneering is relocating its U.S. headquarters to Tennessee as part of the collaboration.

The project will investigate technologies intended to capture energy from fusion reactions and support the production of tritium fuel, addressing engineering challenges that must be resolved before fusion can become a practical commercial energy source.

The collaboration combines ORNL's expertise in materials science, neutron research, and high-performance computing with advanced fusion engineering capabilities. AI-enabled modeling and digital twin techniques will also support development and analysis.

Fusion should not be regarded as a near-term solution for data center power demand. However, its inclusion in the expanding Oak Ridge research ecosystem underscores the region's longer-term role in developing technologies that could eventually influence industrial energy systems.

Workforce Development Becomes a Critical Constraint

The region's growing concentration of nuclear projects presents a substantial workforce challenge.

In October, Oak Ridge Associated Universities (ORAU) released its East Tennessee Nuclear Workforce Demand Assessment, projecting that employment among participating nuclear industry companies could increase from approximately 17,000 workers to 21,000 by 2032.

The assessment identified potential shortages in several occupations, including nuclear reactor operators, chemical plant operators, electricians, pipefitters, and production supervisors. Construction labor demand is expected to become especially pronounced around the end of the decade, while the need for specialized operating personnel will continue beyond that period.

The problem is familiar to data center developers. Large AI campuses require many of the same skilled trades and technical professionals needed to construct nuclear facilities, electrical substations, manufacturing plants, and other industrial infrastructure.

Electricians, mechanical contractors, controls specialists, commissioning professionals, and experienced project managers are already important constraints on large data center construction schedules.

The concentration of new nuclear projects around Oak Ridge could intensify competition for these workers even as regional institutions seek to expand training capacity.

That challenge prompted another significant development on November 18, when the U.S. Department of Commerce and Tennessee announced a new nuclear workforce partnership. Under the arrangement, the state will align more than $12 million in workforce training funds with broader federal nuclear workforce development efforts, while the Economic Development Administration intends to provide a $750,000 technical-assistance grant.

Regional institutions, including the University of Tennessee, Roane State Community College, ORAU, and other technical education providers, are also expanding their involvement in workforce preparation.

Kairos Power's Nuclear Center for Advanced Manufacturing and Precast initiative brings together the company, ORNL, educational institutions, construction organizations, and regional schools to investigate advanced manufacturing techniques and train workers for the construction of nuclear facilities.

These initiatives could improve the region's capacity to deliver complex energy projects. In the near term, however, the pace of announced development may continue to exceed the available supply of qualified personnel.

Power Availability Remains the Central Development Question

The most important limitation facing Oak Ridge's emergence as an AI infrastructure center is also the challenge confronting the broader data center industry: when sufficient electricity will actually become available.

TVA's 2026 Integrated Resource Plan, approved by the utility's board in August, identifies a potential need for approximately 11 GW to 32 GW of additional generating capacity through 2040, depending on future demand and resource assumptions.

The utility is pursuing a combination of natural gas generation, storage, solar power, demand-side resources, and longer-term nuclear technologies. The strategy reflects the practical reality that different technologies operate on very different development schedules.

New natural gas generation and grid infrastructure may be capable of addressing some nearer-term requirements. Large-scale nuclear development, including SMRs now advancing through regulatory and demonstration stages, is generally associated with longer construction and commercialization timelines.

For AI data center developers seeking electricity within the next two or three years, many of Oak Ridge's proposed advanced nuclear projects will not provide an immediate answer.

This is a crucial distinction in evaluating the region's prospects. Announced generating capacity is not the same as available capacity, and an approved reactor design does not automatically translate into electrical service for a commercial facility.

Transmission infrastructure, utility interconnection, financing, equipment availability, environmental requirements, and workforce capacity remain important variables.

As Chernicoff and Vincent have previously emphasized in DCF's Nuclear Momentum Meets the Megawatt Test, the industry's next challenge is not simply announcing nuclear projects, but converting regulatory approvals, investment commitments, demonstration systems, and fuel development into reliable commercial generation.

Even the DOE initiative to make federal property available for private AI data center development must contend with those requirements. A suitable industrial site does not necessarily come with the power capacity required to support a substantial computing campus.

The opportunity at Oak Ridge is therefore best understood as a long-term industrial and technological development rather than an immediate solution to the AI industry's power constraints.

What Oak Ridge Means for the Next Data Center Frontier

For much of the data center industry's history, facility operators could assume that electric utilities would provide sufficient power to support development, allowing data center engineering to concentrate principally on reliability, efficiency, computing capacity, and mechanical infrastructure.

The scale of modern AI computing is challenging that separation.

Hyperscalers and other large operators are increasingly participating in discussions about new generation projects, transmission expansion, energy procurement, fuel availability, and the operation of large electrical networks. At the same time, advanced nuclear developers are looking toward data centers as potential long-term customers capable of supporting substantial capital investment.

Oak Ridge offers an unusually concentrated example of these developments coming together.

The region now hosts operational AI and exascale computing infrastructure, advanced nuclear demonstration projects under construction, commercial fuel manufacturing expansion, proposed microreactor facilities, prospective nuclear recycling operations, and a federal initiative to attract private AI data centers onto DOE property.

The opening of Lux is significant because it adds another tangible computing capability to that ecosystem. The system is operational today, unlike many of the proposed energy projects whose commercial impact will depend on years of construction, licensing, and investment decisions.

The significance of Oak Ridge may ultimately have less to do with how many commercial AI data centers are built within its boundaries than with how many of the technologies used to power, cool, connect, and operate data centers elsewhere are developed and demonstrated there.

Advanced cooling architectures, grid-responsive computing, modular nuclear generation, high-performance networking, and domestic fuel manufacturing all address constraints that increasingly determine where and how AI infrastructure can expand.

Oak Ridge is beginning this transition with something many proposed energy and computing hubs lack: a long-established foundation of scientific research, industrial infrastructure, specialized manufacturing, and institutional experience.

The community that helped establish the technological foundations of the nuclear age is now positioning itself to influence another industrial transformation.

With Lux joining Frontier at the center of its computing infrastructure, Oak Ridge is demonstrating that the relationship between energy and artificial intelligence runs in both directions: AI requires increasingly sophisticated power and cooling systems, while AI itself is becoming a tool for developing the energy technologies that may eventually support its continued expansion.

For the data center industry, that convergence may prove to be Oak Ridge's most important contribution to the next frontier of digital infrastructure.

text:
Environmentalists in Michigan and other states are raising the alarm about a bill that would sideline many federal clean water and air reviews.

The U.S. Senate is acting quickly to pass the 500-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA).

The bill would limit environmental reviews to speed up nuclear energy, electricity grid, and data center projects across the U.S.

The bill has the support of a wide range of the U.S. energy industry, including the American Petroleum Institute, Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), American Clean Power (ACP), Advanced Energy United, and American Council on Renewable Energy (ACORE), as well as industry groups representing major data center operators and some labor groups.

The bill is facing opposition from environmental and civil rights organizations, including Sierra Club, Earthjustice, the National Wildlife Federation, the National Congress of American Indians, and the American Civil Liberties Union.

On a Zoom call Thursday, activists fighting for stronger PFAS regulation spoke against the bill.

“I think it’s a very complex bill,” said Sandy Wynn-Stelt, co-chair of the Great Lakes PFAS Action Network. “I don’t know why we’re acting like we have to get this done by New Years.”

Wynn-Stelt would prefer the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress consider the bill rather than the outgoing Republican-controlled Congress during its lame duck session.

On Wednesday, the U.S. Senate voted 65-31 on a procedural vote to advance BAAJA. While the legislation is expected to pass the U.S. Senate, it faces a more uncertain future in the U.S. House, with many pieces of legislation and a federal funding bill to pass crowding the lame duck agenda.

text:
BMW Group opened Plant Woodruff in South Carolina, its first high-voltage battery site in the United States. The company says the plant assembles sixth-generation batteries for the electric iX5 built 15 miles away at Plant Spartanburg, with more than 300 employees and around 250 robots on the line.

Press release · Issued by BMW Group. The summary above is EVXL's; the text that follows is the issuer's own, published as issued and not edited or endorsed by EVXL. Source: BMW Group

The release, as issued by BMW Group

Plant Woodruff begins assembly of Gen6 high-voltage batteries for electric vehicles produced at Plant Spartanburg.

Fourth site in Gen6 production network to start series production

Efficient production using AI and VR

Highest quality standards through consistent zero-defect approach

Local for Local: only 15 miles from Spartanburg vehicle plant

Woodruff, South Carolina, USA. The BMW Group officially opened its new Plant Woodruff in South Carolina today, marking the start of series production. The facility will supply sixth-generation (Gen6) high-voltage batteries for installation in the new BMW iX5 and future electric vehicles at BMW Group Plant Spartanburg, which is located just 15 miles away. The iX5 is BMW’s first fully electric model to be assembled in the United States. “Electromobility is our most important growth area. That is why we are systematically electrifying our portfolio, with the US playing a key role: By 2030, we will be assembling at least six fully electric models at Plant Spartanburg, says Raymond Wittmann, Member of the Board of Management of BMW AG, responsible for Production. “The start of series production of Gen6 high-voltage batteries in Woodruff is therefore much more than the successful launch of a new site: it lays the foundation for the first-ever series production of fully electric BMW vehicles at Plant Spartanburg and on the American continent. This marks the beginning of the next chapter in the success story of the largest plant in our global production network.” Following Debrecen (Hungary), Irlbach-Straßkirchen (Germany) and Shenyang (China), Woodruff is the fourth site in the BMW Group production network to begin series production of Gen6 high-voltage batteries. With AI-supported production processes, digital twins and virtual reality applications, the new plant is setting industry standards for the assembly of high voltage vehicles.

Henry McMaster, Governor of South Carolina: “BMW continues to deliver on its commitments to South Carolina. Just a few years ago, I stood on this site with BMW leadership to break ground on this facility. Today, we are seeing that investment come to life and marking another milestone in BMW’s commitment to South Carolina. BMW has been a strong partner to our state, and this latest investment reinforces what we have built together and the opportunities ahead.” Robert Engelhorn, President and CEO of BMW Manufacturing Co., LLC in Spartanburg: “We said we would begin assembling fully electric BMW vehicles in the US by the end of 2026 – and we are delivering on that commitment. With today’s opening of Plant Woodruff, we are further expanding our footprint in South Carolina and strengthening the close integration of battery and vehicle production. High-voltage batteries assembled at this state-of-the-art facility will power the next generation of fully electric BMW X models from Plant Spartanburg.”

Local for local: Five Gen6 high-voltage battery sites.

Assembly of the Gen6 high-voltage batteries takes place at five new facilities, which the BMW Group built close to its vehicle plants, in line with its “local for local” principle. In addition to Woodruff, four more state-of-the-art high-voltage battery assembly plants have also been built: Debrecen (Hungary), Irlbach-Straßkirchen (Germany), Shenyang (China) and San Luis Potosí (Mexico). Gen6 high-voltage batteries have been series produced in Debrecen, Hungary, since October 2025. Plants Irlbach-Straßkirchen and Shenyang began series production in October 2026. Plant San Luis Potosí will follow in 2027. “With the opening of our Woodruff plant, we are expanding our global Gen6 network: high-voltage battery assembly is now in place in Europe, Asia and North America. This creates a key prerequisite for producing fully electric Neue Klasse vehicles on three continents,” says Wittmann. “The rapid establishment of our Gen6 sites demonstrates the strength of our production network: we share know-how across locations and industrialize our new battery technology worldwide at speed. In doing so, we combine the strength of our global network with regional manufacturing, in line with our ‘Local for Local’ principle.”

Intelligent production for maximum quality.

The BMW Group has established state-of-the-art, intelligent and efficient production processes for its in-house developed Gen6 high-voltage battery. The new cylindrical round cells are integrated directly into the high-voltage battery, based on the “cell-to-pack” principle. All production steps are continuously monitored inline and comprehensively documented in real time. AI assistants and agents developed inhouse analyze this data and, together with more than 300 employees and 250 robots at Plant Woodruff, help ensure zero-defect battery production. At the same time, the extensive use of artificial intelligence enhances Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) in production. Well before commissioning, digital twins of production and virtual reality applications support planning and employee training.

Training in a virtual factory.

All production staff at Plant Woodruff complete a VR training program developed on site. Within a virtual factory, they can practice real manufacturing operations under realistic conditions. This virtual environment replicates the plant’s production lines in meticulous detail. The training helps employees develop an understanding of relevant processes and builds confidence in operating the equipment before they use it for the first time in actual production.

From start of construction to series production in just over three years.

Following the official groundbreaking in June 2023, construction of the new plant began in September 2023. Just one year later, in September 2024, while construction was still under way, installation of the manufacturing equipment began, with the first test and pre-series batteries rolling off the assembly line in summer 2025. “With today’s opening of Plant Woodruff, we demonstrate how quickly we can scale a new battery concept to industrial production,” said Rich Everly, Vice President Responsible for Manufacturing at BMW Group Plant Woodruff. “The key factor here is the interaction between a skilled and committed team and the continuous sharing of experience within the production network.”

The Gen6 battery cells for the BMW iX5 include a high proportion of secondary materials in their cobalt, lithium and nickel content. Renewable energy is also used in the production of anode and cathode materials, as well as in cell manufacturing. Compared with the Gen5 cell used in the BMW iX, CO₂e emissions have been reduced by around 28 percent per watt-hour. Plant Woodruff does not use any fossil fuels during normal operations, while the site’s industrial trucks are powered by hydrogen.

How the BMW Group builds its Gen6 high-voltage batteries.

The BMW Group sources battery cells for its high-voltage batteries from leading cell manufacturers. The highest technical standards apply. Upon receipt of goods, additional measurements – such as voltage checks – are carried out. This is followed by so-called cell clustering, where the battery cells are connected to coolers. This step ensures optimal insulation and cooling of the cells. The cell clusters and cell contact system are then laser-cleaned and welded with pinpoint precision. The in-line inspection continuously monitors each weld seam in real time, while an innovative foaming process ensures that all elements are protected as a mechanical unit. The hardened foam guarantees the safety, stability and durability of the high-voltage battery. The housing is then closed, sealed and riveted. In the final assembly step, the Energy Master – the central control unit – is installed onto the high-voltage battery. Finally, each high-voltage battery undergoes a 100% end-of-line inspection. From Woodruff, the high-voltage batteries are transported to Plant Spartanburg, located just 15 miles away.

Questions and answers.

Why is the BMW Group building high-voltage batteries in Woodruff?

The site’s proximity to BMW Group Plant Spartanburg is a major advantage. The Gen6 high-voltage batteries assembled in Woodruff are transported only 15 miles to Spartanburg, where they are installed in the new BMW iX5, the first fully electric vehicle assembled in the United States. In this way, the BMW Group is implementing its “local for local” principle and closely integrating battery and vehicle production in South Carolina.

Will battery cells also be produced in Woodruff?

No. In Woodruff, supplied battery cells are assembled into Gen6 high-voltage batteries. The BMW Group sources the battery cells from leading cell manufacturers, which manufacture them to the company’s specifications. At the plant, the cells are inspected and then integrated directly into the high-voltage battery, based on the “cell-to-pack” principle. The BMW Group maintains its product and process expertise for battery cells through its own competence centers in Bavaria. What role do AI and automation play in production? All production steps are monitored inline and documented in real time. AI assistants and agents developed in-house analyse the data generated in this way, support production processes and ensure quality. More than 300 employees and around 250 robots work together at Plant Woodruff. Each high-voltage battery also undergoes a 100-percent end-of-line inspection.

What are the advantages of Gen6 battery technology?

The new round cells offer more than 20 percent higher energy density than the previous cell generation. Charging times are reduced by up to 30 percent and range is 30 percent higher – even more in certain models.

Over what period did the BMW Group build Plant Woodruff?

Following the groundbreaking in June 2023, construction of the plant began in September 2023. Just one year later, while construction was still under way, installation of the manufacturing equipment commenced. Production of the first test and pre-series batteries began in summer 2025. The official inauguration marks the start of series production. This means just over three years elapsed between the start of construction and the start of series production.

About BMW Group in the U.S.

BMW Group began operations in the U.S. over 50 years ago. In addition to the sales, marketing, and distribution of BMW, MINI, Rolls-Royce, and BMW Motorrad vehicles, BMW Group’s business in the U.S. spans 30 locations in 12 states including BMW Group Financial Services, BMW Manufacturing, Designworks, BMW Technology Office USA, and BMW i Ventures. The company’s U.S. plant in South Carolina is the largest single BMW production facility in the world and the global center of competence for BMW Sports Utility Vehicles. The BMW Group sales organization is represented by a nationwide network of 355 BMW retailers, 147 BMW motorcycle retailers, 104 MINI passenger car dealers, and 38 Rolls-Royce Motor Car dealers. Taken together, BMW Group’s business activities in the U.S. provide and support over 120,000 jobs and contribute more than $43.3 billion to the U.S. economy annually.

text:
I’m really proud of the work Colchester Institute are doing to train our future workforce in clean energy and sustainable construction. The young people I met on a recent visit will be delivering clean, home grown energy that will help to reduce bills and tackle climate change. The government are investing millions into future training opportunities in Colchester’s Clean Energy Technical Excellence College and the wider region. I was pleased to raise this with Ministers and look forward to them meeting with Colchester students in the new year so we can further develop the opportunities available locally. #Colchester #cleanenergy #skills #training

I’m working with local charities and businesses to make sure Colchester’s young people get the very best opportunities. I raised the work I’m doing with the Education Secretary in Parliament. I want a new settlement for young people - a guarantee of training and a job - with a range of routes into work with apprenticeships and tailored support. I also want to support young people with disabilities and mental health challenges so we give them opportunities rather than writing them off as has happened before.

Today in Parliament we were debating Private Members’ Bills and I was pleased to speak on cancer care and the importance of enhanced reporting of data to deliver the ambitions of the National Cancer Plan. More on the National Cancer Plan here: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-cancer-plan-for-england #colchester #cancer #cancersupport

The Stanway School in Colchester were at the forefront of research on the impact of smartphones in schools. I’m glad that the government have announced new guidance that will mean pupils do not have access to their phones during the school day. Technology can be a brilliant tool for learning, but children's safety has to come first. The government are also running a consultation on the safety of technology and AI used in schools https://consult.education.gov.uk/edtech-regulation-policy-team/education-technology-safety-assurance-certificatio/

I recently co-led an event with Advance to discuss how we can put the needs of girls and young women on the Essex devolution agenda. Alongside Marie Goldman MP and representatives from early years services, education, prisons, probations, and other local organisations, we discussed the challenges facing girls and young women across Essex and how we can work together to address them. It was a fantastic opportunity to hear from organisations working directly with women and girls, and I look forward to continuing to work with Advance to ensure their needs are heard and addressed in local decision making. #womenandgirls #essex advancecharity mariecgoldman

Today I asked the Prime Minister what more the government is doing to support access to treatment for endometriosis. I've heard from many women in Colchester who have endured ongoing pain and trouble getting help. The Women's Health Strategy is committed to making it easier for women to get faster diagnosis and treatment and I'm following up with local services to see what more we can do to locally to make further improvements. #endometriosis #womenshealth #endometriosisawareness #colchester #essex #pmqs

Today I joined local and national campaigners on endometriosis in Westminster for the launch of a new report - Endometriosis (Not) in the Workplace. No one should have to choose between managing their health and building their career. And we need to do more to ensure workplaces are supportive to women with endometriosis and other menstrual health conditions. I’ll continue to work in Colchester and in Westminster to ensure we are providing the necessary support to women to lead full lives. #endometriosis #colchester #womenshealth

We still need more answers from Essex County Council about Operation Vanguard. How was the contract awarded? Why did no consultation take place with Essex Police and Colchester City Council before the private security guards costing at least £150,000 were introduced? I’m glad the Prime Minister is now also asking Reform-led Essex County Council for answers. #colchester #essex #operationvanguard

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee; Mike Lee (R-Utah), Chairman of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources (ENR) Committee; Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the EPW Committee; and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the ENR Committee, released a substitute amendment to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA). The substitute amendment includes clarifying, conforming, and technical edits to reflect feedback received since BAAJA’s introduction in September.

“This substitute amendment preserves the foundation of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, while making targeted changes based on feedback from our members and stakeholders to further build support. I’m thankful for my colleagues’ efforts to strengthen this legislation, the contributions from members of the House, and the support of countless organizations from across the country. I urge the swift passage of BAAJA to make life more affordable for American families,” EPW Committee Chairman Capito said.

“We have spent months working across party lines on both sides of Capitol Hill and with President Trump to deliver permitting reform that makes it easier to build in America. This substitute amendment reflects that work and brings us closer to getting the job done. Our permitting system takes too long, costs too much, and leaves too much uncertainty for the people trying to build what our country needs. We have an opportunity to lower costs for American families, and get America building again. It’s time to finish what we started,” ENR Committee Chairman Lee said.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves BAAJA and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received. Now’s it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs,” EPW Committee Ranking Member Whitehouse said.

“I’ve worked hard to incorporate the feedback we’ve heard from Tribes and New Mexicans into this Substitute Amendment, and I’m proud to join my colleagues in releasing it today. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will help lower energy costs, strengthen Tribal consultation, and create more good-paying jobs. It also makes sure data centers pay for the energy they use and the grid upgrades they cause, instead of passing those costs on to New Mexico families. Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” ENR Committee Ranking Member Heinrich said.

At least four western Oklahoma cities are interested in being the site of the proposed nuclear energy campus.

The cities of Alva, Elk City, Mangum and Altus are among those who have informed the Oklahoma Department of Commerce they would like to be one of the hosts of the Trump administration-backed energy project as announced last summer when Oklahoma was one of five finalists.

The Oklahoman reported the governments in those four cities notified state officials they want to be considered, should Oklahoma be chosen as the site. The finalists for the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus project were announced in July by U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who signed a memorandum with Oklahoma and the states of Utah, Tennessee, Idaho and Louisiana.

The western Oklahoma cities see the potential in perhaps reversing a falling population as well as economic benefits.

“Western Oklahoma has been slowly declining in population for a long time, and we feel like this might be a great opportunity to reverse that,” Gary Jones, Altus city manager, told The Oklahoman. He was among those who attending a meeting in Oklahoma City in September where the state’s plan was unveiled to dozens of officials from across Oklahoma.

“We have a lot of wide open spaces and we feel like we can provide what they are looking for,” Jones said.

State Rep. Nick Archer, R-Elk City, a supporter of nuclear power said Elk City is interested in hosting such a campus.

“There is no community in the state of Oklahoma that has received a definitive yes or no,” Archer said. “We can’t select a community unless the (U.S.) Department of Energy selects us a winner.”

The Department of Energy is expected to announce the winning states by the end of the year.

text:
RALEIGH, N.C. (WNCN) -- A North Carolina Utilities Commission board member has resigned, effective at the start of 2027, according to the North Carolina Treasurer.

The North Carolina Utilities Commission is an agency that regulates the rates and services of all investor-owned public utilities in the state.

Donald van der Vaart, who submitted his resignation just days after state regulators approved higher Duke Energy rates, disagreed with parts of the Duke Energy decision.

He joined the North Carolina Utilities Commission board in April 2025, N.C. Treasurer Brad Briner said Wednesday when announcing the resignation.

van der Vaart is stepping down more than four years before his term expires and two days after he raised concerns about who could end up paying for the state's growing number of data centers.

He wrote a lengthy section in the Duke Energy report, partially dissenting from the decision. (PDF - Starts on page 292)

On Monday, the utilities commission voted to raise electricity rates by more than 9 percent for residential customers over the next two years.

The commission also approved new requirements for large data centers, aimed at making sure they pay their share of the costs.

The new rate schedule requires large data centers to sign long-term contracts, pay for at least 75 percent of the power they reserve, even if they don't use it, and pay upfront for certain infrastructure built specifically for them.

But van der Vaart argued those protections still don't go far enough. In his dissent, he pointed out that new power plants can last 35 years, while data center contracts might last just 15.

And if those data centers leave, he warned that families and businesses could be left holding the bag.

van der Vaart, a former N.C. Department of Environmental Quality Secretary, is an engineer and attorney by trade, with a background in the energy and utilities sectors.

On Wednesday, North Carolina Governor Josh Stein (D) wrote about Duke Energy and the commission's decision:

Energy costs are rising, and we need to be doing everything we can to bring people relief. This rate increase is too high and moves us in the opposite direction. And the Utilities Commission is wrong to let Duke Energy off the hook for building a clean energy future. Their order eliminates plans for wind, scales back solar, and delays new nuclear while increasing our dependence on price-volatile natural gas and coal. While the orders on large load tariffs provide multiple important consumer protections and help to ensure data centers pay for some of their costs, it is far from the end of our work. We still need a separate rate class so data centers clearly pay for their own energy usage, as well as a requirement for data centers to bring their own clean energy to protect North Carolinians from the full cost of data centers.

text:
The Union County, Ohio, factory that first surfaced in an Ohio EPA application in October is now official. Honda said on Nov. 9 it will spend $3 billion on its fourth Ohio auto plant, on land between its Marysville and East Liberty plants, with production expected to start in 2029, "pending final government approvals."

The state had signed off on its piece before the speeches in Marysville began. The Ohio Tax Credit Authority approved a tax credit for the project that morning, according to Gov. Mike DeWine's office, which did not say what the credit is worth. The Ohio Department of Development told Columbus station WSYX that the board approved amending Honda's existing Job Creation Tax Credit, rather than writing a new one.

That puts the hybrid plant on the same paperwork trail as the last big promise Honda made in Ohio. The most recent Honda job credit I found in the authority's records was approved on Oct. 31, 2022, for the electric-vehicle battery plant in Fayette County and the retooling of existing Honda plants, according to the governor's office. The meeting minutes show a 1.871% credit running 30 years, from Jan. 1, 2025, through Dec. 31, 2054, in exchange for Honda Development & Manufacturing of America creating 2,527 full-time-equivalent jobs with $117,603,200 in new annual payroll, and retaining $578,716,093 in existing payroll, by Dec. 31, 2033. One of its project sites is Allen Township in Union County, where the Marysville plant sits. The department has not published the amended agreement, so it is unconfirmed whether the Nov. 9 vote rewrote that 2022 deal or another Honda agreement, and what changed in it.

What Ohio's 2022 EV Hub Deal Promised

Honda announced the EV hub on Oct. 11, 2022: $700 million to retool the Marysville and East Liberty auto plants and the Anna Engine Plant for electric vehicles, plus $3.5 billion with LG Energy Solution for a Fayette County battery plant that would create at least 2,200 jobs, according to JobsOhio. The governor's office counted 327 new jobs from the retooling on top of the existing workforce.

The battery plant was built. The Honda EVs it was meant to supply were not. On March 12, 2026, Honda canceled the Honda 0 SUV, Honda 0 Saloon and Acura RSX, all three planned for U.S. production, saying "the demand for EVs is declining significantly." It estimated losses tied to the reassessment at up to ¥2.5 trillion across the current and future fiscal years.

The joint venture that runs the Jeffersonville battery plant, L-H Battery Company, announced on July 1 that it had started mass-producing cells there for grid energy-storage systems, not cars. CEO Chahun Ku said storage is part of the plant's future "along with production of battery cells for application in hybrid-electric vehicles." Honda's Nov. 9 release lists that plant as one reason it picked Ohio for the new factory, describing it as able to build cells for both hybrids and EVs.

How Ohio's Job Creation Tax Credit Pays Out

The credit is set out in Section 122.17 of the Ohio Revised Code. It equals the company's Ohio payroll above an agreed baseline, multiplied by the percentage in its agreement. It is refundable, so if the credit is larger than the tax the company owes, the state pays the difference. Most agreements are capped at 15 years; the statute allows up to 30 for qualifying megaprojects.

At the 2022 terms, the yearly figure is small next to a $3 billion factory. By my math, 1.871% of $117,603,200 in new payroll comes to about $2.2 million a year, or roughly $66 million over 30 years before raises. The Dayton Daily News reported the credit's estimated value at $71.3 million. Because the credit is calculated on payroll, it pays nothing for jobs that never arrive.

The statute also gives the authority room to bend. If a company falls short, the board may amend the agreement to reduce the rate or the term, and it decides any repayment at its own discretion after letting the company explain. A company that shuts down operations at the site before the credit's term ends can be made to repay up to 100% of what it received. An amendment is how the board changes jobs, payroll, deadlines or sites in an existing deal, and the statute lets Ohio point an existing credit at the jobs Honda is now offering. Taxpayers are owed the new terms in writing, and as of Nov. 18 the department had not posted them.

JobsOhio and Union County Have Not Set Their Terms

The governor's office put Honda's full new commitment at 2,390 jobs and $3.38 billion, counting work at the Anna Engine Plant and the Honda Transmission Plant in Russells Point, where a transmission line is being converted into a second hybrid-system line. JobsOhio, the state's privately run development corporation, will disclose any aid only after a final agreement is signed.

Property taxes are a separate negotiation. Union County economic developer Eric Phillips told WSYX the county is working out tax exemptions but has not received an official application from Honda, and that any abatement would apply to the new factory, not the land. "The district itself doesn't give Honda any automatic tax abatements," Phillips told the station.

Georgia's handling of a similar project shows what a disclosed package looks like: its draft agreement with Audi lists $958 million in first-phase incentives and an 80% clawback. None of Ohio's three Honda numbers is public yet.

Honda Moved Its Ohio Money From EVs to Hybrids

Honda reported first-half results the day after the Marysville event. EV-related losses took ¥484.8 billion out of operating profit for the six months through September, the Associated Press reported, yet Honda raised its full-year operating profit forecast to ¥780 billion from ¥650 billion, an increase of 20%. The company is paying for the canceled EV program and building hybrid capacity in the same state in the same year.

Capacity was already tight. As The Auto Wire reported in September, Honda had spent heavily making its existing Ohio lines flexible and still ran short of room. The new plant adds 240,000 vehicles a year and, per Honda, can build hybrid, gasoline and battery-electric models, flexibility Honda says will let it adapt as demand and electrification trends change.

What Changes for Honda Buyers Before 2029

Buyers feel this before the new plant opens. Honda said on Nov. 12 that the redesigned 2028 CR-V, due next year, will be sold only with a two-motor hybrid system. It will still be built at East Liberty, at Honda's Indiana plant and in Alliston, Ontario, with its hybrid unit from the Russells Point transmission plant. Honda says hybrids are already more than half of CR-V sales and about 30% of Honda-brand sales. It has not announced CR-V pricing, so shoppers who chose the gas CR-V as the cheaper version do not yet know what the new entry price will be.

Gas prices are pushing the same direction: hybrids hit a record 16% of U.S. sales this fall while EV share slipped. Honda is building for that demand, with the Union County plant as the largest single piece.

What to Watch in Union County and Columbus

Three documents will show what Ohio is giving Honda: the amended tax-credit agreement from the Department of Development, the JobsOhio agreement, and Union County's abatement terms once Honda files an application. Honda has not said which "final government approvals" are still outstanding. If the 2022 hiring deadline still applies, it falls on Dec. 31, 2033, and the new plant is not scheduled to build its first car until 2029.

When a company drops the project a 30-year tax credit was approved for, should Ohio be allowed to amend the existing deal for a new plant, or should the company have to reapply from scratch?
