text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Since four Senators from across the political spectrum introduced their Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act last week, a broad coalition of labor leaders, energy producers, and nonprofits has voiced support for the permitting reform plan, noting that it will deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth. The legislation was drafted by U.S. Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee; Mike Lee (R-Utah), Chairman of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources (ENR) Committee; Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the EPW Committee; and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the ENR Committee.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act delivers cheaper energy, more well-paying jobs, and responsible growth by accelerating the permitting and construction of critical energy and infrastructure projects while maintaining key environmental and historic preservation safeguards. The legislation provides greater certainty for projects that have already been permitted and financed, including by preventing future administrations from arbitrarily blocking entire classes of energy projects, while establishing clear timelines for environmental reviews and legal challenges. It also includes targeted reforms to expand and modernize the electric grid, speed the development of geothermal and other energy projects, and ensure that rapidly growing data centers pay the full cost of their associated transmission needs rather than passing those costs on to families and small businesses. The legislation reflects input from members of Congress on both sides of the aisle and a diverse group of stakeholders.

The bill text is available here.

Labor

“For LIUNA, the key consideration is whether a permitting package will translate to good union jobs, with prevailing wages and robust apprenticeship opportunities. S.5653 exceeds those standards while maintaining proper regulations and safeguards that protect both our members on the job as well as the local communities in which projects take place. Moreover, it will lower energy costs for all Americans at a time when prices of everyday living expenses are at an all-time high,” said LIUNA General President Brent Booker. “For more than a decade LIUNA has testified before Congress, submitted comments, participated in roundtables, and endorsed numerous iterations of permitting bills only to see every effort and attempt fail in final hours of the congressional calendar. Congress has another opportunity to get this done. We urge lawmakers in both parties to seize this moment, pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, and finally deliver meaningful permitting reform. It is time to stop making permitting reform the Groundhog Day of Congress.”

“In our industry, uncertainty means one thing: unemployment. It is long past time that Congress enacts meaningful permitting reform to put UA members to work faster delivering reliable and affordable energy to American communities. Today’s announcement is the culmination of a long process to reach a bipartisan deal and take a critical step towards a long-overdue modernization of our country’s permitting process. This bipartisan legislation, led by Chairs Lee and Capito and Ranking Members Heinrich and Whitehouse, will increase project certainty, streamline federal review timelines, and create thousands of good-paying jobs – all while maintaining reasonable environmental safeguards and opportunities for public input. The UA looks forward to continuing our work with members of both parties in the Senate to advance this critical legislation and with all members in the House to ultimately pass it into law,” said United Association of Union Plumbers and Pipefitters (UA) General President Mark McManus.

“We have seen too many projects unnecessarily delayed for years through litigation, and other projects abandoned by contractors or terminated by the federal government because of our nation’s antiquated permitting process. As a result, thousands of good-paying union jobs have been lost, and taxpayers have been deprived of safer infrastructure and more affordable energy,” said John L. Downey, General President of the International Union of Operating Engineers. “Passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will result in building energy transmission capacity faster, delivering more energy to the grid, creating greater certainty for projects permitted and financed across administrations, and setting clear deadlines for environmental reviews. These reforms will put thousands of Operating Engineers to work, along with other highly skilled crafts people, while making energy more affordable and reliable for American families.”

Nonprofits

“If America is going to meaningfully reduce our emissions and truly address climate change, we need to connect much more clean energy to the grid,” said Citizens Climate Lobby’s Executive Director Ricky Bradley. “This bill will make remarkable, rapid progress toward that goal. We’re proud to endorse it, and we’re excited to mobilize our grassroots volunteers in full support.”

“For decades, the Club for Growth has championed deregulation and permitting reform. We commend President Trump and Senate leaders for moving this agreement forward with legislative text. These reforms are critical to expanding American energy production and lowering energy costs for families and businesses. Excessive regulation has constrained production and contributed to higher costs for American consumers. We urge the Senate andHouse to act swiftly and pass these important permitting reforms,” said David McIntosh, President, Club for Growth.

“The Climate Leadership Council is encouraged by progress on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. Council analysis projects U.S. electricity demand to grow nearly 60% by 2050, and meeting that demand will require building energy infrastructure faster than our current system allows. Permitting reform is essential to keep pace with the demands of a modern economy, and the energy infrastructure it unlocks is what drives clean energy deployment and innovation. CLC looks forward to continued engagement with stakeholders and policymakers as the bill moves forward,” said Erin Alejandre, Director of Policy at the Climate Leadership Council.

“On behalf of grassroots activists across the country, we strongly applaud the introduction of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). Your work over much of this Congress to negotiate the details and make a bipartisan package a reality is a major step forward for the American people and for our energy, technological, and national future,” said Brent Gardner, Chief Government Affairs Officer, Americans for Prosperity.

“After years of working toward this goal, lawmakers from both parties have reached a deal to fix the broken system that keeps America from building the power plants and power lines that would bring costs down. This is a huge bipartisan win at a moment when our politics has made wins like this rare,” said Inclusive Abundance Action President Derek Kaufman. “Families are paying too much for electricity because new energy projects wait years on government reviews, then years more in court, and even once they clear, partisan politics can still take them out. That scarcity is a choice. Today, Congress is choosing differently.”

“The need for reform is one of the few things Republicans and Democrats agree on, and these Senate leaders have translated that consensus into a comprehensive, bipartisan bill. Permitting reform cannot wait, and the time to act is now,”said Michele Stockwell, president of Bipartisan Policy Center Action. “BPC Action has long argued that durable permitting reform must be bipartisan, technology-neutral, and maintain strong environmental standards. We urge swift action and look forward to working with members of both parties to get this bill to the president’s desk this Congress.”

“Pacific Legal Foundation strongly supports the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026,” said John Nagle, federal policy manager at Pacific Legal Foundation. “Americans should not have to navigate years of costly and unpredictable government processes simply to build a home, develop new energy resources, or create the infrastructure our communities need. Reforming our permitting system is essential to removing unnecessary government barriers that delay projects, drive up costs, and discourage investment. We encourage Congress to move quickly to pass this bill to lower costs for Americans, protect property rights, and restore America’s ability to build.”

“Today, one of America’s most important supply lines is its electric grid, and we are not building it fast enough to meet the moment. Our military installations depend on the same civilian grid as every American household. When a transmission line takes a decade or more to approve, that is not just an economic problem. It is a strategic vulnerability, and our adversaries are not waiting years to build. This bill addresses that vulnerability. It sets firm deadlines on environmental reviews, speeds approvals for the transmission lines and power projects the country needs, and gives the federal government tools to move interstate power lines forward when they stall. Just as important, it ensures that once a project is permitted, no administration can revoke it for political reasons. At the same time, it preserves the government’s ability to act in the face of a genuine safety or national security threat, and it keeps reasonable environmental safeguards and opportunities for public input in place. That kind of certainty matters for every form of American energy, including the clean energy that will power our future,” said Major General Paul D. Eaton, U.S. Army (Ret.), Senior Advisor at VoteVets.

“[The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act] is better than I could have expected. Sens. Capito (R-WV), Heinrich (D-NM), Lee (R-UT), and Whitehouse (D-RI) negotiated a compromise bill where each side got real, meaningful wins. This bill would fix our permitting processes so that we can review and build efficiently, reducing costs, improving quality of life, growing our economy, and improving economic outcomes. It’s truly a win-win. I’m optimistic that this incredible bill can be signed into law this year,” said Xan Fishman, Vice President, Energy, Bipartisan Policy Center.

“Permitting reform has stalled for years because Democrats feared losing environmental protections and Republicans feared a deal that would only help renewables. Sens. Heinrich, Lee, Capito and Whitehouse have shown there is a bargain that works for both sides,” said Colin Mortimer, Senior Director of Partnerships at the Progressive Policy Institute. “This bill would get power lines, clean energy and critical infrastructure built faster and lower costs for families while keeping strong safeguards in place.”

“If you care about decarbonizing the economy or reshoring American manufacturing, or cutting bills for ratepayers, then you should support this bill. No agreement is perfect, but there’s something in this permitting reform agreement that will, on net, benefit everybody. And there isn’t a better deal out there,” said Jane Flegal and Pavan Venkatakrishnan of the Searchlight Institute.

Bill Owens, Chairman of the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) said, “NAHB applauds Senators Lee, Capito, Heinrich and Whitehouse and for their leadership and bipartisan approach to crafting the most meaningful reforms in decades to several key federal environmental permitting programs. The housing sector stands to benefit from many of these federal permitting reforms, including an increase in acreage thresholds under the Clean Water Act’s (CWA) Nationwide Permit program along with extending the statutory timeframe from five to 10 years for the CWA permit programs. These provisions provide the industry with needed clarity and consistency during the federal permitting process.”

Energy Companies and Associations

“The American Clean Power Association greatly appreciates the leadership of Senators Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich in developing strong, technology neutral permitting reform legislation that includes an Administration commitment to approve wind projects. All energy industries must be able to confidently rely on the durability of federal permitting decisions. The transmission provisions will also enhance grid reliability and enable economic growth. If adopted, the legislation will substantially increase the deployment of clean resources. Passage before the end of the year is essential to enable the construction of critical energy infrastructure and lower consumer prices,” said Jason Grumet, CEO of American Clean Power Association.

“Washington has a generational opportunity to fundamentally transform a broken permitting system and help address the affordability challenges facing American consumers,” API President and CEO Mike Sommers said. “President Trump and Senators Capito, Lee, Whitehouse and Heinrich deserve credit for working across party lines to bring durable reform within reach. The bipartisan package would modernize NEPA, reduce duplicative reviews and unnecessary litigation, and provide greater certainty for critical projects. Congress should seize this moment and finish the job—making it easier to build the infrastructure America needs and helping keep costs down for consumers.”

“We support this bipartisan effort and applaud Senators Capito, Heinrich, Lee, and Whitehouse for advancing meaningful reforms to help meet America’s growing energy needs. As one of the nation’s largest electric utilities and the operator of the country’s largest transmission network, AEP understands firsthand the critical need for diverse generation and transmission infrastructure to serve our customers and help meet the unprecedented demand for electricity. The process to permit, site and construct energy infrastructure can take years due to unnecessary hurdles that delay projects needed to support reliability, affordability and economic growth. This legislation will help accelerate the process to bring critical infrastructure projects online, supporting the investments required to enhance reliability for our customers, reduce costs, and create new economic opportunities in the states we serve. Congress should pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 now,” said American Electric Power (AEP) Chairman, President and CEO Bill Fehrman.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 represents an historic opportunity to modernize the grid and meet customers’ electricity demand with reliable, affordable power. If enacted into law, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 would safeguard critical environmental standards while providing greater process certainty for environmental reviews and ensure that the customers we serve benefit from our nation’s diverse energy resources. It will also unlock trillions of dollars in private sector investment and job creation to expedite the construction of critically needed energy infrastructure,” said Mark Hewett, President and CEO of Berkshire Hathaway Energy.

“Independent oil and natural gas producers are ready to build, produce, and create jobs, and permitting delays and uncertainty can turn attractive projects into missed opportunities—especially for small producers. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 gives Congress an opportunity to deliver bipartisan permitting reform with clear and enforceable timelines, greater levels of certainty, and fewer unnecessary delays—without compromising the environmental and safety standards that protect our communities and natural resources. Republicans and Democrats should seize that opportunity and move swiftly. American energy shouldn’t have to wait in line for Washington’s bureaucracy. American energy shouldn’t be held back by a permitting system that doesn’t keep pace with energy demand. This is an opportunity to celebrate what bipartisan cooperation can accomplish, providing real solutions to the complex problems that surround America’s broken permitting system,” said Edith Naegele, President and CEO of the Independent Petroleum Association of America (IPAA).

“This is the kind of bipartisan action America needs to meet growing energy demand, put downward pressure on energy prices, and deploy more affordable, exactly reliable solar and storage for American families and businesses,” said Tim Pawlenty, CEO of the Solar Energy Industries Association.

“Affordable advanced energy resources, including solar, wind, storage, and transmission are delivering for America, but opaque, politicized, and endless red tape is getting in our industry’s way of building as much as is needed. That’s why we welcome technology-neutral permitting reform from Congress. This bill text demonstrates bipartisan support for building more advanced energy, faster. With fair competition, better planning, and less red tape, we can move more electrons and tamp down energy costs. Thank you to Sen. Capito, Sen. Mike Lee, Sen. Whitehouse, and Sen. Heinrich on their leadership. We encourage Congress to build on this progress and to prioritize these critical reforms,”said Heather O’Neill, President and CEO of Advanced Energy United.

“Constraining abundant, domestic clean energy could cost the U.S. at least $121 billion in additional energy expenses in the coming years,” CEBA CEO Rich Powell said. “This bipartisan package is a generational opportunity to unleash American energy through faster infrastructure permitting and improved transmission planning. Thank you to Chairs Shelley Moore Capito and Mike Lee, Ranking Members Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich, and President Donald Trump for your leadership on this critical issue. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act presents an incredible opportunity for clean energy, and we look forward to seeing it cross the finish line.”

“This bipartisan breakthrough goes big to durably reform a broken permitting system that needlessly drives up energy costs and puts America’s energy security at risk. These comprehensive reforms would unlock generational investments to make energy more affordable and position America to win the global energy race that will define our future. We urge the Senate to act with the urgency this moment in history demands by passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act,” said Anne Bradbury, the American Exploration & Production Council (AXPC) CEO.

Without reform, we will continue to pay more for the grid.”

“Pass the frickin’ bill so we can start building things again,” said the U.S. Oil & Gas Association.

Business and Manufacturing Groups

“Manufacturers are all in on this game-changing agreement and getting it across the finish line. Our nation’s permitting system is outdated and burdensome, delaying projects across industries and contributing to rising costs across the economy. Costly, duplicative permitting delays are costing manufacturers $8 billion annually, limiting manufacturers’ ability to hire new workers, build and expand their operations. Removing these barriers would unlock greater investment and growth. Manufacturers are ready to build, and modernized permitting will help us race to the future,” said National Association of Manufacturers President and CEO Jay Timmons.

“BCSE commends the continued bipartisan work in Congress to modernize the nation’s permitting system and the further development of a comprehensive legislative permitting reform package. Building on the important progress made by the House of Representatives, Congress now has an opportunity to advance comprehensive, durable permitting reform that can provide greater certainty for investment and accelerate the deployment of critical energy infrastructure,” said Lisa Jacobson, President of the Business Council for Sustainable Energy (BCSE).

“We appreciate all the work that made this strong package possible. Any bipartisan compromise will have trade-offs, but the permit certainty, transmission, and grid modernization components of this deal are strong, and now is the time to deliver reforms that allow us to build the clean energy infrastructure we need to reduce costs for American businesses and consumers,” said Zach Friedman, Senior Director of Federal Policy at Ceres. “We look forward to continuing to work with companies, partners, and key lawmakers to meet the moment and advance this package to drive down costs by accelerating deployment of affordable, homegrown clean energy infrastructure.”

This vital legislation would create a faster, more durable permitting process that gives businesses the certainty they need to invest, build and grow,” said Business Roundtable CEO Joshua Bolten. “Advancing wide-ranging permitting reform is one of the most consequential steps Congress can take to unlock America’s economic potential. By accelerating approvals for critical infrastructure projects, this bill would help lower costs, create good-paying jobs and strengthen America’s long-term competitiveness.”

“For too long, America’s broken permitting system has turned the ability to receive a permit into a barrier to job creation and economic growth. This bipartisan agreement represents a major step toward changing that. By establishing more reliable timelines, creating greater certainty and breaking down longstanding barriers to building, Congress can help ensure that projects across the economy move from the drawing board to the job site,” said Steel Manufacturers Association Executive Vice President Brandon Farris.

“The legislation would modernize federal environmental review and permitting processes for infrastructure projects, provide greater certainty for federal permits and authorizations, and help enable the all-of-the-above energy resources needed to meet America’s growing energy and manufacturing demands,” said the American Chemistry Council. “America cannot build, power, and compete without modern infrastructure. Whether it’s expanding energy production, strengthening manufacturing, building next-generation infrastructure, projects cannot move forward if permitting delays and regulatory uncertainty stand in the way. This bipartisan legislation is an important step toward creating a permitting system that is more predictable, transparent, and effective.”

Standing in our way is a permitting process mired in duplication, endless litigation and uncertainty that has hobbled U.S. competitiveness with the second longest timeline in the world to bring a mine online. We applaud the work that has been done to date and urge Congress to pass commonsense, much-needed reforms that will benefit all Americans,” said Rich Nolan, President and CEO of the National Mining Association.

State and Local Government

“The National Governors Association and its partners are encouraged by the introduction of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 and look forward to working with Congress to further develop this legislation. Working with governors, NGA has long championed commonsense permitting reform to build the infrastructure our country needs. With priorities centered on federal partnership, interstate cooperation, and sound energy and environmental policy, NGA worked across the aisle and across sectors to deliver federal reform recommendations to Congress, using states as proving ground. Reform will help grow our economy, reduce costs, and improve quality of life for all Americans,” said Brian Tatum, CEO of the National Governors Association.

This legislation would modernize the federal permitting process, reduce unnecessary delays, accelerate project delivery and ensure local expertise is incorporated into federal decision-making. Counties applaud Senators Lee, Heinrich, Capito and Whitehouse for their leadership and urge Congress to advance this bipartisan permitting reform package.”

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is an opportunity to change that. By bringing greater certainty and accountability to the permitting process, we can unleash American energy dominance, strengthen our grid, bring manufacturing and investment back home, and ensure the United States leads the next generation of economic growth,” said 21 governors in a statement.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee; Mike Lee (R-Utah), Chairman of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources (ENR) Committee; Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the EPW Committee; and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the ENR Committee, introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 to reform the federal environmental review and permitting processes. This groundbreaking agreement will deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth across the United States.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act provides certainty that permitted energy and infrastructure projects will retain their permits absent extraordinary circumstances, violations of law, or court order, as well as targeted reforms for various energy projects. This legislation reflects input from members of Congress on both sides of the aisle and from a diverse group of stakeholders. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act also forces data centers to pay their fair share by requiring them to pay for all of their associated transmission costs.

“For far too long, our broken and outdated federal environmental review and permitting processes have stood in the way of energy reliability, secure jobs, modern infrastructure, and economic growth. The bipartisan reforms we secured in this deal will transform our nation’s ability to power our economy and fuel future growth, while continuing to protect the land, water, and wildlife we all cherish. I look forward to working with our colleagues in the Senate and the House, and President Trump to get this essential legislation signed into law so we can build the infrastructure America needs to grow and thrive,” said EPW Chairman Capito.

“We once built projects like the Hoover Dam, the Golden Gate Bridge, and the Empire State Building in years, not decades. America still has the resources and the talent, but what too often stands in the way is a permitting system that takes too long and costs too much. After years of work in Congress and many months of negotiations, I’m proud we’ve reached a bipartisan agreement to fix this broken process and get America back to building,” said ENR Chairman Lee.

“The American people want lower energy bills, and they want more clean energy. Our permitting reform plan gets us a long way toward both of those goals. If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share. Like all major pieces of bipartisan legislation, this bill is a compromise. We believe it is a compromise that will result in a brighter, cleaner, more affordable future,” said EPW Ranking Member Whitehouse.

“America is entering a new era of energy demand. We have an enormous opportunity to build big things again to meet that moment – to build more generation, expand our grid, create more jobs, lower energy costs, and make sure we have the energy we need to compete. It should not take decades to build the infrastructure our country needs. Our Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will help us get to ‘yes’ or ‘no’ on energy projects faster, while protecting important environmental safeguards and protecting the ability of Tribes to formally consult during these processes. It will mean more energy on the grid, more good-paying jobs, and lower electricity costs for families and businesses. And as data centers drive demand for more power, it will ensure they pay their fair share of the grid upgrades they require – not leave that bill to American families. Our bill puts teeth behind that principle,” said ENR Ranking Member Heinrich.

The bill text is available here.

text:
The following letter was sent to Rhode Island Senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Jack Reed and U.S. Representatives Seth Magaziner and Gabe Amo by Save The Bay, RI Conservation Law Foundation, Clean Water Action, and the Audubon Society of RI about the Bipartisan American Affordability & Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), now making its way through Congress.

For more on BAAJA, see:

Steve Ahlquist: Senator Whitehouse: This is who he is

Aaron Regunberg: The Democrats’ First Move After Their Big Win? A Giveaway to Big Oil.

Peter Nightingale: Strange Bedfellows: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller

Providence Preservation Society’s statement opposing proposed changes to the National Historic Preservation Act outlined in US Senate Bill

Barry Schiller: A bill in Congress would speed up project approval. Is this good or bad?

Dear Senator Whitehouse:

On behalf of the undersigned environmental, conservation, and advocacy organizations in Rhode Island, we write to express our concerns about the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability & Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), commonly referred to as the permitting reform bill. While we recognize the importance of improving the efficiency, transparency, and predictability of federal permitting processes to expand clean energy and combat climate change, we are concerned that the legislation, as currently proposed, would significantly weaken longstanding environmental protections and undermine Rhode Island’s ability to protect its waters, wetlands, and natural resources.

Our organizations support common-sense permitting reforms that facilitate responsible energy development while maintaining strong environmental safeguards. Unfortunately, despite certain changes in the substitute amendment, the BAAJA still raises significant concerns about several cornerstone environmental laws, including, but not limited to, the Clean Water Act (CWA) and the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). This legislation would diminish state authority, limit public participation, and reduce state and federal agencies’ ability to respond to emerging environmental threats and changing conditions.

We are particularly concerned about the following provisions:

Clean Water Act – Section 401 Water Quality Certifications

Section 401 of the Clean Water Act provides states with an important role in ensuring that federally permitted projects protect state water quality standards and designated uses. This authority is particularly important to Rhode Island, where our rivers, wetlands, coastal waters, and Narragansett Bay support fishing, swimming, wildlife habitat, and other vital uses.

For interstate pipelines and energy transmission projects, the bill would limit state certification conditions to direct point-source discharges, potentially excluding broader project impacts such as stormwater runoff from construction sites, erosion and increased turbidity in nearby waterways, and pollutant releases from disturbed soils. These changes would restrict Rhode Island’s ability to address the full range of potential environmental impacts associated with federally permitted projects.

The substitute amendment clarifies Section 401, including the authority of states to determine which conditions are necessary to ensure compliance with water quality requirements. However, it retains the fundamental restrictions that concern us. States would still have to demonstrate, through clear and convincing evidence, that less burdensome conditions would not adequately protect water quality, and any conditions imposed would still have to meet a least-burdensome standard. The bill also retains restrictions on a state’s ability to deny certification based on problems identified after the designated review period.

These requirements would place an unreasonable burden on Rhode Island regulators and could make it considerably more difficult to protect state waters and wetlands from harmful project impacts. We are concerned that these changes would substantially undermine an important tool that states have historically relied upon to protect their water resources.

Clean Water Act – Sections 402 and 404 - Permit Terms and General Permit Presumption

We are also concerned about the proposal to extend National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) and Section 404 General Permit permit terms from five to ten years. Regular permit review provides an important opportunity to incorporate advances in pollution control technology, address newly identified contaminants, and respond to changing environmental conditions.

The substitute amendment does not address this proposed extension. Extending permit durations would reduce opportunities for regulators and the public to ensure that permitted discharges reflect current scientific understanding and available pollution prevention technologies. At a time when emerging contaminants, such as PFAS chemicals, and other evolving water quality threats, such as microplastics, require continued attention, maintaining the ability to periodically review and update discharge permits is essential.

The bill further directs that effects associated with discharges into less than two acres of navigable waters would be considered a “minimal adverse environmental effect,” creating an assumption of impact disassociated from the reality of impacts on sensitive ecosystems. The Clean Water Act established that general permits under this section were to be reserved for projects that may cause minimal individual and cumulative impacts. By unilaterally categorizing discharges with impacts of less than two acres of navigable waters as “minimal,” it limits the ability of federal and state governments to carefully review actual potential impacts to our state’s navigable waters since the general permit process eliminates individual review.

Project Certainty - Restrictions on Federal Permitting Agency Authority

The BAAJA would also significantly restrict federal agencies’ ability to revoke or modify previously issued permits, even when new information emerges, environmental conditions change, or a project violates its permit requirements.

The substitute amendment adds exceptions that would allow agencies to act in response to threats to human health and the environment, as well as actions required under applicable laws and regulations. While these changes are improvements, the exceptions remain narrowly drawn. For example, the exception concerning human health and environmental harm requires a showing of immediate, specific, urgent, substantial, and proximate harm. This high threshold could prevent agencies from responding to serious threats before they cause immediate, demonstrable damage.

The bill’s restrictions would apply broadly to federal permits and authorizations for many types of projects, not simply renewable energy infrastructure. In practice, these provisions could prevent agencies from updating permit requirements to reflect improved technologies or changing environmental standards. They could also limit agencies’ and courts’ ability to respond meaningfully when permitted projects violate permit conditions and cause environmental harm.

Environmental protections must adapt to new scientific information and changing circumstances. Restricting the ability of government agencies to address permit violations or respond to newly identified environmental threats would place Rhode Island’s natural resources at unnecessary risk.

National Environmental Policy Act – Public Participation and Environmental Review

We remain concerned about the proposed changes to the National Environmental Policy Act. NEPA serves a critical function by requiring federal agencies to evaluate the potential environmental consequences of proposed actions, consider alternatives that could reduce environmental harm, and provide opportunities for public review and comment.

The BAAJA would narrow the types of projects subject to environmental review, limit the scope of alternatives analyses, and significantly limit opportunities for public participation and judicial review. The substitute amendment adds further project exclusions, including certain federally funded broadband projects, and allows agencies to rely on existing environmental analyses prepared for different but similar projects. The substitute amendment also retains provisions that condition a party’s ability to seek judicial review on having participated in the public comment process. While the amendment clarifies that this restriction would not apply retroactively to projects whose comment periods occurred before enactment, the limitation would still apply to future projects. This could prevent individuals and organizations with legitimate environmental concerns from obtaining judicial review because they did not participate in an earlier comment period.

Public participation is not simply a procedural requirement or a box to be checked. It allows local communities, conservation organizations, and other stakeholders to bring important information and perspectives to the permitting process. It also helps ensure that agencies consider less damaging alternatives and account for advances in pollution prevention and environmental protection. Weakening these opportunities would undermine an important mechanism for transparency and accountability in federal decision-making.

Conclusion

Taken together, these provisions represent a significant shift in the balance between facilitating needed infrastructure development and maintaining the environmental protections that safeguard our nation’s natural resources. While the substitute amendment clarifies and improves the original legislation, it does not resolve many of our fundamental concerns.

We recognize that improvements to the federal permitting process are warranted, and we support efforts to make those processes more efficient and transparent. However, permitting reform should not come at the expense of states’ ability to protect their waters, federal agencies’ ability to enforce environmental laws and regulations, or the public’s ability to participate in decisions that affect their communities.

We respectfully urge you to consider taking no votes on this legislation this session, and to instead consider permitting reform in the next Congress. Permitting reforms should improve efficiency and transparency without undermining the Clean Water Act, NEPA, the Endangered Species Act, and the other foundational environmental laws that protect our communities and natural resources.

Thank you for your continued leadership on environmental protection and climate change, and for considering our concerns. We would welcome the opportunity to discuss these issues further with you or your staff.

Topher Hamblett, Executive Director, Save The Bay

Darrèll Brown, Vice President, Rhode Island Conservation Law Foundation

Emily Howe, RI Director, Clean Water Action

Maxwell McFarland, Director of Advocacy, Audubon Society of RI

description:
(WO) – The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has approved GHGSat’s DATA.AIR Gen2 aerial methane measurement system as an alternative test method for periodic screening under the Subpart OOOOb methane rule.
Oil and gas operators can now use the system’s aerial surveys to meet periodic screening requirements for fugitive emissions at the 10-kg/hr threshold.
Mounted on an aircraft, DATA.AIR Gen2 uses a short-wave infrared spectrometer to map methane concentrations over oil and gas sites.
In a blinded controlled-release study in southern Alberta, with 110 measurements at release rates of 2.5 kg/hr to 22.5 kg/hr, the system achieved 90% probability of detection well below the 10-kg/hr threshold, according to GHGSat.
Testing at Colorado State University’s Methane Emissions Technology Evaluation Center (METEC) found 90% probability of detection at 3.5 kg/hr.
text:
(WO) – The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has approved GHGSat’s DATA.AIR Gen2 aerial methane measurement system as an alternative test method for periodic screening under the Subpart OOOOb methane rule. Oil and gas operators can now use the system’s aerial surveys to meet periodic screening requirements for fugitive emissions at the 10-kg/hr threshold.

Mounted on an aircraft, DATA.AIR Gen2 uses a short-wave infrared spectrometer to map methane concentrations over oil and gas sites. GHGSat analysts then use the maps to locate and quantify emissions at the equipment level. GHGSat said a single flight can cover many facilities in a day, including remote sites, without ground crews at each location, and it delivers results within hours as a service. The aircraft complement GHGSat’s satellite constellation, which provides wider monitoring for larger emissions.

In a blinded controlled-release study in southern Alberta, with 110 measurements at release rates of 2.5 kg/hr to 22.5 kg/hr, the system achieved 90% probability of detection well below the 10-kg/hr threshold, according to GHGSat. Testing at Colorado State University’s Methane Emissions Technology Evaluation Center (METEC) found 90% probability of detection at 3.5 kg/hr.

text:
Europe’s clean transition supports decarbonisation, competitiveness and resilience

This summer’s climate extremes, during what European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called a “summer of truth”, were a recurring theme at our 2026 Energy and Climate Summit. Record heat, drought and wildfires have shown how exposed the continent is to a changing climate, while the war in Iran and the disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have pushed Europe into its second energy crisis of the decade. Over two days in Brussels, policymakers, business leaders, experts, and representatives from civil society organisations debated how Europe can respond to both crises at once, and how its clean transition can become a strategy for competitiveness, security and resilience rather than a cost to be managed.

Setting the scene

The conversation began the evening before, at an off-the-record pre-summit dinner bringing together senior officials from European institutions, members of the European Parliament, national representatives, key private sector actors, civil society organisations and academics. Their starting point was that energy, security and sovereignty have become inseparable. The rules-based order that once underpinned Europe’s prosperity has fractured, energy prices now shape geopolitics as much as treaties and alliances do, and supply chains are increasingly driven by power rather than market logic. With the war in Iran choking off supplies, consumer energy prices have reached their highest level since the post-COVID recovery began, showing the volatility the energy system has been exposed to, and participants stressed that the poorest households are those paying the heaviest price.

Around the table, participants spoke frankly about a political mood that has shifted markedly in recent months. In the European Parliament and in several capitals, voices are calling openly to “undo” the Green Deal and to deregulate further, and carbon pricing is under growing pressure. The concerns raised at the summit were reflected in the European Council discussions just days later, on 15–16 October, when Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary, Italy and Greece asked to postpone the new emissions trading system for buildings and road transport (ETS2), already delayed to 2028, until at least 2030; a majority of member states opposed the move, and leaders only asked the Commission for an updated impact assessment. While such calls are presented by various stakeholders to protect jobs and living costs, participants cautioned against misdiagnosing the problem. Taking the example of Europe’s car industry, a representative from a major environmental NGO argued that its loss of competitiveness stems above all from lost market share in China and a lack of speed and commitment in innovation, not from EU climate rules. The real challenge for the sector, in other words, is to compete in electric vehicles at a time of growing Chinese overcapacity.

The methane regulation has become a case in point of how energy security concerns are now reshaping climate policy. Its import requirements, which oblige importers of oil, gas and coal to monitor, report and verify the methane emissions linked to their supplies, were due to apply from January 2027. After importers and fossil fuel producers warned that they could not secure enough compliant supplies in time, and amid pressure from the United States and France, the Commission proposed on 14 October to postpone these obligations by one year, and the European Parliament has since backed a longer, three-year delay.

Dinner participants warned that delaying the methane rules will do nothing to solve Europe’s security or affordability challenges, and that the file matters above all to fossil fuel exporters rather than to Europe’s own industrial base. More broadly, they agreed that climate policy cannot succeed if it is imposed against people, and that public support has to be earned through measures that are fair and visibly beneficial. Europe can be flexible on the means, for instance on timelines, transitional support or simpler rules, but should not weaken the goals themselves, since lowering ambition would only undermine the certainty that citizens and investors need.

This backsliding sits uneasily with public opinion, which remains firmly behind climate action: according to the 2025 Special Eurobarometer on climate change, 85% of Europeans consider climate change a serious problem and 81% support the EU’s goal of climate neutrality by 2050, and tens of thousands of people marched for climate action in Brussels on the weekend before the summit, with little political response. What is missing, participants argued, is leadership, and a narrative that presents the transition as an investment in Europe’s future rather than a cost. Disinformation feeds the story that “nothing works in Europe”, when much is in fact working: electrification is spreading from cars to trucks and ships, and countries with largely decarbonised power systems, such as Spain and France, now enjoy far lower prices than those still reliant on fossil fuels. Outside Europe, too, the expectation remains that the EU will lead.

Even where the political will exists, delivery is held back by very practical barriers, and participants described permitting delays of up to seven years for wind and solar projects, which simple fixes such as one-stop shops and digital procedures can cut sharply, and stressed that permitting is ultimately about people: mayors and local communities who must be listened to. Cash-strapped local authorities, some of which have resorted to taxing electric vehicle charging points, lack the means to renovate social housing, and the poorest households cannot afford heat pumps on their own. Companies ready to be front-runners in decarbonisation still face regulatory and infrastructure obstacles in Europe. Participants called for public money to enable rather than compel, for industrial policy that prioritises instead of spreading resources thinly, and for the same “war room” urgency that Europe has recently shown on defence. Above all, they insisted that decisions remain grounded in science, because, as one participant recalled, you cannot do business on a dead planet.

Climate resilience: protecting Europe from growing risks

The scientific picture was laid out in stark terms the following day. Opening the first session, Connie Hedegaard, former European Commissioner for Climate Action and trustee of Friends of Europe, recalled that tens of thousands of people died prematurely in Europe this summer, harvests are expected to fall, and economists estimate that the cost of this summer’s extreme events equals the EU’s projected growth for 2026. In opening the afternoon sessions, Ulrike Sapiro, Managing Director of the Jacques Delors Friends of Europe Foundation, stressed the same point, also adding that 1.7mn hectares of forest were destroyed over two fire seasons, which is half the land surface of Belgium. Frank Elderson, Executive Board Member of the European Central Bank, put it starkly: this summer was very warm,

but it’s probably going to be the coolest summer of the rest of our lives – Frank Elderson

“This needs to go across the economy,” said Jan Dusík, European Commission Deputy Director-General for Climate Action, previewing the EU Framework for Climate Resilience, which the Commission went on to publish on 27 October together with a proposal for a first European Climate Resilience Law. He noted that the number of people displaced in Europe this summer was the highest since the Second World War, describing it as “an appetiser of living in the era of climate change”. His call for resilience by design, now a guiding principle of the new framework, means embedding climate risk in investment and planning, with clearer ownership of who manages which risks. Only around a quarter of climate-related losses are currently insured, leaving a wide protection gap that public budgets alone cannot close.

Building that resilience depends on reliable data, and Simonetta Cheli, Director of Earth Observation Programmes at the European Space Agency (ESA), described how ESA’s 24 satellites in operation, including 13 in the Copernicus constellation run with the European Union, “take the pulse of our planet”. Satellite data now lets insurers reimburse farmers for hail damage within 24 hours. Cheli stressed the importance of turning scientific knowledge into decisions: “We have to valorise those data […] to make sure that everything which we have in terms of information can be turned into action.” Pierfrancesco Maran, Chair of the European Parliament Committee on the Environment, Climate and Food Safety, linked this to the need for visible protection for citizens today: “We should do more on this point to demonstrate that we don’t have only a strategy for the future, but also action for the present.”

Nature itself emerged as one of Europe’s most effective lines of defence, as Ruth Davis, the UK Special Representative for Nature, illustrated with aerial photographs from this summer, showing that areas where rivers and wetlands had been restored stayed green while everything around it was brown and potentially burning. Nature-based solutions hold water in the land during droughts and slow it down during floods, she said: “These are actual physical solutions to the problems that our citizens are facing on the ground.” Davis also stressed the international dimension. Deforestation in the tropics is drying out the “green water towers” that feed much of the world’s agriculture, pushing up the price of coffee, cocoa and soy. Because these supply chains cannot simply be replaced at home, nature protection abroad is also a security concern for Europe.

Sandrine Dixson-Declève, Executive Chair of Earth4All, called for systemic thinking that recognises these connections: a drought is no longer just a drought when water shortages cut nuclear output in France and Hungary, and a fire is no longer just a fire when it forces neighbouring countries to coordinate across borders.

Nowhere are these links clearer than in water, with water stress already affecting around 34% of the EU’s territory and 40% of its population while around a third of public water supply is still lost through leaking infrastructure. Leena Ylä-Mononen, Executive Director of the European Environment Agency (EEA), reported that only 38% of Europe’s surface waters are in good ecological status, while two-thirds of the EU’s drinking water comes from groundwater that, in some areas, can no longer replenish itself. Calling for less waste and more reuse, she said that water is “a critical resource, and we have been a bit too sloppy with preserving that resource”. The EEA’s new foresight report, Competitive by Nature, makes the case that Europe’s competitiveness depends on a stable climate and healthy ecosystems.

Filip Hebbrecht, Business Relations Manager at Natuurpunt, explained why even a famously rainy region like Flanders ranks 18th in the world for water stress, “in good company with Morocco and Yemen”. Some 50,000 square metres of land disappear under concrete every day, while centuries-old ditches still drain water to the sea. He called for a shift from this “evacuation landscape” to a “sponge landscape” that retains water in soils and wetlands, noting that every euro invested in wetland restoration can return up to €50 to society. Investors are paying attention too. Jonathan Barnes, Associate at KKR’s Global Impact Fund, explained that the global investment firm, which manages around $800bn in assets, treats water resilience both as an investment theme and as a risk across its wider portfolio. Its impact strategy backs companies whose core business addresses environmental or social challenges, such as Axius Water, a nutrient-removal business that has kept more than 530 million kilograms of nutrients out of waterways and grown sixfold under KKR’s ownership. Water also features in the due diligence for other deals: concerns over water extraction in water-scarce regions recently led KKR to walk away from an investment in a consumer water company. Clear demand signals and regulatory frameworks, Barnes added, give investors the confidence to back such solutions for the long term. Rising demand from data centres reinforced the need to consider water in every planning decision.

water is “a critical resource, and we have been a bit too sloppy with preserving that resource – Leena Ylä-Mononen

The politics of the transition: urgency meets fading appetite

While the science grows clearer, the politics are moving in very different directions, and the concerns raised at the dinner was echoed throughout the summit as governments struggle to balance long-term climate goals with immediate pressure from voters and industry.

The geopolitical backdrop has only made this balance harder to strike, and Hedegaard observed how the US President’s willingness to deal with Vladimir Putin on diesel imports, together with the crisis around Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, illustrates how intertwined energy prices, security, social stability and competitiveness have become. Dan Jørgensen, European Commissioner for Energy and Housing, began his intervention with a frank overview of what is taking place in Europe. He stressed that Europe was facing a price crisis rather than a security-of-supply crisis. Europeans are paying twice as much for diesel as they did in February and 140% more for gas, placing industries and vulnerable households under severe strain.

Faced with that pressure, many governments are reaching for short-term relief. Sapiro cited the Jacques Delors Institute’s tracker of national responses, which estimates the cost of the crisis for the EU at nearly €140bn : some €33bn in public support measures, most of them aimed at bringing down fuel prices, plus around €104bn in additional spending on fossil fuel imports. Energy inflation, she added, still stands at 4.2%. Maran pointed to his own country, Italy, where the room the EU’s fiscal rules now allow for energy investment, through the energy component of the national escape clause, amounts to roughly €6bn a year, less than Italy has spent in the past eight months alone on supporting fuel prices. Dixson-Declève added that fossil fuel subsidies have doubled globally in a decade. Such measures may bring relief at the pump today, but they lock in the very dependency that caused the crisis. Europe already spends almost €1bn a day on imported fossil fuels, noted Yvan Verougstraete, Vice-Chair of the European Parliament Committee on Industry, Research and Energy.

Jørgensen warned against letting the price crisis derail the structural response: “It would be a terrible paradox if we, because prices went up because of the situation in the Middle East, took decisions that would in fact prevent us from doing the structural changes that we need in the long term to prevent us from coming in these crises again.” Support for companies and households can be necessary, he said, but it must be targeted and temporary and should channel as much as possible into measures that reduce dependency over time, such as renovating buildings, replacing gas and oil boilers with heat pumps, expanding district heating and switching to electric vehicles. For industry, speakers pointed to lower taxes on electricity, long-term clean power contracts and support for the higher operating costs of electrified processes, such as the carbon contracts for difference introduced in Germany, as ways to help energy-intensive companies move away from fossil fuels.

Maran, for his part, argued that Europe can protect its industry while keeping its climate tools intact, noting that the ETS has cut emissions from covered sectors by around 50% in two decades and that the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), once opposed by companies, is now in demand because it protects them from unfair competition. In his words, the aim must be to “save the world with citizens and companies, not against them”.

If Europe is to move away from fossil fuels, the obvious question is what will replace them, and Elderson framed the scale of the task. Around 48% of Europe’s electricity is now generated sustainably, but electricity makes up only about 23% of final energy use, leaving much of Europe’s energy consumption dependent on fuels rather than electricity. The alternative, he said, is “current sunshine that we can harvest right here”.

“It would be a terrible paradox if we […] took decisions that would in fact prevent us from doing the structural changes that we need in the long term – Dan Jørgensen

Clean industry and electrification: where Europe needs to go

On the answer, speakers broadly agreed that Europe’s future lies in a clean industrial base powered by electricity. Miguel Gil Tertre, Head of Cabinet to European Commission Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera, argued that electrification simultaneously addresses Europe’s dependence on imported fossil fuels, its industrial competitiveness and its climate objectives: “There is no more trilemma for the EU. We need to electrify.” Hedegaard noted that the eight member states with the lowest energy costs also have the highest share of renewables. Europe, she said, has already identified the key ingredients; “what we need to be better at is executing and implementing.”

The benefits are already visible in prices, as Antonio Lopez-Nicolas, Chief Economist at the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Energy, explained: wholesale electricity prices in countries such as Spain, France, Sweden and Finland are almost half the level of those in other parts of Europe because of their high share of clean power. “So now we see that this can be done,” he said. Electrification is the way to pass those benefits on to industry and households, he said, facilitating the uptake of long-term contracts such as power purchase agreements and contracts for difference.

Mobilising investment on the scale required will depend above all on predictability. Elderson estimated that meeting the EU’s 2030 climate target requires around €477bn of additional green investment every year, roughly 80% of which must come from private sources. Investors need stable goals and consistent policies, he said, since “one step forward, two steps backwards” does not help those who have already invested. He also called for deeper capital markets: “The capital needs to flow cross border. It needs to find business opportunities wherever there are. We need to pool capital in a way that we have not been doing in Europe.”

On the demand side, too, change is under way, with Jørgensen reporting that heat pump sales have “exploded” since February and that electric vehicle sales in Germany have now overtaken combustion engine cars, while Verougstraete noted that more than half of new cars sold in Belgium in September were electric. Road freight, however, shows how much remains to be done. Raluca Marian, General Delegate of the International Road Transport Union (IRU), explained that around 90% of Europe’s roughly one million road transport operators are small or micro companies with fewer than ten vehicles. For them, electric trucks and buses only make business sense if they can be charged at the operator’s own depot, typically overnight, where electricity costs between a quarter and a half as much as it does at public charging points along motorways: “Massive scaling up of electrification in Europe cannot happen if the ecosystem of the charging infrastructure does not include both public and depot charging.” Depot charging, however, depends on grid connections that are slow to arrive. The Port of Rotterdam, where tens of thousands of trucks load and unload every day, will only get the grid capacity it needs in 2035, five years after the 2030 transport targets fall due, so an opportunity that exists today risks being lost.

Massive scaling up of electrification in Europe cannot happen if the ecosystem of the charging infrastructure does not include both public and depot charging – Raluca Marian

Clean tech depends on critical raw materials

Any clean industrial strategy also needs a strategy for the materials it runs on, since batteries, grids, data centres and defence systems all depend on critical raw materials and rare earths, most of which are refined in China. Ke Wang, Global Lead for Energy Minerals and Circularity at the World Resources Institute, noted that despite a surge of new policies worldwide, production has become more concentrated. Rather than trying to secure everything, she urged Europe to choose: “Europe cannot reduce every dependency at once. And it does not need to, because not all dependencies carry the same risks.” Europe should identify the dependencies that pose the greatest risks and accept those that do not, she said, and remember that securing minerals achieves little without the industries to turn them into products.

Bart Sap, Chief Executive Officer of Umicore, linked affordable clean energy with Europe’s industrial future, highlighting energy, defence, data and AI, and pharmaceuticals as the sectors where Europe must secure its capabilities. He argued for “balanced collaboration”, using Europe’s purchasing power to attract clean-tech investment, including from China, on Europe’s terms. Yet regulation often stands in the way of recycling. Moving batteries and waste across European borders means complying with different local rules in each country, Sap explained, and a single error in the procedure sends the whole process “back to start”, like the board game everyone played as a child. The consequence is that waste is exported outside the EU instead of being recycled at home. He called for a “one-click certification system”, under which recyclers and transport companies would be audited once and then able to move waste freely to recycling facilities. “Circularity is a source of independence,” he said. “That’s what we have to go for.”

Europe cannot reduce every dependency at once. And it does not need to, because not all dependencies carry the same risks – Ke Wang

Circularity will be just as decisive in meeting Europe’s targets. Cillian Lohan, Chief Executive Officer of the Green Economy Foundation and President of the Civil Society Organisations’ Group of the European Economic and Social Committee, described circularity as primarily a business model rather than an environmental initiative. According to Eurostat, only 12.2% of the materials used in the EU came from recycled sources in 2024, just one percentage point more than a decade earlier, while the Clean Industrial Deal aims to double this circularity rate by 2030. Wang pointed to a concrete opportunity: millions of electric vehicle batteries will soon retire with 70–80% of their capacity left, and reusing just 40% of them could meet the EU’s stationary storage needs by 2040. New extraction in Europe will also depend on public consent: Wang noted that 60% of mining permit delays stem from community opposition and environmental concerns. Lohan argued that giving communities a share of the value, and being transparent, is the most effective answer:

In an age of misinformation and disinformation, transparency is actually our friend – Cillian Lohan

Grids and interconnection: making electrification work

None of this will work unless Europe can move clean power to where it is needed, which is why Gil Tertre described grids as the starting point for everything else: around 40% of Europe’s grids are 40 years old and were never designed to absorb today’s volumes of renewables, heat pumps and electric vehicles. “If this investment does not happen now, then all the other investments will not come.”

Jørgensen set out why a connected Europe matters, warning that average figures for Europe’s energy prices hide huge differences between member states. The decisive factors, he said, are how much renewable energy a country has and how well connected it is to its neighbours. “We need a true energy union where we are actually connected.” According to the EU Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (ACER), Europe already saves more than €30bn a year through integration, with at least €10bn more to gain. Jørgensen said the European Grids Package, which aims to accelerate permitting and improve cross-border infrastructure planning, would “slash permitting times fundamentally from five to ten years to six months as a general rule”, while introducing Europe-wide planning and rules for sharing the costs of cross-border projects. The Commission’s December 2025 proposal sets a maximum of six months for permits for projects such as stand-alone storage and charging stations and a two-year cap for transmission and distribution lines, which the Council’s position, adopted in June, would allow to be extended to 30 months. Even so, the reform would mark a sharp acceleration: legal analyses of the package put average permitting times today at around five years for transmission grids and up to nine years for renewable energy projects, and the electricity industry association Eurelectric has described it as delivering a simpler and faster process with a maximum approval period for many projects.

Beatriz Corredor Sierra, Chairwoman of Redeia, the holding group that integrates Red Eléctrica, the Spanish electricity transmission and system operator (TSO), showed what an integrated, renewables-based system can deliver. Spain integrates up to 95% of the renewable energy it produces, with curtailment below 5%, and securely generates around 60% of its electricity from renewables. Yet the Iberian Peninsula has less than 3% interconnection with the rest of the continent, less than Ireland, which is “very bad for us, but very bad for Europe”. Corredor Sierra also stressed that grids themselves are not the bottleneck for new demand: in Spain, six gigawatts of grid access have been granted to data centres, yet “zero kilowatts” have been connected. Transmission system operators, she argued, are “the spine, the backbone” of electrification, and their deployment depends on involving local communities.

Grid investment also has to remain affordable for consumers. “Is there enough money? Yes,” said Edward Calthrop, Head of the Sustainability and Climate Office at the European Investment Bank (EIB), but the cost of capital is critical: “If we don’t keep a handle on the cost of capital, there is a risk that we end up with ultimately high electricity bills for consumers, which works against electrification.” The EIB has increased its support for grids eightfold in five years, reaching €12bn last year, including €1.6bn for the Bay of Biscay interconnector between Spain and France, and is developing new instruments such as hybrid bonds. Verougstraete called for more creative European financing to lower the cost of grid investment: “We will pay the price afterwards if we don’t do it today.”

Stronger grids are also central to closing the price gap between electricity and fossil fuels. Lopez-Nicolas pointed out that in some countries electricity is four times more expensive than gas, largely because of the taxes, levies and charges loaded onto electricity bills: “We cannot electrify if in some countries electricity is four times more expensive than gas.” The Commission’s Electrification Action Plan recommends that member states bring this ratio down to around two for industry. Jørgensen made the same case for lower taxes on electricity: “any economist will tell you that this is the way to do it”.

If we don’t keep a handle on the cost of capital, there is a risk that we end up with ultimately high electricity bills for consumers, which works against electrification – Edward Calthrop

AI and data centres: rising demand, shared responsibility

The need for grids is all the more pressing because electricity demand is growing fast, driven in part by data centres. Global electricity demand from data centres grew by 17% in 2025, and by around 50% for those optimised for AI, according to Alex Martinos of the International Energy Agency, and is set to roughly double by the end of the decade. At the same time, Europe’s share of global data centre capacity has fallen from around 25% ten years ago to around 15%. Ian Catlow, Head of London’s European Office, noted that London already hosts more than 90 data centres and expects their energy demand to grow tenfold over 25 years.

Melanie Nakagawa, Chief Sustainability Officer at Microsoft, described how data centres can integrate sustainably into the grid, helping to finance new clean power and to make better use of existing networks. She framed their role as that of an enabler, an innovator and a collaborator, pointing out that Microsoft has signed agreements for more than 40 gigawatts of clean energy worldwide, including over 9 gigawatts in Europe, while AI-powered tools are already helping grid operators move more power through the lines they have. She also called for clarity on grid connection queues, so that “projects that are first ready should get first served”, based on clear milestones such as land permits and secured financing. Speakers nonetheless stressed that computing capacity must develop alongside generation, storage and grids, without shifting costs onto other consumers.

projects that are first ready should get first served – Melanie Nakagawa

Adam Elman, Sustainability Director at Google, presented the company’s energy blueprint for responsible data centre growth, built on three pillars. The first is to make data centres an asset for the grid rather than passive power consumers: in Finland, where Google has announced a €13bn expansion, its largest single investment in Europe, the new data centres are sited in the north, away from congested parts of the grid, while in Belgium battery storage helps to relieve the grid at peak times. The second is to bring new clean energy onto the grid so that other consumers do not face higher prices, with around 4.5 gigawatts already contracted in Europe as part of Google’s goal to run on carbon-free energy around the clock. The third is to support the communities that host its sites, for example by supplying waste heat from its data centre in Hamina, Finland, which meets 80% of local heating needs at no cost. On policy, Elman called for grid connection rules that give priority to projects that are ready to be built, noting that connections can currently take seven to thirteen years.

Corinna Grajetzky, Director for European Affairs at ENGIE, described the goal as “not only a twin transition, it’s a twin development”, with data centres planned together with generation, transmission and flexibility, and powered by additional, dedicated carbon-free energy. She pointed to ENGIE’s partnership with Google in Germany, the first 24/7 carbon-free energy agreement in Europe, which is designed to match 80% of Google’s German electricity consumption with carbon-free power on an hourly basis. Flexibility, she added, is essential: “We need to have flexibility in mind, because otherwise decarbonisation costs by 2050 will be 70% higher than they need to be.”

The European Compact for AI Infrastructure, a policy paper published by Friends of Europe at the summit, proposes shared responsibilities between industry, public authorities, grid operators and communities to support this joint development. Speakers also cautioned that AI brings new risks for critical infrastructure, from cybersecurity to rising water use, which must be managed as carefully as the opportunities.

The challenge is therefore not simply to accommodate growing electricity demand, but to ensure that digital infrastructure develops in a way that strengthens energy systems, safeguards water resources and delivers tangible benefits for local communities.

We need to have flexibility in mind, because otherwise decarbonisation costs by 2050 will be 70% higher than they need to be – Corinna Grajetzky

A transition that must work for citizens

Affordability remained central throughout the summit, not least because even in an average year, as Jørgensen noted, around 47 million Europeans struggle to heat their homes adequately, and this year will be worse. “We will never decarbonise if we don’t deal with inequality and poverty at the same time,” said Dixson-Declève, warning that failure to address the affordability of energy and food will push more voters towards populism. She called for taxing the windfall profits of fossil fuel companies to fund a just transition.

Dinner participants stressed that the poorest households cannot afford heat pumps or renovation without support, and that public money must enable the transition, as Europe has done for defence. Corredor Sierra summed up the human dimension: “The missing word here is people.”

We will never decarbonise if we don’t deal with inequality and poverty at the same time – Sandrine Dixson-Declève

Conclusion

Taken together, the discussions pointed to a clear roadmap: protect people and ecosystems from a climate that is already changing, resist short-term fixes that deepen fossil fuel dependency, and make electrification work through clean industry, secure supply chains, connected grids and responsible growth in digital infrastructure. The obstacle is less a lack of solutions than the time it takes to deliver them, as Jørgensen acknowledged: “the biggest problem is the discrepancy between the need for action now and the fact that most of the action we can do will not work tomorrow or the day after, even next year.” Yet, he added, “things are going in the right direction. But it’s not going fast enough.”

Gil Tertre made the closing case for consistency, reminding the audience that industrial transformation unfolds over 30 to 40 years, and planning and regulation, far from working against the private sector, provide the certainty that investors need in an unstable world. “You cannot change your energy strategy every year or every two years. That does not make sense,” he said. “It is extremely important that we stay the course.” With climate, security and competitiveness now pointing in the same direction, there is, as he put it, “no more trilemma for the EU”.

The challenge for Europe is no longer simply to define its climate and energy ambitions, but to create the political consistency, investment conditions and public trust needed to deliver them at the necessary speed and scale.
