text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

November 19, 2026

CONTACT

Amelia Covington

(919) 265-9996

amelia@downhomenc.org

Ridge Graham

(828) 994-7444

ridge@appvoices.org

A coalition of community-based organizations — including Appalachian Voices, Down Home North Carolina, North Carolina Asian Americans Together, North Carolina League of Conservation Voters, North Carolina Black Alliance and Robeson County Cooperative for Sustainable Development — denounces the North Carolina Utilities Commission’s decision to allow Duke Energy to raise its electric rates and exacerbate the ever-increasing affordability crisis in North Carolina.

On Nov. 16, the North Carolina Utilities Commission approved rate hikes of approximately 9.5% over two years for Duke Energy Carolinas customers (Charlotte, Triad, Piedmont and Western North Carolina) and 9.3% for Duke Energy Progress customers (Triangle, Eastern North Carolina and Asheville area) over the next two years. The commission also approved a return on equity, or a guaranteed profit from customers, of 9.8%, higher than the national average of 9.7%.

Duke Energy customers have seen their bills increase by almost 45% since 2020 as a result of a multi-year rate hike approved in 2023 and four annual fuel adjustment increases tied to rising fossil fuel costs. As of this August, one in five customers are a month behind on payments. These additional increases will impact communities across the state already struggling with high bills.

Duke Energy is also building and requesting to build many new electricity generation plants across the state to meet the company’s projected demand from data centers, which will lead to more requests from Duke Energy to raise customers’ bills. Most of these new plants are gas-fired, which will make annual fuel adjustments more dramatic, as spikes in the price of methane gas will result in significant increases.

Organizations across the state are encouraging North Carolinians to contact their state legislators and urge them to enact stronger policies next year to protect ratepayers from further rising costs.

Coalition statements::

“Duke Energy has few incentives to lower its energy costs. The NC Utilities Commission has approved a return on equity of 9.8% that is too high for a company that is legally allowed to charge its customers for the cost of building new infrastructure before it is complete and even if it is never finished. The state legislature needs to seriously consider reforming this as other states have. If Duke Energy was required to cover 10% or more of its energy costs, ratepayers would save tens of millions of dollars.” – Ridge Graham, North Carolina Program Manager, Appalachian Voices

“This year, North Carolinians turned out in record numbers to demand relief from skyrocketing bills, calling out Duke Energy’s corporate greed. By joining together across the state and raising our voices, Duke Energy was forced to slash its original rate hike of 18%, but a 9.5% hike is still too high a burden on families already struggling to meet skyrocketing costs of gas, groceries, housing and healthcare. Now is the time for our state legislators to heed the call and deliver clean, affordable, reliable energy to power our lives.” – Amelia Covington, Statewide Climate Coalition Coordinator, Down Home North Carolina

“North Carolina is growing, but working families shouldn’t foot the bill for that growth. Electricity is a necessity, not a luxury, and affordability must come before corporate profits. Duke may have the power to raise rates, but communities will hold it accountable. Voters’ power doesn’t expire on Election Day. We stand ready to support decisionmakers who will create policies that place all ratepayers ahead of corporate bottom lines.” – Shruti Parikh, Director of Education and Policy Engagement, NCAAT

“This ruling by the NC Utilities Commission, the majority of whom were appointed by Republican leadership at the General Assembly and the state treasurer, is a slap in the face to North Carolinians trying to make ends meet. Instead of putting our people first, they continue to prioritize sweetheart deals for Duke Energy and its shareholders.” – Carrie Clark, Executive Director, NC League of Conservation Voters

“With the continual rise of ratepayer utility rates and growing concerns about hurricanes, droughts, forest fires and data centers, perhaps it’s time for North Carolina to pass a law that bans regulated utilities from making political donations. They are not the same as independent, private corporations that don’t have a public service mission. If this ban on monetary political influence was placed on the ballot as a constitutional amendment, it would most likely pass with votes across the political spectrum.” – Rev. Mac Legerton, Co-Director, Robeson County Cooperative for Sustainable Development

Dive Brief: Google has signed an agreement to purchase 50 MW of electricity from Project Obsidian, a geothermal power project that Quaise Energy is developing near Newberry Volcano in central Oregon, the companies announced this week.

Dive Brief:

Google has signed an agreement to purchase 50 MW of electricity from Project Obsidian, a geothermal power project that Quaise Energy is developing near Newberry Volcano in central Oregon, the companies announced this week.

The project is intended to supply firm, carbon-free electricity to Google’s data center operations in The Dalles, Oregon, possibly as early as 2030. The deal is valued at more than $500 million, a Quaise spokesperson told Utility Dive.

The initial development phase will use conventional drilling technology; a subsequent phase will use millimeter-wave drilling technology to access superhot geothermal conditions. Altogether, the two-stage buildout is expected to cost about $350 million.

Dive Insight:

Google’s agreement with Quaise gives superhot geothermal an important commercial partner as developers seek to move enhanced geothermal systems from demonstration projects to utility-scale deployment.

“Geothermal energy remains largely underutilized. It supplies less than 0.5% of global electricity and is limited to just a handful of states in the U.S.,” Diane Hughes, senior vice president of marketing and communications at Quaise, said in an email.

Unlike conventional geothermal plants, which depend on naturally occurring underground hot-water reservoirs that are geographically constrained and rarely exceed 400 degrees Fahrenheit, enhanced geothermal uses engineered reservoirs to access heat in deeper rock formations.

Quaise is developing millimeter-wave drilling designed to ablate rock without mechanical contact. The company is designing wells to reach depths of up to 65,000 feet, where rock temperatures can exceed 932 degrees Fahrenheit and conventional drill bits cannot withstand the heat, according to Hughes.

“Superhot wells like these can produce up to 10x more power per well than what’s currently in play and bring geothermal to places where it isn’t viable or economical today,” she said.

The agreement comes as technology companies increasingly seek firm power sources to meet data center demand. Google has signed nearly 35 GW of clean energy purchase agreements globally since 2010, including previous investments in next-generation geothermal, according to its most recent environmental report. Google says its three Oregon data center campuses are sourced with 83% carbon-free energy.

Google is also pursuing other emerging technologies, including advanced nuclear power and long-duration energy storage, as part of its efforts to achieve net-zero emissions.

title: Data Centers' Power Grab Threatens U.S. Climate Progress

text:
Why are some of the largest tech companies in the United States many of which have publicly committed to fully decarbonizing their energy supply—planning to build massive on-site fossil fuel generators to power their data centers? The way that the industry is planning to meet its need for speed threatens to set back U.S. climate progress, generate harmful air pollution, and hurt surrounding communities for decades. It doesn’t have to be this way.

The United States is experiencing an unprecedented build-out of large-scale data centers that often each consume the same amount of energy as an entire city. By 2030, data centers could consume as much as 649 terawatt-hours (TWh) a year, representing more than a tenth of all electricity consumed in the country. Yet growth of this magnitude hinges on the ability to rapidly increase energy supply at a speed and scale that the United States hasn’t accomplished in more than 50 years, and grid interconnection processes (which have been slow and arduous, long before the data center boom) now face backlogs of five to seven years in some regions.

The AI industry is highly competitive and incredibly well financed, and it values the speed of building new data centers above all else. As a result, many data centers are speeding up their energization by supplying their own power with new fossil fuel resources on-site, independent of the grid, aka, behind the meter (BTM).

Data centers with BTM generation still often connect to the grid for supplemental power supply to maintain 24/7/365 power supply rather than being “islanded,” which means being totally powered without a grid connection (though there are an increasing number of proposals for islanded data centers).

Even so, BTM gas generation is more polluting than supplying a data center 100 percent from the grid, even when much of the grid electricity comes from gas-powered plants. (This is because more conventional grid-connected combined cycle gas plants are less polluting, more efficient, and better regulated than many of the fossil assets being pursued in BTM constructs, such as reciprocating internal combustion engines, repurposed jet engines, etc.).

The scale of the potential build-out is alarming. The number of BTM gas projects in the United States doubled in the first half of 2026 alone, with experts tracking anywhere from 90 gigawatts (GW) to 177 GW of proposed BTM gas projects. This could generate the same amount of electricity that 68 million to 133 million average households consume in a year (assuming the new generators operate at 90 percent of their full capacity).

title: Environmentalists Have a Wish List for Democrats - Earth Island Institute
authors: Jason Dove Mark, Kang-Chun Cheng, Rahiem Shadad, Carolyn Murphy, Dan Sedran, Hilary Beaumont, The Guardian, Camilla Capasso
description:
Antipathy to data centers is based, in part, on worries about the water-guzzling and sprawling landscape impacts.
And when Democrats take control of Congress and many states come January, environmentalists hope they will be able to incorporate some of their goals into Democrats’ legislative priorities.
Environmentalists say one way to tackle administration corruption is to call attention to the unseemly nexus between Trump and Big Oil.
Which brings us to the final item on environmentalists’ wish list.
Data centers are top of mind, Chieffo says.
text:
Some people have made the case that the nearly unprecedented blue wave was a “green wave,” too. That seems a bit overstated to me; climate change barely registered as a motivating factor for most voters, who cast their ballots based on frustrations over affordability and anger at the Trump administration’s greasy corruption.

But squint just right, and you can see a seafoam-green edge to the Democratic tsunami. Concerns over high energy prices and the war against Iran obviously connect to climate and energy policy. Antipathy to data centers is based, in part, on worries about the water-guzzling and sprawling landscape impacts. It’s not hard to draw a straight line from voter rage over the Trump family’s self-dealing to the White House’s giveaways to the oil, gas, and coal industries.

Environmental groups — including the Center for Biological Diversity, the League of Conservation Voters, and the Sierra Club — are confident that they can surf the blue wave. And when Democrats take control of Congress and many states come January, environmentalists hope they will be able to incorporate some of their goals into Democrats’ legislative priorities. Here’s a rundown of some of the green groups’ aspirations.

Reclaim the Power of the Purse

Article I of the Constitution is unmistakably clear that the “Power To lay and collect Taxes … to pay the Debts and provide for … the general Welfare” resides with Congress. The Republican-controlled 119th Congress, to its unending discredit, surrendered that power as it allowed the Trump administration to illegally impound or rescind funds appropriated by Congress. Environmentalists are hoping a Democratic-controlled Congress will use the power of the purse to repair some of the federal agencies in charge of environmental stewardship and research that were hollowed out by DOGE and Republican legislators’ supine acquiescence.

“While we were hiring 70,000 ICE officers, we were firing thousands of [Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)] officials and Fish and Wildlife Service officials,” Brett Hartl, government affairs director at the Center for Biological Diversity, tells me. “And I think at least now there’s the opportunity that we can sort of rebalance things and bring a little more semblance of normalcy back to just the basic functioning of government.”

Expect to see environmental groups not only push for a restoration of federal budgets for the EPA, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the Department of Energy, and the Department of the Interior back to a Biden-administration baseline, but to also demand that appropriation bills include minimum staffing levels — the kind of explicit directive that will make it difficult for the White House to attempt illegal work-arounds.

Help with High Energy Costs

It’s all but certain that one of Democrats’ first moves in 2027 will be to pass some kind of bill(s) that speak to voters’ worries about affordability. Environmental groups say that addressing energy costs must be part of a broader affordability agenda. “Trump’s failed energy policies were an economic disaster, and a political disaster for Republicans across the country,” says Sara Chieffo, senior vice president for government affairs at the League of Conservation Voters. Step one to addressing that failed energy policy, Chieffo tells me, will be to provide people with immediate relief from skyrocketing energy bills. “What lives in that bucket? Helping families through low-income heating assistance programs, through weatherization, through direct bill assistance, through banning shutoffs of energy for a certain segment of the population that are really carrying a huge amount of energy debt.”

Step two will be to reinvest in renewable energy sources like wind, solar, and battery storage, which are now the cheapest energy sources to bring online. Expect environmentalists to push members of Congress to restore household renewable-energy tax credits for things like rooftop solar and heat pump installation that were created by the Inflation Reduction Act before getting trashed by Republicans in 2025.

End Fossil Fuel Giveaways

According to some polls, government corruption eclipsed even high prices as a top voter concern in the midterms. Environmentalists say one way to tackle administration corruption is to call attention to the unseemly nexus between Trump and Big Oil. “Back in the [2024 presidential election], Trump said at Mar-a-Lago, ‘Give us a billion dollars and we’ll do whatever you want,” Chieffo says. “And you’ve seen polluters being given the keys to the administration.”

One tactic for highlighting the collusion between the White House and the fossil fuel industry would be to repeal the sweetheart deals oil and gas developers have been given for drilling on federal lands. “Let’s return the royalty rate to what it was under the Biden administration for drilling on public lands,” Katharine Groetzinger, from the Center for Western Priorities, tells me. “Putting back into place a methane royalty would be great.”

Here’s an even more ambitious notion: Institute a windfall profit tax on oil corporations. The oil industry has made a killing off the Iran War, earning $130 billion in profits from April to September, according to The New York Times. This is nearly a direct transfer of wealth from ordinary Americans’ wallets to Big Oil coffers, as Americans have spent an extra $147 billion on gasoline and diesel since the Trump administration launched its reckless conflict.

Chieffo says the League of Conservation Voters is looking at a windfall profits tax. So is the Sierra Club. “We’re going to work to hold big polluters accountable, close loopholes, enact a windfall profits tax, and eliminate subsidies that the fossil fuel industry has enjoyed,” Patrick Drupp, the organization’s director of climate policy, told Sierra Club members in a post-election call.

Enforce Accountability

In addition to the power of the purse, one of Congress’s most important constitutional functions is its oversight of the executive branch. “I want to see [congressional Democrats] use their constitutional authority and prerogative and bring impeachment inquiries to the officials in the government,” Hartl says.

Top of his list is Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum. “What the heck was Doug Burgum doing in Venezuela? People kind of forget that we took over a country illegally, installed our own leader, and now we are running their entire economy and making all of these weird oil and mineral deals.”

The US has collected at least $12 billion in Venezuelan oil revenue since the American military abducted Nicolas Maduro at the beginning of the year. Although the US government says 99 percent of those funds have been returned to Venezuela, Democratic lawmakers are likely to continue asking tough questions about the arrangement — questions now backed up by subpoena power.

Also expect green groups to push for investigations into the Bureau of Land Management’s moves to put data centers on public lands and the White House notion of trading away part of Yosemite National Park.

Defend Public Lands

Just a week after the election, the Department of the Interior released a four-year plan that, among other things, calls for selling off federal public lands. Conservation groups hope they’ll be able to work with allies on Capitol Hill to short-circuit such a scheme.

A good place for them to begin is by making a fresh attempt to pass some version of the Public Lands in Public Hands Act. Old-fashioned lands protection is overwhelming popular, with support crossing partisan lines, and conservationists think they have a good chance of passing a public lands bill, perhaps even with a veto-proof majority.

“I think that [congressional Democrats] should push hard and make Republicans pick a side for real,” Groetzinger says. “Even if Trump doesn’t sign it, I think that’s a strong messaging bill that would force people to express their values.”

Lean into Transportation and Farm Bills

The incoming Congress has a raft of multi-year funding bills to consider, and environmentalists are focused on two of them: the Surface Transportation Reauthorization and the Farm Bill.

The Biden-era, bipartisan infrastructure bill expired in September, and environmentalists are hoping to help craft a new multi-year transportation law that will make new investments in rail and other forms of mass transit while also funding EV charging infrastructure. “There’s a big upcoming opportunity around the Surface Transportation Reauthorization Bill to make it a much bigger bill that really centers infrastructure investments,” Chieffo says. “Transit helps people with some of those high energy costs.”

Hartl points out that — due to the see-sawing control of Congress in recent years — this will be the first time in two decades that Democrats will have the chance to write the Farm Bill, which normally is reauthorized every five years. The Farm Bill is about much more than farmer subsidies and food assistance. “The farm bill has billions of dollars in play when it comes to on-the-ground conservation, climate change mitigation, water pollution,” Hartl says. “These seem like relatively dull, in-the-weeds, wonky things. But when you put them all together, they make a difference I think is huge.”

Challenge Data Centers

If there was any marquee election issue that was explicitly environmental, it was the widespread concern about data centers. In case you missed it, people hate ’em. They don’t like data centers’ sprawl; they don’t like the noise they generate; and they are worried about how they might impact energy prices and overall carbon pollution (more than 25 million metric tons of carbon dioxide annually, or more than all of Denmark). They’re also concerned about how much water they use to cool down all the servers that are serving up AI slop.

What might this look like? At the very least, it could involve higher taxes on data center companies, requirements that they bring their own energy (ideally, renewable energy) to the grid, and more environmental safeguards around their operations. Another idea is a national moratorium prohibiting data center construction on federal lands. “I think the numbers are there for that,” Groetzinger says. “That would put Trump in the very awkward position of having to either veto that or sign it.”

Ultimately, though, most decisions about the fate of data centers are made at the local and state level. Which brings us to the final item on environmentalists’ wish list.

Drive Environmental Progress in State Houses

In addition to their sweeping gains in Congress, Democrats also scored big at the state level, as they flipped more than 500 state house seats, won governors races even in Texas and Georgia, and secured full Democratic control, known as a “trifecta,” in six new states. Environmentalists will be looking to their Democratic allies at the state level to help advance their local climate change and conservation priorities.

Data centers are top of mind, Chieffo says.

So is passing state laws to speed the transition to renewable energy. In Wisconsin, lawmakers hope to revive legislation that would set clean energy targets for the state’s utilities and establish carbon pollution-reduction goals. Ditto for Arizona, where legislators want to lock into law renewable energy requirements that the state canned earlier this year. In Pennsylvania, environmentally-minded elected officials want to pass climate legislation and make new investments in public transit. And environmentalists are maneuvering to replicate a major victory that occurred in Michigan, where voters overwhelmingly passed a ballot measure to ban political donations from utilities, their high-level employees, and their lobbyists.

Altogether, the 2026 elections represent an unmistakable rebuke to Trumpism. But, of course, the myriad threats to the environment — from biodiversity loss to water scarcity to greenhouse gas pollution — remain. For environmentalists, the victory of their closest political allies is only a provisional win. “This election was sort of a tourniquet on the bleeding,” Groetzinger says.

Now that environmentalists have friends in high places, it’s time to start the healing.

description:

[9] Ford Energy recently announcing a five-year framework agreement with EDF power solutions North America for up to 20 GWh of battery energy storage systems.
Energy Storage Contracts, Performance Warranties, and Product Liability Moving from EVs to stationary storage is not just about retooling.
Authors The authors are available to discuss energy storage, data centers, supply chain and related matters.
[14] Q1 2026: Data Center Watch Report, Data Ctr.
text:
Key Takeaways:

Energy storage offers automotive manufacturers and suppliers a potential outlet for underused EV battery capacity, as demand from utilities, the grid, and data centers continues to grow.

Pivoting from EVs to energy storage requires more than retooling manufacturing lines. Companies should assess existing incentives and financing arrangements, § 48E tax credit requirements, supply-chain restrictions, and contract terms before committing capacity.

Energy storage creates distinct warranty, operational, and product liability risks, particularly around long-term battery performance, project delays, data center service requirements, cybersecurity, and fire and environmental exposure. Companies should structure contracts, insurance, and liability protections accordingly.

The automotive industry prepared for an electric vehicle (EV) future that has not yet come to fruition. In 2024, forecasters projected that EVs would account for 46% to 50% of U.S. passenger vehicle sales by 2030; more recent projections put that figure at just 20% to 24%.[1] At the same time, demand for energy storage systems (ESS) is surging, driven by utility and grid needs and, increasingly, by the power demands of data centers and the artificial intelligence (AI) economy. A growing number of EV manufacturers and suppliers are now redirecting underused battery capacity toward stationary energy storage. The opportunity is real, but so are the risks: storage is a different business, with different customers, contract structures, and liability exposures. This article outlines the key incentive, contract, warranty, and product liability issues that in-house legal and business leaders should address before making the pivot from EV to ESS.

Why EV Battery Manufacturers Are Pivoting to Energy Storage Systems

EVs reached a record 10.6% share of U.S. new-vehicle sales in the third quarter of 2025, as buyers rushed to claim expiring federal incentives.[2] That share then fell to roughly 5.8% in the first half of 2026, reflecting federal policy changes and rising production costs.[3] [4] Although third-quarter 2026 sales reached their highest volume in a year,[5] few in the industry expect a near-term return to the growth curves that justified recent EV capacity investments.

The energy storage market offers a timely outlet for idle EV capacity. According to a September 1, 2026 report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), the market is growing 32% year-over-year.[6] The U.S. installed a record 18.9 GWh of battery storage in the second quarter of 2026.[7] At least eight major battery plants in the U.S. are being retooled for energy storage.[8]

Major automakers are already moving. Ford and GM have both entered the energy storage market.[9] Ford Energy recently announcing a five-year framework agreement with EDF power solutions North America for up to 20 GWh of battery energy storage systems.[10] For suppliers, these moves signal both a new customer base and a new competitive landscape.

Energy Storage Tax Credits, Financing, and Incentive Clawback Risks

Many EV lines were financed with state and local incentives, federal loans, and joint venture capital, often tied expressly to vehicle programs. Before redirecting a line to energy storage, companies should review those governing documents to confirm that the new use is permitted, that any job-creation, investment, and production commitments can still be met, and whether lender, agency, or joint venture partner consents or amendments are needed to avoid clawbacks or covenant defaults. Approaching grantors and lenders early, with a plan that preserves headcount and investment, generally puts a company in a stronger position than seeking relief after a milestone has been missed.

Federal tax rules add another layer of complexity, particularly for customers that depend on the energy storage tax credit. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act added new definitions of “prohibited foreign entity” and “material assistance” to the Internal Revenue Code and bars the § 48E investment credit for energy storage technology that includes disqualifying material assistance from such an entity.[11] For energy storage, a project fails the test if less than 55% of its manufactured-product costs are free of prohibited foreign entity content for construction beginning in 2026, rising to 75% for construction beginning after 2029.[12] Interim IRS guidance issued in February 2026, Notice 2026-15, allows taxpayers to rely on existing safe harbor tables or signed supplier certifications to make that calculation, as discussed in Foley’s prior client alert. It also confirms that a license with a covered foreign entity entered into or modified on or after July 4, 2025 can disqualify a project from the credit.[13] Proposed regulations and new safe harbor tables are still to come, so the rules may change during a multi-year supply term. Because storage developers and their financiers often rely on that credit, foreign-entity compliance is not just a tax issue; it is a commercial term that can determine whether a supplier wins the business. Manufacturers that license battery technology, or source materials and components, from foreign parties should review those arrangements before extending them to storage products. They also should expect customers to demand supply-chain certifications, documentation and cooperation covenants, and indemnities for lost credits.

Energy Storage Contracts, Performance Warranties, and Product Liability

Moving from EVs to stationary storage is not just about retooling. It also means moving into a different commercial model, with different customers, risk allocation, and performance expectations. Supply terms built for vehicle programs rarely fit without significant revision. Data center customers, in particular, may procure storage directly, through developers and integrators, or through utility and power purchase arrangements, and the supplier’s obligations will often be shaped by contacts to which it is not a party.

Offtake structure. Storage offtake looks different from a vehicle supply program, where volumes typically follow an OEM’s production schedule and releases. Suppliers of energy storage components should consider minimum-volume or take-or-pay commitments, price adjustment mechanisms for commodity and tariff changes, and schedule relief when a customer’s own permitting or interconnection delays push out delivery dates.

Data center requirements. Data center owners and operators commonly impose uptime, availability, and service-level commitments on their vendors, and may seek to flow those commitments down to storage suppliers through system integrators. Suppliers should resist open-ended service-level credits tied to the customer’s own uptime obligations, define their performance commitments at the equipment level, and expect requests for site-specific safety certifications, on-site service response times, and spare-parts commitments. Because storage systems are frequently monitored and updated remotely, suppliers also should expect cybersecurity, data-access, and confidentiality requirements, and should address in the contract who owns and may use system operating data.

Project delay and cancellation risk. Energy storage demand is more exposed to external factors than automotive supply. Fire codes, local permitting, and utility interconnection queues all affect project timing. Local opposition to data centers, a growing source of storage demand, is also mounting. Data Center Watch reports that local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 data center projects worth about $130 billion in the first quarter of 2026[14] and another 45 projects worth about $68 billion in the second quarter.[15] Not every delayed data center project includes energy storage, but each delay can ripple through the supply chain. Supply contracts should specifically address cancellation and suspension rights, termination charges, and who bears the cost of warehousing finished product when a customer’s project is delayed.

Warranty exposure. Standard automotive warranty terms are often a poor fit for storage. Stationary systems may be expected to cycle frequently, often daily, operate continuously, and endure site-specific environmental conditions. Buyers commonly seek long-term commitments on capacity retention, round-trip efficiency, and availability, often with serial-defect remedies and obligations to augment capacity as cells degrade. These obligations can run a decade or more, and much of the risk sits in system integration and operating conditions rather than in the cell itself. Suppliers should tie warranty coverage to defined duty cycles, temperature limits, and access to monitoring data; cap aggregate warranty liability; and align upstream cell and component warranties with downstream commitments so the supplier is not left holding the gap.

Product liability and fire risk. Product liability is always a significant concern for automotive suppliers, but the economic and legal stakes may be greater for energy storage, where large volumes of cells are concentrated at a single site. A single thermal event at a battery installation can damage a significant share of the cells on site, cause government-supervised environmental cleanup, and prompt negligence, nuisance, and other claims from neighboring residents and businesses. As a result, exposure can extend well beyond the value of the product. Suppliers should revisit their insurance programs, indemnity and limitation-of-liability provisions, and compliance with applicable safety standards and fire codes before entering the market.

A Hedge, Not a Replacement

Energy storage can keep EV-era plants productive, but it is a competitive market subject to rapidly shifting demand. Even as overall installations hit records, utility-scale installations fell 8% year-over-year as key markets became saturated.[16] Domestic producers’ advantages also rest on tax and trade policies that may change. The strongest hedge is flexibility: plants, contracts, and licenses that allow capacity to shift between vehicle and storage products as demand moves.

Before committing manufacturing capacity to energy storage, stakeholders should ask:

Do our joint venture, incentive, loan, and license documents permit the change, and what consents are required?

Do our technology licenses and supply chain allow customers to claim the § 48E credit, and are we prepared to certify and stand behind that compliance?

Are customer commitments firm enough to support the investment, and who bears the risk of project delays?

For data center customers, have we limited flow-down of uptime and service-level commitments, and address cybersecurity, remote access, and data rights?

Are our insurance coverage, indemnities, and liability caps calibrated to the fire and environmental risks of large-scale storage?

Have we priced and reserved for long-term performance warranties under realistic operating conditions?

Can our plants, contracts, and licenses shift capacity back to vehicle programs if EV demand recovers?

Companies that treat the move from EVs to energy storage as a legal and commercial restructuring, not merely a retooling, will be best positioned to capture the opportunity while managing the risks inherent to the transition.

Authors

title: Reflections on the just energy transition and sustainable development deliberations at COP31
description:
highlighted the potential of renewable energy, particularly solar and wind, to support sustainable development across Africa.
Although renewable energy deployment is progressing, the continued reliance on fossil fuels presents a significant obstacle to achieving the 1.5°C goal.
The discussion on China's role in green industrialisation further developed this argument by examining how international partnerships can support renewable energy development and industrial capacity in the Global South.
A noteworthy example discussed was the Philippines, where collaboration with local government units has supported the development of renewable energy roadmaps.
China's involvement included pledges to support these initiatives through distributed renewable energy systems, alongside assistance in addressing limitations in electricity transmission infrastructure.
text:
Themes on energy justice

The session Renewables, Modern Grids, and Just and Affordable Electrification: What, Where and for Whom? highlighted the potential of renewable energy, particularly solar and wind, to support sustainable development across Africa. The emphasis on electrification as a tool for development demonstrated how access to energy can create employment opportunities, improve resilience and support electric mobility. The example of interconnectivity between Kenya, Ethiopia and Sudan illustrated the importance of regional cooperation in expanding energy access. This highlighted a broader consideration: energy transitions cannot be approached solely through individual national strategies, as regional infrastructure and collaboration are equally important in achieving affordability and accessibility.

This perspective was reinforced during a mandated event examining the socioeconomic impacts of response measures under the Global Stocktake (GST) and net-zero pathways. Although renewable energy deployment is progressing, the continued reliance on fossil fuels presents a significant obstacle to achieving the 1.5°C goal. However, accelerating the transition must not come at the expense of countries' differing development priorities. The economic implications vary considerably between countries such as Australia, Pakistan and emerging energy markets in Africa. While new industries may generate employment, existing jobs and export revenues can be lost, with particular communities bearing disproportionate consequences. The discussion around cross-border modelling and cooperation highlighted the limitations of applying universal net-zero pathways to countries with vastly different economic circumstances. It demonstrated that equal expectations do not necessarily produce equitable outcomes.

Value chains, investments and the role of China

Other sessions such as Just Energy Markets: Accelerating an Inclusive & Just Energy Transition through Economic Opportunity further explored the economic dimensions of an inclusive transition. Mexican Ambassador Patricia Espinosa Cantellano emphasised the importance of investing in research, infrastructure and skills to strengthen domestic industries. Discussions surrounding Indonesia illustrated how mineral-rich countries can remain economically dependent when they export raw materials without developing domestic manufacturing capacity. Similarly, the challenges facing micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) demonstrated how unequal access to finance can prevent smaller businesses from participating in the transition. These discussions raised important questions about who owns, finances and ultimately benefits from emerging green industries. A transition cannot be considered just if its economic opportunities remain concentrated among established industries and larger businesses.

The discussion on China's role in green industrialisation further developed this argument by examining how international partnerships can support renewable energy development and industrial capacity in the Global South. A noteworthy example discussed was the Philippines, where collaboration with local government units has supported the development of renewable energy roadmaps. China's involvement included pledges to support these initiatives through distributed renewable energy systems, alongside assistance in addressing limitations in electricity transmission infrastructure. This demonstrated how international cooperation can help countries overcome infrastructural barriers to electrification. The discussion also considered the importance of developing domestic manufacturing capabilities rather than remaining dependent on exporting raw materials and importing finished technologies. This was particularly relevant to mineral-rich African countries, where scholars emphasised the importance of building regional rather than exclusively national capacity to create economies of scale and strengthen domestic industries. These examples highlighted the potential of international partnerships to accelerate green industrialisation, while raising an important question about whether such cooperation creates lasting economic independence or reinforces existing dependencies within global supply chains.

Calls for international collaboration

The Fourth Annual High-Level Ministerial Round Table on Just Transition reinforced the significance of recognising different national circumstances within the UNFCCC framework. Nepal's intervention was particularly illustrative and seemed to voice the concerns of many developing countries, namely that despite contributing relatively little to global emissions, the country faces climate disasters that threaten its clean energy infrastructure. This exemplifies the disproportionate challenges faced by countries that have contributed least to climate change but encounter significant financial and technical barriers to achieving their climate objectives.

So far, COP31 has demonstrated that climate action cannot be evaluated solely through emissions reductions or the achievement of net-zero targets. Its success must also be measured through its socioeconomic outcomes, the distribution of opportunities and its contribution to sustainable development. The discussions reinforced the importance of differentiated national pathways, international cooperation and meaningful inclusion in ensuring that the energy transition is not only environmentally sustainable but also economically and socially just.

text:
Egypt is rapidly expanding its solar power capacity as part of its goal to source 42% of its electricity from renewables by 2030 and 65% by 2040.

The country currently gets most of its energy from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and petroleum, which account for roughly 87% of Egypt's electricity generation. Renewables make up around 13%, divided between 6% hydropower and 7% wind and solar.

Egypt’s solar PV capacity is projected to grow from roughly 2.9 GW to 34.3 GW by 2035, driving total national renewable capacity toward nearly 49.7 GW.

Egypt sits within the global “solar belt,” with the Western Desert and Upper Egypt receiving an exceptional solar irradiance of 2,000 to 3,200 kWh/m² annually.

Natural gas has long fueled Egypt's electricity grid. Scaling up solar power reduces domestic gas consumption, freeing up valuable gas reserves for export and foreign currency generation. Related: 5 Oil and Gas Stocks That Crushed Third-Quarter Earnings Estimates

Egypt faces massive costs from fossil fuel subsidies (around $7 billion annually) and soaring import expenses. Solar power is significantly cheaper to generate, costing roughly $0.02/kWh compared to over $0.06/kWh for fossil fuels, helping relieve public debt and state budgets.

Rising domestic demand and summer rolling blackouts have strained traditional power plants. Solar energy offsets daytime loads on conventional plants, increasing grid stability.

Egypt aims to source 42% of its electricity from renewable energy by 2030 and 60% to 65% by 2040 under its Integrated Sustainable Energy Strategy (ISES 2035). Large-scale installations like the Benban Solar Park, and the development of a solar energy plant in Upper Egypt with batteries supplied by a battery manufacturing facility in the Suez Canal Economic Zone are central to this transition.

Other major solar initiatives include the Obelisk Solar Power Project and Shams El-Senaa/ Industry Sun.

Developed with $600 million in investments and Chinese technology, the Obelisk solar farm in southern Egypt generates around 1.1 GW of electricity and features extensive battery storage and automated solar-powered cleaning robots.

The Egyptian government launched Shams El-Senaa targeting 1,000 MW (1 GW) of solar capacity across approximately 7,000 factories, alongside ongoing rollouts of solar systems on public and government building rooftops to cut operating costs and curb natural gas consumption.

Earlier this month, Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly reviewed implementation mechanisms with Minister of Electricity and Renewable Energy Mahmoud Esmat, directing that later phases be extended beyond factories to government buildings and other facilities, according to a Nov. 4 post on Instagram by CairoScene.

Madbouly said the initiative is intended to diversify energy sources, reduce production costs, improve industrial competitiveness and support the localization of solar manufacturing. He also stressed the need for efficient operation and maintenance, including regular inspections of panels, transformers, connection systems and control equipment, backed by specialized technical training.

Esmat said the program is expected to reduce factories’ electricity bills and natural gas consumption while supporting production efficiency and export competitiveness. He added that the initiative should also increase local content in renewable energy components and strengthen related industrial value chains.

A separate nationwide project is also being prepared to install solar power systems on government building rooftops. Both programs form part of the national energy strategy to increase the share of renewables in the energy mix and improve electricity-use efficiency.

As we reported in June, the government has sought external support for its energy strategy and the development of a diversified energy mix, with the European Commission having contracted the management consulting firm Cowater International to assess Egypt’s energy strategy over the next two decades.

In line with a greater openness to private investment, the government had signed around 32 Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) with private developers by 2025 to produce 1,465 MW of renewable energy, with additional agreements underway.

A May report by GlobalData says that, alongside solar, wind power capacity is expected to rise to nearly 15.1 GW, with the Gulf of Suez and Red Sea regions considered key locations.

Egypt is also preparing to introduce nuclear energy into its power mix. The El Dabaa nuclear power plant is expected to contribute around 4.4 GW to the national grid once operational. (Africa Energy Portal)

name: Clean Energy
title: BAAJA Doesn't Do Enough for Clean Energy In the Southeast
authors: Maggie Shober, Shelley Robbins, Eddy Moore, James Hauser
description:
In the Southeast in particular, where it is already much easier to permit and build fossil fuel infrastructure, the removal of impediments to both clean energy and fossil fuels is likely to help fossil fuels more than clean energy.
The intent of the permitting bill is clear — to ease impediments to building clean energy at the speed required to meet the demands of the clean energy transition.
SACE has long advocated for building more clean energy faster to reduce pollution, mitigate climate change, and lower customer bills.
These are all good and necessary steps to getting more clean energy through the interconnection grid and onto the grid faster.
Parts of BAAJA would help advance clean energy in the Southeast but are not applicable given our utility structure.
text:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), a federal permitting reform bill that represents a compromise between clean energy and fossil fuel industries and was first introduced in September, is under Senate consideration.

BAAJA contains several major infrastructure policy overhauls, including modernization of transmission planning that would support clean energy and undermining of existing biodiversity protections that would help fossil fuels.

In the Southeast in particular, where it is already much easier to permit and build fossil fuel infrastructure, the removal of impediments to both clean energy and fossil fuels is likely to help fossil fuels more than clean energy.

Proponents of the bill argue that the lack of proactive regional transmission planning is stalling clean energy deployment, and that BAAJA will lead to transmission that can unlock it. Proponents claim that better transmission planning will level the playing field for clean energy to compete against fossil fuels.

Critics argue that fossil fuel projects already have an easier time getting built, and bringing down potential roadblocks for them does not level the playing field, particularly in the Southeast, where vertically integrated utilities control transmission planning instead of an independent, wholesale transmission operator.

The intent of the permitting bill is clear — to ease impediments to building clean energy at the speed required to meet the demands of the clean energy transition. SACE has long advocated for building more clean energy faster to reduce pollution, mitigate climate change, and lower customer bills.

While we support the intent and key aspects of the bill, SACE cannot support a permitting bill that gives fossil fuels so much of a giveaway and doesn’t do enough to level the playing field for clean energy here in the Southeast.

If BAAJA is going to promote clean energy for the Southeast, it must be reworked to strengthen provisions for non-market regions and soften the giveaways to the fossil fuel industry.

The Good: Modernized Transmission Planning

BAAJA’s transmission provisions include changes to both planning and permitting. Since the Southeast is behind the rest of the country on planning, and permitting comes later in the transmission-building process, the bill’s transmission planning provisions are more immediately relevant in the Southeast.

BAAJA codifies existing regional transmission planning regulations, requires inter-regional transmission planning, empowers state commissions to investigate a utility if it has concerns that the utility’s local transmission planning practices are harming customers, and requires transmission organizations to speed interconnection for generation resources. These are all good and necessary steps to getting more clean energy through the interconnection grid and onto the grid faster. However, the Southeast, with its vertically-integrated utility structure, will be left behind.

First, the important steps toward a consolidated planning process between transmission and generation, that is both transparent and proactive, are what SACE has been advocating for in the Southeast for years. However, the manager’s amendment removes this requirement for vertically integrated regions. This is very convenient for the vertically-integrated utilities in the Southeast.

Second, the strengthening of FERC’s oversight of local transmission planning is also important. However, the bill’s provision on this matter leaves it up to state Commissions to petition FERC for this oversight. Many state Commissions in the Southeast are captured by the utilities they regulate and believe the utilities when they are told that transmission planning is going just fine and there’s no need for additional oversight.

The bill’s provisions on regional and interregional transmission planning apply to the Southeast and would help improve reliability and affordability in the long run, as well as potentially speed interconnection through stronger regional and interregional grids. However, in the Southeast, transparency and bias in transmission planning are ongoing issues, and the bill does nothing to fix the “black box” or utility incentives to continue to check the box for regional transmission planning while only building local transmission lines.

In addition to its planning provisions, the bill provides FERC the ability to backstop permitting for transmission in the national interest. If FERC had had that authority ten years ago, the Clean Line transmission line proposal that would have connected Oklahoma wind to the Southeast through Memphis could be energized today. With that line, Southeast utilities might not have had to resort to blackouts during Winter Storm Elliott in 2022.

The bill also specifies four categories of grid-enhancing technologies and requires utilities to use the best available technologies when the benefits exceed the cost. FERC must penalize any public utility that fails to deploy advanced transmission technologies when the applicable benefit-cost ratio exceeds one.

In the long run, many, but not all, transmission sections of the bill would benefit clean energy in the Southeast. But key transmission sections neglect the Southeast because of our vertically-integrated structure.

The Bad: Weakening Environmental and Consumer Protections

The Clean Water Act

Under BAAJA, benthic communities and wildlife, i.e., plants and animals that live on the bottom of the waterways, would no longer be considered in assessment for 401 state certification under the Clean Water Act, making the water quality itself the only metric for certification.

This provision would render Endangered Species Act reviews, which would also be shortened under BAAJA, effectively useless.

Also under this provision, transmission line and interstate pipeline assessment would be limited to “direct point sources,” meaning that damages caused by upland erosion during construction, a recurring issue in pipeline construction, and impacts to wetlands would no longer be considered in water quality standards assessments. Although pipeline construction poses numerous risks to water quality, it has few to no “direct point sources,” meaning states would have little grounds to deny 401 certification of a pipeline or transmission project.

Several additional water permitting weaknesses exist in BAAJA, but the direct point source restriction makes most of them moot.

The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)

Secretive Precedent Agreements

One proposed reform to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) states that “no federal agency shall be required to consider any specific or technical research that becomes publicly available after the date of publication of a notice of intent or a decision to prepare an environmental document for a proposed agency action.”

Under this regulation, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) could continue to depend exclusively on the secretive precedent agreements that pipeline companies sign with utilities to establish the “need” in a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) for a new pipeline project. Utilities profit from building gas infrastructure, have captive customers to pay the secret pipeline costs, are often affiliated with pipeline companies, and can be incentivized to self-deal. In these scenarios, the captive utility customers shoulder the risk if the pipeline capacity isn’t actually needed.

We think it’s important to look beyond a contract signed in secret to determine whether a project is in the public interest. SACE and partners have submitted research to challenge assumptions about data center load growth, market constraints, and design-day calculations by local gas distribution companies, adding to the context available to FERC to establish “need.” This work would be futile if BAAJA passes as-is.

Judicial Review

Currently, pipeline projects under NEPA judicial review are handled under the Administrative Procedure Act. BAAJA section 1110 changes the standing requirements for these reviews. At present, any party adversely affected by an agency decision can sue for any reason or issue raised by any other party in the comments. Under BAAJA, plaintiffs can sue only if they submitted comments, and only on the specific comments they submitted.

Challenging agency decisions has historically been a collective effort. Typically, organizations with different specialties — such as water, wildlife, or health impacts — analyze applications based on their expertise and submit comments accordingly. Given the short period citizens and advocacy groups have to analyze large applications, it is unlikely that one person or entity — even one with the means to sue — can identify every egregious or unlawful issue in the allotted time.

This update under BAAJA also prevents the court from vacating a permit or Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity, no matter how insufficient the NEPA documents are. The court may remand the deficient document back to the agency for correction, but the project authorization remains valid. The NEPA review process is severely weakened under these circumstances — agencies will be less likely to be sued due to restrictions on plaintiffs and comments, and even if they are sued, the project will continue.

A Major Weakness: The Certainty Provision

The “certainty” provision is advertised as a solution for companies whose permits have been revoked or modified by the federal government, such as a pipeline canceled after the Biden Administration revoked its permit, or offshore wind projects killed by the Trump Administration. Unfortunately, in the case of BAAJA, the solution may be worse than the problem.

BAAJA allows energy project proponents to sue the federal government if it unfairly delays permits for specific types of projects more than previous administrations did over 10 years. For instance, a proponent of a new gas pipeline project in 2029 could sue the federal government, alleging that it is delaying fossil fuel projects more than prior administrations did from 2019-2028. Because the Trump Administration held office during most of that prior period, it might be easy to show that the new administration is not as quick to permit fossil fuel projects, even if the delays are meant to protect public health and the environment.

Alarmingly, BAAJA states that the federal government would pay out tax dollars to these companies to compensate for any proven delays, costs that could run into the billions of dollars.

Obfuscated Language Works in Polluters’ Favor

Beyond creating a biased baseline, these provisions invite endless litigation from some of the largest monied interests in the country. Making the permitting process fast and irrevocable inherently advantages large, polluting projects over smaller clean energy projects, most of which are significantly cheaper and faster to build.

BAAJA also invites litigation over any effort to reduce pollution from existing power plants. For instance, if a future administration seeks to limit the number of hours that a highly-polluting power plant runs near a densely populated neighborhood, it would have to prove that the action is “necessary to prevent immediate, specific, urgent, substantial, and proximate harm or damage to life, property, human health, the environment, national security, or defense that is based on new information that was not considered in the underlying environmental review process or final agency action for the federal authorization or permit.”

If the new administration failed to meet these requirements, BAAJA would protect the “normal” operations of the power plant, which have no specific definition. We can expect power plant owners to argue that almost any rule or action limiting pollution will impair “normal” operations.

The language around this provision is elusive, making it nearly impossible to challenge polluters successfully. Even the severity of harm could be called into question — harm to human health or the environment would not be actionable if the government could not prove it was “immediate” or “proximate.” Even if “immediate, proximate harm” could be proven, the power plant owner could still argue that the limit is invalid because the underlying information was already considered in an earlier environmental review. Corporate lawyers will have a field day with this novel, extensive verbiage, and the likely result is that future public officials will simply leave existing power plants alone, even as science increasingly shows they harm human health.

A Bill That Works for Everyone

Parts of BAAJA are promising for the future of clean energy in the Southeast, particularly the requirement for regional and interregional transmission planning and the federal backstop for important transmission projects. Parts of BAAJA would help advance clean energy in the Southeast but are not applicable given our utility structure. Electric utilities in the Southeast have clean energy projects tied up in the interconnection process, but BAAJA applies its consolidated planning process only to regions with independent transmission operators. And perhaps most importantly, the Southeast has a bonanza of new fossil fuel projects, both pipelines and gas plants, driven by speculative data center demand projections. Locking the Southeast into continued reliance on fossil fuels by making them even easier to build does not outweigh the benefits the region would see from clean energy.

description:

Delegation members emphasized the need to prioritize policies that strengthen energy systems and reduce pollution by deploying affordable clean energy, as well as the importance of ensuring that America can compete in building an advanced clean energy economy.
The turnout of congressional, state, and business leaders at COP31, and their engagement with international partners on clean solutions and electrification, adds support for an ambitious COP31 agreement.
Clean energy is the fastest and cheapest way to meet rising power demand and address affordability.

text:
I am back home in Washington, D.C., after a fruitful long weekend at the 2026 United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye. My time there was filled with valuable conversations with companies, investors, policymakers, and advocacy partners about how the U.S. can deliver on affordability, security, and competitiveness by speeding up clean solutions and electrification.

The energy on the ground reflected growing demand in the U.S. for affordable clean energy. Voters in the recent midterm elections supported leaders at all levels of government who campaigned on solutions to bring down energy costs. The newly elected leaders must now deliver, and clean energy is the fastest way to do so.

COP31 is a moment to strengthen global momentum toward cleaner, affordable energy. That means expanding clean electrification, enacting durable national policies that give businesses certainty to invest in clean solutions, and scaling transition finance to build a stronger, more resilient economy.

Here are four major takeaways as COP31 heads into its final days of negotiations:

1/ U.S. Congress, businesses, and state leaders are committed to delivering affordable, clean electrification

At events throughout COP31, leaders from Congress, states, cities, and businesses across America reinforced their dedication to advancing a clean economy. Governors and mayors highlighted local climate solutions that are lowering energy costs, growing jobs, and cutting pollution in American communities. They also described how faster action can deliver cost savings and health benefits to American families and communities now and in the years ahead.

Businesses reaffirmed their support for shifting toward a clean, electrified economy. More than 180 companies representing more than $1.69 trillion in combined revenue signed on to the Seizing the Electric Advantage statement, organized by our partners at the We Mean Business Coalition, calling on governments to act with urgency on electrification and make clean electrification as a central pillar of economic and industrial strategy.

Our partners at the Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition (SEEC) Institute brought a delegation of 18 U.S. House members to COP31 to strengthen international partners and exchange solutions on shared climate, energy, and economic challenges. Delegation members emphasized the need to prioritize policies that strengthen energy systems and reduce pollution by deploying affordable clean energy, as well as the importance of ensuring that America can compete in building an advanced clean energy economy.

2/ U.S. and EU leaders are exchanging lessons on building a clean economy

I participated in several discussions with policymakers and business leaders from the U.S., Australia, Brazil, the UK, the European Union (EU), EU member states, South Africa, South Korea, and others on how to work together to advance clean power and electrification, and what it means for competitiveness and lower energy costs.

With newly elected leaders in the U.S. heading to Capitol Hill and statehouses across the country, there is an opportunity to deepen work with international partners and strengthen American leadership in advancing global goals. The turnout of congressional, state, and business leaders at COP31, and their engagement with international partners on clean solutions and electrification, adds support for an ambitious COP31 agreement.

3/ There is global momentum for clean electrification

Many governments, including Canada, Denmark, the European Union, Germany, Japan, Norway, Kyrgyzstan, South Korea, Spain, and the UK, are pushing to include the COP31 Presidency’s 35×35 goal to raise electricity’s share of global final energy demand to 35% by 2035 in the final agreement. The goal builds on previous commitments to triple renewables, double efficiency, and transition away from fossil fuels.

Electrification is a critical lever for economic growth and competitiveness. An agreement to scale electrification could help deliver lower energy bills, more secure energy supplies, cleaner air, and good-paying local jobs.

4/ Policymakers must follow through on pledges with practical action

To realize those benefits, leaders must advance policies that make electrification possible. Clear policies give investors and companies the direction and stability they need to invest. To deliver the benefits promised by past climate pledges, policymakers need to follow through with action.

So, what does that mean here in the U.S.? We need to streamline our permitting processes and modernize our power grid and transmission planning to be ready to meet the demands of an electrified economy. Clean energy is the fastest and cheapest way to meet rising power demand and address affordability. But the U.S. power grid is constrained by aging infrastructure and long waits for new projects to connect. Congress has an opportunity to fix these challenges with targeted clean energy incentives and permitting and transmission reforms to modernize our electric grid, build much-needed transmission lines, and speed the build-out of affordable, homegrown clean energy.

States and the federal government will be working on additional policies to secure the grid, accelerate the interconnection of clean energy resources, and expand energy efficiency and demand flexibility programs. Together, these policy solutions can help spur clean energy deployment and reduce costs for consumers.

name: North Carolina Environment
title: Modest fixes, major risks: North Carolina carbon plan and rate case order puts households at risk
description:
The rate cases for the first time begin to assign the grid costs incurred by data centers to their operators.
Then came the Carbon Plan order—and with it, a doubling down on expensive, risky fossil fuels.
Important issues unresolved Nowhere is the disconnect between utility planning and consumer protection clearer than on the issue of hyperscale data centers.
Data centers account for roughly 80% of the projected surge in new economic development electricity demand across the Carolinas.
At the same time, lawmakers should re-examine generous state tax breaks for data centers so taxpayer subsidies are tied directly to clean energy and grid-flexibility commitments.
text:
Key Takeaways

Families Face Higher Bills and Risky Fossil Bets: The Carbon Plan order doubles down on costly natural gas and coal instead of maximizing cheaper clean energy and federal tax credits.

Data Centers Still Leave Ratepayers Exposed: While the new Large Load Tariff is a modest first step for facilities over 50 MW, it leaves roughly half of projected infrastructure costs potentially on everyday customers and lacks clean energy and grid-flexibility requirements.

Lawmakers Must Act in 2027: With the NCUC falling short, the General Assembly needs to require data centers to pay 100% of incremental costs and bring clean energy, tie tax incentives to clean and flexibility rules, and share volatile gas price risk with Duke.

This week, the North Carolina Utilities Commission issued two sweeping decisions that will shape our state’s energy landscape, climate trajectory, and household budgets for decades to come. Together, the Commission’s rulings on Duke Energy’s multi-year rate case and its updated Carbon Plan and Integrated Resource Plan represent a major missed opportunity to lower power bills, modernize our grid, and hold massive data centers energy users accountable.

The Carbon Plan, by failing to maximize near-term clean energy deployments, leaves billions of dollars in federal clean energy tax credits on the table and exposes North Carolina ratepayers to decades of volatile natural gas fuel costs-which have been the biggest driver of bill increases in recent years.

The rate cases for the first time begin to assign the grid costs incurred by data centers to their operators. But by failing to assign the full costs to data centers, require them to reduce energy use during peak hours or ensure that these massive power users are being used to add clean energy to the grid instead of gas and diesel, the message to everyday North Carolinians is clear: families and small businesses will still be on the hook when the bill comes due for an outdated, fossil-fuel-heavy buildout.

Now, the North Carolina General Assembly must step up to protect ratepayers from the cost burden of over investing in expensive and dirty fossil fuels by implementing important safeguards, closing loopholes, and requiring data centers to bring their own clean energy.

Higher bills today, risky bets for the future

First, let’s look at the rate case order. North Carolina households are already squeezed by rising costs across the board, yet regulators approved a framework that raises residential electricity rates by an average of 3.7% over the next two years and locks in a 9.8% return on equity for Duke Energy’s shareholders. Even worse, the cost-recovery structure shifts a disproportionate share of grid upgrade expenses onto everyday residential customers thanks to legislation passed last year. While the order includes $20 million in shareholder funding for low-income bill assistance and weatherization, that is a drop in the bucket compared to the systemic rate pressure families face.

Then came the Carbon Plan order—and with it, a doubling down on expensive, risky fossil fuels. Despite clear evidence from Duke Energy’s own numbers that utility-scale solar, battery storage, energy efficiency, and grid-enhancing technologies are the fastest and most affordable ways to meet demand, the Commission largely greenlit Duke’s plan to build costly new natural gas plants while delaying the retirement of aging, uneconomic coal units.

Here’s a breakdown of what the Commission approved for Duke Energy’s Near Term Action Plan:

Under the shadow of Senate Bill 266—which stripped away North Carolina’s interim 2030 carbon reduction target and opened the door for utilities to charge customers upfront for power plants still under construction—this Carbon Plan puts our 2050 net-zero mandate in serious jeopardy and opens the door for a huge, risky bet on gas.

Important issues unresolved

Nowhere is the disconnect between utility planning and consumer protection clearer than on the issue of hyperscale data centers.

Data centers account for roughly 80% of the projected surge in new economic development electricity demand across the Carolinas. Modeling from Governor Josh Stein’s bipartisan Energy Policy Task Force recently confirmed what EDF has warned about for years: if we handle this load growth poorly, data centers could add tens of billions of dollars in system costs by 2050, sending residential bills skyrocketing. Conversely, when large loads bring their own new clean energy and operate flexibly, they actually lower costs for everyone else by up to $20 billion-and slash carbon pollution.

In its rate case order, the Commission took a modest first step by establishing a Large Load Tariff for facilities exceeding 50 megawatts, including minimum contract commitments and a “Stranded Generation Charge” intended to prevent ratepayers from getting stuck with the tab if a project folds. That is a welcome baseline that EDF fought hard for throughout these proceedings. Our testimony was cited extensively in the final order explaining the Commission’s decisions to enact a more protective framework than that proposed by Duke Energy and the hyperscalers.

But, as Commissioner Donald Van Der Vaart, who resigned on November 18th, noted in his dissent, the proposed charge would cover only about half of projected transmission and generation costs for new data centers:

“As an example, the commission calculated that a hypothetical 500 megawatt data center could require Duke to build about $674 million worth of new electric infrastructure. But if that data center leaves after 15 years, it would pay only $338 million of those electric costs, the other $335 million would fall to everyday customers. In the end, it falls to this Commission to be the counterweight — to ensure that the utility’s legitimate duty to its shareholders, and the data centers’ legitimate interest in lower costs, do not become an obligation of the families, small businesses and manufacturers who remain on the system.”

More broadly, between the Carbon Plan and Rate Case orders the Commission left critical gaps wide open:

No Mechanism For Data Centers to Pay for their own Clean Energy: Regulators declined to include an optional clean transition tariff or “bring your own clean energy” requirement. Without a clear mechanism for tech companies to procure new, dedicated solar and storage to match their 24/7 power needs, Duke’s default response to every new data center announcement will remain the same: build more gas plants backed up by hundreds of diesel generators.

Missing Flexibility Mandates: The orders fail to require or adequately incentivize data centers to curtail or shift load during peak grid stress—one of the most effective tools for avoiding expensive peaker plants and safeguarding reliability during extreme weather.

Unchecked Speculative Forecasts: Regulators largely accepted utility load projections without rigorous, binding guardrails to ensure we aren’t overbuilding fossil infrastructure for projects that may never fully materialize.

Lingering Cost-Shift Loopholes: While stranded generation charges help, transmission and distribution network upgrades triggered by data center growth face a year of stakeholder negotiations before we know how much of those costs will actually be assigned to data centers and how much families will continue to subsidize multi-billion-dollar tech conglomerates.

The General Assembly must step up in 2027

The North Carolina Utilities Commission had an opportunity to draw a firm line protecting ratepayers and our climate, and it fell short. That means the spotlight now shifts squarely to the North Carolina General Assembly.

When lawmakers reconvene in 2027, modernizing our energy laws to govern large-load growth must be at the top of the agenda. Legislators should enact clear statutory rules requiring hyperscale data centers to pay 100% of their incremental grid and generation costs, bring new clean energy capacity onto the system, and participate in grid-stabilizing demand response programs.

At the same time, lawmakers should re-examine generous state tax breaks for data centers so taxpayer subsidies are tied directly to clean energy and grid-flexibility commitments. Finally, they should give Duke energy skin in the game on volatile gas prices and force the utility, not just ratepayers, to bear some of the cost when prices come in higher than anticipated.

North Carolina shouldn’t have to choose between economic growth and affordable, clean electricity. But until our laws require big tech and monopoly utilities to play by fair rules, regular North Carolinians will keep paying the price.
