title: Study reveals data centers' long-distance damage to air quality | MIT News
description:
Some Midwestern states had among the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita attributable to data centers, even though much of the data center electricity demand was concentrated in Virginia and Texas.
But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region.
That proportion has likely increased as new data centers continue to be built at a rapid pace.
The study shows that rural populations are expected to have significantly higher mortality risk from data center electricity demand than urban populations, Chen says.
They could also study the flexibility of data center operations, and how adaptively adjusting electricity demand could impact air quality.
text:
The rapid expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence causes negative health and air quality impacts in regions far from where the brick-and-mortar facilities are located, according to a new study by MIT researchers.

The team estimates that additional air pollution from the electricity demands of data centers in 2023 resulted in about 650 premature deaths across the United States.

Some Midwestern states had among the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita attributable to data centers, even though much of the data center electricity demand was concentrated in Virginia and Texas.

The researchers built a modeling framework that captures how the electricity demanded by data centers propagates through the nation’s interconnected power grid. The model also considers how atmospheric conditions impact the formation of air pollution in different regions.

The framework identifies power plants across the country whose emissions increase in response to data center electricity demand. In parts of the Midwest, these emissions combine with atmospheric conditions that favor the formation of fine particulate matter, a pollutant that can cause heart attacks, stroke, and lung disease.

The researchers say these results underscore the importance of considering unintended regional health impacts of data centers, and how the location and operations of these facilities affect public health on a broader scale.

“When people think about the negative impacts of data centers, they usually focus on the neighbors. But our study indicates that the air quality impacts of data centers are very widespread across a large region. Even if you don’t think you are affected because there is not a data center near you, think again,” says Noelle Selin, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS); director of the Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy; and senior author of the study.

Selin is joined on the paper by Yuang (Albert) Chen, an MIT graduate student; as well as others at MIT, the University of California at Irvine, and Yale University. The research appears today in Environmental Research Letters.

Capturing regional impacts

The Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that electricity demands of data centers represented about 4 percent of total U.S. energy demand in 2023 and resulted in about 4.4 percent of the nation’s overall emissions.

That proportion has likely increased as new data centers continue to be built at a rapid pace.

Many prior studies estimate impacts using average electricity-grid emissions. Like those studies, the researchers assume data centers draw power to run computing tasks 24/7. Their approach also identifies which generators respond to that additional demand hour by hour, allowing them to trace where the resulting emissions and health impacts occur, Chen explains.

“Generators that respond to additional electricity demand are often natural gas plants, although the response varies by place and hour,” he says.

To drill down on regional health impacts, the MIT researchers developed a modeling approach that enables them to identify which generators are contributing to data center electricity demand within each modeled region.

This allows them to incorporate a spatial component into the analysis.

They built an electricity system model that simulates how much electricity each generator produces and pumps into the grid every hour. This model also considers how that electricity is transmitted between regions.

It gives the researchers data on emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and sulfur dioxide (SO2) for each generator across the United States. NOx contributes to the formation of ground-level ozone, or smog, while both NOx and SO2 contribute to the formation of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) in the atmosphere.

“It was a challenge to gather all the data,” Chen says. “There are more than 10,000 generators in the U.S. grid, and we needed to make sure the data provided for each generator is valid and validated across other data sources.”

The researchers incorporated these data into a chemical transport model. This model simulates how pollutants form and travel through the atmosphere across regions.

From there, they translated the additional air pollution from data center operations into premature mortality rates using evidence from epidemiological literature.

The model estimates that emissions from data centers caused about 650 premature deaths in 2023 (513 from PM2.5 and 137 from smog), which represents about 5.3 percent of the nation’s total electricity-related mortality.

“While it is not surprising that any additional source of air pollution will result in mortalities, with data centers, when and where these deaths are occurring are different than you might expect,” Selin says.

A pollution mismatch

The premature mortality rates were highest in Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas, but the bulk of the electricity demand was concentrated in northern Virginia and in Texas. Premature mortality rates in Virginia and Texas are only about half as much as most Midwestern states.

One reason for this mismatch is the interconnected nature of the power grid, Chen says.

Generators that respond to the increased electricity demand in Virginia are likely located in the Ohio Valley, where there is a higher proportion of older power plants that generate more emissions from burning coal and natural gas.

“Different regions have different mixes of power. If you turn on a major new demand source, by plugging a data center into the grid, you might have to fire up your really dirty power plant to meet that new demand,” Selin says.

Plus, due to atmospheric conditions, many pollutants generated in these regions are transported to downwind states.

Midwest states like Nebraska and Iowa are traditionally agricultural regions. Additional ammonia in the atmosphere from fertilizer enhances the formation of PM2.5. The estimated health impacts also extend to Kansas, South Dakota, Missouri, and Arkansas, illustrating that the effects can reach states with relatively few data centers.

The study shows that rural populations are expected to have significantly higher mortality risk from data center electricity demand than urban populations, Chen says.

“When people are thinking about data center siting and operations, it is important to consider more than just things like land and energy prices. They should also take air quality considerations into the equation,” he says. “This is a good baseline to think about where we should build data centers and how we should supply those data centers with electricity.”

In the future, the researchers want to consider air quality impacts of onsite generation — a growing trend where data centers incorporate power plants that supply electricity. They could also study the flexibility of data center operations, and how adaptively adjusting electricity demand could impact air quality.

This research was funded, in part, by the MIT Energy Initiative Society of Energy Scholars and the MIT Martin Family Society of Fellows for Sustainability.

text:
As COP31 draws to a close, new evidence from across 27 countries shows that the biggest barriers to an inclusive clean energy transition are often not technological, but financial, institutional and social.

As attention shifts from negotiation to delivery, a new research synthesis report ‘From Clean Energy Transition to Just Energy Futures’ offers a practical answer to a difficult question: How do clean energy ambitions become change that people can feel?

The report is published by the Clean Energy for Development: Knowledge Translation and Communications Support programme, led by IDS. It draws on 189 outputs from projects providing lessons and recommendations for policy and practice, identifying four key findings:

1. Start with livelihoods, not technology

The answer is to start with how people make a living. Clean energy gains traction when it raises productivity, incomes and resilience, not simply when it becomes available. Evidence from Bhutan, Bolivia, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Kenya, Senegal, Uganda and Vietnam shows that people take up clean energy when it improves their farming, businesses and incomes. In Bhutan, farmers became much more interested in solar irrigation pumps once proof-of-concept projects showed the savings and productivity gains compared with diesel pumps. In Bolivia, fish farmers were more likely to adopt solar-powered oxygen generators over gasoline pumps after visiting pilot projects and seeing the cost savings first-hand.

2. Turn policy ambition into implementation

Strong policy support was not enough on its own. Fragmented responsibilities across energy, agriculture and water institutions slowed implementation in Bhutan. The project responded by developing planning tools and strengthening coordination between agencies, helping bring productive uses of renewable energy into the country’s National Energy Policy 2025.

3. Finance alone isn’t enough

Finance matters, but it is rarely enough. In Vietnam, fewer than half of surveyed farmers were willing to adopt solar water pumps even when preferential loans were available. The guide finds that affordable capital works best when paired with knowledge, confidence, mentoring and market access. Local businesses often provide the missing link, installing and maintaining equipment and helping technologies reach farmers and households. But they also need support ranging from finance and mentoring to skills and enabling regulation. In Tunisia, 65.3 per cent of surveyed small businesses reported insufficient financing for renewable energy investment

4. Design for equity, not just access

The research also challenges assumptions about who benefits. Women and young people are often central to clean energy value chains but remain excluded from ownership, leadership and higher-value roles. In Kenya, they were heavily represented in sales and distribution but far less present in manufacturing, technical and leadership positions. In Africa’s solar sector, only 5.3 per cent of venture capital reached companies with women founders.

In Bolivia, women operated renewable energy systems and took part in productive enterprises, yet strategic decisions about investment, maintenance and expansion often stayed with men. Labour-saving technologies often saved time, but did not necessarily redistribute unpaid care work or increase women’s control over resources and decisions. Inclusion takes active effort: in Ghana, Senegal and Côte d’Ivoire, the research project adapted its selection processes and linked women and youth innovators with mentors, finance and farming communities.

Read the report

What needs to happen next

For policymakers, practitioners and investors, the guide recommends designing interventions around productive uses such as farming and enterprise; combining finance with skills, mentoring and maintenance support; aligning energy, agriculture, finance, gender and climate institutions; and tracking who controls assets, income, time and decisions, not only who gains access.

The challenge is no longer simply how to deploy clean energy at scale, but how to do so in ways that expand opportunity, strengthen local economies, support inclusive development, and build lasting public support for change.

text:
Justice Denied is a series examining how the Justice Department under President Trump shuttered investigations and cases — and what happened to the people and communities who say they were denied justice.

In late 2024, Justice Department prosecutors learned of insiders with a jaw-dropping claim about Southern Coal and its sister companies, a powerful mining conglomerate found to have polluted waterways near its mostly Appalachian mine sites for years.

Former employees said they had information that this coal empire, owned by Republican Sen. Jim Justice of West Virginia and largely run by his son, had falsified lab tests meant to detect water pollution from its operations, according to two people familiar with the case. The people who spoke to MS NOW were granted anonymity in order to speak freely about a DOJ investigation.

This worrisome new lead, the details of which have not been previously reported, set off alarm bells for members of the Justice Department division that enforces environmental laws, according to the sources.

In February 2025, DOJ prosecutors opened a criminal investigation, concerned that Southern Coal officials might be intentionally violating the law and a settlement the company struck with the Justice Department in 2016. In that deal, Southern Coal avoided paying a maximum of $880 million in fines for more than 23,000 alleged pollution violations across five states — by agreeing to pay a $900,000 fine, upgrade pollution controls and comply with the law.

But just when the Justice Department team was poised to check the insiders’ claims, the office of then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche ordered the prosecutors to withdraw subpoenas they had just issued for company records. The team was told to shut down the criminal investigation entirely, the sources told MS NOW.

The order, they said, came soon after James McDonald, an attorney from Sullivan & Cromwell, a Manhattan law firm representing Southern Coal, contacted Blanche’s office to raise objections. Blanche and McDonald had both worked as personal lawyers defending Donald Trump against a New York hush money case that had resulted in his 2024 criminal conviction.

Former Justice Department officials say the sudden intervention of top appointees to withdraw subpoenas and close the Southern Coal case deviates dramatically from the department’s norm.

“It’s unheard of,” said Rick Mountcastle, a former U.S. attorney in the Western District of Virginia, whose office helped bring the civil lawsuit against Southern Coal and its affiliates.

“To have a case shut down before the investigation is anywhere near completion,” he said, “it’s really troubling.”

In an email, the Justice Department told MS NOW it “did not shutter any investigation.”

Steven Ruby, a lawyer for Sen. Justice’s family businesses, said that the companies believe the allegations came from disgruntled former employees and that after Southern Coal and related businesses gave the Justice Department evidence refuting its claims, it “found no basis to continue an investigation.”

Sullivan & Cromwell did not reply to MS NOW’s request for comment.

But the probe’s quick death is part of a broader pattern in President Trump’s second term, a six-month investigation by MS NOW has found.

Since early 2025, Trump’s political lieutenants in the Justice Department have shut down numerous investigations when the subject has been a powerful corporation or a well-heeled ally of the president and his administration. This story focuses on a string of environmental cases in which those lieutenants ordered federal prosecutors and career attorneys to walk away from compelling leads and evidence of potential wrongdoing and environmental danger. Legal experts told MS NOW that in prior administrations the department would have normally pursued those leads.

In the early weeks after Trump’s return to office, the division canceled a long-planned trial of a chemical company emitting the carcinogen chloroprene, which was blamed for dramatically increased cancer rates in the adjoining neighborhood. Over the ensuing months, it shut down criminal probes into Southern Coal and its affiliates as well as a major commercial fishing operator in North Carolina. When Trump ally Elon Musk’s company opened an unpermitted power plant, considered one of the largest sources of air pollution in the nation, Trump’s DOJ not only declined to act, but tried to block citizens from suing Musk’s company.

The Southern Coal example showcases the ways Trump appointees have gutted the Justice Department’s efforts to enforce environmental laws that seek to protect American’s air, water and, ultimately, public health, former department officials told MS NOW.

Laura Thoms, a supervisor and an attorney who departed DOJ’s Environment and Natural Resources Division last year, calls Trump’s second presidency an “open season for polluters” and finds “the consequences for polluting have all but vanished.” Enforcement cases brought by the section have “fallen off a cliff” since Trump’s inauguration, she found in a review, less than a third of the previous year.

And the civil penalties collected against polluters have quickly cratered too. In 2024, the DOJ collected $1.88 billion in civil environmental penalties. In 2025, after Trump took office, his DOJ collected $15 million — less than 1% of the previous year.

Since Blanche officially renamed it the Energy and Natural Resources Division in September, the once powerful unit is estimated to be down to almost half its staff since Trump took office, due to forced exits and departures.

In the faraway Appalachian mountain towns of southern West Virginia, residents say they are paying the price for what they believe is the Justice Department’s retreat from enforcing environmental laws — and a full investigation of Southern Coal and its affiliated companies. Without probing for answers, experts tell MS NOW, neither the government nor the public can determine whether a coal empire owned by a Trump ally and one of the Senate’s richest members is polluting the local drinking water, or whether it’s another company in the area. These communities will not learn who is responsible for their tainted water and the ailments they say they continue to suffer.

Residents MS NOW interviewed in West Virginia’s Wyoming County said they have been unable to safely drink or bathe in the water that comes from their faucets at home. They said independent water tests had found high levels of heavy metals, including lead, arsenic and manganese, sometimes 10 or even 100 times higher than what the Environmental Protection Agency considers safe.

Richard Altizer, a resident and community advocate, showed MS NOW places where creeks and rivers had turned bright orange, white and even black from suspected mine contamination. He said the community was relying on the DOJ probe to get answers — and protection.

“So somewhere along the line, these places have contaminated people’s drinking water and shower water. We know that,” he said. “But dropping that investigation … The Justice Department was the only hope we had.”

Residents and their family members have been diagnosed with cancers, liver failure, thyroid dysfunction and other diseases often associated with heavy metal exposure. Many pay hundreds of dollars a week for water to drink and cook with.

“From the water, I have third-stage kidney failure,” said Pansy Keene, a local resident who said she also suffered from rashes and a high risk of liver disease. She and many fellow residents blame the polluted drainage from local mining sites, including those owned by the Justice companies.

Residents complain that they backed Trump for president but feel he turned his back on them.

“I’m 100% in support of Donald Trump. But I want to say this much: Show me you care,” said resident Barry Brooks. “The people in this state backed you, backed you to the hilt. Now it’s time for you to back us.”

“He should be ashamed of himself,” Keene said. “He wouldn’t want not one member of his family to have to live like we are.”

Kate Waldeck, a West Virginia pediatrician, said that among the local children she treats, there is a high frequency of ailments often linked to heavy metals. Local water tests reveal a toxic risk, she said; her most urgent advice to local parents is not to use tap water to make infant formula.

She said the Justice Department owed the people of West Virginia a full investigation.

“If the federal government thought that there was sufficient evidence to meet the bar of criminal activity affecting the people’s health in the state and nothing is being done about it, I think that that is unethical,” Waldeck said.

The first hint of what Trump and his team planned for the Justice Department’s efforts to curb pollution and enforce environmental laws came within days of his inauguration. A string of supervisors were reassigned or demoted.

Tom Mariani, a 40-year veteran and well-respected chief of the environmental enforcement section of the Environment and Natural Resources Division, had spent considerable time trying to assure career attorneys in his section that he would try to shield them if he had to so they could continue their mission. But hours later, he was notified that he was being transferred to a “sanctuary cities” project that had no actual duties.

The next blow came a few short weeks later. ENRD attorneys had been preparing for their upcoming civil trial against a company called Denka, which operated a neoprene plant releasing the probable carcinogen chloroprene in a Louisiana industrial corridor known as “Cancer Alley.” A public health survey in 2021 titled “Waiting to Die” found residents of this census tract in St. John the Baptist Parish had the nation’s highest risk of cancer from air pollution due to the chloroprene emissions from the Denka plant.

Robert Taylor, founder of a parish advocacy group seeking to hold polluters accountable and inform residents, said that for years he and his neighbors saw community members die from cancer without understanding the risk in their community. He said he didn’t learn the cancer risk from the Denka plant emissions until EPA officials shared their air toxics study of the area in 2015.

“I could go on endlessly talking about the horrors of watching my close relatives die of cancer,” he said. “It’s a horrible way to die.”

In 2023, under the Biden administration, the Justice Department filed an emergency lawsuit against Denka under the Clean Air Act, after the EPA determined that the plant created an “imminent and substantial” risk to the adjoining neighbors, most of whom were Black.

But in March 2025, on the eve of a preparatory hearing on the Denka trial that was to start in April, DOJ supervisors notified the trial team attorneys that political appointees concluded their case was too “novel,” according to people with knowledge of the discussions. The case would be dismissed, they said.

The trial team, as well as attorneys across the DOJ, were stunned by the department press release that quickly followed the same day.

It claimed that the dismissal helped fulfill Trump’s promise to eradicate “radical” race-based policies. In the release, the division’s acting assistant attorney general, Adam Gustafson, said the DOJ would now enforce environmental laws “fairly, without regard to race.”

“We do not regulate through litigation, nor do we stretch statutes beyond their plain meaning to advance political agendas,” his statement read.

In a statement, a DOJ spokesperson said the complaint against Denka “relied on the Clean Air Act’s rarely invoked ‘Emergency Powers’ provision,” based on the EPA finding “imminent and substantial” danger to the public.

But the spokesperson said the department dismissed the Denka case after finding that the Biden administration used that provision to further its “ongoing effort to advance environmental justice.”

The DOJ also said that while it “sympathize[s] with anyone who has lost a loved one,” it had “no information attributing any particular illness or mortality to neoprene production.”

Early in 2025, prosecutors at ENRD believed they had a solid factual basis to launch a criminal investigation into Southern Coal and the mining empire of Sen. Justice. A key part of the case came from whistleblowers.

In the previous six years, records show, the Justice Department had been going to court to get Southern Coal and its affiliates to comply with the settlement agreement the Justice family companies had promised to abide by in 2016. The government argued that the company had violated the agreement in several ways, including failing to pay penalties and to meet a deadline for promised pollution controls in Tennessee.

Most importantly, DOJ said, Southern Coal companies were flouting the law by letting some of its pollution discharge permits expire and not properly reporting pollution leaking into waterways. Southern Coal responded that the consent decree did not expressly state that it had to renew its pollution permits.

A federal appellate court called out the “absurdity” of Southern Coal’s logic, saying that the settlement broadly required the company to comply with pollution laws. It couldn’t do an “end-run” to ignore the law by letting its permits expire, the court ruled.

Amid this battle, the DOJ learned of two former employees who said they had information indicating that Southern Coal or its sister companies were falsifying some water test results, people familiar with the discussions said. Such tests were supposed to detect whether and when the companies’ mining operations violated pollution limits.

ENRD’s environmental crimes section swung into action in early 2025, and later that year sent subpoenas for internal company records, which the office of Assistant Attorney General Stanley Woodward approved, the people said. Prosecutors issued a second set of subpoenas, this time to obtain the lab test results. Southern Coal went to court to block the request for its records, claiming they should be withheld because of attorney-client privilege.

In February 2026, attorneys later learned, while prosecutors awaited the judge’s decision on getting the company records, McDonald contacted Blanche’s office to object. Shortly after, Blanche’s deputies ordered the ENRD supervisors to have their team withdraw the subpoenas for the company records and the water test results. They were also told to shut down the criminal probe, the people said.

Representatives for Southern Coal and the DOJ both said in statements to MS NOW that there was not sufficient evidence to pursue a criminal probe.

An attorney for the Justice family said it had a “nearly 20-year professional relationship” with Sullivan & Cromwell “that has nothing to do with President Trump.”

“We take seriously our duty to ensure all Americans have clean air and water,” a DOJ spokesperson said. “We work with investigating agencies to follow the facts of any case and ensure any violations are appropriately addressed.”

In an interview outside his Capitol Hill office, Justice said questions about Southern Coal should be directed to his son, who runs the business. But the senator disputed that any water tests were falsified.

“I think every bit of that is bogus as bogus can be,” he said. “There is no chance, no chance whatsoever, that we’ve been involved in anything like that.”

Justice said his family business would not harm residents of his state.

More articles

“And do I believe that we’re the cause of people having bad water or we’re the cause that people having water that they can’t bathe in and everything else?” Justice said. “If you look at Jim Justice and how he loves the people of West Virginia, and how he’s treated the people of West Virginia, that is so blatantly false at some point. “

He declined to answer additional questions and left with his staff to prepare for a birthday party he was hosting for his beloved bulldog, Babydog.

But the residents in West Virginia say they feel abandoned by the DOJ decision. They say they considered the federal investigation their only hope for a solution.

Community members told MS NOW they couldn’t move away because it’s too hard to sell homes with undrinkable water. Altizer, the community advocate, has spent his own money testing water to show the problem. He said the Trump administration’s decision made him feel his work and research had been a waste.

“Because if you’re not going to hold the people accountable, then why even try to fix the problem?” Altizer said. “And that just gives [the company] a license to create anything they want to do back here.”

Stephen New, an attorney for some residents who are suing companies owned by the Justice family, said the Trump administration had a duty to first protect West Virginians who can’t safely drink from their faucet, not the company profits of a wealthy Republican politician.

“We’re spending a billion dollars a day in a war in Iran that doesn’t need to be fought,” New said, “while our people live in a Third World country situation.”

In the early spring of 2026, ENRD prosecutors had taken a big step in a long-simmering criminal probe of a major commercial fishing operation in North Carolina and a man known in the area as “the King of Shrimp.”

They drafted a criminal indictment of Brent Fulcher and his company, Beaufort Inlet Seafood, according to two people familiar with the plan. The prosecutors proposed charging Fulcher with wire fraud and obstruction of justice, based on evidence that he and his firm fraudulently underreported their fish catches to avoid violating limits.

It is a federal crime to underreport fish catches that exceed legal quotas set for some fish. Underreporting allows dishonest operators to flood the market with cheaper, undocumented seafood, and such secret overfishing can lead to the collapse of a fishing stock.

The investigators had video evidence of Fulcher and other company officials on his company docks, from November 2021 to January 2022, to receive fish catches as they were hauled out of the fishing boats and weighed.

Then, one morning in late January 2022, federal investigators raided the offices of a Fulcher seafood business and carried out boxes of records.

The federal team found that thousands more pounds of fish were delivered onto Fulcher’s docks, as seen on the video, than the amount his company reported it had received to regulators, according to people with knowledge of the case. Fulcher and his company, the team concluded, had underreported $1 million and $2 million worth of fish.

The investigation stretched on for several years, exploring different leads, and neared the end in early 2026, when prosecutors drafted their indictment. But on June 11, as the DOJ team considered when to bring charges, its prospective defendant appeared on television as an Oval Office guest of Trump’s in a public ceremony about marine fisheries. The event was held for Trump to sign a proclamation to reopen some Pacific waters for commercial fishing.

“I’m from North Carolina but support you 100%,” Fulcher said as video cameras broadcast his effusive praise for the president. “You have done more for this nation in the seafood space than any president before you in my lifetime. Thank you, sir.”

In the next several weeks, Justice Department supervisors told their team they were reviewing the merits of the Fulcher case, people familiar with the discussion said. Then, in August, supervisors told prosecutors that political appointees had decided against pursuing criminal charges. Investigators were frustrated, believing the evidence warranted prosecution. Instead, the people said, DOJ leaders proposed civil penalties against Fulcher and his company.

A White House spokesperson denied any improper political interference by the White House in the DOJ case.

A DOJ spokesperson said the department “pursues or declines to pursue cases based on the facts and the law,” and “is unwavering in its commitment to working on behalf of the American people and upholding federal law.”

Separately, a White House official, who declined to be named in order to discuss internal planning, told MS NOW that the White House was “not aware of any investigation into Fulcher” and that the U.S. Department of Agriculture recommended he be invited to the Oval Office event.

Fulcher did not respond to email requests for comment, but as he attended a North Carolina seafood festival in Morehead City in September, MS NOW asked him in person about the DOJ’s proposed indictment and evidence.

“I really don’t have any comments,” Fulcher said. “But I think a lot of what you just told me, I don’t think is exactly correct. … I don’t have any comment about it until it’s all resolved.”

Days after we spoke with Fulcher, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration sent him and his company a letter concluding that they had violated federal fishing laws and imposing a $1.2 million fine.

Fulcher’s legal team declined our questions on the matter.

But North Carolina fishermen and conservation advocates say they find the DOJ’s closure of the criminal case a terrible message to alleged scofflaws — and to the broader public.

“If you don’t enforce the laws, then … the resources don’t restore or recover,” said Louis Daniel, the former director of the state’s Division of Marine Fisheries. “And so any time you get a case that’s dismissed for whatever reason, that sends a message that it’s OK or it’s the cost of doing business.”

“I can’t describe how important it is to me as a Marine that we have justice, because everything is meaningless without it,” said Steven Brewster, a veteran, recreational fisherman and advocate for local fisheries. “And what you’re telling the people of North Carolina is that you don’t need to follow the rules.”

In 1970, when Congress passed the landmark Clean Air Act, lawmakers recognized that the federal government might fail to enforce environmental laws, so the public needed special protection in that case. They created a special right for citizens to sue polluters on their own if the government was sitting on the sidelines.

Former Attorney General Ramsey Clark said at the time that years of experience had taught Americans that “government will never have the manpower, the techniques or the awareness necessary to enforce the law for all.”

“It will be impossible for government enforcement to control all significant acts of pollution,” Clark said. “Private enforcement of those laws is the only way the individual can be assured that the rights cannot be violated with impunity.”

Congress added similar rights for citizens to sue to several environmental statutes that followed, including the Clean Water Act and the Toxic Substances Control Act.

That would prove important after Thoms, the former DOJ attorney, left ENRD in 2025 and joined the legal team of Earthjustice, a nonprofit environmental public interest group.

An interesting case came to her attention not long into her tenure at her new job: the enormous power plant that xAI, one of Elon Musk’s companies, was building in Mississippi to help power his data centers nearby. The company did not obtain air permits before installing methane gas turbines, which regulators normally deem illegal. It began with 27 turbines and later grew to 69 turbines.

Musk’s company said it was exempt from permitting because the turbines were movable and temporary. It later obtained permits for some of the turbines.

Earthjustice said the plant is one of the largest sources of air pollution in the nation, and pollutants from turbine engines, including nitrogen oxides (NOx), particulate matter and formaldehyde, are associated with increased cases of asthma, heart disease, respiratory illnesses, certain cancers and premature death.

A new study from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology found that the plant’s turbines release nitrogen oxides at levels 19 times higher than what is allowed under the law. MS NOW has reached out to xAI for comment on the study but has not yet received a response.

Thoms knew a Clean Air Act violation when she saw one. She and Earthjustice colleagues joined with the Southern Environmental Law Center to file a citizens’ suit on behalf of the NAACP and the predominantly Black communities surrounding the power plant.

Then Trump’s DOJ took an unprecedented step. It filed to intervene in the case and to block the NAACP’s citizens’ suit from going forward. The government claimed that the suit could harm national security by cutting power to data centers for artificial intelligence that supports the Defense Department.

In mid-October the district court judge handling the xAI case denied the government’s motion to dismiss the case and said there was “no ‘fairly possible’ interpretation of the Clean Air Act that would give the United States the right to unilaterally dismiss a citizen suit once it intervenes.”

As the Southern Environmental Law Center put it: “The District Court ruled that the DOJ does not have the right to unilaterally block the case and rejected the department’s argument that xAI should be allowed to break the law solely because the Trump administration says so.”

Thoms says she is heartened that the court recognized the citizens’ right to sue. She and national legal experts remain floored that Trump’s DOJ didn’t just fail to enforce the law, it denied residents’ right to protect themselves.

“This is an administration that not only refuses to enforce bedrock environmental laws, it’s shutting down lawsuits against the president’s allies and donors,” Thoms said. “Now, Trump’s DOJ is trying to take away the right of ordinary people to protect themselves from illegal pollution when the government fails to act.”

“All communities deserve clean air,” she added, “and whether the protections promised by environmental law are real shouldn’t depend on if a powerful industry or friend of the president is involved.”

You can see more of this reporting on “State of Play” on MS NOW on Thursday, Nov. 19, at 11 a.m. ET.

text:
Elections & Politics Brief | Shannon Roxborough | November 19, 2026

Democrats won both chambers of Congress on November 3 and take control when the new Congress convenes in January. For nearly two years Republicans ran both chambers and backed the administration’s push to expand fossil fuel production, loosen environmental rules and roll back parts of the clean-energy agenda.

Democrats will be able to demand records, hold hearings and question agency officials. A hearing cannot reverse a policy. The president keeps his veto, and agencies keep their executive powers.

The question is whether the new Congress uses oversight to hold companies and agencies accountable where environmental protection and workers’ rights meet.

Analysis: Five areas where the election could change the debate

Federal environmental enforcement. The Environmental Integrity Project counted 16 Justice Department civil suits filed on EPA’s behalf in Trump’s first year back, 76 percent below Biden’s first year. EPA called the report erroneous and says it prioritizes compliance over penalties. Congressional committees can request the enforcement records and ask which cases stopped and why.

Fossil fuel subsidies and clean-energy funding. Brief #171 covered emergency orders that keep coal plants open 90 days at a time. Michigan’s J.H. Campbell plant had cost its owner a net $259 million by June. Congress can ask what the orders cost and whether workers get retention terms. If the administration or the owners will not answer, committees can subpoena records, and Congress can write retention terms into spending bills. If the answer is that no terms exist, workers at plants kept open by emergency order face the same job uncertainty when an order ends as they did before it.

Workers’ rights and labor enforcement. OSHA’s federal inspectors fell from 846 in February 2024 to 736 in June 2025. The NLRB, which handles union and unfair-labor-practice cases, spent most of 2025 without a quorum. Committees can ask whether companies with federal contracts, loans and subsidies should owe workers more. If they conclude companies should, Congress can write it into law, such as wage and safety terms on contracts, loans and tax credits. That needs the president’s signature or a veto override, and most Senate bills need 60 votes. Without a law, only agencies can set such terms, and they answer to the administration.

AI infrastructure. On November 9 the Senate voted 73 to 25 to begin debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. The bill would make data centers above 20 megawatts pay for the grid costs they add. Backers say it would also cut the time new energy projects wait for approval. More than 100 environmental, faith and labor groups urged senators to reject it, and House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said it falls short on environmental protections. President Trump has endorsed it but has said he will not approve wind permits even if it passes.

The three goals are different. Faster building means shorter reviews and fewer delays before a project starts. Environmental safeguards are those reviews and the power of states, tribes and courts to slow or stop a project, such as under the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. Ratepayer protection concerns who pays: whether data centers cover the grid upgrades they require or pass them to households. The bill pairs the first with the third. Critics, including legal scholars who wrote to the Senate, say it pays for that pairing with the second. The current Senate holds this vote, and it previews the new Congress’s choice among the three.

Clean-energy manufacturing jobs. Brief #170 showed that Section 45X pays factories by output with no prevailing wage requirement. At Ultium Cells in Lordstown, Ohio, workers won a $26.91 starting wage by organizing, not by federal rule. They voted to join the United Auto Workers in late 2022 and won a raise from $16.50 to about $20 an hour in an interim agreement. They were then folded into General Motors’ national contract after the union’s 46-day targeted strike in 2023. Congress can ask whether subsidized plants produce lasting jobs that pay well. If they do not, Congress can add a wage floor to 45X or redirect the credit. Otherwise the subsidy keeps flowing whether or not the jobs are good ones.

Five changes the new Congress could pursue

Not all of these are within Congress’s power alone. Oversight is: committee chairs can hold hearings, demand documents and issue subpoenas, and the Government Accountability Office can review agency spending at their request. Changing law is different. A bill must pass both chambers and either win the president’s signature or survive a veto by a two-thirds vote, and most Senate bills need 60 votes to clear a filibuster. Democrats will need Republican votes, or a must-pass spending bill the president signs. Each change below says which applies.

Strengthen environmental oversight. Committees can request enforcement, inspection and exemption data now. A rule requiring regular public reports would need a law.

Attach labor conditions to federal subsidies. This needs a law, such as wage, safety and workforce-retention terms in a spending bill or tax-credit rewrite.

Protect clean-energy investment. Committees can review how tax credits and funding programs are working, including changes made by the 2025 budget law. Restoring anything those changes cut needs a law.

Investigate energy affordability. Committees can summon utility and data center executives and demand cost data now. Cost-allocation rules, such as the permitting bill’s, need a law, and states and federal regulators set electricity rates.

Require worker-transition plans. This needs a law. Companies receiving federal fossil fuel support would have to provide retraining and protections for displaced workers.

The midterms changed the balance of power in Washington. Whether they change the conditions facing America’s workers and communities will depend on what Congress does with that power.

BlueGreen Alliance: Read its work on clean-energy job quality.

description:
Federal and state legislatures have included affirmative emergency powers in numerous environmental statutes across the nation.
Further, this Article grapples with whether common critiques of broader executive emergency powers have salience for affirmative emergency powers.
Indeed, like other forms of emergency authority, the use of affirmative emergency powers involves trade-offs between expediency and process.
It details the statutory provisions granting affirmative emergency powers to officials under the CAA, CWA, SDWA, and state analog statutes.
Part II explores affirmative emergency powers’ capacity to advance environmental protection.
text:
Introduction

Environmental law has always been entwined with emergencies, with their interplay acting as a persistent force in shaping statutes and their implementation. Mass chemical exposures, oil spills, and toxic waste leaks spurred our landmark environmental legislation. Today, some environmental emergencies are unforeseen disasters, and others have their roots in long-term failures of risk assessment or gaps in the law. Indeed, not all modern environmental emergencies resemble sudden, high-visibility crises that dominate public attention.

Take the St. Croix Limetree Bay Refinery in the U.S. Virgin Islands. From above, the refinery pierces a cyan gradient of turquoise waters and verdant hills. But when the refinery restarted in 2021 after a hiatus in operations, it subjected 20,000 people to harrowing conditions. That February, an “oily mist” rained down on the refinery’s downwind communities, coating housing, contaminating water cisterns, and leaving gardens slick and soiled. For weeks, people reported nausea and other symptoms linked to exposure to toxic chemicals, particularly hydrogen sulfide. A community survey revealed the severity of health and property damage from these choking emissions. Residents near the refinery reported a “dense fog” entering homes and daycares; intense sensations of suffocation; burning in their eyes, noses, and throats; workers and children collapsing. One resident described being “overt[aken]” by a cloud of emissions, then feeling “like it was eating [their] nervous system from the inside.”

In response, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) did something extremely rare: it issued an emergency order under Section 303 of the Clean Air Act (“CAA”). The EPA ordered the refinery to cease operations, conduct audits, and submit a plan to undertake corrective measures. As Section 303’s sixty-day limit on administrative orders approached, the federal government filed a civil action seeking injunctive relief to continue the order’s protections. At the same time, Limetree Bay agreed by joint stipulation to keep the refinery idled unless it satisfied corrective requirements designed to eliminate endangerment from the facility’s emissions.

This Article uses the term “affirmative emergency powers” to refer to the type of provisions in environmental statutes that the EPA invoked against the Limetree Bay Refinery. These provisions authorize officials to sue for or order the immediate abatement or prevention of conditions that endanger health, welfare, or the environment. Federal and state legislatures have included affirmative emergency powers in numerous environmental statutes across the nation.

Affirmative emergency powers differ from conventional enforcement actions—the far more common and familiar administrative or civil judicial suits for permit violations or unpermitted pollution. Environmental permits generally grant a holder limited rights to pollute. Conventional enforcement actions address compliance with permit limits for regulated pollutants or whether a polluter holds the appropriate permit. Permitting regimes across air, water, and land also tend to focus on individual sources or single pollutants, oftentimes without considering their collective effects on a particular location. And though they are a powerful check on violations of environmental law, conventional enforcement actions are sometimes insufficient to address serious threats.

When that happens, affirmative emergency powers can function as a critical backstop for environmental protection because they center risk and harm rather than numeric permit limits. So unlike conventional enforcement actions, officials can invoke affirmative emergency powers even when: polluters are in compliance with a permit; rulemaking or standard setting has yet to address new threats; regulatory systems result in toxic hotspots; pollution control approximations in permits or standards have drifted out of sync with real-world conditions; or individual facilities operate in compliance with their permits but nonetheless contribute to acute cumulative environmental burdens.

This distinctive ability of affirmative emergency powers to mitigate dangerous conditions regardless of permit status can enable them to protect people and places from urgent hazards, including data center pollution, climate-driven environmental and health threats, severe cumulative pollution, and “forever chemicals.” This is one reason I argue that affirmative emergency powers should not be seen as exceptional departures from democratic governance, a framing that understandably troubles many scholars. Rather, they should be understood as corrective mechanisms that re-anchor environmental governance to its underlying protective purpose when regulatory systems or conventional enforcement mechanisms fail and when unforeseen circumstances inevitably arise. Accordingly, affirmative emergency powers are—to borrow a phrase used by Professors Elena Chachko and Katerina Linos—“emergency powers for good.”

Despite these benefits, the use of affirmative emergency powers is exceedingly rare under three of the nation’s most commonly enforced environmental laws, namely the CAA, the Clean Water Act (“CWA”), and the Safe Drinking Water Act (“SDWA”). For example, the EPA has issued orders under Section 303 of the CAA fewer than twenty times since 1970. Even in situations as extreme as the Flint Water Crisis, the EPA’s deployment of SDWA-based emergency powers has been infamously belated.

Why affirmative emergency powers are so rarely deployed under these laws remains unclear, in part because they have not been the subject of significant scholarly attention. The Flint Water Crisis inspired a spate of scholarship exploring emergency powers under the SDWA, but research has since waned. Other scholarship has focused on discrete uses of the provisions, such as cleanups at federal facilities or their application under a single statutory provision. For instance, Professors Robert Glicksman and Johanna Adashek recently analyzed the affirmative emergency powers provision of the CAA within a larger project to identify authorities to address contaminants known colloquially as “forever chemicals.”

This Article builds on the limited literature on these provisions and extends environmental enforcement scholarship by foregrounding underexamined authorities to fill gaps in regulatory design and implementation. It engages with the principles of environmental justice and supporting scholarship to consider the goals of protection from disproportionate environmental burdens, but also of participatory power in decision-making. Further, this Article grapples with whether common critiques of broader executive emergency powers have salience for affirmative emergency powers.

Indeed, like other forms of emergency authority, the use of affirmative emergency powers involves trade-offs between expediency and process. This conceptual tension and associated criticisms feature prominently in the abundant literature on emergency powers vested in or delegated to the President. A deep bench of scholars has raised due process, pretextual use, emergency normalization, and other objections to constitutional and statutory-based executive emergency powers. But in the environmental context, I adopt Chachko and Linos’s contention that these eminently justified critiques nonetheless “miss[] . . . part of the picture. Emergency powers can be used in constructive ways that promote public goods.” Building on that view, I argue that when deployed with practices that increase procedural transparency and participation, affirmative emergency powers can be reconciled with democratic norms and environmental justice aspirations for self-determination.

Threaded throughout this Article is an urgency to better understand and harness existing authorities at a time when the landscape of legal options to advance environmental protection shrinks under federal retrenchments and burgeoning doctrinal barriers. Those retrenchments are reflected in diminished agency capacity, extensive rollbacks of environmental rules, and repudiation of longstanding statutory public health and welfare mandates. Contemporaneously, the U.S. Supreme Court’s reworking of administrative law principles has constrained agencies’ interpretive authority and capacity for proactive regulation. Affirmative emergency powers, however, rest on clear, longstanding statutory delegations and operate at the level of individual facilities. Therefore, as detailed below, their use is comparatively well-insulated from many of the novel doctrines that could hinder more transformative regulatory strategies.

This Article also intervenes in a larger reimagining of environmental law necessitated by these changes to core aspects of administrative and environmental governance. My views here are animated by scholars across law, political science, and ecology who recast times of significant instability as predicates for reform. Within this framing, I argue it is time to revisit affirmative emergency powers with a fresh lens.

This Article proceeds in three parts. Part I is descriptive. It details the statutory provisions granting affirmative emergency powers to officials under the CAA, CWA, SDWA, and state analog statutes. To elucidate their scope, I highlight the statutes’ operative terms and standards, identify triggers for action, and describe the types of orders various officials may impose. I then briefly highlight the differences between these authorities and the far more prevalent emergency powers that circumvent environmental protections and processes.

Part II explores affirmative emergency powers’ capacity to advance environmental protection. First, it identifies key benefits regarding responsiveness to instances of dire environmental injustices and to threats that do not involve permit violations. It then outlines the reasons why deployment of affirmative emergency powers avoids much of the doctrinal upheaval inflicted by recent Supreme Court decisions. I conclude that affirmative emergency powers are neglected yet powerful tools for environmental protection and justice, and particularly so in this era of administrative law constraints and regulatory inertia. This Part also surfaces potential counter-considerations. I assess the merits of theoretical and practical challenges, while sketching the limits and drawbacks of using these authorities.

Part III offers a prescriptive framework to guide more effective deployment of affirmative emergency powers. It enumerates contexts where these interventions are especially well-suited to advance environmental protection because conventional enforcement tools have failed to respond adequately or contemporary regulatory regimes have left persistent gaps. I also set forth proposals to inform the use of affirmative emergency powers in ways that complement environmental justice values and diminish common concerns over broad executive emergency authorities.

text:
Growing electricity demand, including from AI-driven data centers, creates a unique opportunity to scale clean firm power technologies, but targeted policy reforms are needed to unlock full potential

WASHINGTON — The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven data centers, among other factors, is increasing U.S. electricity demand, creating new challenges for the power sector but also offering an opportunity to accelerate investment in the next generation of clean, reliable energy technologies, according to a new report released today by the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions (C2ES).

The report examines how growing electricity demand from AI data centers is creating new markets for technologies capable of providing reliable, 24/7 power while reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Through a series of case studies involving hyperscalers, utilities, and energy developers, the report explores how AI-driven investments could help accelerate the commercialization of clean firm power technologies such as traditional and advanced nuclear, next-generation geothermal, long-duration energy storage paired with clean energy sources, natural gas with carbon capture and storage, and biomass energy with carbon capture and storage.

After two decades of relatively flat demand, U.S. electricity consumption is rising again as AI adoption accelerates, manufacturing expands, and more sectors electrify. Some projections suggest data centers could consume as much as 9 to 17 percent of U.S. electricity generation by 2030, more than double their current share. At the same time, many of the world’s largest technology companies must meet the around-the-clock power and capacity requirements of AI data centers while advancing ambitious sustainability commitments, creating strong incentives to seek reliable, low-carbon sources of power.

Among the projects highlighted in the report are agreements supporting advanced nuclear development in Virginia, the restart of the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in Pennsylvania, next-generation geothermal deployment east of the Rocky Mountains, long-duration energy storage projects in Minnesota, and carbon capture projects in Illinois and beyond. While these projects differ in technology and geography, they share a common theme: AI-driven electricity demand is helping create new pathways for the commercialization of technologies that may be nascent, capital-intensive, or face longer deployment timelines than conventional firm options like unabated (without carbon capture) natural gas generation.

“Growing electricity demand presents a significant opportunity to strengthen the energy system America will need for decades to come,” said Katie Ott, vice president, Sustainability, Constellation. “Constellation stands ready to invest in our existing generation fleet while exploring solutions to bring new firm, emissions-free power to the grid. With the right policy frameworks and continued long-term commitments from customers, we can unlock private investment to add megawatts, enhance system reliability, and help manage costs for consumers.”

The report finds that hyperscalers such as Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft are increasingly supporting clean firm power technologies through long-term power purchase agreements, innovative utility tariffs, and direct investments. These arrangements can reduce investment exposure for utilities and energy developers, demonstrate proof of concept to build investor confidence, and support higher-cost technologies as they scale and move down the cost curve.

“Today’s clean firm investments are valuable not because they will transform the grid overnight, but because they help build the foundation for medium to long-term power sector decarbonization,” said Diandra Angiello, Technology Innovation Policy Associate Fellow at C2ES. “These investments enable “learning by doing,” which, over time, can improve project financeability, crowd in additional private capital, and drive the adoption of clean firm technologies in applications far beyond data centers.”

The report cautions, however, that these investments alone are unlikely to deliver a low-carbon power sector in the near term. Despite growing interest in clean firm technologies as long-term power options, hyperscalers must meet rapidly growing electricity demand today, not years from now. As a result, unabated natural gas continues to play a dominant role in meeting the electricity needs of U.S. data centers. Ultimately, the climate impact of AI will depend in part on how quickly clean firm power technologies can capture a meaningful share of the growing electricity demand from data centers and how effectively hyperscaler investment can accelerate the deployment of these technologies into the broader power sector.”

To maximize the opportunity presented by AI-driven investment, the report outlines a series of federal and state policy recommendations that can further accelerate clean firm adoption. These include advancing permitting reform, improving transmission planning and interconnection processes, establishing a federal clean electricity standard and performance standard for data centers, strengthening support for carbon capture infrastructure, extending tax incentives for clean electricity technologies, supporting federal energy financing programs, and encouraging state policies that promote the deployment of clean firm power resources while protecting ratepayers.

Rising demand, technological innovation, and private-sector investment are converging in ways that could accelerate the deployment of technologies necessary for maintaining reliable, affordable, and increasingly clean electricity. The report concludes that the United States is at a pivotal moment for the future of its power system, and complementary policy is needed to reduce costs, shorten deployment timelines, and create durable investment signals.

Over the past several years, C2ES has engaged closely with leading companies across sectors to examine challenges and solutions to decarbonizing the U.S. economy by 2050. To inform policymakers considering these near- and long-term questions, C2ES launched a series of “Closer Look” briefs to investigate important facets of the decarbonization challenge, focusing on key technologies, critical policy instruments, and cross-sectoral challenges. These briefs explore policy implications and outline key steps needed to reach net zero by mid-century.

text:
US electric vehicle and clean energy company Tesla has applied for a Texas property tax limitation for a proposed $3.1 billion polysilicon refinery near Robstown, Nueces County, saying it would not build the plant in the state without the incentive.

The application, filed with the Tuloso-Midway Independent School District under the state’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETI) program, has been published by the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts.

Tesla describes the plant as “under consideration for development” and as the “upstream component of Tesla’s vertically integrated domestic solar manufacturing platform.” It says that “in the absence of the agreement the applicant would not make the proposed investment in this state” and that it is assessing locations in other jurisdictions.

The plant would produce ultra-high-purity polysilicon for single-crystal silicon ingots and N-type, high-efficiency solar cells. Its equipment list includes a hydrochlorination and trichlorosilane synthesis unit, chlorosilane distillation and purification trains, silicon tetrachloride recycling loops and Siemens chemical vapor deposition reactors. The filing does not state the plant’s production capacity.

Investment timeline

An economic impact analysis prepared for Tesla by EY puts construction between 2027 and 2030. Of the planned capital spending, $1.5 billion is earmarked for engineering and construction, $1.4 billion for equipment and $183 million for utility infrastructure, with more than 80% spent in 2028 and 2029.

Tesla plans to hire 260 workers in 2030, rising to 515 once the plant is fully operational in 2032, at average total compensation of $130,000, according to the analysis. Construction would support an average of 550 direct jobs a year. EY estimates the project would generate about $63.5 billion in economic output in Texas through 2065.

Tesla said in the filing that more than 90% of the world’s solar-grade polysilicon is produced in China.

Under the schedule in the EY analysis, the project’s taxable value for school-district maintenance and operations taxes would be cut to zero from 2028 to 2030 and halved from 2031 through 2040. The Comptroller must review the application, and both the Office of the Governor and the school district’s board must approve an agreement before it takes effect.

The application follows Tesla’s JETI filing for Project Crystal Sun, a proposed solar cell and module factory in Fort Bend County, Texas, with planned investment of about $10.1 billion. That project cleared a key tax hurdle in September when the local school board backed its limitation.

The US government’s Section 232 tariffs and minimum import prices on polysilicon, which also impose a 15% duty on imported ingots, wafers, cells and modules, take effect on Dec. 4. The minimum import prices are designed to force foreign suppliers to match US production costs, raising the value of domestic feedstock in a market where US polysilicon production remains limited. Solar manufacturer Toyo secured US polysilicon supply to navigate trade barriers in January.

text:
From: Mercom India

esVolta, a developer, owner, and operator of utility-scale battery energy storage projects, has secured $181.2 million through two financing transactions for its City Breeze and Boxcar battery energy storage projects in Texas.

Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe advised esVolta on both transactions. Winston Taylor advised MUFG Bank on the project financing transaction. So far, the company has secured more than $1 billion in funding.

esVolta closed a $126.1 million project financing facility with MUFG Bank for the City Breeze energy storage project in Bay City, Texas. The financing comprises a construction loan, tax equity bridge loan, letter of credit facility, and term loan. The funds will support the project’s construction and long-term operations.

Once completed, City Breeze will provide 140 MW/280 MWh of energy storage capacity to the Electric Reliability Council of Texas market.

Separately, esVolta closed a $55.1 million tax equity financing with East West Bank for the City Breeze and Boxcar energy storage projects. The Boxcar project, located in Wylie, Texas, will provide 150 MW/300 MWh of battery storage capacity to the ERCOT grid.

“Closing these financings with MUFG and East West Bank reflects the strong confidence our partners have in esVolta’s strategy, our disciplined approach to development and financing, and the strength of our Texas portfolio,” said Randolph Mann, CEO at esVolta. “Together, City Breeze and Boxcar add 290 MW/580 MWh of flexible capacity to ERCOT, where rapid load growth makes energy storage essential to grid reliability and to meeting rising electricity demand.”

In June, the company expanded its corporate credit facility to up to $450 million to support new energy storage projects across North America. Nomura Securities International, a global investment bank in the energy and infrastructure sectors, led the transaction.

According to the release, the company has more than 1.5 GWh of projects operating and under construction in Texas. These projects account for most of its 2 GWh portfolio of operating and under-construction projects.

text:
General Motors Co. in Detroit has announced its largest clean-energy project to date — a utility-scale solar generation facility in Branch County, south of Marshall, and the accompanying Lake Iris solar project in St. Clair County (Port Huron).

Both projects were developed by NorthStar Clean Energy with GM as the primary customer through a virtual power purchase agreement. The cost of the two developments was not provided.

As energy demand grows and the grid evolves, locally connected sources of renewable generation can support both business and community resilience.

The projects build on GM shared earlier this year: In 2025, it secured enough renewable energy to match 100 percent of its electricity use across all its U.S. facilities — making GM the first U.S. automaker to reach this goal.

GM plans to apply the renewable energy credits generated by these projects toward the emissions associated with electricity purchased for its manufacturing operations. The automaker reports it reduced operational emissions (known in greenhouse gas accounting as scopes 1 and 2) by 52 percent since 2018, as it seeks to meet its vision of a zero-emissions future.

In addition, securing long-term, low-cost renewable energy helps improve price predictability and reduce exposure to fuel-market volatility.

The automaker state the value of Branch and Lake Iris extends beyond the electricity to be produced. The two projects together created more than 550 full-time local construction jobs during their development.

Overall, GM reports its renewable projects have generated nearly $2 billion in economic impact and supported about 1,500 construction jobs each year in communities across the U.S.

In related news, Branch helped Bethel Township receive a $1 million Renewables Ready Communities Award, supporting local priorities including township hall expansion and road improvements.

Lake Iris plans to incorporate a pollinator habitat across the solar facility grounds. Native plantings can help reduce long-term maintenance needs while supporting solar-panel efficiency and local biodiversity. GM is supporting the habitat effort, which creates an opportunity to partner with researchers to study pollinator habitat and regional value creation.

text:
The United States has surpassed 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of cumulative installed energy storage capacity, highlighting the rapid expansion of battery storage across the country. The industry added 14.3 GWh of new capacity during the third quarter of 2026, taking total installations for the first nine months of the year to 48.3 GWh, according to the U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026 released by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.

The growing deployment of energy storage is helping improve electricity grid reliability, manage energy costs and support the integration of renewable energy. The report also increased its forecast for cumulative U.S. energy storage deployment by 3.7%, projecting total installations of 708 GWh by 2030 across grid-scale and behind-the-meter applications. Installations during the first nine months of 2026 increased 20% compared with the same period last year.

The industry is also calling on Congress to accelerate permitting reforms and support the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). More than 300 solar and energy storage companies recently sent a letter to Congressional leadership urging the legislation’s swift passage. The proposed measures are expected to accelerate storage deployment, reduce project costs and expand access to affordable and reliable electricity for households and businesses.

SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty said increasing energy storage deployment is helping address electricity affordability concerns. He urged lawmakers to pass the legislation to strengthen America’s energy infrastructure and put downward pressure on electricity prices.

Texas led the country in utility-scale energy storage deployment through the third quarter, adding 12.3 GWh of capacity. Arizona followed with 7.7 GWh, while California recorded 6.8 GWh. According to recent SEIA analysis, the expansion of solar and energy storage helped reduce average wholesale electricity prices by 42% in Texas and 51% in California between summer 2021 and summer 2026.

The report also highlighted strong growth across state markets. Eleven states, including Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama and Illinois, surpassed their previous annual energy storage installation records during the third quarter, with three months remaining in 2026.

Manufacturing capacity is expanding alongside project deployment. New battery cell manufacturing facilities opened in Tennessee in July and Indiana in October, bringing total U.S. battery cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, representing a 50% increase.

Utility-scale projects accounted for most installations during Q3, with 12.2 GWh deployed. Commercial and industrial installations contributed 1.3 GWh, while residential storage added 746 MWh, demonstrating the expanding role of energy storage across different electricity market segments.

description:
Clean energy project developers are encouraged to put forward bids in this new renewables auction.
This latest auction round will continue the government’s journey to clean power and net zero, with budgets being set as COP31 nears its close.
Energy Minister Michael Shanks said: Delivering clean, homegrown power is the route to lower bills, greater energy security and new investment across the country.
We’ve already approved enough clean power to power the equivalent of more than 20 million homes and unlocked over £110 billion of private investment.
Our new approach to this renewables auction maximises transparency and control over what we buy, ensuring we get the clean power we need at the right price.
text:
During the final week of COP31, the government is announcing the budget for the next renewables auction, with an evolution in approach to ensure clean power continues to drive down bills. Clean energy project developers are encouraged to put forward bids in this new renewables auction.

Allocation Round 8 (AR8) will continue the government’s push to clean power and net zero, while continuing to make tackling the cost of living crisis our top priority by creating as much transparency and control in the bidding process as possible.

Prices across all wind and solar technologies will be visible to ministers before they confirm which projects to procure. This builds on the approach taken in the previous auction round for offshore wind, which secured a record amount of offshore wind at a price 40% cheaper than the alternative of building and operating new gas power plants.

Our procurement of renewables generation will continue to focus on delivering value for billpayers, and the government will ensure it procures clean power in the right place and at the right price. This greater control will help deliver this, ahead of more substantial reforms for Allocation Round 9.

This latest auction round will continue the government’s journey to clean power and net zero, with budgets being set as COP31 nears its close. This follows the news last week that energy company RWE confirmed a £12 billion investment in Vanguard offshore wind projects, as part of the previous successful auction round.

Following a year of instability in the Middle East, record-breaking heatwaves and wildfires, the need for renewables and the transition away from volatile fossil fuel markets to build our energy security has never been clearer.

Energy Minister Michael Shanks said:

Delivering clean, homegrown power is the route to lower bills, greater energy security and new investment across the country.

We’ve already approved enough clean power to power the equivalent of more than 20 million homes and unlocked over £110 billion of private investment.

These reforms build on that progress by making the auction process more transparent and competitive, so we secure the best projects at the best price for consumers while accelerating the transition to clean power.

Exchequer Secretary to the Treasury Dan Tomlinson said:

More clean power is the primary route to lower bills while building a more secure and affordable energy system.

Our new approach to this renewables auction maximises transparency and control over what we buy, ensuring we get the clean power we need at the right price.

Initial budgets have been set at a notional £1, because the government now has full visibility over all bids, so will only set a final budget after bids have been submitted. The greater transparency built into our new approach gives more control to government and means that budgets can be increased where we are confident bidding projects offer value for money and deliver on our ambition for cheap clean power.

This auction round reflects an evolution in how clean power is delivered, ensuring we buy the best value new renewable capacity, while government continues to deliver the grid infrastructure needed to carry the electricity being produced. Budgets will be set to ensure that Allocation Round 8 will lower bills and delivers a good outcome for energy security and the climate.

Previous auction rounds have already secured around 24GW of offshore wind capacity since the scheme began. Looking ahead to AR9, as set out at the Budget, government continues to progress reforms to the Contracts for Difference scheme.

Neil McDermott, CEO Low Carbon Contracts Company:

The Contracts for Difference scheme is a world class mechanism enabling investment in clean power and LCCC is proud of our role as counterparty.

This allocation round builds on the scheme’s success and we look forward to working with the successful applicants over the life of the contract.

description:
