text:
A large permitting reform bill co-sponsored by a New Mexico U.S. senator and stirring debate across the country passed another procedural vote Werdnesday in the U.S. Senate.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act passed a cloture vote 65-31, which ended debate on the proposed package. The cloture vote was the third of three procedural votes on the bill faced Wednesday.

The bill has further votes in the Senate and House and potential amendments ahead of it before it could head to the president’s desk. Wednesday’s cloture vote showed lessened support for the bill from the 73-25 procedural vote on Nov. 9.

The bill, co-sponsored by Democratic U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, seeks to remedy delays in national energy and infrastructure projects. The bill has received wide support from the Citizens Climate Lobby, labor unions, the Solar Energy Industries Association and oil and gas industry leaders. But it has raised concerns over its potential to weaken bedrock environmental protections and historic preservation efforts, and limit public input and tribal consultation.

Heinrich and the other co-sponsors of the bill — Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va.; Mike Lee, R-Utah; and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I. — say the bill would accelerate green energy projects, lower costs for ratepayers and force data center companies to pay for their connections to electric grids.

Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska called the policy the “most substantive bipartisan agreement on permitting reform” in her time in Congress.

“You can’t do much in Alaska without a federal permit,” she said Wednesday on the Senate floor. “Almost every project that eventually makes it through the process still winds up in court.”

U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján, Heinrich’s fellow senator from New Mexico, again voted against bill0 Wednesday. The bill has drawn opposition from other members of New Mexico’s all-Democratic congressional delegation as well.

“There is no question the system is broken and America must rebuild our infrastructure,” New Mexico U.S Rep. Melanie Stansbury said during a House floor proceeding Tuesday. “But that cannot be the building of infrastructure and transmission at any cost.”

A spokesperson for Stansbury said the bill and manager’s amendments are still under debate and negotiation.

“It is unclear what, if any, substantive amendments will be considered and voted on,” Stansbury spokesperson Felecia Pohl wrote in an email. “Once we see the final Senate bill, we will determine the next course of action. At the present time, the base bill and manager’s amendment are actively opposed by Tribal nations, civil rights, and environmental organizations across the country and the Congresswoman cannot support the bill in its current form. “

A spokesperson for U.S. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández of New Mexico said she too does not support the bill as it stands.

The Rhodium Group, an independent research organization, conducted an analysis of the policy’s potential impacts on the U.S. energy system, electricity prices and greenhouse gas emissions prior to amendments to the bill. Its models found the policy could reduce average electricity bills for residential customers by $50 to $78 a year in 2040. The study also found it could reduce greenhouse gas emissions by between 5 million and 148 million metric tons annually in 2040, and lead to more clean energy projects.

In the hours preceding the vote, some senators argued these positive impacts are not enough.

“Under this bill, big tech gets to build cheaper, faster and without consequence,” U.S. Sen. Ed Markey , D-Mass., said Monday evening. “Communities will be forced to witness the degradation of their land and suffer from more cancer-causing pollution in exchange for the promise of marginal savings, in addition to the $5 a month savings in 15 years, even modelers supporting this bill have found with modest to nonexistent climate and affordability benefits for our country.”

The Center for Western Priorities also pushed back on the Rhodium Group’s findings, saying the analysis did not count “the emissions from the drilling, mining, and gas-powered data centers the bill would lock in on public lands.”

text:
Would-be presidential contenders are hunting for donors, seizing media attention, and trying to generate some buzz.

Summary

Looking at the current leading Republican and Democratic contenders for the Presidential nomination, there's a huge gap between the parties on climate change and clean energy. There are interesting nuances, however, within each party.

The midterms are over, which means that the Presidential election has begun in earnest. We can’t tell yet who the nominees will be. In fact, since 2008, Presidents have tended not to be the obvious nominees when the campaign began. Still, we can at least get a sense of what the field looks like and how the potential candidates differ in their views about climate change and clean energy.

Let’s start with the Republicans. Vance, Rubio, and Cruz seem to be the three who are mentioned most often at this point.

JD Vance has quickly morphed from clean energy advocate to Trump clone. Until at least 2020, Vance said we “have a climate problem” and needed to move to solar energy. When seeking Trump’s support for his Ohio Senate bid, Vance reversed direction, and he actively opposed clean energy as a Senator. He managed to achieve a lifetime score from the League of Conservation Voters (LCF) of 0%, apparently never voting for anything that favored the environment. Presumably, that wasn’t a problem when Trump picked him as V.P. As Veep, his stance seems indistinguishable from Trump’s.

Marco Rubio also went through a metamorphosis, though not quite as abruptly as Vance. As Florida House Speaker he favored clean energy, energy efficiency, and rooftop solar, but he reversed course as a Senator. Rubio had a lifetime score LCV score of 7% in the Senate, making him a flaming environmentalist compared to Vance’s zero score. As a Trump subordinate in his present position, he echoes the party line, like Vance.

Ted Cruz is a climate denier and believes that China is behind lawsuits against oil companies. His lifetime LCV score is 3%, right between Vance and Rubio. He has favored an all-of-the-above approach, including wind and solar, which makes sense in term of Texas’s energy mix. For example, two years ago, he posted, “Oil, gas, wind, solar, nuclear — Texas is the energy capital of the world.” His support for renewables alongside fossil fuels used to the be the standard Republican position. Weirdly, today it places the arch-conservative Cruz to the left of Rubio and Vance.

On the Democratic side, support for climate action is widespread but there are differences in degree. The Democratic field is larger and more fluid than the Republican field, where one person will carry outsized weight. There seems to be a consensus that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (AOC) and Gavin Newsom are serious contenders, but after that things become more debatable. Jon Ossoff also makes the lists a lot, although he says that he has no interest in running. Could be true, but since everyone says that until the day they announce, the statement doesn’t mean much. It’s certainly easy to imagine that others such as Andy Besheer or Peter Buttegieg might make serious runs. I decided to stick to the first three as at least indicative of the kind of candidates the party might favor.

AOC clearly represents the progressive wing of the party. She has a lifetime LCV score of 98%. She introduced the Green New Deal in Congress along with Sen. Ed Markey. But she proved pragmatic in the runup to passage of Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act, leading to some criticism from the Left.

Gavin Newsom has been a stronger supporter of climate action during his time as governor of California. However, he’s been willing to bend where necessary given pressure to keep gas prices under control and respond to pressure for greater affordability.

Jon Ossoff has an LCV score of 96%. He opposed the Green New Deal and introduced bills to boost solar manufacturing and subsidize solar panels and energy efficiency for lower-income groups. He has also been a spokesman for renewable energy in international gatherings.

There’s obviously a huge gulf between all the Republicans and all the Democrats I’ve discussed. That’s not a surprise: there is about a 30% gap between the LCV scores of the most liberal Republican (Susan Collins) and the most conservative Dermocrat (John Fetterman). There are some nuanced variation, however, within each party.

Six months from now, the list of contenders might look quite different. But at least for now, that’s what the situation looks like.

description:
The Texas Tribune recently reported that state environmental regulators have resumed reviewing permits for data centers.
The move comes after Governor Greg Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) to conduct a comprehensive verification and audit of all data centers advancing through ERCOT’s interconnection process back in August.
According to The Texas Tribune, Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) received notice from the governor’s office on Friday that state electrical grid officials had finished gathering information on potential community impacts from data centers.
“The agency has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations,” TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said in a written statement.
Advocates from environmental groups such as Public Citizen and FracTracker Alliance are criticizing the decision, citing that TCEQ has not publicly released its findings on potential community impacts of data centers or explained how those findings will influence permit decisions.

description:

Quaise Energy says this first-of-its-kind deal will help catalyze the commercial development of superhot geothermal energy.
Quaise Energy says superhot geothermal is a virtually limitless energy source that uses the Earth’s natural heat to generate up to 10 times more clean power per well than traditional geothermal systems.
“Together with Google, we are building the commercial foundation for superhot geothermal and cementing the United States as the global leader in geothermal power,” Quaise Energy’s CEO and president Carlos Araque said in a statement.
Recent breakthroughs and growing interest from AI hyperscalers could supercharge superhot rock geothermal development.
text:
The AI boom and the hyperscalers’ need for round-the-clock clean energy for their data centers meet the next-generation geothermal energy technologies developed by a number of start-ups.

In a world first, Google this week signed an agreement with Quaise Energy to use power from the superhot rocks in the Newberry Volcano in Oregon for its existing data center operations in The Dalles.

Quaise Energy, which develops utility-scale superhot geothermal energy, has signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) under which Google will buy 50 megawatts (MW) of superhot geothermal power from Project Obsidian, Quaise’s flagship project in Central Oregon, beginning in the early 2030s.

Quaise Energy says this first-of-its-kind deal will help catalyze the commercial development of superhot geothermal energy.

Traditional geothermal energy is limited to regions with naturally occurring hot-water reservoirs that rarely exceed 600 degrees F. But superhot rock is a kind of enhanced geothermal that digs miles into the Earth to reach temperatures of nearly 800 F. Once superhot temperatures are reached, cold water is injected to create steam, which powers turbines.

Quaise Energy says superhot geothermal is a virtually limitless energy source that uses the Earth’s natural heat to generate up to 10 times more clean power per well than traditional geothermal systems. Related: 5 Oil and Gas Stocks That Crushed Third-Quarter Earnings Estimates

At Project Obsidian, the company expects to be the first in the world to use millimeter wave drilling, a technology that can plug into existing drilling rigs to economically reach superhot geothermal conditions.

Millimeter wave drilling is the keystone of superhot geothermal, Quaise Energy says, noting it is the only way to access the resource at scale while reaching economic and power parity with fossil fuels.

“Together with Google, we are building the commercial foundation for superhot geothermal and cementing the United States as the global leader in geothermal power,” Quaise Energy’s CEO and president Carlos Araque said in a statement.

For Google, the agreement is more than just another PPAs for clean energy as the tech giant built its first owned-and-operated data center in The Dalles, Oregon, in 2006.

Oregon’s Newberry is also the site of a superhot geothermal project under development by another start-up, Mazama Energy, which just this week announced a first-of-its-kind chilling technology to protect critical equipment in 645°F superhot rock while increasing drilling speed by 20%. These breakthroughs address key barriers to competitive geothermal power, Mazama Energy says.

“We can now address geothermal economics from both directions: lowering the cost of drilling each well and accessing hotter rock that can deliver far more energy,” Mazama Energy’s chief executive officer Sriram Vasantharajan said.

“That is how utility-scale geothermal can become a truly competitive source of firm power.”

Mazama in September raised $135 million in new capital to accelerate superhot rock geothermal commercial development, with strategic investors Shell Ventures and ConocoPhillips alongside John Arnold’s Centaurus Capital, Doerr Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Gates Frontier.

Recent breakthroughs and growing interest from AI hyperscalers could supercharge superhot rock geothermal development.

The Clean Air Task Force estimates that just 1% of the superhot rock (SHR) geothermal potential in the United States could produce 4.3 terawatts (TW) of firm, flexible power. That’s nearly four times the current total installed electricity-generating capacity in the United States.

Superhot rock geothermal energy could help meet part of the soaring power demand from data centers while providing 24/7 clean energy to the hyperscalers’ facilities.

Goldman Sachs Research last month said that it now expects global data center power demand to soar by 170% between 2025 and 2030, with more than 60% of that growth coming from within the United States.

“Power is probably the forever bottleneck,” said Jason Tofsky, global head of Digital Infrastructure Investment Banking at Goldman Sachs.

text:
You probably got the letter.

Rocky Mountain Power recently began mailing out notices of a $4 monthly fee that will be added to electricity bills unless customers opt out. It’s all part of an initiative being pushed by a coalition of cities and counties across the Beehive State, which will fund clean energy projects that would then plug into the power company’s grid.

The Community Clean Energy Program, as it’s called, is set to “advance renewable energy solutions,” according to Rocky Mountain Power’s website. If the notice the company sent to you ended up in the pile of mail on your counter, here’s what you need to know about it:

What is the fee?

The program means Rocky Mountain Power customers will be paying an extra $4 per month on their energy bills unless they opt out. Customers can decline to participate online by logging into their account at rockymountainpower.net, over the phone by calling 800-895-0614, or by mailing an opt-out form to Rocky Mountain Power (this form should have come with your notice).

What is the deadline to opt out?

Customers are automatically enrolled in the program, and must opt out by Jan. 1 to avoid the charge. You can cancel by May 1 of next year without facing a fee. Any cancellations after May 1 incur a $30 charge.

Who will pay?

The fee will charge customers in Alta, Castle Valley, Emigration Canyon, Francis, Holladay, Midvale, Millcreek, Moab, Oakley, Ogden, Park City, Salt Lake City and Springdale. Customers who live in the unincorporated areas of Grand County, Salt Lake County and Summit County will also be subject to the extra charge.

These places are part of Utah Renewable Communities, a group created by a 2019 law to work with Rocky Mountain Power toward the goal of providing net 100% renewable energy by 2030.

Lower-income customers enrolled in Rocky Mountain Power’s Home Electric Lifeline program will be able to participate for free, so the charge to customers will also help offset the cost for their neighbors who may make less.

What will it pay for?

The fee goes toward developing “new, utility-scale renewable energy sources,” including solar, wind, and geothermal projects, according to a newsletter from the Healthy Environment Alliance of Utah, commonly referred to simply as HEAL Utah.

Carmen Valdez, HEAL Utah’s radioactive and toxics program manager, has led the organization’s work with Utah Renewable Communities for the past seven years. Building new utility-scale energy requires funding, so the fee is a way for communities to partner with Rocky Mountain Power and determine what energy projects fuel their power grid, she said in an interview.

“Anytime we look at a bill and see an increase, it could be a little bit of a shock factor,” Valdez said. “But this time, this is a good fee. This is going to helping ensure that Rocky Mountain Power is committed ... to bringing those clean energy sources on the grid.”

The funding from the fee will be pooled, Valdez said, and allocated toward clean energy projects approved by the Utah Renewable Communities board. Each municipality has a representative on the board, she added.

“It’ll be projects that can directly interconnect to the PacifiCorp transmission system, so it could be located in Idaho, Utah or Wyoming,” Valdez said. “But the energy for [Utah] communities will be achieved 100% net, which means it’ll be offset by that clean energy coming onto the grid.”

That means not all the power going to somewhere like Salt Lake City would be generated by renewable energy, but clean energy investments that residents pay into would balance out other sources.

Could it go to nuclear power?

Utah’s law that created the Community Clean Energy Program does define energy derived from nuclear fuel as a “clean energy resource,” but the communities within the program determine what kinds of projects are funded by the fee, Valdez said.

The coalition of municipalities evaluated projects through a request for proposals that only considered wind, solar, geothermal and hydroelectric resources, so those are the types of projects the group plans to pursue moving forward, according to its website.

Why did HEAL fight to get this?

HEAL has been pushing for Utahns to have a say in what projects power their grid for years, Valdez said, and getting involved in the program is a great opportunity for the Beehive State to lead with this first-of-its-kind, community-led energy project and plan.

“We hope that this is really just the start of seeing similar programs throughout the state as well as throughout the nation when it comes to community-led energy resources,” Valdez said.

text:
Polara, a Quebec company that builds charging infrastructure and energy software for electric fleets, said it ranked 139th on Deloitte’s Technology Fast 500 after growing 515 percent between 2022 and 2025. It says it has delivered 165 charging projects and manages 290 sites through its Cleo platform.

The release, as issued by Polara

LONGUEUIL, Quebec, Nov. 19, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Polara, a North American provider of charging infrastructure, software and energy services for electric fleets, today announced that it ranked number 139 on the Deloitte Technology Fast 500™, a ranking of the 500 fastest-growing tech companies in North America, now in its 32nd year. Polara grew 515% during 2022 to 2025.

“Our growth comes from solving the full operational challenge, not just installing chargers”, said Polara’s Chief Executive Officer, Sébastien Fournier. “We bring together infrastructure, fleet operations, software and energy expertise to help customers deploy and operate electric fleet. Our smart platform Cleo optimizes charging sessions and strengthens the economics of electrification.”

Polara’s growth is rooted in the expertise gained through complex fleet-electrification projects across the United States and Canada. This hands-on experience allows the company to design solutions around each fleet’s operational, charging and energy requirements rather than treating charging as a stand-alone equipment purchase.

A key technology supporting this approach is Cleo, Polara’s smart charging and energy-management platform. Cleo connects vehicles, charging stations, buildings and power-grid signals, helping fleets schedule charging around vehicle availability and site constraints while managing demand and energy costs.

On the hardware side, CHRGPK, Polara’s proprietary modular power platform for fleet depots, delivers more than 95% efficiency, IEEE-compliant harmonic mitigation and utility-grade metering and protection, making depots easier to connect, maintain and expand as fleets grow.

Scale demonstrated in the field

Polara’s North American footprint now includes:

165 charging-infrastructure projects delivered;

290 sites managed through Cleo, optimizing thousands of charging stations;

Nearly 150 electric fleets have entrusted Polara with the management of their carbon credits.

This scale is reflected in projects that address different fleet, energy and grid requirements:

New York State’s largest electric school bus fast-charging project for GVC Ltd.;

Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) infrastructure for Fremont Unified School District in California;

Canada’s first municipal vehicle-to-everything (V2X) charging station in Victoriaville, Quebec.

Extending the business case through energy and carbon markets

Beyond infrastructure and smart charging, Polara helps fleets across North America unlock additional value from their transition to electric vehicles and equipment. Through carbon credit management, Polara enables fleets generate recurring revenue that complements energy and maintenance savings, strengthening the business case for fleet electrification.

“The next stage of fleet electrification will be measured by operational and financial performance,” said David Cantin, Vice President, Finance at Polara. “By optimizing charging, accessing energy services and capturing carbon-market value, we help customers turn electrification into a long-term operating advantage.”

“The 2026 rankings demonstrate that established momentum and breakthrough growth can drive sustained market leadership,” said Justin Yahr, Audit & Assurance partner and National Emerging Growth Company leader, Deloitte & Touche LLP. “Nearly 70% of this year’s award winners returned as repeat honorees, reflecting the power of disciplined and sustained execution. More than 30% made the list for the first time, illustrating how quickly new players are shaping their respective sectors. Furthermore, private companies represented almost 80% of the list, a clear indication that the agility and strategic focus of private enterprises remain essential to scaling in competitive markets.”

About Polara

Polara provides charging infrastructure, software and energy services for electric vehicle fleets in the United States and Canada. Its integrated offering spans fleet and site analysis, charging infrastructure with its CHRGPK power platform, smart charging and energy management through Cleo, V2G and V2X applications, and carbon-credit monetization through Polara Carbon. Polara works with fleet operators, school transportation providers, manufacturers, municipalities and public-sector organizations to improve charging reliability, control energy costs and unlock additional value from electric assets.

For more information, visit polara.energy, follow Polara on LinkedIn or explore the Resources section.

About the 2026 Deloitte Technology Fast 500™

Now in its 32nd year, the Deloitte Technology Fast 500™ ranks the fastest-growing public and private technology companies in North America based on percentage revenue growth from fiscal 2022 through fiscal 2025. Eligible companies must be headquartered in the United States or Canada, have been in business for at least four years, own proprietary intellectual property or technology that contributes significantly to operating revenue, report at least US$50,000 in base-year operating revenue and at least US$5 million in current-year operating revenue, and achieve revenue growth of at least 50%.

text:
RALEIGH, N.C. (WBTV) - North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein called Duke Energy’s approved rate increase “too high,” days after state officials signed off on it.

The North Carolina Utilities Commission approved the rate hike Monday, Nov. 16. It takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Calling the commission’s decision “wrong,” Stein said its order abandons wind plans, reduces solar development and delays new nuclear projects, leaving the state more dependent on price-volatile natural gas and coal.

--> Related: Duke Energy Carolinas bills could rise nearly $10 per month in 2027

Duke Energy said North Carolina’s population growth and the need to improve storm resilience require new power plants and electric grid upgrades.

“This outcome keeps affordability at the forefront while allowing us to make the investments needed to strengthen reliability and support North Carolina’s continued growth,” Duke Energy said. “That balance is what we were working to achieve.”

Looking at the numbers

Duke Energy Progress customers will see an average increase of 3.4% over two years, including 4.7% for residential customers. Duke Energy Carolinas customers will see an average increase of 3.7%, including 4.8% for residential customers.

The company said a typical Progress customer’s monthly bill will rise by $6.53 on Jan. 1, 2027, and another $4.66 on Jan. 1, 2028. A typical Carolinas customer’s bill will rise by $9.62 and $5.89 on those respective dates.

“Energy costs are rising, and we need to be doing everything we can to bring people relief,” Stein said. “This rate increase is too high and moves us in the opposite direction.”

text:
The first politician to refer to an “all of the above” energy strategy, according to the Times, was Benjamin Gilman, a Republican congressman from the Hudson Valley, who used the phrase in a speech that he delivered on the floor of the House, in 2000. The country, Gilman said, needed to promote the use of all forms of power, including coal, natural gas, ethanol, wind, and solar. An “effective national energy policy,” he said, “must, at a minimum, allow for all of the above.”

Over the next few decades, the phrase became a bipartisan rallying cry. John McCain used it in his unsuccessful Presidential campaign against Barack Obama in 2008; then Obama took it up. Donald Trump embraced it, and so, too, did many of the Democrats who ran on anti-Trump platforms this year. James Talarico will “keep Texas the world’s energy leader with an all-of-the-above strategy that protects good-paying oil and gas jobs and grows wind, solar, and geothermal,” the senator-elect’s campaign website declared.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a.k.a. the Senate permitting bill, might perhaps more aptly be named the All of the Above Act. The four-hundred-plus-page bill would make it easier to obtain federal permits for a wide variety of energy and energy-related projects, including transmission lines, wind farms, natural-gas pipelines, data centers, and coal mines. The Senate is expected to take up the permitting bill before the weekend. If approved, the bill will then head to the House, where it’s unclear whether it has enough support to pass. Whether it should pass is even more doubtful.

BAAJA was negotiated by a quartet of senators: Shelley Moore Capito, a Republican of West Virginia; Mike Lee, a Republican of Utah; Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island; and Martin Heinrich, a Democrat from New Mexico. The four—and many, many others—agree that the federal permitting process is too cumbersome, and that this discourages investment in many sorts of energy projects. High-voltage transmission lines, which are used to transport electricity over long distances, are a key illustration of the problem; the U.S. has been building such lines at the rate of about five hundred miles per year, when, it is estimated, five thousand miles’ worth per year are needed to meet the country’s growing demand. A lack of transmission capacity can, in turn, prevent electricity-generating projects from coming online, or even being built. BAAJA seeks to encourage the construction of transmission lines by, among other things, giving the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) more power over planning for the country’s electrical grid. Proponents say that, by speeding the addition of transmission lines, the bill will also foster the construction of more carbon-free energy projects. “Removing permitting, transmission, and interconnection barriers would disproportionately accelerate clean energy deployment,” the trade group American Clean Power Association wrote in support of the act.

But BAAJA goes way beyond power lines and FERC’s jurisdiction. And the bill’s multitude of other provisions have many groups—including the National Congress of American Indians, the N.A.A.C.P., the Natural Resources Defense Council, and Earthjustice—up in arms. The current federal permitting process, which has been in place for decades, gives states, communities, and tribes an opportunity to weigh in on major projects and to challenge agency reviews that they find faulty or inadequate. BAAJA “reforms” the process by limiting states’ and tribes’ input, eliminating various kinds of environmental harm from consideration, and curtailing judges’ ability to evaluate whether permits have been properly vetted. In a recent op-ed in Bloomberg Law, David Tatel, who served for three decades on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, wrote that, while on the bench, he had heard “dozens of cases” involving federal agencies’ reviews of projects under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).

NEPA “ensures the federal government takes a ‘hard look’ before, say, greenlighting a new pipeline or uprooting hundreds of trees on a Washington golf course,” Tatel wrote. The permitting bill, he said, would make NEPA challenges so difficult as to render such suits “virtually futile,” and the implications of this would extend far beyond energy infrastructure. “Just last month, a federal judge relied on NEPA to stop the current Administration as it bulldozed hundreds of trees at the East Potomac Golf Course,” Tatel observed. “Earlier this year, a federal judge in Maryland halted the conversion of a warehouse in Maryland into an ICE detention center because it violated NEPA. Neither result is likely to be repeated if the permitting bill becomes law.”

Perhaps the bill’s most surprising—and dangerous—provision is one that would allow companies to sue a federal agency for “disparate treatment” of an energy source. On the upside, this provision could conceivably prevent a future wind-hating President from cancelling green-energy projects simply because he doesn’t care for them. But it could also tie the hands of any future Administration that wants to responsibly promote green energy over fossil fuels. As it is written, the disparate-treatment provision would, some legal experts argue, effectively lock in America’s reliance on oil, coal, and natural gas. In a statement of support for the bill, issued last week, the Trump Administration pointed to the “disparate treatment” provision, saying that it would insure that permits are granted “without bias against fossil fuels.”

The permitting bill was introduced on the Friday before Election Day, and it’s the first major piece of legislation Congress has taken up since the ballots were counted. The bill’s backers—who reportedly include the President’s new chief of staff, Stephen Miller—are eager to see it enacted this session, before Republicans relinquish control of the House and the Senate. It’s not hard to see why the G.O.P. and groups like the American Petroleum Institute—which has been lobbying for the bill by handing out free tacos on Capitol Hill—would be in a hurry to see it passed. It is tougher to understand why congressional Democrats would acquiesce to the rushed timetable, given that in six weeks they’ll be in power.

In an editorial urging passage of BAAJA, the Times argued that Democrats should “take the deal” because Trump would veto any better permitting bill that they might try to pass next year, and that “time matters, especially for the climate.” Lawmakers, the editorial continued, could return in 2027, and approve “other bills that would do even more good.” (Why the President wouldn’t veto those bills, the newspaper did not explain.)

The Times’ argument, which doubtless has been influential, unfortunately doesn’t make much sense, on political or on environmental grounds. As the editorial notes, Trump is going to be in the White House for two more years, during which he will continue to control the federal permitting process. Expediting that process will therefore expedite precisely the kinds of projects that he and his donors like most. Asked recently about BAAJA, Trump said he backed it, but added that he still would “not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.” If the bill passes, challenging the permits that the Trump Administration hands out to, say, pipelines or liquefied-natural-gas terminals will, per Judge Tatel, become “virtually futile.”

text:
Agreement advances early coordination between engineering, procurement, and manufacturing to secure U.S. power infrastructure supply

Hitachi, Ltd. (TSE: 6501, “Hitachi”) and Bechtel today announced an enterprise agreement designed to improve how critical electrical equipment for electrical energy infrastructure is planned, engineered, and procured for Bechtel projects in the United States. The agreement establishes a framework for distribution and power equipment supply, bringing the companies together earlier to support delivery of the infrastructure needed to meet growing electricity demand.

“Demand for electricity is growing faster than it has in decades and meeting it will take more than new factories. It will take partners who are willing to plan together for the long term,” said Bruno Melles, Executive Vice President and General Manager, Hitachi Energy. “Bechtel builds some of the most complex energy and infrastructure projects in the world, and this agreement reflects the trust between our two companies. We see it as a model for how manufacturers and builders can work together to accelerate the building of the grid.”

“Our customers need confidence that the equipment critical to their projects is being planned for from the start,” said Tarek Amine, Principal Vice President and Chief Supply Chain Officer, Bechtel. “This agreement brings our engineering and procurement teams together with Hitachi earlier, so we can align designs, anticipate demand, and reduce repeated work across projects. It’s one of many ways Bechtel is helping customers achieve more predictable delivery of the power infrastructure the United States needs.”

Growing demand and long lead times for power equipment can complicate planning for new power infrastructure. The agreement is designed to address those challenges earlier, aligning Bechtel’s project forecasts and engineering requirements with Hitachi’s manufacturing planning to support more predictable delivery for customers. Hitachi is helping address these constraints by bringing standardized solutions and coordinated execution to the effort, support more predictable delivery.

As the United States invests in new energy infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, and other electricity-intensive industries, coordination across the infrastructure supply chain is increasingly important. Bringing engineering, procurement, and manufacturing perspectives together earlier in project development is essential. Hitachi’s ability to integrate advanced AI into these processes is a differentiator. text:
Ford has reached an important milestone in its electric vehicle strategy, with the first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells now rolling off the production line at its BlueOval Battery Park Michigan facility in Marshall. The batteries are being shipped to Louisville, Kentucky, where they will be used in prototype versions of the upcoming Ford Fathom electric pickup.

The development brings Ford one step closer to launching its next-generation affordable electric vehicle platform, with the Fathom expected to enter production in 2027. It also marks the beginning of Ford’s own domestic LFP battery manufacturing operations, giving the automaker greater control over a technology it considers essential for reducing EV costs.

The first production-grade LFP prismatic battery cells have started leaving BlueOval Battery Park Michigan after years of development and factory preparation.

The facility, located in Marshall, Michigan, is owned and operated by Ford. It was established specifically to manufacture lithium iron phosphate batteries for mainstream electric vehicles, making it a significant part of the company’s efforts to build more affordable EVs in the United States.

Ford says the factory’s production lines can assemble approximately 40 battery cells per minute, placing it among the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly operations outside China.

The facility is designed for an annual production capacity of approximately 20 gigawatt-hours, providing Ford with the ability to supply batteries for future electric vehicles at a much larger scale.

However, the first cells are not heading directly into customer vehicles. Instead, they will be transported to Louisville Assembly Plant, where they will support the development and testing of Ford Fathom prototypes.

Ford plans to begin battery pack assembly in Marshall in 2027, ahead of the electric pickup’s planned production launch.

Lithium iron phosphate batteries are becoming increasingly important in the electric vehicle industry, particularly for manufacturers looking to lower vehicle prices without sacrificing long-term durability.

Unlike nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) batteries, LFP chemistry does not require nickel or cobalt. These materials can add significant costs to battery production, making LFP an attractive alternative for more affordable electric vehicles.

LFP batteries also offer several advantages, including strong durability, good resistance to repeated charging cycles, and access to more widely available raw materials.

There are some trade-offs. LFP batteries generally have lower energy density than comparable NMC alternatives, meaning they can require more space or weight to deliver the same amount of energy. They can also experience greater performance limitations in very cold temperatures.

Ford’s approach is to compensate for these limitations through vehicle efficiency and intelligent battery integration rather than simply installing a larger battery pack.

The company believes this strategy can help deliver the driving range and everyday practicality customers expect while keeping manufacturing costs under control.

Ford’s new battery operation is also the result of a technology licensing agreement with Chinese battery manufacturer CATL.

Rather than establishing a traditional joint venture, Ford acquired the rights to use CATL’s LFP battery technology and manufacturing expertise. CATL engineers also helped prepare the Michigan facility, train employees, and establish production processes and quality-control systems.

The arrangement allows Ford to own and operate the manufacturing facility while benefiting from experience developed by one of the world’s largest battery manufacturers.

Ford says the prismatic LFP cells being produced at the Michigan plant have been developed specifically for its requirements rather than simply being existing CATL products.

The partnership is particularly important because the United States has historically relied heavily on overseas battery manufacturing and technology. Establishing domestic production gives Ford more control over battery supply, manufacturing processes, and the development of future affordable electric vehicles.

The upcoming Ford Fathom will be the first vehicle based on the company’s new Universal EV Platform.

One of the platform’s most important engineering decisions involves integrating the battery pack into the vehicle’s structure instead of treating it as a separate component housed underneath the chassis.

Ford selected rectangular prismatic battery cells because their shape makes them suitable for structural integration. This approach can reduce the number of additional components needed to support and protect the battery.

The company has also simplified electrical connections and sensing systems by combining them into flexible circuit boards and integrating compact power electronics into the battery pack.

These engineering decisions are intended to reduce weight, simplify manufacturing, and lower overall vehicle costs.

Ford says its Universal EV Platform requires approximately 20% fewer components and 25% fewer connecting elements than a conventionally developed vehicle.

The platform is also designed around a more efficient electrical architecture, consolidating multiple vehicle functions into fewer central electronic modules.

Rather than competing primarily through increasingly large battery packs, Ford wants to achieve competitive driving range through improved efficiency and a more carefully optimized vehicle design.

Affordability is expected to be one of the biggest selling points of the Ford Fathom.

Ford has previously announced a starting price of $28,350 for the Standard-Range version in the United States. Including the mandatory $1,595 destination charge, the starting price comes to $29,945 before taxes and registration fees.

That positions the Fathom just below the $30,000 threshold, an important target for Ford as it attempts to attract customers who might otherwise purchase a conventional gasoline-powered pickup.

The combination of LFP battery chemistry, structural battery integration, fewer vehicle components, and a redesigned manufacturing process is central to making that price possible.

Ford is also developing bidirectional power capabilities for the Fathom. With the appropriate home equipment, the electric pickup is expected to support applications that allow it to supply electricity to a home, adding another potential benefit beyond everyday transportation.

Specific battery capacity, EPA-estimated driving range, and maximum charging power have not yet been officially disclosed.

text:
UNIS/SGSM/1636

19 November 2026

The Secretary-General

Message for Africa Industrialization Day

20 November 2026

On Africa Industrialization Day, we celebrate the continent’s determination to transform its economies, create productive jobs for its people, transition to clean energy, and build a more prosperous and sustainable future.

Africa is embarking on this ambitious mission at a critical moment. High-growth sectors are rapidly emerging and creating major opportunities for the continent — from electric vehicles, to batteries, computer chips and renewable energy.

These sectors offer opportunities to diversify economies beyond resource extraction, and build links to regional and global value chains rooted in the processing of critical minerals, innovation, sustainable infrastructure and green industries.

The African Continental Free Trade Area, bold actions towards Agenda 2063, the start of the Fourth Industrial Development Decade for Africa and the continent’s burgeoning leadership in renewable energy are all giving these sectors further momentum and potential for growth.

But fully realizing these opportunities hinges on reliable energy and transport systems, enabling policy and regulatory environments, and investment in skills development, lifelong learning and education.

Above all, as this year’s theme reminds us, African industrialization requires financing and investment, from the public and private sectors alike.

Many African countries face significant financing constraints and crushing debt service burdens that limit investment in infrastructure, energy, technology, skills and productive capacity. The recent launch of the Africa Credit Rating Agency by the African Union and key partners is one key Africa-led initiative that seeks to help address these issues.

The Sevilla Commitment, agreed in 2025, shows a pathway to mobilize more finance — both domestic and international, public and private — to spur sustainable development, while addressing the debt burdens faced by developing countries. It also calls for long-overdue reforms to the global financial architecture to better support, and represent, the needs and participation of developing economies.

By mobilizing resources, partnerships and political will, we can accelerate Africa’s industrial transformation and build a future of shared prosperity for all.

The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties to U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump met in recent days with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

"That's why this is such a monumental success story," Whitmer said. "We are leading the world here and we are gonna out-compete and beat China."

title: Trump wants the Supreme Court to let his EPA cancel billions in Biden-era climate grants
description:
A favorable outcome at the high court could help his administration defeat other grant lawsuits, according to the government’s filing this month.
The EPA canceled the nonprofits’ grants soon after the start of Trump’s second term in January 2025, with EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin accusing the groups of mismanagement and potential fraud.
It demands access to their grant money so they can run the program.
The EPA says the $16 billion at stake is the largest grant cancellation case ever and is another reason it warrants Supreme Court review.
The courts have so far tried to thwart the administration’s priorities, the EPA wrote in its petition to the Supreme Court.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is appealing to the Supreme Court in its push to cut $16 billion in grants for a climate program, the largest grant cancellation case ever and one that could affect Republican President Donald Trump’s push to defund the priorities of prior administrations.

The justices have not said whether they will take the case.

If they do, it could resolve a fight over grants that the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded in 2025. Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration awarded the money under a 2022 law to finance clean energy projects and accelerate the transition from fossil fuels. Trump has targeted other grants, such as those considered to be supporting diversity, equity and inclusion. A favorable outcome at the high court could help his administration defeat other grant lawsuits, according to the government’s filing this month.

At issue is the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, commonly referred to as a “green bank.” Climate United Fund and other nonprofits were picked to operate the program authorized by the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act. If the justices decline to take the case, the groups could regain access to their money because a federal appeals court already ruled in their favor.

The EPA canceled the nonprofits’ grants soon after the start of Trump’s second term in January 2025, with EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin accusing the groups of mismanagement and potential fraud.

The nonprofits’ lawsuit argues that the EPA broke the law and violated the Constitution. It demands access to their grant money so they can run the program. The administration says it is immune from legal and constitutional claims and contends the groups filed their case in the wrong court.

If the justices eventually side with the EPA, it could “have far-reaching implications for the government’s ability to reshape grant programs and to terminate grants that do not advance a particular administration’s policy priorities,” said Romany Webb, deputy director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University who has supported Climate United’s arguments.

The EPA says the $16 billion at stake is the largest grant cancellation case ever and is another reason it warrants Supreme Court review.

The courts have so far tried to thwart the administration’s priorities, the EPA wrote in its petition to the Supreme Court.

The EPA and Climate United declined to comment.

Federal appeals court sided with the nonprofits

In August, a divided federal appeals court in Washington sided with the nonprofits and said the administration improperly terminated the grants. The release of any money was paused to give the Supreme Court a chance to weigh in.

The justices ruled for the administration recently in decisions over canceled National Institutes of Health grants and teacher training grants.

The administration has built its arguments around the Tucker Act, which gives the Court of Federal Claims exclusive authority over contract disputes. The claims court can award money, but not direct the government to take certain actions in the way federal courts can.

The nonprofits argued the way the EPA canceled the grants did not upend a contract with the federal government, but was done illegally and undercut spending on entire programs Congress had required, a constitutional violation. The government argues the matter is a contract dispute.

The administration’s broad use of contract cancellations to enact policies is a novel approach, according to Bob Wagman, president of the Court of Federal Claims Bar Association and a partner at the firm White & Case.

“I would hate to think that the only programs that could be supported have a four-year life,” he said, mentioning cancer research as an example of a grant program that would need longer than a single administration to pay off. “It is just not good for the country.”

Government rushed to cancel grants and criticize the nonprofits

Zeldin last year told Fox News that he suspected the green bank “was a clear-cut case of waste and abuse.”

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan said that when the government was asked for evidence of fraud, the EPA did not provide it and shifted its position to more general concerns about the level of oversight over the program. Chutkan said the government cannot terminate the contracts in violation of the law and that the groups should have access to some of their frozen money, which is held in an account at Citibank.

The administration has been adamant that nothing requires them to make these grants to these groups.

Passage of the Inflation Reduction Act created the green bank. Trump’s tax and spending bill passed last year rescinded part of the law that established the bank and the money that had not already been obligated to its recipients. The EPA has said that those changes mean it should not have to release any money to the groups.

___

Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott in Providence, R.I., contributed to this report.

This Q&A examines how the midterm results could affect data center growth and electricity prices.
It suggests that near-term plans to build hundreds of gigawatts of data center capacity could be scaled back.

text:
This Energy Explained post represents the research and views of the author(s). It does not necessarily represent the views of the Center on Global Energy Policy. The piece may be subject to further revision. Contributions to SIPA for the benefit of CGEP are general use gifts, which gives the Center discretion in how it allocates these funds. More information is available here. Rare cases of sponsored projects are clearly indicated.

Midterm voters gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress and flipped governorships in states central to data center development, including Texas, Georgia, and Ohio. Electricity affordability and data centers featured prominently in the campaigns, with many candidates pledging to pause new data center projects or review their tax incentives, and nearly all saying developers should “pay their own way.” Voters also supported greater limits on data center development in several local ballot measures.

This Q&A examines how the midterm results could affect data center growth and electricity prices. It suggests that near-term plans to build hundreds of gigawatts of data center capacity could be scaled back. “Pay their own way” policies, including the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), can help protect other ratepayers from the costs of serving data centers, but they may be insufficient on their own because they do not address all the ways that data center demand can affect wholesale capacity and energy prices.

Why did data centers emerge as a major issue in the election campaigns?

Data centers sit at the intersection of several voter concerns, including rising energy bills, local effects such as water use and noise, tax incentives for large technology companies, and broader unease about the effects of AI on jobs. Polling reflects that unease. A UMass poll found that nearly two-thirds of respondents oppose data centers in their own communities, and an NBC News exit poll found that over half of voters cited pushback on data centers and AI as a major factor in their congressional vote.

Have data centers actually contributed to higher electricity prices?

Until recently, load growth, including from data centers, had not been a principal driver of electricity prices, except in PJM (the mid-Atlantic states) where capacity auction mechanisms and ceiling prices pushed prices up. Detailed data analysis published by LBNL found that average residential prices roughly tracked inflation from 2019 to 2024. While many blamed data centers for that inflationary growth, LBNL pointed instead to increases in equipment costs (some attributed to tariffs) and fuel costs (especially natural gas), as well as equipment upgrades and replacements necessitated by aging infrastructure and storm recovery, as the principal drivers. These findings do not mean that data center demand had no effect on prices, however. A more recent Dallas Fed working paper estimates that data center demand raised wholesale electricity prices by 6.9 percent nationally by 2025, with regional impacts reaching as high as 15 percent.

At the same time, integrated resource plans in territories served by vertically integrated and regulated utilities reflect significant increases in capital requests, and regulatory commissions are approving more of them, leading to higher prices. These developments point to a changing dynamic in the US power system, in which electricity demand growth driven by electrification, increased manufacturing, and, in some markets, large loads from data centers and other commercial and industrial users is occurring alongside the need to replace and upgrade aging infrastructure. This combination is driving inflationary price pressures.

However, load growth itself does not always translate into price increases. In markets with ample available generation and transmission capacity, increased load led to lower prices by spreading those fixed costs over greater sales volume. Moreover, states with the highest demand growth from 2019 to 2025 generally saw inflation-adjusted prices fall by more than one cent per kilowatt-hour, with Nebraska, New Mexico, and North Dakota absorbing large industrial and data center additions while prices declined. If rapid data center growth continues in states with supply or delivery constraints, and without appropriate tariff structures, electricity prices could rise, necessitating greater protections for vulnerable households.

What have AI companies and data center developers done to secure more power quickly when grid interconnection is delayed?

Developers are increasingly turning to behind-the-meter generation. Around 2 GW of behind-the-meter generation was operational as of mid-2026, with a further 7.5 GW under construction and 60 GW-plus in the pre-construction stage. Most of this capacity is expected to be powered primarily by natural gas, which accounts for roughly 80 percent of the identified behind-the-meter resources. Although the five-year cost of on-site gas generation is estimated at $101-107 per megawatt-hour (MWh) versus an average US industrial price of $86 per MWh, many hyperscalers are prioritizing speed to power over higher electricity costs.

The growing use of behind-the-meter generation has broadened the debate over how data centers should be powered and regulated, with the public increasingly focused not only on electricity prices and who bears the cost of new infrastructure, but also on local community impacts of data center development. These concerns have spurred policy discussions of strategies and regulatory measures such as bring-your-own-power, bring-your-own-clean-energy, and large load tariffs, as well as increased scrutiny of air permitting, local ordinances, and local approvals.

What are the limits and trade-offs of going off-grid?

Going off-grid will not be an easy choice for many data center developers. A global shortage of gas turbines has led some developers to repurpose used jet engines, which are less efficient and more polluting. Developers will need access to reliable natural gas supplies and pipeline infrastructure. In contrast to areas where natural gas availability may be constrained, Texas’s Permian Basin has an abundance of gas, but limited pipeline capacity to transport it. These constraints have repeatedly pushed gas prices at the Waha Hub below zero. In this context, behind-the-meter data centers could offer producers a new local market for surplus gas. Over time, however, that demand could compete with other domestic users and LNG exports, pushing up local gas prices.

Going off-grid also does not eliminate local permitting challenges. Projects may still face increased local opposition over water use, noise, land use, traffic, and air quality.

How might BAAJA and the new Congress affect data center development?

As written, BAAJA would require large computational loads to pay the embedded and incremental costs of serving them and would limit shifting those costs to other customers. However, those protections do not address wholesale capacity and energy prices, a principal driver of price increases in PJM. Even so, Rhodium estimates BAAJA would reduce household bills by $50-78 by 2040, while Grid Strategies estimates that about $55 billion in transmission costs could be collected from data centers.

The new Congress, under Democratic majority control, could shape the debate in two ways. First, Democrats have said they plan to introduce a new wave of bills in January to protect consumers from data center-related electricity costs. Any new legislation would still face a presidential veto and Senate filibuster rules. Second, congressional committees could increase oversight through hearings on data center-related energy costs.

How might the election results change state-level data center policy?

Thirty-six states held gubernatorial elections, with Democrats flipping governorships in several states central to data center growth, including Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa, and Nevada. New Mexico, another state central to data center growth, remained under Democratic control. Multiple governors-elect, including those in Texas and Georgia, campaigned on conditional pauses or moratoria on new data center projects. Others, such as Nevada’s governor-elect Ford, pledged to pause and review data center tax abatements. These positions suggest that, in the near term, data center development will depend not only on the speed of grid interconnection, but increasingly on state-level conditions, including cost-allocation requirements, incentive reviews, and local approvals.

Another likely area of change relates to the allocation of electricity costs. Nearly every candidate took the position that data centers should “pay their own way” rather than shift costs onto other ratepayers, especially residential ratepayers. This position aligns with the recent use of large load tariffs and recent federal efforts to protect ratepayers. However, as noted above, while large load protections cover costs incurred by the serving utility, they do not cover higher wholesale capacity and energy prices. “Pay their own way” clauses may therefore be insufficient on their own to prevent higher electricity bills.

Finally, the election results could increase pressure on developers to address local concerns, including noise, water, and traffic, and to negotiate substantive community benefit agreements. In their campaigns, most governors-elect acknowledged local authority over permitting decisions, reflecting growing opposition to data center development. That opposition is also evident in ballot measure results: of the 47 ballot measures related to data center development decided by voters in 2026, voters favored greater limits on data center development in 46.

Will data center growth slow down?

About 185 GW of announced data center demand is in the pipeline across the 20 states, roughly 53 percent of the national total. The five flipped states with large pipelines (Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Nevada and Iowa) are estimated to account for 142.5 GW of that total demand, about 41 percent of the national total. Based on the current state of development and the possibility that campaign pledges translate into policy, slowdowns or moratoriums could affect up to about 50 GW of data center buildout in the next two to three years. Much of this would likely be in Texas, given its outsized pipeline. Other states that might see slowdowns include Georgia, Ohio, New Mexico, and Nevada. If political pauses are shorter and developers make greater efforts to address local concerns, strengthen community engagement, and establish realistic build schedules, slowdowns or short-term moratoriums may affect less than 10 GW of anticipated demand. Alternatively, if campaign statements on slowdowns or moratoriums were translated into policy in all 20 states, nearly 100 GW of anticipated demand could be affected, potentially slowing overall data center load growth over the next few years.

Beyond data center policy, what can incoming governors do to address electricity affordability?

Aside from data center tariffs, governors have other levers to address electricity affordability, including greater scrutiny of utility capital plans and rate cases; performance-based regulation that rewards cost-control rather than capital spending; faster interconnection processes; deployment of grid-enhancing technologies such as dynamic line rating and advanced conductors; and programs that encourage flexible data center loads. These levers address long-standing price drivers, including equipment inflation, storm and wildfire costs, and rising utility capital spending.

name: Clean Energy
title: Expert Q&A: What a New Transmission and Permitting Bill Means for Energy in the US
authors: Andrea Hohman, Jacqueline Kantor, Alicia Cypress
description:
A new bipartisan federal energy transmission and permitting bill aimed at speeding up energy and infrastructure projects is advancing through the Senate.
It’s designed to also be a grid bill and a data center bill, all in one package with permitting reform.
The primary focus of this bill is really about energy costs, as the gap between our energy demand and our energy supply is raising energy costs for Americans.
It requires federal energy data to track data centers’ electricity use, giving regulators and the public better information.
For clean energy, the expanded grid investments, faster interconnection and streamlined permitting would accelerate development of clean energy projects, including solar energy projects and batteries, which have been the fastest growing in recent years and are poised to accelerate without permitting and grid barriers.
text:
A new bipartisan federal energy transmission and permitting bill aimed at speeding up energy and infrastructure projects is advancing through the Senate. It’s one of the most significant energy reform bills since the 1970s, proposing the biggest changes to how the U.S. power grid is built since the Energy Policy Act of 2005. The bill aims to make electricity more affordable, secure and reliable at a time when demand — including that from artificial intelligence and data centers — is drastically increasing, while the infrastructure of the aging U.S. grid is deteriorating.

We asked WRI energy experts Mark Falinski, Lori Bird, Alex Smith and Katrina McLaughlin to help explain the key energy provisions of the bill (known formally as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, or BAAJA) and their significance, as well as its impact on a clean energy future. While the bill is sweeping and covers many different topics, here, we focus on the important questions and topics in which WRI has deep expertise.

What is this energy bill designed to do?

While this legislation is often referred to as a "permitting bill," it does much more than that. It’s designed to also be a grid bill and a data center bill, all in one package with permitting reform.

At its core, the bill aims to make it easier, faster and cheaper to build the energy infrastructure the U.S. needs. It also aims to streamline federal and state processes, while advancing new technologies. It contains provisions designed to reduce the amount of time it would take to permit projects, limits the time projects are subject to litigation and legal review, and prevents current and future presidential administrations from retroactively canceling projects that have advanced through the permitting process.

The bill also helps accelerate the modernization and expansion of the grid so supply can keep up with America’s rapidly growing energy demand. The bill looks to bridge this gap by streamlining processes to bring new power sources online faster, connecting America’s many grids together, advancing technologies that make the most of the power sources we already have and building out grid infrastructure to move energy from where it is generated to where it is needed. These changes to the grid are particularly important to expand clean energy.

Additionally, there are parts of the bill that are designed to protect Americans from high electricity prices that can come from the increase in new data centers or other large electricity-driven infrastructure.

Ultimately, the bill is trying to make it easier to build the infrastructure necessary to modernize American electricity infrastructure, the buildout of which is currently lagging well behind other developed countries.

The bill is titled ‘Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act’ — what is the potential economic impact? How does it address affordability and jobs?

The primary focus of this bill is really about energy costs, as the gap between our energy demand and our energy supply is raising energy costs for Americans.

This bill won’t drive down electricity bills overnight, but modeling from Resources for the Future suggests that it will lower the cost of the entire power system compared to what it would have been without these new provisions by 3.5% to 7%. This should help slow the rise, or potentially even lower, electricity prices. Similarly, modeling from Rhodium Group suggests that this bill would reduce household electricity bills by $50 to $78 per year in 2040, compared to the bill not passing.

Most of the jobs that will result from this bill are expected to come from the manufacturing, construction and energy sectors that would be needed to build more power lines and energy projects, with Employ America estimating the creation of up to 105,600 industrial jobs. The bill also helps federal agencies hire and keep the staff needed to meet new review deadlines, while still conducting thorough reviews. It includes funding for wildlife and historic preservation reviews, a new fund to strengthen permitting teams and more flexibility for federal power agencies like the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to recruit the experts it will need to carry out the bill’s new transmission and data center rules.

How is this bill expected to impact emissions from the American power system?

Four major modeling studies published since the introduction of the bill use detailed energy models to simulate what would be built with and without the bill. All four agree that the bill would bring more clean power onto the grid and could slow the buildout of fossil-fuel power, relative to the status quo. Depending on the study and scenario, they project 17 gigawatts (GW) to over 300 GW of additional wind, solar and batteries versus without the bill. The high end of that range is roughly equal to all the solar capacity installed in the U.S. today. Most also estimate tens of gigawatts less new gas capacity and a lower share of electricity from coal and gas.

The impact on emissions is more nuanced and a little less clear. Projections range from virtually no change in emissions to large reductions over the next 10 to 15 years, depending on the underlying assumptions, the provisions being modeled, and the future they are compared against.
