text:
GM drivers who have enrolled in the Energy Pass scheme from their respective GM apps (myChevrolet, myGMC and myCadillac) can now use automated Plug and Charge payment at participating Electrify America stations.

The hands-free process is available for GM EVs with native CCS charge ports, and those with native NACS charge ports will receive the functionality in early 2027, the company says.

Drivers using Electrify America stations connect their vehicle to the charger and charging begins inside around 45 seconds, the company says, without paying manually on the app or at the charging point screen.

"Loading an app, reading a touchscreen, swiping a card, it all takes valuable minutes," said Wade Sheffer, vice president, GM Energy. "We're making it easier for drivers to start a charging session and get back on the road, with an experience that has fewer steps than swiping a credit card to get gas."

GM integrated the Electrify America network into the myChevrolet, myGMC and myCadillac apps in January this year, giving their drivers access to 350kW fast charging at around 6,200 Electrify America charging points. All GM apps can be used to find compatible stations, start and end charging sessions, check the EV's charging status, pay, view charging history and manage receipts.

GM launched Energy Pass as a single point of payment for public EV charging in June that lets drivers pay on-app at supported charging networks. General Motors announced in July that Energy Pass had been extended to ChargePoint's network. The company says Energy Pass can be used at present at approximately 60% of US public fast-charging stations.

Plug and Charge technology first became commercially available in 2020, with EV manufacturers integrating the ISO 15118-based standard into vehicles from 2019, and ISO-15118-2 the currently-observed standard in vehicle/grid communications. In the EU, ISO 15118-20 will be mandated from 2027, which adds bidirectional V2G and wireless connectivity to the communications protocol.

The Plug and Charge capability, such as that available to Energy Pass users, is based on an encrypted connection between the vehicle and the charging point carried by the charging cable. Once the vehicle or its driver's identity is verified, a secure data session opens between the vehicle and charging hardware, passing charging data (power level, current charging duration, cost of energy, etc.) between the two. Each session's details are recorded against a unique transaction ID. In the case of Energy Pass users, the cost of the charging session is debited from the registered card on the user's account.

title: How solar and storage are powering a new era of American manufacturing - Canary Media
description:
Cypress Creek Energy is developing, and will own and operate, what will be the largest solar project with energy storage in America.
The ambition to power American industry The Steel River Energy Center is notable for a host of reasons.
The Steel River Energy Center is the largest solar and storage project Google has sourced energy from worldwide.
Whether it’s the project’s size, offtake agreement, job creation, or tax revenue, much about the Steel River Energy Center attracts superlatives.
Watch Driving Steel – a new mini-documentary that takes you inside the American supply chain powering Steel River Energy Center, America’s largest solar project with energy storage to break ground to date.
text:
In the early 2020s, U. S. Steel launched a nationwide search to find the best location for a new factory. The company had recently completed its acquisition of the Big River Steel mill in Osceola, Arkansas. The goal of the expansion: Replicate the success of Big River Steel, which supplies the automotive, construction, and renewable-energy industries and can produce over 3 million tons of steel annually.

After an exhaustive search, the company realized there was no reason to look beyond Northeast Arkansas. ​“We went to 48 states and narrowed the site selection down to 20, 10, five, and then three,” said Dan Brown, U. S. Steel’s executive vice president of advanced technology steelmaking and CEO of Big River Steel. ​“We built another plant one mile from where we’re at.” At close to $3.5 billion, the investment in what is now called Big River Steel 2 was the largest in U. S. Steel’s storied 125-year history.

A variety of factors go into determining the ideal location of a steel plant, including proximity to large customers, good railroad and river transportation, and a solid local workforce. Arguably most important, however, is access to reliable and affordable electricity, because producing steel requires an enormous amount of power. ​“If that isn’t number one, it’s in the top two,” Brown said. ​“You have to have a good electricity provider and a good electricity source.”

The reliable, affordable energy source that will help power the growth of one of America’s most iconic manufacturers is solar and energy storage. To that end, the Steel River Energy Center, which broke ground this past July, is a 2.46-gigawatt solar and 2.94-gigawatt-hour battery storage facility that will be built in three phases and is expected to be fully operational in 2029. Cypress Creek Energy is developing, and will own and operate, what will be the largest solar project with energy storage in America.

The ambition to power American industry

The Steel River Energy Center is notable for a host of reasons. The grid-connected project represents $4.5 billion in private investment and is expected to create 1,400 construction jobs in its first two phases and generate $300 million in local tax revenue over its lifetime. Google also signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with Cypress Creek Energy to secure the energy produced by the first two phases of the project. The Steel River Energy Center is the largest solar and storage project Google has sourced energy from worldwide.

Whether it’s the project’s size, offtake agreement, job creation, or tax revenue, much about the Steel River Energy Center attracts superlatives. But less obvious, and more meaningful for U.S. communities far beyond Mississippi County, Arkansas is the example it provides of solar and storage’s ability to power even the most energy-intensive industries and the many benefits of a robust domestic supply chain.

“Ten years ago, solar was still pretty niche, and battery storage was hardly on the radar,” said Kevin Smith, CEO of Cypress Creek Energy. ​“Steel River is proof that solar and storage have crossed a threshold. This is not niche energy dependent on incentives. This is the foundation of American industrial competitiveness, because we can beat alternatives on price and speed, both of which are critical to businesses that depend on affordable and reliable energy.”

A model to be replicated

The Steel River Energy Center is unique because of its size and because the Entergy Arkansas utility can connect the facility effectively to its transmission grid. While that scale can’t be achieved everywhere, Smith said, the modularity and flexibility of solar and storage can meet the needs of industries anywhere in the country. ​“This is very replicable. Not every location can have gigawatts of solar, but it can be built in 100-to-500-megawatt blocks across Arkansas, the Midwest, the Southeast, the West, everywhere,” Smith said. ​“This should be a standard story going forward.”

What could also become the norm is the strong relationship between domestic manufacturers and their customers, so evident at the Steel River Energy Center. The domestic supply chain supporting Steel River is a significant departure from the situation just five years ago, when utility-scale solar plants relied heavily on cheap steel imported from China. By contrast, Steel River is being built with 100% U.S.-made structural steel. The first two phases of the project will be built on about 400,000 steel piles driven into the ground to support more than 3 million solar panels. Fabricated by PACO Steel in nearby Blytheville, Arkansas using coils produced at the Big River Steel 2 mill in Osceola, each pile bears a stamp reading ​“Proudly made in Mississippi County.”

All the solar panels are being made at the First Solar U.S. factories, and trackers from California-based Nextpower are being built with domestically produced steel, much of it from Big River Steel. Battery storage systems provided by LG Energy Solution Vertech are assembled domestically using cells made in North America.

When price drives decisions

As much as the Steel River Energy Center is a story about domestic manufacturing and the ability of solar and storage to provide the energy big American industries need, it is also very much a local tale. After working in traditional steel manufacturing locations such as Indiana and Michigan, Brown has been in Northeast Arkansas for the past five years and has witnessed the transformation being driven by so much construction and manufacturing activity. ​“You can already see the difference,” said Brown, who lives just five minutes from the Big River Steel plant in Osceola. ​“People are spending money at the stores. There are more restaurants and more people in town.”

It’s a story that is more likely to be repeated in rural communities across America because, as Smith pointed out, more utilities and corporate energy users are moving beyond the politicization of energy to focus on the financial benefits. ​“They are making decisions based on economics, and the economics of solar and storage are unambiguous,” Smith said. ​“That’s why so much renewable manufacturing and deployment is going into red states. It’s not about ideology. It’s arithmetic.”

title: BMW Begins US Production of All-Electric iX5 Ahead of 2027 Launch - Serrari Group
description:
BMW Starts Production of Its First US-Built Electric Vehicle BMW has started building the all-electric iX5 at its plant in Spartanburg, South Carolina, the first fully electric BMW assembled in the United States.
Roughly 70 iX5 electric SUVs are rolling off the assembly line every day, alongside gas, diesel, and hybrid-powered models.
Woodruff is the fourth BMW production facility to begin series production of Gen6 batteries, following facilities in Hungary, Germany and China.
Outlook BMW’s iX5 production launch is an important milestone in the company’s transition towards a broader electric vehicle manufacturing portfolio in the United States.
The all-electric BMW iX5 is being assembled at Plant Spartanburg in South Carolina, United States.
text:
BMW has begun assembling the all-electric iX5 at its Spartanburg plant in South Carolina, marking the first time the German automaker has produced a fully electric vehicle at its US manufacturing facility. The move follows a $1.7 billion investment in the state and forms part of a wider strategy to manufacture at least six fully electric models in the United States by 2030. Production currently stands at approximately 70 vehicles daily, with US dealership deliveries expected in early 2027.

Key Takeaways

BMW has started assembling the all-electric iX5 at Plant Spartanburg, its first fully electric model built in the United States.

The facility is producing approximately 70 iX5 SUVs daily, with deliveries expected in early 2027.

The 2027 BMW iX5 60 xDrive starts at $79,800 and features a 144-kWh battery.

BMW’s new Woodruff facility has started producing sixth-generation (Gen6) batteries for its upcoming electric X models.

The automaker plans to manufacture at least six fully electric models in the United States by 2030.

Suppliers have reportedly been given a production target of 60,000 US-built EVs in 2027, although BMW has not officially confirmed the figure.

BMW Starts Production of Its First US-Built Electric Vehicle

BMW has started building the all-electric iX5 at its plant in Spartanburg, South Carolina, the first fully electric BMW assembled in the United States.

The development represents an important step in BMW’s efforts to expand electric vehicle production beyond its existing manufacturing locations and strengthen its presence in the American market.

BMW began building the iX5 at its sprawling Spartanburg, South Carolina plant this week. It marks the first time an EV has been assembled at the U.S. factory – the largest manufacturing complex BMW operates worldwide.

The company is currently producing approximately 70 iX5 vehicles daily. The electric SUV is being assembled alongside the conventional petrol, diesel and hybrid versions of the X5, using the same flexible production line.

Roughly 70 iX5 electric SUVs are rolling off the assembly line every day, alongside gas, diesel, and hybrid-powered models. All X5 powertrain versions are based on the same architecture, enabling the car manufacturer to share the same assembly line for multiple fuel types.

This arrangement allows BMW to manufacture different powertrain versions within the same facility rather than establishing a completely separate production line for its electric model. It also gives the company flexibility to adjust production according to demand for petrol, diesel, hybrid and fully electric vehicles.

The iX5 is expected to begin arriving at US dealerships in early 2027, giving customers their first opportunity to purchase a fully electric BMW manufactured

BMW Expands US Battery Manufacturing Through $1.7 Billion Investment

The start of iX5 production is supported by a wider investment in BMW’s South Carolina manufacturing operations, which includes a new battery assembly facility in nearby Woodruff.

BMW has invested $1.7 billion to expand operations at Plant Spartanburg. That includes a new battery manufacturing facility located near the main assembly complex. The new batteries will be used for iX5 and other EVs going forward.

The Woodruff facility, located approximately 15 miles from Plant Spartanburg, officially opened on November 13, 2026, and began series production of BMW’s sixth-generation electric vehicle batteries.

BMW officially opened its new Plant Woodruff in South Carolina on November 13, marking the start of series production of its sixth-generation (Gen6) EV batteries.

These battery packs will support BMW’s upcoming electric X models, beginning with the iX5. The proximity of the two facilities also connects battery assembly with vehicle manufacturing within the same regional production network.

Woodruff is the fourth BMW production facility to begin series production of Gen6 batteries, following facilities in Hungary, Germany and China.

Initially, the battery cells used in the iX5 will come from China, with BMW planning to transition towards locally manufactured cells later in the decade.

A BMW spokesperson confirmed that the iX5 will initially use battery cells from China before switching to U.S.-sourced cells from LG Energy Solution’s Arizona plant by the end of the decade.

LG Energy Solution is expected to supply BMW’s US facilities with locally produced cells, while Samsung SDI will supply European factories. BMW has also added both companies as battery cell suppliers for its US and European electric vehicles.

The shift towards US-sourced battery cells is significant because it would give BMW a more locally integrated supply chain for its American electric vehicle operations. It also connects the expansion of vehicle assembly with investment in battery manufacturing and component sourcing.

What Does the 2027 BMW iX5 Offer?

The 2027 BMW iX5 60 xDrive is the first model being produced under the new US manufacturing programme. It combines a large battery, dual-motor all-wheel drive and BMW’s latest Neue Klasse technology.

The 2027 BMW iX5 60 xDrive starts at $79,800.

The vehicle is equipped with a 144-kWh battery, with BMW estimating that it can deliver up to 456 miles of driving range. This is an improvement from an earlier estimate of 435 miles.

Charging performance is another major feature. During a demonstration in Southern California in October, the iX5 reached a peak charging rate of 464 kilowatts (kW). BMW said this could add up to 170 miles of driving range in approximately 10 minutes.

The vehicle also supports a 10% to 80% charging session in approximately 22 minutes, according to the supplied specifications.

Its dual-motor all-wheel-drive system delivers substantial performance, with the vehicle capable of accelerating from zero to 60 miles per hour in 4.4 seconds and towing up to 6,000 pounds.

Inside, the iX5 incorporates BMW’s Neue Klasse design and technology, including a 17.9-inch infotainment touchscreen and a Panoramic Vision display that stretches across the lower section of the windshield. Customers can also opt for a 14.6-inch passenger screen, creating an additional display for the front passenger.

The exterior features BMW’s new Double-X lighting signature, which combines the headlights, daytime running lights, side lights and turn signals into one unit.

These features position the iX5 as more than an electric version of the existing X5. The vehicle brings together BMW’s latest electric powertrain, battery technology, digital displays and updated design.

BMW Targets Six US-Built Electric Models by 2030

The iX5 is the first vehicle in a much larger electric vehicle manufacturing plan for BMW’s South Carolina operations.

It’s a big moment for the German automaker in the U.S., but it’s just the beginning of a much larger plan, which will include no fewer than six U.S.-built EVs by the end of the decade.

BMW’s plan is to assemble at least six fully electric models at Plant Spartanburg by 2030. The iX5 is expected to be followed by additional electric models, potentially including the iX7, iX6 and a performance-oriented iX5 M.

The expansion would allow the company to use its existing manufacturing infrastructure to support a wider range of electric vehicles while maintaining production of conventional and hybrid models.

BMW Manufacturing President and CEO Robert Engelhorn said the company was delivering on a commitment it had previously made regarding US electric vehicle production.

“We said we would begin assembling fully electric BMW vehicles in the US by the end of 2026 – and we are delivering on that commitment,” Engelhorn said.

The company also sees the expansion as part of a broader global shift towards electric mobility.

Engelhorn told Automotive News in an interview that “there’s a clear trend globally for EVs,” adding that “We will contribute to this growth from the BMW side.”

However, the pace of expansion will depend partly on how demand for electric vehicles develops in the United States and other markets.

BMW Revises Its Initial Production Target Amid Slower US EV Demand

Despite the expansion of its manufacturing capacity, BMW is entering the American electric vehicle market at a time when demand has weakened.

US electric vehicle sales have fallen sharply following the end of federal tax credits in September 2025. This has created a more challenging environment for manufacturers planning to expand their electric vehicle production.

BMW’s initial production target for the iX5 was reportedly at least 100,000 vehicles in 2027. However, suppliers have since been asked to plan for about 60,000 US-built electric vehicles in that year.

The automaker has not officially published its production volume estimates, meaning the 60,000 figure should be treated as a reported supplier forecast rather than a confirmed BMW target.

BMW’s longer-term supplier projections reportedly indicate that production could increase to as many as 175,000 electric vehicles annually from 2028.

The company’s expectations are also linked to the share of electric vehicles within the broader X5 range. A BMW representative indicated that approximately one in four X5 models would be electric in the near term.

Kavit Antani, BMW’s general manager of vehicle assembly, also highlighted the current market outlook.

“Currently, the market is looking like 20-25 percent EVs for the immediate three months,” said Kavit Antani, general manager of vehicle assembly. “As the market sees these vehicles come through, it might shift.”

This suggests BMW is adjusting its production expectations to reflect market conditions rather than simply building towards its original projections. The company’s ability to increase output will depend on how quickly customer demand develops and whether the US electric vehicle market recovers.

BMW’s US Manufacturing Expansion and Tariff Discussions

BMW’s decision to manufacture the iX5 in South Carolina also comes amid discussions over US import tariffs and the company’s wider manufacturing and export operations.

The Spartanburg facility is particularly important to BMW’s global business because it produces vehicles for both the domestic market and international customers.

Spartanburg assembled about 400,000 vehicles last year and shipped roughly half to 120 foreign markets, while BMW imported about 215,000 foreign-built models into the US.

The company has been seeking tariff relief from the Trump administration, with its US manufacturing and export operations forming part of the discussions.

Robert Engelhorn, president and CEO of BMW Manufacturing, said the company remained in contact with the federal government over trade conditions.

“Our business model is to export, so for sure we are in close contact with the federal government,” Engelhorn said. “We are looking towards free trade. We are looking toward the lower tariffs.”

BMW’s position reflects the importance of international trade to its US operations. Although the company manufactures vehicles in South Carolina, a substantial share of production is exported to overseas markets. At the same time, BMW imports vehicles manufactured in other countries for American customers.

The iX5 adds a fully electric model to this manufacturing and export network, potentially expanding the range of vehicles that BMW can produce in the United States.

The Bigger Picture

BMW’s decision to begin producing the iX5 in South Carolina demonstrates how established automakers are adapting their manufacturing operations as the global automotive industry shifts towards electrification.

Rather than relying entirely on imports or building separate electric vehicle facilities, BMW is using its existing Spartanburg manufacturing complex to assemble electric, petrol, diesel and hybrid models on a shared production line.

The accompanying Woodruff battery facility also shows the importance of developing local manufacturing capabilities alongside vehicle assembly. Battery production is a critical part of electric vehicle supply chains, and BMW’s investment creates a closer connection between battery manufacturing and finished vehicle production.

However, the company’s revised production expectations show that manufacturing expansion does not automatically translate into higher sales. The US electric vehicle market remains sensitive to consumer demand, affordability, charging infrastructure and government policy.

BMW’s longer-term ambitions will therefore depend on whether it can attract enough customers to support higher production volumes while remaining competitive in an increasingly crowded electric vehicle market.

Why Does This Matter Now?

The iX5 launch matters because it marks a new stage in BMW’s US electric vehicle strategy. The company is moving from importing or manufacturing electric vehicles elsewhere to assembling a fully electric model at its largest global production complex.

For the US automotive industry, the investment also highlights the importance of local battery production, manufacturing employment and supply-chain development as automakers compete in the electric vehicle market.

For consumers, the iX5 introduces another premium electric SUV option, with a stated range of up to 456 miles, rapid charging capabilities and a starting price of $79,800.

For BMW, the immediate challenge will be converting its manufacturing investment into sustainable customer demand, particularly as the US electric vehicle market adjusts to the removal of federal tax incentives.

Outlook

BMW’s iX5 production launch is an important milestone in the company’s transition towards a broader electric vehicle manufacturing portfolio in the United States. With approximately 70 vehicles being assembled daily and dealership deliveries expected in early 2027, the company is preparing to introduce its first US-built fully electric BMW to customers.

The next major developments to watch will include the iX5’s market reception, the pace of production growth, the transition towards US-sourced battery cells and the introduction of additional electric models at Plant Spartanburg.

BMW’s ambition to manufacture at least six fully electric models in the United States by 2030 signals a long-term commitment to the market. However, whether it achieves its reported production ambitions will depend on the recovery of EV demand, the competitiveness of its models and the wider trade and policy environment.

Frequently Asked Questions

1. Where is the BMW iX5 being manufactured?

The all-electric BMW iX5 is being assembled at Plant Spartanburg in South Carolina, United States. It is the first fully electric BMW model to be assembled at the facility.

2. When will the 2027 BMW iX5 be available to US customers?

BMW expects the iX5 to begin arriving at US dealerships in early 2027, with deliveries planned for the first quarter of the year.

3. What is the starting price and estimated range of the BMW iX5?

The 2027 BMW iX5 60 xDrive starts at $79,800 and has an estimated driving range of up to 456 miles, supported by a 144-kWh battery.

4. How many electric vehicles does BMW plan to manufacture in the United States?

BMW plans to assemble at least six fully electric models at Plant Spartanburg by 2030. Suppliers have reportedly been given a production target of 60,000 US-built EVs in 2027 and as many as 175,000 annually from 2028, although BMW has not officially confirmed those production figures.

text:
Canada has the abundant energy and ambition it takes to master our destiny and become an energy superpower in a rapidly changing global economy. We are accelerating major projects, attracting capital and diversifying our economic relationships. Our path to net zero supports this nation-building effort through four pillars -- build, switch, transform and innovate -- drawing on Canada's strengths, resources and regional diversity to strengthen energy security, improve affordability and build a more climate competitive economy.

Key to Budget 2026's plan is Powering Canada Strong, our National Electricity Strategy. Under the strategy, the federal government is investing over $50 billion to double our grid and connect it from coast to coast to coast; enhance domestic manufacturing; create and fill jobs for skilled workers; and reduce emissions.

To support these aims, on November 18, at the Marine Renewables Conference in Ottawa, the Honourable Sean Fraser, Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, announced nearly $10 million in funding for 24 clean electricity and innovation projects across Atlantic Canada, including:

Nearly $8 million to support clean technology innovation in batteries and carbon capture, utilization and storage

$1.2 million to support clean electricity projects

$500,000 for Indigenous and coastal communities to engage on offshore wind development

Nearly $375,000 to support renewable energy and energy efficiency initiatives in Indigenous communities in Nova Scotia

These investments also support the Atlantic Economic Panel's call to develop the region's energy resources and strengthen its electricity system. In its report, Bolder Ambitions: Greater Prosperity for All, the panel highlighted reliable, affordable power and clean technology as foundations for attracting investment, growing businesses and creating jobs across Atlantic Canada.

As countries race to build cleaner, more competitive economies, the Government of Canada is investing in clean energy and innovation that will strengthen energy security, reduce emissions and ensure Atlantic Canada has reliable, affordable electricity to power communities, attract investment, create jobs and compete in a net-zero future.

title: COP31: Businesses, governments, investors, cities and initiatives rally behind electrification
description:
Cities: Through the Yearly Offer of Action of C40 Cities and the Global Covenant of Mayors, 37 cities joined the charge either reporting electrification progress in 2026 or announcing electrification actions for 2027.
Businesses: More than 260 businesses with over US$4 trillion annual revenue announced or profiled actions at COP31, either individually or as part of a coalition.
Investment: At COP31, AIB announced that it is doubling its 2030 green and transition lending target from €30 billion to €60 billion, building on €28 billion already deployed since 2019.
Octopus Energy launched an Asia Electrification Fund at COP31 aiming to raise $600 million for solar, wind, storage and electric vehicle (EV) charging projects, already backed by $50m from Japanese investors.
And BBVA announced at COP31 that it has channeled nearly €60 billion in sustainable business activity linked to electrification from January 2025 to September 2026.
text:
ANTALYA, Türkiye, 19 November 2026: The COP31 Global Climate Action Agenda Electrification Delivery Package – bringing together billions in clean energy investment plans, stronger grids, expanding electricity access and progress in electrifying transport and industry – was presented to Parties today in support of the global opportunity of an electrified economy.

In a formal first for a UN Climate Summit that has put real economy action at the heart of the conference, the Package sets out new actions and updates profiled or announced at COP31, involving over 150 countries plus the European Union, 37 cities and more than 260 businesses across six continents:

Countries: From small island states to the world’s largest economies, more than 150 countries plus the EU – representing over two-thirds of global GDP – are taking action either individually or collectively to shift to clean and electrified energy.

Cities: Through the Yearly Offer of Action of C40 Cities and the Global Covenant of Mayors, 37 cities joined the charge either reporting electrification progress in 2026 or announcing electrification actions for 2027.

Businesses: More than 260 businesses with over US$4 trillion annual revenue announced or profiled actions at COP31, either individually or as part of a coalition.

Grids: Enough grids to stretch more than half way around the world were built, as members of the Utilities for Net Zero Alliance (UNEZA) announced the deployment of more than 21,000 km in 2025. UNEZA also announced combined annual investment plans of at least $156 billion across grids, renewables and storage, 5% higher than last year and 35% higher than in 2024.

Transport: Thirteen zero-emission freight corridors are in development across six continents, covering more than 29,000 km of roads — roughly three-quarters of the way around the planet. Electric vehicle sales in countries that have signed the ZEV Declaration reached 2.1 million in the first half of 2026, while six cities committed to some 2,200 new electric buses in 2027.

Climate finance: AMPLIFi, the Climate Investment Funds (CIF) new financing mechanism, announced it is now operational with its first set of projects and first large donor contribution from the UK of £400 million, aiming to mobilise up to £5 billion in clean power, grids, storage and electrification in emerging markets and developing economies.

Investment: At COP31, AIB announced that it is doubling its 2030 green and transition lending target from €30 billion to €60 billion, building on €28 billion already deployed since 2019. Octopus Energy launched an Asia Electrification Fund at COP31 aiming to raise $600 million for solar, wind, storage and electric vehicle (EV) charging projects, already backed by $50m from Japanese investors. And BBVA announced at COP31 that it has channeled nearly €60 billion in sustainable business activity linked to electrification from January 2025 to September 2026.

name: Congress
title: Can You Negotiate With a Warming Planet? - Atmos Magazine
description:
COP31 attendees are still focused largely on calling out the industries and countries most responsible for warming temperatures.
And the fact is, climate change does not stay in its lane.
Stateside, a wet El Niño season, boosted by the impacts of climate change, gained intensity this fall.
U.N. leaders say they plan to keep the pledge open to signatories until next year’s COP conference.
One framework supports putting fines on industrial sectors responsible for air pollution that contributes to climate change.
text:
Whether you watched in August as flash floods floated away Nepalese homes, were in western Europe or the continental United States during their hottest summers on record this year, or have read about the ocean swallowing Solomon Islands shorelines at a rate of 10 millimeters every year since the ‘90s, it’s increasingly impossible to deny that climate change is a present and ongoing threat that requires mitigation.

That reality is the central tenet of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference in Türkiye, where representatives from more than 190 countries and the European Union—along with environmentalists, activists, and major business leaders—are actively debating how best to address an ever-warming globe.

As is often the case at COP, a major power dynamic is on display between developing nations, rich countries, and the industries responsible for creating the climate crisis.

COP31 attendees are still focused largely on calling out the industries and countries most responsible for warming temperatures. They’re urging action to remediate consequential climate impacts in vulnerable communities, and asking for a firm recognition of fossil fuels as the main source of climate change—and for a commitment to pivot away from them now.

“The actions from those in power here are completely detached from reality,” activist Greta Thunberg remarked at the international climate summit last week. “The planet is not dying; it is being killed, and we know by who, and it’s being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue. No one is coming to our rescue.”

Outgoing U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres used his final COP31 address to appeal for immediate climate intervention.

“You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” he said. “Facts are facts. And the fact is, climate change does not stay in its lane. It drives hunger and displacement around the world. It wipes out development gains built over decades. It pushes countries deeper into debt. It aggravates competition for land and water. It fuels instability. And, increasingly, it threatens the very existence of communities and countries.”

But already it seems the prevailing belief is that it might be another year of limited agreement and achievements.

COP31 discussions are happening against a background of climate realism.

Estimates suggest this year’s record-setting summer heat in Western Europe led to more than 50,000 deaths in urban areas across the continent. Stateside, a wet El Niño season, boosted by the impacts of climate change, gained intensity this fall. Rising ocean levels sent massive waves and catastrophic flooding to West Coast communities from central California to Washington. In Türkiye, extreme weather is leading to a crisis for some farmers. And in Australia, the co-host of this year’s COP, El Niño is on full display as residents prep for an even higher-than-usual fire risk as they head into their summer.

Climate-related issues recently led to some political gains for environmentalists, including Brazil’s recent re-election of left-wing leader Lula da Silva, and Democratic landslide victories in the U.S. midterms that voters delivered in large part as a rebuke to high gas prices and data centers.

But at COP, there still appears to be a reluctance, and no consensus, among major world leaders on committing to any binding climate language.

And that’s a big problem.

Last year, how world leaders left the summit was widely seen as a COP-out and failure. The hope was that countries would leave the conference with a commitment, or even a framework, for transitioning away from fossil fuels by a certain timeline. They didn’t. Instead, there was some lip service about making gains at some future time. This past April, over 50 countries met in Colombia under a pledge to make the transition. Eleven—including Germany, France, the Netherlands, and Ireland—have now released their own fossil fuel phaseout road maps. But in terms of a COP-wide commitment, agreements were essentially kicked down the line to this year’s meeting.

Now, attendees are considering a draft agreement that appears far from final, with no clear main initiative or takeaway. The 18-page “cover decision” was introduced Monday after a week of negotiations, but still represents more of a wishlist of competing ideals than a compromise. Part of the challenge is that, in the years it’s taken for countries to come anywhere near an agreement on these climate points, the playing field has changed dramatically.

Parts of the world have already surpassed 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming over pre-industrial levels. One recent study estimates that with current global emissions policies in place, temperatures could “overshoot” and surge to 2.7 degrees of warming by 2100. Negotiators want that fact taken into account for any final goals.

Climate finance is a major issue, especially as developing nations are already in debt from dealing with climate-related disasters. Wealthy countries had pledged in 2009 to mobilize $100 billion per year by 2020 to help other nations with climate mitigation, but they missed their target. The crowning achievement at last year’s COP was a promise to deliver more money to developing countries hit hardest by climate change, but that pledge is already off to a slow start. One assessment suggests that the annual climate finance goal could fall $840 billion short of its ultimate target of $1.3 trillion.

A new issue permeating COP this year is AI. Both AI and data centers were central focuses at September’s Climate Week NYC, much to the frustration of some climate activists and political scientists, including Leah Stokes, who told me in an interview that AI doomerism was overshadowing the impact of fossil fuels.

But AI is a big concern globally. Hyperscale data centers in the U.S. emit as much as the entire country of Denmark, according to a recent report from Harvard University researchers. COP31 attendees rolled out what they call the Antalya AI Pledge, which recognizes AI’s potential to cut and track emissions while cautioning against its climate risks. The pledge further asks for a commitment from governments and companies to run AI products with clean energy. Just nine countries so far have signed, along with Chinese global tech and e-commerce corporation Alibaba. U.N. leaders say they plan to keep the pledge open to signatories until next year’s COP conference.

Attendees are also pushing for a commitment to make polluters pay. One framework supports putting fines on industrial sectors responsible for air pollution that contributes to climate change. On Tuesday, the United Kingdom signed on to support the statement, joining Spain and five other African, Oceania, and Asian countries.

Missing from the global discussions this week was a major world player and the second-largest contributor of global emissions: the United States.

The Trump administration sent no official representatives to the conference, and joined Afghanistan and Myanmar as the only three countries not to send negotiators. Instead, President Donald Trump is meeting in China with its President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin for the APEC Summit. The two-day economic meeting is expected to revolve around nuclear arms control, AI chips, and the war in Ukraine.

Eighteen members of Congress are at COP31 of their own accord to reaffirm Americans’ commitment to mitigate global warming.

“The United States has retreated from the world stage, and the world is moving on,” Democratic Illinois Rep. Jonathan Jackson told media outlet Devex. “We want to catch back up and let people know that not everyone in the United States agrees with the current direction.”

Outgoing California governor and likely presidential hopeful Gavin Newsom is also attending. Newsom was a bit of a star at last year’s summit.

The timing is admittedly awkward: COP talks are happening as Congress is expected to pass a permitting reform bill this week, which some environmentalists consider to be a sweetheart deal for the fossil fuel industry and tech companies who want to see more data centers built. Others praise the bill for opening up federal land to more clean energy.

Both negotiations in Türkiye and in D.C. highlight the pitfalls of striving for a climate compromise between mutually exclusive, competing interests.

That’s because the atmosphere doesn’t understand a climate pledge or a compromise backed by a handshake. It deals in facts alone. Science shows that fossil fuels must ultimately be phased out to avoid the worst-case climate scenarios.

And while oil and gas and clean energy companies can co-exist in a happy equilibrium that benefits industries and the energy sector, that sort of compromise only leads to a compromised planet.

title: Sunrun and Overview Energy CEOs say the answer to AI's energy problem is already on the grid
description:

And I think that is the future of energy.” Sunrun CEO Mary Powell, whose company installs rooftop solar and home batteries, agreed.
“Ultimately, it is about having power generated right where it’s needed,” she said in the session, moderated by Fortune‘s Allie Garfinkle.
“We sit on top of right now gigawatt-hours of energy,” Powell said.
“We’re creating solar power at night,” Al-Shakarchi said.
text:
“We need more generation, that’s true, but we already have all these assets on the grid that we’re just not taking advantage of,” said Abdullah Al-Shakarchi, co-CEO of Overview Energy, onstage at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit this week. “Gas plants are 60, 70% utilized based on where you are. Transmission often sits doing nothing. And so what are the right solutions that we can build to take advantage of what we’ve already got? Because that lets us lower the amount of things that we need to build. And I think that is the future of energy.”

Sunrun CEO Mary Powell, whose company installs rooftop solar and home batteries, agreed. “Ultimately, it is about having power generated right where it’s needed,” she said in the session, moderated by Fortune‘s Allie Garfinkle. “I mean, the grid was constructed as it is over 100 years ago. And it’s just time that we really advance it.”

Sunrun had about 1.06 million subscribers and 5 gigawatt-hours of networked home battery storage as of Sept. 30, according to its third-quarter results. “We sit on top of right now gigawatt-hours of energy,” Powell said. “Some of it’s being used by the grid, but I really see the next couple of years as an opportunity to crack that wide open and have all of those resources used in a way that can then make the grid more financially viable for everybody.”

The push for efficiency comes as data-center politics have become impossible to ignore. In this month’s midterms, the AI buildout became an affordability issue: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s Senate race arguing that data centers should pay for their own power, and at least 14 Ohio municipalities passed data center bans or restrictions on Election Day.

“The voters told us what we knew, right?” Al-Shakarchi said. “Energy prices are high. People are scared of data centers. We need these data centers. They’re clearly inevitable in many ways. And the grid needs to step up to fix these challenges.”

That anxiety hits household budgets that are already stretched. “Electric rates have gone up, what, 35% in the last five years. And people are really concerned,” Powell said. If anything, she was conservative: Fortune has reported that U.S. electricity prices rose roughly 40% on average over the past five years.

Solar at night, from orbit

Overview Energy’s pitch sounds like science fiction. The company is building satellites that collect sunlight in space, where it’s always shining, and beam it down as near-infrared light onto existing utility-scale solar farms, so those farms can keep producing after dark. “We’re creating solar power at night,” Al-Shakarchi said.

He argued the payoff comes from hardware that’s already built. “If in the U.S. you build no more utility-scale solar farms by the year 2030 and you simply switch them on at night, we can power a quarter of the country’s load growth over the next decade without building anything new on the ground,” he said.

The idea has a marquee customer. In April, Meta signed an agreement for early access to up to 1 gigawatt of Overview’s space solar capacity, with an orbital demonstration planned for 2028 and commercial delivery expected by 2030. Al-Shakarchi credited cheaper, reusable rockets for making the economics work. “That makes us competitive with something like natural gas,” he said.

Charging the battery twice

Asked whether rooftop batteries and space-beamed solar compete, Al-Shakarchi called it “a great partnership.” Overview could power a solar farm overnight and send that energy over transmission lines that would otherwise sit idle, topping off home batteries before a storm or an evening peak.

“If we can charge the battery not only once during the day but during the day and night, all of a sudden the cost of that battery to the consumer is lower,” he said.

Powell, who has made a “storage-first” strategy central to Sunrun, as she told Fortune‘s Diane Brady last year, said the bigger opening now is regulatory. Some parts of the country still don’t let home batteries send power back to the grid, she noted, and she expects more markets to change that over the next year or two.

From NIMBY to BANANA

Powell spent roughly two decades at Vermont’s Green Mountain Power, much of it as CEO, before joining Sunrun, and she says speed is now the whole game. “Utility solutions, I ran a utility for a couple decades; they take a long time. And in many ways, they’re getting harder to build,” she said. “It’s really gone from NIMBY to BANANA. Build absolutely nothing anywhere near anyone.”

Both executives were bullish on prices over the long run. Asked whether electricity will be cheaper or more expensive in 2036, Al-Shakarchi said: “I don’t know if it will be cheaper or the same, but it won’t be more expensive.” Powell said the real path to affordability is giving people “more direct ownership over your energy future.”

When Garfinkle asked what they would most want a crystal ball to reveal about the year ahead, Powell’s answer wasn’t about technology at all. She wants to know how many “awakened regulators” and how much market reform the next year brings.

“The solutions are sitting there,” Powell said. “We have solutions sitting on the grid. We just need enlightened market reform and changes to make it happen.”

BATON ROUGE, Louisiana — Today, weeks after a national election revealed a country fed up with high prices and data centers, Louisiana residents and organizations rallied in downtown Baton Rouge against gas plants for a massive Meta data center. Marching and rallying with signs and megaphones, the group urged the Louisiana Public Service Commission (PSC) to reject Entergy’s proposal to build seven expensive, polluting gas plants for Meta’s Hyperion campus.

Entergy wants PSC approval to build seven additional gas plants for the Meta data center, which will need more energy than a city four times as large as New Orleans. The utility doesn’t want to implement the common-sense customer protections requested by numerous groups intervening in the case. Sierra Club has been urging rejection of this proposal for months because it presents a “substantial cost” that Entergy’s existing customers may be required to bear.

Due to Gov. Jeff Landry’s “lighting speed” initiative and a previous decision by a majority of PSC commissioners, the agency is rushing this proposal through and planning to provide only one opportunity for the public to speak out against this proposal: a December meeting when commissioners are scheduled to also vote on the proposal minutes later. Much of the analysis Entergy has submitted to the PSC has been shielded from public view by NDA restrictions.

In response to the PSC’s upcoming decision, Louisiana residents and Sierra Club staff, issued the following statements:

“It’s clear by now that Meta and Entergy don’t care much for normal Louisianans, but the PSC has a mandate to do just that. Instead they have denied us a meaningful opportunity to speak on a project that will impact our state for generations,” said Margie Vicknair-Pray, project coordinator for the Sierra Club and a Louisiana resident. “Commissioners must know that the people will not sacrifice Louisiana for one big, risky, expensive, polluting experiment. They must vote no on this outrageous corporate favor.”

“Any claims that Meta is fully paying its own way are false,” said Darryl Malek-Wiley, a senior field representative for Sierra Club and a Louisiana resident. “These seven gas plants will guzzle our water, pollute our air, – and customers will be on the hook to pay if Meta walks away. We’re here to tell commissioners that we are done footing the bill for big tech – especially considering the extreme lack of transparency surrounding this project.”

Background:

In its testimony to the PSC urging rejection of Entergy’s proposal, Sierra Club called for:

Restructure the depreciation terms to protect Entergy ratepayers from the risk that Meta will abandon the project at any point and leave customers to pay the remaining bill, often called a stranded asset risk.

Require Meta to pay the full cost of a large transmission line associated with the data center.

Make Meta responsible for 100% of its gas fuel costs.

Amend contract language to assure that Meta is responsible for the lifetime costs of all the proposed gas units.

In negotiations, Entergy showed little willingness to consider or agree to any of these stipulations.

Separately, in Meta’s application to the LDEQ, it wants to modify its existing permit to add 44 fossil-fuel water boilers that will operate and emit pollutants around the clock. Because this would send total pollution for the permit beyond the minor-source permit limits, Meta said that – instead of applying for a major source permit as required by the Clean Air Act – it simply wouldn’t count emissions from the previously approved 31 diesel generators when those are operating during emergency hours.

Sierra Club has urged LDEQ that it must consider emissions from those diesel generators running during emergency operations.

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

Plans to build a solar farm in the Moss Bluff area have been cancelled, according to the project’s developers, with plans now shifting to bring the industry to the DeQuincy area.

Officials with Orion Renewable Energy Group, the company behind the proposed Persimmon Energy Center, announced on Wednesday that the project’s plan was revised after evaluating feedback received from community members and elected officials.

“Over the last several months, Orion Renewable Energy Group has engaged with the community, listened to residents and elected officials alike, and we are taking meaningful action,” a statement from Amanda Hoffman, Orion’s senior project developer, reads. “As a result of the feedback we have received, Persimmon Energy Center is no longer pursuing development in Ward 1.”

Hoffman said the decision reflects the company’s commitment to responsible development and its willingness to make significant changes in response to community feedback.

She said Orion continues to evaluate development opportunities in Ward 6, but has not made any final decisions on the project’s revised size or configuration.

“Our objective remains unchanged,” Hoffman said. “To develop a responsible energy project that respects community priorities while creating lasting economic value for Calcasieu Parish. We believe meaningful engagement requires more than listening. It requires action, and that is exactly what we are doing.”

As of Wednesday, parish officials said Orion has not requested a permit for any development in Ward 6.

Orion’s decision to change course was celebrated by District 35 State Representative Brett Geymann, who called it a “huge victory” for the Moss Bluff community.

“It really is a David versus Goliath story,” Geymann said. “The whole community was so united in its opposition to big industry coming here, it was amazing to see. Things never got ugly or nasty; it was simply a clear and united effort to protect this community, and I applaud Orion for recognizing that and for their willingness to change their plans. I hope that this serves as a model for other communities across the nation who are taking on this battle.”

Geymann said the opposition was never against the industry itself, but about the location.

“The people in Moss Bluff moved here to get away from industry, and they want to protect that,” he said.

The proposed Persimmon development met opposition on several aspects recently. In October, parish officials ordered the company to stop making public claims of property tax reductions after it failed to produce documentation to back those claims.

That same month, the Calcasieu Parish School Board deadlocked on a vote to enter into a contract with Orion for long-term funding for schools located near the proposed Moss Bluff site.

Now, community members question whether the change in plans for the solar farm will affect plans for a data center also proposed for the Moss Bluff area.

In September, Azimuth Renewables confirmed it was exploring options to build a data center in the vicinity of an estimated 1,100 acres it had the option to purchase between Paul White Road and North Perkins Ferry Road.

Geymann said he has not heard of any substantial discussions on the data center since the initial announcement, but said he hopes those developers take note of Orion’s decision.

“I would hope that the people considering that project read up on this (solar farm) project and understand that it will be an uphill fight for them as well,” he said.

text:
Antalya, Türkiye, November 19, 2026 – The International Energy Agency (IEA) released its flagship World Energy Outlook 2026 today, showing that this year’s fossil fuel crisis could meaningfully accelerate the decline of oil and curtail liquefied gas (LNG) demand, but governments must rapidly scale up credible roadmaps for a fossil fuel phaseout, and provide the public finance needed to get on track toward a livable climate. People around the world are suffering from conflict, high fuel prices, and worsening climate disasters, while oil majors reap windfall profits. The IEA’s analysis shows the rollout of renewables, electric vehicles and batteries is already delivering energy security gains, and the Hormuz crisis is boosting uptake. It should embolden governments to commit to accelerating a just renewable energy transition at COP31 and beyond. That means embracing renewable-powered electrification, energy efficiency, and a fast, fair and funded fossil fuel phaseout.

In response, David Tong, Global Industry Lead at Oil Change International, said:

“The key takeaway from the IEA’s latest World Energy Outlook is simple: fossil fuels are driving chaos and high energy bills, and the energy choices we make now will shape all our futures. After yet another fossil fuel crisis, governments cannot afford to keep people and economies hooked on volatile oil and gas markets. The IEA has yet again reiterated that there is no room for new oil, gas, and coal beyond existing fields to limit global warming to 1.5ºC.

“At COP31, governments have a choice: remain trapped in the volatility, conflict, and rising costs of fossil fuel dependence, or build a more secure, affordable, and prosperous future powered by renewable energy. We need credible roadmaps to phase out fossil fuels, backed by the public finance needed to ensure a fast and fair transition, especially for countries in the Global South. We need to electrify almost everything, powered by the wind and sun, but that must go hand in hand with actually phasing out fossil fuels.”

The WEO sets out several future energy scenarios:

The Net Zero Emissions scenario (NZE) is consistent with the Paris Agreement goal to hold global warming well below 2ºC and limit it to 1.5ºC by 2100. The NZE delivers the lowest household energy bills, highest number of jobs, and fastest universal access to electricity and clean cooking. While it is the only IEA scenario that accounts for climate limits, it would still lead to dangerous peak warming of nearly 1.7°C, triggering widespread harm and irreversible damage.

The Net Zero Emissions scenario delivers 5% lower household energy bills overall by 2035, and 10% lower household energy bills in fossil importing countries. NZE also delivers 15.6 million net job additions in the energy sector by 2035, the most of any IEA scenario.

The Net Zero Emissions scenario shows a rapid fossil fuel phaseout aligns with these benefits, if governments adequately plan and fund it. Oil and gas demand declines by around 4% each year by 2035 and then by 7% per year to 2050.

The Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS) reflects current levels of policy ambition, including new plans and targets responding to the Hormuz crisis that accelerate renewables, efficiency, and electrification. It shows that we’re on track to peak global coal and oil use by around 2030, and gas soon after, but warm the planet by a perilous 2.5ºC by 2100.

The misleadingly named Current Policies Scenario (CPS) assumes governments backslide on policy ambition and technological progress stalls. It also does not factor in many policy responses to the Hormuz crisis. This results in continued fossil fuel dominance and a catastrophic 2.9ºC of global heating in 2100.

An Additional Response Case (ARC) finds that full implementation of emerging policy responses to this year’s energy crisis would speed declines in oil and cut into gas demand by 2035, with oil demand 4.4 million barrels per day lower by 2035 compared to STEPS, as electric vehicles, renewables, and efficiency solutions scale up faster to reduce exposure to fossil fuel imports.

The agreement, announced at the EU-Jordan Investment Conference, will facilitate and encourage EU foreign direct investments and contribute to long-term economic cooperation between the EU and Jordan.

"Today’s launch of negotiations for an EU-Jordan Sustainable Investment Facilitation Agreement is an important milestone. The SIFA will drive EU investment in Jordan by making it simpler, safer and more transparent. It will strengthen economic relations between trusted partners, ensuring win-win outcomes for both sides," said EU Trade and Economic Security Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič.

By improving transparency, simplifying administrative procedures and strengthening cooperation between public authorities and investors, the agreement will reduce obstacles to investment in Jordan, enhancing investor confidence and unlocking new business opportunities whilst upholding standards concerning the environment, labour and climate.

The SIFA’s goal is to create a more transparent, predictable, and efficient investment climate for EU businesses of all sizes. It aims to attract and maintain investments in sectors with significant growth potential in Jordan, such as manufacturing, renewable energy, clean technologies, water management, construction, ICT, transport, and logistics. The SIFA will build on the Free Trade Area established by the EU-Jordan Association Agreement and allow investors to take further advantage of it.

The SIFA with Jordan is the first one negotiated with a country of the Middle East and North Africa region.

Background

On 17 November 2026, the Council of the European Union adopted a decision authorising the Commission to open negotiations on behalf of the European Union regarding an agreement on sustainable investment facilitation with Jordan and Egypt.

The EU is Jordan’s second-largest trading partner, accounting for over 15% of Jordan's trade in goods with the world in 2025. Total trade in goods between the EU and Jordan stood at €6.1 billion in 2025 and two-way trade in services amounted to €1.8 billion in 2024. EU foreign direct investment in Jordan amounted to €3.6 billion in 2024.

SIFAs are also complementary to the EU’s Global Gateway initiative. By improving the domestic regulatory framework, the SIFA will help attract more investment to Jordan, which is also the ambition of the Global Gateway and its projects. Through the SIFA, and the improvement in the investment climate, partners can enhance the positive spillovers created by investments under the Global Gateway, attracting further foreign direct investments. This applies to projects under the Trans-Mediterranean renewable Energy and Clean Tech initiative (so-called T-Med) in the MENA region.

The EU’s first SIFA with Angola entered into force on 1 September 2024. In January 2026, the EU’s second SIFA was concluded with Ecuador. SIFA negotiations with Côte d'Ivoire are ongoing.

text:
ANTALYA, Türkiye (November 19, 2026)—The International Energy Agency (IEA) released its annual World Energy Outlook today detailing trends in and scenarios for energy demand, supply, and what that means for emissions and economic development. The report highlights how the U.S.-Israel war on Iran has caused lasting changes to the global energy system and reinforced the benefits of a clean energy transition and electrification for countries. However, the report also makes clear that additional policies and investments are needed to deepen and accelerate these trends, ensure universal access to affordable, clean energy, and keep the world within reach of climate goals. As COP31, the annual U.N. climate conference underway in Türkiye, enters its final days, the report underscores the need for world leaders to ratchet up the pace and ambition of the talks.

Below is a statement from Dr. Rachel Cleetus, Climate Program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS). She is currently attending the U.N. climate talks in Antalya, Türkiye until November 22 alongside other UCS experts.

“The IEA’s latest report makes clear that the fossil energy crisis unleashed by the US-Israel war on Iran has irrevocably changed the global energy system, adding to the many reasons why countries would benefit from a rapid transition to clean energy and electrification. Despite the headwinds, solar power and electrification have increased significantly, already delivering economic advantages. But without explicit, ambitious policies and investments to drive forward a transition away from fossil fuels, the world could be on track for a catastrophic 2.5 to 2.9°C of global warming by 2100.

“The future of the energy system and our climate are inextricably intertwined. World leaders at COP31 must stand up to fossil fuel enablers and commit to a fast, fair transition away from all fossil fuels to renewable energy, and ramping up energy efficiency. Rapid, economywide electrification is crucial and must be based on clean energy to avoid driving up heat trapping emissions. Richer, major emitting nations must live up to their obligations on climate finance to make this transition possible for lower income nations. The current impasse in the COP31 climate finance negotiations is deeply unjust and jeopardizes necessary progress exactly when we need far more ambition.

“The Trump administration’s attacks on clean energy policies and boosting of fossil fuels is only serving the interests of large fossil fuel polluters who are raking in billions in profits while people struggle to afford basic necessities. It’s time for the newly elected Congress to reverse the harms, keep the administration in check and hold fossil fuel companies accountable for the damages they are causing.

“With the world on the brink of breaching 1.5°C of global warming and climate impacts rapidly worsening, world leaders must drastically change course and help secure a healthier, safer world powered by clean, affordable energy for all.”

The US state of Texas has resumed environmental permit reviews for data centres, the Texas Tribune reported on 17 November 2026. Governor Greg Abbott had ordered a pause in September. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) said applications would undergo its normal review process. Applicable state and federal requirements remain in place.

The restart followed notification from Abbott’s office that grid officials had completed collecting information on community impacts. His earlier directive sought information about electricity, water, tax incentives and neighbourhood effects. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas received responses from 93% of 465 projects. Full findings are scheduled for presentation in December.

Environmental group Public Citizen criticised restarting permitting before the findings were shared publicly. It also questioned how TCEQ would use them in decisions. The agency handles permits covering air pollution and construction site stormwater runoff. Community opposition has included concerns about grid reliability, gas generation emissions and water demand during drought.

Digital Watch previously reported on how data centre oversight became an issue in the Texas election debate. It also covered the state’s audit of data centre resource needs, including electricity and water use. Another report focused on water reporting and enforcement, highlighting scrutiny of how facilities account for their consumption. The resumption of environmental permit reviews moves the story from a pause on approvals back to decisions on individual projects and their local impacts.

text:
Ford Motor (NYSE:F) has commenced production of low-cost battery cells at a new plant in Michigan, US, using technology licensed from Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL) (HKG:3750).

The cells are made with a lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) chemistry and are being shipped to a plant in Louisville, Kentucky, to be used for the company’s forthcoming Fathom midsize electric truck.

Ford’s Vice President of advanced development projects Alan Clarke has spoken to the media about the use of CATL battery technology, noting that it is the fastest way for the company to build affordable electric vehicles (EVs) in the US.

“CATL being the biggest in the world, it means that they’re the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn how to produce LFP cells,” Clarke says.

The move has drawn criticism from the US Government, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy saying in September that the agency was “deeply alarmed” by the company’s use of licensed technology from CATL.

As previously reported, LFP batteries are gaining global momentum due to their long-life attributes, low cost, and high-safety characteristics. In 2025, LFP batteries accounted for over 55% of all EV batteries globally, up from nearly 50% in 2024.

Unlike nickel-manganese-cobalt chemistries, LFP batteries rely on lithium carbonate rather than hydroxide.

The chemistry has traditionally been concentrated in China and is popular in more urban markets rather than for longer-range vehicles.

While LFP usage is not as widespread in the US, more than 50 gigawatt-hours of battery manufacturing capacity was redirected towards LFP production in 2025, across several companies including Ford and LG Energy Solution.

Ford Motor’s Fathom is expected to launch in early 2027, joining the Mustang Mach-E in the company’s line of consumer EVs.

As recently reported at Benchmark Week 2026 in Shanghai, CATL is focused on industry collaboration and sharing its expertise through global partnerships.

As US automakers balance geopolitical pushback against the need for affordable EVs, licensing established LFP technology highlights how global partnerships remain central to scaling North America’s battery manufacturing and EV industry.

text:
The National Wealth Fund has today announced its backing for two nationally significant battery energy storage projects in Eccles and Kilmarnock, Scotland, through a new equity investment alongside Matrix Renewables UK Limited.

Matrix will retain a majority stake in both projects, with the National Wealth Fund’s investment supporting their development and delivery alongside Matrix. The projects will boost employment in the area, with more than 200 jobs expected to be created or supported throughout the construction and operation phases.

Strategically located along key transmission corridors between Scotland and England, the two projects will provide a combined 1 GW power capacity and 2 GWh energy storage. The projects will play a key role in the UK’s clean energy objectives by enhancing grid flexibility, managing network constraints and enabling greater integration of renewable energy.

Once operational, the two facilities will collectively support energy storage capability equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of around 520,000 households.

Construction is already underway at Eccles, with commercial operations expected to commence in October 2027. Construction at Kilmarnock is expected to begin in December 2026, with commercial operations targeted for September 2028.

This investment builds on the National Wealth Fund’s track record in energy storage and its role in mobilising private capital to support the UK’s energy transition.

The projects underpin Matrix Renewables’ strategy in the UK, where the company intends to invest further capital in generation and storage projects.

Oliver Holbourn, CEO of the National Wealth Fund, said:

“Battery storage is critical to building a cleaner, more secure and more flexible energy system. text:
Batteries lose capacity over time. EV-haters have spun this fact into a fantasy in which EV batteries die after a few years, sending the cars to the junkyard and their owners back to gas-guzzlers.

EV owners and makers are more optimistic (for one thing, all EVs sold in the US come with an 8-year battery warranty), but it’s only recently, now that modern EVs have been on the road for a couple of decades, that robust data on long-term battery health has become available.

The latest set of data points comes from Ford, which has analyzed five years of battery state-of-health data for its Mustang Mach-E, which debuted in model year 2021. The Class of 2021 includes over 36,000 vehicles, which have driven a collective two billion miles. Ford analyzed the entire fleet, and found that the average battery health retained after five years was 92%.

Kevin Vander Laan, Technical Leader of High-Voltage Battery Cells and Systems at Ford, reminds us that averages can hide variation, so it’s important to look at the spread between the highest and lowest figures. Ninety-five percent of the vehicles report remaining battery capacity between 87% and 97%.

More than 2,000 Class of 2021 owners have surpassed 100,000 miles on their original batteries, averaging more than 91% remaining capacity. Some 30 drivers have passed 200,000 miles, averaging 88%. One owner has driven over 400,000 miles on his original battery.

As part of its quality control process, Ford models battery performance, runs physical tests, and exposes packs to heat, cold, and different charging profiles. The company’s packs are designed to last at least 10 years.

Ford uses field data from vehicles on the road to inform current and future EV programs such as the Universal Electric Vehicle platform and the upcoming Fathom electric pickup.

Mr. Vander Laan lists a few habits can help support long-term battery health:

Charge on Level 2 at home for daily driving and save DC fast charging for when it’s necessary.

Try to manage temperature extremes when possible. Precondition while still plugged in, and park in the shade in summer.

Follow charge-level recommendations in the Ford App for your specific vehicle.

description: (The Center Square) - The U.S. Senate on Wednesday passed a sweeping energy and infrastructure permitting bill that supporters say would lower utility bills and shield residential ratepayers from the
text:
A low-angle view of a steel power transmission tower. Photo: Jason Richard / Unsplash

(The Center Square) - The U.S. Senate on Wednesday passed a sweeping energy and infrastructure permitting bill that supporters say would lower utility bills and shield residential ratepayers from the cost of connecting artificial intelligence data centers to the grid.

The 494-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act directs federal regulators to overhaul grid pricing rules so that large data centers—rather than residential utility customers—pay their share for existing infrastructure and also cover the full cost of the transmission upgrades needed to bring them online.

Lawmakers voted 65-31 to pass the legislation, authored by Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah along with Democratic Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico. The bill now heads back to the House for a final vote before going to President Donald Trump's desk.

Capito, the bill's lead sponsor, said Wednesday on the Senate floor that the package addresses permitting bottlenecks that have delayed new power plants and grid upgrades for decades.

"This bill delivers what families and businesses have been asking for: a permitting process that is faster, clearer and built to keep energy reliable and affordable," Capito said. "Today's vote shows what happens when we put common-sense solutions ahead of partisan gridlock."

The legislation would reshape how federal regulators approve grid connections, pipelines and power plants, limit court challenges to environmental reviews to 150 days, and set strict deadlines for agency decisions. The president promoted the legislation in a Nov. 8 Truth Social post, writing it would lower energy costs for families and allow the U.S. to build pipelines, mines and power plants faster.

"This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs," Trump wrote. "It also guarantees that Data Centers will build and pay for their own Electricity, so American Families don't pay more on their Utility Bills."

Whitehouse said the reforms would deliver immediate relief for households facing higher power bills and also accelerate clean energy production. The Rhode Island senator argued during floor debate last week that the bill's passage will advance stalled wind, solar and battery storage projects nationwide.

"This is something we can grab now and that will pay dividends soon in lower energy rates," Whitehouse said. "The day of data center freeloading ends when this bill passes."

The vote cut across party lines, with Democrats including Georgia Sens. Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock, John Fetterman of Pennsylvania and Mark Warner of Virginia voting in favor, while Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota—who previously objected to provisions allowing federal regulators to override states on contested transmission lines—was a no.

Democratic Sen. Jeff Merkley of Oregon called the Senate floor amendment process "bogus as hell" during Tuesday's floor debate, saying the legislative package "opens the gates to a flood of natural gas for data centers while leaving expanded transmission of renewable energy subject to Trump's obstruction."

A coalition of 11 Tribal organizations argued the bill's changes to the consultations required under the National Historic Preservation Act and shortened response periods after large energy projects are proposed will severely weaken federal protections for sacred sites.

National Congress of American Indians President Mark Macarro called the legislation "an existential threat to Indian Country in the way that we try to protect our religion, our culture, our homelands."
