text:
Washington, D.C. – This week, 18 members of the House of Representatives, including House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition (SEEC) Vice Chairs Reps. Don Beyer (VA-08), Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), Sean Casten (IL-06), and Mike Levin (CA-49), as well as Reps. Jared Huffman (CA-02), Yassamin Ansari (AZ-03), Ami Bera (CA-06), Kathy Castor (FL-14), Salud Carbajal (CA-24), Adriano Espaillat (NY-13), Maxine Dexter (OR-03), Jonathan Jackson (IL-01), Teresa Leger Fernández (NM-03), Lucy McBath (GA-06), Dave Min (CA-47), Emily Randall (WA-06), Raul Ruiz (CA-25), and Nikema Williams (GA-05), joined the international climate community at the 31st Conference of Parties (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye to renew and strengthen U.S. engagement on climate leadership on the global stage. The member delegation reaffirmed partnerships and highlighted shared challenges, including topics ranging from energy affordability and clean electrification to food security and disaster resilience. Members returned to Congress with new relationships and new ideas to build a more affordable, clean, and healthy future for our nation and the world.

SEEC members participated in events across 8 themes.

Forests, Nature, and Natural-Capital Resilience

SEEC members highlighted how protecting and restoring ecosystems can preserve nature’s capacity to absorb and sequester carbon, while bolstering climate resilience for our planet.

“For millions of people around the world, forests sustain their livelihoods, provide clean water, and store the carbon we desperately need to keep out of the atmosphere,” said House Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member Jared Huffman (CA-02). “As climate change fuels more destructive wildfires and floods, protecting the forests we still have and restoring those we’ve lost is essential to protecting communities, supporting local economies, and giving people a say in the future of the lands they depend on. We’ll fight to keep public lands in public hands, restore the lands and waters our communities depend on, and cut the pollution that’s making these disasters worse.”

Adaptation, Disaster Resilience, & Community Preparedness

SEEC members joined panels and discussions on adaptation, disaster resilience, and community preparedness to highlight how adaptation must be a central pillar of climate action.

“Extreme weather threatens our critical infrastructure and makes life more expensive – something my neighbors in Tampa Bay know too well,” said Congresswoman Kathy Castor (FL-14). “At COP, we showed up to work with and learn from our international partners to address these shared challenges together. We’re ready to put SEEC Institute’s Thriving Economy Project into action – our blueprint to lower costs, strengthen American leadership, and make our communities safer.”

Clean Electrification, Climate Finance,and Private-Sector Competitiveness SEEC Members engaged with experts in the clean electrification and climate finance space, and engaged with private sector voices from around the world.

“Anyone who can access electricity, heat, and transportation without burning fossil fuels not only lowers their costs, but also cuts down on pollution and helps provide a livable planet to our children and grandchildren,” said Congressman Sean Casten (IL-06). “Clean electrification is the moral and economically smart path forward for anyone interested in helping both their pocketbooks and our future. It's an imperative next step in addressing both the cost-of-living crisis and climate crisis."

Ocean, Science, & Coastal Resilience SEEC Members participated in events related to ocean, science, and coastal resilience to highlight how the climate crisis is transforming marine ecosystems and coastal livelihoods.

“The ocean has given us time we did not earn,” said Congresswoman Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01). “It has absorbed our emissions, buffered our climate, and fed our communities. The challenge now is whether we will answer that generosity with responsibility. If we get the science right, and we get the trust right, ocean carbon removal will have a fair chance to prove itself and we will have the evidence to decide wisely. The ocean, and the communities that depend on it, deserve our best evidence and our full partnership.”

Transatlantic Industrial, Trade, and Energy Policy SEEC Members highlighted how the U.S. and Europe must work together to transition away from fossil fuel dependence.

“The United States and Europe have a shared responsibility to lead the global transition away from fossil fuels,” said Congressman Mike Levin (CA-49). “That means working together to accelerate clean energy deployment, strengthen our economies, and reduce our dependence on fossil fuel markets. Our transatlantic partnership is essential to building a cleaner, more secure, and more affordable energy future.”

Climate Equity, Mobility, and Community Leadership

SEEC Members highlighted how the climate challenge exacerbates existing social inequities and climate solutions must expand economic opportunity, while giving communities agency in shaping their futures.

“The families with the least wealth, insurance, and political voice are hit first and recover last, from Chicago to the Horn of Africa to the Caribbean. Congress’ job is to help people stay home safely where they can, and move with dignity when they can’t,” said Congressman Jonathan Jackson (IL-01). “I am proud to lead the Congressional Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Caucus in the House of Representatives. Equity should not be a controversial topic, and I am proud to be here with you today to discuss how we can work together on equitable solutions to the climate crisis.”

Climate, Energy, and National Security SEEC Members joined discussions on how climate resilience, clean energy deployment, and international cooperation are essential to our collective security.

“Now more than ever – it’s important to show the world that Democrats in Congress are committed to engaging with the global community to ensure that we are living up to our obligations to protect our planet and our future,” said Congresswoman Emily Randall (WA-06). “I’m grateful to bring the stories and experiences of my neighbors in Washington’s 6th district who face climate threats like coastal erosion and wildfires, and hear from other leaders and organizations that are both domestically and globally situated to help our communities achieve a climate-secure future.”

Food Security, Agricultural Innovation, and Trade SEEC Members participated in events related to food security, agricultural innovation, and trade that spoke to solutions to help farmers adapt to the climate crisis, build more resilient food systems on a global level, and ensure that feeding the world and protecting the planet go hand in hand.

name: Indiana American Energy
title: Guest Column: Utility regulation: Too much or not fast enough?
description: In 2022, America’s utilities planned for about 24 gigawatts of new peak electricity demand over the following five years. By 2025, according to the consulting firm Grid Strategies, their forecasts
text:
Ober

In 2022, America’s utilities planned for about 24 gigawatts of new peak electricity demand over the following five years. By 2025, according to the consulting firm Grid Strategies, their forecasts called for 166 gigawatts, more than six times as much. Data centers account for more than half of that growth, and manufacturing is the next largest driver.

Those forecasts describe a different industry from the one I helped regulate. During my years on the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission, the question before us was usually whether a utility was building too much. Today’s question is how quickly a growing economy can get the power it needs, and on what terms, and the public-interest standard that answers both has held steady.

When I joined the commission in 2018, American electricity demand had grown at well under 1% a year for two decades. Indiana’s coal fleet, which had supplied 90% of the state’s electricity as recently as 2010, was aging, and by 2020 its share had fallen to about 53%. Our work was to pace that transition: how quickly old plants should close and what should replace them.

The clearest test of that era came from Evansville. Vectren (now CenterPoint) had coal units scheduled to retire in 2023, so the issue was how much to build in their place and in what form. Its own forecast showed customers’ demand on the hottest summer days growing by fewer than 100 megawatts over 17 years, yet it proposed a single plant of roughly 850 megawatts, enough for about three-quarters of that peak, at a cost of $781 million. In 2019, the commission denied the request, and our order explained why. It found that the request for bids had been “unduly restrictive,” ruling out combinations of smaller resources; that one facility would have carried most of the utility’s baseload; and that the plant’s economics depended on wholesale market sales with no firm contracts behind them, a revenue stream the order called “a speculative influence that we find must be materially discounted.”

That caution followed from how utilities earn money. A regulated utility earns an return on what it builds and owns, while power it buys from others under contract generally earns it nothing. The arrangement attracts the long-term investment the industry needs and inclines a utility toward building. Our job was to check that inclination before customers paid for a plant they might never use.

When we decided the Evansville case, we believed we were serving through the most consequential period in the industry’s history, which we called the energy transition. Our order considered how a changing industry might leave customers with an uneconomic plant, yet every change we imagined pointed toward the plant becoming unnecessary. Our decision fit the record before us, but within seven years, a short time for plants built to run 40, the outlook reversed, and a forecast like today’s would have made for a very different record.

Today the pressure runs toward building, and talk of transition has given way to talk of abundance. Data centers and new manufacturing are the kind of investment states compete hard to attract, and available power has become the first filter in choosing a site.

Under that pressure, the commission’s job is to test need on the record. A faster pace does not lower the utility’s burden of proof or the duty to keep rates fair for Hoosier households and businesses. Cost causation protects both: Large new customers carry the cost of serving them, backed by long-term commitments, so households are not left holding the bill if that demand never arrives.

Expectations of regulators have also risen with their audience. Utility cases that once drew mainly lawyers and analysts now draw public comment and press coverage. That attention is healthy, because customers pay for every decision, and it rewards decisions that can be explained plainly and defended on the evidence.

Whether the question is how much to build or how fast, the answer has to come from the record, built through sworn testimony and cross-examination, with the state’s consumer advocate at the table for customers and the utility required to prove its case. That design weighed flat demand in 2019 and suits the growth Indiana is pursuing now. Forecasts will keep changing, and a public, evidence-based process remains the surest way for a state to build quickly and build well.

David Ober is an Albion native who represented northeast Indiana in the Indiana House from 2012 to 2018 and chaired the House Committee on Utilities, Energy and Telecommunications. He served on the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission from 2018 to 2022. Find this and other commen tary at indianacapitalchronicle.com .

title: US could ease paths for energy projects. There are risks as well as benefits.
authors: Story Hinckley, Caitlin Babcock, The Christian Science Monitor
description:

This includes renewable energy projects that would over time build a more sustainable America, say Senator Whitehouse and other BAAJA advocates.
Some important elements of the bill: It would change core aspects of environmental laws that define how infrastructure and energy projects are built.
Many environmental advocates and groups appreciate the proposed improvement of transmission lines and fast-tracking of renewable energy expansion.
But climate advocates like Senator Whitehouse say that renewable energy will have the leg up due to market demand.
text:
Fossil fuel and renewable energy advocates have long shared a similar sentiment: It’s too expensive and too time-intensive to build new energy projects in America.

The 303-mile Mountain Valley Pipeline through West Virginia and Virginia opened in 2024, a decade after it was introduced, due to years of permitting delays and litigation that caused its cost to more than double. In New Mexico, the SunZia Wind Project, the largest wind farm in the United States, came online in June – 18 years after developers applied for federal approval and 15 years after the Obama administration “fast-tracked” the project. It was beset by federal and state permitting delays and lawsuits.

Proponents of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), who include Republican and Democratic legislators, the president, and industry groups, say the bill would streamline the permitting process at a time when it is desperately needed. Electricity demand in the U.S. is projected to increase by 25% by 2030, and average electricity prices continue to climb – part of the affordability issue that many midterm voters said was a top priority.

“We need the savings for consumers and the improvements to the environment right away,” says Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island who is one of the bill’s lead negotiators.

The Senate could vote on the bill as soon as Wednesday evening and send it to the Republican-controlled House. But environmental groups – and many Democrats – say the bill would weaken bedrock environmental laws and expedite fossil fuel projects.

What would the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act do?

A group of Republican and Democratic senators and the White House negotiated for more than a year and agreed on the almost 500-page bill that seeks to fully reform the permitting process while making it harder for presidents to revoke permits and cancel projects already underway.

Some lawmakers have pushed for this kind of reform for years. The landmark environmental laws of the 1970s gave the public a say in projects that could pollute their communities, but they added years or decades to some projects’ timelines. This includes renewable energy projects that would over time build a more sustainable America, say Senator Whitehouse and other BAAJA advocates.

Some important elements of the bill:

It would change core aspects of environmental laws that define how infrastructure and energy projects are built. Currently, if a court finds that a project violates the National Environmental Policy Act, a project must stop until it complies with the law. But BAAJA would allow projects to continue, and would expand the type of projects that are exempted from NEPA review. The Clean Water Act would only apply to “direct point source discharge” into U.S. waters, rather than the entire project. Similarly, select projects would be exempted from the Endangered Species Act, and federal agencies would have less time to review a project’s impact on an endangered species.

A less controversial change involves transmission lines, which transport electricity to different parts of the country. They are how New Mexico’s SunZia project powers parts of California, for example. Transmission line shortages and delayed upgrades have created a bottleneck for new renewable energy projects, but BAAJA could cut the timeline for new lines from a decade down to five years by reducing individual states’ ability to delay projects and streamlining the permitting process.

While BAAJA would speed up that process for data centers, another key voter concern in the midterms, it would also require data centers to pay for their own grid infrastructure updates and additional costs associated with connecting to the system.

Who opposes this and why?

Many environmental advocates and groups appreciate the proposed improvement of transmission lines and fast-tracking of renewable energy expansion. As climate scientist Zeke Hausfather noted earlier this week, the obstacle to renewable energy in the U.S. is no longer cost but rather the yearslong wait to be approved and the lack of transmission lines to move energy from solar and wind farms across the country.

“This is ultimately not the bill that I or many climate advocates would have written,” writes Dr. Hausfather. But, he adds, “Every year a solar farm spends waiting in line to connect to the grid is a year a gas or coal plant runs in its place.”

Critics argue that BAAJA unnecessarily weakens key environmental safeguards. They’ve specifically criticized what they call “forever permits,” which limit the government’s ability to cancel or suspend already issued permits. (This has happened under presidents of both parties: President Joe Biden revoked a permit for the Keystone XL natural gas pipeline in 2021 and President Donald Trump suspended five offshore wind projects in 2025.)

The bill would benefit fossil fuel projects (particularly natural gas). But climate advocates like Senator Whitehouse say that renewable energy will have the leg up due to market demand.

Liz Zepeda, federal regulatory director at the Southern Environmental Law Center, says the bill will lock in our current system, which is “so heavily weighted” in favor of the fossil fuel industry. That industry benefits more from less stringent environmental law, while litigation that slows renewable energy projects is “not a serious issue.”

Ms. Zepeda is particularly worried about a section that would allow energy developers to sue the government for “disparate treatment.” If developers could prove the same kinds of energy projects aren’t being approved at the same rate as in the previous 10-year period, then taxpayers could be forced to pay developers for 100% of their project’s cost. This means that the Trump administration would be required to approve wind projects at roughly the same rate as the Biden administration, but a future president would be required to approve coal projects at roughly the same rate of the Trump administration.

“It’s a huge disincentive to roll back fossil fuels in the future,” says Ms. Zepeda. “It’s pretty crazy when you think about it in the long term.”

What’s next?

The bill has strong support in the Senate, despite opposition from a sizable cohort of Democrats. The House is a different story. While Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has not outright opposed the bill, he’s indicated he has serious concerns.

Some Democrats say they are worried Mr. Trump would refuse their priorities but approve Republican ones, and that the bill could make it harder for a future Democratic administration to undo new projects the president approves.

Others want to wait until the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, giving Democrats a sizable majority and theoretically more leverage to shape the bill.

Many Democrats, and a few Republicans, are open to permitting reform but take issue with specific sections of the bill.

Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota, one of two Republicans who voted against advancing the bill Monday, says he’s concerned it would move certain energy decisions away from local control, and he’s hearing pushback from tribes.

“They don’t feel as though they’ve had the ability to actually communicate their concerns,” he said.

Those concerns also resonate for Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona, which has a large Native American population. Asked what it would take for him to vote yes, he simply said, “Take out Title III,” which opponents say would limit tribal consultation for new projects.

Mr. Trump supports the bill and is expected to sign it into law if it passes Congress.

text:
European and British car makers have joined forces to demand “pragmatic” solutions to stop new barriers harming businesses on both sides of the Channel.

Ahead of a joint EU-UK summit on Friday, 20 November, politicians have been urged to take united action to stop a €1.8 billion (£1.5bn) EV tariff hit in 2027 caused by new rules of origin and “Made in Europe” regulations.

The UK’s Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) and the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA) warn that with just six weeks before new trade tariffs are due to kick in, urgent agreements are needed to avoid harm to both sides.

The two groups are demanding measures to include UK-built cars in Made in Europe policies. Under the current proposed EU Industrial Accelerator Act, UK-built vehicles, parts and batteries would be denied incentives and procurement opportunities available to manufacturers in mainland Europe. This, the bodies argue, would significantly damage the viability of UK-made vehicles and components.

At the same time, tougher rules of origin for EVs under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement come into force, threatening manufacturers on both sides of the divide. Under the new trading rules, an estimated 82% of all electric and plug-in hybrid cars produced in the UK and EU will be subject to a 10% import tariff from January 1.

The potential bill for such tariffs is estimated at almost €400 million on UK exports to the EU, and €1.4 billion on EU exports to the UK in 2027 alone.

With the EU and UK each other’s biggest export markets, there are fears that such additional costs could leave local manufacturers under even more threat from Chinese imports.

A large part of the problem around rules of origin is the slower-than-necessary development of local battery manufacture. Despite an estimated €72 billion invested in European battery and EV manufacturing facilities since 2017, the EU still imports around two-thirds of its lithium-ion batteries, mostly from China. The UK’s manufacturing base is even smaller still and the SMMT and ACEA say neither market will have enough qualifying supply by 2027 to avoid the rules of origin tariffs.

Mike Hawes, SMMT chief executive, said, “Europe cannot build a stronger automotive industry by cutting the UK out of the markets that make it competitive. ‘Made in Europe’ must recognise UK-built vehicles, parts and batteries as part of that industrial strength. We also need to maintain pragmatic rules of origin that keep electric vehicles tariff-free and affordable while safeguarding battery supply chains’ localisation efforts.

“These are two tests of the same partnership neither side can afford to fail. European and British leaders must use the forthcoming summit to agree a resolution to both issues.”

Sigrid de Vries, ACEA director general, added: “The EU and UK automotive industries face the same competitive pressures, and our ability to address them depends on continued close cooperation. We cannot afford to create new barriers where practical solutions are within reach.”

title: Trump and Democrats' energy bill threatens environmental protections.
description:
You wouldn’t think a piece of legislation with these kinds of friends would be of high priority for congressional Democrats.
The bill has been moving along in the Senate, behind closed doors, and will soon head to the House of Representatives.
It’s a framework for “permitting reform” that purports to speed up the approval and installation of fossil fuel and clean energy projects—along with power lines to transmit said energy.
But some powerful, influential Democrats, like climate hawk Sheldon Whitehouse, are still dedicated to BAAJA in spite of these flaws.
There are strong cases to be made in favor of streamlining energy permits so we can hasten our existential energy transition.
text:
President Donald Trump devoted one of his premium Truth Social posts to singing this bill’s praises. Stephen Miller also considers it an urgent legislative priority. The American Petroleum Institute wants so desperately to pass the act that it handed out free tacos on Capitol Hill in a promotional spree.

You wouldn’t think a piece of legislation with these kinds of friends would be of high priority for congressional Democrats. Yet their support is indeed robust, as evidenced by the act’s name: The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, co-sponsored by self-identified progressives (Sheldon Whitehouse, Martin Heinrich) and MAGA loyalists (Mike Lee, Shelley Moore Capito). The bill has been moving along in the Senate, behind closed doors, and will soon head to the House of Representatives. It’s a framework for “permitting reform” that purports to speed up the approval and installation of fossil fuel and clean energy projects—along with power lines to transmit said energy. The package is so urgent for both parties that the upper chamber even convened on Veterans Day (typically a holiday for the Senate) to bicker over whether to speedily pass the bill as is, or to spend more time amending the legislation in order to address the myriad concerns from energy experts, legal observers, Indigenous tribes, the NAACP, myriad Democratic state attorneys general, and John Podesta.

The issue is that if BAAJA is passed as is, the Trump administration will use its lame-duck leverage to keep easing pipeline expansions from already thriving fossil fuel and mining companies while indiscriminately suppressing renewable projects. (Trump all but copped to this in a now-infamous press conference.) Worse, the act would shield dozens of major fossil fuel projects from legal or financial accountability around their environmental damages, leaving them off the hook as they wreck essential biodiversity, run roughshod over beloved public lands and historic sites, and lock in greenhouse gas emissions. Further, the bill as currently written will, in the long haul, gut key provisions of historic laws like the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the Clean Air Act—most of which have already been weakened throughout the past decade, under Presidents Trump and Joe Biden. (A former federal judge appointed by President Bill Clinton points out that BAAJA would even kneecap the ability of protesters to successfully sue the Trump administration and stop boondoggles like the forest-ravaging East Potomac golf course.) All for a bill that wouldn’t bring down energy costs that much, according to think tank projections, or even site as many transmission lines as we need.

But some powerful, influential Democrats, like climate hawk Sheldon Whitehouse, are still dedicated to BAAJA in spite of these flaws. From their vantage point, the importance of permitting reform for the future of American energy—and for the fight against climate change—is worth the other risks, especially if those concessions can earn them buy-in from their Republican colleagues.

The permitting-reform concept, which became something of a wonk buzzword during Biden’s presidency, addresses a very real issue holding up the otherwise-booming clean energy revolution: We are not able to build enough interstate power lines, at a fast enough rate, in order to connect new solar and wind and geothermal energy with the grid and ensure people everywhere can realize their benefits. By truncating environmental and preservation review timelines, and limiting the ability of concerned citizens to register any opposition, energy developers could potentially build even more plants at a wider scale—and ensure they get connected to the broader grid.

BAAJA’s most fervent liberal advocates believe this is a rare bipartisan opportunity to work with climate deniers on behalf of renewables development. Not only does the pileup of clean energy projects stuck in federal compliance review make this worthwhile, but it also allows Dems to build on their successful midterm election focus on affordability with a bill that at least gestures toward a path to cheaper energy. Liberal “abundance” advocates like Ezra Klein also believe pro-development bills like BAAJA disproportionately benefit greener energy, while providing a check on the ability of NIMBYs to sue project developers on environmental grounds. The liberal case in favor of BAAJA, which is not an unreasonable one on its face, essentially purports that Dems can address the cost of living by making it easier for all energy developers to supersede government bureaucracy and trust the free market.

There are strong cases to be made in favor of streamlining energy permits so we can hasten our existential energy transition. But BAAJA’s advocates tend to rely on market-based reasoning at a moment when the playing field is catastrophically skewed in favor of fossil fuels, thanks to an administration that’s all but gone to war with the renewables sector on behalf of Big Oil and encouraged the ongoing gas-powered data center boom.

The bill’s most aggressive provisions have been striking enough to give even permitting-reform proponents some pause. Bill McKibben, who favors large-scale solar buildouts, notes that the act rolls backs decades’ worth of environmental protections—and undermines historic sovereignty afforded to tribal nations—while failing to guarantee any substantive emissions reductions down the line. David Bookbinder, former counsel for the centrist Niskanen Center, wrote in a letter that the act presents “a serious threat to American democracy,” noting that one portion of it effectively “limits the enforcement of all federal laws against any project with any federal permit.” Even Sens. Whitehouse and Heinrich were displeased with the initial permitting proposal—before letting it roll on through the Senate, thinking this is the best they’re gonna get. (Other consistent pro voters, like Michigan’s Elissa Slotkin, have nodded to “concerns” around the bill, while Nevada’s Catherine Cortez Masto has withdrawn her initial support because of state tribe objections.)

“I don’t disagree that permitting reform is needed, but this bill was developed behind closed doors, and no one asked us what was going wrong with the NHPA and what didn’t work,” Sarah Lowry, director of geophysics at New South Associates, told me. The Georgia-based business works to identify cultural and historic sites, like cemeteries, via reviews mandated by Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act—the very provision BAAJA is attempting to override. “If you don’t identify those cemeteries before groundbreaking, you can’t protect them, and if a cemetery is discovered by a bulldozer, they have to stop their work. Ironically, it would actually be more costly and add more delays than just going through the process where you identify it and then attempt to avoid it.”

Lowry, who notes that Trump is particularly fixated on nullifying Section 106, told me that if BAAJA rolls back compliance standards with Section 106, “It would decimate cultural resource management in this country—not just my company, even though about 70 percent of our business relates to that work.”

The more everyday people actually learn about everything on offer in this legislation, the more they oppose it—yet the process for its passage has been notoriously obscure, allowing pretty much no one real insight into what’s going on here. One thing is certain, however: BAAJA is more utopian than it is concrete, simply asking millions of Americans to gamble their faith in a Congress they already do not trust in the wake of an election in which voters often signaled an embrace for environmental progress. During these midterms, Colorado voters refuted a ballot measure that would have enshrined natural gas production as a “constitutional right.” In the heart of Texas’ oil country, a clean-air activist beat out a former fossil fuel executive in a key congressional race. The first Montana Democrat to be elected to the House of Representatives in three decades is a former smokejumper who’s already been challenging the Trump administration’s sell-offs of public lands. And throughout the country, Americans approved more funding for car-free public transit.

It’s likely because of those victories that pro-BAAJA Dems want to get it passed right now; they realize the tradeoffs are as intolerable to other lawmakers and constituents as both Whitehouse and Heinrich initially believed them to be. And yet, they’re ready to rubber-stamp a Trumpian agenda that could make the next two years even more destructive for public monuments and our heating atmosphere. We can and should do better than this, for the planet and the future of our civilization. But to some Democrats, this insufficient arrangement might just be good enough, purely because it’s bipartisan.

text:
The US has installed more than 200 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of battery storage, with nearly 50 GWh coming online in the first nine months of 2026 alone.

The US added 48.3 GWh of battery storage through September, up 20% from the same stretch last year, according to the latest report from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Q3 was a little slower: The US installed 14.3 GWh in those three months, down 1% year over year.

Texas is in the lead

Texas added 12.3 GWh of grid-scale batteries through September, more than any other state. Arizona came in second at 7.7 GWh, followed by California at 6.8 GWh. And 11 states had already broken their annual storage installation records with three months to go – Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois.

Utility-scale batteries did most of the work in Q3, accounting for 12.2 GWh of new capacity. Businesses and industrial sites added another 1.3 GWh, and residential added 746 megawatt-hours (MWh). That was the best Q3 yet for home batteries, though installs through September were still down 12% year over year. Some homeowners moved up their installations last year before the federal residential clean energy tax credit ended.

Advertisement - scroll for more content

“States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” said Pete Tillotson, a senior analyst at Benchmark. In September, New York awarded contracts for eight battery projects that can deliver about 950 megawatts (MW) combined. SEIA and Benchmark now expect 708 GWh of storage across the grid, homes, and businesses by 2030, up 3.7% from their previous forecast.

The US can also make more battery cells here. A Tennessee factory opened in July and an Indiana factory opened in October, bringing US cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, up 50%.

What about people’s electric bills?

Solar and batteries helped bring down average summer wholesale power prices by 42% in Texas’s ERCOT market and 51% in California’s CAISO market between 2021 and 2026, according to SEIA’s inflation-adjusted analysis. When batteries had power to spare during peak hours, grid operators could call on expensive power plants less often.

You wouldn’t know it from looking at the total on residential electric bills. The cost of generating power for households fell in both markets, but the cost of delivering it to homes rose. Overall, residential bills rose 22% at the two California utilities SEIA examined and 3% across its Texas utility sample, driven by higher transmission and distribution costs. California is upgrading its grid to reduce the risk of wildfires. Texas is expanding its grid for rising demand and make it more resilient to storms.

More than 300 solar and battery storage companies in the US wrote to Congress last week asking it to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty says the permitting bill would help get projects built faster and ease pressure on power prices. However, many Democrats feel this bill falls short. The Senate voted 70–27 on Monday to end debate on the amendment containing the bill’s text, moving it closer to a final vote.

text:
This week, Ford began shipments of the first lithium iron phosphate electric vehicle battery cells from its new BlueOval Battery Park in Marshall, Michigan, to its Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky. There, the prismatic cells will power early Ford Fathom electric pickup truck prototypes and validation vehicles. The automaker invited me into the plant to meet the people who build the batteries and to see how the so-called “jelly roll” is made.

In 2025, consumers lost access to the clean vehicle tax rebates of the Inflation Reduction Act, but the program and its incentives remain in the law for automakers and suppliers. So bringing this US-based, domestically owned battery plant online is kind of a big deal for Ford. It’s an important milestone for the automaker’s plan to make its new Universal Electric Vehicle, or UEV, platform a reality and to bring the Fathom — its upcoming electric pickup truck — to market in 2027 at a price that EV-eager customers can stomach.

Ford expects to sell the upcoming Fathom at an estimated price of $28,350 (well, $29,945, including the $1,595 destination and delivery fee), with the first preorder expected to open early next year.

More from CNET

Inside BlueOval Battery Park

BlueOval Battery Park Michigan is a $3 billion, 2 million-square-foot facility with a targeted annual production capacity of 20 gigawatt-hours. That’s a whole lot of batteries. Ford is expected to employ 1,700 people at the site across two 12-hour shifts, running around the clock to reach that capacity.

The plant is a clean facility, so getting in meant donning a clean suit, mask, hairnet, gloves and two layers of shoe booties. I then crossed special magnetic and sticky floor panels designed to pull any metal particles off the bottoms of those booties, before passing through multiple air-blower airlocks that blasted my body clean of loose dust.

From the outside, the building is huge and difficult to take in completely. On the inside, the scale truly comes into focus as I stare down a massive hallway just under a mile long end to end. Raw materials — rolls of copper and aluminum sheet, plus the chemical powders that coat them — enter the plant at the eastern end, move in a straight line through the facility, and completed battery packs exit at the western end. The first 0.7 mile of the fab belongs to cell production, split between isolated cathode and anode lines that join halfway through for final cell assembly.

Why Ford picked LFP prismatic

Ford engineers, battery experts and executives tell me that the automaker chose lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, chemistry in a prismatic (rectangular) format for its affordability and structural benefits. LFP uses no nickel or cobalt, which keeps costs down, and Ford found the chemistry well suited to bidirectional charging.

To keep costs low enough to deliver a reasonably priced car, Ford couldn’t use a Chinese supplier and still qualify for IRA manufacturing credits. So it licensed the technology from one, working with a company called CATL, which one Ford exec described as “the world’s leading battery manufacturer,” whose batteries power 30 million vehicles worldwide.

Despite working with a Chinese company, Ford says the plant is completely US-owned, staffed and operated and is totally IRA-compliant, with no foreign entity of concern, or FEOC, involvement beyond the licensing agreement.

Charles Poon, who leads vehicle hardware engineering, said Ford didn’t simply copy a catalog part.

“We designed a unique cell that does not exist in the CATL catalog, specifically for the UEV,” Poon said, adding that the taller and simpler cell delivers “the energy density, the affordability, the durability that [Ford is] looking for” and allows the automaker to more completely integrate the cells and battery pack into the vehicle’s design.

Ford also had to build the supply chain, Poon said, sourcing an IRA-compliant stream for a battery chemistry that is only just entering the mainstream in North America, and working with approved global partners and North American suppliers.

Building the ‘jelly roll’

On the cathode and anode assembly lines, meter-wide rolls of copper and aluminum are first coated with a chemical slurry that is baked on. The large rolls are then split into 10 smaller rolls, with tabs notched into their exposed edges at set intervals. As the continuous rolls pass through multiple machines like gigantic cassette players, AI-powered vision systems watch the foil for coating defects, scratches and wrinkles, marking problem sections so they can be automatically removed.

Next, the cathode and anode foils are layered and rolled into a cylinder, then pressed flat into what Ford calls a jelly roll. Imagine a roll of toilet paper mashed in a hydraulic press, and you’ll have a good idea of what it looks like: a flat rectangle with rounded ends.

The jelly rolls are then gathered in pairs, and the previously exposed tabs are folded together and ultrasonically welded to more solid terminals, which are in turn laser-welded to a cap. The jelly roll couple is then laser-sealed into an aluminum box, about the size and weight of a masonry brick, to form a nearly complete prismatic cell. Engineers vacuum out the air, check for leaks by pressurizing the cell with helium, and fill it with liquid electrolyte. Bob’s your uncle: you have a finished LFP prismatic cell.

Ford says the assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, which plant manager Tracy Church says makes BlueOval Battery Park “among the fastest LFP prismatic lines outside China.”

From cells to packs and beyond

From the cell line, completed prismatic cells would normally pass through a door and straight into pack manufacturing, where full battery packs with integrated “e-box” electronics, integrated cooling and wiring are built. That part of the plant is still undergoing validation, so for now Ford is shipping just the cells to Louisville, not complete battery packs. The company plans to have pack manufacturing up and running in Marshall ahead of Fathom’s launch, with full pack deliveries to Louisville planned in 2027. Church told me that the plant aims to produce 50 battery packs per hour.

Ford hasn’t officially specified the energy capacity of the cells or the completed battery packs and wouldn’t comment when asked about expected range for the Fathom. The automaker wouldn’t even confirm how many cells go into the EV’s pack, but I estimate between 90 and 108 cells based on a cutaway of the finalized unit I examined (but wasn’t permitted to photograph) during my tour. I expect Ford is holding off on finalizing details until closer to the EV’s 2027 launch window.

Battery Park Michigan isn’t just sending cells to Kentucky; it’s also sending expertise. Ford’s Glendale Kentucky plant — which used to build batteries for the F-150 Lightning full-size electric pickup — is currently being retooled to build LFP cells for Ford Energy for large-scale energy storage applications, and the lessons Ford learns in Michigan are already being shared with the manufacturing teams there.

text:
Connecticut is making progress in reducing its greenhouse gas emissions, but new projections show the state is unlikely to meet its target by 2030 – making it harder to stave off the local impacts of global warming.

“Cutting greenhouse gas emissions is critical,” said Emma Cimino, acting commissioner for Connecticut’s Department of Energy and Environmental Protection.

“Preventing the worst impact of climate change is far, far cheaper than repairing the damage that more and more extreme weather events can have on our infrastructure, our natural resources, and our public health,” she said.

Cimino pointed to a rain bomb in September that dumped more than 7 inches of precipitation in Fairfield County, flooding homes, businesses and parts of I-95.

“When it rains, it can rain much harder. This means more pressure on roads, drainage systems, homes, businesses, and public infrastructure,” she said. “Addressing climate change is an affordability issue for our state.”

Connecticut’s greenhouse gas emissions are 28% less than what they were in 2001, but in order to meet its target by 2030, the state will need to bring that reduction to 45%. Current projections show the state is likely to miss that goal by about 9%.

What CT’s climate projections show

Greenhouse gas emissions from homes, commercial buildings and electric power decreased from 2023 to 2024, according to data released by the Governor’s Council on Climate Change in November.

Emissions from buildings are down as more people switch from home heating oil to natural gas, while the number of people using electricity has risen to approximately 20%. That’s according to Michael Malmrose, associate research analyst with DEEP’s Office of Energy Supply and Infrastructure.

Emissions from electric power are down as dirtier power plants are being replaced with gas generators and the Millstone Nuclear Power Station has been online for all of 2024, Malmrose said.(Reactors at Millstone were offline for 89 days for refueling in 2023).

Cimino called the emission reductions “real progress”.

“This is really significant because emissions continue to stay below pre-pandemic levels, even as Connecticut’s economy has recovered,” she said.

But emissions from transportation increased by approximately half a million metric tons from 2023 to 2024. That’s equivalent to the amount of gas emitted by more than 110,000 motor vehicles in an entire year, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.

“The numbers are a little daunting,” Cimino said.

What’s driving transportation emissions

A spokesperson for DEEP said the uptick was largely driven by increased gasoline consumption. Part of that was caused by a 2% bump in the number of miles travelled, but it’s not clear what else could be contributing to the rise.

One thing is certain – state environment officials don’t expect the issue to get any better now that the Trump administration has rolled back regulations on air pollution and fuel efficiency standards for new cars.

“Connecticut cannot meet our goals on our own. We need our federal partners to engage as well. Unfortunately, we’re seeing the opposite of that right now,” Cimino said.

The transportation sector is the highest source of greenhouse gas emissions in Connecticut, releasing more than twice as much carbon as residential buildings.

One way to fix that? Electric vehicles.

description:

text:
Once online, this always-on, carbon-free energy is slated to support Google’s existing data center operations in The Dalles, Ore. and the region’s communities. The agreement will help catalyze the commercial development of superhot geothermal energy, providing benefits for ratepayers and helping protect the environment.

Beginning as early as 2030, Google will purchase 50 MW of power from Project Obsidian. The initial phase of development will use conventional drilling technology to access superhot geothermal conditions at commercial scale. Superhot geothermal is a virtually limitless energy source that uses the Earth’s natural heat to generate up to 10x more clean power per well than traditional geothermal systems. The second phase of development at Project Obsidian is expected to be the first in the world to use millimeter wave drilling, a technology designed to uniquely access superhot geothermal conditions worldwide.

“We started Quaise to make the Earth’s most abundant energy source universally accessible — and this agreement marks a critical next step, not just for Quaise but for the entire clean energy sector,” said Carlos Araque, CEO and President of Quaise Energy. “Together with Google, we are building the commercial foundation for superhot geothermal and cementing the United States as the global leader in geothermal power.”

Unlike traditional geothermal energy, which is limited to regions with naturally occurring hot water reservoirs rarely exceeding 400°F, Quaise develops Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) at superhot conditions, which are expected to enable utility-scale projects to compete with today’s most efficient power plants. Quaise is simultaneously advancing the development of millimeter wave drilling, a technology that can plug into existing drilling rigs to economically reach superhot geothermal conditions.

The agreement builds on Google’s clean energy portfolio and pioneering support of geothermal energy. From 2010 to 2025, Google signed more than 240 agreements to purchase nearly 35 GW of new clean energy, including more than 29 GW in North America across 148 projects. As demand for electricity continues to grow across the country, Google remains committed to ensuring that energy is affordable, reliable, and accessible for families and businesses.

Google pays for 100% of the power its data centers use, and as the company builds data centers, Google covers the infrastructure needs directly driven by its growth. In Oregon, the company’s three data center campuses have already achieved 83% carbon-free energy, with residents of Northern Wasco County People’s Utility District’s service territory having the third-lowest energy rates in the state. Today’s partnership further extends Google’s clean energy and geothermal leadership, while accelerating the development of superhot geothermal as a cost-effective, clean energy resource for Oregon residents and businesses.

“Google data centers are long-term investments in the communities we call home,” said Lucia Tian, Head of Advanced Energy Technologies at Google. “This collaboration with Quaise on superhot geothermal will help fuel local economic growth while helping to build a more robust and affordable energy future for Oregon.”

This new investment extends Google’s track record as a leader powering economic growth in Oregon. Google has proudly called Oregon home since 2006, when it built its first owned-and-operated data center in The Dalles. In the last 20 years, Google has invested more than $7 billion in the state, ranks as the largest taxpayer in Wasco County in recent years, and in 2025, the company helped provide $9.3 billion of economic activity for tens of thousands of Oregon businesses, nonprofits, publishers, creators, and developers.

Quaise’s agreement with Google is the latest milestone in a period of significant momentum for the company. In August 2026, it closed a $180 million Series B financing round, including a $35 million investment from Nabors Industries.

Project Obsidian represents a significant economic opportunity for Central Oregon. The project is expected to support 200 to 400 jobs during construction, more than 50 permanent high-skilled jobs in engineering and operations, and establish the region as a hub for superhot geothermal development. Grid upgrades associated with the project will strengthen reliability for local consumers, and royalties from electricity sales will provide lasting economic benefits to the region.

Technology proven at Obsidian is expected to reduce development costs for future superhot geothermal projects across the United States, where abundant subsurface heat remains inaccessible with conventional methods.

text:
As storms batter California this week, EV drivers could be in for more than just traffic and dangerous road conditions.

Fire officials are urgently warning electric vehicle drivers, e-bike riders and e-scooter users against the potential danger brought on by flooding.

The risk — known as delayed thermal runaway — occurs when an electric vehicle with a lithium-ion battery drives through saltwater. But the reaction can happen even after flooding has cleared the streets.

Fires resulting from these reactions can start "hours or days" after saltwater has entered a vehicle's battery compartment, San Francisco Fire Chief Dean Crispen said in a social media video. He explained that this risk is not unique to electric cars, but anything with a lithium-ion battery.

"Those should not be driven through standing saltwater with King Tides. We have great concerns of folks driving through on either e-bikes or vehicles and those micromobility devices or cars igniting days later," Crispen said.

While the risk has already heightened in San Francisco — which received half an inch of rain on Wednesday morning — the fires can ignite in any electric vehicle facing saltwater exposure.

King Tides, which are the highest predicted tides of the year, are set to continue statewide through the end of January 2027. As the Super El Niño brings flooding and sea levels to historic highs, Californians can expect more frequent and severe saltwater flooding across the entire Pacific coast.

EV giant Tesla said that car owners should treat their vehicle "as if it has been in an accident" if it's been submerged and keep it at least 50 feet from flammable materials.

The San Francisco Fire Department encourages electric vehicle owners to park their cars, e-bikes or scooters on the street if they believe they have driven through standing saltwater.

"Please contact a professional vehicle technician if you suspect your vehicle or device has been subjected to saltwater exposure and have it inspected," the department warned.

Due to the potential for hours- or days-long delays, officials also caution EV owners against charging their batteries until they have been inspected by a certified professional.

The initiative’s Nov. 10 launch at Momentum’s headquarters brought together representatives from stakeholders in the critical minerals sector.

text:
Carrollton-based Momentum Technologies recently helped launch a national initiative to bolster U.S. recovery and processing of critical materials. The company makes modular plants that recover critical minerals from used lithium-ion batteries and other e-waste.

“Modern life — phones, medical devices, electric vehicles and defense systems — runs on critical minerals, yet only a fraction of critical minerals are recycled today,” Mahesh Konduru, CEO of Momentum Technologies, said in a statement. “We’re giving new life to yesterday’s batteries and magnets to help the United States get the minerals it needs.”

ASCEND, or the Accelerator for Supply Chain, Economy and National Development, is a collaboration among Idaho National Laboratory, the National Laboratory of the Rockies and Oak Ridge National Laboratory. The Department of Energy’s Advanced Materials and Manufacturing Technologies Office funds the initiative.

The initiative’s Nov. 10 launch at Momentum’s headquarters brought together representatives from stakeholders in the critical minerals sector. They included electronics manufacturers, mineral processors and refiners, investors, government officials and researchers.

“The ASCEND collaboration is exciting because it will give industry a voice in weighing the costs and help us best align with [the Department of Energy] to support the growth of critical materials recycling in the United States,” Konduru said.

Spurring U.S. production of critical minerals

Participants at the Nov. 10 event discussed recovery of critical materials from used electronics like cellphones, laptops and hard drives, and toured Momentum’s lab and plant. The event featured a look at Momentum’s proprietary membrane solvent extraction, or MSX, technology.

Momentum developed MSX in partnership with Oak Ridge National Laboratory. MSX converts old batteries and magnets into rare earth minerals, using more than 95% of the material at 99% purity, the company said.

China currently dominates the global market for extraction and processing of critical minerals. In support of U.S. competitiveness and national security, ASCEND said it wants to decrease reliance on China and other countries for supplies of critical minerals.

“Recycling rates have long stagnated, not because technologies haven’t advanced, but because there is immense alignment needed — across the value chain, with local and regional policies, among stakeholders and in markets,” Shannon Bragg-Sitton, associate director of Idaho National Laboratory, said in the statement.

“An ecosystem like ASCEND can support that alignment and help companies navigate the complexity.”

ASCEND said feedback collected at the event will help guide Department of Energy investments in critical-minerals processing.

“ASCEND will determine the most impactful opportunities to expand critical materials production through domestic electronics recycling,” Chris Saldaña, deputy assistant secretary of the Department of Energy, said in a statement announcing the initiative.

Modular recycling plants

Momentum opened its Carrollton headquarters and R&D lab in 2024.

The company relies on its MSX technology to recover, separate and process high-purity rare earth elements such as neodymium, dysprosium and terbium. The technology also applies to battery materials like lithium, nickel and cobalt. Its feedstocks include mined ore, used batteries, mining byproducts, old magnets and industrial e-waste.

Momentum installs modular recycling plants that the company said can be permitted and built in one year rather than several years. The company’s customers include energy storage facilities, gigafactories, waste handlers and original equipment manufacturers.

text:
Texas has resumed reviewing environmental permit applications tied to data center developments, and one of the first beneficiaries appears to be Elon Musk.

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) approved an air permit 16 November for a proposed Space Exploration Technologies (SpaceX) gas-fired generation project in South Texas that will power a planned $24bn supercomputing campus.

TCEQ told Argus Wednesday it has "resumed its normal permit review process" after being notified that the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) had gathered information for community impact reviews of pending data center projects.

Texas governor Greg Abbott (R) ordered TCEQ in September to pause reviews of data center permit applications earlier while state officials assessed the potential effect of large new loads on the electric grid and host communities. The review process was expected to restart after ERCOT completed an initial assessment of projects included in the first group of large load projects seeking interconnection under a new process called Batch Zero. The audit results were scheduled to be announced 10 December.

ERCOT did not comment on whether it had informed TCEQ about the audit. ERCOT told Argus it presented an update on the Batch Zero Eligibility Verification and Community Impact Study process at a 5 November meeting of the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT). The grid operator said it plans to provide full findings to the commission on 10 December, with discussion scheduled for a 17 December open meeting.

The permit covers SpaceX's proposed Boca Chica facility in Cameron County. The development includes a gas-fired power plant and super-computing facility on a roughly 444-acre site near the southern tip of Texas.

The plan calls for an initial fleet of 35 simple-cycle turbines totaling roughly 748MW, according to SpaceX's 8 September permit application. The temporary fleet would include GE Vernova TM2500, Mitsubishi FT8 and Solar SMT-130 turbines.

Those units would eventually be replaced by eight permanent GE Vernova 7E turbines totaling about 705MW, according to the filing. The turbines are "used and/or refurbished existing units rather than freshly manufactured units" that SpaceX acquired on the secondary market rather than directly from turbine manufacturers, it said.

The approvals may complicate the incoming administration's approach to data-center development and pressure newly-elected officials to look retroactively at permits approved after the election.

Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) campaigned on a platform to rein in the sector, including a moratorium on data-center approvals until lawmakers could adopt new rules. Investors generally expected new restrictions would apply to future projects but this latest move changed TD Securities' view.

"We believe Hinojosa will now need to look retroactively as well, with a particular focus on all permitting decisions made post-election," they wrote in a note Wednesday. "For developers, this introduces a new level of risk and uncertainty as issued permits no longer carry certainty guarantees."

text:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on Nov. 18 announced the completion of the Master Plan for Responsible Advanced Nuclear Development in New York.

“Demonstrating New York’s leadership role in the national effort to develop new nuclear energy, the Master Plan is a comprehensive statewide roadmap to achieve the Governor’s Nuclear Reliability Backbone to create five gigawatts (GW) of new nuclear power,” Hochul’s office said.

Co-authored by the New York State Energy Research Development Authority (NYSERDA) and the New York State Department of Public Service (DPS), and unveiled at the State’s third Nuclear Summit in Rochester, N.Y., the master plan outlines coordinated state actions to support the safe and timely development and deployment of advanced nuclear power plants in upstate New York.

“Expanding emission-free, round-the-clock nuclear power is a cornerstone of my all-of-the-above approach to ensure we have enough energy to keep the lights on and costs down for New Yorkers,” Hochul said. “The completed Advanced Nuclear Master Plan can serve as a national model by pairing our ambitious target of five gigawatts of new nuclear generation with a comprehensive strategy to support thoughtful development and deployment of what will be the largest buildout the country has seen in more than three decades.”

The master plan was developed in response to Hochul’s 2025 directive to establish a framework supporting advanced nuclear energy development in New York.

Now, the master plan will help facilitate the development of the Nuclear Reliability Backbone, which Hochul directed the creation of in her 2026 State of the State, that will add 5 gigawatts of new nuclear generation to the 3.4 gigawatts already in existence.

DPS on Nov.18 also issued a White Paper with policy recommendations to help enable the commercial viability of advanced nuclear development, potential cost reductions and other considerations for advancing the Governor’s Nuclear Reliability Backbone.

In addition, the New York Power Authority also continues to move forward to develop and construct at least one gigawatt of nuclear energy in Upstate New York.

“Advanced nuclear energy in Upstate New York will strengthen grid reliability, drive economic growth, expand workforce opportunities, and deliver reliable, emissions-free power around the clock for generations to come,” said New York Power Authority President and CEO Justin E. Driscoll. “Responsible nuclear development will require collaboration across government, industry, academia, and local communities. The Advanced Nuclear Master Plan establishes a framework for moving those efforts forward together in advance of Governor Hochul’s goal to establish an 8.4-gigawatt backbone of reliable nuclear power. NYPA will leverage the critical insights detailed in the plan as part of its ongoing effort to develop at least 1 gigawatt of new nuclear generation to supply New York’s electric system.”

The announcements “advance New York’s commitment to a reliable, zero-emission electricity system, proving that a clean energy strategy can support statewide economic development,” Hochul’s office said.

Advanced Nuclear Master Plan

The 30-point Advanced Nuclear Master Plan supported by 12 studies and more than 1,000 pages of research and analysis identifies New York State actions to further assist with responsible advanced nuclear development.

It provides detailed findings and conclusions that address the interconnected requirements for deployment, including commercial viability, siting considerations, community partnerships, state regulatory processes, workforce readiness, and supply chain capacity.

The Master Plan identifies several areas of focus to support responsible advanced nuclear development, including:

• Advance a policy framework to support deployment: Enable State actions on cost reductions and project commercial viability.

• Capitalize on investments: Build on federal investments and opportunities such as Project Janus at Fort Drum.

• Maximize New York’s nuclear supply chain opportunities: Establish a nuclear supplier readiness program, connect New York businesses with nuclear project opportunities, and develop a coordinated, longer-term state supply chain strategy.

• Build the workforce for nuclear energy – starting with existing skills and resources: Leverage existing workforce funding and programs, upskill experienced workers, and support transitions from adjacent sectors while aligning specialized training investments with deployment.

• Identify potential sites and partner with communities to prepare for development: Establish a process to identify interested host communities, evaluate suitable sites, including brownfields, and support early site characterization and evaluation.

• Adapt state regulatory processes while maintaining uncompromising safety: Review State regulatory processes, identify opportunities to better align requirements, and equip local governments with tools to prepare for potential development.

NYSERDA will host a public webinar on January 13, 2027 at 12:00 p.m. ET to provide an overview of the Advanced Nuclear Master Plan. Register for the webinar to join.

White Paper

The white paper was directed by the Public Service Commission’s Nuclear Reliability Backbone Initiating Order. Key White Paper recommendations to be considered by the Commission include a proposal for a comprehensive, integrated suite of support policies to help ensure projects are commercially viable and unlock cost reductions.

The White Paper follows the filing of the Advanced Nuclear Policy Options Paper by NYSERDA and DPS Staff in June 2026. It complements the Advanced Nuclear Master Plan by offering formal policy recommendations for the Public Service Commission to consider as part of the Nuclear Backbone proceeding.

The White Paper incorporates public comments and feedback from a technical conference hosted by DPS in October 2026.

NYPA Nuclear Progress

In June 2025, Hochul called upon NYPA to lead the development of an advanced nuclear power project in Upstate New York capable of generating at least 1 GW of zero-emissions electricity.

Since then -- in parallel with the development of this Master Plan -- NYPA has advanced a focused predevelopment effort.

The Power Authority has solicited information from interested host communities and potential development partners, invested in building a nuclear talent pipeline through major workforce development funding, expanded international partnerships to share expertise and strengthen project delivery, and grown its leadership team with seasoned nuclear experts to guide siting, licensing, financing, and deployment efforts.

title: Outage fears rise, but batteries — and gas — are buffering the grid | Latitude Media
authors: Catherine Boudreau, Nate Kinsey, Lara Pierpoint, The Green Blueprint, Stephen Lacey, Open Circuit, Nick Zenkin, Jeff Young
description:
The North American power grid is less at risk of blackouts this winter than it was this time last year, according to a reliability watchdog.
Canadian provinces including Quebec and Nova Scotia are also at elevated risk, mainly because gas pipelines are constrained.
Will the power grid fail?
NERC’s assessment comes as Americans grow increasingly concerned about the reliability of the U.S. power grid.
Utilities and grid operators are struggling to modernize and expand their systems fast enough to keep up with demand from data centers, reshored manufacturing, and a more electrified economy.
text:
The North American power grid is less at risk of blackouts this winter than it was this time last year, according to a reliability watchdog.

The North American Electric Reliability Corp. found that just three areas are at “elevated” risk during cold snaps — meaning there wouldn’t be enough reserved capacity to meet peak demand — down from seven a year ago.

NERC attributed the improvement to the addition of more than 26 gigawatts of winter peak capacity, driven by about nine gigawatts of both battery storage and gas generation. California and Texas led the pack in terms of deploying storage, while Texas, northern Mexico, and the Mountain West accounted for the largest gas expansions.

The Department of Energy’s emergency orders allowing grid operators to order data centers and other large facilities to shift to backup generators during peak demand — even if it involves breaching air pollution limits — is also helping shore up the grid, NERC found. So are DOE orders keeping six fossil fuel plants online past their scheduled retirement dates, even as they raise costs for customers and greenhouse gas emissions.

In the U.S., just North and South Carolina remain in the “elevated” risk category amid rapid growth in residential electric heating and the arrival of large data centers and industrial loads. That growth has steadily eroded reserve margins, NERC said, particularly during early morning hours before solar generation ramps up. Canadian provinces including Quebec and Nova Scotia are also at elevated risk, mainly because gas pipelines are constrained.

Will the power grid fail?

NERC’s assessment comes as Americans grow increasingly concerned about the reliability of the U.S. power grid. Outages are getting longer, mainly due to more extreme weather as global temperatures rise from burning fossil fuels. Utilities and grid operators are struggling to modernize and expand their systems fast enough to keep up with demand from data centers, reshored manufacturing, and a more electrified economy.

And in recent days, fears of nationwide blackout spread across TikTok and other social media platforms due to a false, manipulated clip of President Donald Trump from an account pushing cryptocurrency, Politifact reported. Further fueling the anxiety have been a series of technology failures impacting air travel, banks, Microsoft, and Apple.

Beyond reliability, NERC also oversees cybersecurity threats to the bulk power system, including by enforcing mandatory standards for utilities and grid operators aimed at preventing cyber and physical attacks on electric, natural gas, and transmission infrastructure. NERC is also the primary hub for companies to share sensitive cyber incident data, indicators of attacks, and vulnerability alerts.

In January, NERC said that these mandatory security controls remain critical, but they aren’t being updated fast enough to keep up with changing threats. That report said a major vulnerability can be addressed by requiring employees or third-party vendors connecting remotely to smaller energy sites to use two-step login verifications. That includes solar, wind, and battery projects, as well as substations and fossil fuel plants. This is already required of the largest power plants, transmission hubs, and regional control centers.

It typically takes several years before updated NERC standards are approved by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and enforced.

NERC didn’t reply to a request for comment by the time of publication.

text:
Concerns include fire danger, environmental issues, cybersec…

The moderator stated that Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton …



State Sen. Charles Perry. (The Texan/Meridith Dyer)

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) lifted a permitting pause this week that Gov. Greg Abbott had previously ordered.

In September, Abbott, in a letter to the TCEQ, directed the state agency to “halt all permits sought by data centers.” The order followed Abbott's directives to the Public Utility Commission (PUC) and Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) to “thoroughly audit” data centers seeking connection to the Texas grid, as well as the order to the Texas Water  Development Board to “compel data centers to comply with water use reporting requirements.”

The TCEQ permit pause was intended to last until ERCOT completed its review of data center projects. The state agency regulates certain environmental permits and assesses the environmental impacts of water quality, air pollutants, and wastewater relating to data center projects.

Following its November 17 decision to lift the pause, the TCEQ told The Texan in a statement, “TCEQ has been notified that ERCOT has gathered information for the community impact review for pending data center projects. The agency has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations.”

In other data center-related news, state Sen. Charles Perry (R-Lubbock) filed legislation related to water consumption and the creation of a new regulatory framework for data centers after the Texas Legislature's bill pre-filing period opened on November 9.

Senate Bill (SB) 338 , authored by Perry, joins the chorus of new House and Senate filings aimed at regulating data centers in the state. The newly filed bills address data center regulations ranging from prohibiting tax abatements to repealing sales and use tax exemptions.

Perry’s bill specifically aims to establish “new safeguards for water consumption, transparency, and the impact of data center development on Texas communities,” according to his press release. The legislation garnered support from 15 bipartisan co-authors.

Perry cited a September hearing as a major impetus for drafting the bill: “At our hearing in September, we heard from Texans who are concerned about what these developments mean for their water, their property, and their quality of life.”

He called the concerns “legitimate,” adding that “Texans should not have to sacrifice their water resources or the peaceful enjoyment of their own homes to accommodate a new development."

Regarding water, the legislation seeks to establish “new standards for future data center developments” and require companies to implement water-efficient cooling techniques, according to the press release.

About water usage by data center companies — a topic that has been shrouded in uncertainty due to a lack of data from the data centers themselves — Perry stated, “We cannot responsibly plan for Texas' future if we do not even know how much water these facilities are using or where that water is coming from."

During the aforementioned hearing, the PUC reported that only 155 out of 377 data center companies reported water usage information.

SB 338 also seeks to further regulate the tax incentives that counties and cities provide data center companies, and revise abatement conditions to include water-related stipulations. The bill states that a Texas city cannot offer a property tax abatement to a data center that covers more than 50 percent of the property’s otherwise taxable value in a given year.

It also states that the Jobs, Energy, Technology, and Innovation Act agreements that data center companies have with school districts — 10-year property tax limitation contracts with a local school district, a company, and the Governor’s office — would be limited by the same water and environmental stipulations.

Texas Policy Research (TPR) stated that the bill’s “cooling mandates, siting rules, and disconnection penalties single out one industry for treatment no other large user faces, and they leave the real cost question unaddressed.”

TPR concluded, “Texas should stop subsidizing data centers, stop singling them out, and do the harder work of building the power and water supply a growing state needs.”

According to research from Power Hopper — a Texas electricity broker that also maintains a public repository tracking Texas legislative filings — data centers and large load users were the most frequently cited in electricity-related bill filings between November 9 and November 13.
