Energy decisions are socially embedded Within the home, energy use is woven into daily routines that household members share and negotiate.
text:
From heat pumps and electric vehicles to wind farms and carbon removal, technologies to reduce emissions are rapidly advancing. But these technologies can do little to cut emissions unless people support and use them effectively. A new book examines these human dimensions of the energy transition.

The De Gruyter Handbook on the Psychology of Energy Transitions, edited by Kim Wolske, research professor at the Harris School of Public Policy and a scholar with the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC), brings together 24 chapters from researchers across the US, UK, Europe and Australia. The premise of the book is that members of the public are integral to what the energy transition becomes and how it unfolds. Understanding the psychology behind people’s choices can help anticipate how people will respond to new technologies and policies, and can guide the design of initiatives that fit how people make decisions in everyday life.

“The inspiration for the book came from conversations I had with students and practitioners who have worked in the energy field,” says Wolske. “How the public responds to new energy policy initiatives can sometimes seem mystifying. People may pass up incentives that would make efficiency upgrades affordable and lower their bills. Or people may object to proposed renewable infrastructure projects despite being broadly supportive of a renewable energy future. This book gathers what we know about human behavior to improve the design and implementation of energy policy, so it can better account for the way people actually think and behave.” The book is written for students, researchers, policymakers and practitioners, including those who are not necessarily psychology experts.

Organized around practical challenges of the transition, the book examines the psychological dimensions of four broad topics: everyday household energy use, household adoption of efficient and renewable technologies, public support for energy policies and community responses to large-scale infrastructure projects. Chapters range from the design of energy labels and demand response programs to local acceptance of solar and wind projects and emerging technologies like carbon dioxide removal. Others consider how political ideology and policy design shape public support for energy policies, and how the costs and benefits of the transition are distributed across groups. Across these topics several themes run through the volume.

Information is rarely enough

“It’s tempting to assume that people just need more information, either about the need for a clean energy transition or the benefits of the technologies that will get us there,” says Wolske. “The book reveals the multitude of psychological factors that shape behavior beyond knowledge—and thus the multiple opportunities we have to better align energy programs and outreach with the needs of the people they are meant to serve.”

“Many energy policies build on the assumption that people carefully weigh costs and benefits before making energy-related decisions,” says Lukas Engel, co-lead of the chapter on cognitive biases and PhD student at the University of Basel. “In reality, energy decisions are often complex and subject to time constraints. As a result, people rely on mental shortcuts that help them make time-efficient decisions, but can also lead to suboptimal behavior.”

Other chapters show that people interpret energy and climate information through existing beliefs and mental models that can differ sharply from the ones experts use. Even generous incentives can go unused when claiming them takes too much time or effort, and awareness campaigns alone often fail to change that.

Context matters

The same technology or program can be met with very different responses depending on the setting in which people encounter it. Whether a household adopts a heat pump depends not only on whether it sounds beneficial in the abstract, but on whether it fits the home and household budget, and on the availability of incentives and trusted contractors.

“Our chapter looks at home electrification as a process, exploring how people’s needs change as they learn about technologies, weigh their options, find a contractor and start using a new system,” says Beth Karlin, founder and CEO of the See Change Institute. People may need support well past installation, as households that don’t learn to use new equipment effectively may see smaller savings than expected and tell their neighbors it wasn’t worth the investment.

Context also includes the information environment, where facts often compete with misinformation. “In hyperpolarized, oversaturated media landscapes, no one is completely immune to misinformation,” says Meaghan Guckian, faculty member at Antioch University New England and author of the chapter on energy misinformation. “The challenge is building people’s resistance to false narratives so that public support for the energy transition isn’t left to claims intentionally (and unintentionally) attempting to derail it.” False beliefs, once formed, can be difficult to correct, so advocates can try to “prebunk” myths by helping people recognize when they are being misled.

Energy decisions are socially embedded

Within the home, energy use is woven into daily routines that household members share and negotiate. Switching to an induction cooktop, for example, isn’t just a decision about energy. It can change how a family cooks together, and the person pushing for the switch may not be the one who does most of the cooking.

What peers do outside of the home also shapes what seems normal and worthwhile to do. Because energy use is mostly invisible, people often guess at what their neighbors do, and those guesses can be wrong. Home energy reports that show households how their energy consumption compares with similar neighbors illustrate how social comparison can be leveraged to prompt change.

Social influence also extends to the larger groups people identify with, such as their community or political party. People tend to act in line with what they believe those groups expect, and group identity shapes which sources people trust and whether a proposal is seen as something “people like us” support or oppose.

Trust and fairness shape local responses

Support for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in general doesn’t necessarily result in support for specific infrastructure projects. Psychological factors, like risk perceptions, fit with community character and whether the process feels fair, can play a role in how people come to support or oppose a local infrastructure project like a solar or wind farm.

“Public responses to wind energy are informed by an interplay among identities, values, emotions, and relationships to place, as well as trust in decision-makers,” says Shannon Howley, contributing author of the chapter on wind energy and assistant professor at the University of Central Florida. “These attitudes are dynamic and can change over time as people encounter new information and gain direct experience with project planning and development. Understanding how people form judgments about wind energy technology is essential in planning projects that are responsive to the concerns of affected communities.”

There are no shortcuts to public acceptance. Genuine community involvement in infrastructure development is necessary but does not guarantee success. Understanding how people perceive a project’s risks and benefits is a place to start.

“Energy policymaking in times of rapid transformation cannot rely on scientific data alone; it must incorporate the concerns, beliefs, and perceptions of individuals and communities,” says Ortwin Renn, professor emeritus at the University of Stuttgart and author of the chapter on risk perception. “This implies, first, that policymakers and planners must be aware of how the public perceives the risks and benefits of energy systems, and what drives their concerns. Second, it requires robust feedback loops to ensure these insights are effectively absorbed and processed by decision-makers in both the private and public sectors. Ultimately, perception research provides vital guidance for prudent and equitable policymaking.”

Attention to psychology can make energy policy and outreach more effective and better matched to the needs of the people and communities they affect. The De Gruyter Handbook on the Psychology of Energy Transitions brings that research to the professionals who design and carry out these efforts. “I’m honored to contribute to this book,” says Karlin. “It brings behavioral science into the real-world decisions energy professionals face every day.”

The book is open access and free to download from De Gruyter Brill.

title: COP31: Can data centres support AI without undermining the energy transition?
description:
At COP31, this tension raises a practical question: how can we build the computing capacity needed for scientific discovery and better services while cutting emissions and securing public support?
A study in Nature Climate Change links data centres built after 2020 with nearby coal-fired generating units remaining open longer.
Within energy systems, AI can improve renewable-generation forecasts, support grid operations and reduce waste in buildings and industry.
Some computing tasks can move to times or places with more clean electricity and spare grid capacity.
Earning public support Better engineering gives communities more credible options, but it cannot decide who should pay or which developments should proceed.
text:
On 9 November, Prime Minister Andy Burnham identified AI as a priority for Britain's 2027 G20 presidency. Yet in the US elections days earlier, voters favoured limits on data-centre development in 40 of 41 local ballot contests tracked by Ballotpedia. The mix of bans, restrictions and advisory votes highlights the tension between national AI ambitions and local willingness to host its infrastructure.

At COP31, this tension raises a practical question: how can we build the computing capacity needed for scientific discovery and better services while cutting emissions and securing public support?

Who bears the costs

The International Energy Agency's central projection sees global data-centre electricity use almost doubling, from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to around 950 in 2030. These figures cover all data centres, not AI alone. When demand grows faster than clean power and grid connections, securing electricity quickly can undermine climate commitments.

A study in Nature Climate Change links data centres built after 2020 with nearby coal-fired generating units remaining open longer. This is an association, not proof of causation. Meanwhile, US research in Nature Energy finds that wholesale-price pressures and rules for sharing grid costs can leave rural and lower-income households disproportionately exposed. The effects depend on local systems and policy choices.

For neighbours, the questions are immediate: will bills rise, will water remain available during droughts, and will promised jobs justify construction disruption, noise and land use? Benefits may reach users worldwide while pressures fall on particular communities. That uneven distribution makes data centres a key part of the COP debate about a fair transition.

Why the opportunity matters

The case for AI extends far beyond convenient answers. It can help researchers investigate disease and identify promising materials for batteries and other clean technologies. Better weather forecasts can help communities prepare for extremes, while AI-based flood warnings can support climate adaptation where monitoring is limited. Within energy systems, AI can improve renewable-generation forecasts, support grid operations and reduce waste in buildings and industry. These uses connect the same infrastructure that draws on local resources to urgent challenges in health, energy security and climate adaptation.

These are substantial opportunities, but their value depends on reliable applications reaching those who need them. Access to computing and skills matters alongside investment in facilities. Nor do potential benefits automatically cancel out environmental costs: more efficient hardware and software can reduce energy per task while wider adoption increases total consumption.

Engineering for local conditions

Engineering can ease these pressures. Smaller models, where reliable, and fewer idle servers reduce unnecessary demand. Some computing tasks can move to times or places with more clean electricity and spare grid capacity. Immediate-response services and costly interruptions to training limit this flexibility.

New facilities should be planned alongside additional clean generation, storage and grid capacity. Annual renewable-electricity purchases alone cannot establish that clean power is available where and when it is needed.

Cooling choices must reflect local conditions. Treated wastewater can reduce reliance on drinking water. Recirculating coolant and releasing heat without evaporation can cut on-site water consumption, although mechanical cooling may require more electricity. Water used in power generation and manufacturing still counts. Waste heat can warm nearby buildings where suitable networks and demand exist; the benefit depends on the heating displaced and the electricity required.

More experimental options include solar-powered computing in orbit. Google's Project Suncatcher has reported prototype AI computation in space, suggesting a possible way to ease terrestrial resource pressures. Its environmental value remains unproven: launches, manufacturing, hardware replacement, disposal and radiating waste heat all present challenges.

Earning public support

Better engineering gives communities more credible options, but it cannot decide who should pay or which developments should proceed. Grid agreements should assign costs fairly and protect households if projected demand never materialises. Developers also need predictable requirements to make investments that can take years to deliver. Communities need a meaningful say over whether, where and on what terms projects proceed, with enforceable commitments on water, noise and local benefits.

Public reporting should show absolute electricity and water use, supply-chain emissions and benefits actually delivered, including lasting employment and useful heat supplied to neighbouring buildings. This lets residents and policymakers judge whether a project merits support. Opposition may lead to better proposals, delay construction or move pressures elsewhere; treating it simply as an obstacle to investment misses the choices at stake.

The challenge is to connect AI's wider promise with conditions people can trust where its infrastructure is built. Clean power, fair cost sharing and meaningful public influence should develop alongside computing capacity. This is where COP31 comes in, where political ambition can translate into lasting public benefit.

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Nevoya is developing a new electric truck corridor on I-10 between San Bernardino, California, and Phoenix, Arizona, in partnership with Facebook and Instagram parent company Meta.

Meta is buying environmental certificates to lower its emissions profile to support the buildout of the route, which will include charging stations. The route is expected to begin operations with 25 trucks in 2027, according to a Nov. 12 news release.

“The agreement helps scale electric trucking in a region central to Meta’s infrastructure with the I-10 being a key route for moving data center construction materials across the southern United States,” the release said. The deal doesn’t involve moving Meta’s own goods, the announcement also noted.

The social media company previously established a partnership with the full-service electric trucking company for a Houston-Dallas route, also set to start in 2027.

Nevoya partners previously noted that the Texas setup involves a book-and-claim system in which companies buy environmental attribute certificates, where environmental benefits from the freight transportation itself are separated and transferred to a company seeking to reduce its emissions.

“Meta coming back for a second corridor is a strong signal that this model works,” John Verdon, Nevoya co-founder and chief commercial officer, said in the news release. “Electric trucks already win on the corridors we run; what unlocks them at scale is multi-year demand that drives financial and operational innovation. That is what this agreement does, and we intend to repeat it corridor by corridor.”

Meta noted in another announcement the Arizona-California corridor charging stations will support other commercial fleets, too.

In early 2027, the Texas route will launch first, Verdon told Trucking Dive in an email. Greenlane is developing that infrastructure.

The I-10 corridor route between the Inland Empire and Phoenix will develop later in the year as charging comes online, Verdon added. A charging infrastructure partner is still being developed for the second route.

“We’re continuing to ramp hiring in Texas and are building the California–Arizona team ahead of more trucks arriving on the I-10,” he also said. “Our model helps: these are regional, home-daily lanes in new electric trucks, which is a job a lot of drivers want.”

title: Where do people want to see Britain's climate action plan working? On their own doorstep
description:
But we know sustained climate action can work.
And I am equally proud of our record on climate action abroad.
We exceeded our five-year international climate finance commitment, spending £12.8bn between 2021-22 and 2025-26 against a pledge of £11.6bn.
Finally, the Climate Change Committee has warned that Britain must adapt for our changed climate – and we are doing exactly that.
We also know that the climate crisis is now a national security issue and we must prepare for future threats.
text:
In this cold weather, it is easy to forget that Britain has just been through its hottest summer on record, part of our new reality as the climate crisis reaches our doorstep. For millions around the world, the consequences have already been more devastating for the communities that did the least to cause this crisis.

That is the backdrop to Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, where I arrive on Tuesday as the UK’s chief negotiator. As I have prepared for these negotiations, I’ve been reflecting on the gap between the science and the political debate in Britain. Early predictions by the Met Office indicate that 2027 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record globally as El Niño rips through the Pacific. This is a sobering reality. And yet, the Conservatives and Reform UK want to bury their heads in the sand and break the consensus on delivering net zero. But we know sustained climate action can work.

Yes, the world will overshoot 1.5C of global heating in the coming years. But without the Paris agreement, the world would have been on track for a 4C increase. International commitments, finance and adaptation are working, and multilateralism has never been more vital to our future. Every fraction of a degree we prevent means lives protected and communities given a better chance at surviving. Setbacks bring frustration, but resistance is the sign of progress.

Britain has a responsibility to lead, and we are determined to do so. I am proud of the progress we have made to cut emissions by 54% since 1990 and the action we are taking to achieve net zero by 2050. And I am equally proud of our record on climate action abroad. We exceeded our five-year international climate finance commitment, spending £12.8bn between 2021-22 and 2025-26 against a pledge of £11.6bn. Britain exceeded its £3bn nature target and tripled annual adaptation funding from £500m to more than £1.5bn.

And the real measure of that investment is what it has achieved. Since 2011, UK climate finance has helped an estimated 159 million people across the world better adapt to the climate crisis, reduced or avoided 201m tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions and mobilised about £26bn in public and private finance.

So, what next? At Cop31, Britain will push for action. And what does that look like? A faster clean-energy transition, cuts to methane, protection for forests and oceans, and better access to finance. The drive for electrification, in particular, is a huge global opportunity. Investing in homegrown clean power is a win-win. It allows us to break our dependence on volatile fossil-fuel markets and protect families from price shocks, while reducing the carbon we use. And through the rollout of solar energy, batteries, clean heat and electric vehicles, communities in Britain will directly benefit from this energy transition through lower bills and a stake in the energy system of the future.

Finally, the Climate Change Committee has warned that Britain must adapt for our changed climate – and we are doing exactly that. We also know that the climate crisis is now a national security issue and we must prepare for future threats. That’s why we are protecting homes from flooding and making them better able to withstand extreme weather. We’re building nine new reservoirs in England to secure our water supplies and restoring the natural systems that help protect communities from floods. I know we have more to do. Here in Britain and around the world, the longer governments wait, the more families will face the upheaval of losing homes to extreme weather and the more it will cost to put it right. The first duty of government is to protect people: cutting emissions and preparing for changes already under way.

I know these commitments feel remote, even when what we agree at Cop31 matters here at home. I understand why people question whether governments will maintain their resolve when politics gets difficult. On the doorstep, people want to see progress, not more promises. So I share here what I say there: I will keep pushing for greater ambition on climate and for results people can see: warmer homes, secure jobs, lower exposure to energy-price volatility and communities better protected from extreme weather.

We have too much to lose by stepping back, and everything to gain from leading. Our security, prosperity and the lives of generations to come depend on what we do now.

text:
Two major offshore wind projects in southern New England are now fully operational and are expected to help stabilize household energy prices as winter approaches.

More than 120 turbines operated by Vineyard Wind and Revolution Wind can generate enough energy to power 750,000 homes across Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island.

Anxhela Mile, staff attorney for the Conservation Law Foundation, said the projects are clear examples of what states can achieve when they invest in homegrown clean energy.

“These developers have contracted for the power to be supplied for 20 years within stable contracts, which is a stark contrast to what we’re experiencing with price shocks from fossil fuels,” Mile pointed out.

The Vineyard Wind project alone is expected to save Massachusetts ratepayers more than $1 billion over the next two decades. New England homes reliant on heating oil have paid more than $200 in additional costs since the Iran War began in March.

Both projects faced significant pushback from the Trump administration, which has labeled offshore wind as a threat to national security and repeatedly sought to revoke construction permits. Earlier this year, it paid a French energy company $1 billion to abandon its plans to build wind farms along the East Coast.

Mile argued wind power is the future of the energy economy and more will be needed to reduce emissions and counter climate change. She stressed despite federal resistance, states can begin to lay the groundwork for future projects.

“They can still expand construction within their region in terms of port development. They could train workforces, and they can also look at new ways to contract energy within the states. So there still is a lot of state discretion in terms of supporting offshore wind,” Mile outlined.

Alpitronic Americas, Inc. (Alpitronic), a manufacturer of DC fast-charging hardware and technology for electric vehicles, today announced it selects York County for its first South Carolina operations. The company’s $33.94 million investment will create 70 new jobs.

Alpitronic produces EV charging equipment used by charge network operators and customers serving passenger vehicles, commercial trucks, buses and fleets. The company’s North American headquarters are in Charlotte, and its global headquarters are in Bolzano, Italy. At its new 173,315-square-foot facility, located at 3560 Stateview Blvd. in Fort Mill, Alpitronic will manufacture various chargers in its Hypercharger line, including the HYC400 and highly anticipated HYC1000. The site will also be used for warehousing functions and include a testing lab along with repair, logistics and office spaces.

Initial operations are expected to be online in February 2027. Individuals interested in joining the Alpitronic team should visit the company’s careers page.

The Coordinating Council for Economic Development approved job development credits related to the project. The council also awarded a $200,000 Set-Aside grant to York County to assist with the costs of building improvements.

The company’s $33.94 million investment will create 70 new jobs.

At the Marine Renewables Conference in Ottawa, Ontario, on November 18, 2026, the Honourable Sean Fraser, Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, announced nearly $10 million in funding for 24 clean electricity and innovation projects in Atlantic Canada.

Energy Innovation Program

The Energy Innovation Program advances clean energy technologies that will help Canada maintain a competitive, reliable and affordable energy system while transitioning to a low-carbon economy.

Recipient: Salient Energy Inc.

Location: Halifax, Nova Scotia

Funding amount: $3,431,497

The Atlas will provide the datasets, models, methodologies and technical information required to support carbon management planning and policy development and to evaluate carbon storage opportunities by the public, industry, academia and governments.

Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program

The Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program is designed to build a cleaner, more modern, reliable electricity grid system by supporting the deployment of grid modernization, energy storage and renewables across Canada.

Location: Annapolis County, Nova Scotia

Recipient: Municipality of the County of Kings

Funding amount: $202,576

The Clean Energy for Rural and Remote Communities (CERRC) program is dedicated to reducing reliance on diesel and other fossil fuels for heat and power in Indigenous, rural and remote communities.

title: Mexico Risks Missing Out on AI Data Center Boom as Energy Crunch Bites
description:
Lugo says local laws haven’t been updated to facilitate building permits for data centers, leading to dizzying permit applications and delays.
Recently reelected President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva even urged more data center investment in his victory speech.
AI infrastructure, including data centers, is the biggest part of a global AI spending spree seen reaching nearly $3 trillion this year.
Even the most upbeat projections for Mexico’s data center build-out pale by comparison.
To date, Querétaro has been the one bright spot for Mexico’s data center ambitions.
text:
If location were everything, Mexico would be having a data center boom. Digital information can zip across the border to the world’s largest economy almost as quickly as if it were coming from inside the US itself.

And so far, Mexicans have shared little of US voters’ political rancor against the AI tech industry. Immensely popular President Claudia Sheinbaum insists she wants exactly this kind of investment, and she needs it to juice a tepid economy.

The problem is that Mexico isn’t ready to take advantage of the moment. The electricity grid needs a massive upgrade. Investors say there’s too much red tape to get a new project going. And other Latin American nations, while further away from the US, are providing robust competition. Brazil hosts 225 of the more than 500 data centers in Latin America, compared with Mexico’s 71. Much smaller Chile has 66, according to the Data Center Map.

Countries across the world have begun to face infrastructure and resource constraints as they seek to become major data center hubs. But Mexico is battling to latch onto the explosion in new technology and investment. Sheinbaum has pledged to streamline regulations, and her government has approved the construction of at least four major data centers since last year, representing a projected investment of nearly $10 billion. Her industry chief insists key infrastructure will be ready in time.

“We are living through a shift in an era,” Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard told Bloomberg News in response to questions about the country’s AI build-out. “For some of the data centers that have been announced in Mexico, power stations and transmission lines are currently being built with the private sector,” he said.

“This is important for the country because it serves as a conduit for artificial intelligence, and there are only two options: Either you have it, or you don’t.”

Last year, CloudHQ announced a $4.8 billion investment plan for six data centers in the industrial hub of Querétaro in central Mexico. But even CloudHQ’s vote of confidence comes with a note of caution.

“It takes at least eight months under normal circumstances to get an electricity connection contract. Factoring in questions, answers and reviews, it can take up to three years,” said Luis Lugo, CloudHQ’s top Mexico executive.

Lugo says local laws haven’t been updated to facilitate building permits for data centers, leading to dizzying permit applications and delays. “Not counting the energy ones, I have had to apply for about 111 permits for several issues,” he said.

Compounding the extra cost and prolonged timelines, there just aren’t enough power plants to support the sector’s growth.

“The limitation on the electricity supply is a major problem in Mexico,” said Daniel Valdez Ramírez, commercial and product director at Risoul Y Cia, an electrical equipment and automation company.

Sheinbaum has pledged to add 32 gigawatts of generation capacity by the end of her term in 2030, which would mark growth of more than a third compared to the national grid’s current capacity of around 91 GW. But by law, state-owned power company Comision Federal de Electricidad (CFE) must produce most of it, limiting the role of would-be private producers and discouraging investment.

The CFE declined to comment on how it might streamline permitting or its plans to expand energy infrastructure for data centers.

More Obstacles

Mexico’s longstanding dependence on fossil fuels is another impediment to attracting more of the facilities that increasingly power the digital economy, from streaming services like Netflix to new virtual assistants like Meta’s Muse.

Mexico’s top business lobby CCE and data center industry group MEXDC point to Big Tech’s climate commitments. Both business associations argue that much more renewable energy is needed to lure investment from AI companies to Mexico, where electricity overwhelmingly comes from burning natural gas.

Sheinbaum, a former climate scientist, is pushing for more green power. By the time she leaves office in 2030, she wants 38% of all locally produced electricity to come from renewables, up from about a quarter today. Her government says 121 solar and wind projects will come online next year as tie-ups between CFE and private companies tick up.

But more than two years into her term, the push has barely moved the needle: Mexico’s total share of renewable energy is up only 2 percentage points.

“We aren’t competitive in that regard,” said MEXDC head Juan Carlos Mondragón. He pointed to abundant renewables in Brazil as a major factor behind its data center growth. Recently reelected President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva even urged more data center investment in his victory speech.

While Sheinbaum announced a plan last year to spend $8 billion for more than 200 new transmission lines through 2030, the CFE’s slow pace building them is another bottleneck.

“Investments of this kind at the federal level take a long time. The customer needs projects completed in 12 or 14 months,” Mondragón said. But the CFE often takes much longer. “We’re ready to get involved with big investments, but regulations need to be improved. Building a transmission line now is a major challenge.”

Without a power sector overhaul, Mexico will struggle to cash in on the high-tech bonanza that’s already playing out.

AI infrastructure, including data centers, is the biggest part of a global AI spending spree seen reaching nearly $3 trillion this year. Mexico’s inability to attract more of it coincides with massive data center spending in the US, followed by a growing backlash. The complaints north of the border often focus on fears they push up electricity bills and use too much water. They played an outsized role in the US midterm elections earlier this month as voters in some states approved data center moratoriums or outright bans.

The incoming governor of Texas, Gina Hinojosa, has already pledged stiffer regulations.

In spite of the headwinds, US capital investment in the facilities shows little sign of slowing. It totaled some $387 billion in 2025, and is on pace to reach $700 billion by the end of this year, according to estimates from Moody’s Investors Service.

Even the most upbeat projections for Mexico’s data center build-out pale by comparison. MEXDC estimates just over $20 billion in total direct investments over the next four years.

One Bright Spot

Some analysts speculate that changing political winds in the US could lead to more opportunities for its southern neighbor.

Mexico can point to significant strengths. It’s latency edge allows data to travel faster to US end-users, an advantage for AI-powered customer service and chatbot apps, among other uses. Other assets include a large pool of skilled labor and dozens of free trade deals that nurture the country’s large manufacturing base. Growing trade with Asian economies already supplies local factories with electronics to make computer servers, many of them exported to the US to propel AI projects there.

“Mexico has everything it takes to become the primary hub for data centers in Latin America,” said Manuel Calvillo, project coordinator for energy infrastructure company Fermaca. The company has recently expanded into data centers and AI computing. “The geographic location is excellent due to proximity and economic integration with the United States.”

While Fermaca is building three data centers in Mexico, including what’s expected to be the country’s largest, only a handful of other firms have major investments in the pipeline.

Some in the sector pin their hopes for growth on Querétaro state, located just a few hours north of Mexico City and close to other industrial centers including Guanajuato and San Luis Potosí.

To date, Querétaro has been the one bright spot for Mexico’s data center ambitions. The state has a long history of automotive and aerospace manufacturing and today hosts cloud computing and other digital infrastructure companies, plus universities that train specialized engineers.

It’s currently home to around 70% of Mexico’s existing data centers, run by sector giants like Amazon Web Services and Google.

But bringing more data centers to Querétaro could prove difficult due to electrical infrastructure that wasn’t designed for intensive energy consumers like the new AI facilities. The situation is likely to get worse as power demand in the state from announced data center projects is on track to grow more than six fold by 2031.

“The Querétaro area is already very saturated,” said Mondragón.

If Mexico ultimately misses its data center moment, it might come to resemble its failure to harness an earlier global shift that led to massive gains just across the border: the shale revolution that transformed the US into the world’s top oil and gas producer over the past couple decades.

While Sheinbaum has taken small steps to consider some fracking projects many years later, a Mexican shale boom is far off despite sharing much the same geology near the US border.

“The comparison with fracking is useful because of the risk of being left behind in a global transformation,” said Banamex economist Arely Medina. “Mexico could miss out.”

For decades, the DGA has been at the forefront of efforts to keep film and television production here at home.

text:
With the midterm elections behind us and Congress back in Washington, we want to update you on the DGA’s ongoing efforts to secure a federal film and television production tax incentive — a critical priority in our fight for jobs.

For decades, the DGA has been at the forefront of efforts to keep film and television production here at home. We’ve successfully advocated for stronger production incentives in states across the country, including California, New York, Illinois, Georgia and others. Now, we’re building on that progress by fighting for a federal incentive that — when coupled with incentives in the states — will help America compete with countries around the world and bring more jobs and opportunities back to our members.

The stakes couldn’t be higher. A recent study commissioned by the DGA and our fellow entertainment unions found that over the past 25 years, America’s share of production for the 25 highest-budget feature films has fallen from 74% to just 34%, while the share of major studio television production spending in the U.S. has dropped from 94% to 64%. Behind these numbers are lost jobs, fewer opportunities for our members, and communities losing the economic benefits of production.

After years of advocacy, we reached an important milestone in September with the introduction of the bipartisan Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act (MPTERA). This legislation represents a major step toward establishing a federal incentive that would help reverse these trends and strengthen domestic production.

The recent elections have created a more complicated political environment, and Congress now has only a narrow window to act before the end of the year during their lame duck session. But our commitment has not changed. Your DGA leadership is actively reaching out to the key Congressional decision makers as part of the push for MPTERA to be attached to a viable tax package if one moves forward. And we are continuing to engage Congressional leaders in both parties, working alongside our industry partners, and pressing for action while there is still an opportunity to pass this legislation in 2026.

We have made tremendous progress in building bipartisan support for this effort, and we intend to keep that momentum going. Whether Congress acts in the coming weeks, or the fight continues into 2027, we will not let up until we have a federal incentive that helps bring film and television jobs back home.

We need your voice in this fight! We encourage every DGA member to contact their representatives in Congress and urge them to support MPTERA. Tell them why keeping production in America matters to you, your family, and your community. A sample letter and resources to help you take action are available at this link.

Together, we can help secure a stronger future for American film and television production and the workers who make it possible.

text:
TEXAS — State environmental regulators have resumed reviewing data center permits, bringing an end to an earlier directive from Gov. Greg Abbott ordering a pause on permit approvals related to data center projects.

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality received notice on Friday from Abbott’s office that officials at the state’s electric grid had completed gathering information on potential community impacts from data centers — one of multiple issues Abbott asked grid officials and electricity regulators to evaluate.

“The agency has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations,” TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said in a written statement.

In August, Abbott had called on the Electric Reliability Council of Texas and electricity regulators to audit all data centers trying to connect to the grid, as well as gather information about tax incentives, power use, water use and potential neighborhood impacts. Abbott at that time paused approval of any grid interconnections for data centers while the audit was completed.

In his Sept. 21 letter to TCEQ calling for the environmental permitting pause, Abbott said the agency needed to wait until ERCOT “completes its review.”

Environmental advocates at Public Citizen, responding to the news of the resumed permits, called on TCEQ commissioners to resign.

“The TCEQ is asserting that ERCOT has concluded its assessment of the community impacts of data centers, and without sharing those results with communities or detailing how the TCEQ will incorporate the findings into permitting decisions, agency leadership has begun unilaterally issuing data center permits,” said Kathryn Guerra, the TCEQ watchdog campaign director for Public Citizen, in a statement.

Intense opposition to data centers had been growing all year in communities across the state, where Democrats and Republicans alike fought projects they worried would destabilize the electric grid, lead to more pollution from new gas-fueled power generators and guzzle up water in a state with serious drought concerns.

TCEQ handles permits related to air pollution at facilities and stormwater runoff on construction sites. The agency faced criticism in October from Public Citizen and FracTracker Alliance. The groups noticed that some data center-related construction permits were being cleared anyway — counter to Abbott’s order.

TCEQ said it suspended the permits and then it shut down its entire automated electronic filing system and required physical applications be submitted for staff to review.

Then in a staggering upset on Nov. 3, Abbott lost his reelection to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who on the campaign trail vowed to keep data center approvals paused until legislators pass new state laws.

Neither Abbott’s office nor Hinojosa’s media team on Tuesday immediately responded to a request for comment.

“Texans are tired of this political theatre,” said Sam Law, researcher at FracTracker Alliance, in a written statement shared by Public Citizen. “We need real leadership, transparency, and a true moratorium on data center development.”

ERCOT provided an update on its review of community impacts to electric regulators at the Public Utility Commission of Texas on Nov. 5. ERCOT reported receiving responses from 93% of 465 projects, which provided enough information for “a statistically meaningful analysis for the final report.”

ERCOT officials plan to report their full findings to the PUC on Dec. 10 and discuss them at the next PUC open meeting Dec. 17. Texas.

text:
FORT MILL — An electric vehicle charger manufacturer will establish its first South Carolina operations in Fort Mill, investing nearly $34 million and creating 70 jobs.

Alpitronic Americas, Inc., a manufacturer of direct current fast-charging hardware and technology for electric vehicles, announced the $33.94 million expansion Nov. 18.

At its new 173,315-square-foot facility located at 3560 Stateview Blvd., Alpitronic will manufacture various chargers in its Hypercharger line.

The site will also be used for warehousing functions and will include a testing lab along with repair, logistics and office spaces.

Initial operations are expected to begin in February 2027. Individuals interested in joining the Alpitronic team should visit the company’s careers page.

The company’s global headquarters are in Bolzano, Italy, and its North American headquarters are in Charlotte, N.C.

“We’re pleased to welcome Alpitronic to York County and to see the company choose our community for its new manufacturing operation,” said Christi Cox, chairwoman of the York County Council. “With its North American headquarters already in the Charlotte region, this is a natural fit as the company expands its U.S. operations. We appreciate Alpitronic’s investment and look forward to the new jobs and opportunities it will bring.”

Alpitronic produces EV charging equipment used by charge network operators and customers serving passenger vehicles, commercial trucks, buses and fleets.

“North America is central to our next phase of growth, and investing in our manufacturing capabilities is key to supporting that expansion,” said Patrik Herrnegger, CEO of Alpitronic Americas. “Our Fort Mill facility will put U.S. production under our direct control, bringing us closer to our customers and enabling us to serve them more efficiently. We thank South Carolina and York County for their partnership as we prepare to begin production in early 2027.”

text:
MADISON, Wis. (WMTV) - Gov. Tony Evers and the Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation announced that the state will provide up to $15 million in tax incentives to support Realta Fusion’s relocation.

The WEDC Board of Directors approved the performance-based Enterprise Zone tax credits for the project on Tuesday.

The entire project is slated to cost $800 million and will move the company’s corporate headquarters to the site of the former Oscar Mayer plant in Madison.

“We don’t have to choose between a clean energy future and supporting good-paying jobs and a strong economy,” said Governor Evers. ”We can and should do both, and that’s exactly what this partnership will do.”

Realta Fusion is a Madison-based fusion energy startup, which was founded in 2022.

“Fusion energy is not only good for our planet and our power grid, but it builds on all our strengths as a state with our world-class research universities, research laboratories, and an incredible manufacturing and supply chain network supported by our highly skilled workforce,” Governor Evers said.

The amount of credits the company will receive depends on the amount of capital invested and the number of jobs created. WEDC says the incentive package is its largest investment in fusion energy to date.

“Realta Fusion is part of the great tradition of the Wisconsin Idea, where research at the University of Wisconsin produces innovations that change the world,” said WEDC Secretary and CEO John W. Miller.

During the 2026 Wisconsin State of the State address, Governor Evers said fusion research is a top priority for Wisconsin.

He announced a partnership between the PSC and the UW–Madison Department of Nuclear Engineering and Engineering Physics to conduct the state’s nuclear energy siting study.

description:

text:
Washington, D.C. — 65 senators just voted to invoke cloture on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), advancing a massive giveaway to Big Tech and Big Oil at the expense of our communities and our climate. Nearly two-thirds of the Democratic caucus voted against the measure, including every Democrat on the Environment and Public Works Committee except for BAAJA co-sponsor Senator Whitehouse.

BAAJA eviscerates our bedrock environmental protections to accelerate the buildout of risky, polluting fossil fuel projects, AI data centers, and ICE detention facilities. It would radically curtail the ability of communities, Tribal Nations, and states to challenge projects that threaten their air and water, while robbing future administrations of the tools to stop the climate crisis. As a result, it would increase exposure to toxic pollution for Black, Brown, and Indigenous communities, exacerbating environmental racism.

BAAJA fails to deliver relief to the millions of Americans hit hard by skyrocketing electricity costs. Even the American Petroleum Institute, a major BAAJA supporter, admits that BAAJA wouldn’t stop energy bills from climbing. Other analyses find that BAAJA could drive gas prices to double over the next decade by accelerating gas demand.

BAAJA was rammed through the Senate following closed-door negotiations without a single hearing, markup, or opportunity for public participation. The fossil fuel industry has spent millions of dollars to shape this bill, which goes above and beyond fulfilling its Project 2025 wishlist.

The bill now requires just a simple majority vote in the Senate before it’s sent to the U.S. House of Representatives. Advocates urge members of the House to listen to the voters who demanded Congress rein in data center development, stop corruption, and bring down electricity costs in the midterms. They must not repeat the Senate’s anti-democratic process and rubber-stamp this bill without adequate consideration of the threats it poses to our communities.

QUOTES:

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) is a corporate power grab, advancing the interests of Big Oil and Big Tech at the expense of people and the planet. By racing to pass this bill, the Senate has betrayed the trust of the public who voted overwhelmingly against corporate corruption in our political system barely two weeks ago.” Basav Sen, Climate Policy Director, Institute for Policy Studies

“BAAJA may give us savings of a mere $15 a month in 15 years, while exponentially increasing asthma and cancer-causing pollution in our neighborhoods. This is the ‘affordability win’ we are supposed to be grateful for? Instead of being beholden to billionaires, the Senate should be delivering on the mandate set by the people: protect the people, our health, our land, and our pocketbooks rather than making working people sacrifice these basic protections for big monopolies that drive up costs, pollute our communities, and use their money and influence to write the rules. Enough is enough!” Mar Zepeda Salazar, legislative director at Climate Justice Alliance

“The Senate’s vote to advance BAAJA is a slap in the face of Americans who just weeks ago overwhelmingly voted for lawmakers to address the affordability crisis and to stop the explosion of data centers. BAAJA is a giveaway to Big Oil and Big Tech that will accelerate the buildout of hundreds of proposed gas power plants and pipelines and AI data centers that run on gas, which will worsen the climate crisis and raise families’ electricity bills. The House of Representatives must reject this bill and deliver real solutions for working families.” Elizabeth Bast, Executive Director, Oil Change International

“Senators who voted for this bill should be ashamed. Americans made clear they want politicians to put people ahead of corporate profits, but instead the Senate just advanced a giant giveaway to Big Tech and polluters. Calling this a bipartisan compromise doesn’t change what it is: a reckless attack on our clean air, clean water, wildlife, public lands, oceans, and communities. We urge the House to do what the Senate will not — put people first and vote ‘no’ on BAAJA.” Erich Pica, President of Friends of the Earth U.S.

“Any senator who votes for the BAAJA is sending a clear message to all of the Tribal Nations that they will not honor Tribal sovereignty and will sacrifice our sacred sites for political gains. Tribes and Indigenous Peoples have made our message clear: do not use this bill as a vehicle to alter Tribal consultation. Any vote other than a no vote on BAAJA lets all of Indian Country know who stands with us and who stands against us.” Jordan Harmon, Policy Specialist, Indigenous Environmental Network

“This rushed backroom permitting reform deal is an outright betrayal of people across the country, especially environmental justice communities who deserve to have a say and be protected from pollution, harmful infrastructure like data centers, and growing climate impacts. The fossil fuel industry has warmed the pockets of those in Congress to create this bill, which would remove necessary and hard-earned protections that defend our health, environment, and rights. We demand the House block this insidious bill. Let’s work with a new Congress to advance real clean, renewable energy solutions, not data center grifts and fossil fuel billionaire giveaways.” Leslie Fields, Chief Federal Officer, WE ACT for Environmental Justice

“Just two weeks ago, voters across the country demanded change from a status quo that is enriching billionaires and corporations at the expense of our communities. People across the country are pushing back against not only a reckless build-out of data centers but also the expansion of polluting energy infrastructure to power these projects – all to benefit the wealthiest tech and energy corporations on earth. For the Senate to rush this bill through now, severely limiting any opportunity for the public to challenge huge giveaways to Big Tech and Big Oil at the expense of our communities, is emblematic of the problems at the core of the bill itself.” Jenna Ruddock, Advocacy Director, Free Press Action

“Time and again throughout this Congress, Senator Schumer has supported the status quo. But the American people are loudly demanding real change. Schumer must step down from party leadership for good. The House has an opportunity now to acknowledge the clear will of the American people and rein in Big Tech’s data center attack. It must start by rejecting this terrible pro-polluter, anti-environment permitting bill, and in so doing, demonstrate what political courage and common sense look like.” Jim Walsh, Policy Director, Food & Water Watch

“BAAJA is a betrayal of public lands, waters, wildlife, and communities in the western U.S. What’s worse is that this bill is being deceptively pushed as an ‘affordability’ bill when those benefits are at best meager, speculative, and won’t be felt for more than a decade while the harms to the people and places we love will start the moment this abomination of a bill is signed into law. It’s a glaring signal that Congress, even after the midterms, remains captured by powerful tech, energy, and finance billionaires.” Erik Schlenker-Goodrich, Executive Director, The Western Environmental Law Center

“This is one of the most anti-environmental bills in recent memory and should not be rushed through during the lame duck session of Congress. There is a reason why the bill is supported by President Trump, Stephen Miller, Exxon, and other plastic producers. It is a gift to fossil fuel companies and the bad provisions greatly outweigh the positive provisions.“ Judith Enck, former EPA Regional Administrator and President of Beyond Plastics

“Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines, and LNG terminals while sacrificing fundamental, commonsense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S. Any benefits for renewable energy are swamped by the likely increases in climate, air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry that will haunt us for decades to come. This is not ‘reform,’ but a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America that is being rushed through in the lame duck session of Congress without any hearings or opportunity for input from the American people.“ Jen Duggan, Executive Director of the Environmental Integrity Project

“Black people are consistently told that we are the ‘backbone’ of the Democratic Party, yet BAAJA is now stabbing Black people in the back. Certain Democrats will need to explain to our people why they are supporting a bill that will exacerbate environmental racism and increase exposure to pollution in Black communities like Cancer Alley and throughout the Gulf South. BAAJA is nothing more than an abundance of betrayal to Black communities who are sick and tired of being America’s premier energy and economic sacrifice zones.“ Anthony Karefa Rogers-Wright, Black Alliance for Peace

“We are profoundly disappointed by this Senate outcome on S. 5653, BAAJA. The votes in favor don’t align with the spirit of election outcomes in 2026. Most Americans heard a resounding popular demand for federal accountability to people and place. We love our neighbors too much to accept this outcome without objection. We commit to educate our representatives and call them to love people and ecosystems.“ Pablo DeJesús, Executive Director, Unitarian Universalists for Social Justice

“Democrats won sweeping victories at the ballot box, but instead of empowering newly energized Democrats, the Senate is choosing to advance a mostly Republican bill with mostly Republican votes. And Senate Democrats who vote for the Billionaires’ Abundance and Anti-Justice Act are showing their contempt for their voters.”- RL Miller, political director of Climate Hawks Vote

About the Mass Clean Energy Center The Mass Clean Energy Center is a state economic development agency dedicated to accelerating the growth of the clean energy and climatetech sector across the Commonwealth to spur job creation, deliver statewide environmental benefits, increase affordability, and secure long-term economic opportunities for the people of Massachusetts.
text:
ROXBURY — The Healey-Driscoll Administration today awarded nearly $20 million in grants through the Mass Clean Energy Center (MassCEC) to grow the state’s clean energy and climatetech workforce. The awards were announced during an event at Roxbury Community College that brought together stakeholders from across the state, including community colleges, state agencies, employers, labor organizations, workforce partners, and legislators. The funding is expected to prepare over 5,500 residents for high-demand occupations that drive the state’s clean energy development and climate resilience efforts, bolstering Massachusetts’ innovation economy and tradition of skilled trades.

“Massachusetts is a leader in clean energy and climatetech, and we want more residents to benefit from the jobs and opportunities this growing industry is creating,” said Governor Maura Healey. “We're investing nearly $20 million to help more than 5,500 people get the skills and hands-on training they need to pursue good-paying careers. This is how we grow our economy, support our businesses and make sure Massachusetts workers are prepared for the jobs of today and tomorrow.”

“Connecting people to good jobs has to start with making sure the right training, equipment, and career opportunities are available to them,” said Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll. “These grants will help Massachusetts organizations meet people where they are, introducing adults of all ages to new career possibilities, and creating more pathways into the clean energy workforce.”

MassCEC's workforce development awards will support 77 awards across five programs: Equity Workforce Training Implementation; Climate-Critical Workforce Training; Equipment and Infrastructure; Climate-Critical Underrepresented Business Support; Students and Young Adults Equity Workforce Career Awareness and Training, and the Climate Service Corps.

The awards will expand training and upskilling opportunities for residents, provide hands-on career exposure for students and young adults, fund equipment and facility upgrades that strengthen training programs, and increase support for underrepresented businesses in the clean energy sector.

“Building out Massachusetts’ clean energy infrastructure requires a skilled workforce that can install, operate, and maintain these systems,” said Energy and Environmental Affairs Secretary Rebecca Tepper. “These grants will give training programs the equipment and resources they need to prepare workers for the demands of the industry and keep critical energy projects moving forward.”

“Clean energy and climatetech reduces energy costs and emissions. To build those solutions, we need a workforce that is ready to deliver. Our role is to strengthen the foundation of our workforce training system so that the residents and businesses it serves can grow together,” said Mass Clean Energy Center CEO Ben Downing.“These grants do that by helping organizations expand their reach, strengthen their programs, and open doors for more people to take part in Massachusetts’ clean energy industry.”

“As Massachusetts continues to lead in clean energy innovation, we need to make sure our workforce has the skills and opportunities to grow alongside this emerging economy,” said State Senator Jake Oliveira (D-Ludlow), Senate Chair of the Joint Committee on Labor and Workforce Development. “These investments are about more than preparing workers for the jobs of tomorrow. They're about creating pathways to good-paying, family-sustaining careers today, strengthening our skilled trades, and ensuring that opportunities reach every corner of the Commonwealth.”

“These investments show our commitment to preparing Massachusetts residents for the jobs of tomorrow while strengthening our clean energy and climatetech workforce,” said State Representative Paul McMurtry (D-Dedham), House Chair of the Joint Committee on Labor and Workforce Development. “These grants will create clear pathways to good-paying, high-demand careers by expanding training programs, upgrading facilities, giving young people hands-on experience, and increasing support for underrepresented communities.”

Equity Workforce Training Implementation grants fund the launch and growth of training pathways into high-demand roles, especially for residents of Environmental Justice communities and other underrepresented groups. text:
This is the first plant in the U.S .to build lower cost LFP batteries, under a license from Chinese battery maker CATL. But Ford stresses that it is running the plant, and has incorporated many of its processes.

Batteries are the most expensive parts of an electric vehicle. If you lower the battery cost, Clarke says you lower the cost of the EV.

“Not only are we focused on making the battery cost less money, making it affordable for our customers, but we are focused on using less battery.”

For taking reporters on a tour of the plant, which is so high tech that operators never touch the end product. They run machines that actually make the product to very precise tolerances.

It’s so clean that anybody walking in must wear gowns, masks, gloves and other coverings, and must go through an “air shower” to blow off the dust.

The process starts with raw materials, which are made into cathodes and anodes. Those are combined into something called “jelly rolls”--named for the shape used in early batteries. Those are combined into the cells. The cells are combined into packs. It’s all done on site.

Production is slow now, but the goal is to have forty cells per minute coming off of each of the two assembly lines.

“That puts us right there among the fastest LFP battery producers, outside China, in the world,” said plant manager Tracy Church.

“Eventually the plant will employ 1700 people. Church expects to have about 800 workers hired by the end of the year.

“Over 70 percent of the team members are from the local area.”

This is all part of Ford’s effort to build electric vehicles that are affordable, but also make a product. The company’s Louisville plant is being overhauled to make vehicles as part of Ford’s new Universal Electric Vehicle program.

When the Fathom electric pickup reaches the market next year it will be the first vehicle from that new program. It will have a sticker price of under 20 thousand dollars. Clarke says the lower priced batteries will enable Ford to include a lot of the features that customers want.

“We know customers want not just the long range and low cost, they want a big center display with high definition images. They want autonomy. They want BlueCruise in their vehicle. They want secure lockable storage.”

text:
NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Texas has resumed issuing air permits for data centers, state regulators said on Wednesday, after pausing the practice last month as part of the state's broader attempt to manage the server warehouses and their effects on the electrical grid, communities and the environment.

• The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality "has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations," TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said.

• Texas Governor Greg Abbott halted the connection of new data centers to the state electric grid in August and ordered an audit of the projects, rattling one of the world's fastest-growing hubs for data center development. Abbott followed up by temporarily blocking air permits for all data center projects.

• The air permit resumption came after the Texas grid operator notified the TCEQ that it had collected "community impact review" information for proposed data center projects, Lopez said.

• Abbott, a Republican, lost his reelection bid in this month's midterm elections to Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa, who has promised to impose a moratorium on data centers once in office in January.

• The most recent permitting decision may generate more pushback from incoming Texas Democratic lawmakers and politicians in the new year, analysts said.

• "TD Cowen sees Abbott's lame duck permitting push as likely to strengthen the Dem-stakeholder demand that Hinojosa take a firm stand, reducing hopes for a near-term policy agreement between Hinojosa and data center developers," the firm said in a note.

The facility operates stationary and portable concrete batch plants and associated material handling, crushing, and screening equipment to produce concrete blocks.

What: Public hearing on D.R. Allen & Son air quality permit

Location: Cumberland County Historic Courthouse, Courtroom No. 3

Address: 130 Gillespie St, Fayetteville

title: Illinois recognizes the need to move beyond natural gas, but utilities still control the alternatives
description:
Rising pipeline infrastructure costs are a major driver, raising an important question: Can Illinois meet customers’ energy needs without continuing to invest billions in traditional gas infrastructure?
Through its Future of Gas proceeding, the Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC) is exploring how cleaner alternatives to natural gas can help deliver affordable, reliable and safe energy.
For example, some Illinois gas utilities have proposed blending green hydrogen into existing gas pipelines, despite research commissioned by EDF showing that this approach is costly, inefficient and delivers minimal emissions reductions.
The Commission acknowledged that Illinois’ gas system must change to meet the state’s clean energy goals.
These alternatives could save money, reduce pollution and avoid locking customers into decades of additional gas infrastructure costs.
text:
Illinois households are paying more for natural gas service even as they use less gas. Residential gas bills have increased by roughly 8% annually over the past five years, while average household gas consumption has declined by about 26% since 2014. Rising pipeline infrastructure costs are a major driver, raising an important question: Can Illinois meet customers’ energy needs without continuing to invest billions in traditional gas infrastructure?

Through its Future of Gas proceeding, the Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC) is exploring how cleaner alternatives to natural gas can help deliver affordable, reliable and safe energy. Small-scale pilot projects can play an important role in this transition by testing promising solutions and evaluating their effectiveness before deploying them more widely. But not all proposed solutions are worth pursuing.

For example, some Illinois gas utilities have proposed blending green hydrogen into existing gas pipelines, despite research commissioned by EDF showing that this approach is costly, inefficient and delivers minimal emissions reductions. By contrast, electrifying buildings with efficient heat pumps offers far greater environmental benefits while using significantly less energy.

To clarify its authority over pilot projects, the ICC opened a separate proceeding. On October 29, the Commission issued a decision addressing seven questions about how pilots can be approved, funded and overseen. The decision recognizes the need for change but leaves a significant obstacle in place: Utilities largely retain control over which alternatives get tested, even when other approaches could better serve customers and communities.

A step forward, but not far enough

Environmental Defense Fund argued that Illinois regulators already have the authority to require utilities to explore alternatives that could lower costs, reduce pollution and limit unnecessary investments in gas infrastructure.

The Commission acknowledged that Illinois’ gas system must change to meet the state’s clean energy goals. But it concluded that it cannot require utilities to carry out pilot projects proposed by outside groups without utility support. It can approve projects utilities voluntarily propose or those specifically authorized by state law.

This creates a fundamental challenge: Gas utilities earn returns for shareholders by investing in infrastructure, giving them a financial incentive to continue investing in pipelines rather than exploring alternatives. As a result, promising solutions like energy-efficient heat pumps may never get tested, even if they could deliver greater benefits to customers.

Regulators can still require utilities to provide studies and planning information, giving them a way to scrutinize proposed investments and evaluate potential alternatives.

Why does this matter?

Imagine a neighborhood where aging gas pipelines need to be replaced. Rather than automatically investing in new pipelines, a utility could explore helping households switch to efficient electric heating or using a shared heating and cooling system that serves multiple buildings.

These alternatives could save money, reduce pollution and avoid locking customers into decades of additional gas infrastructure costs. Yet under the Commission’s decision, communities, local governments and clean energy advocates have limited ability to advance promising solutions without utility support.

Protecting customers and their wallets

EDF also pushed for stronger safeguards to ensure pilot projects deliver real benefits without leaving customers responsible for unnecessary costs. The Commission confirmed that utilities must meet existing standards before recovering pilot project costs from customers. Those costs must be reasonable and justified, and investments must support safe and reliable energy service.

However, the Commission stopped short of requiring utilities to establish clear measures of success before launching a project or rules for ending projects that aren’t working. Instead, it pointed to state legislation as a possible way to establish those protections. The decision also clarified several important points:

More flexibility: Regulators can consider certain pilot projects outside traditional utility rate cases.

Outside expertise: Utilities can partner with other organizations and companies to carry out approved projects.

Customer choice: Households cannot be denied natural gas service simply because an alternative is available through a pilot project.

Privacy protections: Customer information must remain protected, although certain data can be shared with consent or without identifying individual customers.

These are useful steps. But Illinois still needs a stronger approach to ensure promising alternatives receive a fair evaluation and customers benefit from the results.

What comes next?

title: Data Centers and Electricity Costs: Bad Assessment Leads to Bad Policy
description:
Critics argue that energy prices will explode as electricity demand from data centers grows in response to AI adoption.
Source: LBNL Retail Electricity Price Trends and Drivers: Data Update−2026 Edition Data centers are also not primary drivers of nominal price increases.
