Source: LBNL Retail Electricity Price Trends and Drivers: Data Update−2026 Edition Data centers are also not primary drivers of nominal price increases.
“Emergency” legislation to impose a moratorium on data center construction is therefore simply not necessary to protect Americans from rate increases from data centers.
text:
Following recent success in the U.S. midterm elections, multiple Democrats have renewed calls for federal legislation to halt construction of new data centers, driven in part by concerns about AI raising electricity costs for consumers. Critics argue that energy prices will explode as electricity demand from data centers grows in response to AI adoption. But the evidence to date does not support this view, and there are very good reasons to believe it won’t be true in the future either.

Electricity prices are up since 2010, but only in line with general inflation, as shown in Figure 1. In real terms, national electricity prices now are 6 percent lower (although that varies a lot by state – see discussion of Maine below).

Source: LBNL Retail Electricity Price Trends and Drivers: Data Update−2026 Edition

Data centers are also not primary drivers of nominal price increases. Electricity prices closely follow fuel prices, especially natural gas (as shown in Figure 2) which now powers 45 percent of U.S. electricity generation.

Source: LBNL Retail Electricity Price Trends and Drivers: Data Update−2026 Edition

Beyond fuel costs, utilities in many areas buy reliability through “capacity auctions,” where providers bid to supply grid systems with backup power. In the PJM Interconnection, the largest regional grid that covers 13 states, costs in the most recent auction aimed at ensuring sufficient future capacity to guarantee a reliable grid were up from approximately $60 per kWh in 2024 to over $300 per kWh in 2025. This spike did not come from planned new data centers. Prices reflect uncertainty: variable energy sources require more backup capacity, electricity demand has become less predictable, and volatile natural gas prices increase the cost of relying on gas peaker plants as the primary grid backup.

Utilities are also spending more on capital expenditures, up 13 percent each in 2023 and 2024, and by 23 percent in 2025. Some of that expense is driven by data centers, but costs have increased too: gas turbine prices are up almost 200 percent since 2019. And capex for transmission is also up, as utilities replace old equipment at current prices, harden infrastructure against natural disasters (e.g. wildfires), and respond to more damaging storms. New data centers account for only a small share of new transmission costs.

Costs also vary by region, and that helps to show the limited impact of data centers on prices. For example, electricity costs in Maine have risen very sharply, up 50-70 percent from 2021, among the biggest increases in the United States. But there are no significant data centers in Maine, and it seems unlikely that any will be built in the face of intense local opposition. Those increases have been driven by the cost of substantial storm damage in 2024-2025 and the need for subsequent infrastructure hardening, increased gas prices partly driven by growing competition for resources from export-oriented LNG development, and the cost of greening the grid, including attractive net metering rates for distributed solar power.

In short, data centers are a long way down the list of factors that caused recent nominal electricity price increases in the United States.

But what about the future? Will massive new data center overwhelm the grid?

Large cloud service providers (“hyperscalers”) and data center companies have announced more than 240 GW of new data centers to power the AI revolution, much planned for deployment by 2030. That’s approximately 20 percent of current U.S. electricity demand; without matching new supply, that suggests we could expect shortages and potentially dramatic price spikes.

But that conclusion is quite wrong. Electricity price hikes can be avoided without a moratorium or even a pause in data center construction, for four reasons.

First, the pace of data center construction will be slower than anticipated, and actual deployment will likely be smaller than announced.

▪ Capital crunch. Anthropic alone needs $900 billion to meet its needs; that’s challenging on the basis of ~$33 billion in revenues for the first nine months of 2026. . Even Google and Meta are taking on debt to pay for their commitments.

▪ Permits take time. Average time to acquire the necessary land use permits has been 6-18 months. Larger projects take longer.

▪ Design and construction takes 20-54 months, more for large projects especially given shortages of both people and materials).

▪ Grid connections take a long time. In the PMJ region, projects approved in 2025 had been in the queue for8 years. More time equals more cost, raising the capital burden.

Projected new data center deals fell about 50 percent between the 3rd and 4th quarters of 2025. Actual construction fell 6 percent year on year in 2025 to about 6GW.

As a result, the amount of energy built to power new data centers will be considerably lower than headline announcements suggest, and that new demand will take a lot longer to hit the grid.

Second, data centers can manage their demand. Electricity grids are designed to meet peak power demand, not average power demand, because they must ensure that customer needs will always be met. More peak demand equals more generation and more energy infrastructure, and massive new data centers appear to add to peak demand, as they seek to serve their own customers 24/7. Figure 1 shows that the California grid hits maximum utilization for only a few hours a year; most of the time there is plenty of spare capacity.

Source: CAISO Historical EMS Load

But in reality, demand peaks for only a few hours per year. The rest of the time, there is plenty of capacity available. So if data centers can manage their demands on the grid to avoid peaks, they can access plenty of power without increasing peak demand at all. In fact, they may even improve overall capacity utilization, which could reduce rates for existing ratepayers. Hyperscalers are taking steps to do exactly that.

Third, hyperscalers know they must bring their own power, often by placing those generating assets off the grid right where data centers are built (“behind the meter” or “BTM”). Most facilities will still need a grid connection for backup, but that’s not the same as depending on the grid for power 24/7. Grid-connected data centers can help with reliability, and BTM also helps avoid expensive transmission upgrades.

Fourth, utility contracts with data centers can be structured to protect existing ratepayers via “large load tariffs” (for new projects seeking 50MW of electricity or more). Options include:

▪ Data center funding for upfront costs such as engineering studies or power delivery infrastructure.

▪ Minimum contract periods (often 15 years).

▪ Minimum load guarantees (typically 85 percent of anticipated load), which apply even if the data center changes course and does not need that electricity.

▪ Defined ramp-up schedules so there are no sudden and unexpected hits on the grid.

▪ Exit fees in case a data center wants to exit the contract.

▪ Incentives such as faster interconnection to encourage demand management and BYOP.

▪ Hold harmless guarantees – some hyperscalers (e.g. Microsoft) have directly committed to ensuring that ratepayers will not pay the price for data center expansion.

▪ Higher rates for large loads.

These elements have to be implemented properly, and badly designed models like PJM’s capacity auctions have to be fixed, but these four key points mean that big new data centers can become a collaborative partner for electric grids, protecting existing ratepayers and managing the addition of new loads without adding to peak demand. None of this is theoretical – new contracts in Viginia, Ohio, and other states all include these elements. Over time, it seems likely that data centers will add a great deal of new generation, but that it won’t be paid for by other customers.

“Emergency” legislation to impose a moratorium on data center construction is therefore simply not necessary to protect Americans from rate increases from data centers. Concerns that data centers must drive up energy costs and potentially reduce reliability are misplaced; there are plenty of options to ensure a smooth path to growth. A national moratorium is also risky: it could bottleneck U.S. AI development, creating an opportunity for Chinese companies in particular to close the gap with American AI companies. And it could devastate the economics of the industry, frightening off the capital necessary to reach scale. Blocking the growth of a key industry on the basis of imaginary energy concerns is simply unnecessary.

text:
A new Forum publication picks 10 technologies that could help countries cut emissions and reduce their exposure to energy shocks.

Over the past four years, energy shortages and price spikes have exposed the vulnerability of countries heavily reliant on fossil fuels, forcing governments and companies to rethink where their power comes from.

At a corn-processing plant on Hungary’s Great Plain, part of the answer is a tank of salt.

KALL Ingredients, in Tiszapüspöki, can heat its production line with biomass, natural gas or a Heatcube – a tank of molten salt that stores electricity as heat. The Heatcube charges when power is cheap and plentiful, then releases the stored heat as steam when needed, at a lower cost than gas.

This plug-and-play system is designed to supply more than 30 gigawatt-hours of heat and cut up to 8,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions a year.

“Sustainability is central to our operations,” says Maarten Welten, managing director of KALL Ingredients. The Heatcube offers “a stable and cost-effective supply of clean process heat, helping us reduce energy costs and move towards full reliance on renewable energy,” he adds.

Morten Bülow, chief executive of Kyoto Group, the Norwegian developer of the Heatcube, says demand for such solutions is growing. Businesses still want to cut emissions but also need reliable, affordable energy. The Heatcube addresses both. “If you can kill two birds with one stone, you also get higher security of supply,” says Bülow.

It can also help the grid work better, Bülow argues, by shifting electricity consumption to quieter, cheaper periods. “What we would like to do is use the nighttime, and stay off the road in the daytime, when prices are high and the roads are busy.”

Why energy security is changing the case for clean energy

The World Economic Forum's (WEF) Top 10 Emerging Technologies for Planetary Health: Energy Edition picks 10 technologies it says could ease pressure on the planet and make energy systems more reliable.

All 10 solutions, developed with Frontiers and chosen by an 18-member committee of experts from 10 countries and six regions, have a credible path to deployment by 2030.

We have grouped the 10 by their role in the energy system, covering generation, storage, grid coordination and building. The report sorts them differently, by the bottleneck each addresses.

Some replace a scarce material with a common one, and others close the gap between when the grid generates power and when it is needed.

These technologies cannot be pulled apart. “Power systems are systems,” says Doug Arent, a senior fellow at the World Resources Institute and a committee member. “All the different components need to advance and the grid itself, which connects them, also needs to advance.”

For Ann Mettler, president of Catalyse Europe and a former head of the European Commission’s in-house think tank, recent shocks have changed the logic of the transition. After the 2022 gas shortages, Europe diversified its fossil fuel supplies but largely preserved the existing system.

In 2026, war in the Middle East disrupted oil and gas flows through the Strait of Hormuz, triggering what the IEA called the largest supply disruption in history. The case for clean energy now rests on security, sovereignty and cost, Mettler argues: “These technologies provide the alternative.”

The emerging technologies changing how we generate, store and use energy

On generation, the report highlights technologies that produce more energy from clean sources. Conventional silicon solar cells can convert no more than about 29% of sunlight into electricity in theory. Tandem cells add a thin layer of perovskite on top and can break that limit without needing more land. The report puts their realistic ceiling at 42–43%, but the panels must still prove they last about 25 years outdoors, longer than today’s ageing tests can confirm.

Floating offshore wind reaches deep waters where fixed turbines cannot go, unlocking some 80% of the world’s offshore wind resource, according to the Global Wind Energy Council. It costs roughly 1.5 to 2 times as much as fixed-bottom wind today, with forecasts of the two converging by around 2030 to 2032 if platform designs are standardised. Modular nuclear reactors offer round-the-clock clean power using standard factory parts, with the promise of cheaper production as it scales.

On storage, the report foregrounds a crucial mismatch: as wind and solar spread, hours of nearly free power have become common. Storage captures that surplus for use when needed through industrial heat batteries, such as the Heatcube, batteries built from sodium, zinc or iron, and next-generation lithium batteries with greater energy density.

However, the report warns, dependencies can shift rather than disappear. Almost all sodium-ion cells are still made in China, and relying on a single supplier carries some of the same risks as relying on imported fuel.

For grid connections, the report highlights subsea high-voltage cables that move electricity from areas of surplus to those in need.

Viking Link opened in late 2023, connecting Denmark and England beneath the North Sea to balance supply and demand. Tunisia and Italy have also contracted the first subsea cable between Europe and North Africa, potentially bringing Tunisian solar power to European markets. The report also flags the risk. A damaged cable or converter station can take a large amount of power offline, and repair ships and replacement equipment are limited.

Virtual power plants coordinate the grid from the other end, linking batteries, electric-vehicle chargers and smart thermostats so operators can draw on them collectively, rather than relying on extra power stations. “If you aggregate tens of thousands or millions of them, you get to the size of those large power stations,” Arent says. Octopus Energy in Britain runs a prominent example, while US company Voltus has agreed to supply Google with up to a gigawatt of capacity this way.

The report also highlights technologies that turn buildings into power sources. Building-integrated photovoltaics incorporate solar panels into roofs, façades and windows, as seen at London’s King’s Cross station and Copenhagen International School, whose façade features 12,000 panels. The opportunity is large because cities occupy just 2–3% of the world’s land but account for 70–80% of its energy use. The report adds a financial catch. Only 13% of these projects make sense on electricity savings alone, rising to 62% once the roofing or cladding they replace is counted as a saving.

Finally, the report looks at lower-carbon cement, a priority given that the material accounts for around 8% of global CO2 emissions. Calcined-clay limestone cement (LC3) replaces up to about half of the clinker, cement’s most carbon-intensive ingredient, with clay heated at a lower temperature and finely ground limestone. The report says this can cut emissions by up to 40%.

In Colombia, Cementos Argos supplied around 4,650 tonnes for DAVIarena, a new events venue near Medellín, avoiding an estimated 1,200 tonnes of CO2 emissions across the cement and concrete used, according to the company.

How lower-carbon cement can make construction more sustainable

For María Isabel Cárdenas, Argos’ sustainability senior director, the technologies that last are those that deliver on every front. “We work across three dimensions: environmental, social and, of course, economic,” she says. “We know that long-term sustainability also depends on economic viability. Without it, even solutions with strong environmental and social benefits can be difficult to sustain over time.”

Many routes to cleaner cement, such as capturing carbon at the plant, are scientifically proven but not yet commercial, she adds, especially in countries without Europe’s subsidies and research support. Calcined clay, by contrast, is “more applicable, closer to hand” and delivers a cement that is “strong, durable” and fit for purpose.

Argos has made calcined clay cement at its Rio Claro plant since about 2020. The site pulls three levers that Carlos Augusto Orozco, Argos’ cementitious solutions R&D manager, considers “key” for the industry, namely volume, logistics and quality. The plant sits next to a viable clay deposit in Colombia’s Central Cordillera, far from the ports and coal plants that supply alternatives such as slag and fly ash.

Clay is found across much of the world, especially near the Equator, putting the technology within reach of many fast-growing economies in Africa, South Asia and Latin America, where much of the world’s future construction will happen. But its success depends on investment in calcination plants and a mindset shift among concrete producers, in what Orozco describes as “a very conservative” industry.

Other challenges remain. Low-carbon cement “has never had a chance to prove itself”, says Mettler, and policymakers are wary of approving materials whose performance over decades is not yet known. The report notes that LC3 has already outperformed ordinary Portland cement in early strength tests, but that testing and buyer confidence remain key bottlenecks.

Who gets the benefits

The report also tests each technology on who benefits, and the answer is rarely everyone.

A solar façade can lower a building’s electricity bill, but tenants will not see their share of the savings unless a lease or regulation distributes them. An offshore wind farm may create jobs, but they will not necessarily go to the fishing communities that use those waters unless local hiring is built into the contract.

Cheaper cement does not automatically mean cheaper housing either, because savings may not pass down the value chain.

What policy and investment still need to do

China, Mettler argues, saw the link between energy and security early. Like Europe, it has few oil and gas reserves of its own, so it treated the energy transition as a matter of security and sovereignty as much as climate, conceiving it as a system rather than a collection of technologies.

Policy is beginning to follow suit elsewhere. The European Commission’s Electrification Action Plan proposes cutting network charges for industrial users who shift consumption to off-peak hours, narrowing the price gap that has long favoured gas.

In Brazil, net metering helped unlock more than 50 gigawatts of small-scale solar, much of it rooftop, according to the Brazilian Solar Photovoltaic Energy Association (ABSOLAR). In Colombia, the cement standard sets performance targets rather than fixed recipes, says Orozco, so producers can use as much clay as they like, as long as the cement performs.

Mettler argues that governments also need better evidence. Most energy systems, she says, are “unbelievably unproductive.” She proposes a new measure, resource productivity, to assess how effectively countries use existing infrastructure. She also calls for “a circular economy but on steroids” to recover and reuse critical materials and reduce import dependence.

Habits may be the final barrier, for businesses and consumers alike. “If you go to a regular factory that’s been running on gas for the last 100 years, nobody thinks there’s any alternative,” says Bülow. Homebuyers, Cárdenas adds, focus on a house’s appearance and location, “but not necessarily on the attributes of its materials.”

Yet the choice between clean and cheap energy is getting less stark. Several of these technologies could lower costs as well as emissions, though none is guaranteed to. The question now is whether policy can keep up.

text:
Many lithium-ion batteries in cars and consumer electronics already contain a bit of silicon oxide to boost energy density. Sila, and competitors like Group14 Technologies and Nexeon, are making advanced silicon-carbon materials that incorporate higher levels of silicon, which further increases storage capacity.

The research firm Benchmark Mineral Intelligence estimates that, by 2035, engineered anode materials with high silicon content could reach about 3% of the total anode market, measured by gigawatt-hours.

Over the last several years, many US battery materials projects have been canceled or delayed because of the slow growth in the electric vehicle market. But silicon anode firms have maintained their momentum.

The deal with Panasonic follows a commitment Sila announced in August for a $1.4 billion loan from the US Department of Defense and a $300 million private fundraising round announced in July.

Nexeon raised $70 million in August. In October, Group14 raised $169 million to finance a plant in Spain. The firm started production at a plant in South Korea earlier this year.

So far, these companies are getting the most traction in markets that require high performance. For example, Group14’s material is already used in batteries for electric supercars and heavy-lift cargo drones.

Parker says silicon’s high power output and fast charge rate make the material attractive for batteries that quickly charge and discharge to smooth out data centers’ fluctuating energy consumption. “The same thing we’re putting in the air is what needs to be in data centers, but for slightly different reasons,” he says.

In March, Panasonic said it was considering a plan to convert some car battery manufacturing lines in Kansas and Japan to make batteries for data centers. Sila says its material will go into Panasonic’s US-made batteries across its portfolio of applications.

While customers in performance-sensitive markets may be willing to pay a premium, the applications are low volume, says Sam Adham, head of battery value chain research at the consulting firm CRU International. The real prize is still mass-market electric cars.

In 2022, Sila announced plans to put its silicon anode materials into a luxury SUV made by Mercedes-Benz by the middle of the decade. Now, Sila says Mercedes has backed away from that project. Sila says it’s still working with Mercedes generally and expects its material to eventually go into other cars.

Adham says the automotive market is still difficult to reach. The fact that silicon expands during charging remains a technical barrier for car batteries. In addition, advances in conventional lithium-ion batteries that give them longer ranges and faster charging speeds are eroding the advantages that advanced silicon-based materials can provide.

“They’ve done it in wearables and consumer electronics, but it has not really worked in cars,” Adham says. “They ran into technical challenges.”

text:
The US energy storage market has crossed 200 GWh of cumulative installed capacity, as battery deployments continue to expand across all segments, as per a new report. The total 215.9 GWh includes 14.3 GWh of new capacity in Q3 2026, taking installations during the first nine months of the year to 48.3 GWh.

The figures are from the U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026 (ESMO), released by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.

According to the report, utility-scale projects accounted for the bulk of Q3 installations, adding 12.2 GWh. Three GW-scale projects came online during the quarter, supporting growth in the utility-scale segment. Commercial and industrial (C&I) storage contributed 1.3 GWh, while residential systems added 746 MWh.

The report said battery energy storage system (BESS) installations in Q3 at 14.3 GWh remained flat quarter-on-quarter (QoQ), but increased 23% year-on-year (YoY) for the first three quarters of 2026.

Overall US installations were up 20% YoY during the January-September period. Texas led utility-scale storage deployment through Q3, adding 12.3 GWh. Arizona followed with 7.7 GWh, while California recorded 6.8 GWh.

The report also highlighted the impact of solar and energy storage deployment on electricity prices. According to SEIA analysis, the growth of these technologies helped reduce average wholesale electricity prices by 42% in Texas and 51% in California between summer 2021 and summer 2026 (see Solar & Storage Cut Wholesale Electricity Prices In CAISO & ERCOT).

Eleven states had already exceeded their previous annual energy storage installation records by the end of Q3, despite three months remaining in 2026. These included Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama, and Illinois.

As states move from targets to centralized procurements, Benchmark Minerals Senior Analyst Pete Tillotson says energy storage pipelines are growing across utility mandates and bulk capacity contracts, thanks to “investment appetite and flexibility requirements”.

In 2026, analysts project the annual installed BESS capacity of the US to reach 73.8 GWh, up 26% from 59 GWh installed in 2025 which was an increase of 30% over the previous year, comprising both utility and behind-the-meter (BTM) installations. This implies around 26 GWh of new additions in Q4 2026.

SEIA and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence have raised their forecast for cumulative installations by 2030 by 3.7% to 708 GWh across grid-connected and behind-the-meter (BTM) applications. Annual installations are projected to exceed 129 GWh by 2030.

Along with installations, domestic manufacturing is also seeing an uptick as per the report. Ultim Cells of LGES and General Motors began Lithium-ion Phosphate (LFP) commenced cell production for stationary storage in Tennessee in July 2026, while Samsung SDI opened LFP production at its StarPlus Energy facility in Indiana in October. This brought the total US battery cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, a 50% increase, according to the report.

Battery module manufacturing capacity exceeded 109 GWh following the opening of an additional facility in Q3. Analysts forecast that LFP will account for 92% of lithium-ion BESS deployments in 2026, up from 77% in 2023. Lithium-ion batteries are expected to account for over 97% of all BESS installations in 2026.

Other technologies, including flow batteries, sodium-ion and lead acid batteries, continue to lag behind lithium-ion. Recently US flow battery and sodium-ion cell manufacturer ESS Tech filed for relief under Chapter 7 (see US Battery Maker ESS Tech Files For Chapter 7 Bankruptcy).

The complete report is available for purchase on Benchmark Mineral Intelligence website.

Meanwhile on the policy front, following the results of the mid-term elections in the US, SEIA said more than 300 solar and storage companies recently urged Congressional leaders to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA).

The industry says the legislation could accelerate storage deployment, reduce project costs, lower prices, and improve access to affordable electricity.

title: Ford Starts U.S. LFP Battery Cell Production - Briefs Finance
description:
What happened in Marshall, Michigan Ford said Wednesday it has started U.S. battery cell output for its next wave of electric vehicles using technology licensed from China's CATL.
Ford framed this as a step toward wider use of lithium iron phosphate cells - the lower cost LFP chemistry - in U.S. vehicles.
The automaker said moving faster on throughput will help lower battery costs.
As the largest producer of U.S. vehicles, Ford has consistently highlighted its American heritage, employment, and factories while both the Biden and Trump administrations press for more domestic production.
The bottom line: Ford is anchoring its next EV wave to lower cost LFP cells and a licensed design from the world's biggest cell maker.
text:
What happened in Marshall, Michigan

Ford said Wednesday it has started U.S. battery cell output for its next wave of electric vehicles using technology licensed from China's CATL. The first cells rolled out last month at the Marshall complex, and they are already shipping for prototype builds of the Fathom small electric pickup that CEO Jim Farley has positioned against Tesla and Chinese competitors.

Ford framed this as a step toward wider use of lithium iron phosphate cells - the lower cost LFP chemistry - in U.S. vehicles. The chemistry was developed in the U.S. but reached commercial scale largely in China. Alan Clarke, who oversees advanced development projects as a vice president at Ford, said the CATL license enables Ford to introduce the low-cost chemistry in the United States as rapidly as possible. While guiding visitors through the plant on Tuesday, Clarke said, "If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible." "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells."

Capacity, pace, and the ramp

Ford says the highly automated Marshall operation should be able to turn out 40 battery cells per minute, equating to roughly 20 gigawatt-hours a year for its EV lineup and energy storage business. That goal is below the company's earlier plan that called for up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually, reflecting an EV slowdown at Ford and across the sector. The company also said the site has room to add capacity if needed.

Ford remains at an early phase of certifying its processes and plans to ramp cell production next year ahead of the Fathom's expected launch in the fourth quarter of 2027. The automaker said moving faster on throughput will help lower battery costs.

When new technologies reshape industries, stay grounded with the free Market Briefs newsletter that explains markets clearly every day

The political backdrop and why it matters

In Michigan, the decision to build CATL-licensed batteries drew rebukes from certain members of Congress as well as U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who objected to Ford's relationship with the Chinese battery giant. In September, Duffy sent CEO Jim Farley a letter expressing "profound concern" about Ford's relationships with Chinese companies that he said could harm the automaker and the U.S. auto sector. The White House a day later commended the company for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

As the largest producer of U.S. vehicles, Ford has consistently highlighted its American heritage, employment, and factories while both the Biden and Trump administrations press for more domestic production. The bottom line: Ford is anchoring its next EV wave to lower cost LFP cells and a licensed design from the world's biggest cell maker. For your portfolio, watch certification progress, the ramp toward 20 GWh, any capacity add-ons, and whether Fathom lands its late 2027 debut on schedule.

text:
The European Commission, the EU’s executive branch, has approved an amendment to German state aid schemes, allowing the country to combine electricity subsidies for energy-intensive companies this year, it said in a press release.

Lower electricity costs could accelerate the transition towards a net-zero economy and help industry introduce clean production processes.

Companies can now receive relief through both the so-called industry power price scheme, and the compensation scheme which covers their indirect emission costs incurred under the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). Both schemes are designed to keep European industry competitive despite high energy prices and fierce competition from countries with less ambitious climate policy, but the EU initially rejected Germany’s pleas to combine subsidy packages. Today’s decision also makes it easier for German companies to apply.

“The price of electricity is a key factor in determining where companies will produce and invest in the future,” said Katherina Reiche, German economy and energy minister. “In Brussels, we have secured an agreement allowing particularly energy-intensive companies to combine the industrial electricity price and electricity price compensation from 2026. This will provide greater relief, particularly for key industries such as chemicals, steel, glass and battery cell manufacturing.”

German steel industry association WV Stahl welcomed that companies in the sector could combine the subsidies, but it added: "A solution limited to this year does not yet provide planning security. But that is precisely what our steel companies need if they are to have genuine prospects for the future in Germany." The lobby group called on the government to implement "further, long-term measures".

Germany could spend an extra 1.6 billion euros per year between 2026 and 2030 as a result of this decision, the Commission said. A recent analysis from consultancy Aurora Energy Research suggested that the subsidies could cost the government one billion euros more per year than planned because wholesale electricity prices are higher than expected.

text:
Springfield, Mass.-headquartered Eversource Energy and the University of Massachusetts Amherst on Nov. 12 renewed a non-binding memorandum of understanding to cut campus energy use, lower greenhouse gas emissions, and connect students with cooperative study and internship opportunities.

The three-year agreement, which runs through 2028, continues their decade-long partnership, which also supports the university’s carbon mitigation goals, while helping the university manage its overall energy costs.

“Over the past 12 years, our partnership with UMass Amherst has demonstrated what can be achieved when organizations work together toward shared energy and sustainability goals,” said Tilak Subrahmanian, vice president of energy efficiency and electric mobility at Eversource.

“This renewed agreement builds on that momentum, creating new opportunities to improve energy efficiency, reduce peak demand, and advance the university’s decarbonization goals in a cost-effective manner,” Subrahmanian added. “Together, we look forward to supporting innovative projects that will help create a more resilient and sustainable campus for years to come while also helping the university manage its energy costs.”

Specifically, the agreement includes joint efforts to maximize energy efficiency on new construction and major renovation projects, supported by Eversource incentives through the Mass Save® program. This is the third agreement signed by the university and Eversource since 2014.

Working with Eversource over the last 12 years, the university said it has accumulated annual electrical use savings of 34,000,000 kWh at the campus, the equivalent of taking roughly 3,100 homes worth of electricity off the grid.

The campus also reduced summer peak electrical loads by 3,950 kW through cumulative efficiency upgrades.

Among the partnership’s notable projects are the new Computer Science Laboratories and Sustainable Engineering Laboratories, served by the newly constructed North Energy Exchange Center and its 640-ton-ground-loop heat-pump system.

By connecting both facilities to a shared district energy loop rather than constructing separate geothermal systems for each building, UMass Amherst is improving efficiency while reducing infrastructure costs, according to Eversource.

Other efforts under the partnership have focused on testing and implementing cutting-edge energy and sustainability technologies, by converting buildings from fossil fuels to electric power, upgrading older buildings to operate more efficiently, and optimizing cooling systems to make laboratory space more sustainable.

“Renewing our strategic partnership with Eversource will support the university’s commitment to sustainability and enable further emissions reductions through the 2050 target year set by the commonwealth,” said Andrew Mangels, vice chancellor for administration and finance. “We are proud to have reduced our carbon emissions as of 2025 by more than 20 percent, an example of the shared commitment of the university and Eversource.

“Importantly, our partnership also benefits the university’s bottom line, helping to ensure we can meet our clean energy goals in a financially sustainable manner,” Mangels said.

Eversource and UMass Amherst are also exploring ways to reduce the campus’s electricity demand during periods of peak grid use through demand response initiatives, battery and thermal energy storage, and enhanced building management controls.

The renewed agreement also supports workforce development and the university’s broader transportation goals.

Eversource also said it will help connect UMass students with available cooperative study and internship opportunities, and the partners will collaborate on UMass Amherst’s electric mobility roadmap by continuing to install EV charging stations to reduce carbon emissions from fleet and personal vehicles.

description:

Along with data centers, BAAJA would incentivize development of energy systems deemed both clean and dirty, including gas pipelines and solar projects.
"Voters emphatically rejected AI data centers, delivering a Democratic majority – then Senate Democrats turned around & voted for an AI bailout," wrote Tlaib on X.
It's also strained American energy infrastructure and communities, and forced ratepayers to grapple with elevated electric bills.

text:
Down to the wire, Republicans, industry groups and some Democrats are throwing their weight behind a permitting reform bill that targets the issues that defined the midterm elections: data centers, energy and affordability.

Seventy senators voted Monday to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA, which faces a final Senate vote and a divided House with little time to spare before the new Democratic majority kicks in.

↑ X

Embed code copied to clipboard

Your browser does not support HTML5 video.

NOW PLAYING What The Midterm Shift Means For Oil And Gas Markets

Supporters of the bill say it streamlines new grid infrastructure, generation projects and mines to meet soaring energy demand and lower inflated prices. Opponents highlight how BAAJA weakens bedrock environmental protections and reviews, limits community engagement on nearby projects, and accelerates the unpopular artificial intelligence buildout right after voters resoundingly rejected it.

Why Investors Should Care

BAAJA is an attempt to rationalize what has thus far been an ad hoc scramble to power the surge in computing demand — created first by bitcoin mining and then compounded by the rise of AI.

Shares of bitcoin miners-turned-data center operators, names like Iren (IREN) and Tetrawulf (WULF), have been hard hit by fears of waning AI compute demand. A broad group of suppliers of power equipment, including GE Vernova (GE) and Caterpillar (CAT), also felt the bite of investors' concerns.

Makers of chips and memory, meanwhile, face an uncertain slowdown in demand. At the top of that heap, Nvidia (NVDA) reported that it carries $118 billion worth of financial guarantees tied to AI infrastructure. That was up $9.5 billion from the prior quarter, and makes the company vulnerable to client project cancellations, delays and cost hikes.

The largest hyperscalers aren't as likely to have their data center projects threatened. But smaller players, particularly middlemen neoclouds like CoreWeave (CRWV), have fallen sharply under heavy debt loads and unclear outlooks.

The BAAJA legislation attempts to reconcile the large part of that outlook tied to supply, demand and pricing of electrical power.

The bill also makes way for some nascent efforts to modernize the grid and guard ratepayers from demand peaks. It forces grid operators to allow distributed energy networks within 18 months, expanding the virtual power plant market for players such as Tesla (TSLA).

'Larger Increases For Fossil Fuels'

"This is fuel neutral," said Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer. "We truly do need whatever fuel we can use at any particular spot to generate electricity at a good cost," he added.

Along with data centers, BAAJA would incentivize development of energy systems deemed both clean and dirty, including gas pipelines and solar projects. But one report finds potentially lopsided benefits for oil companies.

A Purdue University report predicts the bill will boost energy company revenues and jobs, "with larger increases for fossil fuels." It estimates BAAJA will raise greenhouse gas emissions and "domestic mortality attributable to air pollution from fossil fuels."

'Voters Emphatically Rejected AI'

At least five current House Democrats oppose the bill, including Reps. Rashida Tlaib, Jared Huffman, Adelita Grijalva, Summer Lee and Melanie Stansbury, according to The Hill.

"Voters emphatically rejected AI data centers, delivering a Democratic majority – then Senate Democrats turned around & voted for an AI bailout," wrote Tlaib on X. "They advanced a 'permitting reform' bill that'll allow Big Tech to poison our communities while doing nothing to bring down utility costs."

Nationwide, Americans voted during the midterm elections to restrict data centers in 44 out of 45 ballot measures. Up ballot, they also crushed pro-data center reelection bids, adding to the market pressure already roiling the debt-saddled stocks of the AI boom.

'A Better Day' May Never Get Here

One of the House Democrats supporting the bill, Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, said it's "not a bad deal," and it could be all Congress can manage under President Donald Trump. "You may look for a better day down the road, and then that day never gets here," Gonzalez told The Hill.

When it comes to passing energy legislation, the Democrats could instead try to negotiate a bill that's better aligned with environmental and tribal organizations once they take control of Congress.

Passing permitting reform in the Senate would still take 60 votes. Democrats would need some Republican backers, and for the next two years, they also face Trump's veto.

$44 A Year By 2035

Republican Rep. Harriet Hageman has called BAAJA "one of those compromise bills that benefits everyone." She added, "You don't have affordability unless you have reliable and affordable energy."

The AI infrastructure boom has propelled GDP growth and electricity demand. It's also strained American energy infrastructure and communities, and forced ratepayers to grapple with elevated electric bills.

A midpoint projection from Rhodium group shows the legislation could save Americans around $44 a year on their electric bills by 2035.

Changes To The National Historic Preservation Act

The 494-page package would make building all sorts of new power infrastructure speedier and easier through reforms to permitting laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.

Ira Matt, executive director of the National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Offices, blasted the proposed changes to the NHPA in a message to the group's members. "What began as a termination-era approach of cutting tribal nations out has shifted to an assimilation-era tactic of telling us how and when we can participate, what matters to our cultures, and which harms we must accept," he wrote, according to Heatmap.news.

Free Tacos

Among the industry groups backing the bill, the American Petroleum Institute reportedly handed out free tacos around the Capitol building with signage that read, "Pass permitting reform. Lower energy costs. Brighter Opportunities."

description:

text:
The U.S. energy storage industry installed 14.3 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of new capacity in the third quarter, according to the U.S. Energy Storage Market Outlook Q4 2026 (ESMO) produced by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.

The third quarter numbers bring total installations in the first nine months of 2026 to 48.3 Gwh, up 20 percent year-over-year. U.S. energy storage capacity installed has now exceeded 200 GWh to date as grid operators, utilities and energy buyers turn to storage to lower energy costs and strengthen grid reliability.

Further, the outlook for energy storage continues to strengthen, with the report increasing its 2030 cumulative U.S. deployment forecast by 3.7 percent to 708 GWh across grid and BTM.

Texas led the nation in utility-scale storage deployment through Q3, adding 12.3 GWh of capacity. Arizona and California followed with 7.7 GWh and 6.8 GWh, respectively. Recent SEIA analysis shows that rapid growth in solar and energy storage helped drive down average wholesale electricity prices by 42 percednt in Texas and 51 percent in California from summer 2021 to summer 2026. Also, 11 states surpassed their previous annual energy storage installation records in Q3, even with three months remaining in 2026. Those 11 states are Colorado, Massachusetts, Utah, Michigan, Georgia, Mississippi, Virginia, Iowa, Montana, Alabama and Illinois.

“States are moving from targets to centralized procurements,” Pete Tillotson, senior analyst at Benchmark Minerals, said. “Across utility mandates and bulk capacity contracts, energy storage pipelines are growing as a result of both investment appetite and flexibility requirements.”

Utility-scale projects accounted for the vast majority of Q3 installations, with 12.2 GWh deployed, followed by 1.3 GWh of commercial and industrial storage, and 746 MWh of residential storage. U.S storage manufacturing continues to accelerate, as a new battery cell manufacturing facility opened in Tennessee in July. In October, a new cell manufacturing facility opened in Indiana, bringing total cell manufacturing capacity to 92.4 GWh, a 50 percent increase.

The U.S solar and storage industry is urging lawmakers to send the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) to the President’s desk.

“Voters made it clear that they want lower prices, and the growing deployment of energy storage is helping make that happen. We’re urging Congress to pass BAAJA to build out America’s energy infrastructure and put downward pressure on prices,” SEIA CEO Tim Pawlenty said.

Last week, more than 300 solar and storage companies sent a letter to Congressional leadership urging swift passage of BAAJA. The legislation will accelerate energy storage deployment, reduce project costs, and expand access to lower cost, reliable electricity for households and businesses.

name: American Energy
title: A Message to Data Centers Going Off-Grid: Do Better | Third Way
description:
Americans are deeply concerned about the rapid development of AI data centers, with impacts on energy and water among their greatest worries.
Many data centers are getting built alongside high-emission natural gas infrastructure to quickly and fully power their compute needs.
It is time for data centers to do better.
Going Off-Grid Doesn’t Eliminate Costs for the Public Electricity equipment costs are skyrocketing, and supplies are tightening.
And while data centers aren’t the cause of this shortage, their off-grid power solutions are making it worse and more expensive.
text:
Americans are deeply concerned about the rapid development of AI data centers, with impacts on energy and water among their greatest worries. But instead of putting forward real fixes, developers often turn to less-than-optimal solutions to power their facilities–solutions that don’t address the public’s frustrations with energy costs, water use, and pollution.

Many data centers are getting built alongside high-emission natural gas infrastructure to quickly and fully power their compute needs. While grid operators, utilities, policymakers, and supply chains may not be responding quickly enough to deliver cleaner, grid-connected power that meets the AI industry’s business objectives, this alternative approach is unsustainable and carries tremendous downsides.

It is quickly depleting already-short supplies of electricity equipment, materials, and labor, leaving other energy customers in the lurch. It is prioritizing natural gas over a diversified energy portfolio that can protect against market fluctuations and lower emissions. And while most off-grid developers say they intend to connect to the grid in the future, they are not sufficiently planning for the gigawatt-scale impact their data centers, new supply additions, and the industry writ large will have on the system and economics affecting all electricity users.

Certainly, policymakers must address interconnection processes, permitting bureaucracy, and energy policy uncertainty that push some data center developers toward subpar methods of securing power. But because of its intensive electricity demand and proximity to everyday communities, this industry has a unique responsibility to mitigate and avoid its own impacts.

It is time for data centers to do better.

Going Off-Grid Doesn’t Eliminate Costs for the Public

Electricity equipment costs are skyrocketing, and supplies are tightening. Critical components such as turbines, transformers, and switchgear have increased by roughly 50% over the last five years. And while data centers aren’t the cause of this shortage, their off-grid power solutions are making it worse and more expensive.

Data centers require a lot of power and can’t afford to go dark. Hyperscale facilities need more than 15 times as much electrical equipment as a standard large load. And without the reliability offered by the grid, data centers using on-site electricity need roughly 50% more equipment to support local integration, stabilization, and management than a grid-connected facility.

As data center developers build out their own energy supply, they are outcompeting utilities for the electricity equipment needed for standard grid operations, maintenance, and investment. Consider a utility procuring equipment to replace turbines in an aging power plant, to harden the local distribution network to withstand storms, and to install a major high-voltage transmission line to alleviate congestion.

What might have cost a utility $100M in 2021 could now cost upwards of $150M. This will affect everyday customers.

These equipment prices are just one example of the rising costs that come with aggressive off-grid power and surging demand. Everything that goes into building and maintaining an electricity system–minerals, equipment, labor–will become more and more expensive as unprecedented demand drives up costs. It will be families and businesses connected to the grid, not tech companies, that bear those added costs.

The Risks of a Gas-Heavy Strategy

Data centers are, by and large, opting to power their facilities with natural gas because it provides a stable baseload power source and the US has large domestic reserves. While natural gas is, and will continue to be, an important part of the US electricity mix, it is not immune to supply and price shocks.

The data center industry accounts for half of forecasted load growth, and favoring gas power so heavily puts long-term diversification at risk. Why does energy supply diversification matter? Increased reliance on gas could put upward pressure on energy prices and make the US energy system more vulnerable to global market fluctuations.

Building large amounts of less efficient, single-cycle gas-fired generation increases demand for the same fuel that supplies much of America’s power, industrial, and home heating needs. Whether that demand raises prices for other consumers–and by how much–will depend on how quickly production and pipeline capacity can respond.

Cost isn’t the only risk of a gas-focused energy strategy. The public is concerned about impacts on water and air, and rightly so. These co-located gas power systems will contribute to local pollution, worsen air quality, and use substantial amounts of water. Natural gas may be better than backup diesel generators, but it still contributes to a data center industry that is moving the country’s emissions in the wrong direction.

Instead of using the grid more efficiently and investing aggressively in cleaner energy, a diversified energy supply strategy, and grid infrastructure that benefits everyone, data centers are relying on an outdated, fossil-fuel-first power mix to serve their own needs.

What Doing Better Looks Like

Companies will continue to invest in natural gas power, and that’s OK. Where it becomes a problem is when gas is the overwhelming energy source, with little diversity in the portfolio. Similarly, it’s OK for data center developers to pursue interim solutions to power facilities while the grid catches up, as long as their plans account for what the larger system ultimately needs. It is understandable that companies want to protect commercially sensitive and proprietary data, but they still need to provide sufficient information to planners and the public to assess the impacts of development in their communities.

The tech industry has capital, an innovation mindset, and technology that can purportedly solve intractable problems. No one is suggesting it will be easy to prioritize diversification over speed to power, to better plan across fragmented power systems and market structures, and be more transparent, but hyperscalers can apply their considerable resources to contribute to a more efficient, affordable, reliable, and clean grid. If the tech industry wants to show the public it intends to “do better” on its energy and resource impacts, the following guidelines are a good place to start.

Be good grid stewards. Don’t overbuild high-emission, lower-efficiency generation. Even if it eventually connects to the grid, it will lock us into a suboptimal resource mix. Instead, work with states, grid operators, and utilities to invest in capacity additions and transmission upgrades that align with their development objectives. Commit to demand flexibility and power management tools that maximize energy use during low-demand periods to more efficiently use existing power plants and backup generation, shave peak demand, and alleviate pressure on the grid during emergencies.

Pay your real fair share. Cover both the costs to power a facility and the indirect costs that the scale and speed of data center development are having on energy prices. This would include the rising costs and competition for equipment, fuel, labor, etc.

Pay to expand technology adoption. Prioritize investment in commercially available clean generation, storage, and grid-enhancing technologies. Increase the investments many tech companies are already making to commercialize advanced nuclear, geothermal, hydrogen, carbon capture, long-duration storage, demand-side management, and advanced transmission technologies.

Be open with the public. Provide grid operators, utilities, and regulators with accurate data on project development plans and anticipated electricity demand that distinguish between speculative siting and actual development. Report power and water usage and forecast data–with appropriate limits to protect commercially sensitive data–to the Energy Information Administration (EIA) as well as regulators, grid operators, and other authorities.

Don’t Wait to Do Better

There is no single entity to blame, nor is there a single entity that can fix the grid and build a better electricity system. These changes don’t happen in a vacuum. While the public is asking more of tech companies, federal policy should enable positive changes. That includes permitting reform, ratepayer protection requirements, supply chain and workforce strategies, and data reporting standards.

But the tech industry is the most visible and rapidly growing contributor to energy, resource, and cost issues; it has access to enormous resources to avoid and address problems, and it has the most to gain by finding swift solutions that resolve public concerns.

Shortcuts and workarounds are not a sustainable strategy. For their own success, for the long-term strength of the US energy grid, and in response to a frustrated public, the data center industry has every reason to “do better.”

text:
This is the fourth in a series of blogs on the BlueGreen Alliance’s Reserach. Follow along to read more about BGA’s impactful research throughout the years.

By: Roxanne Johnson, BlueGreen Alliance Vice President of Research

The midterm elections saw voters overwhelmingly elect new governors, state legislators, and members of Congress who promised to address issues of affordability and corruption. Working people know that nothing is affordable if you don’t have a good job—wages have stagnated compared to inflation and the increases in costs of living, which came through loud and clear in the election. Voters took a stand against corruption and exploitation, refusing to have their lives and livelihoods scarified to give tax breaks to billionaires.

Now, incoming elected officials have an opportunity to actually deliver for the working people and communities who sent them to office. To do so, they will have to take on the close-to-home issues that drove voters to the polls, like healthcare, immigration, foreign wars, and cost of living. They will also be tasked with restoring decimated institutions, holding those responsible accountable, and rebuilding a government that serves the people. That’s a tall order.

With so many crises to handle at once, emissions reductions may seem minor, but in fact efforts to expand clean energy and fight climate change are powerful tools to help solve the affordability crisis. Candidates ran and won by arguing that taking back power from elites and investing in clean power and technology built by union labor can bring down costs. E2’s latest annual U.S. Clean Energy Employment Report found that the clean economy is currently a major source of jobs, employing more than 3.5 million workers in all 50 states. However, 2025 saw a decline of nearly 37,000 clean economy jobs after four sustained years of growth.

The BlueGreen Alliance (BGA) was founded on the belief that we don’t have to choose between creating good jobs and protecting the environment, that we can and must do both. For 20 years, BGA has brought together the labor and environmental movements to develop broadly supported policies that solve problems and create good jobs in a clean economy. This will be even more relevant in 2027 given the impacts the Trump administration and the Republican Congress have had on clean energy, manufacturing, and working people.

Our new Research Hub hosts resources and guides that policy makers can use to create good jobs and benefits for communities, improve resilience, and reduce emissions, including:

Bait and Switch: The Impacts of Trump Administration Policies at the Intersection of Clean Energy, Manufacturing, and Labor: Detailed accounting of the whole of government attacks on clean energy, working people, and communities across the country.

Tracking Trump’s Wasteful Offshore Wind Buyouts: The U.S. Department of Interior (DOI) has paid off energy companies to walk away from offshore wind commitments. Our tracking website tallies impacts of these buyouts and abandoned projects. As of today, these impacts include $3.9 billion in taxpayer money spent, more than 85,000 projected jobs that will no longer materialize, and 21.15 GW of power generation capacity that won’t get built.

Fallout: Where Attacks on the Clean Economy Hit Home: Use our interactive tool to explore the 223 manufacturing, clean energy, and industrial projects canceled or delayed by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) and learn about how they could have benefitted communities across the country. Dig deeper into more than 3,000 additional sites subject to stricter tax eligibility requirements under OBBBA.

2026 Federal Policy Playbook: more than 80 existing federal bills that can help build a worker and community-centered clean economy.

Robust policy development and advocacy relies on good data that allows us to map the breadth and depth of the clean economy and to see impacts of policies to jobs and other economic outputs. The three other blogs in this series highlight BGA’s research and analysis on manufacturing, the automotive sector, and jobs impacts. BGA operates within an ecosystem of organizations that track the clean economy in different ways, and we leverage the broad knowledge and data generated by everyone in our policy work.

This ecosystem of clean economy research includes regular reports and analysis such as the annual U.S. Department of Energy U.S. Energy & Employment Report (USEER), authored by BW Research, and E2’s annual U.S. Clean Energy Employment Report which and builds on a subset of that data with additional analysis. During the Biden-Harris administration, investment trackers proliferated to capture impacts of federal awards and investments on the ground in real time. While not all of them stuck around, some remain (our friends at the Big Green Machine have listed many of them here) and we’re using them to see what has changed due to Trump administration actions and the OBBBA.

Fallout, our recently released interactive tool, pulls together data from five existing trackers (Rhodium / MIT’s Clean Investment Monitor (CIM), Atlas Public Policy’s Clean Economy Tracker (CET), Wellesley College’s Big Green Machine (BGM), E2’s Clean Economy Works Project Tracker (E2), High Road Analytics’ Invest in America tracker) plus BGA’s electric vehicle supply chain data. Aggregating the data in this way allowed us to show the 223 canceled and stalled projects as well as more than 3,000 sites that now have curtailed tax support, including sites that are indirectly affected by a reduction in demand because they supply components to impacted technologies. We used this data to generate total estimates of private investment and jobs at risk for our Bait and Switch report, which we previewed at the Senate Democrats’ Clean Energy and Manufacturing Jobs Roundtable. The next version of the tool will be a more comprehensive map of the broader clean economy and incorporate additional BGA supply chain data.

Robust policy development and advocacy within a coalition also relies on developing a shared analysis of the problem and potential solutions with our coalition partners, who each bring different perspectives and deep expertise as well as on the ground experience to ground truth our ideas. For example: in 2019, BGA released Solidarity for Climate Action, a set of coalition-approved principles and policies to get to net zero by 2050. Executive Director Jason Walsh talked about the process on America’s Work Force Union podcast. He highlights that taking the necessary time (which turned out to be 8 months and 24 drafts) to negotiate a policy platform that could be fully owned by both sides of the movement enabled us to agree on policies that weren’t just the lowest common denominator. Many elements of that platform appeared in the Inflation Reduction Act, which passed in 2022.

BGA has been convening the labor and environmental movements for 20 years to develop robust policy with wide-reaching support that creates good jobs in the clean economy. Our tools and resources can help new and existing policy makers across the country solve the problems that drove voters to the polls, deliver real benefits for working people, and build a more resilient and clean economy.

About This Series

The BlueGreen Alliance operates in a unique space in the movement for good jobs in a clean economy and our coalition has a wealth of knowledge, expertise, and experience in the areas in which we work. BGA research is developed by staff across the organization and equips partners and allies with robust data and analysis to support our shared work towards a clean, prosperous, and equitable economy. Our dedicated Research Department leverages an array of expertise to generate robust, evidence-supported research and data products and to inform data-driven analysis and policy recommendations.

As we celebrate our 20th anniversary in 2026, this four-part blog series reflects on 20 years of research at the BlueGreen Alliance.

text:
Across the country, large data centers have become a charged political issue. But basic information, including how much energy they use and how much pollution they emit, has been largely lacking.

A paper recently published in the journal Nature Sustainability documents the consumption and output of the largest and most powerful data centers across the United States. Those roughly 400 hyperscale centers use almost as much electricity in a year as massive, mature industries like steel and aluminum and even as much as all the collective homes, businesses, and facilities in some individual states.

“It's pretty extraordinary—a few hundred buildings are consuming as much as an entire state,” says Gianluca Guidi, a data scientist at Harvard’s T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the study’s lead author.

Most of the electricity comes from burning fossil fuels, causing the combined centers to emit more than 25 million metric tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) a year, the study found. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas largely responsible for climate change.

(Solar panels that plug into your wall are about to be everywhere.)

Hundreds more hyperscale data centers, each of which contain tens of thousands of computer servers that power the artificial intelligence industry and cloud computing, are planned or under construction, so their electricity demands are poised to grow significantly, Guidi says.

“Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step,” Gina McCarthy, the former administrator of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, said in a statement.

The researchers calculated the number of hyperscale centers using a database from a commercial research company along with satellite imagery documenting their size. Then, using the research company’s information along with their own calculations of size and operating hours, they estimated annual electricity consumption for each facility. Finally, data from the Environmental Protection Agency revealed the mix of electricity sources used by utilities serving each center. The study covers the year between May of 2024 and April 2025.

Collectively, the centers required between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity (a terawatt is a trillion watts) during the study year. Roughly half, 54 percent, came from fossil fuels, including natural gas (38 percent) and coal (15 percent). Another 21 percent used nuclear energy, and a quarter employed hydropower, solar, wind, and other renewables.

Prior to this calculation, the last estimate quantifying hyperscale centers’ energy consumption published in a scientific journal appeared five years ago, using data from 2018. It calculated cumulative energy use then at 23 terawatt hours. “This was before the AI boom rapidly expanded the number of these centers. Our data shows it’s now at least three time higher,” says Francesca Dominici, a Harvard data scientist and coauthor of the paper. The earlier research also found carbon emissions were roughly three times lower than they are now.

The implications of this much electricity consumption go beyond the strain many electric grids are currently experiencing. The study authors say their future research will study how much these data centers take a toll on human health. Research clearly links emissions from fossil-fuel-based energy generation with changes to the climate, as well as health harms like lung and heart disease.

Even low levels of chronic exposure to pollution, including from fossil-fuel power plants, damages the heart, according to a study published in July in the journal Radiology. Cardiac computed tomography (CT) scans that had been performed in more than 11,000 Canadians concluded those living in areas with higher fine particulate pollution have more calcium plaque and artery obstruction. This occurred even in places where the particulate matter fell below allowable government standards.

“There was no lower level at which we didn't see an association, which indicates there may be really no safe level of air pollution exposure,” says Kate Hanneman, a cardiac radiologist at the University of Toronto, who conducted the research.

(Debunking three myths about air pollution.)

Exposure to emissions from coal-powered plants—some 15 percent of the hyperscale centers’ energy consumption—may be particularly harmful, says Corwin Zigler, an environmental scientist at Brown University. Older people exposed to its sulfur-dioxide-laden pollutants have especially high death rates, Zigler reported in Science in 2023. In recent years, coal plants have installed technologies reducing their emissions, but “still, the burden is not zero,” Zigler says.

The Nature Sustainability study found very large data centers are concentrated in specific parts of the country, with four states—Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa—consuming more than half of the electricity use reported.

This concentration means some locations bear more burden than others. Research published last year by the same authors, examining computer centers mining for bitcoins, found higher concentrations of particulate pollution in some regions of the country. Some of that pollution remained close to the data centers, but other particulates appeared hundreds of miles away, thanks to wind and atmospheric patterns that disperse them.

Similarly, coal power pollution impacts health far from the plant locations. “If you live in Boston, some of that pollution you're breathing came from Ohio or Kentucky or Missouri or Indiana,” Zigler says of his research.

Communities with a concentration of data centers can also struggle to get the power they need, especially on hot days when air conditioners are running, Shaolei Ren, an electrical and computer engineer at the University of California, Riverside, said in an email. His ongoing research, not yet published, also finds health issues associated with living near data centers “can be very uneven across communities. In the most affected counties, the per-household health burden can be about seven times the national average,” his email stated.

Data centers can also deplete another resource, water. Some is used to keep computers from overheating, but as much as three-quarters of the usage is linked to electricity generation, according to early research by the Harvard researchers that has not yet been peer-reviewed by other scientists.

The rapid growth of data centers “should be a wake-up call” for communities and regulators, who are only starting to grapple with how to reliably and safely power this fast-growing industry while not straining the grid, polluting the air, harming the climate, or raising prices for other energy users, says Kasparas Spokas, who directs the electricity program at the research and advocacy nonprofit Clean Air Task Force. “How the demand for those data centers will be met will shape power sector emissions for decades,” he says.

Of nearly two dozen planned hyperscale data centers, only about half intend to source electricity from grids adding new renewable energy to their mix, according to an analysis in September by the nonprofit EnergyTag.

Some states are exploring options to demand that new, large data centers consume more clean energy, such as by charging them “large-load” tariffs or mandating that a high percentage of their power comes from renewables, Spokas says. “It's a difficult balance that communities and policymakers have to strike between promoting economic development while still prioritizing the economic and environmental concerns of local communities,” he says.

Hoffman said the decision reflects the company’s commitment to responsible development and its willingness to make significant changes in response to community feedback.

She said Orion continues to evaluate the opportunities for developing in Ward 6, but said no final decisions have been made regarding the project’s revised size or configuration.

“Our objective remains unchanged,” Hoffman said. “To develop a responsible energy project that respects community priorities while creating lasting economic value for Calcasieu Parish. We believe meaningful engagement requires more than listening. It requires action, and that is exactly what we are doing.”

text:
By Skip Descant.

California is making new funding available for school districts transitioning to electric school buses.

The California Air Resources Board (CARB) and the California Energy Commission (CEC) have allocated at least $55 million for the Zero-Emission School Bus and Infrastructure (ZESBI) incentive program to continue to advance zero-emission school buses. The funds are administered by Catalyst Mobility, formerly CALSTART.

Zero emission buses (ZEBs) make up roughly 9.5 percent of the San Diego Unified School District (SDUSD) bus fleet, which comes to 43 buses, said John Burciaga, fleet manager for the Transportation Services Department at SDUSD, indicating the district aims to pursue funding for an additional 50 ZEBs.

The buses “are actively utilized in daily route operations and are strategically deployed in service areas near the Port of San Diego,” Burciaga said in an email, noting the strategic use of the emissions-free vehicles in an area historically overexposed to air pollution.

There are now 2,265 zero-emission school buses operating or delivered to school districts in California, according to data from the Electric School Bus Initiative, with more than 8,600 delivered or operating electric buses (e-buses) nationwide. The technology has been credited with improving the overall safety of students by not exposing them to diesel exhaust and also with saving money for school districts.

Burciaga credited the e-buses for their “significant operational savings.”

“The cost of electricity required to charge the buses is substantially lower than the cost of diesel fuel, resulting in considerable fuel savings,” he said. “In addition, electric buses have simplified drivetrains with fewer moving parts, reducing maintenance requirements and associated costs by an estimated 50 percent compared to conventional diesel-powered buses.”

Despite reports of operational challenges in areas where buses travel long distances or experience reduced range in cold weather, electric buses should not be overlooked, officials said.

“Like any vehicle, [zero-emission] ZE school buses can be easier to operate in certain conditions, but ZE school buses have also been successful on cold and rural routes,” said Jennifer Smith, senior project manager for public engagement and media relations at Catalyst Mobility.

Route planning can help school transportation officials best locate electric buses where they make the most sense, she said.

“When deciding which routes to electrify first, criteria such as route length and operational schedule should be front of mind,” Smith said. “Very rarely, if ever, are we seeing a fleet go from 100 percent internal combustion engine buses to 100 percent ZE school buses in one go. Phased transitions let them adjust to the technology and operational shifts it brings while helping fleets maintain their vehicle replacement schedule, setting them up for long-term success.”

The 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act made $5 billion available for the purchase of electric and other clean school buses through the federal Environmental Protection Agency’s Clean School Bus Program. The Donald Trump administration has halted the process and is revamping the program, prompting states to develop their own incentives.

The ZESBI program was first structured around the Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit, a federal incentive program to encourage businesses or nonprofits to purchase plug-in electric or fuel cell commercial vehicles, Smith said. That program is also no longer available.

“Since the tax credit is no longer available, CARB decided to cover that gap and any further gaps that may result from tariffs with an additional $40,000 in funding for each ZE school bus,” she said.

Skip Descant writes about smart cities, the Internet of Things, transportation and other areas. He spent more than 12 years reporting for daily newspapers in Mississippi, Arkansas, Louisiana and California. He lives in downtown Yreka, Calif.
