text:
MARSHALL — Ford Motor Co. launched production batteries here at the country's first lithium-iron-phosphate battery plant for automotive applications, and packs are being shipped for pre-production Fathom all-electric pickups on the road undergoing testing.

The $3 billion plant launched production on Oct. 10, and at full ramp-up, Ford expects BlueOval Battery Park Michigan will produce 40 battery cells per minute on each of the two lines. With batteries representing about 40% of the cost of an electric vehicle, the batteries built here using technology licensed from Chinese battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. are key to unlocking affordable pricing for the $28,350 Fathom, whose deliveries will begin in the fourth quarter of 2027.

"The bottom line is that the cost of the product is lower," said Alan Clarke, vice president of advanced development projects, "and by doing that, we've given ourselves more opportunity to put more technology and capability into the vehicle that the customers will actually care about."

The Fathom is a midsize truck and the first vehicle Ford is launching off its new Universal Electric Vehicle Platform, the product of its originally separated, small "skunkworks" team charged five years ago with disrupting the now-123-year-old company to compete with low-cost Chinese EVs. The UEV is key to helping Ford turn around its money-losing Model e EV business by 2029.

"It's not an affordable, boring vehicle," said Charles Poon, vice president of vehicle hardware engineering, referencing features like autonomous driving and embedded maps. "When you step on it, it's going to peel away like a Mustang GT."

Many EVs, including many of Ford's first-generation EVs, on the road use lithium ion nickel-manganese-cobalt batteries that have a high energy density. But their materials also are more expensive than the LFP batteries built here. Additionally, LFP batteries have higher durability. So, while Ford executives expressed confidence that Fathom will offer the 300 miles of range many consumers look for, they also emphasized its capability to power a home during outages or peak-rate times, to charge to 100% compared to the recommended roughly 80% for NMC batteries that have less durability, and to last for a decade or more.

Ford manufacturing the batteries itself, known as vertical integration, also offers it cost-competitiveness in the United States without mark-ups, full control over technology and process advancements and the ability to take advantage of federal battery production tax credits as a result of efforts to find material sourcing from allied nations, executives said. It expects the facility can accommodate other chemistries in the future, as well, such as lithium manganese-rich. Poon said Ford is researching its second-generation of LMR batteries.

"Having domestic LFP cell production and also the full pack assembly here as well," said Sam Abuelsamid, vice president of market research for auto communications firm Telemetry Agency, "is key to bringing down the cost of the UEV architecture and getting it to the point where it's at a price point that's going to be attractive to consumer, but also at some point should be profitable for Ford, as well, as opposed to having to buy parts, buy batteries from a supplier."

The manufacturing process in the one-mile-long facility with hundreds of robots and machines starts on one side and ends at the other. A cell is made in six-and-a-half days, including a five-day aging process. Ford expects to have nearly 800 employees in Marshall by the end of the year of the 1,700 it has committed to employing at the plant.

Initially, the building is split into two areas for anode and cathode creation, the sides of the battery with negative and positive polarity, respectively. Their separation helps to reduce cross-contamination. Employees have to wear special jumpsuits, shoes or shoe coverings, hair nets and other personal protective equipment and go through air showers whose floor coverings are replaced four times a day between sections to reduce contaminants. Air moisture also is tightly monitored to protect quality.

Quality is critical because the battery cells aren't serviceable once they end up in a battery pack, which is the floor of the Fathom. There are multiple quality checks throughout the manufacturing process, and Ford has contracted CATL employees to be in the plant through ramp as it works to train operators and technicians on machines and achieve defects measured as parts-per-billion compared to a higher frequency of errors typically recorded in the auto space.

The decision to license from a Chinese company has received backlash from the Trump administration and other Republican legislators, but Clarke emphasized how Ford is using it to propel the domestic manufacturing industry.

"If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States," Clarke said, "we need to also do it the fastest way possible, and the fastest way possible is you go to a company that has made hundreds of gigawatt hours of factories, not tens. And CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells."

At the start, materials are mixed in large vats to create anode and cathode slurry, a black, wet mixture that is spread onto both sides of foil — copper for anode and aluminum for cathode. After each side is coated, the foil goes through massive ovens heated to hundreds of degrees Fahrenheit to dry the anode to a matte finish and the cathode slurry to glossy. Once dried, the foil turns into almost-2,000-pound, 3,000-meter jumbo rolls that are transported by robots.

It next goes to a slitting and calendaring process, which separates the five lanes of coated foil into individual lanes and presses down the material, because the more surface area it covers, the greater the range. It's like applying the weight of four elephants on a postage stamp, said Austin Evans, process engineer. A visual system inspects for defects. Scrap is set aside for recycling, and Ford has a recycling facility on-site.

These now-smaller "whopper" rolls then go to tab formation, which uses lasers to cut out figure eight-shaped excess foil, leaving behind foil tabs like those in a binder. The coated foil then is rolled once again into roughly 500-pound "pancake" rolls.

At this point, the anode and cathode processes converge. Each foil is wound together with a ceramic separator material between to create a 4-to-5-pound "jelly roll." More than 300 jelly rolls can be made from a pancake roll. It's important that the tabs line up during winding, or else it can take longer for electrons to get where they need to go, which affects range and can be dangerous in the case of free currents. The jelly rolls are photographed, and X-rays check for proper winding inside.

Once passed, a jelly roll is paired with a second, and connectors are sonically welded to them to attach the jelly rolls. Lasers weld the top cap to the connector nodes and then the cell gets a mylar wrapping for additional protection and finally an aluminum can, which is laser welded to the cap. The cell is placed in an air-tight chamber with helium pumped into the cell to test for leakage. If there is, a separate welding rework can address the issue there nearby to avoid slowing down production.

Next, a baking process to remove any residual moisture before electrolyte is added to the cell, which allows it to be charged and discharged in a process called formation. It now goes through about five days of aging to check the voltage drop to ensure there's nothing wrong with the battery. Batteries are charged to 28% to comply with shipping regulations for under 30%.

After final quality checks, the cells then through a hole in the wall on a conveyor belt enter the packing plant. There is no door from the cell manufacturing plant into the packing plant, because Ford fully owns the packs, and CATL employees aren't allowed in that area.

A display of the Fathom pack and a busbar overlay of the cells showed a grid the size of 18 cells by six cells in a steel stamping to make up the pack. The pack also consists of an e-box, a consolidated power module that includes the 48-volt architecture to power electronics, has an inverter to support bidirectional charging and components for fast-charging. The e-box and charging equipment are accessible under the rear seats for service.

Abuelsamid noted the pack itself is simple in design compared to that of other EVs, especially those like General Motors Co.'s or Ford's current-generation EVs that use pouch cells over these new prismatic cells.

"They slice up the electrodes, and they stack the anodes and the cathodes and separators and put it together, and that's a little more complicated process and is a little more potentially trouble-prone, as we've seen with some of the recalls," Abuelsamid said of pouch cells, referencing the a major recall on the Chevrolet Bolt, Hyundai Kona EV and Porsche Taycan. He added about the simplification: "All of these things cascade to give you a cheaper overall cost."

Ford has about 170 Fathoms on the road being tested in all weather and road conditions, addressing issues that weren't caught in development or simulation like noise issues.

"I think it's normal at this phase of product development to have a lot of dirty laundry. The important part is to have the velocity to fix it," Clarke said. "We're giving ourselves the time to fix them if we find issues between now and then. We're not setting up a Hail Mary-delivery plan that has no chance of success. It's quite the opposite."

As the industry talks about "China speed," referencing the often-cited 18 months Chinese automakers say they are going from development to a new model, Clarke said that's a target for Ford now with the UEV in place. However, he emphasized some skepticism over some of the timetables in China depending when the companies start their clocks and noted its market of dozens of competitors emphasize spec wars and often small changes that flood the market and generate pricing wars that hinder profitability.

"We will take our time," Clarke said, "making sure we know that we can build less thing at higher volume versus many things at low volume."

title: GM implements Autocharge to enable seamless charging at Electrify America EV charging stations
description:
The latest player to implement a seamless charging system is GM.
Drivers of GM EVs can now plug and walk at participating Electrify America stations.
At the moment, there are two different standards for seamless charging in the US.
Chargepoint is throwing in its lot with Plug & Charge, while EVgo is using its own version of Autocharge.
“Electrify America has been a pioneer in making public charging more seamless, enabling drivers to authenticate and start a charge simply by plugging in,” said Robert Barrosa, President and CEO of Electrify America.
text:
As regular Charged readers know, the EV charging industry is gradually moving towards seamless charging—no apps or credit card readers, just plug in and walk away (as Tesla drivers have always done).

The latest player to implement a seamless charging system is GM. Drivers of GM EVs can now plug and walk at participating Electrify America stations. The feature is now available for GM EVs with native CCS charging ports, and will be enabled for vehicles with native NACS ports “in early 2027.” (Using seamless charging requires signing up with GM’s new Energy Pass app.)

At the moment, there are two different standards for seamless charging in the US. GM’s system uses Autocharge, which is based on DIN Spec 70121. Plug & Charge (the popular name for a feature included in the ISO 15118-20 standard) is generally considered the more advanced standard, but the two aren’t really competing standards, because EVs and chargers can support both.

Charging providers are hedging their bets. Chargepoint is throwing in its lot with Plug & Charge, while EVgo is using its own version of Autocharge. An EVgo spokesperson told Charged: “We are committed to rolling out the Plug & Charge standard once the intricacies around certification and implementation have been addressed. In the meantime, we continue to support Autocharge+ as our current solution.”

Using GM’s Autocharge-based system, a driver simply connects their vehicle to a compatible Electrify America charger, which automatically initiates charging. Internal GM testing found that energy flow begins within approximately 45 seconds.

“We’re making it easier for drivers to start a charging session and get back on the road, with an experience that has fewer steps than swiping a credit card to get gas,” said Wade Sheffer, Vice President, GM Energy.

“Electrify America has been a pioneer in making public charging more seamless, enabling drivers to authenticate and start a charge simply by plugging in,” said Robert Barrosa, President and CEO of Electrify America. “Bringing that experience to GM EV drivers is another important step forward.”

text:
MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.

The automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They’ll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.

The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.

The automaker’s decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford’s ties to CATL.

Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible.

“If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible,” Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. “CATL being the biggest in the world means that they’re the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells.”

The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing “profound concern” about Ford’s ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.

Ford’s battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company’s energy storage business. That’s down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.

text:
Around the world, people are demanding a halt to the proliferation of data centres — racks of computers, housed in warehouses, that are powering the boom in artificial intelligence. Communities worry that existing infrastructure will not be able to handle the surge in demand for electricity and water, and that data centres’ energy demands will cause environmental and health problems, including increases in air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions. The question of whether AI is going to stall climate action is explored in the first of a three-part Nature Podcast (Nature https://doi.org/rzqs; 2026).

Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say

People have many concerns about the way AI is being developed, including how it might affect safety, security and jobs. Where energy is concerned, however, any added demand for computing power can, and must, be met in smart, sustainable ways, not by burning more fossil fuels. Achieving this will take some creative thinking, and researchers need to be closely involved. Many argue that there are alternatives to relying on energy-intensive data centres, such as AI models that can run on individual computers or institutional servers, thereby consuming much less power than those run using cloud services. Efforts to develop such options need to be better funded.

Future projections of data centres’ energy demands are hard to make, because they are based on assumptions that could change. If current global trends continue, electricity consumption by data centres will go on rising. Between 2017 and 2024, it grew by around 12% per year. Figures for 2024 from the International Energy Agency (IEA), based in Paris, show most of this demand coming from three regions: the United States (45%), China (25%) and Europe (15%).

The Electric Power Research Institute, a non-profit organization in Palo Alto, California, has projected that the continued growth of US data centres could add up to 94 gigawatts of demand by 2030, equivalent to 17% of the country’s electricity consumption. Data centres currently consume more than 1.5% of the world’s electricity supply, and the IEA’s projections indicate that this figure will more than double in the next few years. By 2030, data centres could consume more electricity than Japan, the agency says.

Why scientists should lead the shift away from AI mega data centres

There are serious concerns that this extra demand will be powered mainly by fossil fuels, when carbon emissions are already at a record high. Research published this week in Nature Sustainability estimates that some 400 data centres in the United States accounted for around 26 megatonnes of carbon dioxide emissions between May 2024 and April 2025, more than those produced by many countries (G. Guidi et al. Nature Sustain. https://doi.org/hcsptc; 2026). And according to a study published last week in Nature Climate Change, data centres’ energy demands could prolong the lifespan of coal-fired power stations (C. Li et al. Nature Clim. Change https://doi.org/rzqr; 2026).

But none of this is inevitable. Governments could mandate that new energy demand be met with renewable sources. And regulators could look at alternative ways to manage existing electric supplies.

Many nations’ electric grid systems are designed to accommodate surges in demand, whether to power extra cooling on hot summer days or extra heating during winter cold snaps. Much of the time, there is excess capacity. This excess could be used to reduce the amount of new energy needed to power data centres.

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown

One solution is to curtail data-centre operations during periods of peak electricity consumption, and ramp up at times of lower demand. An analysis released in 2025 by researchers at Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, found that the US electric grid could accommodate 98 gigawatts of extra demand in this way, without adding any new generation capacity (see go.nature.com/4cdeknm). That 98 gigawatts would be enough to cover most, if not all, of the expected expansion in US data centres over the next few years.

There is potential for this to become a reality. In June, as part of a larger effort to modernize the grid, the US Federal Energy Regulatory Commission instructed grid operators to draw up a plan for how they will cope with extra demand from data centres. The technology industry is understandably paying close attention to how it might mitigate the problems of powering data centres. Earlier this month, OpenAI announced what it is calling a “grid protectors program”, a project to consult with US grid operators, regulators and policymakers to see how the company can work around peaks in power demand.

Meanwhile, Google is paying households and businesses in parts of the Eastern United States to reduce their electricity consumption during periods of high demand. Similar proposals are being considered in other countries.

Why open-source generative AI models are an ethical way forward for science

These are all tentative moves in the right direction, although arguably progress is not being made fast enough. Policymakers and data-centre operators must engage seriously with those who oppose the centres’ expansion. At a minimum, any new energy sources developed to power these centres must be renewable. Existing energy sources can also be better deployed, and researchers working to develop alternatives to energy-intensive data centres should be better supported. More peer-reviewed evidence is needed, especially for countries outside the United States.

There are smarter and more sustainable ways to power the growth of AI, but to achieve them, concerted and coordinated action will be needed. In this way, the harm posed to people and the planet can be minimized, and AI technologies can benefit everyone.

A growing sense of urgency about the climate crisis continues to build, and this winter’s monster El Niño, not even peaked yet, has already brought unprecedented extreme impacts to California, the Southwest, and Florida.

text:
The Regional Industrial Development Corporation (RIDC) will use a $937,500 Industrial Site Reuse Program (ISRP) grant to perform an environmental assessment and conduct asbestos remediation of the Allegheny County site.

Investments like this one by the Shapiro Administration are making communities healthier, increasing Pennsylvanians’ quality of life, and continuing to grow the Commonwealth’s economy.

Harrisburg, PA – Today, Department of Community and Economic Development (DCED) Secretary Rick Siger and Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) Secretary Jessica Shirley announced the approval of a $937,500 grant through the Industrial Sites Reuse Program (ISRP) to the Regional Industrial Development Corporation (RIDC) to perform environmental remediation at the former Westinghouse East Pittsburgh Works property in Allegheny County.

The RIDC will use the ISRP funds for an environmental assessment and lead paint stabilization and asbestos abatement, including paint and other hazardous materials, and the removal and disposal of asbestos throughout the property at 500 Braddock Avenue, Keystone Commons, in East Pittsburgh. Once remediated, the site will be renovated and reused as a multi-tenant manufacturing facility, providing leased spaces for companies, job training, and manufacturing.

“The Industrial Sites Reuse Program is an important tool that feeds economic growth while reusing infrastructure and creating healthier and safer communities across the Commonwealth,” said DCED Secretary Rick Siger. “This investment will strengthen East Pittsburgh by providing a site that will support job training, manufacturing spaces, and encourage business investments in Pennsylvania’s workforce.”

The ISRP provides loans and grants for environmental assessments and remediation carried out by eligible applicants who did not cause or contribute to the contamination. The program is designed to support the cleanup of environmental contamination at industrial sites, thereby bringing dormant land into productive reuse.

“Pittsburgh has long been a hub of manufacturing in Pennsylvania, and with this project will continue to be where America gets made,” said DEP Secretary Jessica Shirley. “Restoring former industrial sites to productive use is a win-win by getting rid of blight bringing in new business and preserving green spaces from development.”

For too long, hazardous waste sites, abandoned mine lands, and abandoned wells have sat vacant and released toxic chemicals into the environment because Pennsylvania didn’t have the resources or the speed to get projects up and running. The Shapiro Administration is working to fix that — building shovel-ready sites, cleaning up abandoned mine land and hazardous waste sites so communities can put those areas back to good use, and aggressively plugging abandoned or orphaned wells that are polluting our air and water.

Since taking office, Governor Shapiro has worked to protect the Commonwealth’s natural environment and defend Pennsylvanians’ Constitutional right to clean air, pure water, and the preservation of the environment. Since 2023, the Administration has plugged over 500 orphaned and abandoned wells — more than in the previous ten years combined. The 2026-27 budget authorizes a one-time transfer of $20 million from the General Fund to the Hazardous Sites Cleanup Program, protecting Pennsylvanians from the most dangerous toxic waste sites throughout the Commonwealth and turning them into shovel-ready sites to turn dirt into jobs.

For more information about the Industrial Sites Reuse Program or DCED, visit the agency’s website, Facebook, X, and LinkedIn.

text:
$800 million project will create more than 500 jobs, build on Evers Administration carbon-free electricity efforts

MADISON — Gov. Tony Evers, together with the Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation (WEDC), announced that the state will provide up to $15 million in tax incentives to support Realta Fusion’s $800 million project to locate its corporate headquarters and research and development facility at OM Station, the site of the former Oscar Mayer plant, in Madison. This comes as Gov. Evers and WEDC announced Realta’s relocation in July.

“For the past eight years, my administration and I have worked hard to boost carbon-free energy here in Wisconsin, which is why I’m jazzed that we can be a part of helping Realta bring the benefits of fusion energy to our state,” said Gov. Evers. “We don’t have to choose between a clean energy future and supporting good-paying jobs and a strong economy; we can and should do both, and that’s exactly what this partnership will do. Fusion energy is not only good for our planet and our power grid, but it builds on all our strengths as a state with our world-class research universities, research laboratories, and an incredible manufacturing and supply chain network supported by our highly skilled workforce. I can’t wait to see all the good that will come from this project.”

The WEDC Board of Directors on Tuesday approved up to $15 million in performance-based Enterprise Zone (EZ) tax credits for the project, which is expected to create more than 500 high-paying jobs. The amount of credits the company will receive depends on the amount of capital invested and the number of jobs created. The incentive package is WEDC’s largest investment in fusion energy to date. The Evers administration has championed fusion as a source of carbon-free electricity to power Wisconsin homes, businesses, and communities.

“WEDC is proud to partner with Realta Fusion in this groundbreaking enterprise,” said WEDC Secretary and CEO John W. Miller. “Realta Fusion is part of the great tradition of the Wisconsin Idea, where research at the University of Wisconsin produces innovations that change the world.”

Wisconsin has emerged as a regional and national hub for fusion research and collaboration, driven by decades of leadership at the University of Wisconsin (UW)-Madison and a growing ecosystem of industry partnerships and startup companies. As part of his 2026 State of the State address this year, Gov. Evers identified fusion research as a top priority for Wisconsin, announcing a partnership between the PSC and the UW–Madison Department of Nuclear Engineering and Engineering Physics to conduct the state’s nuclear energy siting study.

Realta officials said they expect to break ground on “The Realta Forge,” its dedicated research and development facility, where it will begin building the prototype magnetic mirror fusion machine it calls Hammir before the end of this year. Company leaders thanked Gov. Evers and WEDC for their strong support of commercial fusion activities in the state.

“The availability of EZ tax credits through WEDC was a critical factor in selecting OM Station as the best location within the most supportive business environment for us to build The Realta Forge,” said Realta Fusion Chief Operating Officer Dominick Bindl. “Formalizing this agreement allows us to continue moving at the speed required to bring commercial fusion energy to the world as fast as humanly possible.”

This announcement comes as, earlier this year, Gov. Evers signed 2025 Wisconsin Act 165, which exempts capital expenditures on fusion energy projects from state sales and use taxes. In addition, WEDC is providing a $778,000 Ignite Wisconsin grant to the Wisconsin Fusion Energy Coalition to position the state as a national hub for fusion energy commercialization.

Additional background on Gov. Ever’s efforts to build a clean energy future in Wisconsin

Since Day One, Gov. Evers and the Evers Administration have been committed to promoting climate resilience and building a clean energy economy in the state. In his first year in office, Gov. Evers joined the U.S. Climate Alliance and later was the first Midwest governor to serve as an executive board member and co-chair.

The governor, along with his fellow U.S. Climate Alliance governors, is committed to collectively achieving the goals of the 2015 Paris Agreement to combat climate change and has established an ambitious goal of ensuring 100 percent carbon-free electricity consumption in Wisconsin by 2050. In 2019, Gov. Evers also created the Governor’s Task Force on Climate Change, which advised and assisted the governor in developing strategies to mitigate and adapt to the effects of climate change for the benefit of all Wisconsin communities.

In addition to joining the Alliance in 2019, in his first year in office, Gov. Evers signed Executive Order #38 to create the OSCE, charging the office with developing the Wisconsin Clean Energy Plan to promote the development and use of clean and renewable energy across the state, advance innovative sustainability solutions that improve the state’s economy and environment, and diversify the resources used to meet the state’s energy needs.

In accordance with Gov. Evers’ Executive Order #38, the state’s first-ever Clean Energy Plan was in 2022, providing a roadmap for the state to lower energy bills and prices at the pump for Wisconsin families, promote energy independence by reducing reliance on out-of-state energy sources, create an estimated more than 40,000 jobs by 2030, and invest in job training and apprenticeship programs in innovative industries and technologies. Since creating Wisconsin’s Clean Energy Plan four years ago, OSCE has released annual clean energy progress reports to outline the strides the state is making to meet our clean energy goals.

Additionally, in 2023, Gov. Evers created the Green Ribbon Commission on Clean Energy and Environmental Innovation to advise on creating the state’s first-ever Green Innovation Fund. The Green Innovation Fund and its partners work to leverage public and private financing to invest in projects that provide environmental and clean energy solutions to businesses, reduce pollution, lower energy costs for families, and expand access to clean, affordable energy options.

Earlier this year, the PSC announced that Wisconsin is now a national leader in enrollment for the Inflation Reduction Act Home Energy Rebate programs, which have helped residents statewide reduce energy use and lower utility bills. Wisconsin was the very first state to make energy efficiency upgrades available under the Home Energy Rebates (HOMES) Program in August 2024 and remains one of only a handful of states in the country to offer both the HOMES Program and the Home Electrification and Appliance Rebate (HEAR) Program, which was launched a few months later.

Since launching the programs in 2024, $19 million in rebates have been paid to Wisconsin households to install popular energy-efficient measures, including air sealing, insulation, heat pumps for cooling and heating, and electric panels and wiring. More about the state’s efforts through the HOMES and HEAR programs to help Wisconsin households save energy and money with energy-efficient home upgrades can be found on Gov. Evers’ press release page .

In recent years, advancements in nuclear technology and increased demand for energy have led to renewed interest in nuclear energy nationwide, which is why, in addition to signing Act 165, Gov. Evers signed 2025 Wisconsin Act 12 last July to launch a nuclear power siting study, supported by $2 million in funding provided by the 2025-27 Biennial Budget, that will bolster knowledge and understanding of how Wisconsin’s nuclear energy potential can help meet the state’s growing need for carbon-free energy.

The overarching goal of the siting study is to provide foundational information and a thorough evaluation of potential nuclear energy development opportunities in Wisconsin to help guide future actions. The study scope encompasses traditional nuclear power, small modular reactors, and advanced technologies, including fusion energy. It will identify various siting opportunities and analyze site characteristics, suitability, regulatory, and permitting requirements, as well as impacts to local economies and the power grid.

Information from industry experts at the Oak Ridge and Pacific Northwest National Laboratories will be incorporated into the study, as will feedback from recent experiences with the construction and operation of nuclear projects. Act 12 requires the study to be completed by the start of 2027.

As announced by Gov. Evers in his 2026 State of the State address, the siting study will be conducted by PSC and the UW-Madison Department of Nuclear Engineering and Engineering Physics, as UW-Madison has one of the nation’s few remaining teaching and research nuclear reactors and is a national leader in fusion energy research. Gov. Evers toured the University of Wisconsin Nuclear Reactor in March, celebrating the new dynamic partnership and its impact in advancing the goals of Wisconsin’s Clean Energy Plan.

In addition to the nuclear power siting study, in July 2025, Gov. Evers also signed 2025 Wisconsin Act 11, creating a Nuclear Power Summit Board designed to help advance nuclear power and fusion technology and development, and to showcase Wisconsin’s leadership and innovation in the nuclear industry through the hosting of a nuclear power summit in the city of Madison.

In addition to the new partnership between the PSC and UW-Madison, Gov. Evers also announced in his 2026 State of the State address that the state is taking the first steps to continue efforts to purchase renewable energy certificates (RECs) from Wisconsin utilities and renewable energy projects for the next two decades, continuing the state’s long-standing practice of leading by example and ensuring Wisconsinites have access to in-state renewable electricity and building on his administration’s efforts to help bolster clean energy in Wisconsin. The state plans to purchase approximately 225,000 RECs every year for the next 20 years, representing 225,000 megawatt-hours (MWh) of renewable electricity each year, which is enough energy to power more than half a million Wisconsin homes.

Since 2007, the state of Wisconsin has purchased over 1.8 million RECs from Wisconsin utilities. Each REC represents the equivalent of about one MWh of renewable energy. By purchasing RECs, state agencies support Wisconsin-based jobs, local economic development, clean air, and clean water, while offsetting their net greenhouse gas emissions. The RFP seeks proposals capable of delivering RECs starting in January 2031 for a 20-year term, helping position state agencies and universities to achieve Wisconsin’s goal of 100-percent carbon-free electricity by 2050.

name: Detroit American Energy
title: Michigan Democrats should back bipartisan permitting reform | Opinion - Detroit Free Press
description:
We have a federal permitting system so slow that critical projects like power lines can spend more time getting approval than being constructed.
The bill would make it faster and more affordable to build the power grid America needs.
The price and reliability of our power is a major factor for companies deciding to build here.
I voted for the law requiring 100% clean power by 2040 in Michigan.
This bipartisan bill in Congress would speed up clearing this backlog, which is why the American Clean Power Association is backing it.
text:
In Michigan, we know how to build things. We build jeeps at Warren Truck. General Dynamics designs the Abrams tank here. And, at the Detroit Arsenal, the U.S. Army runs its ground vehicle program.

But what’s slowing us down is the electric grid all of that has to run on. It’s not Michigan’s fault. We have a federal permitting system so slow that critical projects like power lines can spend more time getting approval than being constructed.

Congress is working on a bill right now that would fix that, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. The bill would make it faster and more affordable to build the power grid America needs. We need Michigan’s Democrats in Washington D.C. to lead the way on getting it done.

Look at what folks in Detroit have been going through. Since 2024, DTE has filed for five rate increases. Their latest would add nearly 10% to a household’s bill. Families can’t keep up. In 2024, utilities shut off power more than 375,000 times to Michiganders struggling to pay. That means no furnace in the cold months, and no AC during heat waves for our seniors and families with newborns.

Utility companies claim they need the money for the grid. So then let’s fix this country’s outdated permitting system – which is driving up the cost of all these projects ‒ so that we can build the grid we need quickly and slow these rate increases people can keep more money in their pocket. An ICF analysis shows that permitting reform could save households about $55 billion on their electricity through 2035.

This matters to Michigan’s economy too. The price and reliability of our power is a major factor for companies deciding to build here. Manufacturers are feeling the pinch. The National Association of Manufacturers says our broken system is costing them $12 billion a year, and this legislation would cut that by about a third.

I’m a union guy from a union town. I know that money would be better spent on wages and hiring instead of legal battles. I also know that if we can get these projects moving we can put our skilled trades to work.

All of these are commonsense fixes. Like letting utilities upgrade lines in corridors they already use without starting another long review process.

I voted for the law requiring 100% clean power by 2040 in Michigan. If we’re going to meet this, we have to fix the permitting reform process. Nationwide, there are currently more than two terawatts of projects waiting to be connected to the grid. Most of it is solar and wind.

It’s happening here in Michigan too. We’ve had dozens of clean energy projects shelved because of grid congestion. 20 gigawatts of solar in our state is waiting in line to connect. This bipartisan bill in Congress would speed up clearing this backlog, which is why the American Clean Power Association is backing it.

As some Democrats question the bill, it’s worth remembering that two of our party’s strongest clean energy voices helped write it, Democratic Senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich.

Democrats should also note that this would make a federal permit very hard to claw back. In plainer terms, once a clean energy project gets approved, a future Republican administration couldn’t just tear it up on a whim. We need that certainty to meet that 2040 goal.

Democrats have always been at our best fighting for working families.

This is a chance to do exactly that. I hope our delegation and their colleagues vote yes on this.

FY 2027 Transportation Proposal Puts EV Charging Investments at Risk

WASHINGTON, D.C. — On Monday, Senate Republicans released an Appropriations package that proposes to take back nearly $2 billion in federal funding already allocated to states to build out electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act and repurpose it for general transportation uses, putting critical clean transportation investments at risk.

Republicans already clawed back roughly $500 million from the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) Formula Program in the FY 2026 appropriations bill. Now, they are proposing to further divert these funds, even as all 50 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico have approved plans for their use and are working to deliver critical charging infrastructure to their communities. More than half of available NEVI funding has already been committed to projects, and the proposal threatens to upend additional awards that states continue to make to charging developers.

For example, Texas recently made an announcement of $226 million in awards that will support 321 stations. The Senate proposal would threaten Texas’s remaining NEVI funding, along with funding for states like Ohio, which has one of the largest numbers of operational NEVI-funded stations in the country.

In response, Clean Transportation for All Director Katherine García released the following statement:

“It is unacceptable for Senate Republicans to once again seek to claw back critical EV charging investments. Trump’s day-one freeze of NEVI set states back, and they are only now back on track after we successfully challenged that freeze in court. This latest proposal threatens affordable transportation for American families, clean air for communities, and states’ efforts to build the infrastructure of the future. We have successfully defended NEVI against the Trump administration’s attacks, and we will continue fighting to protect the program and ensure these investments reach communities across the country.”

Background:

The NEVI program, established through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law in 2021, provides funding to states to build a nationwide network of EV fast-charging stations. Protecting that investment is essential to expanding charging access, supporting EV adoption, reducing dependence on volatile gasoline prices, and cutting transportation pollution.

Since the Trump administration’s unlawful freeze of the NEVI program was lifted following successful litigation by Sierra Club, its partners, and a coalition of states, hundreds of millions of dollars in NEVI funding have been committed to charging projects.

Congress must preserve funding for EV charging infrastructure while providing dedicated resources for passenger rail, public transit, and other clean transportation priorities.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Congressman Eugene Vindman (Va.-07) introduced a package of four bills aimed at lowering electricity costs, strengthening oversight of utility companies, and protecting Virginia families and small businesses from bearing the costs of unnecessary utility company projects.

As electricity demand continues to grow and utility companies invest billions in expanding and modernizing the electric grid, consumers must not be forced to shoulder costs that could be avoided or fairly assigned back to utility companies.

“Virginians are already struggling with rising electricity bills, and they shouldn’t have to pay even more for utility companies’ poor investments and lack of accountability,” said Vindman. “As energy demand grows, we need to modernize our grid, make sure large energy users like data centers pay their fair share, and protect families and small businesses from being saddled with unnecessary costs. The bottom line is simple: hardworking Virginians shouldn’t be footing the bill for utility companies and massive corporations to protect their bottom lines.”

As we face the rapid expansion of energy-intensive data centers, outdated transmission infrastructure, and unnecessary utility spending, Virginians deserve a grid that is reliable, affordable, and built with ratepayers in mind. This package would promote smarter investments, reduce unnecessary costs, and hold utility companies accountable for putting consumers first.

The following bills are included in this package:

The Make Data Centers Pay Act would protect Virginians from rising utility bills by requiring medium and large data centers to pay the full cost of the power generation, transmission lines, and grid upgrades needed to serve them.

The Lower Electricity Bills Act wouldforce utilities to use low-cost modern technologies whenever they build or upgrade transmission lines, and to deploy them wherever the benefits outweigh the costs. Companies that fail to make these improvements will face penalties from federal regulators.

The Smart Transmission Line Placement Act would cut unnecessary red tape by exempting transmission line upgrades within existing right-of-way corridors from lengthy federal reviews. This policy improvement would make it easier for utility companies to boost grid capacity by modernizing infrastructure already in place rather than building new projects.

The Local Transmission Accountability Act would strengthen oversight of utility companies’ local transmission projects to help prevent unnecessary infrastructure spending from driving up electricity bills for consumers. Utility companies that start projects that harm local ratepayers will face steep fines.

BACKGROUND

Vindman has long been a champion for holding data centers and electric utilities accountable.

He introduced the Make Data Centers Pay Act to protect hardworking Virginia families and small businesses from being forced to shoulder the rising electricity costs associated with the growing electricity demands of data centers.

He also introduced the Smart Data Center Policy Act to prevent data center development near neighborhoods, schools, and parks.

Vindman introduced the Home Energy Affordability Act to limit how often utilities can change residential utility rates and change prices for everyday Virginians, as well as the Utility Hikes Transparency Act, which would create the first comprehensive, machine-readable federal database of retail utility rate changes in the United States.

He has also fought against corruption in the energy sector by championing the Energy Utility Lobbying Ban Act, which would bar former government officials from lobbying on behalf of the companies they used to regulate.

What’s more, Vindman was the first member of Virginia’s congressional delegation to publicly oppose the proposed merger between NextEra and Dominion Energy, raising concerns about its potential impact on electricity rates and Virginia consumers.

He delivered remarks at a Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) public hearing on the proposed merger, urging regulators to reject the proposal and put the interests of ratepayers ahead of corporate profits. Vindman submitted official public comments to the SCC urging them to block the NextEra-Dominion merger.

title: China and the U.S. are still the biggest polluters, but only China is doing better - WVXU
description:
The rise of electric vehicles means China is also reducing its oil use.
But last year, U.S. emissions went in a different direction.
U.S. greenhouse gas emissions rose in 2025, as the country burned more coal for power and oil and gas for heating.
Two-thirds of passenger vehicle sales in China are now electric vehicles, according to recent data from the China Passenger Car Association.
China will be promoting trade of its clean tech technologies at the conference, says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
text:
As more than 200 countries meet in Turkey for the annual United Nations climate talks, COP31, the two largest emitters of greenhouse gases remain China and the United States. Now the countries' stories are diverging.

For years, China's climate pollution was growing, driven by increased coal use. But for the past two and a half years, China's emissions have been flat or falling.

"And that is a remarkable change," says Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

China is driving down emissions by increasing renewable energy and batteries, which is displacing coal. The rise of electric vehicles means China is also reducing its oil use.

"Those are bigger reductions than we expected," Myllyvirta says, "and I think anyone expected."

But last year, U.S. emissions went in a different direction. U.S. greenhouse gas emissions rose in 2025, as the country burned more coal for power and oil and gas for heating. A recent report from United Nations scientists notes that the U.S. sticks out as the only major economy where planet-warming pollution increased significantly last year.

This year, emissions in the U.S. are projected to fall slightly. The country will likely burn less coal than last year. But the U.S. could reduce its emissions more if it were deploying large-scale renewable energy and batteries like China, says Alex Wang, a professor at UCLA Law and an expert on Chinese climate policy.

The problem, Wang says, is the U.S. hasn't had long-term policy support for these climate technologies. The Biden administration increased funding for solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles. The Trump administration reduced that funding and created regulatory hurdles for those industries.

" What we're suffering through these days is the policy whiplash that comes with the political divisions in the U.S.," Wang says.

Here are the four things you need to know about U.S. and Chinese emissions.

China had long-term planning

China started building the infrastructure that is allowing it to reduce emissions about twenty years ago. Back then, China was still known as a manufacturer of low-cost items. Air pollution in major Chinese cities was also reaching record levels.

Chinese leadership made policies to tackle both the country's economic identity and its air quality. Five-year plans from the central government helped provinces pivot into the clean energy sector.

"Because the policy direction was so consistent and clear," Wang says, "they used that to drive the development of all of these industries that really didn't exist before."

The government set up nationwide supply chains for technologies like solar panels, batteries, wind turbines and electric vehicle manufacturing. Today, China is the unparalleled global leader in producing, deploying and exporting these clean energy technologies.

"On the electrification front, they're going gangbusters," Wang says.

These technologies are helping China reduce its emissions, Myllyvirta says. His research group found that last quarter China's emissions dropped 3% – the largest decline since the COVID-19 pandemic.

In the power sector, emissions are falling as coal use decreases and solar, wind, and nuclear energy increase. China has built many new coal plants in recent years, but they often don't run at full capacity and instead are used for backup generation.

Industries like cement and steel manufacturing are also reducing climate pollution. In the transportation sector, electric vehicles are displacing demand for gasoline and diesel. Two-thirds of passenger vehicle sales in China are now electric vehicles, according to recent data from the China Passenger Car Association.

The U.S. has flip-flopped, experts say

While China has consistently invested in clean technologies, that hasn't been the case in the U.S. The U.S. has struggled to scale up climate tech industries that reduce emissions because of flip-flopping by the federal government, Wang says.

Under the Biden administration, Congress passed new financial incentives for renewable energy and electric vehicles, and policies that cut greenhouse gas emissions in sectors like the oil and gas industry. The Trump administration has reversed those policies, putting up roadblocks for solar and wind projects, canceling tax breaks for home solar and electric vehicles, and proposing to cut regulations on methane — a super planet-heating gas.

The Trump administration frequently cites its "energy dominance agenda," which prioritizes keeping coal plants running.

Asked about increased U.S. greenhouse gas emissions last year, White House spokesperson Taylor Rodgers wrote in an email to NPR, "The United States is in a position of strength thanks to the President's energy dominance agenda which has unleashed affordable, reliable, secure energy sources. America is the world's leading producer and exporter of oil and gas, and many nations rely on the United States for their energy supply."

This is a growing problem as the country builds more energy-hungry data centers, says Ben Haley at consulting firm Evolved Energy Research. Most of those data centers are now being powered by fossil fuels like natural gas and coal.

"The pace and scale at which they come online tends to increase emissions," Haley says. "You can't really match that with clean energy deployment at scale, currently."

A new study finds that carbon dioxide emissions from about 400 large U.S. data centers equal almost as much as an entire country like Denmark.

Chinese exports equal emissions reductions

Wang says it's great that China's emissions seem to be plateauing. But he says, "We shouldn't forget the fact that their emissions really are outsized compared to the rest of the world."

Still, the country is exporting clean technologies like solar, batteries and electric vehicles to countries including Pakistan, Nepal and the Philippines. That's helping these countries reduce their dependency on fossil fuels.

Chinese clean tech exports have only increased since the beginning of the U.S. war with Iran, says Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember.

The ongoing U.N. climate talks in Turkey will have a large emphasis on getting countries to commit to increasing electrification. China will be promoting trade of its clean tech technologies at the conference, says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

As China gets a bigger share of the global clean tech trade, it will be harder for the U.S. to compete, he says.

"This dominating position will not go away, and if anything, it will be further consolidated in the coming years," Li Shuo says. "The U.S., I think, will struggle."

title: The grid will fall short of AI's power needs. These 6 resources can close the gap.
description:
I would start somewhere else: Assume the grid will fall short, then ask how to close the gap — and how fast.
6 ways to close the gap, and where each runs out The first four options below address serving data centers through the grid.
Gas offers firm power and a familiar path, but gas turbine supply has become the constraint.
Reliable operation also requires sufficient on-site backup capability or access to grid power during outages and maintenance.
For data center operators, that is a choice between some power sooner and firm power later.
text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Simon Irish is CEO of Terrestrial Energy, a developer of small modular nuclear reactors.

Most planning for artificial intelligence’s electricity demand starts with a forecast and asks whether it is right.

I would start somewhere else: Assume the grid will fall short, then ask how to close the gap — and how fast.

The evidence supports that starting point. McKinsey & Company estimates the U.S. will need 30 GW to 55 GW of additional capacity by 2030 as data center demand grows and aging plants retire. PJM Interconnection, the largest U.S. grid operator, has already seen the impacts of this trend. Its latest capacity auction fell about 6.6 GW short of its reliability requirement and cleared at the price cap.

Forecasts can be wrong, and requested load can be speculative or duplicative. But the PJM result is a market outcome, not a forecast. The useful question is which tools can close the gap, by when and at what cost.

6 ways to close the gap, and where each runs out

The first four options below address serving data centers through the grid. The final two consider generation at or near the data center, with an optional grid connection. These categories overlap; on-site generation is a delivery strategy, not a generation technology, and can use multiple technologies.

Flexible demand. Duke University’s Nicholas Institute estimates the grid could absorb 76 GW of new load if that load accepted curtailment averaging 0.25% of annual consumption, in events of about 1.7 hours. It is the fastest option because it needs no new generation. It makes better use of capacity already on the grid.

But that capacity is finite, and beyond it, further load growth requires new supply. There is also a practical hurdle; to date, many data centers have shown little willingness to curtail AI workloads, because the value of computing far exceeds the cost of power.

Existing nuclear plants. Increasing output at operating plants through uprates and restarting closed plants can add reliable electricity supply, while extending operating licenses keeps existing plants running. A U.S. Department of Energy initiative targets 5 GW of added capacity at existing nuclear plants by 2029, and DOE has closed a $1.9 billion loan to restart Iowa’s Duane Arnold plant, returning 615 MW to service.

The limit is opportunity: Few operating plants remain candidates for significant uprates, and restarts are underway at nearly every plant where one is practical.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Utility Dive free daily newsletter

Natural gas. Gas offers firm power and a familiar path, but gas turbine supply has become the constraint. GE Vernova’s gas turbine backlog and slot reservations reached 116 GW at midyear 2026, and the company has said a heavy-duty turbine ordered today will not arrive until 2031. Buyers also take on fuel-price exposure and decades of emissions.

Wind, solar and storage. These resources can be deployed quickly and at scale. Their limit is that data centers require dependable power around the clock, so matching that requirement takes substantial overbuilding, energy storage and transmission infrastructure to deliver the same capacity as a firm resource.

On-site generation. Building a power plant at a data center can bring electricity online sooner by avoiding some grid upgrades and connection delays, where permitted.

However, it does not speed up equipment deliveries. An on-site gas turbine plant faces the same turbine shortages as one supplying the grid. Reliable operation also requires sufficient on-site backup capability or access to grid power during outages and maintenance. If a project relies on the grid, developers need clear terms defining that access and its cost.

Advanced nuclear energy. Advanced reactors offer firm, clean power and can be built as a fleet. They can serve data centers directly, with an optional grid connection. They will not close the gap this decade, and their real test is cost at fleet scale.

Guiding principles

No single option is fast, firm and large enough on its own. Three principles follow.

Match each solution to its clock.

Flexible demand, uprates at existing nuclear plants, and new wind, solar and storage can help meet near-term electricity needs.

Read More in Generation

Natural gas and on-site generation can help fill the gap while longer-term resources are developed, but only if equipment deliveries, permits and grid interconnection align with the data center’s schedule.

Advanced nuclear energy can contribute in the 2030s and beyond.

Utilities must plan now for both natural gas and advanced nuclear energy. DOE’s long-term modeling indicates 550 to 770 GW of additional firm, clean generating capacity could be needed by 2050, with advanced nuclear energy providing about 200 GW.

Infrastructure built to meet an immediate shortfall should also have a useful role later. A gas plant could provide firming capacity or operate during periods of peak demand as longer-term supply becomes available.

Make flexibility the price of speed. Utilities can offer earlier interconnection to customers accepting curtailment under defined, metered and enforceable terms. For data center operators, that is a choice between some power sooner and firm power later. Customers that can curtail load may get power sooner; those that cannot must wait for firm supply. This converts flexibility from an assumption into a contract and rewards developers whose flexibility is real.

Secure the long-lead items for firm, clean power now.Buyers who reserved gas turbine production slots early secured earlier deliveries; those ordering now may have to wait until 2031.

Firm, clean power has its own long-lead items, including fuel supply and equipment manufacturing capacity. Utilities and data center operators can sign reservation or offtake agreements that give suppliers the demand signal to build capacity before it is needed.

Read More in Generation

These principles also address the forecast debate. Some investments — flexibility, uprates and transmission — remain valuable across demand scenarios. Others are options worth buying, such as reservations for firm supply in the 2030s and beyond.

And some are bets to avoid: irreversible commitments sized to a demand number that may not arrive. If forecasts prove too high, the cost is the price paid to preserve an option. If they prove right and no one bought the option, the cost is the kind of shortfall PJM has already seen.

name: Clean Energy
title: Opinion: Care about affordability? Then you have to care about this. - The Salt Lake Tribune
description:
The status quo has left us completely unable to build the energy system we need.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is the joint work of Sens.
A significant backlog of energy projects is waiting to be built or hooked into our overloaded, archaic energy grid.
At the end of 2025, more than 85% of the energy projects seeking to get plugged into the grid were renewable sources and storage.
The fossil fuel projects of the past are already built and connected; the green energy projects being built are not.
text:
When I say it this way, it sounds like such an easy call: The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 is the largest reimagining of the federal permitting process in a generation. It would make it far easier to build new energy infrastructure of all kinds: wind and solar farms and interstate transmission lines and, yes, natural gas pipelines. It would make it easier to build much else, too: rail and transit infrastructure and affordable housing and broadband internet.

The bill represents Democrats and Republicans deciding that the fight over what gets built should play out in elections and markets rather than in the bowels of administrative agencies and courts. It should be driven by what people want, in public, rather than what they can block, often in private. I do not expect, in every case, that that would lead to outcomes I like. But leaving the system unchanged is a guarantee of calamity. The status quo has left us completely unable to build the energy system we need.

Still, I don’t want this column to read as more confident about this bill than I really am. It is more than 400 pages, with much of it dedicated to technical changes to other laws. I’ve been unnerved, while reporting this story, by Capitol Hill staff members telling me precisely opposite things about the same provisions. Legislation at this scale rarely plays out exactly as its architects expect. The laws that the act would revise, like the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act, work quite differently today than what was expected when they were signed into law in the 1960s and ’70s.

But at its core, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would do the same thing over and over again: It would make it faster and simpler to build energy infrastructure by rolling back the opportunities for delays, lawsuits and vetoes that have proliferated in recent decades. This is a bill that would remove procedural and legal obstacles to building. It would not decide what gets built. Whether the act is part of a Green New Deal or a natural gas resurgence would depend on what Democrats do next.

The single most important climate policy going forward is for Democrats to win elections so that they have the power to set climate policy in the future. The Democrats who won Senate seats, or look likely to win them, in Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas and Alaska ran on an all-of-the-above energy strategy. Democrats everywhere ran on putting affordability first.

The bill is an early test of whether they meant it. A Democratic Party that was saying what voters wanted to hear, but has no intention of doing what voters asked them to do, will not hold power for long.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is the joint work of Sens. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.; Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I.; Mike Lee, R-Utah; and Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va. For Heinrich, the story of this bill goes back almost two decades, to when he first saw the way that delay and lawsuits could be weaponized even against clean, pro-labor projects.

“When I got elected to Congress in 2008,” Heinrich said, “there was an opportunity to build a clean energy project in New Mexico and connect it to the rest of the country with a 550-mile transmission project. Today it’s in service with roughly $20 billion of economic impact across a couple of different states and one of the largest project labor agreements in the history of the Southwest. But it took us roughly 18 years to permit and build — and the build part was like two years and the permit part was like 16 years. That, to me, is the nut that we’re trying to solve.”

The National Environmental Policy Act, for example, originally provided examples of environmental reports that were less than a dozen pages. Now those reports can stretch hundreds or thousands of pages, take years to complete, and invite interminable litigation. That can be deployed to stop bad projects, but it is an obstacle for good ones, too. NEPA, as it is known, does not impose an environmental benefit test on projects. The requirements are purely procedural. Agencies are trying to prevent grounds for a lawsuit or an administrative delay, not prove their project is green. That’s why NEPA, despite its name, can be wielded with equal ferocity against clean and dirty projects alike.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, creates a more neutral and swift permitting system, and green energy advocates believe that system would be of particular benefit to their technologies. A significant backlog of energy projects is waiting to be built or hooked into our overloaded, archaic energy grid. That backlog is overwhelmingly tilted toward green energy. At the end of 2025, more than 85% of the energy projects seeking to get plugged into the grid were renewable sources and storage. The fossil fuel projects of the past are already built and connected; the green energy projects being built are not.

I talked to several Democrats who are skeptical of the act, and those conversations always began the same way — with President Donald Trump. Asked whether he would approve new wind turbines on federal land under the bill, he said, “No, I will not approve wind turbines.” When he was informed that approving those turbines was part of the deal, he doubled down: “I know, but I won’t approve it.”

It’s hard to argue with the Democrats who think it’s crazy to make a deal with a president who has made it clear that he has no intention of upholding his side of the deal, and has often acted lawlessly to boot. “I cannot support a bill that relies on a handshake promise from the same administration that’s spent the last two years waging a war on new clean energy projects to hold up its end of the bargain, and continues to do so even after negotiating the reform proposal,” Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said in a statement.

But capriciously blocking wind power is what Trump is doing now. The bill makes it harder for Trump to sit on wind projects in the future. “His departments have to give an answer, yes or no, and the answer has to be justified, and there’s a time frame by which they have to deliver it,” said Daniel Palken, an energy permitting expert at Arnold Ventures (and a former Senate staffer). The remedies here become severe, including one that says agency heads cannot travel more than 25 miles from their headquarters if a permit is more than 60 days delayed.

There are also fears that Trump will use the bill to pillage public lands. The concern here is somewhat complex. The bill does not remove any protections that public lands currently enjoy. The worry, rather, is that there could be an unintended consequence from something that the Democrats wanted.

Parts of the bill attempt to ensure something called “permit certainty,” wherein a future (or current) president can’t upend existing permits in a discriminatory manner. The genesis of those sections of the bill is that Trump has done exactly that to wind and solar projects, and Democrats want him to stop.

But that’s created a new fear: That Trump would issue all manner of illegal permits to drill on public lands that will then be protected by the bill’s provisions in the future. That is the question that has caused me the most concern while reporting this column. If that’s true, then yes, that’s a huge problem. But the bill’s architects don’t think it’s true. The bill was amended to make it clearer that illegal permits would not stand and were not protected by courts. But multiple environmental groups and Democratic offices still fear the possibility. Further amendments, like one that’s been offered by Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., stating this even more sharply would be welcome.

That said, if Trump were going to be president for another decade, I would be less eager to see this legislation pass. But it will be future presidential administrations that most benefit from the bill, as many of the new rules and new capacities the act envisions will take years to write and implement.

A conversation I had with Brian Deese, director of the National Economic Council under President Joe Biden, drove this home for me. When I asked him what difference the act would have made to the green energy infrastructure push under the Biden administration, he said that “almost everything would have been different.” But it would have depended on when the act would have passed. “If we had passed something like this bill alongside the Inflation Reduction Act, it would have been good,” he said, referring to the 2022 law that included significant incentives for clean-energy projects. “If we passed it two years before the IRA, it would have been game changing.”

That, to me, is the single best argument for the act. If you believe that Democrats will build on the blue tsunami and take the presidency in 2028, perhaps with even larger House and Senate majorities, then the case for this bill is extremely strong. It’s a force amplifier of anything they might do on clean energy. That’s why Janet Yellen and Jared Bernstein, who led Biden’s Treasury Department and his Council of Economic Advisers, both backed the bill.

Others fear that we are too far down a calamitous climate path to allow new natural gas to be built, and that the surge in artificial intelligence data center construction makes the legislation more dangerous than it might have been a few years ago. But I don’t see a scenario in which new demand for energy would not be met. The data center build-out might be stopped by communities organizing against their construction. But once they are approved and built, they are going to be powered.

The problem, right now, is that we cannot meet enough new demand — whether from data centers or electric vehicles or heat pumps or anything else — with renewables. What the act might make possible is the construction of an energy grid where there is enough renewable power to meet new demand. In the absence of that energy system, new demand would be met by fossil fuels. And the absence of that system describes our reality today.

“The gas build-out we’re seeing today is symptomatic of our inability to build enough electricity infrastructure,” said Jane Flegal, a senior fellow at the Searchlight Institute. “The reason there is so much gas build-out is there’s a sudden surge in demand for electricity and our system for siting and permitting renewables and building transmission lines is totally broken. This bill will go a very long way to fixing that.” (It’s also worth noting that the bill includes a provision forcing new data centers to swallow the transmission costs they impose on the grid, rather than making ratepayers foot part of the bill, as often happens now.)

The Senate vote to move forward on the bill was telling. Among Democrats from states that went for Kamala Harris by 10 points or more, the vote was 2-1 against it; among Democrats representing more purple or red states, it was 2-1 in favor. Something Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said last week has been ringing in my ears: “If affordability doesn’t prevail, we’re in trouble,” he said. “We cannot impose on people what we think is important. We have to listen to what’s important to them and then deliver.” (Schumer voted to advance the bill.)

Some Democrats want to wait for the new Congress to be seated so they can renegotiate this bill to gain more leverage and extract better terms. That makes sense in theory, but most analysts I talk to think it would fail in practice. This bill was a bipartisan project from the start. Whitehouse, one of its architects, is perhaps the most relentless climate voice in the Democratic caucus. And it’s hard to imagine the conditions for dealmaking improving when Democrats begin investigating Trump and his administration and family in earnest and as Stephen Miller settles into his new role as White House chief of staff. We are entering an era of renewed partisan collision, not a renaissance of bipartisan dealmaking.

“ The folks that argue that there’s going to be some mythical negotiation in the future, I think that’s just absolute lunacy,” said Rep. Josh Harder, D-Calif., who chairs the Build America Caucus. To Harder, it’s a mistake to present this bill as a painful compromise: “ It’s so rare in Congress that you have an opportunity to strengthen the economy and accelerate growth, create jobs, reduce climate emissions and lower prices for consumers all at the same time. We’ve got to pass this.”

description:
Kate MacArthur, president and CEO of the Ascension Economic Development Corporation, is working on both fronts: building relationships with companies considering the parish while helping existing businesses find room to grow.
One recruitment strategy involves working with lead-generation consultants who identify about 20 potential foreign direct investment prospects annually.
At the same time, Ascension Economic Development aims to meet with 35 to 50 existing companies annually through its business retention and expansion program.

text:
Some of Ascension Parish’s future employers may be years away from choosing a location. Others are already here, trying to find enough skilled workers or resolve an infrastructure problem before they can expand.

Kate MacArthur, president and CEO of the Ascension Economic Development Corporation, is working on both fronts: building relationships with companies considering the parish while helping existing businesses find room to grow.

One recruitment strategy involves working with lead-generation consultants who identify about 20 potential foreign direct investment prospects annually. The consultants evaluate companies that may consider locating along the U.S. Gulf Coast within the next five years, helping the parish build relationships with prospects well before they make location decisions.

“These are kind of long-term relationships,” MacArthur says. “As factors move forward, we have that ability to make sure they’re aware of our assets, what we have here, and continue to talk with them throughout their process of evaluating different site location options for their business.”

The organization also responds to site-selection inquiries, participates in industry conferences and trade shows, and works with Louisiana Economic Development and the Greater Baton Rouge Economic Partnership to identify opportunities.

Recruitment priorities include specialty chemical manufacturing, critical minerals processing, advanced manufacturing, warehousing and distribution. MacArthur says the parish wants to build on its roughly 60-year history in chemical manufacturing, leveraging its existing industrial infrastructure and technically skilled workforce to attract complementary businesses.

“We always will want to build off of our existing competency,” she says. “We have a very skilled and trained workforce, and that’s a big advantage.”

Electric vehicle battery components and other technologies that rely on chemical processing are among the opportunities being pursued.

At the same time, Ascension Economic Development aims to meet with 35 to 50 existing companies annually through its business retention and expansion program. Those confidential meetings help identify operational challenges, workforce shortages and infrastructure concerns that could affect a company’s ability to remain and grow in the parish.

“The ultimate goal is to help the businesses that are here continue to grow,” MacArthur says. “We want them to invest and we want them to hire more people.”

The organization works with partners such as Entergy and River Parishes Community College to address issues ranging from electric service disruptions to shortages of specialized workers. It also informs companies about available incentives, workforce training programs and other resources that could support expansion.

While Louisiana offers most business incentives, Ascension’s Industrial Development Board can pursue payment-in-lieu-of-tax agreements, and local governments can establish economic development districts when projects warrant additional flexibility.

MacArthur says proposed incentives undergo project-specific financial analysis to ensure anticipated tax revenue outweighs the cost of incentives. Decision-makers also consider broader community benefits, including job quality, economic diversification and long-term investment.

Moving forward, the organization plans to continue its recruitment and retention strategies while working with regional and state partners to prepare development-ready sites and respond to changing industry demands.
