text:
Teams from Ole Miss and Southern Miss have partnered to determine whether the Orca Basin could hold valuable critical minerals. Finding extractable critical minerals in the Orca Basin could be a boon to U.S. mineral supply chains and national defense.

Mississippi researchers are investigating whether an unusual deep-sea brine basin off the coast of Louisiana naturally concentrates critical minerals, including lithium.

University of Mississippi geologist Leo Macelloni is partnering with researchers from the University of Southern Mississippi to determine whether the Orca Basin could hold valuable critical minerals, using a $950,000 contract from the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, now called Marine Mineral Administration.

The three-year project will combine water chemistry, seafloor mapping and deep-sea sampling to study whether and how valuable elements accumulate in brine pools.

“We are working together to understand if the brine pools in the Gulf contain significant amounts of critical minerals like lithium,” said Macelloni, director of the Mississippi Mineral Resources Institute and Center for Marine Resources and Environmental Technology at Ole Miss. “These minerals are incredibly important for modern technology – everything from cell phones to car batteries to data chips – but the environment of brine pools is also very delicate.

“So, the challenge is not only to find these minerals, but to determine best practices to steward these resources while preserving marine life.”

Brine pools are deep-sea environments of extremely salty water. The high salt content makes the deep-sea water denser than the surrounding water, forming distinct pools and lakes. These sites are rare worldwide, but common in the Gulf.

Macelloni and USM professors Wokil Bam and Stephan Howden are planning a 15-day research expedition this year to collect water and brine samples. They hope to determine whether critical minerals are forming in one such pool in the Orca Basin.

“The Orca Basin is a fascinating natural laboratory because of its unusual geology and chemistry,” he said. “What makes the Orca Basin especially interesting is that these processes occur within a relatively confined environment, allowing us to investigate the mechanisms responsible for mineral transport and enrichment in greater detail.”

The Orca Basin is about 7,800 feet deep. The brine pool at its base is some 650 feet thick and covers nearly 50 square miles.

“In many ways, the Orca Basin provides a natural experiment for understanding processes that may also occur in other deep-sea environments worldwide,” Bam said.

Critical minerals have been found in brine fluids located beneath land – such as in the Smackover Formation beneath much of central Mississippi – but have not been confirmed in deep ocean brine pools, Macelloni said.

“Because conditions are so extreme there, we need to characterize the area before we can study it further,” he said. “We plan to collect samples of water and sediment to reconstruct the conditions of the area and assess the chemistry of the brine.”

If critical minerals are found in the basin, future projects could explore how to best extract those resources without damaging the brine pool’s environment, Macelloni said.

Finding extractable critical minerals in the Orca Basin could be a boon to U.S. mineral supply chains and national defense, but that is not the study’s only goal, Bam said.

“For us, success is not necessarily about discovering a large mineral deposit,” he said. “It is about developing a better understanding of the processes that control how critical minerals are transported, redistributed and concentrated.

“Even if the concentrations are too low for commercial extraction, we will gain valuable insight into how critical minerals behave in deep-ocean environments.”

This article is republished courtesy of Ole Miss.

title: EV Owners Fear Myths More Than Cost or Charging | The Truth About Cars
description:
Ask people who already drive electric cars what stands in the way of wider adoption, and they do not point first to sticker prices or missing chargers.
It collected answers from 29,547 drivers of electric cars across 34 countries.
More striking, over 2,000 of those vehicles had passed 100,000 miles and still held 91% of their original capacity.
There is a genuine operational point buried in the hype: EV battery fires are harder to extinguish and can reignite, requiring special procedures from emergency responders.
The best-selling Tesla Model Y clears its debt after about 13,000 miles of UK driving.
text:
Ask people who already drive electric cars what stands in the way of wider adoption, and they do not point first to sticker prices or missing chargers. They point to misinformation. In the 2026 Global EV Driver Survey, 74 percent of respondents named myths as a top barrier to adoption in their own country, well ahead of the 49 percent who cited purchase price and the 47 percent who flagged charging access in apartment buildings. Respondents could pick up to three answers, so these are not mutually exclusive, but the ranking is telling.

The survey is not a small one. It collected answers from 29,547 drivers of electric cars across 34 countries. Participants signed up through EV associations and through volunteers and enthusiasts, and the worldwide results were weighted by each country's share of the EV fleet. A caveat worth keeping in mind: this is a sample of people who already own EVs, so it captures owner opinion instead of pinning down why non-owners stay away. Still, the people living with the technology have a clear read on what the rest of the world gets wrong about it.

The top misconception, by a wide margin, concerns the battery. Battery longevity was flagged by 72 percent of respondents as a myth others hold. The idea that EVs catch fire more easily than other vehicles was named by 58 percent. Nearly half, 45 percent, pointed to the claim that widespread EV adoption would collapse the electricity grid. And 40 percent named the belief that EVs do not help the climate.

What stands out is the gap between what owners say others believe and what owners themselves worry about. Battery lifespan tops the list of perceived myths, yet 65 percent of respondents rejected any suggestion that they feared for the lifespan of their own battery, while only 18 percent agreed. The people who have the most direct experience with these batteries are the least afraid of them.

Owners are not in denial about everything, though. They acknowledged that EVs still carry high prices and that charging is hard for anyone without somewhere to plug in at home.

This is the fear owners most often say others carry, and it is the one their own experience most directly contradicts. Batteries lose capacity gradually, and heat and hard charging speed that up. But most modern traction batteries do not become unusable after a few years, and replacing a whole pack outside of warranty defects is rare.

The warranty floor sets a useful baseline. EV battery packs are warranted for a minimum of 8 years or 100,000 miles, and the large majority hold onto most of their capacity long past that mark. The assumption that buyers will face a new battery bill a few years after purchase is itself a persistent misconception.

Real-world fleet data backs this up. Ford gathered battery health figures from 36,000 Mustang Mach-E EVs. The company found that examples from the 2021 model year held on to 92% of usable capacity on average after 5.2 years and 55,000 miles of driving. More striking, over 2,000 of those vehicles had passed 100,000 miles and still held 91% of their original capacity. If you are buying used, a battery certificate or state-of-health report is the way to confirm condition rather than guess at it.

The claim that EVs burn more easily than conventional cars is a persistent myth, and the data does not support it. The available fire figures show gasoline vehicles catch fire at a higher rate per vehicle on the road than EVs do. Insurers reach the same conclusion. The General Association of the German Insurance Industry states that studies show no greater fire risk for electric cars than for petrol or diesel vehicles, and that vehicle insurance statistics give no indication of a higher fire risk.

The fact-checks land in the same place. No examined expert report or statistic shows a higher fire risk for EVs, and vehicle fires have decreased overall even as the proportion of electric cars has risen. The perception runs backward from the evidence.

So why the perception gap? Two reasons. First, clips of electric cars on fire spread fast, and a high-voltage battery fire can look spectacular. Second, EV fires receive outsized media coverage relative to their actual frequency. There is a genuine operational point buried in the hype: EV battery fires are harder to extinguish and can reignite, requiring special procedures from emergency responders. That is a challenge for fire crews, not evidence that the cars burn more often.

The idea that electric vehicles disable the power grid is another persistent myth. The grounded version of the concern is real: more EVs and heat pumps push up electricity demand and require local grid upgrades, and grid operators do have to plan around peak loads.

The leap from there to collapse ignores how charging actually works. Not everyone drives at the same time, plugs in at the same hour, or draws full power. Charging can be shifted to nighttime, cheaper tariffs, or managed through load management, replenishing cars when demand is lower. Grid expansion and smart charging are already the standard tools for absorbing more EVs. The simultaneous national plug-in that crashes everything is a scenario nobody has managed to produce outside a headline.

Here the myth leans on a real fact and stretches it. Building an EV, especially its battery, tends to generate more carbon dioxide than building a comparable combustion car. That upfront debt is genuine. The error is stopping the accounting there.

Lifecycle studies consistently show EVs produce lower total emissions over their service life. The ICCT's 2021 analysis found a European EV would trim emissions by 66 percent to 69 percent versus a conventional car, rising to 74 percent to 77 percent by 2030 as the electricity mix decarbonizes. The ICCT also concludes that combustion cars have lifecycle emissions twice as high as their official tailpipe values, once you account for fuel production and real-world efficiency.

The carbon debt pays off quickly. A Carbon Brief factcheck found a typical EV wipes out the carbon debt from its battery in under two years, and over the full lifecycle, an EV emits around three times less carbon dioxide than an average petrol car. The ICCT puts the European break-even at around 11,000 miles. The best-selling Tesla Model Y clears its debt after about 13,000 miles of UK driving.

Flawed figures keep circulating anyway. Volvo's 2021 report estimated its electric C40 needed around 68,400 miles to break even, but researcher Auke Hoekstra found Volvo overestimated electricity generation emissions, overestimated the petrol car's fuel efficiency, and underestimated fuel production emissions. Corrected, the C40 pays off its debt after about 16,000 miles. Volvo's own report even admitted its assumptions were conservative and likely to overestimate the footprint.

Treat each myth as a stretched truth rather than a pure fabrication. Every one of these claims starts with a genuine core issue and then makes an absolute statement from it. Range, fire risk, battery aging, grid load, and raw materials all deserve serious debate rather than sensational headlines.

If you are evaluating an EV, plan range with a buffer rather than trusting the brochure figure, judge battery economics on total cost of ownership rather than list price alone, and verify a used pack's state of health before buying. When a headline tells you EVs are pointless, check whether it leans on an old study, a corrected figure, or a source with an agenda. The owners surveyed have already done that math, and it is why they are not losing sleep over their batteries.

title: Dems Should Bring Back the Grid Deployment Office - Legal Planet
description:
Restoring the Energy Department’s GDO would lay the foundation for large-scale renewable energy deployment.
Troy Jackson, who defeated Senator Susan Collins in Maine, has been a long-time proponent of renewable energy development.
Yet in their enthusiasm, Democrats should not forget the backbone of the electricity grid: transmission.
There is a smaller-scale, and much less divisive thing, that Democrats could do to achieve similar ends: reestablish the Grid Deployment Office (GDO).
With renewed control over the budget, Democrats should push for a restoration of funding to the Department of Energy, coupled with a demand for the revival of the Grid Deployment Office.
text:
Restoring the Energy Department’s GDO would lay the foundation for large-scale renewable energy deployment.

Renewable energy advocates received welcome news last week, as Democrats swept both the House and Senate in a historic repudiation of the incumbent administration. Solar and wind have gained some reliable supporters. Troy Jackson, who defeated Senator Susan Collins in Maine, has been a long-time proponent of renewable energy development. Sean McCann, who won Michigan’s fourth district, explicitly campaigned on developing renewables and nuclear to support US energy independence. Already, talk of restoring tax credits for green energy production has begun. As electricity demand continues to grow, expanding our clean generation fleet is a sensible idea to keep rates affordable without growing carbon emissions.

Yet in their enthusiasm, Democrats should not forget the backbone of the electricity grid: transmission. The buildout of renewable energy today is not hampered primarily by costs—photovoltaic solar is already the cheapest source of energy, with onshore wind not far behind. Instead, it is the long delays and high costs involved in constructing the transmission lines meant to carry renewable energy to demand centers that are stalling our transition. Accordingly, much has been made of permitting reform to speed up transmission construction. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) recently passed a procedural vote in the Senate, bringing one major piece of legislation meant to speed up transmission deployment closer to enactment. Backers of the proposed permitting reform bill, which is dividing the environmental movement, see BAAJA as a chance to speed up transmission. Yet there’s plenty not to like in the bill too. There is a smaller-scale, and much less divisive thing, that Democrats could do to achieve similar ends: reestablish the Grid Deployment Office (GDO).

Back in 2021, The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act not only awarded tax credits for renewable energy, but also funded a swath of programs meant to facilitate transmission construction. Among other things, the Act created the GDO, an office under the Department of Energy empowered to provide low-cost financing for transmission development, and even take an ownership stake in transmission projects. By doing so, the GDO could exercise eminent domain authority to speed up transmission construction in a way independent transmission developers would otherwise not be able to. In addition, the GDO conducted essential transmission planning studies that identified opportunities for interregional projects with large returns on investment.

The GDO was a promising experiment. Yet it never got the chance to prove its worth. Just a year after getting off the ground, the GDO was gutted under Trump’s restructuring of the Department of Energy. Funding for transmission planning and permitting programs by the Department fell by 90% from 2025 to 2027. The GDO’s funding was cut by 75% from 2025 to 2026, and the Office was largely dissolved into the larger Office of Electricity. In August, the Department of Energy announced it would no longer designate any areas as National Interest Electric Transmission Corridors—a function the GDO used to fulfill—which prevented FERC from exercising siting authority within those areas. More than $2 billion in Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnership grants were cancelled in October of 2025. The GDO’s Transmission Facilitation Program was not officially eliminated, but there has not been a new funding round since Trump took office.

The hollowing out of the GDO coincides with a recognition that transmission buildout is more important than ever. In 2026, the Department of Energy itself reported that there is a “pressing need” for more transmission construction as a result of data center buildout and reshoring of manufacturing. In that same report, the Department hailed the multifold benefits of interregional transmission, the construction of which the federal government is uniquely positioned to facilitate.

With renewed control over the budget, Democrats should push for a restoration of funding to the Department of Energy, coupled with a demand for the revival of the Grid Deployment Office. This may even be a bipartisan issue: Republicans have signaled a desire to work on permitting reform for transmission siting in recent months. The Grid Deployment Office offers an alternative way to speed up transmission construction—one that does not come coupled with BAAJA’s environmental concerns—and its programs would amplify the impact of the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

title: Europe EV sales jump in October as high oil prices, subsidies fuel demand - ET Auto
description:
Registrations of battery electric vehicles in Europe jumped more than 60 per cent in October from a year earlier, as consumers continued to be drawn by government subsidies on their purchase, high oil prices and availability of more affordable models.
BEVs made up around a third of cars sold across 18 key European markets during the month, data from E-Mobility Europe, New Automotive and Fier Automotive showed on Wednesday, amid discussions in Brussels to soften EU car emissions targets for 2035.
BEV registrations reached 295,252 vehicles in October, giving fully electric cars a 32.1 per cent market share So far this year, 2.33 million BEVs have been registered across Europe, up 40.7 per cent from the same period in 2025 France hit a 41.5 per cent BEV market share in October, with 61,958 registrations, while Germany's share reached 37 per cent with 94,069 registrations The Nordic market remained Europe's most electrified during the month, led by Norway at 98.8 per cent share.
Denmark, Finland and Sweden followed with 88.4 per cent, 59.9 per cent and 51.1 per cent share, respectively BEVs accounted for around half of the registrations in Luxembourg, Portugal, Belgium and the Netherlands in October The Czech Republic, Italy and Poland remained among Europe's least electrified markets at 9.3 per cent, 5.9 per cent and 6.2 per cent, respectively

title: Most Canadians Back Chinese EV Investment — With Strings Attached
description:
Of 1,604 Canadians surveyed between Friday and Sunday, 59% said they support allowing Chinese investment in Canada’s EV and battery manufacturing sectors.
Canadians are most open to Chinese involvement in EV manufacturing specifically.
The pattern is consistent: investment is acceptable if it builds something tangible for Canadians.
The Political Context The survey results landed on the same day Prime Minister Mark Carney met with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Canada’s posture on Chinese investment has been complicated by both economic need — the country wants to build a competitive EV supply chain — and security concerns that have led to restrictions in other sectors in recent years.
text:
What the Survey Found

The Angus Reid Institute and the Centre for Strategic Statecraft released the poll on Tuesday. Of 1,604 Canadians surveyed between Friday and Sunday, 59% said they support allowing Chinese investment in Canada’s EV and battery manufacturing sectors. Only 27% oppose it outright. The catch: 46% want additional security or ownership restrictions attached to any such deal.

Support is not uniform across sectors. Canadians are most open to Chinese involvement in EV manufacturing specifically. Appetite narrows considerably when the conversation shifts to electricity generation, transportation infrastructure, critical minerals, and telecommunications.

The Conditions

When asked what safeguards matter most in the automotive sector, respondents were clear. Sixty-six percent said protecting domestic jobs must be a priority. Forty-four percent want automakers required to source parts from Canadian suppliers. Forty-two percent flagged data protection — ensuring data generated inside Canada stays inside Canada.

The pattern is consistent: investment is acceptable if it builds something tangible for Canadians. Investment that extracts value or displaces workers is not.

The Political Context

The survey results landed on the same day Prime Minister Mark Carney met with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The two leaders agreed to strengthen bilateral trade ties and deepen cooperation in energy, EVs, and artificial intelligence. Canada’s posture on Chinese investment has been complicated by both economic need — the country wants to build a competitive EV supply chain — and security concerns that have led to restrictions in other sectors in recent years.

The survey suggests the public position is pragmatic rather than ideological: not a blanket no to Chinese capital, but a conditional yes tied to measurable domestic benefit.

text:
Samsung SDI will supply 16 gigawatt-hours of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries to the energy storage systems operator for its large-scale projects in the United States.

Samsung SDI sealed a deal with Jupiter Power to supply 16 gigawatt-hours of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, the Korean battery maker said on Monday.

The energy storage systems (ESS) operator will use the batteries for large-scale projects in the United States.

The size of the deal has not been disclosed, but industry estimates put it at about 3 trillion won ($2.2 billion).

Production will take place at Samsung SDI’s plant in Indiana, and delivery will take place over three years starting in 2029.

Jupiter Power — owned by BlackRock, the global asset manager, and based in Austin, Texas — has one of the largest ESS project pipelines in the United States.

Samsung SDI’s Indiana factory, which was initially planned as a joint venture with General Motors focused on EV batteries, turned into an LFP battery production line for ESS after the Korean battery maker acquired a 100 percent share in the plant.

Samsung SDI is currently the only non-Chinese maker of prismatic ESS batteries in North America.

Combining the newly inked agreement with earlier orders between the two companies, the total supply comes to roughly 27 gigawatt-hours.

The contract also adds to a run of U.S. orders for Samsung SDI, which secured an ESS LFP supply deal worth more than 2 trillion won late last year. It agreed to a 1.5 trillion won ESS battery deal with a U.S. energy company in March, as well as a 1-gigawatt-hour ESS supply contract with Alpha Omega Power last month.

text:
November 18, 2026 Ottawa, Ontario Natural Resources Canada

Canada has the abundant energy and ambition it takes to master our destiny and become an energy superpower in a rapidly changing global economy. We are accelerating major projects, attracting capital and diversifying our economic relationships. Our path to net zero supports this nation-building effort through four pillars — build, switch, transform and innovate — drawing on Canada’s strengths, resources and regional diversity to strengthen energy security, improve affordability and build a more climate competitive economy.

Key to Budget 2026’s plan is Powering Canada Strong, our National Electricity Strategy. Under the strategy, the federal government is investing over $50 billion to double our grid and connect it from coast to coast to coast; enhance domestic manufacturing; create and fill jobs for skilled workers; and reduce emissions.

To support these aims, today, at the Marine Renewables Conference in Ottawa, the Honourable Sean Fraser, Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, announced nearly $10 million in funding for 24 clean electricity and innovation projects across Atlantic Canada, including:

Nearly $8 million to support clean technology innovation in batteries and carbon capture, utilization and storage

$1.2 million to support clean electricity projects

$500,000 for Indigenous and coastal communities to engage on offshore wind development

Nearly $375,000 to support renewable energy and energy efficiency initiatives in Indigenous communities in Nova Scotia

These investments also support the Atlantic Economic Panel’s call to develop the region’s energy resources and strengthen its electricity system. In its report, Bolder Ambitions: Greater Prosperity for All, the panel highlighted reliable, affordable power and clean technology as foundations for attracting investment, growing businesses and creating jobs across Atlantic Canada.

As countries race to build cleaner, more competitive economies, the Government of Canada is investing in clean energy and innovation that will strengthen energy security, reduce emissions and ensure Atlantic Canada has reliable, affordable electricity to power communities, attract investment, create jobs and compete in a net-zero future.

text:
Government Capacity

Anyone Who Promised Government Would Work Better Should Steal This Experience

11.18.26 | 17 min read | Text by Loren DeJonge Schulman

This is the first in a three-part series on what the federal Life Experiences effort can teach anyone trying to make government deliver for people instead of for the bureaucracy. The series summarizes, excerpts, and takes inspiration from Making Government Work for People: Putting Life Experiences at the Center of Policy and Service Delivery, the retrospective Schulman co-authored with Amira Boland of New America’s New Practice Lab for the IBM Center for The Business of Government. This post covers what worked, what very much did not, and a little of what this Administration and a new Congress and even future transition teams can do about it. Part 2 applies the same lens to fields FAS works on (climate disasters, federal R&D, and clean energy deployment). Part 3 gets meta and asks what government should organize itself around.

In 2018 a farmer walking into a USDA county office could find three doors: one for the Farm Service Agency, one for the Natural Resources Conservation Service, and one for the Risk Management Agency, each handling work questions about the same farm (eventually, Farmers.gov set up a single front door for those farmers, which helped but was a Band Aid). A small group of early federal customer experience folks looked at those doors and silos and, feeling somewhat crazed, asked what felt like a reckless question: what would simplify the doors across the whole government, organizing around the moments in people’s lives instead of the boxes on an org chart?

The effort that grew out of that question eventually touched 36 agencies, dozens of states and territories, and thousands of stories. It ran out of an OMB team that started with just one person and some volunteers and less than $1M and grew to support five cross-agency teams, growing in ambition but less so in resources or enabling infrastructure. The gap between those two is why this essay exists and why I think it’s an important moment to give it attention.

Amira Boland and I just published a retrospective on the Life Experiences initiative with the IBM Center for The Business of Government, Making Government Work for People. It draws on our (mostly her) time running the work at OMB and on a March 2026 convening of more than 40 people who were part of the work. This is the much-summarized version, sharing what someone who is frustrated with how bureaucracy drives work instead of people’s experiences (Permitting? Grantmaking? Procurement? R&D?) could do radically and differently.

Teeing up a new Congress and getting a head start for 2029

November’s election sends a new Congress to Washington in January with 127 new members and also starts the clock on 2029 transition planning. A lot of the people who won promised voters a version of a government that works, whether answering the phone faster, clearing backlogs, cutting paperwork, or making help easier to access.

That’s fantastic, and they have so much fodder to build on! Starting with everything we learned from the Life Experiences initiative. It began as a pilot under the 2018 President’s Management Agenda and expanded under the next Administration’s customer experience executive order. Its Newborn Supply Kit won bipartisan support for scaling in 2025 appropriations, and states and cities (and other countries!) are excited to design their own versions of experienced-based services. We think we got a lot right and also think all these newly energized leaders are well positioned to supercharge what we were often forced to get wrong. So the lessons below are a head start for anyone who just told voters government would work better (or plans to) and now has to figure out how.

TLDR: Life Experiences

The Life Experiences initiative was an attempt to run parts of the federal government the way people experience their lives, starting from a moment in someone’s life and working backward to every program, agency, form, and contact center number they hit along the way. Instead of asking “how do we improve FEMA’s website?” a team might ask what it’s like to have a baby, or to lose a job, or to rebuild after a hurricane, and then go find out how that intersected with government interactions. After a hurricane, for example, a survivor might apply for help from FEMA, the Small Business Administration, HUD, their state, and their insurer, describing the same damage on every application. Based on that the disaster team put together a clear north star: that survivors should only have to share their information once (spoiler: they didn’t quite get there – but we could!).

The overall effort grew in two stages. Three pilots ran between 2018 to 2020 (transitioning to adulthood with an intellectual disability, seeking employment after military service, and recovering from a disaster). In December 2021, Executive Order 14058 formalized the approach, culminating in five life experience initiatives: having a child, recovering from a disaster, facing a financial shock, approaching retirement, and transitioning to civilian life.

Each life experience got a small cross-agency team made up of staff borrowed from the agencies involved, often with designers and researchers from USDS, 18F, and similar groups, all coordinated by the customer experience team at OMB. Teams spent their first several months listening – something government is strangely terrible at, at least on a consistent basis. They interviewed people across the country, sat with frontline staff who already knew what wasn’t making sense, and pulled feedback and administrative data to find any patterns. Their outputs were journey maps (which explain every step a person goes through as they navigate a government system and how that interacts with government review and decision points) and a list of “how might we” problems that seemed worth taking on with the collective might and sway of a White House-led initiative. From there teams picked fixes they could build, piloted them with willing agencies and states, and reported back to senior leaders on how to make it bigger or better. Those fixes ranged from the very small (drafting plain language on webpages that bounced people between SSA.gov and Medicare.gov) to the structural (changing how states handle Medicaid renewals so fewer eligible people lose coverage on paperwork).

Among these pilots, several found permanent homes at SAMHSA, the VA’s Veterans Experience Office, and the Administration for Community Living, and states have picked up the Newborn Supply Kit. Many other pieces–and much of the overall thesis–didn’t survive, for reasons anyone attempting this again might run into. More on that below.

We can have nice things! Ingredients for Successful Life Experience Approaches

A lot of people did this work on top of their day jobs, for years. Here’s what kept them coming back and we think serve as a baseline for anyone trying their own version.

Basic but true: a shared north star is vital. Just describing the big outcome every agency, state, and partner is aiming at, even when each takes its own route, is a set of magic words and yet often lacking in government reform. Governance charters and coordination frameworks were much harder to get anyone excited about, and much easier to drop when leadership changed. For facing a financial shock, it was “apply in 20 minutes, enroll in 24 hours, receive services within a week;” for disaster recovery, survivors should only have to share their information once during the most stressful time of their lives. Other fields could set the same kind of target and leave the methods open.

Championing specific fixes you could explain to your mom (or deputy) in a sentence. Wonks often treat government like foreign language and get lost between actions and goals, but integrating FAFSA with IRS data to make it easier to apply, changing how Medicaid renewals work to make it easier to stay enrolled, and sending a kit of supplies to families with newborns were things a skeptical deputy secretary or appropriations staffer could grasp the merit of immediately and, crucially, defend in the context of their north star.

Showing the problem mattered more than the best memos (and I can write a good memo). A video of a veteran describing their struggle to apply for benefits, or a journey map of every agency a new parent contacts in the first year, made the problems with these systems understandable to colleagues in a way briefing memos or power points just won’t. Demo days for Hill staff and gallery walks for senior leaders kept the work alive through forgetful administrative cycles and staff turnover.

Rethinking which risks count is mindblowing (complimentary). Government is built to see the risks of trying something new and almost blind to the risks of leaving something struggling as is. The early pilots asked agencies “what happens if we do NOT act?” and made the status quo something leaders had to defend. Anyone writing report language, a hearing question, or a transition memo can borrow the move by putting the cost of the current process on the record, so doing nothing stops looking free.

Flexible talent and pilots made it cheaper to say yes. Teams like USDS, 18F, the Office of Evaluation Sciences, and Lab at OPM brought skills agencies couldn’t hire fast enough for life experience initiatives, and outside partners reached communities federal teams couldn’t. That central amd outside capacity got agencies past the feeling that they were too stretched to start. Calling something a pilot let skeptical leaders participate without betting their operating model on it. But all of that requires both the flex to be available to begin with and a transition plan for sustainment.

(As always) Everything depended on the right people inside the agencies. A presidential mandate was necessary but nowhere near sufficient. The life experience initiative made progress in places where someone with operational responsibility and the ear of the Deputy Secretary could drive it. It stalled where everyone agreed it was important and but nothing really changed day to day. Peer pressure for deputies to take off their agencies hats worked, as they tended to care how the White House compared them with their peers. The work also went furthest when long term agency program staff were part of the life experiences team, sitting in on interviews, running parts of workshops, and joining design sessions, instead of receiving updates as clients or outsiders.

And the life experiences frame itself turned out to be a recruitment tool. Organizing around how people live, instead of which agency runs which program, reminded civil servants who they were serving and why they came on board in the first places.

Brakes and breaks and breakdowns: why working across agencies is so tough

The walls that life experiences teams hit were built into how the federal government organizes money, process, authority, and accountability, which means anyone trying to deliver across agency lines (in any field) will find them waiting. Learn out lessons, build better ladders and doors!

Indecision as Policy, or “Nobody” owned journeys. Accountability in the federal government runs vertically, from Congress to agencies to the programs that report up their own chains. A new parent’s experience runs horizontally across all of them. But no one’s really in charge of that overall, or often even in pieces. Charters and steering committees only gave life experiences teams permission to act differently and worked when the people on them had authority. They also took far longer to stand up than anyone expected and their hammer fades over time. Someone who woke up every day in charge of an outcome would have been the difference maker.

Money, money, money. Federal budgets are built two years ahead, so political enthusiasm for a new priority builds a long time after the relevant money is spoken for–not great for fast moving agile projects like life experiences. Individual agencies have far more resources than any central fund that can invest in novel projects, but few incentives and few vehicles to contribute to shared work, so teams assembled funding through negotiated contributions that took time (a long long time). Even cross-agency priority goal funds drew multiple rounds of review from resource management offices at OMB and agency general counsel offices, on questions as basic as whether one agency’s employee could spend time on a cross-agency project. The transaction costs of moving small amounts of money routinely dwarfed the money itself.

The drudgery of folk law. When teams asked general counsel offices “can we?” they often got answers to “should we?” Different agencies reached different conclusions about the same statutes (the Economy Act for moving money, the Paperwork Reduction Act for user research, the Privacy Act for data), and the most cautious reading usually won, and won very slowly. But worst of all, myths of what was not allowed were pervasive, referring to mystery statutes and regs that existing only in fever dreams of proceduralization. Research institutions will recognize this one – a lot of what institutions experience as federal requirements turns out to be someone’s cautious interpretation, layered on top of someone else’s who left five years ago.

Government couldn’t access what it already knew. The whole promise of organizing around life moments depends on agencies making it easier to validate or understand facts about a person or community, so that a new parent or a disaster survivor doesn’t have to prove the same thing five times or we have reliable insights on the barriers they face. In practice, every data-sharing arrangement required its own legal negotiation, and teams learned that the technical problem (moving data between systems) couldn’t be solved until someone settled the governance problem (who is allowed to use it, for what, and with what protections). Agencies define basic terms like family, household, and income in incompatible ways, often because the underlying laws were written decades apart, and there were never any serious efforts at reconciling them. Even within single programs, basic data on who is eligible and who actually enrolls often didn’t exist in usable form.

The invisible infrastructure (the things you expect exist but don’t). Most agencies couldn’t produce a definitive list of the services they provide. The research teams had already completed sat in individual drives. And (I promise this is true) teams coordinating across five departments had no shared calendar or co-editing tool or even access to a common chat platform.

States were vital partners no one has relationship with. Most of what people experience as “the government” is delivered by states, counties, Tribes, and territories, and federal agencies often lack the authority, knowledge, or influence to change how those services run. Teams had to build new networks from scratch and rebuild relationships that were initially mistrustful (and often rightfully so).

Congress was out of the loop The life experiences effort never had a real congressional engagement strategy.Agencies were often reluctant to go to the Hill with cross-agency work that didn’t fit any one committee’s jurisdiction. That also cut teams off from constituent services offices, which hear about the seams between agencies every day.

Pilots proved things and then had nowhere to go. Work that succeeded at small scale often had no route to a permanent program home before the administration ended.

Put all of that together and you get a government that can see a problem spanning five agencies and has almost no way to own, pay for, or staff the fix without driving itself crazy. But! Most of that machinery can be built and yeah, it’s not sexy, but functioning government is.

Steal this report!

Campaign promises about government working better tend to collide with the machinery described above, from folklore legal barriers to months of review on small transfers to lack of ownership. The people who built Life Experiences already found many of the potholes, so the next crew can drive around them – or better yet, fix them! If you just won on a promise like that, or you’re planning for the people who will, steal from it!

For the administration in office now

Restart Life Experiences back up using the bones already in place. The life experiences model has taken a back seat to newer initiatives, but the Trump administration has most of what it would need to restart it. EO 14058 is still on the books, OMB re-released the customer experience requirements in Circular A-11 Section 280, the America by Design executive order created the National Design Studio, and OMB memo M-26-18 is scalingLogin.gov toward a universal sign-on for public services. The newest piece is America.gov, launched in September with GSA as an AI-assisted front door to information from more than 29,000 government websites. A front door works best when what’s behind it is organized around the reasons people show up, which is what Life Experiences built maps for.

Trump Accounts offer a natural place to start. Every eligible child born from 2025 through 2028 gets a $1,000 Treasury deposit, which means every new family now has a federal financial touchpoint in a baby’s first months, tied to the Social Security number and IRS steps parents are already navigating. Building a “Birth of a Child” experience around that moment (one sign-on, one place to set up the account, and a nudge toward the health coverage, nutrition assistance, and supplies a new family may qualify for) would take the program from an account to a service.

What a new Congress can do

Here are some report’s initial recommendations (see the report for many more), sorted by the calendar the new folks in town are about to face.

Ahead of early hearings

Treat casework insights as intelligence. Every new office is building a casework operation from scratch, and caseworkers have superpowers to see the seams between agencies every day. Their insight is invaluable. Our idea to build Legislative-Executive Voice of the Customer Center has a fantastic foundation in the new Constituent Services Institute, which is helping congressional caseworkers get shared perspectives. The mature version of this would send constituent services intelligence and agency feedback in both directions and give agency staff a safe channel to flag statutory barriers.

Take a life experience approach to oversight In first hearings with agency leaders, get ready to ask who owns the handoff between their program and the next agency’s (or state or county) and what happens to a person when it fails.

Ask GAO to map one life moment across the programs a committee oversees.

Be in the room(s) where it happens. Briefings at a contact center, demo days of current delivery pilots, and site visits to field offices give committee staff something concrete to see, which is how the Newborn Supply Kit found its bipartisan support.

Test out some life experience north stars within committee work.

In the first year of the new Congress

Prioritize fixing the laws that make government listening and sharing hard. These aren’t simple or sexy, but work to reform the Paperwork Reduction Act, Privacy Act, and more so they fit iterative customer research and services that move at digital speed is worth it.

Fund shared work so agencies can stop wasting time passing the hat. Create a cross-agency service delivery fund with multi-year appropriations and transfer authority, usable for back-office and data work as well as visible front-end fixes – if that’s too much, pilot it for a specific service. Or just ask a fed about their experience with the Economy Act.

Set an expectation for aligning common benefits definitions across services, authorities, and agencies. Whether a task force, a quarterly federal review process, or an AI agent with a dream, this will simplify so much of anything else you might want to do in this space.

Make customer experience data public. Agencies report plenty of performance measures and very little about what the experience was like for the person – VA is the exception. It has statutory requirements to measure wait times, satisfaction, and complaints, and it publishes trust score you can look up by services. That data has given Congress, veterans service organizations, and VA’s own leaders a shared picture of where service is slipping. Other agencies have no such requirement. Congress could require high-impact service providers to publicly report a standard set of measures (wait times, completion rates, satisfaction and trust, and complaints), so a committee, a caseworker, or a constituent can see whether things improve over time. For cross-agency work, the same reporting would let a life experience publish a baseline against its north star and show progress against it.

Find a bipartisan opportunity around one life moment. Birth to first year already has working pilots and a kit that both parties have voted to fund! Hint hint!

Build relationships state and local delivery partners and start building infrastructure to support them: federally funded, locality delivered benefits struggle with sharing insights, lessons, vendors to avoid, open source software and common artifacts – a role Congress can help with.

Give the center of government a clear mandate for life experiences. The OMB customer experience team was the backbone for this effort, but their work is transient and Congress doesn’t expect much of their leaders for delivery. A center-of-government team with dedicated appropriations and statutory protection could cover three functions: policy (guidance and standards), implementation (hands-on agency support), and surge (responding to opportunities and crises).

For anyone planning a 2029 transition (in either party) – Amira writes more about these recommended activities in the 2026 State Transition memo on CX), but here’s a few ideas:

Use 2027 and 2028 for discovery: what’s the next group of life experiences? The Life Experiences original listening tour took about six months of interviews, feedback data, and analysis. Folks thinking about a next transition can do that before inauguration instead of spending year one on it. Pick one journey and learn it from people who have lived it, from former frontline staff and state and county administrators who know where the skeletons in the closet are (and which workarounds to scale), and from the research archives, journey maps, and public data the last effort left behind.

Arrive with a vision for integrated delivery, not just a plan for individual agencies. The Life Experiences teams spent much of their time improvising infrastructure that should have existed before they started, and a transition team can do that design work in advance. Start with a clear point of view on how delivery should work for the priority experience: what a person applies for once, what government already knows and shouldn’t ask again, and which agency or state owns each handoff. Then sketch the architecture underneath it (what data moves or how it is validated between which agencies and states, on what legal basis, with what privacy protections and consent, and through what shared systems) and an operating model for cross-agency work that covers who owns the experience, how staff and money move between agencies.

Build listening and enabling relationships with states and locality deliver partners before a governing moment.

Recruit and develop a pipeline of leaders who have a delivery and outcomes mindset, and are prepared to think of their roles in terms of the north stars they are aiming at.

Map key services before you’re responsible for them. Leaders can’t coordinate what they can’t see. SSA’s service map and the public reporting under OMB Circular A-11 Section 280 give a transition team a start to build a first-draft service index for its priority experiences, ready to hand to new agency leaders to correct and complete once the team is in place.

Pick at least one cross-agency experience and its owner before day one. Pick an operational lead, plan a path from pilot to permanent program home before launch, and draft the executive order language or management agenda priority that gives that owner authority, budget, and staff in writing. And ask “what happens if we don’t act?”!

Different hallways, same long set of doors

If you work on science, energy, or climate policy, you’ve likely seen every item on that list, just with different descriptions. Almost nothing FAS cares about gets delivered by one agency acting alone – it runs through several federal agencies and then through states, universities, utilities, contractors, and local offices, each with its own rules and its own money. Picture a researcher filling out three agencies’ versions of the same biosketch, or a homeowner chasing a heat pump rebate through a tax credit, a contractor, a permit office, and a utility. (Or a town after a flood describing the same damage to four different programs.)

In Part 2, I’’ll point the same lens at fields FAS works on: recovering from a climate disaster, getting an idea funded and into a lab, and getting clean energy infrastructure built. The journeys are different but the doors look awfully familiar.

In contrast, distributed energy resources (DERs for short) can improve overall resiliency in the face of both natural and human-made disasters, while also enabling ratepayers to take advantage of utility discounts, and even earn revenue from their personal energy assets.
The DERs field includes — but is not limited to — rooftop solar, EV charging stations, and home batteries.
DERs stakeholders have also begun moving into the distributed computing field as well.
The DERs field can include, for example, a new gas power plant commissioned to run an adjacent AI data center.

text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Centralized power plants can trip widespread brownouts or blackouts when under stress. They make fat targets for enemy weapons, too. In contrast, distributed energy resources (DERs for short) can improve overall resiliency in the face of both natural and human-made disasters, while also enabling ratepayers to take advantage of utility discounts, and even earn revenue from their personal energy assets. The DERs field includes — but is not limited to — rooftop solar, EV charging stations, and home batteries. And, we ain’t seen nothing yet. DERs stakeholders have also begun moving into the distributed computing field as well.

The World Of DERs Is Expanding

DERs first surfaced on the CleanTechnica radar in the early 2000’s during the Obama administration, when the US Department of Energy began promoting decentralized, home-and community-based energy resources as the leading characteristic of a modernized and more resilient electricity grid. Made possible by the falling cost of solar, wind, and energy storage, the agency’s embrace of small-scale, localized electricity generation was a sharp contrast with the traditional emphasis on large centralized power plants for energy security (see more DERs background here).

Nowadays the DERs field embraces practically any non-centralized power generation resource, regardless of size or type. The DERs field can include, for example, a new gas power plant commissioned to run an adjacent AI data center.

To get some perspective on the journey of DERs since the early 2000’s, consider the case of the leading rooftop solar installer Sunrun. After launching in 2007, Sunrun segued into energy storage and virtual power plants, with “virtual” referring to smart grid technology that coordinates thousands of far-flung energy producing (and consuming) devices to balance supply and demand at peak periods of consumption.

For the record, Sunrun now presents itself as a storage-first company. The company’s focus remains on renewable energy but the storage field is source-agnostic, embracing practically every energy resource on the planet.

Sunrun CEO Mary Powell also prefers to use “distributed” instead of “virtual” in reference to decentralized power systems, to emphasize that hardware is the foundational element. As of this month, Sunrun ranks as the biggest distributed power plant in the US, with solar and storage assets spread among 164,000 enrolled households.

Distributed Computing Is In The House

Back in 2021, Sunrun entered into an installation partnership with the home energy management startup SPAN, known for its next-generation home electrical panels among other products, and that layed the ground work for a partnership on distributed computing systems. Earlier this year, SPAN introduced XFRA, a new product consisting of computer nodes to be staged at homes and smaller commercial spaces to form a distributed data center. The model is similar in concept to the familiar Internet-enabled citizen scientist platform, except that XFRA deploys its own nodes instead of using a participant’s personal computer.

This past September, Sunrun announced its selection as an authorized installation partner for XFRA with a focus on new home developments, aiming for gigawatt-scale distributed computing networks beginning in Texas and other selected markets. “Sunrun’s battery-plus-solar systems will maintain reliable electricity for both the homes and the XFRA compute nodes, while preventing the overloading of local distribution infrastructure—allowing SPAN to maximize node deployment.,” Sunrun explains.

“By pairing home energy generation and storage with XFRA compute nodes, we are unlocking new economic value for our customers and for Sunrun, while also solving certain speed-to-power constraints that would otherwise limit AI deployment,” Sunrun CEO Mary Powell elaborated in a press statement.

Arch Rao, founder and CEO of SPAN, also chipped in his two cents. “We can now drastically increase our penetration of XFRA compute nodes by pairing them with Sunrun energy systems to deliver cost-effective AI compute capacity at unprecedented speed while also reducing compute cost for certain AI applications,” Rao said.

Pushing DERs To The Next Level

Back when the Energy Department initially began promoting DERs as a function of the energy transition, the agency used the term “prosumer” to describe ratepayers who are empowered to engage with their local power grid as a renewable energy producer, not simply as a passive consumer. The distributed data center adds another layer of engagement to the prosumer mix.

At a personal appearance during Climate Week in New York City in September, Powell referenced distributed computing as the latest demonstration of the company’s ongoing dialog with its customers and other stakeholders, leading to innovative new products that put more power management tools in the hands of ratepayers.

Powell reiterated the point during an appearance at the 2026 “DERVOS” summit at the Brooklyn Navy Yard on November 5, and the DERVOS gathering itself provides further insights into the widening scope of DERs activity.

“DERVOS” is a play on Davos, which is shorthand for the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum. Like the World Economic Forum, DERs stakeholders have emerged in force upon the global economy as well as here in the US, stretching far from its do-it-yourself roots in the off-gridder movement of the 1970’s.

The event itself is the brainchild of the collaborative trade organization DER Task Force. The group formally launched in 2019 but it claims roots much earlier, in the 1970’s-era New York City activist organization Energy Task Force, whose activities were highlighted by the installation of a wind turbine in the city — illegally, of course.

By the time DERVOS 2026 rolled around, the DER Task Force had become an organization with a reach far beyond New York, and it has also embraced the size-doesn’t-matter ethos under the slogan, “Everything is DER.”

“That’s what we mean by Everything is DER: not that everything is small, or even literally ‘distributed,’ but that the center of gravity is shifting toward energy resources that are closer to load and controlled by those who need the power,” the Task Force explains (emphasis theirs).

“Sometimes that shift is bottoms-up, sometimes it’s centrally planned, but either way, DERs aren’t the sideshow anymore. They’re the main event,” they add.

I’ll have much more to report from DERVOS 2026 in the coming days and weeks, but for the time being let’s go back to the foundational idea of improving grid resiliency and security. Climate change aside, in recent years Russia and the US have both provided textbook cases for transitioning out of energy systems that involve building fat, juicy infrastructure targets for attack, alongside precariously long energy transportation systems. If you have any thoughts about that, drop a note in the comment thread.

These state trifectas create a chance to enact policies to advance clean energy and respond to voters’ concerns about energy affordability.
When he took office in January 2025, Trump refused to spend money that Congress had appropriated for clean energy.
It also cut other clean energy provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act, despite the law overwhelmingly benefiting Republican-held districts.
The administration has also intervened in permitting, holding up hundreds of wind and solar power projects.
They can use this authority to investigate the administration’s refusals both to enforce environmental regulations and to spend money allocated for clean energy.
text:
The 2026 U.S. midterm elections are sweeping Democratic majorities into Congress and state legislatures across the country. That’s creating an opportunity to shift the country back to responding to climate change.

But faced with a president who staunchly opposes policies that could help slow climate change, what will these leaders with newfound power actually be able to do?

Democrats in Congress will have a stronger hand to play in their negotiations with the White House come January, and they may have leverage in pursuing climate policies during negotiations over the federal budget. Yet for the next two years, their ability to enact comprehensive climate legislation will likely be limited by President Donald Trump’s promised veto.

Beyond the federal level, six states – Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin – will have new Democratic trifectas: Democratic governors and Democratic majorities in both chambers of the legislature. These state trifectas create a chance to enact policies to advance clean energy and respond to voters’ concerns about energy affordability.

We study the politics and policies around climate change. Here are some ways we see potential for real change.

What can Congress do to restore clean energy spending?

When he took office in January 2025, Trump refused to spend money that Congress had appropriated for clean energy. The courts ruled that the move was illegal.

A few months later, Trump’s federal budget bill eliminated tax credits for producing wind power, investing in solar power and purchasing electric vehicles. It also cut other clean energy provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act, despite the law overwhelmingly benefiting Republican-held districts.

The new Democratic Congress will have authority over taxing and spending, known as the “power of the purse.”

U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, a Democrat from Maine who serves on the House Appropriations Committee, plans to withhold funding for federal agencies if the administration does not spend funds allocated to clean energy. Further, advocates believe Democrats can leverage budget negotiations with the White House to restore wind and solar tax credits.

How can Congress respond to federal agencies’ anti-environmental stances?

In his second term, Trump has doubled down on his wide-ranging effort to eliminate environmental regulations. His administration has handed out exemptions from air pollution rules to many facilities, including 71 coal-fired power plants. The administration has also intervened in permitting, holding up hundreds of wind and solar power projects.

Congressional majorities have the power to exercise oversight of federal agencies, including the ability to subpoena documents. They can use this authority to investigate the administration’s refusals both to enforce environmental regulations and to spend money allocated for clean energy.

Since Congress has limited legal means to force the administration to comply with investigations, its oversight powers give it leverage largely through bad press and lower approval ratings for Trump.

Congress has seen some movement lately on legislation that could boost renewable energy. A proposed bipartisan permitting reform bill could speed up construction of electricity transmission lines and clean energy sources such as wind, solar and geothermal power.

However, many climate advocates oppose the bill for accelerating fossil fuel projects and weakening environmental laws. For instance, opponents warn that the bill removes checks on environmentally harmful projects. U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman, a Democrat from California, has called for the new Congress to renegotiate the legislation.

What can state governments do to slow climate change?

Former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee, a Democrat, contends that “almost every (climate) policy you can think of … can be done at a state level.”

In recent years, unified Democratic control has allowed Michigan and Minnesota to pass ambitious climate laws, such as policies requiring that 100% of electricity comes from clean energy sources by 2040. Both are back under Democratic control, and incoming governors Jocelyn Benson and Amy Klobuchar each campaigned on expanding renewable energy.

Those and other states with new trifectas can now enact legislation that has been stalled for years due to partisan opposition.

In Pennsylvania, for example, Democratic lawmakers have advanced proposals that would allow community solar power, regulate data centers – these are huge electricity users – and require utilities to store excess electricity. But those proposals stalled under Republican control of the state Senate. That could change with Democrats gaining a trifecta.

Democrats also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas. Given Texas’ burgeoning wind industry and solar power potential, a shift in its energy policy could help to significantly reduce emissions. Texas’ renewable energy requirements once drove wind power expansion. But electric utilities successfully pushed for weakening the law’s targets for solar power, and the state’s Republican government repealed the policy in 2023.

While Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas has focused more on affordable energy than renewable energy, she supports wind and solar power as a means of lowering energy costs. Advocates believe her victory will prevent the enactment of two proposed bills that would impose administrative hurdles and fines on renewable energy generators.

Unlike his predecessor, Ken Paxton, incoming Attorney General Nathan Johnson has signaled that he will not bring Texas into litigation against progressive federal policies such as environmental regulations.

What do US voters want?

Climate policies are broadly popular with Americans, though less so among Republicans. They are more popular than most people and politicians think.

In recent ballot measures, such as Nevada’s 50% renewable energy target in 2020 and Washington state’s cap-and-trade repeal effort in 2024, voters have favored climate policy. However, many Americans currently rate other priorities, such as healthcare, the economy and lowering high prices, as more important.

Taken together, this polling data suggests that bold climate actions may be more likely to flop among voters if they are seen as worsening other issues that voters care about. For example, if voters worry that climate legislation will increase costs, they may be less likely to support the politicians behind it.

In contrast, if politicians can reassure voters that their climate policies are complementary to addressing other public concerns, such action may be less likely to backfire and could even boost politicians’ popularity – even potentially among Republican voters. U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island, argues that Democrats should explain how renewable energy can lower electricity prices – a current priority for voters.

Looking back, looking ahead

title: China and the U.S. are still the biggest polluters, but only China is doing better - WUNC
description:
The rise of electric vehicles means China is also reducing its oil use.
But last year, U.S. emissions went in a different direction.
U.S. greenhouse gas emissions rose in 2025, as the country burned more coal for power and oil and gas for heating.
Two-thirds of passenger vehicle sales in China are now electric vehicles, according to recent data from the China Passenger Car Association.
China will be promoting trade of its clean tech technologies at the conference, says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
text:
As more than 200 countries meet in Turkey for the annual United Nations climate talks, COP31, the two largest emitters of greenhouse gases remain China and the United States. Now the countries' stories are diverging.

For years, China's climate pollution was growing, driven by increased coal use. But for the past two and a half years, China's emissions have been flat or falling.

"And that is a remarkable change," says Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

China is driving down emissions by increasing renewable energy and batteries, which is displacing coal. The rise of electric vehicles means China is also reducing its oil use.

"Those are bigger reductions than we expected," Myllyvirta says, "and I think anyone expected."

But last year, U.S. emissions went in a different direction. U.S. greenhouse gas emissions rose in 2025, as the country burned more coal for power and oil and gas for heating. A recent report from United Nations scientists notes that the U.S. sticks out as the only major economy where planet-warming pollution increased significantly last year.

This year, emissions in the U.S. are projected to fall slightly. The country will likely burn less coal than last year. But the U.S. could reduce its emissions more if it were deploying large-scale renewable energy and batteries like China, says Alex Wang, a professor at UCLA Law and an expert on Chinese climate policy.

The problem, Wang says, is the U.S. hasn't had long-term policy support for these climate technologies. The Biden administration increased funding for solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles. The Trump administration reduced that funding and created regulatory hurdles for those industries.

" What we're suffering through these days is the policy whiplash that comes with the political divisions in the U.S.," Wang says.

Here are the four things you need to know about U.S. and Chinese emissions.

China had long-term planning

China started building the infrastructure that is allowing it to reduce emissions about twenty years ago. Back then, China was still known as a manufacturer of low-cost items. Air pollution in major Chinese cities was also reaching record levels.

Chinese leadership made policies to tackle both the country's economic identity and its air quality. Five-year plans from the central government helped provinces pivot into the clean energy sector.

"Because the policy direction was so consistent and clear," Wang says, "they used that to drive the development of all of these industries that really didn't exist before."

The government set up nationwide supply chains for technologies like solar panels, batteries, wind turbines and electric vehicle manufacturing. Today, China is the unparalleled global leader in producing, deploying and exporting these clean energy technologies.

"On the electrification front, they're going gangbusters," Wang says.

These technologies are helping China reduce its emissions, Myllyvirta says. His research group found that last quarter China's emissions dropped 3% – the largest decline since the COVID-19 pandemic.

In the power sector, emissions are falling as coal use decreases and solar, wind, and nuclear energy increase. China has built many new coal plants in recent years, but they often don't run at full capacity and instead are used for backup generation.

Industries like cement and steel manufacturing are also reducing climate pollution. In the transportation sector, electric vehicles are displacing demand for gasoline and diesel. Two-thirds of passenger vehicle sales in China are now electric vehicles, according to recent data from the China Passenger Car Association.

The U.S. has flip-flopped, experts say

While China has consistently invested in clean technologies, that hasn't been the case in the U.S. The U.S. has struggled to scale up climate tech industries that reduce emissions because of flip-flopping by the federal government, Wang says.

Under the Biden administration, Congress passed new financial incentives for renewable energy and electric vehicles, and policies that cut greenhouse gas emissions in sectors like the oil and gas industry. The Trump administration has reversed those policies, putting up roadblocks for solar and wind projects, canceling tax breaks for home solar and electric vehicles, and proposing to cut regulations on methane — a super planet-heating gas.

The Trump administration frequently cites its "energy dominance agenda," which prioritizes keeping coal plants running.

Asked about increased U.S. greenhouse gas emissions last year, White House spokesperson Taylor Rodgers wrote in an email to NPR, "The United States is in a position of strength thanks to the President's energy dominance agenda which has unleashed affordable, reliable, secure energy sources. America is the world's leading producer and exporter of oil and gas, and many nations rely on the United States for their energy supply."

This is a growing problem as the country builds more energy-hungry data centers, says Ben Haley at consulting firm Evolved Energy Research. Most of those data centers are now being powered by fossil fuels like natural gas and coal.

"The pace and scale at which they come online tends to increase emissions," Haley says. "You can't really match that with clean energy deployment at scale, currently."

A new study finds that carbon dioxide emissions from about 400 large U.S. data centers equal almost as much as an entire country like Denmark.

Chinese exports equal emissions reductions

Wang says it's great that China's emissions seem to be plateauing. But he says, "We shouldn't forget the fact that their emissions really are outsized compared to the rest of the world."

Still, the country is exporting clean technologies like solar, batteries and electric vehicles to countries including Pakistan, Nepal and the Philippines. That's helping these countries reduce their dependency on fossil fuels.

Chinese clean tech exports have only increased since the beginning of the U.S. war with Iran, says Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember.

The ongoing U.N. climate talks in Turkey will have a large emphasis on getting countries to commit to increasing electrification. China will be promoting trade of its clean tech technologies at the conference, says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

As China gets a bigger share of the global clean tech trade, it will be harder for the U.S. to compete, he says.

"This dominating position will not go away, and if anything, it will be further consolidated in the coming years," Li Shuo says. "The U.S., I think, will struggle."

title: U.S. used EV sales surge as new market struggles - Canadian Auto Dealer
authors: Canadian Auto Dealer, Todd Phillips, Perry Lefko
description:
Used electric vehicles are gaining ground in the United States, even as the new EV market struggles to build momentum following the expiration of federal tax credits.
According to Cox Automotive’s EV Market Monitor, released November 16, used EV sales climbed 73.2 per cent year over year in October to an estimated 48,678 units.
New EV sales presented a different picture.
New EV days’ supply rose 21 per cent month over month to 85 days, compared with 89 days for internal combustion engine and hybrid vehicles.
The widening gap between new and used EV sales growth highlights the importance of pricing, inventory management and the expanding selection of pre-owned electric vehicles.
text:
Used electric vehicles are gaining ground in the United States, even as the new EV market struggles to build momentum following the expiration of federal tax credits.

According to Cox Automotive’s EV Market Monitor, released November 16, used EV sales climbed 73.2 per cent year over year in October to an estimated 48,678 units. Sales were also up 4.7 per cent from September, supported by a growing selection of off-lease vehicles entering the market.

New EV sales presented a different picture. Deliveries reached an estimated 83,262 units, up three per cent from October 2025 but down 3.9 per cent from September. It marked the first year-over-year increase of 2026, although EV market share slipped to 6.2 per cent from 6.5 per cent the previous month.

Inventory levels also increased. New EV days’ supply rose 21 per cent month over month to 85 days, compared with 89 days for internal combustion engine and hybrid vehicles. Used EV supply reached 38 days, remaining below the 47-day supply for conventional and hybrid models.

Pricing trends offered another contrast. The average transaction price for a new EV increased one per cent from September to US$56,221, while the average used EV listing price declined 0.5 per cent to US$36,582.

Tesla remained the leading new EV brand, accounting for 57.5 per cent of sales. Its Model Y represented nearly 44 per cent of new EV volume.

The widening gap between new and used EV sales growth highlights the importance of pricing, inventory management and the expanding selection of pre-owned electric vehicles.
