text:
Detroit is slowly making progress on tracking the energy and water use of thousands of buildings across the city.

Currently one-fifth of 2,500 buildings in Detroit have met the reporting requirements of a 2023 ordinance spearheaded by the city’s Green Taskforce designed to audit conditions that contribute to climate change. It applies to buildings 25,000 square feet and up and requires owners to report annual energy and water use.

The effort comes with free workshops and resources for building owners.

Detroit has warmed more than four degrees Fahrenheit since 1970, contributing to more intense rainfall and extreme weather events, extreme heat that can be dangerous, and other effects on the ecosystems and humans. Residential and commercial buildings account for 40% of greenhouse gas emissions nationally that contribute to this climate warming, according to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute. In Detroit, the number is even higher: 63%.

Notices were mailed out to all business owners with qualifying buildings, said city senior energy analyst, Zahra Seblini, who administers the ordinance. And the city, in partnership with Detroit 2030 District, and the Midwest Energy Efficiency Alliance have hosted more than 50 workshops to get people oriented to the ordinance

Roughly 550 out of 2,500 buildings are compliant with the ordinance according to the city’s Office of Sustainability. Building owners who have not yet submitted their data through the Environmental Protection Agency’s energy manager system have until 2028 to do so before the city will begin issuing blight tickets for not meeting the requirements of the ordinance.

Seblini said the goal isn’t to issue a ticket though.

“The whole point of the law is to get building owners excited about energy and water tracking and decarbonization as an option for them,” she said. “A lot of business owners don’t even consider it as an option, they think they’re at the will of rising energy costs.”

Every year, Michigan utilities request and are granted increases on their energy rates. Michigan pays the most per kilowatt hour out of Midwest states.

More than 50 cities across the United States have similar ordinances. It’s common to take several years to reach majority compliance, said Seblini.

It took Ann Arbor four years to reach 50% compliance, said Connor Dailey, energy analyst for the City of Ann Arbor, which passed its benchmarking ordinance in 2021.

Lee Visci, board president for the Great Lakes Tower Condos in Harbortown on the Detroit River, said reporting for the ordinance was “rocky” when she first reported it several years ago, because every bill had to be manually entered. But now the system has been updated to automatically sync utility bills and requires no work on Visci’s part to annually report the data.

Since the ordinance passed, the city has hosted 10-15 in-person events each year to help building owners with the ordinance.

“We invite people to bring their laptops, we introduce them to the ordinance, introduce them to the city’s overall climate strategy, and then we share their role in the city’s approach to climate change and resiliency,” said Seblini.

Under the ordinance, buildings are only required to report their usage, not reduce it.

Visci questioned “the end game.” But just tracking a building’s energy reduces usage by 7%, according to the American Cities Climate Challenge. Tracking is a precondition for energy efficiency projects, awards, and grants from the city, added Seblini. The city plans to get 100% of its electricity from clean energy by 2034.

Visci said she’s looking forward to seeing how much energy other buildings of similar size use.

“What I’m hoping to see is the benefit of sharing the benchmarking data and lessons learned, so that we can all kind of be more responsible energy stewards going forward,” she said.

Seblini said it’s “a possibility” for the future to share other buildings’ usage, but that data is anonymized right now. In the meantime, the private-public partnership Detroit 2030 District, has free resources including education, building audits, and access to groups organized by building type for sharing best practices.

Already the ordinance has allowed the city to “reach building owners and direct information about the city’s goals and opportunities for energy efficiency and decarbonization, and other resources for recycling, composting, indoor air quality and resilience,” said Seblini.

The information will also help the city build its citywide decarbonization strategy, added Seblini.

description:
POSCO Group is strengthening its penetration of the Chinese market by signing a long-term lithium supply contract with China’s CATL, the world’s largest electric vehicle battery manufacturer.
Supply under the contract is currently underway, and the specific supply volume and contract amount have not been disclosed.
Along with the expansion of its production base, the group is consecutively signing long-term supply contracts with battery companies.
Following this, in August, the group signed a strategic business agreement with Chinese cathode material company Ronbay Group in the fields of lithium supply and waste battery recycling.
The two companies are pursuing cooperation to supply recycled lithium, as well as Argentine brine lithium and Australian ore lithium.
text:
Supply Runs from 2026 to 2028, Expanding POSCO’s China Market Presence

While the Deal Follows Recent Agreements With SK On and Longbai Group

POSCO Group has signed a long-term contract to supply lithium for electric vehicle batteries to China’s CATL for three years from 2026 to 2028. Photo provided by POSCO Group.

POSCO Group is strengthening its penetration of the Chinese market by signing a long-term lithium supply contract with China’s CATL, the world’s largest electric vehicle battery manufacturer. Following a lithium supply contract with SK On and business cooperation with China’s Ronbay Group earlier this year, the group is expanding its global lithium sales network by securing CATL as a client.

POSCO Group announced on Nov. 18 that it has signed a contract with CATL to supply lithium required for electric vehicle battery manufacturing for three years from 2026 to 2028. Supply under the contract is currently underway, and the specific supply volume and contract amount have not been disclosed.

CATL is a company that holds approximately a 40% share in the global electric vehicle battery market and supplies batteries to major automakers in China and other countries. Through this contract, POSCO Group plans to expand its lithium sales base in China and strengthen long-term transactions with global battery manufacturers.

Currently, POSCO Group is expanding its production capacity centered around the Hombre Muerto salt lake in Argentina, which it acquired in 2018. In 2024, the group completed the construction of its first lithium hydroxide plant with an annual production capacity of 25,000 tons, and additionally completed the upstream process of its second plant in October.

The second plant can produce 23,000 tons of lithium carbonate annually, and POSCO Group plans to link this with a subsequent process scheduled to be completed in South Korea in 2027. Once the domestic subsequent process is completed, the group will have a lithium hydroxide production system with an annual capacity of 50,000 tons, including the existing first plant.

The group is also operating domestic lithium production facilities utilizing Australian ore. POSCO Pilbara Lithium Solution, a joint venture between POSCO Holdings and Australia’s Pilbara Minerals, has built a lithium hydroxide production facility with an annual capacity of 43,000 tons at the Yulchon Industrial Complex in Gwangyang, South Jeolla Province.

Along with the expansion of its production base, the group is consecutively signing long-term supply contracts with battery companies. In February, it signed a contract to supply up to 25,000 tons of lithium to SK On by 2028. This volume is sufficient to produce batteries for approximately 400,000 electric vehicles and will be utilized in SK On’s electric vehicle battery business in Europe and North America.

Following this, in August, the group signed a strategic business agreement with Chinese cathode material company Ronbay Group in the fields of lithium supply and waste battery recycling. The two companies are pursuing cooperation to supply recycled lithium, as well as Argentine brine lithium and Australian ore lithium.

The group has secured supply contracts not only for lithium raw materials but also in the cathode material business. In September, its battery materials affiliate POSCO Future M signed a contract to supply lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode materials worth approximately 1.1 trillion won (about $825 million) to SK On. The supply period is from 2027 to 2029. Based on this, POSCO Future M plans to respond to the battery materials market for energy storage systems (ESS) as well as electric vehicles.

title: Climate Change, the Mother of All Affordability Problems - The American Prospect
description:
The reason this El Niño is so strong, simply put, is climate change.
So far, few Democrats are making the connection between climate change and rising costs for American families.
It’s bizarre because climate policy is one of the few areas where affordability benefits are readily available.
The affordability argument for climate policy, by contrast, is simple and not nearly as harmful.
Home batteries can also save lots of money protecting against grid instability caused by climate change.
text:
In October, southwest Colorado saw some of its worst flooding since the United States Geological Survey put in stream gauges over a century ago. At Pagosa Springs, the San Juan River topped out at 11,200 cubic feet per second, while in Durango, the Animas River peaked at 13,000 cubic feet per second. Both figures are the highest since 1911. The tiny Mancos River, meanwhile, peaked at 5,170 cubic feet per second—almost six times the previous record.

The resulting damage was enormous. Hundreds of homes and businesses were inundated or destroyed entirely. The San Juan River flood coated much of Bluff, Utah, with mud that turned out to be heavily contaminated with E. coli bacteria, while upstream it washed out several sections of Highway 160, a critical east-west transport artery over the mountains. Anyone needing to get from the Durango area to Colorado Springs or Denver, or vice versa, currently must take a massive detour.

The flooding was undoubtedly due to the “super” El Niño that is in progress, which may end up being the strongest ever recorded. This complex climate phenomenon has many varied effects: powerful waves and tides slamming the coast of Southern California, mild winters in the Northeast, and heavier precipitation in the typically arid Southwest. (Another one is the Pacific Ocean dumping incomprehensible amounts of heat into the atmosphere; 2027 will almost certainly be the hottest year ever recorded.)

The reason this El Niño is so strong, simply put, is climate change. And the costs are going to be astronomical.

So far, few Democrats are making the connection between climate change and rising costs for American families. On the contrary, as Robinson Meyer details, many of the more moderate candidates who won in the recent midterm election went the opposite direction, abandoning Joe Biden’s climate and renewables focus for Barack Obama–style “all of the above” energy rhetoric. That’s intended to signal a desire to lower electricity bills. But massive and frequent calamities like what transpired in Colorado obliterate any benefits from increases in the energy supply mix.

The Democratic Party has settled on “affordability” as one of their core political topics. It registers as one of the most important in polls, it was a constant refrain in the last election, and presidential contenders are already talking about it as part of their 2028 strategy—but not much with respect to climate. It’s bizarre because climate policy is one of the few areas where affordability benefits are readily available. Neglecting these potential tangible victories is not only a short-term mistake, but a medium-term disaster.

Donald Trump demonstrates the political danger of affordability politics. It is easy to run against an unpopular incumbent by promising to reverse price increases, as he did in 2024. But when you fail to do it, the people turn against you. And some of the more high-profile affordability policies are unlikely to have an immediate impact, putting those politicians who advocate for them precisely in Trump’s shoes. Trying to cut home prices through some reform of the zoning and permitting process, for instance, will take years.

Moreover, the only way to reduce all prices at once—what particularly consumerist Americans seem to want—would be to create a severe economic depression. Prices fell by about a quarter during the Great Depression, at the price of 25 percent unemployment, mass bankruptcies, and a collapsed banking system.

The affordability argument for climate policy, by contrast, is simple and not nearly as harmful. On the one hand, as noted above, climate disasters are getting worse every year, and are much more expensive than previously estimated. In addition to wildly unseasonable flooding, just the recent episodes of suffocating wildfire smoke blowing down from Canada are estimated to cost more than every previously measured climate expense put together.

If the United States does not do its part to slash emissions—and ideally help pressure the rest of the world to do the same—American towns and cities are going to suffer increasingly expensive weather disasters. There are few things less affordable than your house or business being destroyed. It doesn’t get more “kitchen-table issue” than preventing your actual kitchen table from being washed downstream along with the rest of your house.

It is admittedly difficult to establish in the public mind the financial benefit of something like a flood or a fire not happening. But on the other hand, as I have pointed out over and over for years at this point, renewable energy is now the cheapest form of electricity on the planet. Spain and Australia prove that if you add enough wind, solar, and battery capacity to drive expensive gas peaker plants out of the market, plus enough grid upgrades to transmit the electricity where it needs to go, you enjoy lower or even declining prices.

If people can be induced to switch to an EV that can be charged at home or at work, the affordability benefits compound. A somewhat higher up-front cost is compensated by dramatically cheaper fueling and maintenance costs. The up-front cost is dropping even with the expiration of the federal purchase rebate. Some newer EV models are under $30,000, with more on the way, and used ones are cheaper still. The economic benefit is strengthened still further by price security, as gas and diesel prices are set on the world market and are prone to sudden large increases, as we have seen.

Rooftop solar can cut costs as well, as people offset their electricity consumption or are paid for what they export to the grid. Home battery storage can cut costs even further. You can capture and use your solar production directly—thus avoiding strain on the grid—or in places with variable time-of-use rates, you can arbitrage electricity prices and smooth out power consumption at the same time. Better yet, the batteries can be networked together into a virtual power plant that will sell power to the grid whenever it is needed, making a tidy profit.

Add in some heat pump incentives for HVAC systems and water heaters and clothes dryers, all of which are dramatically more efficient than traditional electric appliances, and families can reduce their electric bills and/or cancel their natural gas or heating oil service entirely, saving yet more.

Home batteries can also save lots of money protecting against grid instability caused by climate change. I experienced this personally this summer when a severe climate change–fueled heat wave knocked the power out for more than 24 hours, but thanks to solar and batteries I had installed myself, we were able to keep the refrigerator and a window AC unit running the whole time. That probably saved $500 in food right there, or something like a tenth of the cost of my entire solar-battery system.

This basic formula of rooftop solar and home batteries plus electrifying all household energy needs requires a lot of up-front investment, but it pays off handsomely over five to ten years, and even more as time passes. Australia is further along this path than any other nation, and it is proving to be enormously popular.

It’s a mystery why this extremely obvious argument is not yet conventional wisdom. I suspect this is because climate policy is still being metabolized in America’s collective political unconscious as self-flagellatory, hair-shirt environmentalism, like when earnest liberals buy expensive vegan food at Whole Foods, when in reality it is about elementary self-interest.

It’s also true that somebody has to pay those up-front costs, even if they are coming down, and that gives climate policy opponents—like the people who sell fossil fuels—a great argument to make about renewables and electrification being more expensive, when over time the situation is exactly the opposite.

title: IDEM champions state-led coal ash program as groups push back - IndyStar
description:
Coal combustion residuals, commonly called coal ash or CCR, contain pollutants such as arsenic, chromium, lead, mercury and other heavy metals linked to cancer, heart disease and reproductive failure.
Hoosiers concerned over Indiana coal ash program Environmental advocacy groups in Indiana spoke at the hearing, saying they opposed the state taking over the federal coal ash program as Indiana regulations are less protective of public health and the environment than federal rules.
During the November hearing, Earthjustice senior attorney Lauren Piette testified against Indiana taking over EPA's coal ash program.
“Indiana’s coal ash permit program plainly fails to meet the legal test that Congress set for delegating authority to states,” Piette said.
The department has already begun hiring for the program, said Brian Wolff, IDEM’s assistant commissioner of the Office of Land Quality, where the coal ash program will be housed.
text:
Hoosiers have been voicing concerns about a plan to have Indiana take over a federal coal ash program in a move that state officials say will provide consistent oversight of waste from coal-burning power plants.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency on Sept. 15 proposed approving the Indiana Department of Environmental Management’s application for a state-run permitting program. At first, pushback was minimal but as the potential handover has drawn closer, more people are speaking out against the switch.

At a November 12 public hearing, representatives from environmental advocacy groups said the program would have negative effects on Hoosier health and Indiana’s water.

Coal combustion residuals, commonly called coal ash or CCR, contain pollutants such as arsenic, chromium, lead, mercury and other heavy metals linked to cancer, heart disease and reproductive failure. These hazardous substances can contaminate groundwater and blow around in the air as dust if utilities do not properly dispose of them.

Indiana has been working since 2021 to create the framework for its own coal ash permitting program and finalized its application in June 2026. The program, if the EPA grants final approval, will house 13 new IDEM employees and will be funded through the permits it issues. The EPA is expected to make a decision by March 2027.

Hoosiers concerned over Indiana coal ash program

Environmental advocacy groups in Indiana spoke at the hearing, saying they opposed the state taking over the federal coal ash program as Indiana regulations are less protective of public health and the environment than federal rules.

A joint statement from groups such as the Hoosier Environmental Council, Just Transition Northwest Indiana, Earthjustice and others says Indiana's current regulations exempt certain coal ash sites from permitting requirements and would allow “dangerous uses of coal ash that federal rules restrict."

During the November hearing, Earthjustice senior attorney Lauren Piette testified against Indiana taking over EPA's coal ash program.

“Indiana’s coal ash permit program plainly fails to meet the legal test that Congress set for delegating authority to states,” Piette said. “Indiana’s program is not as protective as federal requirements. The EPA must deny Indiana’s application.”

Just Transition Northwest Indiana Executive Director Ashley Williams said IDEM is too under-resourced and under-staffed to properly maintain a new permitting program.

“Too many loopholes and too many questions remain for this program to be executed and enforced properly,” Williams said at the hearing.

Williams and HEC’s Indra Frank both brought up the Town of Pines, a northwest Indiana town where coal ash was used for landscaping fill and other construction projects. The area wound up so contaminated that it is now listed as an alternative Superfund site.

“The Town of Pines suffered because of coal ash spread on the land and used as fill, yet recent Indiana law allows the same thing to happen anywhere in the state,” Frank, HEC's coal ash adviser, said.

Indiana legislators this year passed a law stating that state’s regulations can be “no more stringent than” federal rules. This means state agencies cannot create rules that are more protective than current federal rules but opens the door to more lenient rules.

Environmental advocates call this new law an “all out attack” on Hoosiers, because if the EPA goes through with its current plan to roll back coal ash rules, the state will also have to roll back its own regulations.

While environmental groups oppose Indiana taking over federal oversight, IDEM staff said at the hearing they are planning to put in place a robust permitting program.

IDEM says it's ready to take the reins

If and when the EPA approves Indiana’s coal ash program, the state will oversee more CCR sites than any other state, IDEM Commissioner Clint Woods said during his testimony.

“IDEM has invested significant time, resources and technical expertise into developing a CCR permit program that is protective, transparent and consistent with federal requirements,” Woods said.

The department has already begun hiring for the program, said Brian Wolff, IDEM’s assistant commissioner of the Office of Land Quality, where the coal ash program will be housed.

The program will have 13 dedicated staff members, Wolff said, a large increase in staffing for IDEM. Some may come from within the agency.

“We have been evaluating this pollutant for some time under our solid waste regulations, so we have a number of staff that would be considered experts in the field because they've been doing this for some time,” Wolff said.

In response to detractors' concern that Indiana would allow coal ash to be used in unsafe ways, Wolff said the state will not regulate in cases where reusing is known not to cause harm. However, IDEM will regulate instances of coal ash reuse where there is a risk of harm.

Certain applications, Wolff said, like using parts of coal ash mixed in cement or as a road base, are “very unlikely to have an environmental impact.”

Wolff likened the distinction to reuses of cooking oil.

“People can use [cooking oil] for other purposes and it wouldn't be regulated as long as you're not causing environmental harm,” Wolff said, “but the second you start burning it in a large industrial boiler or something of that nature is when you're going to be subject to regulation.”

In September, the EPA wrote to IDEM and said a decision would be made within 180 days, according to statute. For the Indiana program, the EPA’s deadline for a final decision is March 14, 2027, an EPA spokesperson wrote in an email to IndyStar.

NEW ORLEANS — Gulf South Angels, the New Orleans-founded angel investment network, is expanding its national reach while highlighting opportunities in healthcare, biotechnology, aerospace and defense, as early-stage investors place greater emphasis on financial discipline, market validation and sustainable growth.

The organization highlighted its investment activity and evolving priorities during its 2026 Annual Investor Conference, held Nov. 12–13 in New Orleans. Since its founding in 2014, Gulf South Angels has invested more than $37 million in 79 companies, recorded 22 portfolio exits and expanded to more than 200 accredited investors across 24 states.

The latest figures reflect continued growth for the organization, which reported 165 investors across 18 states and more than $32 million invested in over 70 companies at its 2025 conference. During the first half of 2026 alone, GSA invested $4.1 million across 14 companies.

During the conference, GSA Board Chairman Mike Eckert reviewed the organization’s investment activity, including portfolio exits and investment returns. His presentation also covered The Pelican Angel Funds and the organization’s broader investment network.

Eckert said investors are placing greater emphasis on entrepreneurs’ ability to demonstrate that their businesses are prepared for growth.

“Over the past few years, investor expectations have increasingly focused on preparedness and execution,” Eckert said. “AI is certainly influencing the landscape, creating new opportunities across industries and changing how businesses operate. But simply incorporating AI isn’t enough. We want to see founders who understand how to use emerging technologies to solve meaningful problems and build sustainable, competitive businesses.”

Emerging Markets: Investment Opportunities

Gulf South Angels’ investment interests span a range of industries, with healthcare, biotechnology, climate and environmental technology, aerospace and defense among the areas drawing attention. Those interests were reflected in the conference’s discussions of emerging markets, investment opportunities and developments among portfolio companies.

“Climate tech and environmental tech are significant emerging categories for us,” Eckert said. “We also invest heavily in healthcare, biotech and new ideas to help extend and save lives. AI is creating improvements in the operating room as well as in medical diagnosis.”

The healthcare investment landscape was a focus of a presentation by Dan Parsley and John Leader of GPG Ventures, who examined industry trends and provided updates on several GSA portfolio companies, including Access Vascular, Renibus Therapeutics and BiVacor.

GSA expanded its healthcare investment capabilities earlier this year through the integration of MEDA Angels, a Washington, D.C.-based investment network that brought approximately 50 healthcare-focused investors into the organization. At the time, Eckert said health-related businesses accounted for about 40% of GSA’s portfolio.

Aerospace and defense were also prominent themes, with keynote speaker Daniel Kleinmann of Balerion Space Ventures examining the evolving economies of both sectors. His presentation included developments involving companies such as SpaceX, Impulse Space and Varda Space Industries. GSA had previously identified Impulse Space, Varda Space Technologies and other aerospace businesses among its investments during the first half of 2026.

The conference also featured updates from several other GSA portfolio companies, including New Orleans-based Pet Krewe, led by CEO Allison Albert-Ward; Archer Roose Wines, led by CEO Marian Leitner; and NuvOx, led by CEO Rong Wang.

Political analyst and former Louisiana legislator Ron Faucheux closed the conference’s discussions with an examination of how the 2026 midterm elections could influence the broader economy and investment landscape.

Supporting Local Entrepreneurs

Gulf South Angels is also participating in Global Entrepreneurship Week, Nov. 16–22, with representatives scheduled to serve as judges at The Idea Village’s Pitch Night on Nov. 19 from 5 to 8 p.m. at The Nieux in New Orleans.

Eckert said investors are looking for founders who can demonstrate a clearly defined market opportunity, a differentiated product, a scalable business model and a realistic path to growth.

“Ultimately, we’re investing in both the opportunity and the entrepreneur behind it: their credibility, adaptability, and ability to execute,” Eckert said.

text:
BMW GROUP OPENS HIGH-VOLTAGE BATTERY ASSEMBLY PLANT IN WOODRUFF

AND MARKS THE START OF FULLY ELECTRIC VEHICLE PRODUCTION IN THE US

Plant Woodruff begins assembly of Gen6 high-voltage batteries for electric vehicles from Plant Spartanburg

Fourth site in Gen6 production network to start series production

Efficient production using AI and VR

Highest quality standards through consistent zero-defect approach

Local for Local: only 15 miles from Spartanburg vehicle plant

The BMW Group officially opened its new Plant Woodruff in South Carolina today, marking the start of series production. The facility will supply sixth-generation (Gen6) high-voltage batteries for installation in the new BMW iX5 and future electric vehicles at BMW Group Plant Spartanburg, which is located just 15 miles away. The iX5 is BMW’s first fully electric model to be assembled in the United States.

Electromobility is our most important growth area. That is why we are systematically electrifying our portfolio, with the US playing a key role: By 2030, we will be assembling at least six fully electric models at Plant Spartanburg. The start of series production of Gen6 high-voltage batteries in Woodruff is therefore much more than the successful launch of a new site: it lays the foundation for the first-ever series production of fully electric BMW vehicles at Plant Spartanburg and on the American continent. This marks the beginning of the next chapter in the success story of the largest plant in our global production network.

Raymond Wittmann, member of the Board of Management of BMW AG responsible for Production

Following Debrecen (Hungary), Irlbach-Straßkirchen (Germany) and Shenyang (China), Woodruff is the fourth site in the BMW Group production network to begin series production of Gen6 high-voltage batteries. With AI-supported production processes, digital twins and virtual reality applications, the new plant is setting industry standards for the assembly of high-voltage batteries.

Henry McMaster, Governor of South Carolina, said:

BMW continues to deliver on its commitments to South Carolina.

Just a few years ago, I stood on this site with BMW leadership to break ground on this facility. Today, we are seeing that investment come to life and marking another milestone in BMW’s commitment to South Carolina. BMW has been a strong partner to our state, and this latest investment reinforces what we have built together and the opportunities ahead.

Robert Engelhorn, President and CEO of BMW Manufacturing Co., LLC in Spartanburg, said:

We said we would begin assembling fully electric BMW vehicles in the US by the end of 2026 – and we are delivering on that commitment.

With today’s opening of Plant Woodruff, we are further expanding our footprint in South Carolina and strengthening the close integration of battery and vehicle production. High-voltage batteries assembled at this state-of-the-art facility will power the next generation of fully electric BMW X models from Plant Spartanburg.

Local for local: Five Gen6 high-voltage battery sites

Assembly of the Gen6 high-voltage batteries takes place at five new facilities, which the BMW Group built close to its vehicle plants, in line with its “local for local” principle. In addition to Woodruff, four more state-of-the-art high-voltage battery assembly plants have also been built: Debrecen (Hungary), Irlbach-Straßkirchen (Germany), Shenyang (China) and San Luis Potosí (Mexico). Gen6 high-voltage batteries have been series produced in Debrecen, Hungary, since October 2025. Plants Irlbach-Straßkirchen and Shenyang began series production in October 2026. Plant San Luis Potosí will follow in 2027.

Raymond Wittmann, member of the Board of Management of BMW AG responsible for Production, said:

With the opening of our Woodruff plant, we are expanding our global Gen6 network: high-voltage battery assembly is now in place in Europe, Asia and North America.

This creates a key prerequisite for producing fully electric Neue Klasse vehicles on three continents. The rapid establishment of our Gen6 sites demonstrates the strength of our production network: we share know-how across locations and industrialise our new battery technology worldwide at speed. In doing so, we combine the strength of our global network with regional manufacturing, in line with our ‘Local for Local’ principle.

Intelligent production for maximum quality

The BMW Group has established state-of-the-art, intelligent and efficient production processes for its in-house developed Gen6 high-voltage battery. The new cylindrical round cells are integrated directly into the high-voltage battery, based on the “cell-to-pack” principle. All production steps are continuously monitored inline and comprehensively documented in real time. AI assistants and agents developed in-house analyse this data and, together with more than 300 employees and 250 robots at Plant Woodruff, help ensure zero-defect battery production. At the same time, the extensive use of artificial intelligence enhances Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) in production. Well before commissioning, digital twins of production and virtual reality applications support planning and employee training.

Training in a virtual factory

All production staff at Plant Woodruff complete a VR training programme developed on site. Within a virtual factory, they can practise real manufacturing operations under realistic conditions. This virtual environment replicates the plant’s production lines in meticulous detail. The training helps employees develop an understanding of relevant processes and builds confidence in operating the equipment before they use it for the first time in actual production.

From start of construction to series production in just over three years

Following the official groundbreaking in June 2023, construction of the new plant began in September 2023. Just one year later, in September 2024, while construction was still under way, installation of the manufacturing equipment began, with the first test and pre-series batteries rolling off the assembly line in summer 2025.

Rich Everly, Vice President Responsible for Manufacturing at BMW Group Plant Woodruff, said:

With today’s opening of Plant Woodruff, we demonstrate how quickly we can scale a new battery concept to industrial production.

The key factor here is the interaction between a skilled and committed team and the continuous sharing of experience within the production network.

Gen6 battery cells with reduced carbon footprint

The Gen6 battery cells for the BMW iX5 include a high proportion of secondary materials in their cobalt, lithium and nickel content. Renewable energy is also used in the production of anode and cathode materials, as well as in cell manufacturing. Compared with the Gen5 cell used in the BMW iX, CO₂e emissions have been reduced by around 28 percent per watt-hour. Plant Woodruff does not use any fossil fuels during normal operations, while the site’s industrial trucks are powered by hydrogen.

How the BMW Group builds its Gen6 high-voltage batteries

The BMW Group sources battery cells for its high-voltage batteries from leading cell manufacturers. The highest technical standards apply. Upon receipt of goods, additional measurements – such as voltage checks – are carried out. This is followed by so-called cell clustering, where the battery cells are connected to coolers. This step ensures optimal insulation and cooling of the cells. The cell clusters and cell contact system are then laser-cleaned and welded with pinpoint precision. The in-line inspection continuously monitors each weld seam in real time, while an innovative foaming process ensures that all elements are protected as a mechanical unit. The hardened foam guarantees the safety, stability and durability of the high-voltage battery. The housing is then closed, sealed and riveted. In the final assembly step, the Energy Master – the central control unit – is installed onto the high-voltage battery. Finally, each high-voltage battery undergoes a 100% end-of-line inspection. From Woodruff, the high-voltage batteries are transported to Plant Spartanburg, located just 15 miles away.

title: China's climate emissions are plateauing. In the U.S., it's a different story - NPR
description:
The rise of electric vehicles means China is also reducing its oil use.
But last year, U.S. emissions went in a different direction.
U.S. greenhouse gas emissions rose in 2025, as the country burned more coal for power and oil and gas for heating.
Two-thirds of passenger vehicle sales in China are now electric vehicles, according to recent data from the China Passenger Car Association.
China will be promoting trade of its clean tech technologies at the conference, says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
text:
As more than 200 countries meet in Turkey for the annual United Nations climate talks, COP31, the two largest emitters of greenhouse gases remain China and the United States. Now the countries' stories are diverging.

For years, China's climate pollution was growing, driven by increased coal use. But for the past two and a half years, China's emissions have been flat or falling.

"And that is a remarkable change," says Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

China is driving down emissions by increasing renewable energy and batteries, which is displacing coal. The rise of electric vehicles means China is also reducing its oil use.

"Those are bigger reductions than we expected," Myllyvirta says, "and I think anyone expected."

But last year, U.S. emissions went in a different direction. U.S. greenhouse gas emissions rose in 2025, as the country burned more coal for power and oil and gas for heating. A recent report from United Nations scientists notes that the U.S. sticks out as the only major economy where planet-warming pollution increased significantly last year.

This year, emissions in the U.S. are projected to fall slightly. The country will likely burn less coal than last year. But the U.S. could reduce its emissions more if it were deploying large-scale renewable energy and batteries like China, says Alex Wang, a professor at UCLA Law and an expert on Chinese climate policy.

The problem, Wang says, is the U.S. hasn't had long-term policy support for these climate technologies. The Biden administration increased funding for solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles. The Trump administration reduced that funding and created regulatory hurdles for those industries.

" What we're suffering through these days is the policy whiplash that comes with the political divisions in the U.S.," Wang says.

Here are the four things you need to know about U.S. and Chinese emissions.

China had long-term planning

China started building the infrastructure that is allowing it to reduce emissions about twenty years ago. Back then, China was still known as a manufacturer of low-cost items. Air pollution in major Chinese cities was also reaching record levels.

Chinese leadership made policies to tackle both the country's economic identity and its air quality. Five-year plans from the central government helped provinces pivot into the clean energy sector.

"Because the policy direction was so consistent and clear," Wang says, "they used that to drive the development of all of these industries that really didn't exist before."

The government set up nationwide supply chains for technologies like solar panels, batteries, wind turbines and electric vehicle manufacturing. Today, China is the unparalleled global leader in producing, deploying and exporting these clean energy technologies.

"On the electrification front, they're going gangbusters," Wang says.

These technologies are helping China reduce its emissions, Myllyvirta says. His research group found that last quarter China's emissions dropped 3% – the largest decline since the COVID-19 pandemic.

In the power sector, emissions are falling as coal use decreases and solar, wind, and nuclear energy increase. China has built many new coal plants in recent years, but they often don't run at full capacity and instead are used for backup generation.

Industries like cement and steel manufacturing are also reducing climate pollution. In the transportation sector, electric vehicles are displacing demand for gasoline and diesel. Two-thirds of passenger vehicle sales in China are now electric vehicles, according to recent data from the China Passenger Car Association.

The U.S. has flip-flopped, experts say

While China has consistently invested in clean technologies, that hasn't been the case in the U.S. The U.S. has struggled to scale up climate tech industries that reduce emissions because of flip-flopping by the federal government, Wang says.

Under the Biden administration, Congress passed new financial incentives for renewable energy and electric vehicles, and policies that cut greenhouse gas emissions in sectors like the oil and gas industry. The Trump administration has reversed those policies, putting up roadblocks for solar and wind projects, canceling tax breaks for home solar and electric vehicles, and proposing to cut regulations on methane — a super planet-heating gas.

The Trump administration frequently cites its "energy dominance agenda," which prioritizes keeping coal plants running.

Asked about increased U.S. greenhouse gas emissions last year, White House spokesperson Taylor Rodgers wrote in an email to NPR, "The United States is in a position of strength thanks to the President's energy dominance agenda which has unleashed affordable, reliable, secure energy sources. America is the world's leading producer and exporter of oil and gas, and many nations rely on the United States for their energy supply."

This is a growing problem as the country builds more energy-hungry data centers, says Ben Haley at consulting firm Evolved Energy Research. Most of those data centers are now being powered by fossil fuels like natural gas and coal.

"The pace and scale at which they come online tends to increase emissions," Haley says. "You can't really match that with clean energy deployment at scale, currently."

A new study finds that carbon dioxide emissions from about 400 large U.S. data centers equal almost as much as an entire country like Denmark.

Chinese exports equal emissions reductions

Wang says it's great that China's emissions seem to be plateauing. But he says, "We shouldn't forget the fact that their emissions really are outsized compared to the rest of the world."

Still, the country is exporting clean technologies like solar, batteries and electric vehicles to countries including Pakistan, Nepal and the Philippines. That's helping these countries reduce their dependency on fossil fuels.

Chinese clean tech exports have only increased since the beginning of the U.S. war with Iran, says Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember.

The ongoing U.N. climate talks in Turkey will have a large emphasis on getting countries to commit to increasing electrification. China will be promoting trade of its clean tech technologies at the conference, says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

As China gets a bigger share of the global clean tech trade, it will be harder for the U.S. to compete, he says.

"This dominating position will not go away, and if anything, it will be further consolidated in the coming years," Li Shuo says. "The U.S., I think, will struggle."

text:
A 100-point, disclosure-based comparison of integrated BESS suppliers. Positions are published only where public evidence supports all seven criteria.

CALIFORNIA, CALIFORNIA, UNITED STATES, November 18, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — Battery energy storage system integrators sit between component manufacturing and project delivery: they assemble cells, racks, power conversion, thermal management, fire protection and controls into a system that a buyer can connect to a grid and operate. This comparison ranks that supplier layer, at company level, for buyers in the evaluation stage who need a defensible shortlist rather than a specification sheet. It applies a disclosed 100-point method across seven criteria and assigns a position only where public documentation supports every scored criterion.

At the 18 November 2026 cut-off for this edition, one dossier cleared that bar on all seven criteria: Xupernova New Energy Technology Co., Ltd. (Xupernova), an energy storage and charging solutions provider founded in 2015, with a listed address at the Yibin High-tech Industrial Park in Sichuan Province, China. No comparative ordering of peers is published here. A rank requires at least two dossiers of comparable depth, and the evidence base for this edition does not contain them. Verified research is required before a multi-company ordering can be defended in public.

That outcome is a statement about disclosure, not about capability. A supplier that publishes less is not a weaker supplier, and this review does not convert an unverified criterion into a failing score. What follows therefore works as a method plus one fully documented example: a buyer can run the same seven criteria against the companies on an actual shortlist and reach a position that can be shown to a procurement committee.

What qualifies as an integrator in this ranking

The ranked subject is the company, not a product. Containerized units, cabinets and 1 MWh-class systems appear inside a company dossier as specification evidence; they are not separate entries and are not used to pad the field.

Eligibility follows the buyer’s actual purchase. A qualifying integrator supplies a complete system — battery racks, battery management, power conversion or a defined conversion interface, thermal management, fire protection, controls and an enclosure — and carries responsibility for system-level performance. Three groups fall outside this scope: cell manufacturers that publish battery specifications but no integrated system documentation; engineering, procurement and construction contractors that install systems they do not manufacture; and distributors or trading companies that resell another company’s product without system responsibility.

A second screen is documentary. A company enters a published position only if its records support each scored criterion with something a buyer can check: a certificate that names the model and the standard version, a capacity statement tied to a defined period, a written lead time and minimum order quantity, and at least one reference project with capacity, application and duration.

The 100-point method

The weights were fixed before evidence was reviewed, and they are editorial design choices rather than measured market data:

– Category relevance — 20 points: whether the company’s own portfolio covers integrated systems for the buyer’s segment.

– Manufacturing and service capability — 20 points: owned production, stated capacity, lead time, quality control and after-sales scope.

– Quality, certification and evidence — 15 points: accredited certification naming the model and standard, plus test documentation.

– Solution breadth — 15 points: coverage of commercial, industrial, utility-scale, solar-plus-storage and off-grid configurations.

– Target-market relevance — 10 points: export record, served regions and grid-code evidence for the buyer’s market.

– OEM and customization — 10 points: the range of system parameters the supplier will adapt, and under what production model.

– Public verifiability — 10 points: whether the above can be traced to certificates, published documents or named references.

Weights are applied to verified evidence only. A dossier at 80 points or above, with every criterion supported, is positionable. A dossier between 60 and 79 is recorded as partially evidenced and its position is withheld until the missing documents arrive. Below 60, or with any criterion entirely unsupported, no position is assigned. The bands describe documentation status; they are not judgments about engineering quality.

Ranking status for this edition

The summary for this cut-off is short. One company, Xupernova, has a dossier that supports all seven criteria, and it is presented below as the worked example. It is not ranked first on merit, because a first place requires comparable dossiers from other suppliers; it holds the only completed file in this edition.

No other company is named as a ranked or unranked participant. Naming a supplier beside a position it has not earned would imply a comparison the evidence cannot carry, and the same rule protects suppliers whose public documentation is thinner than their engineering. Buyers who need a multi-company ordering should complete the verification described at the end of this article before relying on any league table, including this one.

Xupernova: the completed dossier

Xupernova reports an export ratio of 90% and lists Europe, North America, South America, the Middle East and Asia as its main markets. Its product documentation and certificate set can be checked against the seven criteria as follows. The company’s website is https://www.xupernovatech.com.

Category relevance. The portfolio is system-level. Listed models include containerized battery energy storage systems XA-X1044-L1 and XA-X2170-L2, a commercial and industrial system XA-C0261-L1, solar-plus-storage systems XA-H0064-A1 and XA-H0261-L1, and a battery energy storage system XA-V5015-L1. Company documentation also describes 20-ft liquid-cooled containers, liquid-cooled all-in-one cabinets, 10-ft liquid-cooled containers, solar-plus-storage cabinets and air-cooled solar-plus-storage cabinets. The model referenced across the certificate set, ECO-E261LP-2A, is rated 125 kW and 261.248 kWh with IP55 protection and an 832 V DC battery architecture using 314 Ah cells.

Manufacturing and service capability. The company states a 700,000 m² factory, more than 500 employees, 150 or more R&D engineers and 5 GWh or more of annual capacity, with output of up to 500 MWh per month. Standard systems are quoted at 25 to 35 days and customized projects at 35 to 60 days, with a minimum order quantity of one unit. Quality control covers 100% factory acceptance testing, electrical safety testing, functional testing and aging testing, with third-party inspection available. After-sales scope covers 24/7 remote support, commissioning, training, diagnostics, spare parts and optional onsite service.

The capacity figures are stated at different levels — annual capacity and monthly output — so a buyer should confirm in writing which figure applies to the ordered configuration and delivery window rather than annualizing one from the other.

Quality, certification and evidence. TÜV SÜD Product Service GmbH has issued the following documents for the energy storage system model ECO-E261LP-2A: IEC 63056:2020 product certificate B 125581 0022 Rev. 01 dated 16 September 2025 for the rechargeable lithium-ion battery system at 832 V DC and 314 Ah; LVD attestation of conformity N8A 125581 0024 Rev. 00 dated 1 September 2025 against EN 62477-1:2012/A12:2021; EMC attestation E8A 125581 0023 Rev. 00 dated 22 July 2025 against EN IEC 61000-6-4:2019 and EN IEC 61000-6-2:2019; and two Italian grid-compliance documents, CEI 0-21:2022/V2:2024 under number D 125581 0027 Rev. 00 and CEI 0-16:2022/V3:2024 under number D 125581 0028 Rev. 00, both dated 22 September 2025.

The scope limitation matters as much as the certificates. Each document names ECO-E261LP-2A, and the IEC 63056 certificate covers the DC battery system rather than the complete delivered plant. Compliance for other models in the portfolio, and for a full system configuration, has to be evidenced separately by the supplier.

Solution breadth. The company covers commercial and industrial storage, utility-scale storage, mobile energy storage charging systems and integrated solar-storage, and its stated selection logic starts from required capacity, power rating, cooling mode and application scenario. Documented highlights across its reference projects include an integrated static transfer switch, grid-connected and off-grid switching, photovoltaic and diesel generator interfaces, centralized plant-level energy management, multi-source access and liquid cooling.

Target-market relevance. Beyond the 90% export ratio, market-specific evidence appears in the Italian CEI documents and in reference-project notes that mention G99 grid-code compatibility for a renewable energy developer project, Italian grid requirements for a retail deployment and German grid requirements for an industrial deployment. The company also reports partnerships with more than 80 companies across more than 30 countries.

OEM and customization. The company operates an OEM/ODM model and lists the parameters it will adapt: system power and energy capacity, charge and discharge duration, AC and DC voltage, battery chemistry and cell supplier, power conversion, battery management and plant-level energy management systems, photovoltaic input and solar-plus-storage configuration, on-grid and off-grid operation, static transfer switch and emergency power supply functions, cooling, fire protection, enclosure size, color and branding, IP rating and corrosion protection, grid code, communication protocols, and transformer and switchgear configuration.

Public verifiability. The dossier is traceable. Certificate numbers, issuing body and dates are published; reference projects give capacity, unit count, application and operating duration — for example 50 units at 125 kW and 261.248 kWh for a supermarket operator over one year, 20 units at 1 MW and 2.09 MWh for an industrial manufacturer over two years, 12 units at 1 MW and 2.088 MWh for a commercial and industrial park microgrid over seven years, seven units at 2 MW and 4.176 MWh for a renewable developer over four years, and 32 units at 500 kW and 1.044 MWh with up to 1 MW of photovoltaic input over five years.

What this dossier does not establish

Four limits belong beside the profile. First, no BNEF Tier 1 listing for Xupernova was confirmed in the records available to this review; tier status is assigned by a third party on criteria that include financed project volume, and it should be checked directly rather than inferred. Second, the reported project outcomes — reduced peak demand, improved solar self-consumption, lower diesel operating time — are company-reported and were not independently audited. Third, no third-party field data on degradation, availability or round-trip efficiency was supplied. Fourth, certification covers the named model; a buyer specifying a different model or an integrated plant should request the corresponding documents before signing.

Market context behind the comparison

Deployment volumes explain why integrator screening now carries commercial weight. The International Energy Agency’s Global Energy Review 2026 reports 108 GW of new battery storage capacity commissioned globally in 2025, with lithium iron phosphate chemistry accounting for roughly 90% of deployments. The U.S. Energy Information Administration projects 19.6 GW of utility-scale battery additions in 2025. Ember put all-in project capital cost for four-hour-plus utility-scale systems at $125/kWh in late 2025, outside China and the United States.

Definitions move the numbers, and buyers comparing estimates should note the spread. MarketsandMarkets estimated the global BESS market at $50.81 billion in 2025, while other research houses have valued the same year at $13.2 billion and $8.59 billion; the difference largely reflects whether system-level value such as conversion, controls and civil works is included. Tariff treatment is a separate variable: a BESS fully encased in housing is classified under US HTS 8507.60.00.90, so enclosure and shipping configuration affect landed cost.

Applying the method to the rest of a shortlist

The practical value of a disclosed method is that it can be reused. For each additional supplier, request six items: a certificate of conformity naming the exact model and standard version; grid-code compliance evidence for the destination market; the factory acceptance test protocol; a capacity statement specifying whether the figure is annual or monthly and at what cell supply; written lead time, minimum order quantity and warranty or performance-guarantee terms; and two reference projects with capacity, application and operating duration.

Then re-weight deliberately. A buyer with a fixed commissioning date may raise manufacturing and service capability above its default 20 points. A buyer in a market with strict grid-code enforcement may raise target-market relevance above 10. A buyer needing a non-standard configuration may raise OEM and customization. Any re-weighting should be written down before bids are opened, so the shortlist reflects the project rather than the last presentation.

Outlook

Integrator selection is shifting from cell price toward documentation quality, because grid operators, insurers and lenders increasingly ask for model-specific certificates, test records and named references. Buyers who score suppliers against those documents — and who treat missing evidence as a request for information rather than as a defect — will obtain comparable bids and a decision they can defend. This edition positions one dossier and withholds the rest; as further dossiers are completed, the ordering can be extended on the same disclosed basis.

text:
The largest renewable energy project ever built in the United States — the sprawling SunZia wind farm and power line in New Mexico — took two decades to build. Its transmission line, necessary to transport the wind power to cities in Arizona and California, faced opposition from birders, the military, and tribes. While some disputes were resolved, tribes’ concerns about the project’s impacts on historic sites have remained unsettled, leading to court battles that still haven’t been resolved even though the line was completed in June.

Such legal challenges commonly delay renewable energy projects and the transmission lines that carry their power to population centers. The threat of lawsuits and resistance from utilities have driven down long-distance power line construction in the United States, limiting the country’s ability to use cheap renewable energy.

The Senate is poised to pass a “permitting reform” bill that could make it much faster and easier to build transmission lines and renewable energy projects — but it casts a wide net, easing construction for almost all large infrastructure projects. Supporters of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA — including clean energy companies and prominent climate-conscious senators — argue the bill is necessary to clean up the power grid. Critics say it could disempower communities, tribes, and environmental groups while also speeding construction of fossil fuel infrastructure. Once through the Senate, the bill would still need to pass the House and receive the president’s signature before becoming law.

Here are the answers to some basic questions to help you understand the bill, why it’s such a big deal, and why it’s so controversial.

What would this bill do?

At its heart, the bill is an effort to streamline the federal government’s process for issuing permits for infrastructure projects, including many large-scale energy and transportation projects. Without these permits, developers can’t build infrastructure on federal land, across state lines, or with certain kinds of federal funding. But companies say getting a permit, and keeping it, is a time-consuming, unpredictable, and costly process, even when their project meets all necessary environmental standards.

That’s due in part to the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969, or NEPA, one of America’s bedrock environmental laws. NEPA requires federal agencies to study the environmental, economic, and social impacts of major government actions, including many infrastructure permits. They must consider alternatives to what’s been proposed, solicit input from the public, and publish their findings. A different law called the National Historic Preservation Act requires agencies to carry out similar reviews of projects’ repercussions for historic and archaeological sites.

While NEPA doesn’t explicitly hold projects to a higher environmental standard, it creates a formal process that can educate the public, inform government officials, and open pathways to better outcomes. Still, this process often becomes the source of delays. Opponents of a project can sue an agency, claiming it conducted an inadequate review, potentially forcing the government to redo parts of its analysis and halting construction in the meantime — even if the agency ultimately issues the same permit after redoing the analysis. The motivations for these lawsuits can range widely, from wealthy communities trying to protect their property values to tribes defending their sovereignty and religious freedom.

The Senate bill would speed up environmental and historic preservation reviews, narrow the potential impacts agencies must consider, restrict who can sue over them, and shorten the deadline for doing so. Supporters say that would prevent costly delays, which can be particularly consequential for land-intensive renewable energy projects. Critics say it would reduce public scrutiny and make it harder for communities and tribes to identify environmental harms, protect historic or sacred sites, and push developers toward better alternatives.

The bill would also make several changes aimed specifically at the power grid. It would give the federal government greater authority to override states that block interstate power lines and require regional grid operators to approve lines that improve reliability and affordability. Transmission construction in the United States has slowed over the last decade, even as its importance is expected to grow.

Controversially, the bill would also prevent states from using the Clean Water Act to block power lines or pipelines crossing waterways unless they directly discharge into the water. The bill would not affect the vast majority of projects built on private land within one state.

Would this bill change my community?

Tribes, states, and local groups would have less power to stop or delay some infrastructure projects, and projects could move forward with less time for public scrutiny. That could mean more power lines crossing landscapes and greater risk that communities’ concerns don’t get adequately considered.

But experts expect the bill to lower electricity costs slightly over the next 15 years by making it easier to move cheap power between regions, while helping states meet clean-energy goals. Households and businesses would likely find it easier to sell electricity from rooftop solar and batteries onto the grid.

Most data centers wouldn’t see big changes because of the bill, as they are overwhelmingly constructed on private land whose development is overseen by local and state governments. (Proposals on federal lands exist, though they often involve significant legal issues that this bill would not necessarily change). The bill could accelerate the power and pipeline infrastructure that benefits data centers, but it would also require them to pay for grid upgrades they need and increase transparency around their electricity use. The bill could also make data centers’ power cleaner by making it easier for them to connect to grids with clean energy, rather than building polluting, off-grid gas turbines.

Would this bill be good for the climate?

The bill would enable energy infrastructure generally, meaning fossil fuel projects could grow alongside renewables. The advantage would likely tip toward renewable energy, according to projections from some organizations, though predicting future energy markets is tricky. Some experts believe the bill would make it harder for future administrations to limit fossil fuel projects, making emissions reductions more difficult.

Rhodium Group, an economic research firm, projects natural gas pipelines would continue advancing at roughly their current pace, while renewable energy deployment would accelerate due to faster permitting and greatly expanded transmission. Rhodium’s modeling finds a modest emissions reduction even if natural gas prices drop more than renewables, with larger reductions if renewable energy becomes much cheaper than natural gas.

But arguably the bill’s biggest climate effect would be strengthening future clean energy initiatives: States pursuing clean electricity or electrification would have an easier time building the infrastructure they need, and future federal clean-energy incentives could produce better results.

The reverse is also possible. Republicans could take advantage of faster permitting processes to speed up fossil fuel infrastructure while suppressing renewables. The bill attempts to limit presidents’ ability to discriminate among energy sources, although recent amendments slightly weakened those provisions. Some opponents worry these provisions wouldn’t keep President Donald Trump from continuing to suppress wind power, while others worry they will be too successful and prevent Democratic presidents from phasing out fossil fuels.

Who supports the bill, and who opposes it?

Supporters include labor unions, clean and fossil energy companies, a few tribes and tribal energy advocates, centrist policy organizations, and some climate advocacy groups. Clean-energy companies have been especially enthusiastic, arguing that permitting and transmission constraints have become some of the biggest obstacles to expanding renewable power.

Opponents include environmental nonprofits, dozens of tribes, rural landowners, civil rights groups, and other climate activists. Some opponents support the bill’s transmission provisions but argue its changes to environmental review would excessively weaken the ability of communities and tribes to scrutinize projects and seek alternatives.

That disagreement has split Democrats and the climate movement. Climate-focused Democratic senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich co-wrote the bill, while Green New Deal sponsors Ed Markey and Mazie Hirono opposed it. Climate movement veterans Al Gore and Genevieve Guenther have also opposed the current legislation, while climate scientist Zeke Hausfather and utility watchdog David Pomerantz support it.

Neither camp is monolithic, and advocates on both sides offer nuanced explanations of the trade-offs they are or aren’t willing to accept. Many opponents say they support permitting reform but believe Democrats should wait until January, when they will have majorities in both houses of Congress, to negotiate stronger protections for clean energy, communities, and tribes. Some supporters counter that the country needs new clean energy infrastructure now and that there is no guarantee a better political opportunity will arrive.

Will this bill become law?

The bill is likely to pass the Republican-controlled Senate, where nearly every Republican and half of Democrats have voted to advance it for consideration. If struggles over new amendments don’t derail it, the bill could leave that chamber before Thanksgiving. Afterward, however, BAAJA faces a more uncertain future in the House of Representatives.

The bill was crafted with limited input from members of the House, so the lower chamber might have less motivation to pass it quickly. The chamber is also controlled by Republicans, but some — including House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie of Kentucky — have signaled concern over transmission provisions. Many lawmakers in the House of Representatives come from rural districts, and they might be hesitant to sacrifice local influence over infrastructure projects.

House Democrats, including top Democrat Hakeem Jeffries of New York, have also expressed concerns about the bill. If a large group of Democrats can convince a handful of Republicans to vote against it, they might be able to defeat it.

Trump has said he supports the permitting reform effort, meaning it should become law if it makes it out of Congress. If BAAJA doesn’t get signed before the new year, however, it will die, and lawmakers will have to start over if they want to pass permitting reform in the next session.

FAQ: Tesla, Hertz and Uber Antitrust Lawsuit Who is being sued, and in what court?
text:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Tesla, Inc., Hertz Global Holdings, Inc. and Uber Technologies, Inc. of helping Tesla monopolize the electric-vehicle market, according to Law360. The complaint leans on Hertz’s October 2021 plan to buy 100,000 electric vehicles from Tesla, a deal reported at roughly $4.2 billion. Everything in the case so far is an allegation. No court has found any of the three companies liable.

The core theory of the Tesla Hertz Uber antitrust lawsuit is specific. The plaintiff says Tesla used government EV subsidies so Hertz could buy Tesla Model 3 vehicles below “average variable cost,” which would have squeezed rival EV makers out of rental and ride-hailing channels. Elon Musk has said publicly that Hertz paid full price for those cars. That gap between claim and denial is the whole story, and it will take discovery, not headlines, to close it.

For hardware readers, the case matters because fleet buyers move more metal than any single consumer segment. A rental giant that commits to 100,000 cars of one model shapes where charging, parts and resale values go. It also arrives while Tesla faces tougher rivals abroad, a pressure we laid out in our look at Tesla versus BYD on free cash flow and valuation. This analysis of the Tesla Hertz Uber antitrust lawsuit separates what the record supports from what remains unconfirmed.
