text:
American corn growers are looking to the world’s shipping industry for a potentially massive new source of demand as mounting financial pressure, stagnant commodity markets and consecutive years of farm income losses intensify the need for new markets for U.S. corn.

A coalition of leading agricultural and renewable fuels organizations is urging the Trump administration to make American corn ethanol a top priority in the development of global maritime fuel standards, warning that decisions being negotiated internationally could determine whether U.S. farmers gain access to billions of gallons of potential new ethanol demand.

In a letter to six senior administration officials, the National Corn Growers Association (NCGA), Growth Energy, Renewable Fuels Association (RFA), Indiana Corn Growers Association and 20 other state and national corn and grain policy organizations called on the administration to aggressively advocate for the inclusion of American corn ethanol in the emerging global maritime fuel market.

The letter was addressed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, National Energy Dominance Council Chair Doug Burgum, Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett and Coast Guard Commandant Admiral Kevin Lunday.

The organizations argue that opening the international shipping industry to American ethanol could provide a significant new outlet for U.S. corn at a time when traditional markets are struggling to absorb the nation’s production.

“Corn growers are facing a fourth consecutive year of net income losses, and the outlook beyond 2026 is no better without new, lasting sources of demand,” the organizations warned.

They contend that existing markets, combined with outdated regulatory barriers and restrictions on market access, are not sufficient to absorb the volume of agricultural production American farmers can deliver.

A potentially billion-bushel opportunity

The potential size of the maritime fuel market is enormous.

According to estimates from NCGA, alcohol-capable ships already operating around the world could consume nearly 2 billion gallons of ethanol annually. That would represent demand equivalent to approximately 680 million bushels of corn.

The opportunity could expand dramatically as additional vessels enter service.

Ships already on order could increase potential annual ethanol demand to approximately 7.7 billion gallons, equivalent to roughly 2.7 billion bushels of corn.

For Midwestern corn producers facing mounting production costs, tighter margins and uncertainty surrounding future commodity prices, the prospect of a new market of that magnitude could have significant implications for long-term demand.

And unlike some emerging alternative-fuel opportunities that require years of technological development, the coalition says much of the infrastructure and technology needed to begin using ethanol in maritime transportation already exists.

More than 100 ships currently operating worldwide were built with engines capable of running on methanol. According to the organizations, those vessels can also operate on ethanol with little to no modification.

Every major marine engine manufacturer has now tested ethanol, while leading global shipping companies have begun operating vessels using the fuel.

In September, a deep-sea vessel completed the first ship-to-ship bunkering operation involving 100% U.S. corn ethanol at an American port.

Hundreds of additional alcohol-capable ships are also on order.

The coalition says those developments demonstrate that American ethanol is ready to compete in the global shipping market today.

New demand could strengthen rural farm economies

For corn growers, the potential benefits extend well beyond increased ethanol production.

The organizations emphasize that ethanol plants are economic anchors in agricultural communities, purchasing locally produced grain, supporting skilled manufacturing jobs and contributing to the tax bases of rural communities.

Increased demand from international shipping could also help bring currently idle U.S. ethanol production capacity back into operation without requiring the construction of additional plants.

That could provide an important economic boost for corn-producing regions across the Midwest.

Additionally, increased ethanol production would generate additional distillers grains, a high-protein feed ingredient used by livestock producers.

That creates another potential benefit for the broader agricultural economy by strengthening the connection between corn production, ethanol manufacturing and domestic livestock operations.

The coalition argues that every gallon of American ethanol used in maritime transportation represents an opportunity to move more American-grown corn into a value-added product, support domestic manufacturing and expand U.S. energy exports.

“Every gallon of U.S. ethanol burned at sea is an American-grown, American-made fuel competing in a global market,” the organizations wrote.

International regulations could determine whether farmers get a seat at the table

Despite the enormous potential, the coalition warns that significant regulatory hurdles remain.

The United Nations’ International Maritime Organization (IMO) is negotiating the global rules that will determine how alternative maritime fuels are evaluated and recognized as the shipping industry works to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

Those negotiations could have major consequences for the future of American corn ethanol.

One of the most important unresolved issues is how the carbon emissions associated with ethanol production and use will be measured.

The IMO has not yet established a recognized carbon intensity value, commonly referred to as a carbon score, for U.S. corn ethanol.

Without a fair and scientifically supported carbon score, American ethanol could face a competitive disadvantage against other alternative fuels in the international marketplace.

The organizations are particularly concerned that some proposed sustainability requirements could restrict the use of U.S. corn ethanol while potentially favoring ethanol produced in Brazil.

They want the Trump administration to ensure that international standards recognize the environmental benefits of American agricultural production practices, including conservation measures already being adopted by U.S. farmers.

The letter specifically calls for the administration to make fair treatment of American corn ethanol a top U.S. objective during upcoming IMO negotiations in November and December.

The coalition also wants any alternative to the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework to recognize biofuels that are reducing emissions today and avoid excluding U.S. agricultural feedstocks.

Another priority is maintaining the involvement of the U.S. Department of Agriculture in the international negotiations, ensuring that agricultural expertise and data are incorporated into decisions affecting the future of American biofuels.

The groups are also asking the administration to support the port infrastructure necessary to supply ships with American ethanol.

A critical moment for American corn demand

The organizations say the administration has already taken important steps toward securing fair treatment for U.S. corn ethanol, including submitting proposed carbon emission default values to the IMO.

However, they are urging federal officials to see that effort through as international negotiations continue.

The stakes are significant for an agricultural industry searching for new sources of demand.

With more than 100 alcohol-capable ships already operating, hundreds more on order and global shipping companies beginning to embrace ethanol, the maritime sector represents an emerging opportunity that could eventually consume billions of gallons of American-produced fuel.

For Midwestern corn growers, the difference between capturing that market and being shut out could come down to regulatory decisions being made thousands of miles away.

The coalition is asking for an opportunity to meet with administration officials before the IMO’s November and December meetings and says it is prepared to provide the data and technical expertise necessary to support the U.S. position.

The message to Washington is straightforward: American farmers have demonstrated their ability to produce the corn. American ethanol producers have the capacity to turn that grain into fuel. Now, the organizations want the administration to make sure international rules do not prevent those products from competing in one of the world’s largest transportation markets.

For an agricultural economy facing another year of financial pressure, unlocking the maritime fuel market could represent far more than another outlet for ethanol. It could become a major new source of long-term demand for American corn.

title: “Who Drives Chinese EVs? The Whole World Does”... Hyundai Motor Company's Utilization ...
description:
As the global onslaught of Chinese-made EVs intensifies by the day, Hyundai Motor Company’s utilization rate has fallen sharply this year, according to figures.
According to Hyundai Motor Company’s quarterly report on the 17th, the utilization rate at all nine of its domestic and overseas plants from the start of this year through September stood at just 86.1%.

As the global onslaught of Chinese-made EVs intensifies by the day, Hyundai Motor Company’s utilization rate has fallen sharply this year, according to figures.

According to Hyundai Motor Company’s quarterly report on the 17th, the utilization rate at all nine of its domestic and overseas plants from the start of this year through September stood at just 86.1%. That was down 8.2 percentage points from 94.3% in the same period last year.

The plant in Türkiye fell from 103.9% to 84.8%, while the plant in Indonesia recorded the lowest rate, at just 35.8%. Utilization at domestic plants also declined from 101.7% to 93.6%, amid production disruptions caused by strikes and other factors. Kia’s overall plant utilization rate also fell 1.2 percentage points year on year to 95.1%.

The market sees the onslaught of Chinese-made EVs as a major cause. Chinese-made cars are making strong inroads in the South Korean market. According to the Korea International Trade Association, China’s exports of electric passenger cars to South Korea from January through September this year totaled $3.35991 billion (about 4.488 trillion won), a 99.2% surge from the same period last year. South Korea became China’s fourth-largest EV export market worldwide, after Belgium, Australia and the UK, as well as its largest in Asia.

Export value soared about 174-fold, from $12.32 million in 2020 to $2.14173 billion last year. This year, exports through September alone surpassed last year’s full-year total. The market share of South Korean-made EVs in the domestic market fell from 75% in 2022 to 55% from January through September this year. For passenger EVs alone, the share of South Korean-made cars dropped to 48.7%, below half.

An automotive industry official said, “Policy support, including production tax credits, is urgently needed to maintain the domestic production base.” In particular, there are calls for tax support proportionate to production volume so that tax credits lead to expanded domestic production and investment in facilities. text:
Public charging is becoming more convenient for General Motors (GM) electric vehicle owners, thanks to a new Plug and Charge feature that eliminates the need for charging apps, touchscreen interactions or credit cards at participating Electrify America stations.

Through GM Energy Pass, eligible GM EV drivers can now simply plug their vehicles into compatible Electrify America fast chargers and start charging automatically. The feature is currently available for GM electric vehicles equipped with native Combined Charging System (CCS) charge ports, while models with native North American Charging Standard (NACS) ports are expected to receive support in early 2027.

The update aims to remove several steps from the public charging process, making fast-charging stops more straightforward and reducing the time drivers spend interacting with charging equipment.

According to GM, internal testing shows that energy flow can begin within 45 seconds of connecting an eligible vehicle to a compatible charger.

The new capability allows compatible GM electric vehicles and Electrify America charging stations to authenticate charging sessions automatically.

Instead of opening an app, selecting a charger, scanning a QR code or swiping a payment card, drivers only need to park and connect their vehicle. The charging station recognizes the vehicle, initiates the session and processes payment through the account linked to GM Energy Pass.

Wade Sheffer, vice president of GM Energy, said the company wants to make public charging faster and easier by reducing the number of steps required to begin a session.

The feature also adds a layer of convenience and security by eliminating the need to use a physical credit card at the charging station.

For drivers who regularly rely on public DC fast charging, removing these additional steps could make charging stops feel more like the familiar experience of refueling a conventional vehicle.

The Electrify America Plug and Charge rollout builds on several recent improvements to GM’s public charging ecosystem.

In January 2026, GM integrated Electrify America into its myChevrolet, myGMC and myCadillac mobile applications. The integration brought more than 6,200 Electrify America fast-charging stations into the apps, allowing drivers to locate chargers, plan routes, monitor charging sessions and handle payments without downloading another charging application.

Many of these stations support charging speeds of up to 350 kW, depending on the vehicle’s charging capabilities and station conditions.

The next major step came in June 2026, when GM introduced Energy Pass. The service was designed to simplify access to multiple public charging networks through a single GM account.

Following a one-time enrollment, drivers can use Energy Pass to find compatible charging stations, start and stop sessions, check real-time charging status, make payments, review charging history and access receipts.

The service covers supported charging networks representing approximately 70% of U.S. DC fast chargers, giving GM EV owners a more unified way to manage public charging.

Electrify America CEO Robert Barrosa described the integration as another step toward making public charging more seamless, allowing drivers to spend less time dealing with payment systems and more time on the road.

For eligible GM electric vehicles, using the new Electrify America feature is relatively straightforward.

Drivers first need to enroll in Energy Pass through the myChevrolet, myGMC or myCadillac app. A payment method must then be added, and the Plug and Charge setup instructions must be completed.

Once the setup is finished, the charging process becomes automatic.

At a compatible Electrify America station, drivers simply connect their vehicle to the charger. The vehicle and charging station authenticate the session, and charging begins without requiring additional action.

Payments are handled through the payment method associated with Energy Pass. Charging session information and receipts remain accessible through the corresponding GM mobile application.

Drivers can also continue using Charge by App and other available charging methods while the new capability rolls out.

GM says its electric vehicle customers can access more than 250,000 public charging points across the United States and Canada through its charging ecosystem.

That network includes more than 40,000 DC fast chargers aggregated through Energy Pass, providing access to a growing selection of charging locations for drivers traveling beyond their home charging setup.

The expansion is particularly important as GM continues introducing new electric vehicles and competing in an increasingly crowded EV market. Convenient access to reliable public charging remains one of the major factors influencing the overall ownership experience.

title: Power sector emissions set to fall in US amid lower coal use
description:
Power plants burned 10% less coal through July of this year, according to a new analysis of federal data from think tank Energy Innovation.
This year, though, coal plants are just not running as often.
Through August 2026, coal plants ran an average of 46.7% of the time, compared with 49.7% over the same period last year.
The Department of Energy has been ordering coal plants to stay open past their planned retirement dates on the grounds of an alleged energy crisis.
The DOE also announced hundreds of millions of dollars in funding coal plants, while the Environmental Protection Agency has rolled back regulations on pollution from the facilities.
text:
Power plants burned 10% less coal through July of this year, according to a new analysis of federal data from think tank Energy Innovation. That drop in coal consumption caused power sector emissions to decline in the first half of 2026 — and puts the U.S. on track for a 2% reduction in overall energy-related emissions across this entire year.

This year, though, coal plants are just not running as often. Through August 2026, coal plants ran an average of 46.7% of the time, compared with 49.7% over the same period last year.

The data suggests that coal’s resurgence last year was a blip rather than the start of a boom, even as electricity demand has continued to soar this year.

The Department of Energy has been ordering coal plants to stay open past their planned retirement dates on the grounds of an alleged energy crisis. These orders have burdened consumers with hundreds of millions of dollars in costs, despite some of the plants being too run-down to produce any power. The DOE also announced hundreds of millions of dollars in funding coal plants, while the Environmental Protection Agency has rolled back regulations on pollution from the facilities.

Around 48 gigawatts of coal capacity shuttered in Trump’s first term, far more than in either of President Barack Obama’s terms in the White House. Last year saw a far smaller amount of coal retirements, and so this year, the fleet has shrunk by only 1.6%. It now stands at about 167.5 GW, said report author Robbie Orvis, Energy Innovation’s senior director of modeling and analysis.

What else is picking up the slack? Not combined-cycle gas turbines, the large-format workhorses of the electricity sector. Through August, they ran at a slightly lower rate than they did last year. Overall gas consumption at power plants did tick up 3.8%, however, indicating greater production from different types of gas facilities, like peaker plants, for example.

At the same time, new solar plants have been surging onto the grid, pushing large-scale solar generation up by a projected 21% this year, per federal data. In May, for the first month ever, solar outproduced coal on the U.S. grid, think tank Ember noted. And batteries have kept up their charge, visibly displacing gas in the high-value evening peak hours in California, Texas, and other markets.

text:
Indiana University Bloomington (IU) used its inaugural Climate Week to promote “equity-centered” climate policy, featuring former Biden administration energy official Shalanda Baker, who helped design the race-conscious Justice40 initiative.

IU describes the week as focused on “science-informed, community-driven, and equity-centered solutions” to climate change. Its featured event, “How universities can tackle the climate crisis and environmental justice,” placed Baker at the center of that agenda.

[RELATED: Community college pays students up to $15,000 to train in environmental justice advocacy]

Baker served in the Biden administration as the nation’s first deputy director for energy justice before becoming director of the Department of Energy’s Office of Economic Impact and Diversity.

During her federal tenure, Baker helped develop Justice40, an initiative created under former President Joe Biden to direct 40 percent of certain federal climate and clean-energy benefits toward communities identified as “disadvantaged.”

Baker described her vision for the Department of Energy as making “equity and justice enduring.”

She also said the department sought to place Black, indigenous, people of color, and low income communities “at the core of our energy transition and energy policy.”

Justice40 materials claim that people of color “have been disproportionately and systematically harmed by pollution for decades” and attribute disparities in government investment in part to “racial, ethnic, gender, ability and other biases.”

The Trump administration ended federal Justice40 requirements in 2025 as part of its rollback of diversity, equity, and inclusion programs and race-conscious federal policy.

Baker also co-founded the Initiative for Energy Justice (IEJ), which advocates alternatives to conventional privately operated utility models.

IEJ promotes “community choice aggregation, municipal utilities, public power policies, and other policy solutions” while arguing that the existing regulated-utility system has blocked “affordable, renewable, and democratically managed energy.”

The group emphasizes “community benefits and governance,” including giving communities greater decision-making authority over energy infrastructure.

[RELATED: Indiana University library guide urges resistance to ‘cisheteropatriarchy’]

Baker’s appearance was not the only Climate Week program to frame environmental policy through race and social justice.

IU also advertised “Climate in Common: Environmental Justice,” addressing “distributive justice, procedural justice, and recognitional justice.”

Another event, “Environmental Justice & Racism,” was hosted by the IU Environmental Law Society, Black Law Students Association, and Public Interest Law Foundation and examined “disparate environmental impacts on communities of color in America.”

The week also featured David Watkins and other speakers working on environmental-justice and climate-policy issues, alongside researchers focused more directly on energy economics and federal climate policy.

IU Climate Week was organized by the Environmental Resilience Institute with support from the O’Neill School of Public and Environmental Affairs and other campus partners.

Antalya, Türkiye | COP31, 17 November 2026 — The Government of Iceland, through its Ministry for Foreign Affairs, has recently signed a three year commitment to Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL), reinforcing its strategic partnership to advance climate action and universal energy access. Iceland will fund annually across two core pillars, the renewed collaboration focuses on clean cooking in schools and sustainable cooling solutions, while mainstreaming gender equality and youth empowerment.

The multi-year commitment directly targets two critical priorities detailed in the partnership framework:

Platform for Clean Cooking in Schools: Anchored within the School Meals Coalition, this flagship initiative links food and energy systems to transition school meal preparation from traditional biomass to clean cooking. Building on country action in Tanzania, Uganda, Kenya, Laos, and Sierra Leone, the platform aims to reach an additional 100 million students by 2030. Iceland’s support enables SEforALL to provide technical assistance, support country roadmaps, mobilize pooled co-financing, and establish carbon finance mechanisms.

Sustainable Cooling for All: Addressing extreme heat risks affecting over 1 billion vulnerable people—61 percent of whom are women—this programme delivers sustainable cooling solutions across Sub-Saharan Africa, Small Island Developing States (SIDS), South Asia, and Southeast Asia. The initiative advances data-driven agricultural cold chain planning to protect food security, supports National Cooling Action Plans aligned with the Global Cooling Pledge, and drives youth-led innovation through the #ThisIsCool campaign.

Gender equality and youth empowerment remain woven across both pillars. The partnership scales SEforALL’s activity-based STEM Traineeship Programme, equipping young women with practical technical skills to deploy clean cooking and cooling infrastructure. Furthermore, it leverages SEforALL’s leadership as co-convener of the Gender and Energy Compact—where Iceland serves as a Champion—to elevate women and youth in global policy forums.

The announcement comes as the 2026 Tracking SDG7 report highlights that 655 million people still lack electricity and 2 billion remain dependent on polluting cooking fuels. Closing these gaps requires sustained international cooperation and targeted institutional support.

A partnership delivering lasting impact

"Iceland has consistently demonstrated what meaningful international partnership enables, investing not only in clean energy solutions, but also in the people, institutions and capabilities needed to deliver lasting change. We are deeply grateful for Iceland's continued confidence in SEforALL and our shared commitment to a sustainable energy future for all."

Iceland is proud to continue its partnership with Sustainable Energy for All, supporting practical solutions and strengthening the capacity of countries and communities to benefit from the clean energy transition. Through this commitment, we reaffirm our belief that international cooperation and investment in people are essential to achieving a more sustainable and equitable future."

text:
Utilization at Metaplant America (HMGMA), Hyundai Motor Group's electric vehicle production base in the United States, has fallen below half of capacity. The slide is attributed to a concentrated hit from slowing local EV demand after the U.S. federal government scrapped purchase subsidies.

HMGMA, located in Georgia, operated at 41.4% of capacity in the January-September period, down 26.7 percentage points from 68.1% a year earlier, according to a quarterly report filed by Hyundai Motor (005380) on the 17th. The decline was the steepest among Hyundai's nine global production bases. Output fell to 35,000 vehicles from 52,000.

HMGMA currently builds two Hyundai models, the Ioniq 5 and the Ioniq 9. Combined factory shipments of the two models totaled 25,043 units in the first nine months of this year, down 47.2% from 47,431 a year earlier. The plant began operations in October 2024 as an EV-only facility, but added the Kia (000270) Sportage Hybrid in June this year in response to weaker local EV demand and growing appetite for hybrids.

Industry officials say the impact of the Donald Trump administration's termination of EV subsidies last October has been concentrated at HMGMA because of its focus on electric models. Even though the Ioniq 5 ranks among the best-selling EVs in the U.S. market this year alongside Tesla's Model Y and Model 3, that is not enough to offset the broader downturn, analysts said. Battery-electric vehicle sales in the United States totaled 725,888 units in the January-September period, down more than 30% from a year earlier, according to Cox Automotive.

Hyundai plans to expand HMGMA's annual capacity from the current 300,000 vehicles to 500,000 by 2028 and eventually to 700,000 to 800,000, but those plans risk being derailed if current trends persist. The company intends to respond by broadening the plant's lineup with Genesis models and additional hybrid and electrified vehicles tailored to North American demand.

Hyundai's plants have struggled this year beyond HMGMA, both at home and abroad. Intensifying competition from Chinese brands and production adjustments tied to the shift to electrification are cited as the main causes. Overall utilization across the company's nine domestic and overseas production bases came to 86.1% in the first nine months, down 8.2 percentage points from 94.3% a year earlier. Capacity rose 3.0% to 3.167 million vehicles over the same period, but actual output fell 6.0% to 2.728 million.

In Europe, utilization at the Turkey plant dropped to 84.8% from 103.9%, and at the Czech plant to 79.3% from 85.9%. At the Turkey plant, a narrower model mix and a production gap stemming from the electrification shift weighed heavily: the i10 city car was discontinued in November last year, and mass production of the Ioniq 3 did not begin until August this year. In Asia, utilization at the India plant fell to 83.3% from 92.9%, and at the Indonesia plant to 35.8% from 52.7%.

Domestic plants also saw utilization fall 8.1 percentage points to 93.6% this year from 101.7% last year, hurt by production disruptions from strikes. Output declined to 1.252 million vehicles from 1.388 million.

Still, the Alabama plant, which builds the Tucson and Santa Fe, ran at 101.0% of capacity, and the Brazil plant, which produces the HB20 and Creta, at 105.4%, both maintaining full operation.

text:
The following are highlights from today’s Washoe County Board of County Commissioners meeting:

1. Blight, RV, and obstruction code amendments: The Board of County Commissioners voted to amend the county code related to recreational vehicles and blight. The amendments expand the definition of “public view” to include public access easements and publicly maintained trails. This language is intended to clarify that even though the private property includes the public access easement, it is unlawful to block that easement with vehicles or other materials stored on the property. Current code language only applies to public view from roadways.

The amendments also remove the language referencing reduction of economic value due to blight. This code language is often cited by complainants as the basis for their complaint; however, potential reduction in economic value cannot be determined in a code enforcement proceeding. A condition or action either violates the code or it does not – perceived economic value is not a code standard.

Finally, the amendments clarify that occupying an RV for more than 30 days is a nuisance. RVs are registered vehicles not permanent dwellings. This code amendment will clarify that it is illegal to use an RV as a permanent dwelling.

“I want to thank our county staff in their efforts to strengthen our Code Enforcement,” Vice Chair Mariluz Garcia said. “This is something that has been a huge priority for this commission, something that’s very near and dear to my heart over the past four years, and you’ll see several items today that are either increasing the Code Enforcement fines or clarifying the definition of blight… Our county staff is working very, very hard, not only those in Code Enforcement but also in Northern Nevada Public Health, and we need to keep going and continue to look at ways to improve these efficiencies because we all want clean and healthy neighborhoods.”

2. Animal Services code amendment: The Board approved amendments to the county code related to animals and fowl to comply with Nevada Assembly Bill 418 (2025) by adding a section requiring a training course on handling pets, renewed every two years, for owners and operators of kennels, animal rescue organizations that handle pets, and commercial establishments engaged in the business of handling pets. The requirement does not extend to veterinarians or animal shelters.

3. Solar project sponsorship: The board accepted a $3,750,000 sponsorship agreement from Google LLC to support the Washoe Solar Project and the installation of solar arrays, battery backup systems, and energy efficiency upgrades at Washoe County facilities. The total cost of the project is estimated at almost $4.5 million, a difference of approximately $707,700, which will be requested in the fiscal year 2028 budget cycle.

A tax credit through the Inflation Reduction Act will generate just over $1.2 million in rebates for Washoe County, if the County can complete construction by the end of calendar year 2027 before the credit expires. The proposed locations are:

Washoe County Administration Complex, Building A and the Senior Center

Emergency Operations Center

Gerlach Community Center and Fire Department

Sparks Senior Center

Public Administrator

Nevada Cares Campus

Sparks Library

Downtown Courts lighting control system

“We appreciate Google’s sponsorship of these projects,” Washoe County Sustainability Manager Brian Beffort said. “This investment will bring numerous benefits to the people of Washoe County: lower energy costs, cleaner air, support for renewable-energy jobs, and greater resilience for both our grid and our important community services.”

4. Proclamation: The Board declared November Homeless Youth Awareness Month and presented the proclamation to representatives of the Eddy House, a Reno nonprofit that supports nearly 600 homeless and at-risk youth. It provides emergency shelter, housing programs, counseling, case management, workforce development, and life-skills education to reduce youth homelessness.

description:
The North Carolina Utilities Commission issued an order approving a set of near-term actions in Duke Energy’s Carbon Plan and Integrated Resource Plan, which outlines how the utility plans to meet electricity demand.
The order extends certain coal-unit retirement dates beyond those approved in the commission’s 2024 plan.

The commission also extended through 2028 its authorization for up to $440 million in advanced nuclear development costs.
It also authorizes Duke to prepare and submit amendments to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission for two AP1000 units at the W.S.
text:
The North Carolina Utilities Commission issued an order approving a set of near-term actions in Duke Energy’s Carbon Plan and Integrated Resource Plan, which outlines how the utility plans to meet electricity demand.

The commission said the order was unanimous and bipartisan. It followed a 12-day expert witness hearing and five public witness hearings held across the state and virtually. More than 600 people submitted consumer statements of position, while four parties submitted system modeling evidence and 11 filed expert testimony.

The order extends certain coal-unit retirement dates beyond those approved in the commission’s 2024 plan. Duke must file an updated coal retirement analysis with its next plan.

The commission also extended through 2028 its authorization for up to $440 million in advanced nuclear development costs. That preserves the option to develop either 600 megawatts of small modular reactors or about 1,117 megawatts of large light water reactor generation.

The order opens a new nuclear resources docket and calls for a technical conference in 2027 to examine reactor technology, costs, financing, execution risks and customer protections before the commission decides whether to build a new nuclear plant.

It also authorizes Duke to prepare and submit amendments to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission for two AP1000 units at the W.S. Lee site, and revisions to the combined license application for two AP1000 units at the Shearon Harris site.

The plan calls for pursuing about 2,730 megawatts of new natural gas combined-cycle generation and about 1,111 megawatts of additional combustion-turbine generation between 2030 and 2033. It also includes up to 2,300 megawatts of solar resources to be placed in service between 2032 and 2034.

The commission authorized development and procurement of up to 2,700 megawatts of additional battery storage, which could bring planned system storage to as much as 5,400 megawatts by 2034. Solar procurements must include customer protections such as volume and market-depth adjustment mechanisms and an independent evaluator.

The order authorizes up to $55.6 million for near-term development of Bad Creek II, including work to preserve federal energy tax credits and the option to place 1,760 megawatts of pumped-storage hydropower in service by 2040. It also allows Duke to continue planning to reach a 22% reserve margin by 2031.

The commission said the biennial planning process allows it to adjust to changing electricity-demand forecasts, market conditions, technology costs and resource availability. Duke is expected to submit its next proposed plan in fall 2027.

The complete order and record are available on the commission’s website under Docket No. E-100, Sub 207.

text:
< All Press Releases

BOISE, Idaho — The Bureau of Land Management accepted winning bids totaling $7,924,129 on 23 geothermal lease parcels covering nearly 71,411 acres in Idaho. The BLM may issue the leases after completing its review and receiving payment.

Combined bonus bids, rental payments, and future royalties from the leases will be distributed among the U.S. Treasury, the State of Idaho, and the counties where the leased parcels are located.

Geothermal lease sales support domestic energy production and American energy independence while contributing to the nation’s economic and military security. Consistent with Executive Order 14154, “Unleashing American Energy,” the BLM’s geothermal leasing program helps meet U.S. energy needs and strengthens the nation’s position as a global energy leader.

Leasing is the first step in developing federal geothermal resources. A lease allows the lessee to explore for and potentially develop geothermal resources, but it does not by itself authorize surface-disturbing activity. The BLM reviews proposed activities under the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 and other applicable legal authorities.

Planning documents for this sale are available in the BLM National NEPA Register for parcels managed by the Four Rivers Field Office (link is external) , Bruneau/Owyhee Field Office (link is external) , Burley Field Office (link is external) , and Upper Snake Field Office (link is external) . The BLM conducts lease sales online through Efficient Markets (link is external) .

Geothermal energy is an abundant resource, particularly in the West. The BLM manages geothermal leasing, exploration, and development across approximately 245 million surface acres of public lands and 700 million acres where the United States owns the subsurface mineral estate.

For more information, visit the BLM Idaho Geothermal Energy website or contact BLM Senior Land Law Examiner Judy Duenas at tduenas@blm.gov or 208-373-3866.

The BLM manages about 245 million acres of public land located primarily in 12 western states, including Alaska, on behalf of the American people. The BLM also administers 700 million acres of sub-surface mineral estate throughout the nation. Our mission is to sustain the health, diversity, and productivity of America’s public lands for the use and enjoyment of present and future generations.

title: Note to next Eugene City Council: Keep your hands off clean energy fund dollars
authors: Dylan Plummer, Ben Botkin, Jaime Adame, Lillian Schrock-Clevenger, Letters to the Editor, Shaanth Nanguneri, Oregon Capital Chronicle, Leo Heffron, Tyson Alger
description:
After two years of planning, organizing, signature gathering, door-knocking and campaigning, our coalition passed the Eugene Clean Energy Fund to establish a 2% fee on billion-dollar corporations and direct that money to support climate action and clean energy jobs.
Ensuring Measure 20-388 is implemented as voters intended does not mean turning our backs on the fiscal challenges faced by the city of Eugene.
First and foremost, there is the Community Safety Payroll Tax, which is coming up for renewal in 2027.
While they’re at it, council should consider making the payroll tax more progressive, by lowering the tax rate for low-income individuals and increasing it for the richest members of our community.
No matter what is decided with the Community Safety Payroll Tax, it is critical that council respect the wishes of voters and the historic mandate that was given to the Eugene Clean Energy Fund to support climate action and clean energy jobs.
text:
We did it. After two years of planning, organizing, signature gathering, door-knocking and campaigning, our coalition passed the Eugene Clean Energy Fund to establish a 2% fee on billion-dollar corporations and direct that money to support climate action and clean energy jobs.

And the measure didn’t just squeak by. It is on track to win by close to 20 percentage points. Make no mistake: This is a significant mandate from voters to tackle the climate crisis and build a just transition away from fossil fuels.

Such a margin of victory was possible not only because of the strong popular support for the issue, but also the big tent coalition of over 120 elected officials, organizations, businesses, unions and newspapers that came together to support the initiative.

In its endorsement of the measure, the Lookout Eugene-Springfield Editorial Board recommended redirecting half or more of the fund to pay for unrelated services. Such a proposal may have been worth considering had Measure 20-388 passed by only a narrow margin. Based on the election results, however, any proposal to divert funds away from climate action would subvert the clear will of the voters.

Our coalition will be working with the mayor and City Council to ensure that these funds are protected, and are spent on their intended purpose: reducing emissions, lowering energy costs and creating good-paying jobs here in Eugene.

One of our biggest priorities is funding union-built, publicly owned renewable energy generation, managed by our public utility, Eugene Water & Electric Board. Community solar installations around the city, coupled with battery storage, could generate renewable electricity and lower energy bills, while providing grid resilience and reliability in the face of increasingly frequent, climate-driven extreme weather events.

Additionally, we are eager to support the use of funds to retrofit and electrify existing affordable housing, and to support the building of affordable and social housing with the highest-possible energy efficiency standards.

Ensuring Measure 20-388 is implemented as voters intended does not mean turning our backs on the fiscal challenges faced by the city of Eugene. Thankfully, there are other opportunities to generate revenue to close city budget gaps and maintain social services.

First and foremost, there is the Community Safety Payroll Tax, which is coming up for renewal in 2027. The payroll tax, which was first established in May 2019, has operated as a slush fund for the Eugene Police Department since it was created — ironically, just a year before the Black Lives Matter uprising and amid historic calls for police reform in Eugene and nationally.

The tax, which establishes a 0.21% tax on employers in Eugene, and a 0.44% tax on the income of workers making over $32,344 annually, has generated between $22 million and $25 million a year. Of that, police, courts and prosecutors offices have received the vast majority, about $18 million annually, while core services like our libraries, shelters and firefighters have received only a tiny fraction, and CAHOOTS-like mobile crisis services no longer even exist in Eugene.

The editorial board is correct: Reinstating funding for critical programs like CAHOOTS, and expanding resources for affordable housing development in partnership with organizations like Square One Villages, is extremely important.

And we would argue, these programs fall specifically within the remit of “public safety.” Instead of pilfering funding that was overwhelmingly approved by voters to support clean energy and jobs programs, the City Council should instead amend the payroll tax to require a significantly larger portion of the funding to support nonpolice services such as CAHOOTS-like programs, affordable housing, shelters and firefighting that are central to ensuring public safety.

While they’re at it, council should consider making the payroll tax more progressive, by lowering the tax rate for low-income individuals and increasing it for the richest members of our community.

Currently, only minimum-wage earners are exempt from the tax, which is the same rate for all other incomes. Instead, an exemption should be established for those earning less than half of Eugene’s average median income, and the fee should be increased for those earning more than 150% of the median.

No matter what is decided with the Community Safety Payroll Tax, it is critical that council respect the wishes of voters and the historic mandate that was given to the Eugene Clean Energy Fund to support climate action and clean energy jobs.

In the meantime, the city must get creative with its approaches to generate revenue to reinstate CAHOOTS-like services, while expanding social services and building a safer and more sustainable Eugene for all residents.

text:
Virtual power plant (VPP) capacity in North America increased 25.9% year-over-year to reach 47.2 GW of behind-the-meter flexible capacity, according to a new report from Wood Mackenzie.

The report, “2026 North America Virtual Power Plant Market Report,” found that market growth was driven more by expanding capacity than by an increase in deployments, customers or programs. The number of company deployments, unique offtakers, and monetized market and utility programs each grew by less than 15%.

“Escalating turbine costs, affordability concerns and slow supply response to large loads are driving more interest in VPPs,” said Elham Akhavan, principal analyst at Wood Mackenzie.

Akhavan noted that capital expenditures for heavy-duty turbines have increased more than 80% since 2020, making battery energy storage system (BESS) VPPs more cost-effective on a per-kilowatt basis in 2026. Distributed BESS remained the most cost-effective option during that period.

Residential Market Leads Wholesale Capacity Growth

The residential sector recorded the largest year-over-year increase in wholesale-market VPP capacity, with growth of 155%.

"Residential’s share of wholesale-market VPP capacity more than doubled, reflecting opt-out enrollment and retailer-led battery growth," said Max Issokson, senior research analyst at Wood Mackenzie.

Storage and electric vehicle penetration also increased relative to thermostats, growing 19.7% year over year and exceeding the growth recorded in 2025. Economic participants were the only market segment to contract, declining 13.5% year over year.

Regional Markets and Capacity Opportunities

PJM and ERCOT continue to have the largest utility commitments to data center capacity and the greatest disclosed VPP offtake capacity, according to the report.

Emerging markets, including MISO, along with activity in Arizona, Illinois and Virginia, represent additional opportunities for VPP development.

Summer capacity prices in MISO increased from $30 to $384-$424/MW-day this year. However, aggregation rules continue to limit market growth.

“Arizona, Virginia and Illinois are building new programs that may increase capacity,” said Akhavan. “California has been a strong market in the past, but its future growth depends on SB 913 versus one-off DSGS funding.”

Data Centers and Competition Shape Market Development

The report identified a new development in the VPP market: providers disclosed a 1-GW pipeline of capacity specifically targeting data center loads. This category was not included in the previous year's market scorecard.

Competition among commercial and industrial aggregators is also increasing, with battery ownership and optimization emerging as factors that distinguish providers.

“Financiers are divided on how to account for VPP revenue, with some pricing it directly into storage leases, while others pass it through to customers as a bill credit or direct incentive,” said Akhavan. “How that revenue is treated is becoming a defining competitive variable.”

The report also noted that installed storage capacity does not automatically translate into VPP capacity. Opt-out enrollment models have demonstrated the ability to increase available capacity quickly, while opt-in enrollment models and barriers to data access continue to constrain market growth.

text:
By Sarah McFarlane

Nov 17 (Reuters) – More than 30 countries have joined COP31 host Turkey’s voluntary pledge to boost global electrification as part of broader efforts to curb climate change.

Turkey hopes the pledge will raise power’s share of final energy demand worldwide to 35% by 2035, from just over a fifth today, ushering in an “age of electricity” and be a central part of a ​final deal at the UN climate conference taking place in the Turkish Mediterranean city of Antalya.

Supporters say electric technologies can be cleaner, ‌more secure and more efficient than fossil fuels. But some developing countries are opposed to the plan because of the infrastructure investments required to hit the goal, observers said.

Here are some of the potential impacts if the target is adopted:

EMISSIONS

Achieving what Turkey has dubbed the 35×35 target could reduce planet-warming carbon emissions, but the amount depends largely on whether new power is produced from renewable or fossil fuel sources.

The pledge has no language requiring the increased electricity use to come from renewable sources.

Turkey’s presidency has said such language ‌is not ​necessary because countries already agreed to move away from fossil fuels at past COPs.

The voluntary pledge ⁠would cut around 4.1 billion metric tons of ⁠carbon emissions per year even if governments did not prioritise cleaner power sources, the equivalent of 7% of current global emissions, according to non-profit emissions tracker Climate TRACE.

But if the goal were met by prioritising clean power for new generation, that would roughly double, Climate TRACE said.

SECURITY

The US-Israeli war with Iran has pushed energy security up government agendas and highlighted the risks of relying on imported oil and gas ​supplies.

Electrification, particularly using domestic renewable energy and batteries, can help reduce import dependence and exposure to fossil fuel price shocks, COP31 leaders have said.

“Fossil fuels are not only driving the climate crisis. Dependence on them carries a steep economic and security price – as the crisis in the Middle East ⁠has laid bare,” UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said during the first week of the conference.

EFFICIENCY

Using ⁠electricity directly, such as in electric vehicles, heat pumps and electric industrial equipment, delivers more useful energy and ​is more efficient than burning fossil fuels, proponents say.

For instance, electric vehicles can convert roughly 80% of electricity into movement, while a petrol or diesel engine ​converts only about 20% of its fuel energy into motion, losing most of the rest as heat, according to ‌the World Resources Institute.

Lower energy consumption means lower bills for households and businesses and helps to curb inflation, which has risen sharply because of the disruption to energy markets caused by the Iran war.

“There is very strong economic motivation behind it because of the intrinsic efficiency of electrification and all the different calculations that the countries are doing about their energy security and independence,” said Diana Acconcia, head of the EU delegation to COP31.

In sunny regions, for example, ⁠the lifecycle cost of building and operating solar-plus-batteries projects ranges from $54 to $82 per megawatt hour, compared with $70–$85/MWh for new coal in China and more than $100/MWh for new gas in many markets, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency.

SKEWED ECONOMICS

Increasing clean energy, however, remains a challenge, especially in the developing world.

Managing ⁠fluctuating wind and solar output alongside surging electricity demand ‌requires massive power grid upgrades and battery storage investments, analysts said.

“Wealthy countries that have already built their prosperity ⁠on fossil fuels must move fastest, while developing countries need the finance and technology to electrify their ​economies and bring ‌affordable power to people who still lack access,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Nairobi-based think tank Power ​Shift Africa.

High interest ⁠rates can also weigh heavily on renewable energy projects, posing another constraint for developing countries with less favorable financing terms, according to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis.

That is because most of a renewable energy project’s lifetime costs are incurred upfront. Fossil fuel projects also face higher borrowing costs, but fuel-burning power plants typically incur a larger share of their costs over time.

Critics of the electricity pledge say a single global target fails to reflect the different circumstances of countries, and the G77 bloc of 134 countries wants financial support for any new targets introduced at COP31.

(Reporting by Sarah McFarlane, Additional reporting by ​William James; editing by Barbara Lewis)

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Date: November 16, 2026

Contact: Anja Semanco | anja@alaskawild.org | 724-967-2777

Washington, D.C. —Alaska Wilderness League is calling on Congress to oppose S. 5653, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (also called BAAJA or the permitting reform bill), as it allows for significant environmental concessions that have the potential to harm iconic public lands across the country, notably in Alaska. A manager’s amendment to the bill did not sufficiently address our concerns. Last Monday, the Senate passed a motion to proceed on the bill.

Most concerning for the protection of Alaska’s federal lands: The bill would force fast project reviews with inadequate information, limit or eliminate opportunities for the public to weigh-in, erase judicial checks and balances, and lock in bad—and potentially illegal—government decisions. The result would be faster decisions that come at the expense of careful analysis, public input, and essential science. More specifically, under this presidential administration in which Alaska is under relentless attack, the proposed legislation would fast-track approvals for oil and gas and mining projects across Alaska’s most iconic public lands, while simultaneously curtailing options for a future administration to address any unlawful approvals.

In addition, American taxpayers could be on the line to pay some of the largest multinational corporations for their costs associated with project delays that result from efforts to correct unlawfully issued permits.

“We must seek essential clean energy reform that does not come at the expense of our irreplaceable wild places.” said Kristen Miller, Executive Director of Alaska Wilderness League. “As written, S. 5653 would pave the way for industry to develop some of the most controversial industrialization projects on Alaska’s public lands with limited oversight. The bill would hand corporations almost exclusive control over the fate of projects like the proposed Ambler Road and oil drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. We can achieve energy reform and block unchecked data center growth without forsaking biodiversity hot spots and subsistence resources that will never recover if they are sold to the highest bidder.”

Alaska’s public lands are at a precipice, and going into a new Congress is the time to renew our fierce protection of these special places for the people and wildlife who depend on it, and to help mitigate a warming planet.

text:
Why it Matters

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) finalized changes to South Carolina's air pollution regulations on Nov. 16, approving new permitting and emissions-testing requirements and requiring the state to strengthen its rules for monitoring nitrogen oxide pollution from industrial facilities. The changes take effect Dec. 16, giving South Carolina one year to correct deficiencies in its pollution monitoring and reporting requirements or face federal disapproval of those provisions. ​

The Change

EPA amended 40 C.F.R. § 52.2120, which lists South Carolina's federally approved air pollution regulations, to update provisions governing construction permits, source testing, and NOx emissions. The agency also added 40 C.F.R. § 52.2132 to document its conditional approval of the state's NOx requirements.

EPA approved changes to construction permit requirements and exemptions for smaller sources of air pollution but excluded two sentences that would have allowed facilities to qualify for exemptions at higher emissions levels when no other applicable limits or requirements existed. The agency also approved most of the state's NOx regulations while conditionally approving certain monitoring, record-keeping, and reporting requirements for newly affected facilities.

What it Means for Clients

Industrial facilities and other stationary combustion sources in South Carolina face two different regulatory outcomes. The changes to construction permitting and source testing have received final approval, while portions of the NOx monitoring and recordkeeping rules remain conditionally approved until the state addresses EPA's concerns. EPA also did not finalize proposed changes to public participation requirements for minor source permitting, which were published Aug. 19. Those provisions remain under separate consideration.

Who is Lobbying

EPA Region 4 issued the rule. Two organizations with substantial lobbying disclosures involving air pollution issues are not directly connected to South Carolina's regulatory changes.

LyondellBasell Industries NV reported $690,000 in second-quarter lobbying expenditures, listing Clean Air Act and water pollution permits for plastics manufacturing facilities, product bans, recycled content requirements and EPA funding among its lobbying issues.

Bay Area Air Quality Management District reported $34,000 in second-quarter lobbying expenditures involving federal environmental appropriations, diesel emissions reduction programs, wildfire funding and air pollution issues.

What Next

SC DES must submit revised NOx monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements by Dec. 16, 2027, to satisfy EPA's conditional approval. If the state fails to submit the required corrections, the approval automatically converts to a disapproval under the Clean Air Act. The separate proposal to change public participation requirements for minor source permits remains pending, with no final action date announced.

title: The Trump Administration praised a Georgia manufacturer. Now the company is suing the EPA.
authors: Phil McKenna/Inside Climate News, Mary Landers, Phil McKenna, Inside Climate News

This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment.
In August 2025, Vice President JD Vance and Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin visited cold storage equipment manufacturer Alta Refrigeration to announce plans to roll back regulations the company opposed.
However, Alta wants a permanent reprieve, something it said the head of the EPA previously promised.

text:
This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.

In August 2025, Vice President JD Vance and Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin visited cold storage equipment manufacturer Alta Refrigeration to announce plans to roll back regulations the company opposed.

The EPA followed through in May, giving manufacturers of cold storage and other equipment several more years to continue selling devices that use hydrofluorocarbons with high global warming potential as refrigerants. Now, Georgia-based Alta and the Coalition for the Use of Safe and Efficient Refrigerants—an industry group also based in Georgia and chaired by Alta’s president—are suing the EPA and Zeldin, arguing that the agency did not go far enough.

The lawsuit shows how one company sought to push the Trump administration’s deregulatory agenda even further, revealing tensions between an EPA eager to roll back regulations and industry interests seeking yet more.The case is unfolding alongside a series of legal challenges to the agency’s actions, brought by a broad coalition of major industry groups representing air conditioning and equipment manufacturers, attorneys general from nearly two dozen states and an environmental group, all of whom contend the agency went too far.

The rollback and ensuing lawsuits stem from the American Innovation and Manufacturing Act of 2020, bipartisan legislation signed by President Donald Trump during his first term that mandated a gradual phasedown of hydrofluorocarbons. The chemical refrigerants are potent greenhouse gases, trapping heat in the atmosphere hundreds to thousands of times more effectively than carbon dioxide, pound for pound.

National industry groups supported both the legislation and a related international climate agreement, the Kigali Amendment, because the measures would help boost U.S. manufacturing jobs and exports. In 2023, the EPA issued a rule to help facilitate the required phasedown of hydrofluorocarbons.

The EPA’s May action extended the transition timeline, giving Alta and other manufacturers a five-year reprieve from requirements to use more climate-friendly refrigerants in new equipment. The agency said the delay would benefit companies and lower prices for American consumers. However, Alta wants a permanent reprieve, something it said the head of the EPA previously promised.

“Administrator Zeldin stated plainly that he intended to ‘give ALTA what it was asking for,’ the company argued in a document filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in September.

Before filing their lawsuit, Alta and the Coalition for the Use of Safe and Efficient Refrigerants petitioned the EPA to grant cold storage equipment manufacturers a permanent exemption from the hydrofluorocarbon phasedown. When the agency proposed a reprieve instead, Alta sought help to try to persuade the administration.

A declaration submitted by Alta President Eric Brown describes an exchange between Zeldin and a member of Georgia’s congressional delegation. The documents show screenshots of what appears to be Zeldin explaining that an act of Congress would be needed to make the rollback permanent.

The images show the request came from “Rep Buddy C.”, which may be U.S. Rep. Earl “Buddy” Carter (R-Georgia). Carter and Zeldin, a former U.S. representative from New York, served as colleagues and co-sponsored legislation during Zeldin’s tenure in Congress.

Citing the ongoing lawsuit, the EPA and Carter’s office both declined to comment.

Joseph Goffman, an EPA assistant administrator during the Biden administration who is not involved in the lawsuit, said Brown’s declaration “read as much like somebody throwing a tantrum as it did like a legal document” and praised Zeldin for “actually doing his job.”

Alta Refrigeration declined to comment.

Brown’s declaration said the EPA, through a member of Georgia’s congressional delegation, instructed him to withdraw comments Alta submitted to the White House Office of Management and Budget. Brown wrote that he did so “under duress.”

Goffman said he had never heard of the Office of Management and Budget asking for comments to be withdrawn because the White House disagreed with their content. Goffman said Zeldin’s decision not to permanently exempt Alta from the rule does not undo his earlier decision to give Alta and others a five-year reprieve, which Goffman said should never have been granted.

The industry groups that supported the hydrofluorocarbon phasedown and are now suing the EPA over the rule change represent more than 90 percent of residential and commercial heating, ventilation, air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment manufactured and sold in North America, along with more than 60,000 plumbing and heating, ventilation and air-conditioning professionals.

American companies invested heavily to transition to new technology to comply with the phasedown of climate pollutants, and the 2026 revision disrupted that without adequate explanation, the groups noted.

“It’s bad for the environment, bad for the economy, and it’s opposed by the bulk of the industry,” said David Doniger, a senior attorney and strategist for the Natural Resources Defense Council, the environmental organization that sued over the rule change. “It’s hard to think of something you could do that’s less popular or that does more harm and makes fewer friends than this.”

text:
General Motors is aiming to increase use of robots and other automation by 20% at its North American factories by 2028, two people familiar with the matter said, as the automaker grapples with higher labor and onshoring costs.

The Detroit automaker is developing its own robots and assembling them at its Kokomo, Indiana, plant, the same people and two other people said, and is focused on using autonomous mobile robots to move parts around its plants.

The 20% automation target and production of robots in Indiana have not previously been reported.

Automation is likely to emerge as a key issue in the United Auto Workers’ next round of negotiations with GM, Ford Motor and Jeep parent Stellantis, before the contracts expire in spring 2028.

The UAW, which represents about 50,000 GM factory workers, criticized the company’s automation efforts as a job-cutting tactic.

“Their idea of being more efficient is to cut the very people who create their product and profits,” UAW Vice President Ryan Hiestand said in a statement to Reuters after publication of the initial story. “We don’t need more robots so GM can do another stock buyback.”

GM did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Earlier, the company said it uses automation to improve safety, quality and efficiency. “As competition intensifies globally, we continue to put these technologies to work in ways that support our manufacturing teams,” it said.

GM Asking Suppliers For More Automation

As manufacturers expand the use of robots and AI in their factories to boost efficiency, they risk rankling labor groups that are guarding against job losses.

GM is still buying robotics equipment from outside suppliers while developing its own in-house, an effort that company executives outlined last year.

It also is asking parts suppliers bidding on new contracts to submit automation plans for their own operations, two other people familiar with GM’s supply base said. GM is using a scorecard to rate suppliers’ automation efforts and considering the scores in contract decisions, the people said.

US automakers have increased automation to contain manufacturing costs since the UAW won record contract gains from GM, Ford and Stellantis in 2023. President Donald Trump’s drive to bring more factory work home also has put pressure on production costs.

GM said the 2023 contract would add about $575 in labor costs per vehicle; Ford pegged its added cost at $900 per vehicle. At the time, analysts said the companies likely would increase automation as a way to defray the higher labor costs. GM last year said it had about 100 roboticists, AI engineers and hardware specialists working on advanced robotics systems.

Tensions Stir Over Automation

US automakers have long said their labor costs exceed those of foreign rivals and newer competitors such as Tesla, whose US factories are largely nonunion.

UAW President Shawn Fain already has warned that AI and increased automation pose a threat to workers.

“The fruits of our labor have multiplied like never before, but workers aren’t reaping the harvest. That’s theft,” Fain said at a UAW convention in June. “And if AI continues to be used as an accessory to that crime, it has to be stopped.”

During a February episode of the “Automated” podcast, Mikell Taylor, GM director of robotics strategy, said manufacturers need to design processes that take advantage of the respective strengths of workers and robots.

“How do I get the best out of both the people here and the machines here to get as much efficiency and quality as I can?” she said.

‘Less Hours Into Production’

GM and other automakers have used robots in their factories for decades to weld together body panels, for example, or move supplies between stations.

But they are exploring more ways to integrate robotics and AI into their plants to increase productivity, especially as they grapple with higher costs from rising commodity expenses and efforts to localize supply chains.

“It’s all about the end game: putting less hours into the production of the vehicle so (automakers) can be more efficient and more profitable,” said Laurie Harbour, a partner who specializes in automotive at Wipfli, a tax and advisory firm. She added that increased automation can ease labor shortages for auto manufacturers.

text:
OSLO, Norway--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Myths and misconceptions about electric cars, from battery lifespan and fire risk to grid collapse, are the biggest barrier to EV adoption, according to respondents to the annual Global EV Driver Survey. The 2026 survey draws on responses from more than 29,500 EV drivers across 34 countries.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261117539716/en/

MYTHS. Battery lifespan (72%), fire risk (58%) and grid collapse (45%) top the list of EV myths reported by respondents to the 2026 Global EV Driver Survey, which gathered responses from more than 29,500 EV drivers across 34 countries.

“The EV transition is not just an infrastructure or affordability challenge. It is also an information challenge. Outdated information and misconceptions continue to influence decisions long after the technology has moved on,” says Ellen Hiep, from the Steering Committee of the Global EV Alliance (GEVA).

Myths the greatest barrier

Asked to identify the greatest barrier to EV adoption in their country, 74% of respondents cited myths about EVs, ahead of purchase price (49%) and charging access in apartment buildings (47%).

The most reported myths are that EV batteries do not last (72%), that EVs catch fire more easily (58%), and that the EV transition will eventually cause the electricity grid to collapse (45%).

EV batteries will outlast the car

“It is understandable that people compare EV batteries with phone batteries that need replacing after two or three years. But most EV drivers have a very different experience with their car batteries,” says Ellen Hiep.

In the survey, 65% of respondents disagree or strongly disagree with the statement “I am concerned about the lifespan of my battery”, while only 18% agree or strongly agree.

“Most EV drivers know from experience that modern EVs come with long battery warranties of eight years, and that most batteries will outlast the car,” says Ellen Hiep.

About the annual Global EV Driver Survey

The annual Global EV Driver Survey gathers insights into EV ownership, charging and barriers to adoption from 2024 and onwards. The 2026 edition draws on responses from more than 29,500 EV drivers in 34 countries and is presented by the Global EV Alliance (GEVA), a non-profit network of 71 EV associations across 41 countries. Explore the survey data at survey.GlobalEVAlliance.com , including global findings and country-level results.

title: State report outlines industrial decarbonization roadmap | WEMU-FM
description:
A new state report has detailed how Michigan’s industrial sector can go carbon-neutral by 2050.
The roadmap involves grant programs, tax credits and capping greenhouse gas emissions while investing in renewable energy and storage.
The roadmap estimates industrial emissions could cost the state over $616 million in extra annual health spending by 2050 if nothing changes.
Michigan’s industrial and energy sectors account for nearly half of the state’s greenhouse gas emissions, according to the report.
Other pieces of the plan involve boosting the "Buy Clean, Buy Michigan" plan to encourage more sustainable practices when it comes to sourcing.
text:
A new state report has detailed how Michigan’s industrial sector can go carbon-neutral by 2050.

The roadmap involves grant programs, tax credits and capping greenhouse gas emissions while investing in renewable energy and storage. It began as part of the MI Healthy Climate Action plan, released in April 2022.

Michigan Chief Climate Officer Alessandra Carreon said it’s not “theoretical.”

“It’s grounded in … technology that exists today and practical policy measures, again, that are designed to introduce cost effectiveness for business that translates into cost savings for community members,” Carreon said.

The report breaks steps down into three phases: near-, medium- and longer-term goals. For the nearer-term goals to get done within the next few years, the state needs to start putting resources together, working with stakeholders and conducting research, the report says.

Putting the full plan into action could require a lot of funding and other resources. But Carreon said the more efficient Michigan’s industries can get on the front end, the cheaper things can get down the line.

“It can become easy to say this is really expensive and therefore we shouldn’t do it. But if we don’t think about all the externalized costs that result when you sort of stop there, you’re actually incurring costs, again at the system level, that you could be avoiding,” she said.

The roadmap estimates industrial emissions could cost the state over $616 million in extra annual health spending by 2050 if nothing changes.

Meanwhile, the roadmap authors suggest going all-in on the strategy could lead to lower energy costs. Michigan’s industrial and energy sectors account for nearly half of the state’s greenhouse gas emissions, according to the report.

The plan argues coordination between industry and utilities could lead to a more efficient and cheaper energy grid.

Elizabeth Boatman is with 5 Lakes Energy, the firm that created the report. She used renewable energy as an example.

Boatman said peak hours for renewable energy production don’t always line up with the peak hours for residential use. Without proper storage, some of that excess energy would just get wasted.

But, Boatman said, by building more storage capacity and changing power usage habits during those peak renewable production hours, industrial operations could help solve the problem.

“The more that we have different ways to offtake electricity when there’s excess of it going into the grid ... the more that we can [level] rates and affordability across all the ratepayers,” Boatman said. “Michigan could serve the same amount of load on the customer side by building less solar and less wind in total.”

She said businesses have another reason to stop relying so much on natural gas, as availability and supply chain risks increase.

“It’s not hospitals that have their gas shut off because not enough gas can be brought into a state. It’s not homes or universities or police stations. It’s manufacturers,” she said.

Other pieces of the plan involve boosting the "Buy Clean, Buy Michigan" plan to encourage more sustainable practices when it comes to sourcing.

The Michigan Manufacturers Association said it was still evaluating the plan Monday afternoon and couldn’t weigh in yet. But spokesperson Delaney McKinley said the group believes in working with regulators on future policies.

“Our initial review appreciates the report's recognition of the diversity of Michigan's manufacturing industries and the different operational and energy needs across those sectors," McKinley said in an email.

"As the state looks to support investment in manufacturing, there are opportunities to help manufacturers modernize their operations through voluntary, incentive-based programs such as grants, technical assistance, financing and support for adopting new technologies," said McKinley. "These investments can improve efficiency, strengthen operations and continue to deliver environmental benefits while keeping Michigan manufacturers competitive.”

text:
Moment Energy has begun production of a battery energy storage system made with repurposed electric vehicle batteries, marking a step toward expanding second-life battery applications in commercial and industrial energy infrastructure.

The company's Nova system is the first battery energy storage system (BESS) built with repurposed EV batteries to achieve both UL 1973 and UL 9540 certification, according to Moment Energy. The certifications address safety requirements for stationary battery systems and their use in commercial and industrial applications.

The system is designed to serve commercial facilities and larger energy storage installations, with applications including energy cost management, backup power and grid services. Moment Energy reports that its systems have been deployed at critical infrastructure sites, including airports, hospitals, agricultural facilities and manufacturing operations.

Each Nova unit provides 200 kW of power and 500 kWh of energy. Multiple units can be combined for larger installations, including projects reaching tens of megawatt-hours. The system is designed to accommodate battery packs from different electric vehicle models and uses a battery management system to monitor and manage batteries with varying levels of remaining capacity.

A modular architecture allows individual battery packs to be replaced as they age rather than requiring replacement of the entire installation. Moment Energy estimates the system can operate for more than 20 years with periodic capacity augmentation and battery pack replacement.

The system also incorporates liquid cooling, smoke and heat detection, flammable gas monitoring and deflagration prevention. It has been tested to UL 9540A, which evaluates thermal runaway fire propagation in energy storage systems. The company's manufacturing facility has also received UL 1974 certification, which covers processes for evaluating and repurposing used batteries.

Expanding the Second-Life Battery Supply Chain

The announcement comes as demand for stationary battery storage grows alongside electricity consumption from data centers, manufacturing and other energy-intensive commercial and industrial operations. Repurposing EV batteries offers another potential source of storage capacity while extending the useful life of battery materials and reducing the need for new battery production.

Batteries retired from electric vehicles may retain capacity for stationary applications, where operating requirements differ from those of vehicles. However, assessing battery health, managing variations among battery packs and maintaining long-term system performance are important considerations for second-life storage projects.

Moment Energy said its Nova system is manufactured in North America and has been independently verified as meeting Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements. The company also said the system qualifies for the federal Investment Tax Credit beginning in 2027 under applicable eligibility requirements.

Production is underway at the company's Megafactory 1, with first deliveries planned for the first quarter of 2027. The system was unveiled at RE+ in Las Vegas on Nov. 17.
