text:
INDIANAPOLIS, IN – Americans for Prosperity–Indiana (AFP-IN) today praised the Indiana Department of Environmental Management (IDEM) for rescinding more than a quarter of its non-rule policy documents and urging the U.S. EPA to follow Indiana’s lead.

Under Governor Mike Braun’s Executive Order 25-17, IDEM identified 26 of its 103 non-rule policies as obsolete, duplicative, or no longer grounded in current law. Eliminating them removes roughly 176 pages of “shadow regulations” — guidance that shaped agency decisions without ever going through public comment or legislative review. IDEM has also recommended that the EPA review more than 500 federal guidance documents for consolidation or elimination.

AFP-IN State Director Cody White issued the following statement:

“Hoosier businesses, farmers, and families shouldn’t have to navigate rules that were never actually written into law. Governor Braun and Commissioner Woods are showing what accountable government looks like: review the rules, keep what works, and clear out what doesn’t. Indiana isn’t just cleaning up its own house, it’s pushing Washington to do the same, and we urge the EPA to act quickly on IDEM’s recommendations.”

IDEM Commissioner Clint Woods issued the following statement:

“The top priority of government should be to be accountable to the citizens it serves. By reviewing and removing outdated policies, Indiana is increasing transparency, reducing unnecessary bureaucracy, and ensuring agency actions remain firmly grounded in the law and worthy of the public’s trust.”

Executive Order 25-17 directs state agencies to cut regulatory requirements by 25 percent by 2029. AFP-IN will continue to support the Braun administration and General Assembly in delivering on that goal.

text:
The 50 per cent Domestic Value Addition (DVA) requirement under the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Automobiles and Auto Components remains a challenge for auto-component manufacturers, with the domestic ecosystem for electric vehicle components and advanced automotive technologies still developing, according to the NITI Aayog’s latest report on impact assessment of PLI schemes.

The assessment identifies compliance with localisation requirements as a key challenge for companies seeking incentives under the scheme. Manufacturers must meet the prescribed DVA threshold to qualify for incentive disbursements.

Advt

Only 10 component applicants secure DVA certification

Only 10 applicants under the Component Champion Incentive Scheme have secured DVA certification across 37 variants, according to the report.

The certification process requires companies to demonstrate domestic value addition in their products and submit the necessary documentation to designated testing agencies.

The assessment notes that stringent DVA norms make compliance difficult, particularly as the domestic supply chain for advanced automotive technologies and EV components is still evolving.

Developing domestic supply chain remains critical

The PLI scheme seeks to strengthen domestic manufacturing of advanced automotive technology products. However, meeting the localisation threshold requires manufacturers to build domestic sourcing capabilities across their supply chains.

The assessment highlights the need to develop a wider domestic ecosystem for advanced automotive technologies to help manufacturers meet the DVA requirement.

description:

Henry McMaster, governor of South Carolina, says, “BMW continues to deliver on its commitments to South Carolina.
text:
BMW Group opened Plant Woodruff in South Carolina on November 13, 2026, starting series assembly of Gen6 high-voltage batteries. The packs use cylindrical cells in a cell-to-pack design and supply the new BMW iX5, BMW’s first fully electric model assembled in the United States, at Plant Spartanburg, 15 miles away.

BMW Group has started series production of sixth-generation (Gen6) high-voltage batteries at its new Plant Woodruff in South Carolina, USA, which officially opened on November 13, 2026. The batteries will be installed in the BMW iX5 and future electric vehicles (EVs) at BMW Group Plant Spartanburg, 15 miles away. The iX5 is BMW’s first fully electric model to be assembled in the US.

Raymond Wittmann, member of the board of management of BMW AG responsible for production, says, “Electromobility is our most important growth area. That is why we are systematically electrifying our portfolio, with the US playing a key role: By 2030, we will be assembling at least six fully electric models at Plant Spartanburg. The start of series production of Gen6 high-voltage batteries in Woodruff is therefore much more than the successful launch of a new site: it lays the foundation for the first-ever series production of fully electric BMW vehicles at Plant Spartanburg and on the American continent. This marks the beginning of the next chapter in the success story of the largest plant in our global production network.”

Woodruff is the fourth of five Gen6 battery assembly sites that the company has built close to its vehicle plants under a “local for local” principle. Debrecen in Hungary has produced Gen6 batteries in series since October 2025. Irlbach-Straßkirchen in Germany and Shenyang in China began series production in October 2026, and San Luis Potosí in Mexico will follow in 2027.

“With the opening of our Woodruff plant, we are expanding our global Gen6 network: high-voltage battery assembly is now in place in Europe, Asia and North America. This creates a key prerequisite for producing fully electric Neue Klasse vehicles on three continents. The rapid establishment of our Gen6 sites demonstrates the strength of our production network: we share know-how across locations and industrialise our new battery technology worldwide at speed. In doing so, we combine the strength of our global network with regional manufacturing, in line with our ‘Local for Local’ principle,” Wittmann adds.

Cell-to-pack with bought-in cells

Woodruff does not make battery cells. BMW sources cylindrical round cells from cell manufacturers, which build them to its specifications, and integrates them directly into the pack using a cell-to-pack approach. The company keeps its cell product and process expertise in its own competence centers in Bavaria. According to BMW, the Gen6 cells offer more than 20% higher energy density than the previous cell generation, with charging times cut by up to 30% and range increased by 30%, and by more in certain models.

At the plant, incoming cells undergo additional measurements, such as voltage checks, before cell clustering, where the cells are connected to coolers for insulation and cooling. The cell clusters and the cell contact system are then laser-cleaned and welded, with every weld seam inspected inline in real time. A foaming process binds the components into a single mechanical unit, after which the housing is closed, sealed and riveted. The final assembly step installs the Energy Master, the pack’s central control unit. Every battery then passes a 100% end-of-line inspection before being transported to Spartanburg.

AI and VR in production

All production steps are monitored inline and documented in real time. Artificial intelligence (AI) assistants and agents developed in-house analyze this data to support zero-defect production and improve overall equipment effectiveness (OEE). More than 300 employees and around 250 robots work at the plant. Digital twins and virtual reality (VR) applications were used for planning and training before commissioning, and all production staff complete an on-site VR training program set in a virtual replica of the plant’s production lines.

Robert Engelhorn, president and chief executive of BMW Manufacturing Co., LLC in Spartanburg, says, “We said we would begin assembling fully electric BMW vehicles in the US by the end of 2026 – and we are delivering on that commitment. With today’s opening of Plant Woodruff, we are further expanding our footprint in South Carolina and strengthening the close integration of battery and vehicle production. High-voltage batteries assembled at this state-of-the-art facility will power the next generation of fully electric BMW X models from Plant Spartanburg.”

The groundbreaking took place in June 2023, and construction began that September. Equipment installation started in September 2024 while construction was still under way, and the first test and pre-series batteries came off the line in summer 2025.

Rich Everly, vice president responsible for manufacturing at BMW Group Plant Woodruff, notes, “With today’s opening of Plant Woodruff, we demonstrate how quickly we can scale a new battery concept to industrial production. The key factor here is the interaction between a skilled and committed team and the continuous sharing of experience within the production network.”

Lower-carbon cells

The Gen6 cells for the iX5 contain a high proportion of secondary material in their cobalt, lithium and nickel content. Renewable energy is used to produce the anode and cathode materials and to manufacture the cells. BMW says this cuts carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) emissions by around 28% per watt-hour compared with the Gen5 cell used in the BMW iX. Plant Woodruff uses no fossil fuels during normal operations, and its industrial trucks run on hydrogen.

Henry McMaster, governor of South Carolina, says, “BMW continues to deliver on its commitments to South Carolina. Just a few years ago, I stood on this site with BMW leadership to break ground on this facility. Today, we are seeing that investment come to life and marking another milestone in BMW’s commitment to South Carolina. BMW has been a strong partner to our state, and this latest investment reinforces what we have built together and the opportunities ahead.”

text:
TKTMJ has received a $42.4 million Army contract for construction and site work in Metairie, Louisiana. The Natchitoches, Louisiana-based small business will provide construction access to the work site, demolition, clearing and grubbing, excavation, embankment placement, geotextile and stone installation, and turf establishment and maintenance.

The firm-fixed-price contract was competitively procured through an internet solicitation. The government received four bids.

Work will be performed in Metairie and is expected to be completed by November 15, 2027. The contract is identified as W912P8-27-C-A003.

The full $42.4 million contract amount was obligated when the award was made using fiscal 2027 civil expenses funding.

The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers’ New Orleans District is the contracting activity. The district oversees flood-risk management, navigation, coastal restoration, environmental, and other civil works projects throughout southern Louisiana.

Although the announcement does not name the specific project, the listed activities indicate a substantial civil construction effort involving preparation, earthwork, ground reinforcement, stone placement, and final site stabilization.

Construction access work will allow personnel and equipment to reach the active site. Demolition, clearing, and grubbing will remove existing structures, vegetation, debris, and other obstructions before excavation begins.

Excavation and embankment placement will reshape the site in accordance with the project design. Geotextiles can separate, reinforce, filter, or stabilize soil layers, while stone is commonly used for drainage, erosion control, structural support, or surface protection.

Turf establishment and maintenance will stabilize completed areas and restore ground cover after major construction activity.

The firm-fixed-price structure establishes an agreed amount for the defined scope, placing much of the performance-cost risk on TKTMJ unless the government authorizes changes.

Because the Army Corps obligated the entire amount at award, the $42.4 million represents a funded contract rather than an ordering ceiling or value dependent on unexercised options.

Quehenberger Logistics, a transport provider that operates in 11 European countries, began electrifying its electric truck fleet in 2018. By the end of 2026, the company will have 24 EVs in its fleet, and it plans to add 50 more in the following two years.

The company has built up extensive expertise in fleet electrification, from selecting the right vehicles and planning the charging infrastructure to training drivers and optimizing route planning.

“We are convinced that electric mobility is an essential part of the future of freight transport,” said CEO Christian Fürstaller. “That is why we are consistently expanding our electric fleet and charging infrastructure. Because we’ve been involved from the very start, we understand the practical requirements. We pass this expertise directly on to our customers.”

The key to successful electrification, Quehenberger believes, is the targeted and intelligent deployment of EVs. The company deploys electric trucks where they can fully utilize their strengths: in urban distribution, on predictable routes and in areas with optimal charging infrastructure.

“E-mobility in freight transport does not work on a ‘scattergun’ approach,” said Managing Director Andreas Letsch. “The key lies in the precise analysis of operational profiles, strategic route planning and intelligent integration into existing logistics processes.”

“A high-performance charging infrastructure is the backbone of a successful electric fleet,” added Christian Fürstaller. “That is why we are investing not only in vehicles, but also in the necessary infrastructure.”

title: From pilots to pipelines: Unlocking finance to scale up Nature-based Solutions - IUCN
description:
Co-hosted by the Government of the Netherlands, the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) and the ENACT Partnership, the event examined the financial, institutional and practical barriers preventing promising Nature-based Solutions (NbS) initiatives from reaching scale.
Making nature investment-ready While public finance remains critical for early-stage development and reducing investment risks, attracting private capital requires a different approach to how NbS projects are designed and presented.
Sylvia Wisniwski, Chief Executive Officer of Finance in Motion, stressed that project developers need to understand the perspective of investors.
To attract their interest, NbS projects need to demonstrate financial viability, replicability, a track record and clear exit strategies.
Progress will depend on piloting different approaches, testing a range of financial mechanisms and learning from implementation to identify solutions suited to different contexts.
text:
“Our economies are fundamentally dependent on nature, and Nature-based Solutions offer a powerful means of addressing climate change while delivering broader societal benefits,” said Afke van Rijn, Vice Minister for the Environment and International Affairs at the Government of the Netherlands, opening the discussion. “The challenge now is to move beyond individual projects towards system-level, landscape-scale approaches that integrate nature into development planning.”

The message set the tone for a technical side event held at the UNIDO Pavilion during COP31. Co-hosted by the Government of the Netherlands, the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) and the ENACT Partnership, the event examined the financial, institutional and practical barriers preventing promising Nature-based Solutions (NbS) initiatives from reaching scale.

As Ali Raza Rizvi, Director of IUCN’s Global Climate Change & Energy Transition Team and moderator of the session, highlighted, “Global investment in Nature-based Solutions currently stands at around US$220 billion annually, yet estimated financing needs reach US$571 billion per year to meet global biodiversity, climate and land restoration targets. With approximately 90% of current funding coming from public sources, there remains a significant opportunity to mobilise private capital and scale investment at the pace required.”

From policy ambition to investable projects

Building on the ENACT Partner Dialogue on Innovative Financing for Nature-based Solutions held in July 2026, speakers explored a central finding: the main bottleneck is often not a lack of NbS strategies or pilot initiatives, but the difficulty of turning these into commercially viable, investment-ready projects.

Mechthild Caspers, Head of Division for Climate Policy in the Land Sector and Nature Restoration at Germany’s Federal Ministry for the Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety (BMUKN), highlighted the role of ENACT in bridging this gap. By bringing state and non-state partners together and aligning their efforts, the Partnership can help move beyond fragmented initiatives towards more coordinated, large-scale and long-term implementation.

Switzerland’s experience offered practical lessons on creating the conditions for this transition. Oliver Wolf, Forest Policy Advisor at the Swiss Federal Office for the Environment, emphasised the importance of strong governance, integrated policies and credible impact measurement. Examples such as the Biodiversity Action Plan, integrated forest management and seed funding for urban tree planting demonstrate how targeted public investment and locally tested approaches can create the foundations for wider uptake. Testing innovative approaches at the cantonal level, he noted, can also provide a pathway for scaling successful models nationally.

Making nature investment-ready

While public finance remains critical for early-stage development and reducing investment risks, attracting private capital requires a different approach to how NbS projects are designed and presented.

Sylvia Wisniwski, Chief Executive Officer of Finance in Motion, stressed that project developers need to understand the perspective of investors. Institutional investors may not be familiar with the term NbS, but they do understand investment structures, asset classes, risk profiles and returns. To attract their interest, NbS projects need to demonstrate financial viability, replicability, a track record and clear exit strategies.

In response to this, Karim ould Chih, Chief of the Division of Innovative Finance and International Financial Institutions at UNIDO, underlined that there is a “need to connect policy ambition with project preparation, public support with appropriate private investment, and credible measurement with practical delivery, to mobilize finance at scale for NbS.”

The discussion also highlighted the need to strengthen national planning and enabling conditions. Integrating NbS into Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), National Adaptation Plans (NAPs), National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (NBSAPs) and wider development strategies can help provide the policy coherence and long-term certainty needed to encourage investment.

No single financing model

Closing the discussion, Maria Ana Petrera, Head of Team Global Climate and Energy Policy at Denmark’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, highlighted that although the concepts and policy frameworks for NbS are increasingly established, making projects attractive and viable investments remains a key challenge.

“There is no single financing model that will unlock NbS at scale,” she noted. Progress will depend on piloting different approaches, testing a range of financial mechanisms and learning from implementation to identify solutions suited to different contexts.

Marina Ponti, Deputy to the Director General and Managing Director of UNIDO’s Directorate of SDG Innovation and Economic Transformation, reinforced the importance of connecting policy, partnerships and finance to deliver tangible outcomes: “Clear policies, strong partnerships and accessible finance turn climate commitments into decent jobs and inclusive and sustainable development for people and the planet.’’

The event reinforced a shared message: scaling up NbS finance will require more than new funding sources. It calls for stronger national enabling environments, better-prepared project pipelines, innovative public-private financing approaches and harmonised monitoring, reporting and verification systems that build confidence in the results.

Through continued collaboration and knowledge exchange, the ENACT Partnership and its partners aim to help bridge the gap between ambition and implementation – ensuring that NbS can move beyond isolated pilots to deliver lasting benefits for climate, nature and people.

text:
Shortly after becoming 2027 D.C. Teacher of the Year, Ramon G. Griffin appeared on WHUR 96.3 FM, where his story reached thousands of listeners, including a mother who he said later wrote him a two-page letter in request of guidance for her teenage son.

“I look forward to reaching out to her and assisting her in that process and that goal,” said Griffin, an African-American history instructor at Thurgood Marshall Academy Public Charter School in Southeast. “The meaning of this Teacher of the Year award is that I am able to have a voice and representation on a larger scale so that others can be inspired and so that I can help individuals. It’s my objective to work more closely with young teachers to aid them in their skill set, to make sure our children are being educated properly and effectively.”

On Oct. 26, D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser — flanked by D.C. State Superintendent Dr. Antoinette Mitchell, Ward 8 D.C. State Board of Education Representative Dr. LaJoy Johnson Law, and others — announced Griffin as 2027 D.C. Teacher of the Year during what several students, faculty and staff at Thurgood Marshall Academy PCS thought was an assembly organized in celebration of the school’s 100% college acceptance rate since its inception.

“In my spirit, I can honestly say I knew I won,” Griffin told The Informer. “When she switched it up and said ‘I’m here for a teacher,’ the first thing that came to mind was that this may be it. Then she stated a quote from a documentary that was done on me last year, and she stated where I originate from, and I said I’m about to be awarded D.C. Teacher of the Year. That’s when it set in.”

Griffin, a self-described griot, has 13 years of teaching under his belt, seven of which have been at Thurgood Marshall Academy PCS. That’s where he currently serves as an instructor of AP African-American Studies and African American History through Film and Music. Both courses, he told The Informer, allow him to engage students in storytelling.

Within a couple of months, Griffin’s endeavor to shape the minds of youth continues when Thurgood Marshall Academy PCS hosts yet another “Morehouse Day.” This event, held at several District schools, connects male students with members of the Morehouse Alumni Association Washington, DC Chapter, many of whom graduated from District public and public charter schools before pursuing higher education.

“We have Morehouse men who come in: those who are elders to me, those who were there during my tenure and those who are younger,” said Griffin, a member of Morehouse’s Class of 1998 and key influence in at least three Thurgood Marshall Academy PCS alumni’s matriculation to the HBCU. “What it shows is that we as Black men are not what they portray in the news. We’re not about bringing each other down. We’re about standing out, building, and making sure that our race is looked upon proudly, not for others, but for self and for the next generation.”

An Inside Look: ‘Morehouse Day’ at Thurgood Marshall Academy PCS

The upcoming “Morehouse Day” at Thurgood Marshall Academy PCS is scheduled to take place on Jan. 15, which would’ve been the 98th birthday of Morehouse alumnus the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. This intergenerational gathering also happens around the same time that Howard University men’s basketball team plays its home game against Morehouse College.

For Morehouse alumnus and “Morehouse Day” brainchild Ebbon Allen, it was a perfect storm that only Griffin could help make happen.

“Before we even knew that Ramon was going to be awarded and honored, we’ve been on ‘Morehouse Day’ as teammates for the last two years,” Allen told The Informer. “We definitely had a meeting within the last two or three months to designate ‘Morehouse Day’ for MLK’s birthday weekend. Ramon just shows the epitome of a Morehouse man: well-versed, well-traveled, and definitely educated.”

Speaking more about his fellow Morehouse alumnus, Allen said that Griffin has long put in the work to boost college enrollment among young Black men.

“He’s had a lot of young men going to attend Morehouse College,” Allen told The Informer. “We’re still trying to work on a pipeline to send more young men from Thurgood Marshall Academy down to Atlanta.”

Since the inception of “Morehouse Day” in 2021, Allen and other members of the Morehouse Alumni Association Washington, DC Chapter have spoken to more than 2,000 young men attending: Calvin Coolidge High School; Dunbar High School; Eastern Senior High School; Friendship Technology Preparatory High School; H.D. Woodson High School; Kelly Miller Middle School; and Ron Brown College Preparatory High School.

The upcoming “Morehouse Day” at Thurgood Marshall Academy PCS will be the second seminar of its kind on school grounds. Allen said that students will delve into violence prevention, entrepreneurship, college and career readiness, and the scholarship application process. His goal, he said, centers on providing them space to imagine how to achieve their dreams.

“We wanted young Black men to understand that they can learn about self-advocacy and learn the value of being a Black male in today’s society,” Allen told The Informer. “There’s going to be a new [mayoral] administration so our young men need to get well-versed and become well-educated about their rights and the opportunities to create a space of learning about strong advocacy.”

Allen, who followed in his three uncles’ footsteps to attend Morehouse College, credited the HBCU with exposing him to the different caliber of Black men. He told The Informer that, like him and other Morehouse men, Griffin has embedded in him a passion for working hard and laying a foundation for those coming after him.

“Ramon Griffin sets the bar for other Black male educators about how much of an impact and difference they can make,” Allen told The Informer. “By coming to Thurgood Marshall Academy in Southeast Washington, D.C., he’ll make more young Black men…find out what it takes to get back in a positive light. You don’t always have to be an entertainer. You don’t always have to be in athletics, but you can take an education pathway and still be awarded for your service, commitment and dedication.”

Out of the Mouths of Babes

C’khai Morgan, a senior at Thurgood Marshall Academy PCS, said he counts Morehouse College among his top choices for business management and human resource management, thanks to Griffin.

“He literally embodies the meaning of a Morehouse Man,” C’khai told The Informer. “You go in any classroom he ever had, you’re going to see something Morehouse. You catch him on a good day, he’s probably wearing a Morehouse sweater.”

C’khai, who also applied to Fayetteville State University, North Carolina Agricultural & Technical State University, and Temple University in Philadelphia, was a student in Griffin’s AP African-American Studies course last school year. On his way to scoring a 4 on the Advanced Placement exam and clinching college credits, he participated in Thurgood Marshall Academy PCS’ “My Brother’s Keeper” program, where he got to learn more about the man he now regards as an uncle.

“I started seeing a different side of Mr. Griffin that I never heard of,” C’khai said. “He always wants the best for somebody, but other students who lack maturity or just lack the understanding of his purpose would be like ‘Mr. Griffin be trying hard. He be pressed to get somebody in trouble.’ It reminded me that you can’t let somebody else’s opinions refer to someone as such.”

Students who take Griffin’s African-American History through Film and Music course take a trip through the Jim Crow, the Great Migration, and Harlem Renaissance, among other time periods, to understand how the blues genre originated from Africa, came into form during enslavement, and traveled with African Americans who moved into northern U.S. cities.

Although Griffin has a curriculum, he often deviates from it, as Thurgood Marshall Academy PCS student Kailani Marshall noted, by recounting his family history. She told The Informer about learning African-American history through stories of Griffin’s grandmother who migrated from Mississippi to Detroit, where he was born and raised.

“He makes sure that students actually retain the information and it’s entertaining as well,” said Kailani, a senior who hopes to study sociology either at Georgetown University, Howard University, Spelman College, or Temple University. “I can’t say that about a lot of classes. The way he teaches really allows students to understand topics fully.”

During her junior year, Kailani took Griffin’s AP African-American Studies and African-American History through Film and Music courses. She, too, scored a 4 on her AP exam, due to what she called Griffin’s demand for excellence.

“You can’t be mediocre. It’s not an option,” Kailani said about Griffin. “He’s passionate about instilling confidence and success into students. You can’t say that about a lot of teachers. He really is one of the few teachers who actually care for their students and care for their future.”

During Griffin’s first year of teaching AP African-American Studies at Thurgood Marshall Academy PCS, 87.5% of his students passed the AP exam. This feat follows other achievements at Dunbar High School, where he directed climate and culture, and at Kingman Academy Public Charter School, where he served as a founding member.

Even with Thurgood Marshall Academy PCS’ 100% college acceptance rate, Griffin acknowledged that it takes great effort to earn a bachelor’s degree. That’s what he said he emphasizes to his students as he shares his coming-of-age story and integrates writing and math enrichment into his assignments.

“You don’t want to be a 20-year-old counting on your fingers. You don’t want to be a 20-year-old starting a sentence and ending it at the end of the page with one period,” Griffin said. “You just have to put in the work, and I give them examples of times during my high school years and during my college years. Whatever you want in life, you can have. You definitely will accomplish it, but you have to have a plan. It’s not going to be given to you.”

Based on reporting by Washington Informer.

In the capital city, hundreds of defendants wait in jail for an indictment, sometimes as long as a year or more.

When Vicki Sands learned that her son, Carson, was in a county jail near Jackson, Mississippi, more than 600 miles away from her home in North Carolina, she felt, at first, a strange kind of relief.

Months before his arrest, he left Asheville, launching on a road trip with a new acquaintance he had met in the mountain city’s street-life scene. The journey had ended with a falling out in the Deep South that left Carson homeless.

“I was glad he was off the streets,” said Vicki Sands in an interview with The Marshall Project. “I was glad he was out of the woods.”

ADVERTISEMENT

That feeling didn’t last long.

Since an initial appearance before a judge on Nov. 3, just days after his Halloween night arrest last year, Carson Sands has not been inside a courtroom again. No attorney has requested a preliminary hearing or filed a motion to reduce his $300,000 bond on charges stemming from an alleged gas station robbery. There’s been no routine status conference where a judge might probe the reason for delays and prod prosecutors to move things along. He has not been indicted, convicted, or sentenced — but is stuck in an indefinite legal limbo.

“It’s as if he doesn’t exist,” his mother said.

As of June 30 of this year, Sands was one of 131 people being held for more than six months without an indictment: 56 of whom had been held for more than a year, an analysis by The Marshall Project found.

This article was published in partnership with The Howard Center for Investigative Journalism, an investigative reporting unit and early-career journalism training program based at the University of Maryland Philip Merrill College of Journalism, which is supported by the Scripps Howard Foundation.

ADVERTISEMENT

Such long periods of pre-trial incarceration with no formal charges from a prosecutor are almost unheard of in many other parts of the country, where prosecutors are given a limited amount of time to indict before a defendant must be released — 40 days in Florida, 60 days in Louisiana. In fact, Mississippi is one of only six states with no limits at all, according to a 2023 law review analysis.

In all, almost half of the people in custody at the end of June who had been held for at least 30 days on felony charges were not indicted, the analysis found.

State and local officials have argued and deflected blame about slow-moving criminal cases, backlogs and people literally getting lost in jail for years. A labyrinth of record systems, and questions about their accuracy, has often stymied those conversations. The Marshall Project’s findings are the first of their kind to be released publicly.

Critics say the analysis raises serious questions about whether the court system is depriving individuals of their constitutional right to due process before taking away their liberty.

Those critics include Brad McCullouch, a Hinds County assistant district attorney who was promoted to interim officeholder in July by the state’s governor.

ADVERTISEMENT

He went so far as to compare time spent in jail by some Hinds County prisoners to detention practices seen under authoritarian governments.

“This is not what we do as a country,” McCullouch said. “It’s not based on constitutional principles.”

McCullough touted his efforts to put more resources toward the grand jury process and to help secure the release of people from custody where he thinks appropriate. But he can’t run in next Tuesday’s special election because he doesn’t live in Hinds County, and is in office at most about six more weeks.

One of the five people running to replace McCullouch will help determine whether anything changes. Several have promised reforms, while others have not made it a central focus of their campaign.

Meanwhile, for Carson and others, the wait continues.

ADVERTISEMENT

“Lost in the System”

Carson Sands’ journey into legal purgatory began on Halloween night 2025, when he walked into a Jackson gas station near LeFleur’s Bluff State Park. Far from home, he’d marked his 31st birthday just days earlier, on the streets and huddled in the woods.

Sands placed a water, an energy drink, and a Cayman Jack beverage on the counter. The clerk told him he couldn’t use an EBT card for the alcohol, according to a police report written later. In a scene captured on security video, police said Sands pulled a can of bear spray from a backpack he was wearing. He put the items into the backpack, threatened to rifle through the cash register, and then displayed a knife on his way out of the store with the drinks.

A Capitol Police officer found Sands and arrested him not far away, in some woods near a baseball field.

An arrest like this is only the beginning of a criminal case. In most jurisdictions, a prosecutor must next consider the charges lodged by law enforcement and then decide whether to pursue formal charges in court. In Mississippi, district attorneys must obtain an indictment from a grand jury to prosecute someone for a felony.

During Sands’ initial — and only — court appearance, on Nov. 3, the judge ruled that he would need to post a secured bond of $300,000 to be released from jail while waiting for the next steps in his case. Using a bondsman, that would typically require a cash payment of about $30,000 — a sum he doesn’t have the means to pay.

The inability to pay does not necessarily lead to indefinite detention in many other states. Instead, after a certain amount of time, people in these states can ask a judge to reduce their bond or to outright release them from jail without having to pay any cash.

In Texas, after 90 days, Carson Sands could have asked for a lower bond or to be released without paying any money at all by the end of January.

There are constitutional reasons that many states put time limits on pre-trial detention, but also practical considerations. When a case stalls waiting for an indictment, victims must wait for resolution to their cases. Evidence can go stale or even be missing, making it harder for prosecutors to win a once solid case or for the accused to defend themselves. Defendants with few financial resources, like Sands, are forced to sit out the long wait times in a dangerous jail, while defendants with greater financial means get to spend that time at home.

This gray zone of detention without legal limits sits at the intersection of multiple dysfunctional systems stretched beyond their limits in Hinds County — including a decrepit and deadly jail under federal receivership and a public defender’s office still reeling from a staffing and caseload crisis.

But it’s the district attorney’s office — rocked by recent scandals — that is responsible for taking cases to the grand jury to seek an indictment. It’s also the office most subject to immediate oversight by voters, through next week’s special election. The office has been operating under an interim leader since July, when the previous prosecutor, Jody Owens, resigned as part of a plea deal in a federal corruption case.

Amid this tangle, Vicki Sands has found it very difficult to determine basic facts about her son’s detention, or to discern how to help. She considered trying to file a habeas corpus petition — which can be used to challenge the basis for someone’s detention — but doesn’t even know how to start.

“Carson is simply lost in the system,” said his mother. “He hasn’t been convicted, and yet he is detained going on a year with no end in sight.”

One Day in Court

Over the course of this year, as The Marshall Project conducted its analysis, a reporter spent several days in the county court. The reporter saw a series of unindicted defendants appear before a judge for a thicket of initial appearances, preliminary hearings, bond reductions and status hearings.

Felony cases in Mississippi must move through a series of different courts that don’t always intersect. In Hinds County, the county court is a frequent venue where attorneys bring motions and arguments on behalf of defendants without indictments. But with only a single judge hearing these cases, this is a major chokepoint.

As of April 15, Carson Sands had already been jailed for almost six months. His mother worried he was deteriorating within a dangerous and overwhelming environment. The lights in the jail were always on. A TV blared. She couldn’t mail him books, which had long been a source of calm to him. She sent meditation guides and other reading material through the jail messaging system, but some of her messages were blocked.

“He does not belong in prison,” Vicki had written around this time to a reporter with The Marshall Project. “He needs behavioral health treatment. He needs support for his psychiatric needs. Instead, he is in an environment that is crushing and traumatizing him.”

Carson — yet again — did not make it onto Judge Johnnie McDaniels’ slate of felony cases that day.

But several other people did, people just like him –– arrested, jailed, and simply waiting. Court officials called the case of LaShanti Esco. She’d been arrested last August on serious charges — armed carjacking and armed robbery. She faced a $1 million bond.

As the case was called, Wendy Wilson White, an assistant district attorney, said that the proceedings were moot — the case had finally been indicted, she said, paving the way for a formal arraignment in a higher court.

But Judge McDaniels saw a problem as he flipped through the papers in front of him. He’d heard this claim before.

“It is April,” he said. “The same representation was made in January. Why wasn’t an indictment that occurred in January filed by now? What would be the explanation?”

That can sometimes happen when law enforcement can’t locate a defendant to serve the papers. But Esco had been in the county’s custody the entire time.

“I don’t know that I have an explanation,” White said.

Ultimately, the indictment wasn’t served on Esco until about five days after the hearing, according to court records. It had only been signed by a grand jury that month, not in January.

White is one of five candidates now running in a special election to be the next district attorney in Hinds County.

White told The Marshall Project last week that she will never knowingly misrepresent a case to a judge and emphasized that when handling a case in court, she sometimes has limited information immediately available to her.

“I’m representing the state, and I have to take accountability when there are shortcomings in a case,” White said.

Next up was Jeremy Jordan, arrested in August 2025 on a drug possession charge. Jordan was held without bond due to prior charges from 2022 and 2023 that were still open and not indicted.

That meant, his attorney said, that Jordan had been in jail for 237 days with three criminal charges and not a single indictment on any of them.

In at least some of the cases, the defense attorney said, prosecutors were waiting on results from the state crime lab.

“We know the issues with the state crime lab,” McDaniels said. “Surely three or four years is enough time to get something back?”

McDaniels set a secured bond for $75,000 for Jordan — still a high bond. Jordan stayed in jail for months more, and in June submitted his own motions to dismiss the case for violation of due process.

The cases continued. Adetdrick Burton had been held almost a year on a murder charge and a $1 million bond, with no indictment.

“This case has not been presented to a grand jury,” said White, the assistant district attorney. “The DA’s office is not in possession of the file. The DA’s office requires, or prefers, to have the completed investigative file.”

In response to a question from the judge, White could not say whether the file had been requested from law enforcement by the DA’s office.

“A case is not solved just because an arrest is made,” said McDaniels. “When I’m being told more than a year later that you don’t know what stage a case is at, that should be troubling to us all.”

Next up was Justin Porter, held 609 days without an indictment on home burglary charges. White acknowledged the long delay in securing an indictment, but urged caution, alleging that the burglary in question had been carried out, she claimed, as “an attempt to terrorize the victims.”

“Surely there is an explanation why a defendant charged with attempted burglary of a dwelling has been detained for 609 days without being indicted,” McDaniels asked White. “There has to be an explanation.”

“That’s definitely a good question,” White said. “I don’t know that the state is prepared to offer an explanation that would be satisfactory.”

When cases stall like this, there are several possible reasons in play. Sometimes law enforcement makes an arrest but, as White suggested in court, simply does not turn over the file to the prosecutors, leaving those prosecutors without evidence to present to a grand jury. Sometimes the case has been forgotten, and the district attorney’s office simply hasn’t asked for it. Other times, the investigation may still be ongoing, even after an arrest has been made, or officers are waiting on forensic tests or other evidence.

But even when prosecutors don’t have an explanation at hand, or when defense attorneys haven’t given a case much attention, an area’s senior circuit judge has a responsibility under the state’s rules of criminal court: They must monitor the circumstances and release conditions of people detained in the local jail.

Senior Circuit Judge Winston Kidd and McDaniels, whom Kidd has designated to oversee felony cases before an indictment, did not respond to questions from The Marshall Project about how they handle review of the jail lists.

This requirement was written to prevent people from falling through the cracks, said William Waller Jr., a retired chief justice of the Mississippi Supreme Court who helped write the state’s rules of criminal procedure.

“That was the whole purpose for it,” said Waller. “It was supposed to be a safety net to catch cases.”

A Maze of Faulty Data

A month before Carson Sands was arrested, a jail operations consultant based in Maryland named Wendell France took over management of Hinds County’s Raymond Detention Center on the order of a federal judge.

That followed a decade of litigation brought by the U.S. Department of Justice over unending constitutional violations inside the county’s jail — widespread brutality, deaths and beatings at the hands of other prisoners, rampant contraband, open sewage, and poor or nonexistent medical care.

Once France began to examine the roster of detainees, he noticed something that alarmed him: Significant numbers of people in the jail were held only based on an arrest charge, with no indictment.

He dispatched a letter to local justice system officials, including Owens, who was then the DA. A former civil rights litigator, Owens ran for office in 2019, promising to be a “decarceral prosecutor.”

“I am writing to formally request your office’s immediate attention to the status of pre-trial detainees who have been held without indictment for extended periods,” France wrote to Owens in an Oct. 10, 2025 letter. “These are not merely administrative concerns but fundamental constitutional violations that expose the county to significant legal liability.”

As he had done before when similar concerns had surfaced, Owens responded by pointing out that jail rosters supplied by local jail administration are often riddled with errors.

“I am committed to reducing the delays for criminal detainees wherever possible, but caution you that the conclusions you have drawn in your correspondence are based on inaccurate data,” Owens wrote.

Owens also warned that law enforcement agencies, and not his office, often drive delays by failing to complete investigations promptly, even after an arrest has been made. Those agencies, Owens said, do not quickly turn over files to the DA’s office and sometimes do not even notify the office of cases that are open or arrests that have been made.

Nine months later, Owens resigned as part of a plea deal with federal prosecutors on conspiracy charges involving a bribery scheme.

Not long after these letters were dispatched, an assistant district attorney was also sounding the alarm, claiming that management of the grand jury process had fallen into near complete disarray.

“Cases are lost, defendants are lost, indictments have errors, hundreds of cases have been presented to the Grand Jury but never turned in,” wrote Gwen Agho in December 2025, according to an email she provided.

Agho is also now running for district attorney in Hinds County.

Locally, the accuracy of jail and court records has been a flashpoint in long-running clashes over jail crowding and case delays. Money from the state flowed into Hinds County beginning in 2022 to help reduce a pandemic-linked backlog, but local officials could not reach consensus about where the backlog was. This disagreement was driven, in part, by jail systems, court records, and case management that don’t talk to each other, said State Public Defender André de Gruy.

He identified unindicted cases as a key problem, but acknowledged he was dealing with jail lists widely known to be faulty, with errors in case numbers and indictment status. He didn’t have the resources to laboriously correct and verify those lists line by line.

But that’s exactly what The Marshall Project did.

The news organization started with a list provided by the county of the 848 people in custody on June 30 and then excluded people who had been there for less than 30 days — which is within detention norms nationwide — as well as people held on suspected or confirmed probation violations or other kinds of post-sentencing matters. The analysis also excluded people likely being held on misdemeanor charges and those under the age of 18 when they were arrested. That left 628 held in custody while facing criminal charges.

The Marshall Project examined several thousand pages of public court records, obtained through the Mississippi Electronic Courts portal, including dockets and filings, to match public indictments or circuit court cases to people detained at the jail. Almost half did not have any.

Even those who were indicted while in jail had often waited months for it to finally happen. More than two-thirds of the people who were still waiting for an indictment on June 30, or who had been indicted while held, had gone three months or more without an indictment.

How long had people in the Hinds County jail waited for an indictment?

Hundreds of people who were in jail in Hinds County, Miss., on June 30 of this year had waited more than 30 days in custody without receiving an indictment. Most of them waited more than 90 days.

McCullouch said The Marshall Project’s analysis reached findings similar to those his staff conducted after he took over the office in July.

In a letter to France in September, he touted the role of his office in securing release for 59 people held on non-violent charges. By October, McCullouch told the county’s Board of Supervisors that number had risen to 74.

He called this the “low-hanging fruit” that needed to happen quickly to relieve pressure on the jail before a more careful sifting of cases with violent charges follows. That work will take longer, he said, because of the potential stakes for broader public safety.

In doing that careful sifting, McCullouch — and White, speaking separately about her plans if elected — also touted the significance of new funding from the county for an additional assistant prosecutor’s position.

But the maze of often-faulty data doesn’t help either, said McCullouch.

Justice system officials should have access to reliable, current data of the sort that it took The Marshall Project weeks to produce, said Andrew Davies, research director with the Deason Criminal Justice Reform Center at Southern Methodist University.

“Hinds County urgently needs better systems for tracking this information,” Davies said. “Without them, courts and jails lack the tools they need to deliver justice and treat people with dignity.”

The interlocking nature of the problem, cutting across different systems and different branches of government, means it’s hard to identify one point of failure that can be easily fixed. But it also means that there are several people empowered to push solutions or force the issue onto the agenda — including judges, legislators, and the local district attorney.

And that’s where, McCullouch said, regardless of what judges or police detectives do, or how faulty the jail data happens to be, a prosecutor has power — if they will use it.

Sometimes, he said, that means taking a case with no file to the grand jury, expecting the grand jury to decline an indictment.

So what happens next for Sands?

Earlier this month, The Marshall Project asked McCullouch about the status of the case and why there’d been such a long delay in securing an indictment.

McCullouch turned around in his chair and faced his computer — “You said Sands?” he asked, double-checking as he typed — opening the system prosecutors use to track case files submitted by law enforcement agencies.

There was nothing for Carson’s case. Just an empty screen. McCullouch told The Marshall Project he’d never heard of the case until the news outlet asked. He said his office would try to find out more and take some action.

Capitol Police turned the case file over to prosecutors the next day, according to a spokesperson for the agency.

After 349 days in jail, Sands had been found.

text:
Key Takeaways

As the federal government rolls back climate policies at home and retreats from climate commitments abroad, states are taking up the mantle, creating and implementing climate action plans (CAPs).

More successful CAPs have various non-climate considerations, consistent leadership on climate action, significant public participation, and federal funding mechanisms that support implementation.

States have a massive appetite for investing in planning and technology that provide climate resilience, economic development, and affordability.

Despite strong 67% support from the American public for federal climate action, recent climate policy reversals or rollbacks signal the federal government’s broad retreat from action on climate mitigation, adaptation, and resilience. In its wake, states have been filling the leadership vacuum and taking up the mantle. One key tool in their toolbelts are climate action plans (CAPs).

What Are State CAPs?

A CAP typically establishes greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction targets and outlines strategies to achieve them. These plans are tailored to the state’s demographics, economy, and natural resources, and include elements such as adaptation strategies, energy goals, and social objectives. The strength of a CAP can also vary, from legally binding requirements to voluntary and incentive-based measures (as seen in Tennessee's plan, for example). Usually, CAPs are developed by state officials in collaboration with stakeholders and the public. Various states began some form of climate action planning during the early 1990s. In 2001, just 19 states, along with Puerto Rico, had a CAP. In 2024, 48 states and all five major territories had developed some kind of CAP, though only 24 states have officially enacted their CAPs through legislation, executive orders, or other rules and regulations.

Part of the increase in state CAPs can be attributed to the Climate Pollution Reduction Grants (CPRG) program under the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), which was authorized by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA) (P.L. 117-169). This dual-phased federal program provided nearly $5 billion in planning and implementation grants to states, metropolitan areas, and tribes to develop a CAP or update an existing one under specific guidelines. The first phase offered $250 million in noncompetitive grants for participants to create a Priority Climate Action Plan (PCAP). These plans included a detailed GHG inventory of emission sources and sinks, high-priority GHG reduction measures, a benefit analysis for low-income and disadvantaged communities, and a review of authority to implement. Under the second phase, $4.6 billion was awarded in competitive grants. Participants were required to develop a more in-depth Comprehensive Climate Action Plan (CCAP), requiring GHG reduction projections and targets, plans to leverage other federal funding, and a benefit analysis for the entire state population, among other elements.

Under the CPRG program’s first phase, 45 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico participated in developing PCAPs. Note that three states—Florida, Iowa, and Kentucky—at some point developed their own state CAPs but never opted into the federal CPRG program. For 16 states, CPRG funding resulted in their first-ever CAP of any kind. Almost every participating state went on to submit a CCAP, as well (the exceptions were Alabama, Idaho, Indiana, and Mississippi).

What Makes for a Successful CAP?

In addition to setting out steps to reduce GHG emissions, CAPs often consider factors like environmental justice and equity, job creation, household costs, and economic growth. Many of these elements, like the inclusion of a benefit analysis for low-income and disadvantaged communities, were required by the CPRG program. Because CAPs are not one-size-fits-all, states that can combine their plans with existing goals and agendas can more easily execute their CAPs. Jacob Corvidae, senior principal at RMI, notes that this is especially true if their efforts are well-synced with affordability and economic development initiatives.

For instance, the U.S. Climate Alliance, a collective of 24 states that have CAPs and governors committed to a net-zero future, was able to reduce its collective net GHG emissions by 24% between 2005 and 2023 (while increasing its collective gross domestic product by 34%). During that same period of time, non-Alliance states and territories only reached a 16% GHG reduction. By moving in unison with clear commitments, Alliance states are better positioned to de-risk investments, improve market certainty, and avoid issues like emissions leakage, whereby emission reduction rollbacks in one region result in emission increases elsewhere.

Climate impacts are felt first and foremost by people and communities—through their health and safety, their social well-being, and their wallets. Accordingly, effective climate plans incorporate and address the needs of communities on the ground. Moreover, climate impacts are not felt in a silo. The most equitable and effective plans are those that are multidimensional and holistic. They involve the public, stakeholders across all sectors of the economy, and every level of government throughout the entire planning process. Many states have looked to Maine’s Maine Won’t Wait plan as a leading example of community involvement in planning. A 39-member council of scientists, industry leaders, bipartisan officials, and community representatives created the plan, offering a wide array of perspectives. The council received hundreds of comments through its website, thousands of survey responses, and held public meetings to ensure community engagement and benefit. The plan also created groups such as the Equity Subcommittee and the Industrial Task Force to target underrepresented diverse populations and industry stakeholders, respectively.

Last but not least, an essential ingredient for success in state climate planning is funding. The funding provided by the CPRG program built up states’ capacity to hire necessary staff, conduct analysis, and create and implement their plans. Corvidae noted that many states were able to implement parts of their plans through other IRA funding sources, such as the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Formula Program. However, given the recent rollbacks of federal climate funding programs, states that have their own self-sustaining funding mechanisms can better support their CAPs than those without. For instance, the State of Washington’s Cap-and-Invest program, created by its Climate Commitment Act (S.B.5126), not only sets binding standards to lower emissions, but brings in billions of dollars in revenue by requiring businesses that emit the equivalent of at least 25,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide annually to buy emission allowances from the state. It also requires that at least 35% of the Cap-and-Invest program revenue benefits vulnerable populations in overburdened communities and no less than 10% of revenue goes to projects supported by a Tribal resolution.

What Challenges Do CAPs Face?

Even while CPRG was active, the funds for implementation grants were massively oversubscribed, Corvidae highlighted. Some states built their plans under the assumption that they would have CPRG funding to implement them—only to be hindered when that money did not come in, due to the competitive nature of the implementation grants. Outside of CPRG funds, most states planned on using other federal tax credits and grants that have since been terminated by Congress. Before the cuts were made, a 2025 Brookings Institute study estimated that around half of U.S. states, particularly southeastern and Great Plains states, could potentially roll back their climate-based planning should federal support wane. A University of Maryland study projects that in 2035, all states will see gross domestic product losses if all federal clean energy legislation and regulations are repealed, with states like Texas, Michigan, Indiana, and Montana projected to face $5.3-8.8 billion each in losses.

Beyond funding uncertainty, the federal landscape is changing what states can accomplish without legal challenges. For example, Congress blocked California in its push to phase out the sale of gas-powered vehicles by 2035. The state then sued the EPA and the president in response, landing it in the center of a political battle. In addition, the Trump Administration’s goal of “Unleashing American Energy” has resulted in many executive orders directly halting wind and other renewable energy projects, which states have pushed back against in court.

Finally, states that lack a CAP, or have deprioritized the one they do have, create a “race to the bottom” in which deregulation can reign. An extreme example of this can be seen in Florida, which, despite developing a CAP in 2008, has since dropped its statewide emission reduction efforts, and in fact prohibited municipal governments from passing certain net-zero policies. Furthermore, some states with written or enacted CAPs have directly contradicted their emission reduction goals by passing anti-renewable legislation and increasing fossil fuel generation. For example, Indiana, Louisiana, and Tennessee all passed legislation that includes natural gas as a form of “clean energy.”

States as Policy Laboratories

States should be self-motivated to invest in climate action, not only to mitigate and prepare for adverse climate change impacts, but also for the co-benefits that can be observed locally (e.g., lower electricity costs, cleaner air, green jobs, better public transportation, etc.). States can also act as policy laboratories, testing new policies before they are implemented in other states or at the federal level. On the global stage, without leadership from the Trump Administration, states now represent the U.S. global climate action agenda. Indeed, 28 governors and mayors attended the 2025 UN climate summit (COP30) and at least 10 are expected to attend COP31 currently taking place in Antalya, Türkiye.

The states now have their work cut out for them. One Nature study found that U.S. GHG emissions would drop by 45.7% if 23 states were to achieve 2050 net-zero emission goals—though such a change would still fall short of Paris Agreement targets. Corvidae emphasized that states have a massive appetite for climate planning, pointing to the high level of state participation in the CPRG program regardless of politics or geography. And, though states can and are taking charge of climate action through their CAPs, renewed federal funding support is still necessary to maximize successful implementation.

text:
Ethiopia has seen an impressive increase in electricity access during the last 20 years, but access to clean cooking has not kept pace. Lack of access to clean cooking is acknowledged as the largest energy access challenge in the country. Currently, the access rate is ~13% and Ethiopia’s ambition is to achieve more than 57% access by 2030. With most households continuing to rely on firewood and charcoal, this reliance has far-reaching consequences for public health, the environment, gender equality and household livelihoods.

As Ethiopia works towards its national clean cooking targets, evidence-based planning and investment will be essential to accelerating the transition and ensuring that solutions are affordable, accessible and appropriate for different communities.

Developed by Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) in partnership with the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO), under the umbrella of the Energising Development (EnDev) programme, this report provides a comprehensive cost-benefit analysis of Ethiopia's transition to clean cooking.

The analysis examines the economic, social and environmental costs and benefits of different cooking technologies, including electric cooking, biogas, solar cooking and improved biomass solutions. It also incorporates geospatial analysis to help identify where investments can deliver the greatest impact.

The findings provide evidence to inform national policy, investment decisions and programme design, supporting Ethiopia's ambition to achieve a just, equitable and sustainable clean cooking transition.

Key conclusions and recommendations

Transition to clean cooking: The positive net benefit finding holds up even under pessimistic assumptions, so the case for transitioning is robust rather than contingent on favourable conditions. Because the analysis excludes the cost of the interventions needed to drive adoption, the net benefit calculated here can be read as an upper bound on what the government and donors could spend on price support, financing or awareness campaigns and still come out ahead.

Choice of clean cookstove: No single technology suits every context. A successful transition will need a mix of these technologies matched to local conditions.

Electric cooking: Ethiopia's electrification progress is a strong foundation for electric cooking, but access does not automatically translate into use. Households often keep cooking with biomass for reasons of affordability, reliability and habit. Appliance financing for electric pressure cookers and electric mitads, targeted subsidies, consumer awareness and demand-side management are needed to turn electrification into realized clean cooking outcomes.

Job creation: The employment gains identified are conditional on a supportive local ecosystem. Manufacturing, distribution, installation and repair capacity, together with training for artisans, technicians and entrepreneurs, all need to be built up for the formal jobs to materialize. At the same time, moving away from charcoal will reduce (mostly) informal livelihoods for many of the 1.3 million people in charcoal trade, so reskilling and transition support for these workers should be built into program design from the outset.

Affordability: Upfront cost is an important barrier to adoption. For many transitions, particularly from purchased firewood or charcoal to electricity, biogas or solar, households save money on fuel from the outset but may not be able to clear the initial hurdle of buying the stove or system. Targeted subsidies, appliance financing and Pay-As-You-Go models aimed at this upfront cost may be effective tools to overcome this initial hurdle.

Behaviour change: Long-term health benefits are real, but many households, especially low-income ones, may not be able to invest based on benefits that come far down the line. Awareness campaigns are therefore likely to be more persuasive if they lead with the immediate, tangible savings in fuel and time that many transitions deliver, rather than health messaging alone.

Gender empowerment: The time savings identified translate directly into potential gains for women and girls, who bear most of the burden of cooking and fuel collection today. Clean cooking policies and programs should be explicitly linked to gender equality objectives, with monitoring frameworks tracking gender-related outcomes so progress on time poverty, education and income generation can be assessed directly rather than assumed.

description:
Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, said it is a “pivotal time” for US climate and energy policy.
President Donald Trump has pulled the United States out of the Paris climate agreement twice and is trying to quit the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change.
“We have lost [the] trust of the international community when it comes to climate,” said Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.).
“What they can deliver to the United Nations process is extremely limited,” he said, adding that it’s unlikely there will be any sweeping new climate legislation or climate funding in the next two years.
We’ve got work to do to reclaim our credibility in this institution.” Bob Berwyn is an Austria-based reporter who has covered climate science and international climate policy for more than a decade.
text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—After their big gains in the 2026 midterm elections, a delegation of Democratic US House members appeared at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference Monday, pledging to rejoin the international fight against global warming.

Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, said it is a “pivotal time” for US climate and energy policy.

“The wrecking ball of Donald Trump and this out-of-touch administration, and the temporarily empty chair of the United States at this COP31, does not represent what the Americans want or need,” Huffman said.

President Donald Trump has pulled the United States out of the Paris climate agreement twice and is trying to quit the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The current administration has also tried to cut all funding for climate programs.

Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, the United States has had no formal government presence at the UN talks, but was informally represented by America Is All In, a coalition including local governments, businesses, faith groups, Native American tribes, and universities.

Huffman said the midterm election shows that Americans have rejected the current administration’s efforts to “turn the United States into something like a petro-dictatorship.” The results could pave the way for the country to reestablish a formal presence at the annual talks.

Given legal uncertainties about Trump’s efforts to completely withdraw the US from the UN’s climate framework, the extent of US participation in the talks is unclear. But Huffman said that, in the past, US congressional delegations have attended the annual Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, under both Democratic and Republican majorities.

“The next time we’re here, we will be an official congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives,” Huffman said in an interview with Inside Climate News.

The US would still be excluded from the formal government-to-government negotiations, but a congressional delegation representing the majority party, potentially capable of advancing climate and energy legislation, could make a difference, Huffman said.

“We want to take the best practices that we’ve heard from all of the global partners… and craft them into good, solid climate policy once we get back to Congress,” said Rep. Lucy McBath (D-Ga.).

The new Democratic majority in the House of Representatives can also use its oversight authority to try to ensure that the money the US has promised for climate aid and sustainable development is restored, said U.S. Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.).

Casten said some of America’s European allies are “spending $500, $600 million per day more than before the United States attacked Iran” because of increased oil prices, and that simply stopping those hostilities could free up funding for climate efforts.

“We have lost [the] trust of the international community when it comes to climate,” said Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.).

“I think it is a complete betrayal of our responsibility that Donald Trump has pulled us out of the Paris Agreement not once but twice,” she said. A Democrat winning the 2028 presidential election would help ensure the US can rejoin that agreement, she added.

It will take time to regain trust in the international community, Ansari said.

“But we will come back,” she said, “working 10 times harder, 50 times harder than we did before, to make sure that we are being team players, to make sure that we are… supporting small island developing states and supporting vulnerable African nations.”

Climate activists reacted cautiously to the promises about the United States’ potential return to the international climate arena.

“We welcome the political shift in the United States that puts the brakes on the reckless dismantling of domestic green policies,” said Harjeet Singh, director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. “However, here at COP31 in Antalya, the international community cannot afford to celebrate prematurely or suffer from collective amnesia.”

Singh said the US has a long history of obstructing climate negotiations across successive administrations and regardless of which party holds power.

“As the world’s largest historical emitter, the US carries an outsized moral and legal responsibility to act,” he said. “Real change will not be measured by who walks through the halls of this summit, but by whether Washington finally ends its expansion of oil, gas, and coal at home and delivers hundreds of billions of dollars in grant-based climate finance to developing countries.”

Singh said until the US pays its fair share to help vulnerable countries recover from climate impacts and transition to sustainable energy systems, “warm words from visiting lawmakers mean very little to communities on the frontlines.”

Brandon Wu, with ActionAid USA, said the new Democrat-led House majority must reassert control over the budget and hold the Trump administration accountable for “likely illegal actions like dismantling USAID and gutting foreign assistance” funding approved by Congress.

“What they can deliver to the United Nations process is extremely limited,” he said, adding that it’s unlikely there will be any sweeping new climate legislation or climate funding in the next two years. What members of Congress can do is lay the groundwork for more ambitious action in a post-Trump era, he added.

While meeting delegates from other countries, Huffman said he’s heard both gratitude and optimism, as well as skepticism, about a possible US return to the climate talks.

“The fact is the US has become kind of an unreliable partner and we’ve lost our credibility,” he said. “So we’ve tried to bring humility to this moment. We’ve got work to do to reclaim our credibility in this institution.”

Bob Berwyn is an Austria-based reporter who has covered climate science and international climate policy for more than a decade. Previously, he reported on the environment, endangered species, and public lands for several Colorado newspapers, and also worked as editor and assistant editor at community newspapers in the Colorado Rockies.

This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News.

text:
In one of the first tests for newly re-elected congressional Democrats, the Senate is considering a bill that would overhaul and streamline permitting for energy projects.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects in America — everything from fossil fuel pipelines to transmission lines that would add more clean energy to the grid. And it would roll back environmental and social protections to achieve this goal.

Senators Angus King and Susan Collins both voted yes in a procedural vote to advance BAAJA last week. Both are members of the Senate Climate Solutions Caucus.

In a statement to Maine Public, Sen. King said permitting reform will "speed up the clean energy revolution." The independent senator has been advocating for permitting reform for years.

But President Trump, while in favor of the bill, vowed last week not to approve any wind energy permits even if it passes.

“The bill hasn’t been fully negotiated,” Trump said in comments to reporters. “I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.”

Meanwhile many Maine environmental and climate advocates are opposed to the bill, which would limit state and tribal authority under the Clean Air Act, the Endangered Species Act, and eliminate the need for tribal and state permissions for some projects. Critics have called it a "giveaway" to "Big oil" and data centers.

“This bill trades one environmental harm for another,” said Ivy Frignoca, Casco Baykeeper with Friends of Casco Bay, “and is not in the best interest of Maine’s waters.” Friends of Casco Bay has serious concerns with provisions of BAAJA that weaken the Clean Water Act.

“BAAJA is a bad deal, and we can do better,” said Nick Lund, acting advocacy director at Maine Audubon. “Narrowing environmental review, diminishing state and tribal authority, and constraining public participation are not the way to achieve a cleaner future.”

But Peter Dugas, Maine state coordinator for the Citizen's Climate Lobby, said passing comprehensive permitting reform is needed to greenlight and move along clean energy projects, which are urgently needed to reduce emissions.

"Like any bill that's a bipartisan compromise, it's not going to be perfect," he said. "But what you gain with a with a bipartisan bill is that it's more robust to the ebbs and flows of political power."

"A lot of what we were championing in the Inflation Reduction Act was glorious for the three years it existed, but of course it was leveled by the new administration," he added. "While there are certain parts of this that we certainly would not want to have in there in a perfect world, the research shows that the net benefits to climate emissions reductions is very good."

The Senate will hold a final vote on the bill this week.
