title: As outages persist, Puerto Rico finds a way to help keep the lights on with 'virtual power plant'
description:
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico (AP) — On nearly 20 days in October, an electric utility took energy from a battery attached to Hector Ríos’ house in Cabo Rojo, on the southwest corner of Puerto Rico, and used it to support the power grid.
“There’s nothing virtual about it,” said Javier Rúa Jovet, chief policy officer at the Solar and Energy Storage Association of Puerto Rico.
But when the sun sets and demand rises, Puerto Rico barely has enough power to meet the need.
The utility pays solar providers three times the residential electricity price for the battery energy it takes, recovering the costs through rates.
But experts believe Puerto Rico can think bigger.
text:
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico (AP) — On nearly 20 days in October, an electric utility took energy from a battery attached to Hector Ríos’ house in Cabo Rojo, on the southwest corner of Puerto Rico, and used it to support the power grid.

Ríos was happy to share.

With the U.S. territory's frequent power outages that disrupt daily life and restrain its economy, he likes the idea of helping prevent blackouts for other people. He's also compensated for the energy.

“It just seems like a good deal, to contribute to the community and make money at the same time,” Ríos said.

Ríos, 75, is part of what has become one of Puerto Rico's most effective tools for energy resilience amid nearly a decade of electricity woes: a “virtual power plant,” or VPP, that harnesses batteries from nearly 115,000 households to bolster the grid when its aging and fickle power plants can't meet demand.

Nine years after Puerto Rico's public power utility filed for bankruptcy and Hurricane Maria ravaged its already dilapidated energy grid, residents still face unpredictable blackouts and electricity rates higher than in almost any state. Few new utility-scale power sources have been built since Maria, and most of the federal dollars promised for grid recovery have not yet reached the territory.

But the VPP — the first of its kind in Latin America and the Caribbean, and the U.S.' second largest in terms of capacity — showed its potential this summer, preventing or mitigating outages more than 60 times since June 1, according to Luma Energy, its transmission and distribution utility.

“There’s nothing virtual about it,” said Javier Rúa Jovet, chief policy officer at the Solar and Energy Storage Association of Puerto Rico. “It’s real, and it’s better than a power plant.”

Dozens of states now operate similar networks of distributed energy sources like battery storage systems, electric vehicles and smart thermostats to help manage the grid. Experts expect their role to grow in the U.S. amid energy constraints, rising utility prices, and tech companies’ push to build power-hungry data centers.

As President Donald Trump’s administration promotes fossil fuel expansion and redirects dollars away from solar adoption in Puerto Rico, proponents of the territory's system say it highlights the value of distributed solar and storage, and shows how these systems can bolster resilience for other energy-vulnerable communities.

“There’s a way for this technology to benefit not just the individual buildings that they’re on,” but instead be “in service to the community all the time,” said Nathalie Jordi, community solar lead at Together New Orleans, a nonprofit that championed an upcoming $23 million city program to provide and network over 1,000 batteries on homes and businesses across New Orleans.

A solar revolution after Hurricane Maria

The opportunity to harness a vast network of residential batteries arose after Hurricane Maria in 2017, which left some communities without electricity for nearly a year. Experts linked the infrastructure failure to thousands of post-hurricane deaths.

“We had to procure resiliency in some other way,” said Rúa Jovet, “not a centralized system that will completely fail for a whole year.”

There are now over 207,000 rooftop solar systems on an archipelago of fewer than 3.2 million people, a 20-fold increase from before Maria that was propelled by households who could afford installations, philanthropy, and some federal dollars. Because of the territory's unique need for resiliency, nearly every installation includes at least one battery, a necessary add-on to keep the system running in a blackout.

“The mindset was, get yourself ready for everything,” recalled Ríos, who after Maria bought a diesel generator for his house, then installed panels and a Tesla Powerwall battery in 2023. The system also cut his utility bill in half, from about $400 to $200 in the summer.

Solar panels create an energy boon during the day, charging batteries and sending excess power to the grid. But when the sun sets and demand rises, Puerto Rico barely has enough power to meet the need. Any power plant malfunction can prompt an outage.

In late 2023, Luma launched a small pilot program that would leverage residential battery capacity to offset the shortages. Ríos was among the first to enroll; now over half of solar customers participate.

If Luma predicts an energy deficit, customers are digitally notified that a battery sharing event is coming. They can opt out via app, or adjust how much of their battery — enrollees typically offer 30% — they make available.

The experiment has faced challenges. In a 2026 survey of solar customers by the nonprofit Solar United Neighbors, some participants criticized the compensation structure, which varies by solar provider. Others expressed hesitation to enroll in the program because they did not understand it or feared losing backup power.

Ríos said he’s only had that problem once — when a storm knocked out power right after he shared his battery. He now skips battery sharing events if there's bad weather forecast.

He acknowledged the payment system is “a little vague.” He and his wife received $162 last year, which they happily redeemed as a Marshalls gift card.

Luma told The Associated Press that relying so often on battery sharing has contributed in part to recent rate increases. The utility pays solar providers three times the residential electricity price for the battery energy it takes, recovering the costs through rates.

Rúa Jovet says that expense doesn’t compare to the societywide economic losses of frequent power outages that spoil food, endanger health and shutter schools and businesses. The territory is also set to spend more than $1.7 billion this year importing fuel for most of its power generation.

Creating a consistent energy source

Luma said each battery sharing event, typically about four hours, supports the equivalent of about 80,000 residential customers. Enrolling more households would enable supplemental power for more hours.

But experts believe Puerto Rico can think bigger.

“The VPP in Puerto Rico is like an emergency escape valve, but the batteries should be a grid asset,” said Jigar Shah, director of the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office under former President Joe Biden and comanaging director of the advisory firm Multiplier.

Instead of only being tapped in an emergency, Shah said, the batteries could dispatch power every day — offsetting the need to burn fossil fuels — and help absorb excess energy across the grid when solar panels are producing at their peak. Several states, including California and Texas, use solar and batteries this way.

VPPs “could potentially play a larger role in Puerto Rico’s energy future,” Alejandro Figueroa, Luma chief regulatory officer, told The Associated Press. But, he said, a program used daily would require a different design and compensation structure to be sustainable.

Providing daily power is a natural next step, Rúa Jovet said, and could help Puerto Rico meet its own legal mandate that the archipelago reach 100% renewable energy by 2050. But a virtual power plant alone cannot solve the territory’s energy crisis.

That will require deploying billions of unspent federal recovery dollars, continuing improvements to transmission and distribution infrastructure and building new large-scale generation and storage.

“You don’t want the situation to be a persistent emergency forever,” he said.

title: BMW Begins Production of Gen6 Batteries for iX5 at New South Carolina Plant
description:
Located approximately 15 miles from BMW’s vehicle manufacturing facility in Spartanburg, the new Woodruff plant strengthens the company’s local battery and vehicle production network.
Woodruff is the fourth facility in BMW Group’s global production network to begin series production of Gen6 high-voltage batteries.
By 2030, BMW plans to assemble at least six fully electric models at its largest global production facility in Spartanburg.
AI, Robots and Virtual Reality Support Battery Production BMW is placing considerable emphasis on automation and artificial intelligence at its new Woodruff facility.
BMW Gen6 Batteries Promise a Lower Carbon Footprint Beyond performance and manufacturing efficiency, BMW says its Gen6 battery technology also brings environmental improvements.
text:
BMW has officially opened its new high-voltage battery assembly plant in Woodruff, South Carolina, marking a major milestone in the automaker’s plans to expand electric vehicle production in the United States. The facility has started series production of BMW’s sixth-generation (Gen6) batteries, which will initially power the new all-electric BMW iX5 and future electric models assembled at the nearby Spartanburg plant.

Located approximately 15 miles from BMW’s vehicle manufacturing facility in Spartanburg, the new Woodruff plant strengthens the company’s local battery and vehicle production network. It also represents an important step toward BMW’s goal of assembling at least six fully electric models at Plant Spartanburg by 2030.

The BMW iX5, unveiled in June 2026, marks the first time the popular X5 SUV is available as a fully electric model. It is also BMW’s first fully electric vehicle scheduled for production in the United States. The electric SUV features a 141-kWh high-voltage battery, advanced chassis technology and the latest driver assistance systems.

Woodruff is the fourth facility in BMW Group’s global production network to begin series production of Gen6 high-voltage batteries. The other locations are Debrecen in Hungary, Irlbach-Straßkirchen in Germany and Shenyang in China.

BMW has established five new battery assembly facilities worldwide under its “Local for Local” production strategy. The fifth location, San Luis Potosí in Mexico, is expected to begin operations in 2027.

The strategy involves manufacturing batteries close to the vehicle assembly plants they supply, helping strengthen regional supply chains and integrate battery and vehicle production.

According to Raymond Wittmann, BMW Board Member responsible for Production, the Woodruff facility lays the foundation for the first series production of fully electric BMW vehicles at Plant Spartanburg and represents a major step in the company’s electrification strategy in North America.

By 2030, BMW plans to assemble at least six fully electric models at its largest global production facility in Spartanburg.

Advanced Gen6 Battery Technology Uses a Cell-to-Pack Design

The new Woodruff facility produces BMW’s in-house-developed Gen6 high-voltage battery systems, which introduce several manufacturing and technology improvements.

One of the most important changes is the adoption of a cell-to-pack architecture. Instead of first assembling individual battery cells into conventional modules, BMW integrates the cylindrical cells directly into the battery pack. This eliminates an intermediate production step and helps simplify the overall battery design.

The Gen6 batteries use cylindrical 46120 cells, supplied by AESC. The cells are connected to cooling systems and undergo a series of precision manufacturing processes before being integrated into the finished battery pack.

BMW also uses advanced laser cleaning and welding technology to connect the battery components. An innovative foaming process provides mechanical protection, while the battery housing is sealed and riveted before the central Energy Master control unit is installed.

Every completed high-voltage battery undergoes a comprehensive end-of-line inspection before being transported to Plant Spartanburg.

AI, Robots and Virtual Reality Support Battery Production

BMW is placing considerable emphasis on automation and artificial intelligence at its new Woodruff facility.

More than 300 employees and 250 robots work together to support battery assembly. AI assistants and agents developed specifically for the plant continuously analyse production data to identify potential problems and maintain high manufacturing standards.

Production processes are monitored in real time, with each manufacturing step documented to improve quality control and operational efficiency.

Digital twins and virtual reality technology also played an important role before the plant became operational. BMW used digital simulations to plan manufacturing processes, while employees completed VR training programmes inside a virtual recreation of the factory.

The virtual environment allows workers to practise manufacturing procedures and become familiar with production equipment before operating it in the real facility.

BMW Gen6 Batteries Promise a Lower Carbon Footprint

Beyond performance and manufacturing efficiency, BMW says its Gen6 battery technology also brings environmental improvements.

The battery cells used in the BMW iX5 contain a high proportion of secondary materials in their cobalt, lithium and nickel content. Renewable energy is also used during the production of anode and cathode materials, as well as in battery cell manufacturing.

According to BMW, the new Gen6 cells reduce CO₂-equivalent emissions per watt-hour by approximately 28% compared with the Gen5 cells used in the BMW iX.

The Woodruff facility has also been designed to reduce its environmental impact. BMW says the plant does not use fossil fuels during normal operations, while its industrial trucks are powered by hydrogen.

$1.7 Billion Investment Strengthens BMW’s US EV Strategy

The Woodruff battery plant is part of BMW’s broader investment of approximately $1.7 billion in electric mobility in the Spartanburg area.

The project began with a groundbreaking ceremony in June 2023, followed by construction starting in September of the same year. Manufacturing equipment installation began in September 2024, while the first test and pre-series batteries rolled off the production line in summer 2025.

The official opening and start of series production now complete an important phase of BMW’s US battery manufacturing expansion.

The investment also involves cooperation with local battery cell suppliers, including AESC, reinforcing BMW’s efforts to develop a more integrated North American electric vehicle supply chain.

With the Woodruff facility now operational, BMW is moving closer to its target of producing multiple fully electric models in the United States. The new Gen6 batteries will play a central role in that strategy, starting with the all-electric BMW iX5 and potentially supporting a much wider range of future electric BMW X models.

text:
Stark Future has become the first electric motorcycle company in Europe to reach unicorn status after raising at least €150 million in equity and now plans to expand into larger motorcycle categories, its founder told Reuters.

The raise, led by Highland Europe, alongside Morgan Stanley Investment Management's 1GT and Axon Partners Group, was based on a pre-money valuation of €1.2 billion. A potential second close could see the amount raised rise further, he added.

Advt

The valuation marks a 60 per centbincrease from its previous funding round in September 2025, when it was valued at €750 million. A unicorn is a privately held start-up company worth more than $1 billion.

Anton Wass, founder and CEO of the Barcelona-based company, which made its name in Enduro racing, an off-road endurance motorsport, said Stark expects revenue of roughly €150 million this year.

That would mark a 30 per centbjump from €115 million in 2025. In addition, the company expects to be positive on an earnings before interest and tax basis this year, Wass said, although he declined to disclose a figure.

"The reason we are profitable is that we have quite strong gross margins due to owning all the IP ourselves. We have a really, really short value chain," he said.

Wass said Stark had received takeover approaches but was not interested in selling. Instead, he hoped the latest financing could be its last private round ahead of a potential listing, although that was still "a couple of years away".

The growth has helped Stark capture 5 per centbof the €3 billion market for Motocross, Enduro and Supermoto, Wass said and it would use the money raised in the latest round to expand into markets worth €90 billion, targeting 10%-30 per centbmarket share.

Advt

The strong growth contrasts with mixed fortunes elsewhere in the sector, with Harley-Davidson-backed LiveWire saying last month that there was substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern.

As countries prepare for the second week of negotiations at the COP31 climate talks in Turkey, with faster electrification top of the agenda, Wass said government support was not needed but action could nevertheless accelerate the transition.

"Higher taxes on unsustainable products and lower taxes on sustainable products is the best way forward," he said, while adding that "we need to build our businesses expecting no help."

Wass said Stark's rapid growth was down to designing the bikes to outperform combustion-engine rivals on performance and ease of use, rather than relying on their environmental appeal.

"We're not trying to force people to be sustainable, we simply want to make the sustainable option the best option, even if you don't care about sustainability."

text:
In one of the first tests for newly re-elected congressional Democrats, the Senate is considering a bill that would overhaul and streamline permitting for energy projects.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects in America — everything from fossil fuel pipelines to transmission lines that would add more clean energy to the grid. And it would roll back environmental and social protections to achieve this goal.

Senators Angus King and Susan Collins both voted yes in a procedural vote to advance BAAJA last week. Both are members of the Senate Climate Solutions Caucus.

In a statement to Maine Public, Sen. King said permitting reform will "speed up the clean energy revolution." The independent senator has been advocating for permitting reform for years.

But President Trump, while in favor of the bill, vowed last week not to approve any wind energy permits even if it passes.

“The bill hasn’t been fully negotiated,” Trump said in comments to reporters. “I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.”

Meanwhile many Maine environmental and climate advocates are opposed to the bill, which would limit state and tribal authority under the Clean Air Act, the Endangered Species Act, and eliminate the need for tribal and state permissions for some projects. Critics have called it a "giveaway" to "Big oil" and data centers.

“This bill trades one environmental harm for another,” said Ivy Frignoca, Casco Baykeeper with Friends of Casco Bay, “and is not in the best interest of Maine’s waters.” Friends of Casco Bay has serious concerns with provisions of BAAJA that weaken the Clean Water Act.

“BAAJA is a bad deal, and we can do better,” said Nick Lund, acting advocacy director at Maine Audubon. “Narrowing environmental review, diminishing state and tribal authority, and constraining public participation are not the way to achieve a cleaner future.”

But Peter Dugas, Maine state coordinator for the Citizen's Climate Lobby, said passing comprehensive permitting reform is needed to greenlight and move along clean energy projects, which are urgently needed to reduce emissions.

"Like any bill that's a bipartisan compromise, it's not going to be perfect," he said. "But what you gain with a with a bipartisan bill is that it's more robust to the ebbs and flows of political power."

"A lot of what we were championing in the Inflation Reduction Act was glorious for the three years it existed, but of course it was leveled by the new administration," he added. "While there are certain parts of this that we certainly would not want to have in there in a perfect world, the research shows that the net benefits to climate emissions reductions is very good."

The Senate will hold a final vote on the bill this week.

text:
Lewis County in Washington state has become the first region in North America where developers can lock in insured feedstock costs before committing to a project.

The county’s Bioeconomy Development Opportunity (BDO) Zone for woody biomass has been named the first “Insurable BDO Zone”. The designation was announced by feedstock consultancy Ecostrat, risk specialist New Energy Risk (NER) and the Economic Alliance of Lewis County.

The zone already held an “AA” rating under the BDO Zone Initiative, which assesses the reliability of regional feedstock supply. That has now been upgraded to “AA Insurable” after NER found in a preliminary review that the zone meets its initial pre-screening criteria for Feedstock Supply Insurance (FSI).

FSI caps the delivered cost of feedstock for up to ten years. Projects in Lewis County can now reserve in their own name a share of the zone’s 600,000 bone-dry tons a year of insurable supply, at a set range for the insured cost cap.

Each reservation comes with a fast-tracked, non-binding indication of FSI terms. This gives developers and lenders a view of their feedstock cost protection well before a final investment decision.

Answering the cost question

Todd Chaput, executive director of the Economic Alliance of Lewis County, said investors looking at the area always want to know whether the fibre is available and what it will cost over a plant’s lifetime.

“Our BDO Zone rating answered the first. This designation answers the second,” he said. He added that it gave the county a site-selection advantage that no other region currently has.

Jordan Solomon, president of Ecostrat and chairman of the BDO Zone Initiative, said feedstock risk had long been where promising projects stalled. Combining a zone rating with insurance prequalification gave local economic developers a new tool, he said. He expects Lewis County to set the standard for other regions across North America.

George Schulz, chief executive of NER, said the initiative showed how value streams from wood waste could unlock access to feedstock insurance and support the development of biofuel projects.

text:
Key takeaways

Amazon aims to reduce the carbon emissions for every unit of electricity it uses by 65% by 2030.

The target covers electricity consumed by Amazon’s global operations and follows the International Energy Agency's net-zero pathway.

Amazon has invested in more than 700 carbon-free energy projects globally, with capacity to power more than 12.1 million U.S. homes once completed.

When we co-founded The Climate Pledge in 2019, we committed to reaching net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, knowing that the electricity powering our business would be central to getting there. That's why we’ve built the largest corporate portfolio of carbon-free energy in the world: more than 700 projects globally and over 40 gigawatts of capacity, enough to power more than 12.1 million U.S. homes once completed. Now we’re ready to take the next step.

Today, we’re setting a new goal: By 2030, we aim to cut the carbon intensity of the electricity our global operations use by 65%, compared with 2019. We’re doing this as energy demand rises, because we believe growing our business and cutting emissions can, and must, go hand in hand. Carbon intensity is one of the clearest ways to show that.

We developed this goal and methodology based on the International Energy Agency’s Net Zero by 2050 pathway and reviewed it with leading academics. We commit to updating it so it stays aligned with the latest climate science.

What is carbon intensity and why does it matter?

Carbon intensity tracks emissions per unit of electricity consumed, measured in carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) per megawatt-hour (MWh). Put simply, by 2030 we aim for each unit of electricity we use to be associated with 65% fewer carbon emissions than in 2019. Because it measures progress per unit, it shows whether we’re decarbonizing our electricity supply and decoupling emissions from business growth, however much we grow.

Electricity demand is rising fast across the technology sector, driven by cloud computing and AI. That’s a challenge for the whole industry. A near-term, measurable goal keeps us focused and gives customers a clear trajectory to track our progress against.

How is Amazon investing in carbon-free energy?

Every new carbon-free energy project we bring online can help displace fossil-fuel generation on the grid, lowering the carbon intensity of the electricity we consume. Since 2019, BloombergNEF has consistently recognized us as one of the world’s largest corporate purchasers of carbon-free energy.

Our strategy spans power purchase agreements, utility-scale solar and wind farms, on-site generation, and advanced nuclear and geothermal energy. Together with X-energy, we aim to bring more than 5 gigawatts of new advanced nuclear power online across the U.S. by 2039, the largest commercial deployment target for small modular reactors to date. We focus in particular on countries where new carbon-free energy can make the biggest impact in decarbonizing the grid. Our announcement this week that we plan to invest $7 billion in renewable energy in India by 2030 further supports this goal.

What comes next?

Meeting this goal will mean scaling the carbon-free energy we already invest in and working alongside utilities, grid operators and policymakers to bring more carbon-free power online where we operate. All the while, we’ll seek to ensure these projects benefit local communities.

Through our Built Together initiative in the U.S., we invest in education, job training, energy affordability and water preservation, and fund priorities that communities choose for themselves. This work is guided by the Amazon Data Center Commitment.

We’ll report our progress every year in our Sustainability Report.

text:
PJM Interconnection, the biggest grid operator in the United States, has proposed to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to streamline the processes related to new power generation capacity commissioning and large consumer connections in a bid to speed it all up.

PJM, which operates in 13 states, has been struggling to cope with the sharp demand rise resulting from the proliferation of data centers, which has created a supply shortfall of some 6.8 GW, according to a Reuters report. Unless PJM secures generation capacity to cover that, the grid in those 13 states could become less reliable.

The shortfall was revealed in PJM’s June 2028/2029 electricity procurement auction, organized earlier this year. The amount of capacity is what PJM needs to find before that year to make sure there is enough generation during demand spike periods.

“Neither generation nor transmission is coming online quickly enough to keep pace ‌with new demand growth driven mainly by large loads like data centers,” company spokesman Jeff Shields said. "The factor that PJM planning can influence is how quickly these new resources are studied for reliability."

Last month, PJM had to issue a Maximum Generation Alert as a warm front moving across its area of operation met planned generation capacity maintenance, leading to a supply squeeze as some 62 GW in capacity were offline for maintenance. The unfavorable combination of circumstances prompted electricity prices to shoot up to over $1,000 per megawatt-hour.

To tackle these challenges, PJM has proposed to FERC to reduce the time now required for the study of connecting new demand sources to the grid, from two years to 12 months. By streamlining its processes, the grid operator would also be able to identify the places for the most urgent grid upgrades related to the connection of new data centers.

description:

text:
Leaders have set an ambitious target to deploy 300 GW of offshore wind in the North Seas by 2050. The commitment recognises the strategic importance of replacing dependence on fossil fuels, and the benefits of clean electrification for competitiveness. However, delivery gaps have emerged as technical bodies lack the mandate and agency to deliver the full strategic value of the project. Europe’s leaders must re-inject high-level leadership to drive progress across cooperation on planning, security, and finance.

North Sea leaders affirmed the strategic case at the Hamburg Summit in January 2026 and set out a forward action plan. Delivering on the ambition to deploy 300 GW of offshore wind in the North Seas would set up Europe to develop a new renewables powerhouse for the continent – driving competitive electrification, clean industrialisation, and technology leadership in key sectors.

However, delivering on that opportunity requires leaders to take control of the process. Doing so would be a signal of their resolve to improve competitiveness, affordability and security outcomes for industry and households alike.

The strategic imperative

The North Seas region is one of the few places where Europe can produce vast quantities of clean and homegrown electricity – the energy needed to power an electrified, competitive and more secure European economy. Every 100 GW of North Seas wind could replace approximately 60 bcm of European gas demand, the equivalent of around 15% of the combined fossil gas demand of the UK and EU in 2025. Replacing that fossil fuel dependence could save billions in the EU and the UK, help reduce electricity prices, and ensure a secure and stable supply of electricity.

Moreover, the North Seas present a major industrial opportunity for Europe: powering industry across the continent with clean, competitive electricity and driving the development of critical supply chains, while securing European leadership in pioneer offshore technologies and manufacturing of strategic components.

Finally, as security risks in the North Seas region mount, making the most of the sea basin’s geo-strategic location through cooperation on surveillance, protection and security-by-design, can strengthen Europe’s defences for all.

Forward progress but gaps remain

European leaders re-affirmed the ambition to deliver 300 GW of offshore wind by 2050, including up to 100 GW of joint, cross-border projects, at last January’s North Sea Summit. Moving to implement the action plan agreed by leaders, the Offshore TSO Collaboration (OTC) has set up workstreams to progress actions on planning, cost allocation and financing tools. Informal coordination between security and energy stakeholders has also begun at national level, or in some cases, bilaterally.

However, while these are positive forward steps, they are insufficient to coordinate across the region and deliver on the scale of this industrial project. Key gaps thus remain across the planning, security and financing frameworks needed to deliver the full strategic ambition of the North Seas project.

Five actions for European leaders to reclaim agency

Establish a leader-level sherpa group to ensure strategic objectives are achieved and delivery remains on track in the run-up to the next North Sea Summit.

Re-integrate the UK into the North Seas Energy Cooperation (NSEC) as a full member to enable the closer collaboration required to deliver the North Seas agenda.

Instruct the Offshore TSO Collaboration (OTC) to identify the new, strategic offshore infrastructure necessary to ensure that delivery of the strategic objective of 300 GW by 2050 remains viable and cost effective.

Formalise cooperation between national security and energy stakeholders across the region, to leverage the security dividends of closer cooperation and ensure the timely deployment of resilient infrastructure.

Develop a financing strategy for the North Seas that leverages existing public finance institutions like the European Investment Bank (EIB) and the UK’s National Wealth Fund (NWF) to provide de-risking capital for shared, cross-border infrastructure projects while ensuring coordination across institutions.

title: India's EV market is entering its growth phase, and global automakers risk missing it
description: AMSTERDAM--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov 17, 2026--
text:
AMSTERDAM--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov 17, 2026--

India may be on the verge of becoming the next major electric mobility market. The latest international electric mobility study by management and technology consultancy BearingPoint shows that purchase intentions among urban consumers are running well ahead of the market’s development to date. Among respondents likely to purchase a vehicle within the next three years, 39 percent prefer a new battery electric vehicle (BEV). A further 25 percent would choose a hybrid or plug-in hybrid, while only 17 percent prefer a new gasoline- or diesel-powered vehicle. At the same time, electric vehicles accounted for just four percent of new passenger car registrations in India at the end of 2025, according to FADA. The latest registration figures, however, point to clear momentum: after steady growth through 2026, the share of battery electric vehicles had already risen to more than eight percent by September.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261116485299/en/

“Many manufacturers are currently focused primarily on China. Yet India could become the next major growth engine for global electric mobility. The combination of strong purchase intentions, rising BEV registrations, and the already established position of local manufacturers resembles the early growth phases of other major electric vehicle markets. The window to gain a meaningful foothold will not remain open indefinitely. Companies that fail to establish a robust local market position now risk missing a decisive part of the growth phase,” said Manuel Schuler, Global Leader Automotive at BearingPoint.

Affordability will determine the next phase of market growth

Unlike in many established Western automotive markets, financing plays a particularly important role when consumers in India purchase a new vehicle. For many buyers, the vehicle price is not the only consideration; the monthly cost also matters.

This is clearly reflected in the study results: 43 percent of respondents prefer vehicle financing, while only 34 percent would choose to pay in cash. India is therefore the only market surveyed in which financing options already outpace cash purchases. At the same time, car subscription models also have the highest share among all countries surveyed, at more than six percent.

For manufacturers, this creates a clear opportunity. Beyond the vehicle price, they should focus more on the monthly cost of ownership and make electric mobility more accessible through suitable financing offers. Options include battery-as-a-service concepts, separate financing models for vehicles and batteries, and battery-swapping systems.

Local manufacturers are putting international competitors under pressure

While technological innovation is central in many markets, trust-related factors dominate vehicle purchase decisions in India. Respondents rank vehicle safety (66 percent), warranty coverage (63 percent), battery repairability (62 percent), trust in brand quality (61 percent), and maintenance and repair costs (61 percent) as the most important criteria. Digital features, technological leadership, and design play a significantly smaller role.

Locally established manufacturers are particularly well positioned to benefit from these preferences. Tata Motors and Mahindra & Mahindra not only rank highest among respondents; according to FADA, they also accounted for around 63 percent of all new battery electric passenger car registrations in India in September 2026. The findings indicate that local trust, proximity to the market and a strong service ecosystem currently matter more than global brand recognition alone. This makes it increasingly difficult for international manufacturers to gain meaningful market share without a strong local presence.

Used electric vehicles are emerging as an additional growth engine

The used-car market could also play an important role in the wider adoption of electric mobility in India. Twenty-seven percent of respondents consider purchasing a used electric vehicle very attractive, putting India well ahead of Germany, the US, and the UK.

Trust in the battery remains a prerequisite for further market growth. Forty-four percent of respondents say that a certified battery health report would make them more likely to purchase a used electric vehicle. Battery certificates, warranties, and professional used-car programs could therefore become important components of future business models.

“The strong openness to used electric vehicles shows that many consumers are not necessarily looking for the latest model, but for an affordable and reliable entry point into electric mobility. This gives manufacturers a clear opportunity: certified used-car programs and battery certificates can build trust and lower barriers to entry,” Manuel Schuler added.

Local value creation will determine market success

For international manufacturers, simply exporting electric vehicles to India will not be enough. The study findings and the market’s development show that long-term success requires a strong local presence. Alongside competitive products, local production capacity, regional partnerships, and integration into India’s emerging value chains are becoming increasingly important.

In some respects, this development resembles the early growth years of China’s electric vehicle market. Manufacturers that invest early in local capabilities, partnerships, and value creation can do more than participate in growth; they can actively shape the future competitive landscape.

“Automakers must decide what role they want to play in building India’s electric mobility ecosystem. China shows that early investment in local partnerships and value creation can unlock significant growth opportunities. For many years, international manufacturers benefited from market access, economies of scale, and profitable joint ventures. At the same time, these partnerships helped build an increasingly independent and globally competitive local automotive ecosystem. Whether India will follow a similar path remains to be seen. The strategic principle, however, is the same: companies that build local capabilities and partnerships today will benefit from the growth while helping to shape tomorrow’s competitive landscape,” Manuel Schuler concluded.

About the survey

The BearingPoint study is based on an international survey of drivers and prospective vehicle buyers in Germany, the UK, the US, China, and India. More than 10,000 people were surveyed in total. The surveys were conducted across the five countries between late January and late March 2026. Topics included purchase intentions, preferred powertrain types, usage and financing models, brand preferences, and attitudes toward used electric vehicles. The Indian sample has an urban focus. The findings therefore primarily reflect the perspectives of urban Indian consumers.

text:
When the Trump administration eliminated the federal tax credits for electric vehicle purchases, EV sales fell off a cliff. The third quarter last year saw a record 437,000 new EV sales as Americans rushed to take advantage of the credits before they expired, but then sales cratered.

Since then, the war in Iran has driven gas and diesel prices through the roof. The average price of gasoline across the country has been stuck at over $4 for months, making it considerably cheaper to drive an EV than a gas-powered car.

In response, EV sales are rebounding. Americans bought 262,000 EVs in the third quarter of this year, making two straight quarters of sales growth. The numbers are far lower than last year’s record quarter, but the growth is likely to continue. Eleven states have direct incentives in place for EV purchases and another eight offer utility discounts, charger rebates, or localized incentives.

Automakers are introducing more and better all-electric options. Ford is introducing a new electric pickup that is far more affordable than the previous Lightning truck, and Subaru and Rivian are launching attractive new electric SUVs.

Used EVs are also having a hot streak. Americans bought 44,350 used EVs in August, an increase of 26% from July and 15% over a year ago.

Around the world, EVs continue to have a growing share of the global auto market. There is a good chance that steady, sustainable growth will persist in the U.S. as well, bringing an end to the boom-and-bust cycle of the last few years.
